M. 5, 407: Ephyre,id. H. 12, 27: Isthmos,id. M. 7, 405; 6, 419 sq. Trop.: morbus,of one who practises unnatural unchastity,Aus. Epigr. 131.

bimatris.definition: bĭmātris, e, bis - mater Having two mothers, poet. epithet of Bacchus (v. Bacchus init.): satumque iterum solumque bimatrem,Ov. M. 4, 12; Hyg. Fab. 167; Anthol. Lat. 1, 19, 2 (where it is scanned bīmăter).

bimatus.definition: bimus The age of two years (of animals and plants): ante bimatum,Varr. R. R. 2, 5, 17; Col. 7, 3, 6; 7, 4, 4: (polypi) ultra bimatum non vivunt,Plin. 9, 30, 48, § 89; 11, 21, 24, § 73: neque his bimatu longior vita,id. 9, 30, 48, § 93.—Of children, Vulg. Matt. 2; 16.

bimembris.definition: bĭmembris, e, bis - membrum Having double members: puer,half man, half beast,Juv. 13, 64; most freq. a poet. epithet of the Centaurs (half man, half horse; cf. bicorpor and biformis): Centauri bimembres,Sil. 3, 41: forma bimembris,Ov. H. 9, 99. Subst.: bĭmembres, ium, comm., = Centauri, the Centaurs: nubigenae, * Verg. A. 8, 293 Heyn. and Jahn; Ov. M. 12, 240; 12, 494; 15, 283; Stat. Th. 12, 554.

bimenstruus.definition: bĭmenstruusbis-mensis, = διμηνιαῖος Of two months, Gloss. Cyril.

bimestris.definition: bĭmestris, e (abl. regularly bimestri, Hor. C. 3, 17, 15; by poet. license, bimestre, Ov. F. 6, 158; cf. caelestis, perennis, etc.), bis-mensis Of two months' duration, of two months (rare): consulatus, Planc. ap. Cic. Fam. 10, 24, 7: stipendium,Liv. 9, 43, 6: triticum,which may be reaped two months after sowing,Plin. 18, 7, 12, § 70: porcus,two months old,Hor. C. 3, 17, 15: porca,Ov. F. 6, 158.

bimulus.definition: bīmŭlus, a, um Adj. dim. [bimus], only two years old (very rare, and only of man), Cat. 17, 13; Suet. Calig. 8 fin.

bimus.definition: bīmus, a, um, prob. contracted from bis-hiems, of two winters; cf. Eutych. ap. Cassiod. p. 2311 P., and Aufrecht, Zeitschrift für vergl. Sprachf. 4, p. 415 Two years old, of two years, continuing two years: nuces,Cato, R. R. 17, 2; Varr. R. R. 2, 1, 13: una veterana legio, altera bima, octo tironum, Planc. ap. Cic. Fam. 10, 24, 3; so, semen,Plin. 18, 24, 54, § 195: surculi,id. 17, 14, 24, § 105: plantae,biennial,Pall. Febr. 25, 2: merum, * Hor. C...

binarius.definition: bīnārĭus, a, um, bini That contains or consists of two: formae,i.e. coins of the value of two gold pieces,Lampr. Alex. Sev. 39.

binio.definition: bini The number two, a deuce: jactus quisque apud lusores veteres a numero vocabatur, ut unio, binio, tri nio, quaternio, quinio, senio, Isid. Orig. 18, 65: biniones δηνάρια, Gloss. Philox.

binominis.definition: bĭnōmĭnis, e, bis-nomen, analog. to cognominis, from con-nomen Having two names (only in Ov. and in gen. sing.): binominis, cui geminum est nomen, ut Numa Pompilius, Tullus Hostilius, Paul. ex Fest. p. 36 Müll.: Ascanius (also called Iulus),Ov. M. 14, 609: Ister (also called Danubius),id. P. 1, 8, 11; id. Ib. 415.

binubus.definition: bis-nubo A doublymarried man (late Lat.), Cassiod. Hist. Sacr. 9, 38.

biothanatus.definition: bĭŏthănătus, a, um, , = ] That dies a violent death, Lampr. Elag. 33; Firm. Math. 3, 14 fin.; 4, 1; Serv. ad Verg A. 4, 386.—Collat. form bĭaeŏthănătus, from βίαιος-θάνατος, Tert. Anim. 57.

bioticus.definition: bĭōtĭcus, a, um Of or belonging to common life, used in common life, practical: epilogi,Serv. ad Verg A. 3, 718: metrum, Mar. Vict. p. 2494 P. (in Diom. p. 470 ib. written as Greek).

bipalium.definition: bis-pala A double mattock: solum ad bipalium defodere,Col. 11, 2, 17 Schneid. ad loc. (MSS. ; elsewhere only in abl. sing.): bipalio vertere terram,Cato, R. R. 6, 3: bipalio agrum subigere,id. ib. 45, 1; Varr. R. R. 1, 37, 5; Col. 3, 5, 3; 11, 3, 11; id. Arb. 1, 5; Plin. 17, 21, 35, § 159; 18, 26, 62, § 230.

bipalmis.definition: bĭpalmis, e (access. form bĭpalmus, a, um, App. Herb. 7), bis-palmus Two spans long or broad, of two spans (very rare): tabulae,Varr. R. R. 3, 7, 4: spiculum,Liv. 42, 65, 9.

bipartio.definition: bĭ-partĭo (in MSS. also bĭ-pertĭo), no Perf., ītum, 4, v. a.bis, to divide into two parts, to bisect (as verb. finit. very rare; more freq. in part. and adv.): ver bipartitur, is divided (in respect to weather), Col. 11, 2, 36; so, hiems bipertitur,id. 11, 2, 5 Schneid. N. cr.—Mostly part. pass.: bipartita divisio,Varr. L. L. 5, § 17 Müll.: genus bipartitum,Cic. Top. 22, 85: bipertiti Aethiopes,Plin. 5, 8, 8, § 43: ut faceres imperium bipartitum,...

bipatens.definition: bĭpătens, entis, bis-pateo Opening in two ways, open in two directions (acc. to Serv. ad Verg. A. 10, 5, used by Enn.; cf. Ann. v. 62 Vahl.; but only two exs. in Verg. are preserved): portis alii bipatentibus assunt, i.e. portis duarum valvarum,Verg. A. 2, 330 Wagn.—Of the doors of the dwellings of the gods: considunt tectis bipatentibus,Verg. A. 10, 5 (est autem sermo Ennianus tractus ab ostiis, quae ex utrāque parte aperiuntur, Serv.).

bipeda.definition: bis-pes A tile or flagstone two feet long, for pavements (several times in Pall., elsewh. very rare), Pall. 1, 19, 1; 1, 40, 2 and 5; id. Mai, 11, 2 (twice); Inscr. Fabr. p. 511, 159 (cf. Vitr. 7, 1 fin.: tegulae bipedales).

bipedalis.definition: bĭpĕdālis, e, id. Two feet long, broad, or thick (class. in prose and poetry): fenestrae,Cato, R. R. 14, 2: trabes,two feet thick,Caes. B. G. 4, 17: materia,id. B. C. 2, 10: sol huic (Epicuro) bipedalis fortasse videtur, * Cic. Fin. 1, 6, 20: adulescentulus bipedali minor, * Suet. Aug. 43: tegulae,Vitr. 7, 1 fin.: modulus,Hor. S. 2, 3, 309: hiatus,Plin. 16, 12, 23, § 57: latitudo,Col. 8, 3, 7. Subst.: bĭpĕdāle, is, n., a tile or flag-stone two fe...

bipedaneus.definition: bĭpĕdānĕus, a, um, bis-pes Two feet long, wide, or thick (a rare access. form of bipedalis; most freq. in Col.): scrobs,Col. 4, 1, 2: spatia,id. 4, 30, 5: humus,id. 2, 2, 21 Gesn. and Schneid. N. cr.: latitudo,id. 5, 5, 2; 11, 2, 28: pastinatus,Plin. 17, 20, 32, § 143.

bipennis.definition: bĭpennis (-pinnis), e, bispenna Having two wings, two-winged (very rare): insectum,Plin. 11, 28, 33, § 96 (cf. just before, binis advolat pinnis): plumae, Varr. ap. Non. p. 79, 17.

bipes.definition: bĭpēs (˘˘, Aus. Idyll. 11, 39; Neutr. plur. bipedia, Aug. Mor. Manich. 9), pĕdis, adj. bis-pes, two-footed (mostly poet. or in post-Aug. prose): equi,Verg. G. 4, 389: mensa,Mart. 12, 32, 11: Aegyptii mures bipedes ambulant,on two feet,Plin. 10, 65, 85, § 187: alium bipedem sibi quaerit asellum,two legged ass,Juv. 9, 92: animal genus, mortale species, terrenum vel bipes differens,Quint. 5, 10, 61. Subst., mostly contemptuously, of men: hoc ministr...

biplex.definition: biplex, duplex, διπλοῦς Double, Gloss. Gr. Lat.

biremis.definition: bĭrēmis, e, bis-remus. Twooared, having two oars (rare): lembi,Liv. 24, 40 init.: scapha, * Hor. C. 3, 29, 62.— Also Freq. in an extended signif., having two banks of oars; only subst., a galley with two banks of oars (cf. Dict. of Antiq.; first used by the Erythraeans, acc. to Plin. 7, 56, 57, § 207), Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 20, § 51; 2, 5, 23, § 59; Caes. B. C. 3, 40; Tac. H. 4, 27; 5, 23; Claud. B. Gild. 369; id. Laud. Stil. 1, 367; Suet. Caes. 39; i...

birotus.definition: bĭrŏtus, a, um, bis-rota Twowheeled, with two wheels (post-class.): vehiculum,Non. p. 86, 30.—More freq. subst.: bĭrŏta, ae (gen. plur. birotūm, Cod. Th. 6, 29, 2, § 2; 8, 5, 9), f. (sc. raeda), a cabriolet, Cod. Th. 8, 5, 8, § 1 sqq.

birrus.definition: m. (, , n., Aug. Serm. Divers. 49), = (of yellow color) A cloak to keep off rain (made of silk or wool), Edict. Diocl. p. 20; cf. Salmas. Vop. Carin. 20; Burm. Anth. Lat. 2, p. 408; Cod. Th. 14, 10, 1, § 1; Schol. Juv. 8, 145; Sulp. Sev. Dial. 1, 21, 4; Claud. Epigr. 42.

bisextialis.definition: bĭsextĭālis, e, bis-sextus Containing two sextarii: olla,Marc. Emp. 15.

bisextilis.definition: bĭsextĭlis, e, bisextus Containing an intercalary day: annus,Isid. Orig. 6, 17, 25.

bisolis.definition: bĭsŏlis, e, bis-solea Having two (foot) soles, Edict. Diocl. p. 20. ‡† bĭsōmum, i, n. vox hibrida, from bis-σῶμα, a sarcophagus for two persons, Inscr. Orell. 8; Inscr. Rein. 20, 40; 20, 116.

bison.definition: βίσων [acc. to Oppian. Cyn. 2, 155, named from the Thracian Βίστονες] A species of wild ox living in northern regions, the Urus, the humpbacked ox, bison: Bos bison, Linn.; Plin. 8, 15, 15, § 38; Sen. Hippol. 65; Mart. Spect. 23, 4; Sol. 20.

bisonus.definition: bĭsŏnus, a, um, bis-sono Sounding twice, Serv. ad Verg. A. 9, 618.

bispellio.definition: bis-pellis, only trop. A man with two skins, a cunning man, Dig. 47, 3, 72; also written , Dig. 21, 2, 31.

bisulcus.definition: bĭsulcus, a, um, bis-sulcus (twofurrowed), hence, in gen. Divided into two parts, two-cleft, cloven (poet. and in postAug. prose): lingua, forked, Pac. ap. Non. p. 506, 17; Ov. M. 9, 65: pedes, * Lucr. 2, 356; Ov. M. 7, 113; Plin. 11, 45, 105, § 254: ungula, a cloven hoof, id. 8, 21, 30, § 73; 10, 1, 1, § 1: cauda,id. 9, 29, 46, § 85: forcipes,id. 11, 28, 34, § 97. Subst.: bĭsulca, ōrum, n. (sc. animalia), animals with cloven feet (opp. to the so...

bitumen.definition: cf. Sanscr. gatu, gum Bitumen, a kind of mineral pitch found in Palestine and Babylon, Gr. ἄτφαλτος, Plin. 35, 15, 51, § 178 sq.; Tac. H. 5, 6; 5, 17; Just. 1, 2, 7; Vitr. 2, 6; Lucr. 6, 808; Verg. G. 3, 451; Ov. M. 9, 660; 14, 792; Vitr. 8, 3, 1 sqq.: Judaicum,Veg. 1, 20, 1; 3, 56, 2; 5, 83, 3; 6, 14, 1: Apollonium,id. 6, 14, 1; Vulg. Gen. 6, 14.—For magical or religious use, Verg. E. 8, 82; Hor. Epod. 5, 82; Claud. VI. Cons. Hon. 325.

bitumino.definition: bĭtūmĭno, āre, 1, id. To cover or impregnate with bitumen (late Lat.), Ambros. Hexaëm. 6, 9, 72; cf.: bitumino, ἀσφαλτόω, Gloss. Lab.—Hence, P. a.: bĭtū-mĭnătus, a, um, impregnated with bitumen, bituminous: aqua,Plin. 31, 6, 32, § 59.

bituminosus.definition: bĭtūmĭnōsus, a, um, id. Abounding in bitumen, bituminous (perh. only in the two foll. exs.): terra,Vitr. 8, 3, 9: fontes,id. 8, 3, 4.

blaesus.definition: blaesus, a, um Lisping, stammering, hesitating in utterance, speaking indistinctly (most freq. in poetry): blaesus, cui litterae sibilantes (s, z) molestae sunt vitioseque pronunciantur, Popm. Differ. p. 133; Ov. A. A. 3, 294; Mart. 10, 65, 10.—Of a parrot: sonus,Ov. Am. 2, 6, 24. —Hence, subst.: blaesus, i, m., one who lisps, Dig. 21, 1, 10.—Of intoxicated persons, Juv. 15, 48; cf. Ov. A. A. 1, 598.

blandimentum.definition: blandior. Flattering words, blandishment, complimentary speech, flattery (class.; most freq. in plur. and in Tac.): nec eam (virtutem) minis aut blandimentis corrupta deseret,Cic. Tusc. 5, 31, 87: pessum dedisti me blandimentis tuis,Plaut. Rud. 2, 6, 23; id. Truc. 2, 2, 63: multa igitur blandimenta plebi per id tempus ab senatu data,Liv. 2, 9, 6: captus blandimentis,Plin. Ep. 2, 19, 4: per blandimenta juvenem aggredi,Tac. A. 13, 13; 12, 64: mulie...

blandio.definition: blandĭo, īre, 4 ( Act. collat. form of blandior), to caress, coax, court: cur ego blandirem (mulierem),App. Mag. 87, p. 328 fin.—Part. pass.: blanditusque labor molli curabitur arte, Verr. ap. Prisc. 792 P.: blandiendo duce nutrivit malum,Sen. Hippol. 135.

blandior.definition: blandĭor, ītus, 4, v. dep.blandus. Prop., lit., to cling caressingly to one, to fawn upon, to flatter, soothe, caress, fondle, coax (class.). Transf.

blanditia.definition: (, , in abl., App. M. 9, p. 230, 11), blandus. The quality of one blandus; a caressing, flattering, flattery (mostly in an honorable sense; cf. on the contrary, assentatio and adulatio; class in prose and poetry; most freq. in plur.). Trop., pleasure, delight, enticement, charm, allurement (cf. blandus, II. A., and blandior, II. B.): blanditiis praesentium voluptatum deliniti atque corrupti,Cic. Fin. 1, 10, 33: attrita cotidiano actu forensi inge...

blanditor.definition: blandior A flatterer (late Lat.), Itin. Alex. M. 39 (90).

blandulus.definition: blandŭlus, a, um Adj. dim. [blandus], pleasing, charming: animula vagula, blandula, Hadrian. Carm. ap. Spart. Hadr. 25.

blandus.definition: blandus, a, um, adj.for mlandus; akin to μείλιχος, mollis, mulier; Goth. milds; Engl. mild Of a smooth tongue, flattering, fawning, caressing (class and very freq.). Lit.: blanda es parum,Plaut. Cas. 3, 3, 21: nemini credo qui large blandu'st dives pauperi,id. Aul. 2, 2, 19: ut unus omnium homo te vivat numquam quisquam blandior,Ter. Hec. 5, 4, 21: scis me minime esse blandum,Cic. Att. 12, 5, 4: unum te puto minus blandum esse quam me,id. ib. 12...

blasphemabilis.definition: blasphēmābĭlis, e, blasphemo (eccl. Lat.) That deserves reproach, censurable, Tert. Cult. Fem. 12.

blasphematio.definition: id. (eccl. Lat.) A reviling, Tert. Cult. Fem. 12.

blasphemia.definition: f. (, , n., Prud. Psych. 715), = (eccl. Lat.) A reviling, slander, Vulg. Isa. 51, 7; towards God,blasphemy,Hier. Ep. 62, n. 2; Aug. Verb. Dom. Serm. 11; 14; 15; Vulg. 2 Par. 32, 17; id. Matt. 26, 65.

blasphemo.definition: blasphēmo, āre V.a., = βλασφημέω (eccl. Lat.), to revile, reproach, Vulg. 1 Par. 20, 7; God and divine things, to blaspheme: Christum,Prud. Apoth. 415: nomen Domini,Tert. adv. Jud. 13 fin.; Vulg. Lev. 24, 11; id. Matt. 9. 3; 26, 65.

blasphemus.definition: blasphēmus, a, um, , = (eccl. Lat.) Reviling, defaming: satelles, Prud. στεφ. 1, 75; and subst., of God and divine things, blasphemer, Tert. Res Carn. 26; Hier. Ep. 9; Vulg. Lev. 24, 14 (as transl. of the Heb. ); id. 1 Tim. 1, 13.

blateratio.definition: blatero A babbling (late Lat.), Auct. Idiom. p. 576, 28 Keil.

blateratus.definition: id. A babbling, prating (post-class.), Sid. Ep. 9, 11 fin.: canini,whining,Mart. Cap. 9, § 999.

blatero.definition: blătĕro, āvi, ātum, 1, kindred with βλάξ, simple, stupid, Paul. ex Fest. p. 34 Müll.; cf. blactero. To talk idly or foolishly, to babble, prate (colloq. and mostly ante- and post-class.), Pac. ap. Fulg. p. 561, 17; Afran. ap. Non. p. 78, 32: illud memento, ne quid in primis blateres,id. ib.; Plaut. ap. Non. p. 44, 15: desine blaterare, Caecil. ap. Non. p. 79, 2: cum magno blateras clamore, furisque, * Hor. S. 2, 7, 35; Gell. 1, 15, 17: his et si...

blatio.definition: blătĭo, īre, kindred with blatero To utter foolish things, to babble, prate (anteclass. and late Lat.): nugas blatis,Plaut. Am. 2, 1, 79; so id. Curc. 3, 82; id. Ep. 3, 1, 13; Tert. Pall. 2; cf. Non. p. 44, 11 sq.

blatta.definition: An insect that shuns the light; of several kinds, the cockroach, chafer, moth, etc., Plin. 29, 6, 39, § 139; 11, 28, 34, § 99: lucifuga,Verg. G. 4, 243 (per noctem vagans, Serv.); cf. Col. 9, 7, 5; Pall. 1, 37, 4; Hor. S. 2, 3, 119; Mart. 14, 37; cf. Voss, Verg. l. l.—On account of its mean appearance: amore cecidi tamquam blatta in pelvim, Laber. ap. Non. p. 543, 27.

blatteus.definition: blattĕus, a, um, 2. blatta, II. Purple-colored, purple: tunicae,Vop. Aur. 46, 4: pallium,id. 45, 5: funes,Eutr. 7, 9.

blattiarius.definition: 2. blatta, II. A dyer in purple, Cod. Th. 13, 4, 2 dub.

blennus.definition: A blockhead, dolt, simpleton: stulti, stolidi, fatui, fungi, bardi, blenni, buccones,Plaut. Bacch. 5, 1, 2; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 35 Müll.

blitum.definition: n. (, , m., Pall. Mart. 9, 17: blitus seritur is written prob. from the corrupted or misunderstood blitūseritur, or perh. the obscure blitus eritur of the MSS.) A vegetable, in itself tasteless, but used as a salad, orache, or spinach: Spinacia oleracea, Linn.; Plaut. Ps. 3, 2, 26; Varr. ap. Non. p. 550, 15; Plin. 20, 22, 93, § 252; Pall. Mart. 4, 9 fin.; Paul. ex Fest. p. 348 Müll.; Isid. Orig. 17, 10, 15.

boarius.definition: bŏārĭus (bŏvārĭus, Cic. Aem. Scaur. 11, 23), a, um, bos Of or relating to neat cattle: NEGOTIANTES,Inscr. Orell. 913: forum, the cattle market at Rome (in the eighth district of the city, near the Circus Maximus): in foro bovario,Cic. Aem. Scaur. 11, 23; Paul. ex Fest. p. 30, 5 Müll.; acc. to Ov. F. 6, 478, so called from the large brazen statue of an ox placed there; cf. Plin. 34, 3, 5, § 10; Tac. A. 12, 24; acc. to fable, because Hercules fed h...

boethus.definition: The aid or assistant of a scribe (pure Lat. adjutor), Cod. Valent. 10, 69, 4.

boletus.definition: The best kind of mushrooms, Plin. 22, 22, 46, § 92; Plaut. Curc. 5, 2, 14; Mart. 1, 21; 14, 101; Juv. 14, 8; much valued by the Romans,Mart. 3, 60; 13, 48.—The emperor Claudius is said to have been poisoned by them, Plin. l. l.: Tac. A. 12, 67 dub.; Suet. Claud. 44; Juv. 5, 147.

bolus.definition: A throw or cast (ante- and post-class.; cf. jactus). Lit. Trop., gain, profit, advantage; a haul, winning, piece of fortune, etc.: primumdum merces annua: is primus bolu'st, that's her first haul, Plaut. Truc. 1, 1, 10: intus bolos dat,id. ib. 4, 2, 12: dabit haec tibi grandis bolos,id. Pers. 4, 4, 106; Lucil. ap. Non. p. 46, 13: magnum bolum deferunt aeris,Varr. R. R. 3, 14, 5; 3, 2, 16.—Esp.: aliquem tangere bolo, to cozen, wheedle of gain: qui...

bombinator.definition: The buzzer, hummer, of the bee, Mart. Cap. 9, § 999 Kopp. (al. bombitat ore).

bombizatio.definition: The buzzing of bees: est sonus apium ab ipso sonitu dictus: ut mugitus boum, hinnitus equorum, Paul. ex Fest. p. 30, 2.

bombus.definition: A hollow, deep sound, a booming, humming, buzzing: Ennius sonum pedum bombum pedum dixit, Fortun. Dial. (v. Enn. p. 183 fin. Vahl.); of bees; of a horn; of the clapping of hands: si (apes) intus faciunt bombum,Varr. R. R. 3, 16, 32: cum tuba... mugit, Et reboat raucum regio cita barbara bombum,Lucr. 4, 546: raucisonos efflabant cornua bombos,Cat. 64, 263: torva mimalloneis inplerunt cornua bombis,Pers. 1, 99 Coningt. ad loc.; Mart. Cap. 1, § 67; ...

bombycinus.definition: bombȳcĭnus, a, um, bombyx Of silk, silken (cf. sericus): vestis,Plin. 11, 22, 26, § 76: panniculus,Juv. 6, 260: taenia,Mart. 14, 24; Dig. 34, 2, 23, § 1.—Subst.: bombȳcĭna, ōrum, n., silk garments, Mart. 11, 50, 5; 8, 68, 7; App. M. 8, p. 214, 6.—And bombȳcĭnum, i, n., a silk texture or web, Isid. Orig. 19, 22, 13.

bombyx.definition: m. (f., Plin. 11, 23, 27; Tert. Pall. 3), = . The silk-worm, Plin. 11, 22, 25, § 75 sqq.; Mart. 8, 33, 16; Serv. ad Verg. G. 2, 121; Isid. Orig. 12, 5, 8; 19, 27, 5. Meton.

bona.definition: Bŏna Dea (Dīva) The good goddess, worshipped by the women of Rome as the goddess of chastity and fertility. No man was permitted to enter her temple; but in later times it became the resort of unchaste women, and the scene of license,Macr. S. 1, 12, 21 sqq.; Ov. A. A. 3, 244; cf. also id. ib. 3, 637; Juv. 2, 84 sq.; 6, 314. Clodius invaded this sanctuary, and is hence called by Cicero the priest of the Bona Dea, Cic. Att. 2, 4, 2; id. Har. Resp. ...

bonifatus.definition: bŏnĭfātus, = εὔμοιρος Lucky, fortunate, Gloss. Gr. Lat.

bonitas.definition: bonus The good quality of a thing, goodness, excellence (cf. Caes. B. G. 1, 28 Herz.; class., but mostly in prose). Of concrete objects: bonitas praediorum,Cic. Rosc. Am. 7, 20: agrorum,id. Agr. 2, 16, 41; Caes. B. G. 1, 28: agri aut oppidi,Cic. Agr. 2, 28, 76: praediorum,id. Rosc. Am. 7, 20; Dig. 50, 16, 86: terrae,Lucr. 5, 1247: soli,Quint. 2, 19, 2: aquae,Phaedr. 4, 9, 8: vini,Plin. 14, 4, 6, § 55: arboris,id. 13, 9, 17, § 61: gemmarum,id. 37,...

bononia.definition: Bŏnōnĭa, ae, f., = Βονωνία. A town in Gallia Cisalpina, in the neighborhood of Mutina, a Roman colony founded A. U. C. 563, Cic. Fam. 12, 5, 2; Liv. 37, 57, 7; Vell. 1, 15, 2; Sil. 8, 599; Mel. 2, 4, 2; previously a Tuscan town called Felsina, now Bologna, Plin. 3, 15, 20, § 115; Interpr. ap. Serv. ad Verg. A. 10, 198; Liv. 33, 37, 3; Amm. 20, 1, 3; 27, 8, 6.—Hence A fortress in Pannonia, now Banostor, Amm. 21, 9, 6; 31, 11, 6; Itin. Anton. A to...

bonum.definition: v. bonus, I. 5. and II. A. 5.

bonus.definition: bŏnus (old form dŭonus, Carm. Sall. ap. Varr. L. L. 7, § 26 Müll.; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 67 Müll.), a, um, for duonus, cf. bellum, bis, and cf. root dvi-; hence δείδω, δέος Good; comp.melior, uscf. Gr. μάλα, μᾶλλον, better; sup.optimus (optu-mus, ante-class. and often class.) [root opof ops, opes; cf. copia, apiscor], best. Attributively. As subst.

boo.definition: bŏo (with the digamma bŏvo, Enn.; V.infra), āre or ĕre, from the root bo, kindr. with Sanscr. gu and the Gr. βοάω; cf. Varr. L. L. 7, § 104 Müll.; Non. p. 79, 4; acc. to Paul. ex Fest. p. 30 Müll. directly from the Gr., to cry aloud, roar (mostly ante- and post-class., and in the poets).

boopes.definition: A plant, pure Lat. caerefolium, App. Herb. 104.

boreotis.definition: bŏrĕōtis, ĭdis Adj. f., = βορεῶτις, northern; acc. plur. boreotidas, Prisc. Perieg. 577.

borith.definition: bōrith A plant purifying like soap, soapwort (herbe savonnieère, Jarchi Malach. 3, 2; cf. Ges. and Robinson's Heb. Lex. under ), Vulg. Jer. 2, 22, and Mal. 3, 2.

bos.definition: (prob. orig. form of nom. , , Petr. 62, 13; cf. Varr L. L. 8, § 74 Müll., where, acc. to Cod. B., the read. should be: nunc in consuetudine aliter dicere pro Jovis Juppiter, pro Bovis Bos, pro Strus Strues.—Hence Gen. plur. bŏvĕrum, Cato, R. R. 62 Schneid. N. cr.; cf. Varr. L. L. l. l.: alios dicere Boum greges, alios Boverum; v. Juppiter, nux, rex, sus, and Schneid. Gr. 2, p. 171.— Regular gen. boum very freq.; uncontracted form bovum,Cic. Rep. ...

bostrychus.definition: bostrychus, a, um Curled, in ringlets: crines, Firm. Math. 4, 12. ‡† bŏtănĭcum herbarium dicitur, quod ibi herbae notentur, Isid. Orig. 4, 10, 4.

botellus.definition: dim.botulus A small sausage (rare), Mart. 5, 78, 9; 11, 31, 13; cf. Apic. 2, 3; Sid. Ep. 8, 11.

botronatus.definition: βότρυς An ornament for the hair of a female, in the form of a cluster of grapes, Tert. Cult. Fem. 10; Cypr. Hab. Virg. p. 98.

botruosus.definition: bōtrŭōsus, a, um, botrus Full of clusters (pure Lat. racemosus), App. Herb. 66; Isid. Orig. 17, 11, 8.

botryitis.definition: βοτρυῗτις and βοτρυώδης (cluster-shaped) A kind of calamine, Cels. 6, 6, n. 6; Plin. 34, 10, 22, § 101; Scrib. Comp. 24 and 220. A precious stone in the form of a cluster of grapes, otherwise unknown, Plin. 37, 10, 55, § 150.

botryodes.definition: bŏtryōdes, is In the form of a cluster of grapes: cadmea,Veg. 6 (4), 11, 1.

botulus.definition: (orig. like φύσκη and the Ital. budello, derived from the Lat.; Fr. boyau, an intestine; hence like the somewhat differently formed derivatives, Ital. boldone and boldonuccio; Fr. boudin; Engl. pudding) A sausage (very rare; acc. to Gell. 17, 7, 11, a vulgar word, used by Laber. for farcimen): botulus genus farciminis, Paul. ex Fest. p. 35 Müll.; Mart. 14, 72; Petr. 49 fin; Apic. 2, 5; Arn. 2, 73; Tert. Apol. 9. Meton., a stomach filled with del...

boustrophedon.definition: boustrŏphēdŏn From right to left and back again alternately, forwards and backwards, an ancient way of writing, Mar. Vict. 1, 14, 6 Gaisf. (al. boustrophen, id. p. 2499 P.).

bovarius.definition: bŏvārĭus (boār-), a, um, bos Of or relating to horned cattle: arva, afterwards the site of the Forum Bovarium,Prop. 4 (5), 9, 19. Forum,the cattle-market,Varr. L. L. 5, § 146 Müll.: horam sibi octavam, dum in foro bovario inquireret, postulavit,Cic. Aem. Scaur. 11, 23; cf. Ov. F. 6, 473; Paul. ex Fest. p. 30 Müll.; Liv. 21, 62, 3; 33, 27, 4 Weissenb. ad loc.; 35, 40, 8; Val. Max. 1, 6, 5; 2, 4, 7; Plin. 34, 3, 5, § 10; Tac. A. 12, 24: lappa boari...

bouarius.definition: bŏvārĭus (boār-), a, um, bos Of or relating to horned cattle: arva, afterwards the site of the Forum Bovarium,Prop. 4 (5), 9, 19. Forum,the cattle-market,Varr. L. L. 5, § 146 Müll.: horam sibi octavam, dum in foro bovario inquireret, postulavit,Cic. Aem. Scaur. 11, 23; cf. Ov. F. 6, 473; Paul. ex Fest. p. 30 Müll.; Liv. 21, 62, 3; 33, 27, 4 Weissenb. ad loc.; 35, 40, 8; Val. Max. 1, 6, 5; 2, 4, 7; Plin. 34, 3, 5, § 10; Tac. A. 12, 24: lappa boari...

bovicidium.definition: bos-caedo A slaughtering of cattle, Sol. 1, § 10.

bouicidium.definition: bos-caedo A slaughtering of cattle, Sol. 1, § 10.

bovinator.definition: bovinor. A brawler, blusterer, reviler, acc. to the Gloss.: bovinatores θορυβοποιοί, θρύλλον ποιοῦντες ἠ ταραχήν; v. bovinor. = tergiversator, one who seeks evasions (the figure drawn perh. from the holding back of draught cattle), Lucil. ap. Gell. 11, 7, 9; cf. Non. p. 79, 26.

bouinator.definition: bovinor. A brawler, blusterer, reviler, acc. to the Gloss.: bovinatores θορυβοποιοί, θρύλλον ποιοῦντες ἠ ταραχήν; v. bovinor. = tergiversator, one who seeks evasions (the figure drawn perh. from the holding back of draught cattle), Lucil. ap. Gell. 11, 7, 9; cf. Non. p. 79, 26.

bovinus.definition: bŏvīnus, a, um, , = bubulus [id.] Of or pertaining to oxen or cows: medulla, Theod. Prisc. Diaeta, 15.

bouinus.definition: bŏvīnus, a, um, , = bubulus [id.] Of or pertaining to oxen or cows: medulla, Theod. Prisc. Diaeta, 15.

brabeum.definition: or A prize in the games (late Lat.), Prud. στεφ. 5, 538; Tert. adv. Marc. 3; Vulg. 1 Cor. 9, 24.

bracarius.definition: braca A maker of trowsers or breeches (late Lat.), Lampr. Alex. Sev. 24; Cod. Just. 10, 64, 1; Edict. Diocl. p. 20.

bracatus.definition: brācātus, a, um, id.. Wearing trowsers or breeches. In gen., wearing broad garments: Satarchae totum bracati corpus,Mel. 2, 1, 10.

bracchialis.definition: bracchĭālis (brāch-), e, bracchium Of or belonging to the arm: nervus,Plaut. Poen. 5, 4, 99: crassitudo,the thickness of an arm,Plin. 17, 17, 27, § 123: torques,Vop. Aur. 7.—Hence Subst.: bracchĭāle, is, n. (sc. ornamentum): argenteum,Plin. 28, 7, 23, § 82 sq.; 25, 10, 80, § 129; 32, 1, 3, § 8; and bracchĭālis, is, m. (sc. torques), Treb. Claud. 14, 5 (class. armillae); an armlet, bracelet; cf. Prisc. p. 1220 P.

bracchiatus.definition: bracchĭātus (brāch-), a, um, id. II. C. With boughs or branches like arms (very rare): vineae,Col. 5, 5, 9; 5, 5, 12; 5, 5, 13: arbores,Plin. 16, 30, 53, § 123.

bracchiolum.definition: (), , dim. bracchium. A small, delicate arm: puellulae, * Cat. 61, 181. Transf.

bracchionarium.definition: (), , , = ψέλλιον ἀνδρός A bracelet, Gloss. Gr. Lat. [βραχίων].

bracchium.definition: (less correctly ; Gen. bracchi, Lucr. 6, 434), , n. perh. kindr. with Gr. βραχίων; but cf. Sanscr. bāhu; like frango, Sanscr. bhang, Bopp, Gloss. p. 239 a, the arm; particularly Lit., the forearm, from the hand to the elbow (while lacertus is the upper arm, from the elbow to the shoulder), Lucr. 4, 830; 6, 397: bracchia et lacerti,Ov. M. 1, 501; 1, 550 sq.: subjecta lacertis bracchia,id. ib. 14, 305; Curt. 8, 9, 21; 9, 1, 29: (feminae) nudae bra...

brachycatalectum.definition: (, Serv. Centim. p. 1817 P.), , (sc. metrum), = βραχυκατάληκτον or βραχυκαταληκτικόν; in metre A verse that wants a whole foot or half a metre, Diom. p. 501 P.

brachypota.definition: βραχυπότης A small drinker, Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 15, 120.

brachysyllabus.definition: (sc. pes), = (of short syllables); In metre, another name of the tribrachys, ˘˘˘,Diom. p. 475 P.; Mar. Vict. 2539 P.

bractea.definition: (also ), , perh. kindr. with βράχω, to rattle A thin plate of metal, gold-leaf (thicker plates of metal are called laminae; cf. Isid. Orig. 16, 18, 2: bractea dicitur tenuissima lamina): aranea bratteaque auri, * Lucr. 4, 729: leni crepitabat brattea vento,Verg. A. 6, 209: inspice, quam tenuis bractea ligna tegat,Ov. A. A. 3, 232; Mart. 8, 33, 6; Plin. 33, 3, 19, § 61; cf. argenteae,id. 37, 7, 31, § 105. Trop., show, glitter: eloquentiae, Sol. p...

bractealis.definition: bractĕālis, e, bractea Of metallic plates: fulgor, golden, Prud. στεφ. 10, 1024.

bracteamentum.definition: id. II. Glitter, splendor, Fulg. Contin. Virg. p. 140.

bracteatus.definition: bractĕātus, a, um, id. Covered with gold-plate, gilt (post-Aug. for the class. aureus): sellae,Sid. Ep. 8, 8: lacunar,id. ib. 2, 10. Trop. (cf. aureus, II.).

branchus.definition: Βράγχος A son of Apollo; or, according to others, of Smicrus of Delphi, inspired by Apollo with prophecy, v. Branchidae, Stat. Th. 3, 479; 8, 198 Schol.

brassica.definition: Cabbage; of several varieties (much prized by the ancients, and freq. employed in medicine), Cato, R. R. 156 sq.; Col. 10, 127 sq. Schneid.; 11, 3, 23; Plin. 19, 8, 41, § 136 sq.; 20, 9, 33, § 78 sq.; Pall. Febr. 24, 7; id. Jun. 4; id. Sept. 13, 1; id. Aug. 5, 3; Veg. 3, 15, 12; Plin. Val. 4, 29; Plaut. Ps. 3, 2, 26; Prop. 4 (5), 2, 44.al. (in Cic. N. D. 2, 47, 120, perh. a gloss; v. Orell. N. cr.).—Plur.: , , , varieties of cabbage, Cato, R. R. ...

brephotropheum.definition: or A foundling hospital, Cod. Just. 1, 2, 19.

brephotrophus.definition: One who brings up foundlings (v. brephotropheum), Cod. Just. 1, 3, 42, § 9.

breviatio.definition: id. A shortening (late Lat.): dierum,Aug. Ep. ad Hesych. 18: chronicorum, Jornand. Get. praef.

breuiatio.definition: id. A shortening (late Lat.): dierum,Aug. Ep. ad Hesych. 18: chronicorum, Jornand. Get. praef.

breviator.definition: id.. * An abbreviator, epitomizer, Oros. 1, 8.—* The author of a breviarium (q. v.), Novell. 105, 2, 4.

breuiator.definition: id.. * An abbreviator, epitomizer, Oros. 1, 8.—* The author of a breviarium (q. v.), Novell. 105, 2, 4.

breviculus.definition: Adj. dim. [brevis], somewhat short or small (rare): homo,Plaut. Merc. 3, 4, 54: pinnae, Fronto, Eloq.: grabatulus,App. M. 1, p. 107, 18. Transf., of time: tempus,App. M. 6, p. 183, 35.

breuiculus.definition: Adj. dim. [brevis], somewhat short or small (rare): homo,Plaut. Merc. 3, 4, 54: pinnae, Fronto, Eloq.: grabatulus,App. M. 1, p. 107, 18. Transf., of time: tempus,App. M. 6, p. 183, 35.

breviloquium.definition: brevis-loquor Brevity in speech, Prisc. p. 754 P.; Fulg. Myth. praef. fin.; Serv. ad Verg. A. 1, 561.

breuiloquium.definition: brevis-loquor Brevity in speech, Prisc. p. 754 P.; Fulg. Myth. praef. fin.; Serv. ad Verg. A. 1, 561.

breviloquus.definition: brĕvĭlŏquus or -quis, = βραχυλόγος Short in speech, speaking briefty, Gloss. Lab.

breuiloquus.definition: brĕvĭlŏquus or -quis, = βραχυλόγος Short in speech, speaking briefty, Gloss. Lab.

brevio.definition: brĕvĭo, āvi, ātum, 1, brevis To shorten, abbreviate, abridge, βραχύνω brevio, Gloss. Vet. (post-Aug.; cf. Burm. Anth. Lat. 1, p. 76; most freq. in Quint.); Manil. 3, 461; 6, 431: breviare quaedam,Quint. 1, 9, 2: aliquid callide,id. 5, 13, 41 Spald. N. cr.: prolixa (in scribendo),Lact. Epit. 8, 6; Sev. Sulp. Hist. Sacr. 1, 1: breviatae horae,Paul. Nol. Carm. Nat. S. Fel. 24, 9, 13: umerorum raro decens allevatio atque contractio est. Breviatur en...

breuio.definition: brĕvĭo, āvi, ātum, 1, brevis To shorten, abbreviate, abridge, βραχύνω brevio, Gloss. Vet. (post-Aug.; cf. Burm. Anth. Lat. 1, p. 76; most freq. in Quint.); Manil. 3, 461; 6, 431: breviare quaedam,Quint. 1, 9, 2: aliquid callide,id. 5, 13, 41 Spald. N. cr.: prolixa (in scribendo),Lact. Epit. 8, 6; Sev. Sulp. Hist. Sacr. 1, 1: breviatae horae,Paul. Nol. Carm. Nat. S. Fel. 24, 9, 13: umerorum raro decens allevatio atque contractio est. Breviatur en...

brevis.definition: brĕvis, e, adj. (abl. breve, Varr. R. R. 2, 3, 2; Comp. abl. breviore, Ov. Am. 2, 17, 22) [cf. βραχύς, Fest. p. 26], short, little, of small extent, in space and time (opp. longus; in space, in good class. prose, diff. from parvus, which designates that which fills a small space in length, breadth, and thickness; while brevis is used only of length in its different directions of breadth, height, or depth; and even of a circle, as merely a line, ...

breuis.definition: brĕvis, e, adj. (abl. breve, Varr. R. R. 2, 3, 2; Comp. abl. breviore, Ov. brevitas.definition: brevis Shortness. Lit., in space (cf. brevis, I.) (rare): brevitas angusti freti,the narrowness of the strait,Gell. 10, 27, 6: hominibus Gallis prae magnitudine corporum suorum brevitas nostra contemptui est,smallness of stature,Caes. B. G. 2, 30; cf.: haec habilis brevitate suā est,Ov. Am. 2, 4, 35: spatii,Caes. B. C. 1, 82, 3: crurum,Plin. 8, 34, 52, § 123: chamaeplatani coactae brevitatis,Plin. 12, 2, 6, § 13: guttarum,Vitr. 7, 8, 2.—More freq...

breuitas.definition: brevis Shortness. Lit., in space (cf. brevis, I.) (rare): brevitas angusti freti,the narrowness of the strait,Gell. 10, 27, 6: hominibus Gallis prae magnitudine corporum suorum brevitas nostra contemptui est,smallness of stature,Caes. B. G. 2, 30; cf.: haec habilis brevitate suā est,Ov. Am. 2, 4, 35: spatii,Caes. B. C. 1, 82, 3: crurum,Plin. 8, 34, 52, § 123: chamaeplatani coactae brevitatis,Plin. 12, 2, 6, § 13: guttarum,Vitr. 7, 8, 2.—More freq...

bria.definition: A wine - vessel, εἶδος ἀγγείου, Gloss. Philox.; Arn. 7, p. 235; cf. Hildebr. ad App. Mag. 59 (acc. to Charis. p. 63, : hebria est vas vinarium, unde ebrius et ebria dicitur).

bromosus.definition: brōmōsus, a, um Stinking, fetid: caro,Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 37: qualitas,id. Tard. 3, 2.

bruchus.definition: βροῦχος or βροῦκος A kind of locust without wings, Prud. Ham. 229; Vulg. Lev. 11, 22 al.

bruma.definition: for brevima, breuma = brevissima: dicta bruma quod brevissimus tunc dies est,Varr. L. L. 6, § 8 Müll.: bruma a brevitate dierum dicta, Paul. ex Fest. p. 31 Müll.; cf. Isid. Orig. 5, 35, 6; Gesn. Claud. Rapt. Pros. 2, 106; Ruhnk. ad Ter. Phorm. 4, 4, 28. Lit., the shortest day in the year, the winter solstice, * Lucr. 5, 746; Varr. L. L. l. l.; Ter. Phorm. 4, 4, 28: circa brumam serendum non esse,Plin. 18, 24, 56, § 204 al.—Plur.: solis accessus d...

brumalis.definition: brūmālis, e, bruma. Of or pertaining to the winter solstice, or shortest day: dies,Cic. Div. 2, 14, 33; id. Fat. 3: polus,Varr. L. L. 9, § 24 Müll.: signum,Capricorn,Cic. de Or. 3, 45, 178: flexus,the tropic of Capricorn,Lucr. 5, 615; 5, 639: orbis,Cic. N. D. 3, 14, 37: tempus,id. ib. 2, 44, 112: circulus,Plin. 2, 70, 70, § 177: oriens,Col. 1, 6, 1; Plin. 2, 47, 46, § 119: occasus, id. l. l.: meridies,Col. 9, 5, 1: revocatio,Cic. Univ. 9: hora, t...

brumaria.definition: (sc. herba) [bruma] A plant, also called leontopodium, App. Herb. 7.

brutesco.definition: brūtesco, ĕre V. inch. [brutus], to become brutish, rough, unreasonable (postclass.), Sid. Ep. 4, 1 fin.; Lact. 7, 12, 24; Ven. Ep. praef. carm. 6, 5.

brutus.definition: brūtus, a, um, kindr. with βαρύς, perh. contr. from barutus, a lengthened form of barus, like actutum, astutus, cinctutus, versutus, from actu, astus, cinctus, versus; cf. also βρῖθύς, heavy, weighty; Fr. and Engl. brute, brutal. Lit., heavy, unwieldy, immovable (rare): brutum antiqui gravem dicebant, Paul. ex Fest. p. 31 Müll.: pondus,falling down with heavy weight,Lucr. 6, 105: tellus, * Hor. C. 1, 34, 9 (cf.: terra iners,id. ib. 3, 4, 45: i...

bryonia.definition: A wild vine, the bryony; of two kinds: the white, Plin. 23, 1, 16, § 24; Scrib. Comp. 59; the black, Plin. 23, 1, 17, § 27; Col. 10, 250; App. Herb. 66.

bubalinus.definition: būbălīnus, a, um, bubalus Pertaining to the African gazelle: laridum, Val. Imp. ap. Vop. Prob. 4.

bubalus.definition: būbălus, i, m. A kind of African stag or gazelle, Plin. 8, 15, 15, § 38; Sol. 20, 5; Vulg. Deut. 14, 5.—Hence, bū-bălus, a, um, , of the gazelle: caro,Vulg. 2 Reg. 6, 19; id. 1 Par. 16, 3. The buffalo, wild-ox, = urus, Sol. 20, 5; Mart. Spect. 23, 4; this use of the word is censured by Pliny, 8, 15, 15, § 38.—Collat. form būfălus, i, m., Ven. Fort. Carm. 7, 4, 21.

bubile.definition: (access. form , unus. acc. to Varr. L. L. 8, § 54 Müll.; although used by Cato, acc. to Charis. p. 81; and by Veg. 4, 1, 3), , bos A stall for oxen: (boves) reicere in bubile,Plaut. Pers. 2, 5, 18 Ritschl; Cato, R. R. 4; Varr. R. R. 1, 13, 1; Col. 1, 6, 4; Phaedr. 2, 8, 4.

bubo.definition: m. (f. only once Verg. A. 4, 462; cf. Serv. ad loc.; Non. p. 194, 1.— Hence given erroneously by Prisc. p. 683 P. and Rhemn. Palaem. p. 1370 Fin. ib. as comm.) [βύας, βῦζα], an owl, the horned owl: Strix bubo, Linn., whose cry was considered as ill-boding,Plin. 10, 12, 16, § 34; Verg. A. 4, 462: ignavus bubo,Ov. M. 5, 550: profanus,id. ib. 6, 432 (cf. id. ib. 5, 543: profana avis): funereus,id. ib. 10, 453: Stygius (since Ascalaphus, son of Ach...

bubsequa.definition: (also and ), , bos-sequor A neatherd, herdsman (post-class.), App. M. 8, p. 201, 13; id. Flor. 1, n. 3; Sid. Ep. 1, 6.

bubulcarius.definition: bŭbulcārĭus, = βοώτης A ploughman, Gloss. Gr. Lat. ( = bubulcus).

bubulcito.definition: bŭbulcĭto, āre, v. n. (bŭbulcĭtor, āri, v. dep., Plaut.) [bubulcus] To be a herdsman, to keep, feed, or drive oxen (ante- and post-class., and very rare). Lit.: bubulcitarier,Plaut. Most. 1, 1, 50; App. Flor. n. 6, p. 343, 14. Trop., to cry or bawl like an ox-driver, Varr. ap. Non. p. 79, 29 (Sat. Men. 52, 1).

bubulcus.definition: bos, bubulus, βοῦκος. In a restricted sense, one who ploughs with oxen, a ploughman, = arator (diff. from pastor and armentarius, a herdsman; so most freq. in the Script. rerr. rustt.),Varr. R. R. 2, prooem. § 4 sq.; Juv. 11, 151; cf. Col. 1, 6, 8; 1, 9, 2; 2, 2, 25; 2, 5, 2; 2, 12, 1 sq.; Cic. Div. 1, 27, 57; Ov. Tr. 3, 12, 30; Juv. 7, 116; 11, 151 al. In a more general sense, a herdsman (rare, and not before the post-Aug. per.), Dig. 33, 7, 18...

bubulinus.definition: būbŭlīnus, a, um, bos, for bubulus Of cattle, ox- (post-Aug.; only in Veg.): stercus,Veg. 1, 13, 3: fimum,id. 3, 28, 3: sevum,id. 4, 8, 2: urina,id. 4, 17.

bubulo.definition: būbŭlo, āre, bubo To cry, hoot, or screech like an owl, Auct. Carm. Phil. 37.

bubulus.definition: būbŭlus, a, um, bos Of or pertaining to cattle or oxen (class.): cori,thongs, straps of ox-hide,Plaut. Poen. 1, 1, 11; and humorously, cottabi, the snapping of such ox-whips (cf. cottabus), id. Trin. 4, 4, 4 Lind.; so also monimenta, for lashes, id. Stich. 1, 2, 6; and, exuviae,id. Most. 4, 1, 26: pecus,neat cattle,Varr. R. R. 2, 1, 13: armentum,Col. 1, praef. § 26: fimum,Cato, R. R. 40, 2; Liv. 38, 18, 5: utres,Plin. 6, 29, 34, § 176: lac, cow's...

bucca.definition: (not ), , kindred with βύζω, βυκάνη; Fr. bouche. The cheek (puffed or filled out in speaking, eating, etc.; diff. from genae, the side of the face, the cheeks, and from mala, the upper part of the cheek under the eyes; v. Plin. 11, 37, 57, § 156 sqq.; mostly in plur.; class.): buccam implere, Cato ap. Gell. 2, 22, 29: sufflare buccas,Plaut. Stich. 5, 4, 42: inflare,id. ib. 5, 6, 7: rumpere buccas,to write bombast,Pers. 5, 13: sufflare buccis,Ma...

buccellatum.definition: buccella Soldiers' biscuit, Amm. 17, 8, 2; Vulcat. Gall. Avid. Cass. 5, 4; Spart. Pesc. Nig. 10, 4; Cod. Th. 7, 4, 6; 7, 5, 2.

buccina.definition: buccĭna, buccĭnātor, buccĭno, buccĭnum, and buccĭnus, v. bucina, etc.

bucco.definition: Amplif. [bucca, one who has distended cheeks], a babbler, blockhead, fool (very rare): bucco = garrulus, quod ceteros oris loquacitate, non sensu exsuperat,Isid. Orig. 10, 30: stulti, stolidi, fatui, fungi, bardi, blenni, buccones,Plaut. Bacch. 5, 1, 2: macci et buccones,App. Mag. p. 325, 30.

buccula.definition: (), , dim. bucca. A little cheek or mouth, * Suet. Galb. 4: pressa Cupidinis buccula,App. M. 6, p. 182, 17; 3, p. 137, 40; Arn. 2, p. 73. In milit. lang.

bucerus.definition: būcĕrus (būcĕrĭus, Lucr. 2, 663), a, um Having the horns of a bullock, ox-horned (perh. only in the foll. exs.): bucerum pecus de bubus dicimus, Paul. ex Fest. p. 32 Müll.: bucera saecla,the race of horned caltle,Lucr. 5, 864; so id. 6, 1236; imitated by Ovid: armenta, * Ov. M. 6, 395: buceriae greges,Lucr. 2, 663 (quoted by Non. p. 80, 27, and p. 208, 21).

bucetum.definition: (, , n., Varr. L. L. 5, § 164 Müll.), , n. bos A pasture for cattle, cow-pasture (very rare), Luc. 9, 185; Gell. 11, 1, 1; Sid. Ep. 2, 2.

bucina.definition: (not ) A crooked horn or trumpet (while tuba is usually the straight trumpet; cf. Veg. Mil. 3, 3, 5 Stewech.). Lit., a shepherd's horn, Varr. R. R. 2, 4, 20: bucina inflata,id. ib. 3, 13, 1; Col. 6, 23, 3; Prop. 4 (5), 10, 29. Transf.

bucinator.definition: (), , bucino One who blew the bucina, a trumpeter, Caes. B.C. 2, 35; Petr. 26, 9; Varr. L. L. 6, § 75; Dig. 50, 6, 6; Inscr. Orell. 3522. Trop. (cf. bucina, II. D.), one who trumpets forth, blazes abroad: bucinator existimationis meae, Cic. Fil. ap. Cic. Fam. 16, 21, 2; Inscr. Orell. 3232.

bucino.definition: būcĭno (bucc-), āvi, ātum, 1, bucina To blow the bucina, to sound or give a signal with the trumpet (mostly impers.; cf. Gr. σαλπίζειν): cum bucinatum est,Varr. R. R. 2, 4, 20: saepe declamante illo ter bucinavit,Sen. Contr. 3 praef.: bucinate in neomeniā tubā,Vulg. Psa. 81 (80), 4: Triton conchā sonaci leniter bucinat,App. M. 4, p. 157, 3; cf. bucina, II. C.

bucinum.definition: (), , id.. The sound or blast of a trumpet, Plin. 9, 33, 52, § 103; 11, 10, 10, § 20.—Hence, ad Bucinum, a quarter in Rome, Dig. 14, 4, 5, § 16. A shell-fish used in dyeing purple, Plin. 9, 36, 61, § 129 sq.

bucolicus.definition: būcŏlĭcus, a, um Pertaining to shepherds, pastoral, bucolic. In gen.: Bucolicōn poëma, Virgil's pastoral poetry, the Bucolics, Col. 7, 10, 8; and absol.: Būcŏlĭca, ōrum, n., = τὰ Βουκολικά, Bucolics, Ov. Tr. 2, 538: Bucolica Theocriti et Vergilii,Gell. 9, 9, 4; cf. Serv. ad Verg. E.1. Esp.

bucranium.definition: Oxhead. A place of sacrifice, Inscr. Orell. 2322. A plant like a bullock's head in shape, App. Herb. 86.

buda.definition: colloq., = ulva, Anthol. Lat. 5, 189, 2; Aug. Ep. 88, 6; Don. ad Verg. A. 2, 135.

bugillo.definition: A plant, also called ajuga reptans, Marc. Emp. 8.

bulbus.definition: (), , βολβός. A bulb, bulbous root (tulips, hyacinths, lilies, etc.), Plin. 19, 4, 21, § 61; cf. Cels. 2, 18; Plin. 17, 20, 33, § 144; 21, 5, 11, § 24; 22, 22, 32, § 67 sq. An onion; a garden vegetable of several kinds, among which the Megarean was the best known, Cato, R. R. 8, 2; Ov. R. Am. 797; Col. 10, 106; 4, 32, 2; Plin. 19, 5, 30, § 93; in Apic. 8, 7, and in Edict. Diocl. p. 16, called bulbus fabrilis.

buleuta.definition: ae. A councillor, a senātor, Plin. Ep. 10, 39 (48), 5; 10, 112 (113), 3; 10, 114 (115), 3; Spart. Sever. 17.

bulga.definition: Gallic; now bougette A leathern knapsack, bag: bulgas Galli sacculos scorteos appellant, Paul. ex Fest. p. 35 Müll.: bulga est folliculus omnis, quam et crumenam veteres appellarunt: et est sacculus ad bracchium pendens, Lucil. ap. Non. p. 78 (Sat. 2, 16, and 6, 1); Varr. ap. Non. 78, 2 (Sat. Men. 61, 3). Humorously, the womb, Lucil. ap. Non. p. 78, 14 (Sat. 26, 36).

bulimo.definition: būlīmo, āre, āvi, ātum (βουλιμιῶ), 1 To have bulimy or insatiable hunger, Pelag. Vet. 10; Theod. Prisc. 2, 29.

bulimosus.definition: būlīmōsus, a, um, bulimus Afflicted with insatiable hunger, Pelag. Vet. 10.

bulimus.definition: Great hunger, bulimy; hence also, weakness of the stomach, fainting, Gell. 16, 3, 9; cf. bu; Veg. 5, 34 (3, 35); 5, 37 (3, 38) (in Varr. 2, 5, 4, written as Greek).—Also written , , , Paul. ex Fest. p. 32 Müll.

bulla.definition: root vhal-; Gr. φαλ-; cf. φαλλός, φύλλον Any object swelling up, and thus becoming round; hence A waterbubble, bubble: ut pluvio perlucida caelo Surgere bulla solet,Ov. M. 10, 734: crassior,Mart. 8, 33, 18; Plin. 31, 2, 8, § 12; App. M. 4, p. 145, 7.—Hence Any thing rounded by art.

bullatus.definition: bullātus, a, um, bulla. (Acc. to bulla, I. B.) Quickly passing; acc. to others, inflated, bombastic: nugae,Pers. 5, 19. (Acc. to bulla, II.) Furnished with a boss or stud: cingulum,Varr. L. L. 5, § 116 Müll.—Of the heavens, studded with stars: aether,Fulg. Myth. 1, p. 24 Munck. (Acc. to bulla, III.) Wearing a bulla about the neck: puer, Scip. Afr. ap. Macr. S. 2, 10, 7: statua,of a child,Val. Max. 3, 1, 1: heres,yet a child,Juv. 14, 5; cf. Petr. ...

bullo.definition: bullo, āre, and bullĭo, īvi, ītum, 4, v. n.bulla To be in bubbling motion, to be in a state of ebullition, to bubble. Trop.: indignatione,to boil with rage, fty in a passion,App. M. 10, p. 250, 34: libidinum incendio bulliebant,Hier. ad Eustach. p. 236, 1, 1.

bullula.definition: dim.bulla. A watery vesicle, Cels. 2, 5 fin.; 5, 28, n. 17. A small neck-ornament (bulla), Hier. in Isa. 2, 3, 18.

bumastus.definition: (, , Edict. Diocl. p. 18), , = βούμαστος, sc. ἄμπελος (having large breasts; cf. Bumammus),a species of grape with large clusters,Verg. G. 2, 102 and Serv. ad loc.; id. Cul. 405; Col. 3, 2, 1; cf.: tument mammarum modo bumasti (acini),Plin. 14, 1, 3, § 15; 14, 3, 4, § 42.

bunias.definition: būnĭăs, ădis, f. A kind of Swedish turnip, Col. 10, 422; acc. buniada, Plin. 20, 4, 11, § 21.—Another kind is called būnĭon, ii, n., = βούνιον, Plin. l. l.—Hence, būnītus, a, um, , made from bunion: vinum,Cael. Aur. Tard. 4, 3, 52.

bupaeda.definition: βούπαις A huge youth, Mart. Cap. 1, § 31; 9, § 908 Kopp. (al. pubeda).

buprestis.definition: to swell up). A venomous beetle, whose sting caused a swelling in cattle, Plin. 30, 4, 10, § 30; 31, 10, 46, § 119; Veg. 5, 14, 10; 5, 77, 1; Isid. Orig. 12, 8, 5; Dig. 48, 8, 3, § 3. A kind of vegetable, Plin. 22, 22, 36, § 78.

burdo.definition: (collat. form , , Acron. ad Hor. C. 3, 27, 7) A mule (the offspring of a horse and she-ass, while mulus is the offspring of an ass and a mare; v. Isid. Orig. 12, 1, 61), esp. used for carrying litters, Dig. 32, 49: onus duorum burdonum,Vulg. 4 Reg. 5, 17.

burdunculus.definition: A plant, perh. borage, Marc. Emp. 5.

buris.definition: m. (, , f., Varr. R. R. 1, 19, 2) [acc. to Serv. ad Verg. G. 1, 170 (cf. also Isid. Orig. 20, 14, 2), contr. from βοῦς and οὐρά, ox-tail] The curved hinder part of the plough of the ancients, the plough-beam, Varr. ap. Serv. l. l.—Acc. burim, Verg. G. 1, 170 Serv. and Voss.; Varr. R. R. 1, 19, 2.

burius.definition: A species of animal, otherwise unknown, Jul. Val. Rer. Gest. Alex. M. 3, 31.

burra.definition: burrus. A small cow with a red mouth or muzzle, acc. to Fest. s. v. A shaggy garment, Anthol. Lat. 5, 133, 5.—Hence, plur.: , , , trifles, nonsense (post-class.): burras, quisquilias, ineptiasque, etc., Aus. praef. ad Latin. Pacat. 3.

burranicum.definition: prob. formed from the preced. A kind of vessel, Paul. ex Fest. p. 36 Müll.

burricus.definition: or (), , burrus; Fr. bourrique A small horse, Veg. 6, 2, 2; Paul. Nol. Ep. 29; cf. Schneid. ad Varr. R. R. 2, 8, 1.

bustar.definition: bustum A place where dead bodies were burned, Charis. p. 25 P.

busticetum.definition: id., post-class. for bustum A place where dead bodies were burned, Arn. 1, p. 24; 7, p. 222.

bustualis.definition: bustuālis, e, bustum Of or pertaining to the place where dead bodies were burned, Sid. Ep. 3, 12; Prud. Cath. 9, 52.

bustuarius.definition: bustŭārĭus, a, um, id. Of or pertaining to the place where dead bodies were burned: gladiator,that fought at a funeral pile in honor of the dead,Cic. Pis. 9, 19; Tert. Spect. 11; cf. Serv. ad Verg. A. 10, 519 (Cicero so calls Clodius, in the passage cited, on account of a tumult which he caused at the funeral ceremonies that Cicero's brother made in honor of Marius): moecha,she who prostitutes herself among tombs,Mart. 3, 93, 15: altare,upon whic...

bustum.definition: buro = uro, whence also comburo; cf. burrus, red, orig. The place where the bodies of the dead were burned and buried; later also, in gen., for a tomb: bustum proprie dicitur locus, in quo mortuus est combustus et sepultus... ubi vero combustus quis tantummodo, alibi vero est sepultus, is locus ab urendo ustrina vocatur; sed modo busta sepulchra appellamus, Paul. ex Fest. p. 32 Müll.; cf. Serv. ad Verg. A. 3, 22; 11, 201; Inscr. Murat. 1514, 3. T...

buteo.definition: A kind of falcon or hawk, Plin. 10, 8, 9, § 21; 11, 49, 110, § 263; Arn. 7, p. 280; Paul. ex Fest. p. 32 Müll.; giving auguries by its flight, v. ales, II. E.

buthysia.definition: A sacrifice of oxen, Suet. Ner. 12 fin.

buttuti.definition: buttuti, , Plaut. ap. Charis. p. 216 P.

butyrum.definition: (, Sid. Carm. 12, 7; , Aen. Mac. Herb. c. de ruta. buturum, Edict. Diocl. p. 15), , , = βούτυρον [said to be a Scythian word, but prob. βοῦστυρός; Engl. butter],butter,Cels. 4, 15; 4, 18; 5, 26, 30; Col. 6, 12, 5; Plin. 11, 41, 96, § 239; 28, 9, 35, § 133 sq.

buxeus.definition: buxĕus, a, um, id.. Of or pertaining to the boxwood-tree, made of boxwood, boxwood-: luci,Sol. 52: forma,Col. 7, 8, 7: mola,Petr. 74, 5. Of the color of boxwood: rostra (anatum), Varr. ap. Non. p. 460, 8: dentes,Mart. 2, 41, 7: anuli, perh. ironic. for spurious (on account of the paleness of boxwood), Petr. 58, 10; cf. pallor,App. M. 1, p. 110, 30: luror,id. ib. 9, p. 231, 4.

buxum.definition: id. The wood of the boxtree (cf. Neue, Formenl. 1, 509; 1, 625). In gen.: torno rasile,Verg. G. 2, 449: ora buxo Pallidiora,Ov. M. 4, 134: multifori tibia buxi,id. ib. 12, 158: buxoque simillimus Pallor,id. ib. 11, 417; cf. Plin. 16, 16, 28, § 70. Esp. of objects made of boxwood.

buxus.definition: (cf. Prisc. p. 549, and the letter B). Lit., the pale, evergreen box-tree, Enn. ap. Phylarg. l. l.: buxus densa foliis,Ov. A. A. 3, 691: crispata,Claud. Rapt. Pros. 2, 110: horrida,id. ib. 2, 268: perpetuo virens,Ov. M. 10, 97; Plin. 16, 43, 84, § 230; for its natural history, v. Plin. 16, 16, 28, § 70 sq. For things made of boxwood (cf. Plin. 16, 36, 66, § 172), a pipe or flute: tympana vos buxasque vocant Berecyntia. Verg. A. 9, 619 Forbig. ad ...

byssinus.definition: byssĭnus, a, um Made of byssus: linum,Plin. 19, 1, 4, § 21: vestis,App. M. 11, p. 269, 10; Isid. Orig. 19, 22, 15: opus,Dig. 39, 5, 16, § 7.—Subst.: byssĭnum, i, n. (sc. opus), a garment of byssus; trop.: vestite vos serico probitatis, byssino sanctitatis, purpură pudicitiae,Tert. Cult. Fem. 13; Vulg. 2 Par. 5, 12 al.

byzantium.definition: Bȳzantĭum, ii, n., = Βυζάντιον A city in Thrace, on the Bosphorus, opposite the Asiatic Chalcedon, later Constantinopolis, now Constantinople; among the Turks, Istamboul or Stamboul (i.e. εις τὴν πόλιν), Mel. 2, 2, 6; Plin. 4, 11, 18, § 46; 9, 15, 20, § 50 sq.; Nep. Paus. 2, 2; Liv. 38, 16, 3 sq.; Tac. A. 12, 63 sq.; id. H. 2. 83; 3, 47 al. Derivv.

c.definition: N.indecl., or f., the third letter of the Latin alphabet; corresponded originally in sound to the Greek Γ (which in inscrr., esp. in the Doric, was frequently written like the Latin C; v. O. Müll. Etrusk. 2, p. 295); hence the old orthography: LECIONES, MACISTRATOS, EXFOCIONT, [pu]CNANDOD, PVC[nad], CARTACINIENSI, upon the Columna rostrata, for legiones, magistratos, effugiunt, pugnando, pugnā, Carthaginiensi; and the praenomina Gaius and Gnaeus,...

caballarius.definition: id., = κέλης, ίππεύς A rider, horseman, Gloss. Lat. Gr.: ίπποκόμος (i.e. a hostler) caballarius, Gloss. Vet.; hence, Ital. cavaliero, Fr. chevalier.

caballatio.definition: id. Fodder for a horse (post-class.), Cod. Th. 7, 4, 34; 12, 38, 14.

caballinus.definition: căballīnus, a, um, id. Of or pertaining to a horse, horse. (post-Aug.): caro,Plin. 28, 20, 81, § 265. dentes, id. 30, 8, 22, § 72; flmum,id. 30, 13, 38, § 112: fons,i.e. Hippocrene,Pers. prol. 1.

caballio.definition: dim.id. A small horse, a pony: marini, perh. = hippocampi,Veg. 1, 20, 2; 6, 12, 3.

caballus.definition: [perh. Celtic; hence Ital. cavallo, Fr. cheval, Engl. cavalry, cavalier, etc.; cf. cob, Germ. Gaul] An inferior riding- or pack-horse, a nag (poet. and in post-Aug. prose): tardus, Lucil. ap. Non. p. 86, 15; Varr. ib.: mediā de nocte caballum Arripit,his nag,Hor. Ep. 1, 7, 88; so id. S. 1, 6, 59; 1, 6, 103; id. Ep. 1, 18, 36; Juv. 10, 60; 11, 195; Sen. Ep. 87, 8; Petr. 117, 12; Dig. 33, 7, 15: Gorgoneus, jestingly for Pegasus,Juv. 3, 118.

cabus.definition: LXX. [Heb. kab] A corn-measure, answering to the χοῖνιξ, Vulg. 4 Reg. 6, 25 Müll.

cacabaceus.definition: cācăbācĕus (cacc-), a, um, cacabus Of or pertaining to a kitchen-pot: motus,i.e. like the liquid boiling in a pot,Tert. adv. Herm. 41.

cacabatus.definition: cācăbātus (cacc-), a, um, id. Black, sooty, besmeared like a cooking-pot: aedificia (opp. immaculata),Paul. Nol. Ep. ad Serv. 32, 9.

cacabo.definition: cācăbo ( Auct. Fragm. Aucup. 12), āre To cackle; Gr. κακκαβίζω, as the natural cry of the partridge: cacabat hinc perdix, Carm. Philom. 19

cacabus.definition: () A cooking-pot: vas ubi coquebant cibum, ab eo caccabum appellarunt,Varr. L. L. 5, 27, 36: aeneus,Col. 12, 46, 1: argenteus,Dig. 34, 2, 20; 33, 7, 18, § 3: novus,Col. 12, 48, 5: figuli,id. 12, 41, 2: fictilis,Scrib. Comp. 220; Stat. S. 4, 9, 45.

cacaturio.definition: căcātŭrĭo, īre V. n. desid. [caco], to desire to go to stool, Mart. 11, 77.

cachexia.definition: A consumption, wasting, cachexy, Cael. Aur. Tard. 3, 6, 80 sqq.; 4, 2, 18 (in Cels. 3, 32, as Gr.).

cachinnatio.definition: id. A violent laughing, immoderate laughter: sine ullā suspitione nimiae suspitionis,Auct. Her. 3, 14, 25: ut si ridere concessum sit, vituperetur tamen cachinnatio,Cic. Tusc. 4, 31, 66.

cachinno.definition: căchinno, āvi, ātum, 1, like καχάζω or καγχάζω; Sanscr. kakk; and our titter, onomatop. To laugh aloud, laugh immoderately. Lit. (class. but rare): famulae furtim cachinnant,Lucr. 4, 1176; 1, 919; 2, 976: ridere convivae; cachinnare ipse Apronius,Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 25, § 62; Suet. Vesp. 5; Aur. Vict. Epit. 28.—With the acc. of that which one laughs at: exitum meum cachinnant,App. M. 3, p. 132, 25.—* Poet. (v. Liddell and Scott under καχλάζω, γέ...

cachinnosus.definition: căchinnosus, a, um, cachinno Given to loud laughter (late Lat.), Cael. Aur. Acut. 1, 3, 41.

cachinnus.definition: id. A loud laugh, immoderate laughter, a laugh in derision, a jeering. Lit. (class in prose and poetry; also in plur.): tum dulces esse cachinni consuerant,Lucr. 5, 1396; so id. 5, 1402: in quo Alcibiades cachinnum dicitur sustulisse,to have set up a loud laugh,Cic. Fat. 5, 10; Suet. Aug. 98: tollere,Hor. A. P. 113: cachinnos irridentium commovere,Cic. Brut. 60, 216: res digna tuo cachinno,Cat. 56, 2; 31, 14; 13, 5: securus,Col. 10, 280: perversu...

caco.definition: căco, āvi, ātum, āre, and A.,—κακάω, to go to stool, to be at stool. Neutr., Pompon. ap. Non. p. 84, 2: toto decies in anno, Cat. 23, 20; *Hor. S. 1, 8, 38; Mart. 12, 61, 10. Act., Pompon. ap. Non. p. 84, 1 (Com. Rel. p. 209 Rib.): canes odorem mixtum cum merdis cacant,Phaedr. 4, 17, 25; Mart. 3, 89.—Also, to defile with excrement: cacata charta,Cat. 36, 1 and 20.

cacoethes.definition: (bad state or habit); In medic. lang.,an obstinate, malignant disease,Cels. 5, 28, n 2; Plin. 24, 3, 3, § 7.—Plur. cacoëthe = κακοήθη, τά, Plin. 22, 25, 64, § 132; 24, 10, 47, § 78. —Hence

cacophonia.definition: κακός-φωνή A disagreeable sound formed by the meeting of syllables or words, cacophong, Mod. Lat.

cacozelia.definition: A bad, faulty, awkward imitation, Sen. Contr. 4, 24 fin.; id. Suas. 7; Quint. 2, 3, 9 (written as Greek, id. 8, 6, 73; cf. κακόζηλον; id. 8, 3, 56); cf. Diom. p. 446 P.

cacozelus.definition: căcŏzēlus, a, um A bad imitator (cf. cacozelia), * Suet. Aug. 86; Ascon. Cic. Caecil. 6, 21; cf. Quint. 8, 3, 56 sqq.

cactus.definition: A prickly plant with edible stalks, etc., found in Sicily, Spanish artichoke: Cynara cardunculus, Linn.; Plin. 21, 16, 57, § 97. Trop., any thing thorny, unpleasant: eradicato omni cacto et rubo subdolae familiaritatis,Tert. Pall. 2 fin.

cacula.definition: (cacula, Plaut. Ps. Arg. 2, 13 sq.), , Sanscr. cak-, to help; cf. calon; v. Paul. ex Fest. s. h. v. p. 45 Müll.; Fest. s. v. procalare, p. 225 ib. A servant, esp. the servant of a soldier: cacula = servus militis (militaris? cf. the passage foll., from Plaut.),Fest. p. 35: cacula δοῦλος στρατιώτου, Gloss.: video caculam militarem me futurum,Plaut. Trin. 3. 2, 98; so id. Ps. Arg. 4; and perh., acc. to the MSS., also Juv. 9, 61, where Jahn reads ...

cacumen.definition: etym. dub. The extreme end, extremity, or point of a thing; the peak, top, utmost point. Lit. (whether horizontal or perpendicular; while culmen is an extremity projecting in height; v. Doed. Syn.; in the poets freq.; in prose rare before the Aug. per.; not in Cic.): ut altis Arboribus vicina cacumina summa terantur Inter se,the extreme top,Lucr. 1, 898. —So of tree-tops: umbrosa cacumina,Verg. E. 2, 3: fracta,id. ib. 9, 9; 6, 28; id. G. 2, 29; 2...

cacumino.definition: căcūmĭno, āvi, ātum, 1, cacumen To point, make pointed (prob. formed by Ovid): summas cacuminat aures,Ov. M. 3, 195: saxoque cacuminat ensem,Sid. Carm. 7, 414: ova cacuminata,Plin. 10, 52, 74, § 145: apex in conum cacuminatus,Sid. Ep. 2, 2.

cacus.definition: Κᾶκος Son of Vulcan, contemporary with Evander, a giant of immense physical strength, who dwelt in a cave on Mount Aventinus, and troubled the whole region around by his robberies; he robbed even Hercules of the cattle of Geryon, and was on that account slain by him, Ov. F. 1, 543 sq.; Liv. 1, 7, 5 sq.; Verg. A. 8, 190 sq., and Serv. in h. l.; Prop. 4 (5), 9, 7; 4 (5), 9, 16; Col. 1, 3, 6; Juv. 5, 125; Sol. 1, §§ 7 and 18.

cadaver.definition: cado, I. B. 2.; cf. Isid. Orig. 11, 2, 35, and the Gr. πτῶμα, from πίπτω. Lit., a dead body of man or brute, a corpse, carcass (class.). Meton., the remains, ruins of desolated towns: tot oppidŭm cadavera, Sulp. ap. Cic. Fam. 4, 5, 4.

cadauer.definition: cado, I. B. 2.; cf. Isid. Orig. 11, 2, 35, and the Gr. πτῶμα, from πίπτω. Lit., a dead body of man or brute, a corpse, carcass (class.). Meton., the remains, ruins of desolated towns: tot oppidŭm cadavera, Sulp. ap. Cic. Fam. 4, 5, 4.

cadaverinus.definition: cădāvĕrīnus, a, um, cadaver Of carrion: nidores, Aug. Civ. Dei, 9, 16.— Hence, subst.: cădāvĕrīna, ae, f. (sc. caro), the flesh of a carcass, Tert. Anim. 32, 9.

cadauerinus.definition: cădāvĕrīnus, a, um, cadaver Of carrion: nidores, Aug. Civ. Dei, 9, 16.— Hence, subst.: cădāvĕrīna, ae, f. (sc. caro), the flesh of a carcass, Tert. Anim. 32, 9.

cadialis.definition: cădĭālis, e, cadus Of or pertaining to a jar: resina,contained in it,Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 7, 108.

cadmia.definition: (, Paul. ex Fest. p. 47, 10 Müll.), , , = καδμεία or καδμία An ore of zinc, calamine, cadmia, Plin. 34, 1, 2, § 2; 34, 10, 22, § 100; Paul. ex Fest. l. l.; Isid. Orig. 16, 20, 2 and 11. The dross or slag formed in a furnace, Plin. 34, 10, 22. § 100 sq.; Isid. Orig. 16, 20, 12.

cado.definition: cădo, cĕcĭdi, cāsum, 3 ( Part. pres. gen. plur. cadentūm, Verg. A. 10, 674; 12, 410), v. n. cf. Sanscr. çad-, to fall away. Lit. Trop.

caducarius.definition: cădūcārĭus, a, um, caducus Relating to property without a master: lex Julia (introduced by Augustus), Ulp. Lib. Regul. § 28. Epileptic: homines, Aug. Vit. Beat. med.

caduceator.definition: caduceum. A herald, an officer sent with a flag of truce: caduceatores = legati pacem petentes. Cato caduceatori, inquit, nemo homo nocet, Paul. ex Fest. p. 47: bellantes ac dissidentes interpretum oratione sedantur, unde secundum Livium legati pacis caduceatores appellantur,Serv. ad Verg. A. 4, 242; Liv. 26, 17, 5; 31, 38, 9; 32, 32, 5; 37, 45, 4; 44, 46, 1; Curt. 3, 1, 6; 4, 2, 15 al. A servant to a priest, Arn. 5, p. 174.

caduceum.definition: n. (sc. sceptrum or baculum), or , , m. (sc. scipio or baculus; which form was predominant in the class. per. is doubtful, since neither Cicero, Nepos, Livy, nor Pliny uses the word in the nom.) [kindr. with κηρύκειον, Aeolic καρύκιον, —ῦ—, r changed to d, as ad = ar] A herald's staff, the token of a peaceable embassy (orig. an olive- stick, with στέμματα, which afterwards were formed into serpents, O. Müll. Archaeol. § 379, 3): caduceus paci...

caducus.definition: cădūcus, a, um, adj.cado. That falls or has fallen, falling, fallen (mostly poet.): bacae glandesque caducae, * Lucr. 5, 1362; cf. Dig. 50, 16, 30: glans caduca est, quae ex arbore cecidit: oleae,Cato, R. R. 23, 2: spica,that fell in mowing,Varr. R. R. 2, 2, 12: aqua,id. ib. 3, 5, 2: aquae,Ov. P. 2, 7, 39: frondes,Verg. G. 1, 368: frons,Ov. M. 7, 840; id. Tr. 3, 1, 45: folia,id. Am. 2, 16, 45: lacrimae,id. M. 6, 396: poma,Prop. 2, 32, 40: oliva,C...

cadus.definition: ( Gen. plur. cadūm, v. II. infra), m., = κάδος [Slav. kad, kadĭ; Serv. kada; Magyar, kád; Rouman. Kadŭ]. Lit., a large vessel for containing liquids, esp. wine; a bottle, jar, jug; mostly of earthen-ware, but sometimes of stone, Plin. 36, 22, 43, § 158; or even of metal, Verg. A. 6, 228. Transf., a measure for liquids (in this sense, gen. plur. cadum, Lucil. and Varr. ap. Non. p. 544, 13 and 16; Plin. 14, 14, 17, § 96); syn. with amphora Attica ...

caecator.definition: caeco, prop. one who makes blind, hence He who stops or obstructs a fountain, Paul. Nol. Carm. Nat. S. Fel. 24, 9, 618 (with ref. to Genes. 26, 15).

caecitas.definition: caecus Blindness. Lit. (rare but in good prose), Cic. Tusc. 5, 39, 113; 5, 38, 111; id. Fin. 5, 28, 84; Plin. 11, 37, 55, § 149; 12, 8, 18, § 34. Trop.: furorem autem esse rati sunt mentis ad omnia caecitatem,Cic. Tusc. 3, 5, 11: in furore animi et caecitate,id. Dom. 50, 129: mentis,id. ib. 40, 105; cf.: an tibi luminis obesset caecitas plus quam libidinis,id. Har. Resp. 18, 38.

caeco.definition: caeco, āvi, ātum, 1, id. To make blind, to blind. Lit.: sol caecat,Lucr. 4, 325 (300); Paul. Nol. Carm. Nat. S. Fel. 20, 7; 20, 292: unde caecatus est (Appius Claudius),Aur. Vict. Vir. Ill. 34, 3.—Hence, in gardening: oculum,to destroy,Col. 4, 9, 2; 4, 24, 16; cf. caecus, I. C., and oculus. Transf., to make dark, to obscure: caecantur silvae,Avien. Per. 504.

caeculto.definition: caeculto, āre, contr for caeculĭto, from caecus, as ausculto for ausculito, from auris To be like one blind, to be dim-sighted: caecultare est caecos imitari, Paul. ex Fest. p. 45 Müll.: caeculto άμβλυώττω, Gloss.; Plautus: numnam mihi oculi caecultant? Paul. ex Fest. p. 62 Müll.; cf. caecutio.

caecus.definition: caecus (not coecus; sometimes in MSS. cēcus), a, um, adj. akin to σκιά, σκότος; Sanscr. khāyā, shadow Having no light, devoid of light. Act., not seeing, blind. Pass., that cannot be seen, or trop., that cannot be known, invisible, concealed, hidden, secret, obscure, dark.

caecutio.definition: caecūtĭo, īre (no Perf.), from caecus, like balbutio from balbus, to be blind, to see badly (ante- and post-class.), Varr. ap. Non. p. 35, 4: omnes quodammodo caecutimus, App. Flor. n. 2: utrum oculi mihi caecutiunt, Varr. ap. Non. p. 86, 12; Mart. Cap. 1, § 3.

caedes.definition: ( Gen. plur. regularly caedium, Liv. 1, 13, 3; Just. 11, 13, 9; Flor. 3, 18, 14 al.; but caedum,Sil. 2, 665; 4, 353; 4, 423; 4, 796; 5, 220; 10, 233; Amm. 22, 12, 1; 29, 5, 27; cf. Prisc. p. 771 P), f. caedo. Lit. Meton.

caedo.definition: caedo, cĕcīdi (in MSS. freq. caecīdi, v. Neue, Formenl. 2, 460), caesum, 3, v. a. root cīd- for scid-; cf. scindo; Gr. σχίζω. Lit. Trop.: caedere sermones, a Grecism, acc. to Prisc. 18, p. 1118 P., = κόπτειν τὰ ῥήματα, to chop words, chat, talk, converse, Ter. Heaut. 2, 3, 1; cf. Non. p. 272, 13, and Prisc. p. 1188 P.: oratio caesa,i. e. asyndeton,Auct. Her. 4, 19, 26; Aquil. Rom. §§ 18 and 19; Mart. Cap. 5; § 528.—Hence, caesum, i, n.; subs...

caeduus.definition: caeduus, a, um Adj [caedo], that can be cut without injury, fit for cutting; a t. t. of agriculture, Dig. 50, 16, 30: silva,Cato, R. R. 1 fin.; Varr. R. R. 1, 7, 9; Col. 3, 3, 1; cf. natura,Plin. 12, 19, 42, § 89: fertilitas,id. 16, 37, 68, § 175; 17, 20, 32, § 141; 17, 20, 34, § 147.

caelamen.definition: caelo A basso-relievo (prob. formed by Ovid; rare): clipei caelamina,Ov. M. 13, 291; App. Flor, n. 7; id. de Deo Socr. p 40, 30 Elm.

caelator.definition: caelo An artisan in basso-relievo, a carver, engraver, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 24, § 54; 2, 4, 27, § 63; Quint. 2, 21, 24: argenti caelatores,Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 85: curvus,Juv. 9, 145; Tert. Idol. 3; Inscr Grut. 583, 5 al.

caelatura.definition: id. The art of engraving or carving bass-reliefs in metals and ivory, engraving, celature. Lit.: caelatura, quae auro, argento, aere, ferro opera efficit: nam sculptura etiam lignum, ebur, marmor, vitrum, gemmas, praeterea quae supra dixi, complectitur,Quint. 2, 21, 8: caelatura altior,id. 2, 4, 7; Plin. 35, 12, 45, § 156. Meton. (abstr. pro concreto), the engraved figures themselves, carved work, Suet. Ner. 47: usque adeo attritis caelaturis, ne...

caelebs.definition: caelebs (not coelebs), lĭbis, etym. dub. Unmarried, single (whether of a bachelor or a widower) Lit.: (censores) equitum peditumque prolem describunto: caelibes esse prohibento,Cic. Leg. 3, 3, 7; Plaut. Cas. 2, 4, 11; Quint. 5, 10, 26; Suet. Galb. 5 Baumg.-Crus.: caelebs senex,Plaut. Stich. 4, 1, 37: caelebs quid agam Martiis Calendis,Hor. C. 3, 8, 1; id. S. 2, 5, 47; Ov. M. 10, 245; Mart. 12, 63; Gai Inst. 2, 286; Tac. H. 1, 13; id. A. 3, 34. Tr...

caeles.definition: caelĕs (coel-), ĭtis, caelum; v Corss. Ausspr. II. p. 210 Heavenly, celestial (poet.; access. form of caelestis, but not found in nom. sing.): di caelites. Enn. ap Cic. Div. 2, 50, 104 (Trag. Rel. v. 353 Vahl.): agricolae ( = ruris dei),Tib. 2, 1, 36: Venus (opp. vulgaris),App. Mag. p. 281, 14: regna,Ov. F. 1, 236: sub caelite mensa,Paul. Nol. Carm. 24, 9 al.—Esp. freq. subst.: caelĭ-tes, the inhabitants of heaven, the gods, Enn. ap. Varr. L. L. ...

caelestis.definition: caelestis (coel-), e ( Gen. sing. CAELESTAE, Inscr. Neapol. 2602; abl. sing. regularly, caelesti: caeleste,Ov. H. 16, 277; id. M. 15, 743; cf.: bimestris, cognominis, perennis, patruelis, etc.; gen. plur. caelestum, but caelestium, Enn. Epigr. v. 9 Vahl.; Att. ap. Cic. N. D. 3, 26, 68, or id. Trag. Rel. v. 209 Rib.; Varr. L. L. 6, § 53 Müll.; Lucr. 6, 1274; Cat. 64, 191; 64, 205; Verg. A. 7, 432; Ov. M. 1, 150), adj. caelum, pertaining to heaven ...

caelibatus.definition: (), , caelebs Celibacy, single life (severely punished by the leges Julia and Papia Poppaea; only post-Aug.),Sen. Ben. 1, 9, 4; Suet. Claud. 16; 26; id. Galb. 5; Gai Inst. 2, 144.

caelicola.definition: caelĭcŏla (coel-), ae ( Gen. plur. caelicolūm, Enn. ap. Prisc. p. 1103 P., or Ann. v 483 Vahl.; Verg. A. 3, 21; Prud. Sym. 1, 170: caelicolarum,Juv. 13, 42), caelumcolo. Dwelling in heaven, poet. designation of a deity, a god, Enn. l. l.; Verg. A. 2, 641; 6, 554; 6, 787; Ov. M. 1, 174; 8, 637; Val. Fl. 5, 111; App. de Deo Socr. 6. A worshipper of the heavens, Cod. Th. 16, 5, 43; 16, 8, 19; Cod. Just. 1, 9; cf. Juv. 14, 97.

caelicus.definition: caelĭcus (coel-), a, um, caelum, = caelestis, II. B. Celestial, magnificent (very rare): tecta,Stat. S.2, 3, 14; Mart. Cap 9, § 891; Paul. Nol. Nom. Christ. 64.

caelifluus.definition: caelĭflŭus (coel-), a, um, caelum -fluo Flowing from heaven: fontes,Paul. Nol. Nat. S. Fel. 12, 780.

caeligenus.definition: caelĭgĕnus (coel-), a, um, caelum-gigno Heaven-born: Victoria et Venus,Varr. L. L. 5, § 62 Müll.: stellae, App. de Mundo, p. 57, 29.

caelipotens.definition: caelĭ-pŏtens (coel-), entis Adj. m. [caelum], powerful in heaven: di,Plaut. Pers. 5, 1, 3.

caelitus.definition: caelĭtus (coel-), caelum. From heaven (late Lat. for divinitus or caelo) omnia quae caelitus mortalibus exhibentur, App. Dogm. Plat. 1, p. 8, 31; Lact. 4, 2 fin.; 4, 28; Amm. 23, 6, 34. Transf., from the emperor, Cod. Th. 6, 32, 2; 10, 20, 16.

caelo.definition: caelo, āvi, ātum, 1, 1. caelum. Lit., answering to the Gr. τορεύω, to engrave in relief upon metals (esp. silver) or wory, to make raised work, to carve, engrave; later also, to cast (cf. O. Müll. Archaeol. § 311 sq.; and v. Quint. 2, 21, 8, s. v. caelatura; Fest. s. v. ancaesa, p. 17; Isid. Orig. 13, 4, 1; 19, 7, 4; 20, 4, 7)' ab initio sic opus ducere, ut caelandum, non ex integro fabricandum sit, Quint. 10, 3, 18: hanc speciem Praxiteles cael...

caelum.definition: (, Serv. ad Verg. A. 1, 640), , caedo The chisel or burin of the sculptor or engraver, a graver: caelata vasa... a caelo vocata, quod est genus ferramenti, quem vulgo cilionem vocant,Isid. Orig. 20, 4, 7; Quint. 2, 21, 24; Varr. ap. Non. p. 99, 18; Stat. S. 4, 6, 26; Mart. 6, 13, 1.— Plur., Aus. Epigr. 57, 6.

caelus.definition: caelus, i, v. caelum Init. and I. 2.

caementicius.definition: caementīcĭus (-tītĭus), a, um, id. Of or pertaining to quarried stones, consisting of them: structurae,Vitr. 2, 4: parietes,id. 2, 8 med.: saxum unhewn, quarry-stone (opp quadratum), id. ib.

caementum.definition: n. (access. form , , f., like armenta, ae, to armentum, Enn. ap. Non. p. 196, 30, or Trag. v. 422 Vahl.; v 373 Rib.) [contr. from caedimentum, from caedo; hence Engl. cement]. A rough, unhewn stone, as it comes from the quarry, a quarry-stone, used for walls. Caementa marmorea, pieces that fly off from marble in working, chips of marble: caementa marmorea, sive assulae,Vitr. 7, 6, 1.

caena.definition: caena and its derivv., v. cena, etc.

caenositas.definition: caenŏsĭtas (coen-), ătis F [caenosus], a dirty place; only trop., Fulg. Cont. Virg. p. 156 Munk.

caenosus.definition: caenōsus (coen-), a, um, caenum Muddy, dirty, foul, marshy (rare): lacus. Col. 7, 10, 6: gurges (i. e. Styx),Juv. 3, 266.—Comp.: caenosior liquor,Sol. 49 fin. Trop.: impuritas, Salv. Gub. Dei, 3, 10.

caenulentus.definition: caenŭlentus (coen-), a, um, id. Covered with mud, muddy, filthy: pedes,Tert. Pall. 4.

caenum.definition: (less correctly ), , cunio Dirt, filth, mud, mire (always with access. idea of loathsomeness, diff. from limus, lutum, etc.: omnes stultos insanire, ut male olere omne caenum,Cic. Tusc. 4, 24, 54; freq. and class. in prose and poetry); prop.: pulchrum ornatum turpes mores pejus caeno collinunt,Plaut. Most. 1, 3, 133; cf. id. Poen. 1, 2, 93; 4, 2, 4; Cic. Att. 2, 21, 4; Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 68, § 173; Lucr. 6, 977; Verg. G. 4, 49; id. A. 6, 296; Ov. M...

caepa.definition: (also ), , f., and equally freq. (), , n. ( Gen. caepis, Charis. p. 43 P., without voucher, but the assertion of the gram. Diom. p. 314 ib.; Prisc. p. 681 ib.; Phocae Ars, p. 1706 ib., and Serg. p. 1842 ib., that caepe is indecl., is also unsubstantiated, since the form of the gen. caepe cited by Prisc. l. l. from App. is the well-known later orthog. for caepae; v. Neue, Formenl. 1, 551; 1, 557 sq.; 1, 578; in plur. only caepae or , f.; cf. Don. ...

caeparia.definition: . , caepa A disease in the privy members, Marc. Emp. 33.

caerefolium.definition: (, Col. 10, 110), χαιρέφυλλον, whence the Fr. cerfeuil, and Germ. Kerbel Chervil, Plin. 19, 8, 54, § 170; Pall. Febr. 24, 9; id. Sept. 13, 3; App. Herb. 104.

caerimonia.definition: (; scanned cĕrīmōnĭa, Prud. c. Symm. praef. 1, 5), , f. (collat. form , , n., Gloss. Lat. pp. 50, 69 Hild.; Inscr. Orell. 3188) [kindr. with Sanscr. root kri, = facere; cf. also creo. cerus, Ceres. strictly sacred work, divine rite; cf. Bopp, Gloss. p. 79, a; Pott, I. p. 219; Mommsen, Unterit. Dial.] The sacred. the divine, that which has reference to the Deity (in class. prose) Lit. Meton. (abstr. pro concr.), a religious usage, a sacred rite, r...

caerimonialis.definition: caerĭmōnĭālis, e, caerimonia Pertaining to religious rites, ceremonial; officia. Arn. 7, p. 237.

caerimonior.definition: caerĭmōnior, āri, 1 Dep. a. [id.], to treat with due ceremony, to worship, Aug. Serm. 309; Act. St. Cypr. 3.

caerimoniosus.definition: caerĭmōnĭōsus, a, um. id. Per taining or devoted to religious rites' dies. Amm. 22, 15, 17.

caeruleus.definition: caerŭlĕus, and in poetry equally common, caerŭlus, a, um, cf. cae -sius, κύανος, and Sanscr. cjamas = dark Lit., dark-colored, dark blue, dark green, cerulean, azure, κυάνεος; poet. epithet of the sky, of the sea, and other similar objects (as dark, opp. albus and marmoreus color, Lucr. 2, 771 sq., and syn. with ater, Verg. A. 3, 64; v. under II. A.). Transf.

caesa.definition: caedo (only in the milit. lang. of Veget.) A cut, Veg. Mil. 1, 12.

caesar.definition: Caesar, ăris (CAESERIS, C. I. L. 4, 2308; Inscr. Orell. 4205: CAESARVS, C. I. L. 1, 696), m., = Καῖσαρ [a caeso matris utero, Plin. 7, 9, 7, § 47; cf. Non. p. 556, 32: A caesarie dictus, qui scilicet cum caesarie natus est,Fest. p. 44; cf. Comment. p. 383. Both etymm. also in Isid. Orig. 9, 3, 12, and Spart. Ael. Ver. 2. Better acc. to Doed. Syn. III. p. 17, from caesius, caeruleus, the color of the skin; cf. Rufus], a cognomen in the gens Julia...

caesareus.definition: Caesărĕus, a, um, v. Caesar, II. C.

caesariatus.definition: caesărĭātus, a, um, caesaries (very rare). Covered with hair, having long hair: caesariati comati,Fest. p. 35: miles usque caesariatus,Plaut. Mil. 3, 1, 171: Numidae equis caesariati,i. e. with helmets ornamented with horse-hair,Tert. Pall. 4.—* Trop., ornamented with foliage or leaves: terra, App. de Mundo, p. 67, 37; cf. coma.

caesaries.definition: kindr. with Sanscr. kēsa, coma, caesaries, Bopp, Gloss. p. 85, a A dark (acc. to Rom. taste, beautiful) head of hair, the hair (mostly poet.; only sing.). Barbae, the hair of the beard (very rare), Ov M. 15, 656.

caesim.definition: caesīm, caedo By cutting, with cuts. Lit. Trop., of discourse, in short clauses: membratim adhuc, deinde caesim diximus,Cic. Or. 67, 225 (cf. the same, and § 223, incisim aut membratim); Quint. 9, 4, 126; cf. id. 11, 3, 102 Spald. N. cr

caesitas.definition: caesius Blue, blueness: oculorum, Boëth. ap. Porphyr. Dial. 2, p. 31; id. ap. Aristot. Categ. 3, p. 176.

caesius.definition: caesĭus, a, um, cf. caeruleus Bluish gray; very rare, and only of the eyes, cat-eyed: virgo caesia, Ter Heaut. 5, 5, 18; v. Don. in h. l. and Gell. 2, 26, 19: isto modo dicere licebit caesios oculos Minervae, caeruleos esse Neptuni,Cic. N. D. 1, 30, 83 (cf. in Gr. γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη): caesia, Παλλάδιον, has she gray eyes? she is the impersonation of Pallas, * Lucr. 4, 1161: caesius, Ter Hec. 3, 4, 26 (glaucis oculis, quasi felis oculos habens et...

caeso.definition: ( V. the letter K), , m.a caeso matris utero dictus, Plin. 7, 9, 7, § 47; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 57 Müll.; Isid. Orig. 9, 3, 12, and v. Caesar init., a Roman cognomen in the gens Fabia, Liv. 2, 43, 2; 2, 48, 3 and 4; 3, 11, 6 sq. et saep.

caesor.definition: caedo One who hews something (post-class.): lignorum caesores,hewers of wood,Hier. Ep. 53, n. 6, after the Vulg. Deut. 29, 11: lapidum,stone-breaker,Ambros. Luc. 2, 89 fin.; Vulg. 2 Par. 24, 12; cf. Val. Prob. II. p. 1458 P

caespes.definition: (not ), , caesus, caedo. A turf, sod as cut out: caespes est terra in modum lateris caesa cum herba, sive frutex recisus et truncus, Paul. ex Fest. p. 45 Müll.: caespes χορτόπλινθος, χορτόβωλος, πλίνθος, Gloss.: non esse arma caespites, neque glebas, * Cic. Caecin. 21, 60.— Used for altars, mounds (of tombs), for covering cottages, huts, etc.,Hor. C. 1, 19, 13; Ov. Tr. 5, 5, 9; id. M. 4, 753; 7, 240; 15, 573; Verg. A. 3, 304; Tac. G. 27; id. A...

caespiticius.definition: caespĭtĭcĭus, a, um, caespes Made of turf (post-class.): tribunal,Vop. Prob. 10: murus, Capitol. Anton. Pius, 5.

caesposus.definition: caespōsus, a, um, id. Abounding in turf or grass: litus,Col. 10, 130.

caestus.definition: (not ), , ( Dat. plur. caestis, Varr. ap. Non. p. 492, 11) [caedo], a strap of bull's hide loaded with balls of lead or iron, wound around the hands and arms, a gauntlet, boxing-glove for pugilists (pugiles), Cic. Tusc. 2, 17, 40; Verg. A. 5, 69; 5, 379; 5, 479; Prop. 3 (4), 14, 9; Ov. F. 2, 367; Tac. A. 14, 20; Stat. Th. 6, 764; 6, 829; Val. Fl. 4, 251; Plin. 11, 37, 45, § 124; Sen. Med. 89; cf. Fest. p. 35; Dict. of Antiq.

caesura.definition: caedo A cutting, felling, hewing, hewing off ligni, Plin. 16, 43, 84, § 230; silvae,id. 17, 20, 34, § 151 In metre, a pause in a verse, coesura; called also incisio, Diom. p. 496 P.; Bed. Metr. p. 2368 ib.

caesuratim.definition: caesūrātim, caesura With pauses in short clauses (for the class. caesim): dictio caesuratim succincta,Sid. Ep. 4, 3.

caesus.definition: caesus, a, um, Part., v. caedo.

caeterus.definition: caetĕrus, a, um, with its derivatives; v ceter.

caetra.definition: (better than ), , prob. Spanish A short Spanish shield, Verg. A. 7, 732 Serv.; Liv. 21, 27, 5; 28, 5, 11; Plin. 11, 39, 93, § 227; Tac. Agr. 36; Suet, Calig 19; Luc. 7, 232; Sil. 3, 278; 3, 348 al.— Prov.: quis rotundam facere cetram nequeat? Varr. ap. Non. p. 82, 18.

caetratus.definition: caetrātus, a, um, caetra Armed with a caetra, shield-bearing ( = πελταστής): cohors,Caes. B. C. 1, 39; so Liv. 31, 36, 1: juventus,Sil. 9, 231; and subst.: caetrā-ti, ōrum, Caes. B. C. 1, 70; Liv. 31, 36, 1; 33, 4, 4 et saep.

caiatio.definition: caio A striking, a cudgelling or beating of children, Fulg. Cont. Virg. p. 162 Munck.

caio.definition: cāio, āre To beat, cudgel, Fulg. Cont. Virg.

calamellus.definition: dim.id. A little reed (late Lat.), Arn. in Psa. 150.

calamister.definition: m. (ante- and postclass.; nom. not found; also , , n., Plaut. Curc. 4, 4, 21; Varr. L. L. 5, § 129 Müll.; Non. p. 546, 16; Serv. ad Verg. A. 12, 100; Isid. Orig. 20, 13, 4. Plur.: calamistra, Varr. ap. Charis. p. 61 P.) [calamus], a hollow, tubular iron for curling the hair, a curling-iron, crisping-pin. Lit.: calamistrum quod his calfactis in cinere capillus ornatur, Varr. L. L. l. l.; Serv. l. l.; cf. Isid. Orig. l. l.; 10, 57: meum, Plaut. Cur...

calamistratus.definition: călămistrātus, a, um, calamister Curled with the curling-iron, crisped, curled (of men, a reproach for effeminacy; cf. Serv. ad Verg. A. 12, 100): cinaedus,Plaut. As. 3, 3, 37: coma,Cic. Sest. 8, 18: saltator,id. post Red. in Sen. 6, 13.—Of fops: pueri cincinnatuli et calamistrati,Hier. Ep. 130, 19; so Ambros. Ep. 4, 15.

calamitas.definition: cf. in columis. Lit., loss, injury, damage, mischief, harm: sed ecca ipsa egreditur, nostri fundi calamitas (Ter. Eun. 1, 1, 34). Proprie calamitatem rustici grandinem dicunt, Don.; cf. the same on Ter Heaut. 2, 4, 15: robigo genus est vitii, quo culmi pereunt, quod a rusticanis calamitas dicitur, Serv ad Verg. G. 1, 151: postquam calamitas plures annos arvas calvitur, Pac. ap. Non. p. 192, 30; Plaut. Cas. 5, 2, 34; id. Capt. 4, 3, 4: non ut lega...

calamitosus.definition: călămĭtōsus, a, um, calamitas. Act., that causes great damage or loss, ruinous, destructive. Pass., suffering great damage, exposed to injury, unfortunate, miserable, unhappy.

calamus.definition: . Lit., a reed, cane (pure Lat. harundo; cf. canna),Plin. 16, 36, 65, § 159 sq.; 16, 21, 33, § 80; Col. 3, 15, 1; 4, 4, 1; Pall. Nov. 22, 3 al.: aromaticus (found in Syria and Arabia),sweet calamus,Col. 12, 52, 2: odoratus,Plin. 12, 22, 48, § 104; Veg. 6, 13, 3.—Also absol.: calamus,Cato, R. R. 105, 2; Plin. 13, 1, 2, § 8 sq.: Syriacus,Veg. 4, 13, 4. Meton.

calathiscus.definition: A small wicker basket: virgati calathisci,Cat. 64, 319; Petr. 41, 6 Burm.

calathus.definition: . Lit., a wicker basket, a hand-basket (pure Lat. quasillum, made in the shape of a lily); acc. to diff. uses, a flower-basket, a wool-basket, a thread-basket or a fruit-basket, etc.; cf. Plin. 21, 5, 11, § 23; Vitr. 4, 1, 9; Verg. E. 2, 46; Ov. F. 4, 435: calathi Minervae,Verg. A. 7, 805; Ov. A. A. 2, 219; id. H. 9, 73; 9, 76; Juv. 2, 54; Ov. A. A. 2, 264; id. M. 12, 475. Meton., any other vessel of similar form, of metal or wood.

calator.definition: id.; a servant for calling, etc., a crier; hence Lit., a servant, esp. of priests, Suet. Gram. 12; cf. Serv. ad Verg. G. 1, 268; Inscr. Orell. 2431 sqq.; so freq. in inscriptions. In gen., any servant, attendant; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 38 and 225 Müll.: egomet mihi comes, calator, equus, agaso, armiger,Plaut. Merc. 5, 2, 11; id. Ps. 4, 2, 52; id. Rud. 2, 3, 5.

calatorius.definition: călātōrĭus, a, um, calator Relating to priests' servants, Inscr. Fabr. p. 449, n. 58.

calautica.definition: (in many MSS. and edd. erroneously ), , of uncer.tain etym.; acc. to Beier, Cic. Clod. et Cur. 5, p. 107, perh. kindr. with καλύπτω, as auris, through the Cretan form αὖς, with οὖς A covering for the head of women, which fell down over the shoulders (perh. a kind of veil): calautica est tegmen muliebre, quod capiti innectitur,Non. p. 537, 2 sq.: mitrae, semimitrae, calautica, etc.; cf. Mai and Orell. in h. l. (Orell. Cic. V. 2, p. 336); Cic....

calcar.definition: for carcar; cf. Sanscr. kar, wound; and Lat. calx. Lit., a spur as worn on the heel: calcaria dicta, quia in calce hominis ligantur, ad stimulandos equos,Isid.
