careor.definition: cărĕor, ēri Dep. collat. form of careo in old writers, acc. to Prisc. p. 797 P.

caresco.definition: căresco, ĕre V. inch. n. [careo], to want, στέρομαι, Gloss. Philox.

careum.definition: Cumin, caraway: Carum carvi, Linn.; Col. 12, 51, 2 Schneid. N. cr.; Plin. 19, 8, 49, § 164; Dig. 33, 9, 5 al.

carex.definition: Reed-grass, rush, or sedge, Verg. G. 3, 231; Cat. 19, 2; Col. 11, 2, 62; Pall. 1, 22.

carians.definition: cărĭans, antis, caries Defective, decayed, rotten: tripus,Mart. Cap. 1, § 10.

caries.definition: (other cases appear not to be in use) Decay, caries (prop. of a hard, dry decay, not of rottenness); of wood, Varr. ap. Non. p. 83, 12; Vitr. 7, 3; Col. 11, 2; Plin. 16, 39, 74, § 188; 16, 39, 76, § 197; 16, 40, 78, § 212; Ov. Tr. 5, 12, 27.— Of walls,Amm. 16, 2, 1.—Of bones, Lucil. ap. Non. p. 21, 24; Cels. 8, 2.—Of dry soil, Col. 3, 11.—Of the taste of old wine, flatness, Col. 3, 2, 17; Plin. 15, 2, 3, § 7; 23, 1, 22, § 40; 14, 4, 6, § 55.—Of o...

carina.definition: cf. κάρυον, cornu. The keel of a ship, Plaut. Mil. 3, 3, 42; Caes. B. G. 3, 13; id. B. C. 1, 54; Liv. 22, 20, 2; 28, 8, 14; Tac. A. 2, 6; Curt. 7, 3, 9; 10, 1, 19; Ov. M. 14, 552; id. P. 4, 3, 5.—In the poets very freq. (in Ovid's Met. alone about thirty times). Meton.

carino.definition: cārĭno, āre, for scarinare, root in scortum To abuse, revile, blame ( = irrideo), Enn. Ann. 181; 229 Vahl.; cf. Serv. ad Verg. A. 8, 361, and Paul. ex Fest. p. 47 Müll.: carinantes = illudentes, Gloss. Isid.

cariosus.definition: cărĭōsus, a, um, adj.caries Decayed, rotten. Prop.: palmula,Varr. R. R. 1, 67: terra,too loose, porous,Cato, R. R. 5, 6; 34, 1; 37, 1. Cato's expression, terra cariosa, is explained by Pliny as meaning: arida, fistulosa, scabra, canens. exesa, pumicosa,Plin. 17, 5, 3, § 34; but better by Col. 2, 4, 5, as = varia, i. e. wet on the surface and dry below:—os, Cels. 8, 2: dentes,Phaedr. 5, 10, 5; Plin. 32, 7, 26, § 82: vina,flat,Mart. 13, 120: amphor...

caritas.definition: carus. Prop., dearness, costliness, high price, etc. (opp. vilitas): annonae,Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 18, § 47; 2, 3, 92, § 215; id. Off. 3, 12, 50; Liv. 44, 7, 10; Suet. Ner. 45: rei frumentariae (opp. vilitas annonae),Cic. Imp. Pomp. 15, 44: nummorum,id. Att. 9, 9, 4: olei,Plin. 18, 28, 68, § 273: vini,Suet. Aug. 42.—Also absol. caritas (sc. annonae), high prices, Cato, R. R. 3: ut tum vendas cum caritas est,Varr. R. R. 1, 69: cum alter annus in vilita...

caritores.definition: cārĭtōres1. caro Wool - carders, Gloss. Papiae.

carmelus.definition: Κάρμηλος. Mount Carmel, a high, steep mountain in Phoenicia, on the sea-coast, now Karmel or Karmul; also the town on, and the god of, this mountain, Tac. H. 2, 78; Suet. Vesp. 5: Carmelum promontorium et oppidum,Plin. 5, 19, 17, § 75.—Also called , Vulg. Isa. 29, 17. A small town in Judoea, with a mountain of the same name, near the Dead Sea, Vulg. Josh. 15, 55; id. 1 Reg. 15, 12; 25, 2 al.—Hence, , , , an inhabitant of Mount Carmel, a Carmelit...

carmen.definition: (old form , Varr. L. L. p. 86 Bip.) [Sanscr. çasto declaim, praise; cf.: camilla, censeo] A tune, song; poem, verse; an oracular response, a prophecy; a form of incantation (cf.: cano, cantus, and canto). In gen., a tune, song, air, lay, strain, note, sound, both vocal and instrumental (mostly poet.; in prose, instead of it, cantus; cf. also versus, numeri, modi): carmen tuba ista peregit ( = sonus),Enn. Ann. 508 Vahl.: carmine vocali clarus cith...

carmino.definition: carmĭno, āre, 1. carmen To make verses (post-class.): votivum quippiam,Sid. Ep. 1, 9: verba Graia,id. ib. 9, 15.

carnalis.definition: carnālis, e, 2. caro Fleshly, carnal (opp. to spiritalis; eccl. Lat.): delicta,Tert. Poen. 3: oculi,Min. Fel. Oct. 32: stirps,Prud. Apoth. 1051.—Subst.: carnālĭa, um, n., carnal things (opp. spiritalia), Lact. 4, 17, 21.—Adv.: carnālĭter, carnally, Tert. Bapt. 7 fin.; Hier. Ep. 54, n. 9; Prud. Apoth. 436.

carnalitas.definition: carnalis Fleshli ness, carnality (eccl. Lat.), Aug. Serm. 186; id. Temp. 2.

carnarius.definition: carnārĭus, a, um, 2. caro Of or belonging to flesh; subst. Carnārĭus, ii, m. Car-nārĭum, ii, n.

carnatio.definition: id. Fleshiness, corpulency, Cael. Aur. Tard. 1, 4, 113.

carnatus.definition: carnātus, a, um, id. Fleshy, fat, corpulent, Cael. Aur. Tard. 1, 4, 95.

carneus.definition: carnĕus, a, um, 2. caro Of flesh (post-class.). Prop.: tunica,Aug. Serm. 344: membra, Maximian. Gall. 1, 85. Trop., carnal (opp. spiritalis): lex,Prud. Apoth. 370.

carnicula.definition: dim.2. caro Flesh, Prisc. p. 684 P.

carnifex.definition: carnĭfex or carnŭfex, fĭcis, m. v. caro-facio An executioner, hangman, Plaut Bacch. 4, 4, 37; id. Capt. 5, 4, 22; id. Rud. 3, 6, 19; Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 45, § 118; id. Phil. 11, 3, 7; id. Quint. 15, 50; id. Rab. Perd. 4, 12; Quint. 5, 10, 59; Lucr. 3, 1017; Cat. 97, 12; Juv. 8, 175 al.; this office was considered so disgraceful that he was not permitted to live in the city, Cic. Rab. Perd. 4 sq.; but in the Subura, Mart. 2, 17, 1 sqq. Trop., torment...

carnificina.definition: (), ae. carnifex. The office of executioner or hangman; capital punishment, execution: carnificinam facere = carnificem esse,Plaut. Capt. 1, 2, 23; cf. id. Cist. 2, 1, 1: locus carnificinae,Suet. Tib. 62.—Hence Per meton., the rack, torture, torment: dolores atque carnificinas facere, Cato ap. Gell. 10, 3, 17; and ap. Non. p. 187, 30; so, carnificinam subire,Cic. Tusc. 5, 27, 78: in ergastulum et carnificinam duci,Liv. 2, 23, 6.

carnifico.definition: carnĭfĭco (carnŭf-), ātus, āre, v. a. (carnĭfĭcor, āri, v. dep., acc. to Prisc. p. 791 P.) [id.] To execute, behead: carnifical. (hostes) jacentes,to be cut in pieces, mangled,Liv. 24, 15, 5: vitam cum dolore et insigni cruciatu carnificatus amisit, Sisenn. ap. Prisc. p. 793 P.; Tert. adv. Marc. 1, 2.

carnosus.definition: carnōsus, a, um, 2. caro Abounding in flesh, fleshy.

carnulentus.definition: carnŭlentus, a, um, id. Like flesh (post-class.): tactus,Sol. 2, 41: pectora, Prud. στεφ. 10, 372.

carnutes.definition: Καρνοῦτοι A people in Gaul, on both sides of the Liger, whose chief town was Autricum, now Chartres, in the Départ. d'Eure et Loire, Caes. B. G. 2, 35; 5, 25; 5, 56; 6, 2; 6, 4; 7, 2; 8, 31; ap. Tib. 1, 7, 12.—Adj.: , , of or belonging to the Carnutes, Sulp. Sev. Dial. 3, 2 al.—As subst.: , , , = Carnutes, Plin. 4, 18, 32, § 107 Jan.

caro.definition: cāro, ĕre, cf. Gr. κείρω; Germ. scheren; Engl. sheer To card (very rare), Plaut. Men. 5, 2, 46; and in Naev. acc. to Varr. L. L. 7, § 54 Müll., p. 92 Bip. (cf.: caritores, 2. carmen, 2. carmino, etc.).

carpasum.definition: κάρπασον A plant with narcotic juice, Dig. 39, 4, 16, § 7; Col. 10, 17; the same, called , Plin. 32, 5, 20, § 58.

carpentarius.definition: carpentārĭus, a, um, adj.carpentum Of or pertaining to a wagon or chariot: fabricae,Plin. 16, 8, 13, § 34: artifex, a wagon- or carriage-maker, Lampr. Alex. Sev. 52; cf. fabri,Dig. 50, 6, 6: vehiculu m = carpentum, Treb. XXX. Tyrann. 29. Subst.

carpentum.definition: A two-wheeled, covered carriage, coach, or chariot, esp. used in town and by women, Prop. 4 (5), 8, 23; Ov. F. 1, 619; Liv. 5, 25, 9; 1, 48, 6; 34, 3, 9; Tac. A. 12, 42; Juv. 8, 147 al.; cf. Becker, Gallus, 3, p. 10; Dict. of Antiq.: funebre or pompaticum,Suet. Calig. 15; id. Claud. 11; Isid. Orig. 20, 12, 3: Gallica,Liv. 31, 21, 17; cf. Flor. 1, 18, 27: Cimbrorum,id. 3, 3, 16: Britannorum,id. 3, 10, 17. A wagon or cart for agricultural use (post...

carphologia.definition: of sick persons A picking of pieces of straw from the (mud) walls, Cael. Aur. Acut. 1, 4 and 5.

carpineus.definition: carpīnĕus, a, um, carpinus Made of hornbeam: manubria,Col. 11, 2, 92.

carpisculus.definition: or , , κρηπις, crepida. A kind of shoes, Vop. Aur. 30. In architecture, groundwork, basement, Inscr. Orell. 3272.

carpo.definition: carpo, psi, ptum, 3cf.: rapio, ἁρπάζω, καρπος; Engl. grab, grip, grasp. Lit., of plants, flowers, fruits, etc., to pick, pluck, pluck off, cull, crop, gather (class.; in prose and poetry, esp. in the latter very freq.; syn. decerpere). Trop.

carptim.definition: carptim, carptus, carpo (in the ante-Aug. per. very rare; not in Cic.) By pieces, by detached parts, in parts, separately: favos congerere in qualum,Col. 9, 15, 12: res gestas carptim perscribere,Sall. C. 4, 2 Kritz; cf. Plin. Ep. 6, 22, 2; 8, 4, 7: carptim divisis agris,into small pieces,Suet. Dom. 9: carptim breviterque perstringi,Plin. Pan. 25, 1 Schwarz. Meton.

carracutium.definition: carrus A kind of two-wheeled carriage, Isid. Orig. 20, 12, 3.

carrago.definition: carrus A fortification or barricade made of wagons (postclass.), Amm. 31, 7, 7; Treb. Gall. 13; Veg. Mil. 3, 10.

carroballista.definition: (), , carrus A ballista mounted on a carriage, Veg. Mil. 3, 24; 2, 25.

carroco.definition: Celtic A sea-fish, perh. a sturgeon: Acipenser sturio, Linn.; Aus. Ep. 4, 57.

carruca.definition: and , ae. A sort of four-wheeled travelling and state coach (not before the empire), Plin. 33, 11, 49, § 140; Suet. Ner. 30; Mart. 3, 47, 13; 3, 62, 5; 12, 24, 2; Lampr. Elag. 31 al.; cf. Becker, Gall. 3, p. 12 sq.

carrucarius.definition: carrūcārĭus, a, um, 1. carruca Pertaining to the carruca: mulae,Dig. 21, 1, 38: mulio, Capitol. Max. jun. 4.—Subst.: carrūcārĭus, ĭi, m., a coachman, Dig. 19, 2, 13.

carrus.definition: m. (, , n., Auct. B. Hisp. 6; cf. Non. p. 195, 26, and Isid. Orig. 20, 12, 1) A kind of two-wheeled wagon for transporting burdens, Varr. and Sisenn. ap. Non. p. 195, 26 sq.; Caes. B. G. 1, 3; 1, 6; 1, 26; 3, 51; Hirt. B. G. 8, 14; Liv. 10, 28, 9; Veg. 3, 10; Cod. Th. 8, 5, 47.

cartallus.definition: κάρταλλος A basket, Vulg. Deut. 26, 2; id. Jer. 6, 9.

carthago.definition: Carthāgo (Karth-, and without asp. Kartāgo), ĭnis ( Locat. Carthagini, like Tiburi, ruri, domi, etc., Plaut. Cas. prol. 71; Cic. Agr. 2, 33, 90; Liv. 28, 26, 1 sq.; 31, 11, 7 al.; cf. Schneid. Gr. 2. p. 236; Zumpt, Gr. § 63, note), f., (prop. new town: istam urbem Carthadam Elissa dixit, quod Phoenicum ore exprimit Civitatem Novam, Sol. c. 40 (27, 10 Bip.); cf. Gesen. Gesch. d. Hebr. Spr. and Schr. pp. 228 and 229; and Robinson, Lexic. s. v. ). T...

cartilago.definition: Sanscr. kart, to spin; cf. κάρταλος, cratis Cartilage, gristle; in animals, Cels. 8, 1; Plin. 11, 37, 87, § 216; 9, 24, 40, § 78; 11, 4, 3, § 9. Transf., in plants, a substance harder than pulp but softer than woody fibre, Plin. 15, 28, 34, § 116; 16, 36, 64, § 158.

caruncula.definition: dim.2. caro A little piece of flesh, * Cic. Div. 2, 24, 52; Cels. 2, 7; 8, 4; Val. Max. 3, 7, ext. 6.

carus.definition: cārus (not chārus; in Inscrr. often kārus, Inscr. Orell. 1175; 2417 al.), a, um, Sanscr. kan, to be beloved; kāru, agreeable Dear, precious, valued, esteemed (pass., freq. and class. in prose and poetry; syn.: dilectus, amatus, acceptus, gratus; opp. vilis, neglectus, contemptus; carum esse; syn. diligi); act., loving, affectionate, Verg. A. 1, 646: carum ipsum verbum est amoris, ex quo amicitiae nomen est ductum,Cic. N. D. 1, 44, 122; id. Off. 2...

caryota.definition: (, , Mart. 11, 31; Stat. S. 1, 6, 20) A kind of nut-shaped date, Varr. R. R. 2, 1, 27; Plin. 15, 28, 34, § 116; 19, 5, 29, § 91; Plin. Ep. 1, 7, 6 al.; these the Romans were accustomed to send on the Saturnalia and New Year's day as a present to their friends and patrons,Mart. 8, 33, 11; 13, 27, 1.

casa.definition: Sanscr. khad, to cover; cf.: cassis, castrum Any simple or poorly-built house, a cottage, hut, cabin, shed, etc., Varr. R. R. 2, 10, 6; Lucr. 5, 1011; 6, 1254; Cic. Tusc. 5, 34, 97; Vitr. 2, 1; Verg. E. 2, 29; Tib. 2, 1, 24 et saep.; Cic. Fam. 16, 18, 2; a small country-house, Mart. 6, 43; Caes. B. G. 5, 43 Herz.; Veg. Mil. 2, 10.—Of babyhouses, Hor. S. 2, 3, 247. Esp.: casa Romuli,the thatched cottage of Romulus on the Capitoline Hill,Vitr. 2. 1...

casabundus.definition: cāsābundus (in the best MSS. cassāb-, on account of the first long A, like cassus, caussa, Juppiter, etc.), a, um, caso, ready to fall, tottering, Naev. ap. Varr. L. L. 7, § 53 Müll.; Macr. S. 5, 21, 16; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 48 Müll.

casarius.definition: căsārĭus, a, um, casa Of or belonging to a cottage; only substt. Că-sārĭus, ii, n., a dweller in a cottage, a cottager, Cod. Th. 9, 42, 7. Căsārĭa, quae custodit casam, Paul. ex Fest. p. 48 Müll.

cascus.definition: cascus, a, um, adj.cf. canus Old: cascum significat vetus: ejus origo Sabina quae usque radices in Oscam linguam egit,Varr. L. L. 7, § 28; cf. Müll. Etrusk. 1, p. 41, and v. casnar: quam prisci casci populi tenuere Latini,Enn. Ann. 24 Vahl.; cf. Cic. Tusc. 1, 12, 27; so Manil. and Papin. ap. Varr. l. l.; Att. ib.: sal,Aus. Ep. 22, 27.— Hence, * cascē, adv.: casce nimis et prisce loquens,in an old-fashioned manner,Gell. 1, 10 in lemm.

casearius.definition: cāsĕārĭus, a, um, caseus Pertaining to cheese, cheese-: taberna,in which cheese was smoked and kept,Dig. 8, 5, 8, § 5.

casellula.definition: dim.casa A little hut (late Lat.), Ennod. Ep. 8, 29.

caseus.definition: m. (, , n., Cato, R. R. 76, 3 and 4; Plaut. and Nov. ap. Non. p. 200, 9 sq.) Cheese, Varr. R. R. 2, 11, 3; Col. 7, 8, 1; 12, 12 sq.; Pall Mai, 9; Plin. 11, 42, 97, § 240 sq.; Plaut. Capt. 4, 2, 72; Cic. Sen. 16, 56; Ov. F. 4, 371 al.: facere, Varr. l. l.: premere,Verg. E. 1, 35: figurare,Plin. 16, 38, 72, § 181.—As a comic term of endearment: molliculus and dulciculus caseus,Plaut. Poen. 1, 2, 157 and 179.

casia.definition: (rarely , e. g. Pall. Oct. 14, 13; Veg. 6, 13, 3 and 4), , , = κασία or κασσία. A tree with an aromatic bark, similar to cinnamon, prob. the wild cinnamon: Laurus cassia, Linn.; Plin. 12, 19, 42, § 85, and 12, 19, 43, § 95 sq.; Verg. G. 2, 466; Plaut. Curc. 1, 2, 6; Cels. 5, 23, 1 and 2; Scrib. Comp. 93; 125 al. A fragrant, shrub-like plant, mexereon, also called cneoron or thymelaea, q. v., Plin. 21, 9, 29, § 53; 21, 12, 41, § 70; Verg. E. 2, ...

casito.definition: cāsĭto, āvi, āre V. freq. [cado], to fall repeatedly, to drop down: si ex tegulā casitaverit stillicidium,Dig. 8, 2, 20, § 3 sq.

cassidile.definition: dim.1. cassis A small bag or wallet, Vulg. Tob. 8, 2.

cassis.definition: (access. form , , Prop. 3 (4), 11, 15; Verg. A. 11, 775; cf. Prob. II. p. 1473 P. Lind.; Charis. p. 80 P.; Prisc. p. 698 ib. Also Paul. ex Fest. p. 48, instead of cassilam, the reading should be cassidam), Etruscan, acc. to Isid. Orig. 18, 14, 1; cf. Müll. Etrusk. 1, p. 392; cf. Sanscr. khad, to cover, and Lat. castrum, casa A helmet, commonly of metal (as galea was of leather, Isid. Orig. 18, 14, 1; cf. Tac. G. 6), Plaut. Trin. 3, 2, 100; Caes. ...

cassius.definition: Cassĭus, aold form Casseius; hence, Cassīus, and from this Cassĭus is formed; cf. Ritschl de Sepulcro Fur. The name of a Roman gens; esp. distinguished L. Cassius Longinus Ravilla, a very severe judge; from him the Lex tabellaria Cassia proceeded, A. U. C. 617, by which the judges were obliged to vote with little tablets, Cic. Leg. 3, 16, 35; id. Sest. 48, 103; id. Brut. 25, 97; 27, 106; and Ascon. Cic. Verr. 1, 1, 10, § 30. The consul L. Cassius...

cassivellaunus.definition: A British chief, defeated by Coesar, Caes. B. G. 5, 11; 5, 18.

cassiuellaunus.definition: A British chief, defeated by Coesar, Caes. B. G. 5, 11; 5, 18.

casso.definition: casso, āvi, ātum, 1, cassus (late Lat.). In gen., to bring to naught, destroy, trop., Sid. Ep. 1 fin. In the Lat. of the jurists, to annul, make null or void, = abrogo, Cod. Th. 11, 1, 3 al.

cassus.definition: cassus, a, um Empty, void, hollow. Prop. (syn.: inanis, vacuus; mostly poet.). Trop., vain, empty, useless, futile, fruitless (syn.: inanis, irritus): cassum quiddam et inani vocis sono decoratum, * Cic. Tusc. 5, 41, 119; so, copia verborum,Lucr. 4, 511: vota,Verg. A. 12, 780: fertilitas terrae,Ov. M. 5, 482: fraus,Luc. 5, 130: consilia,Sen. Troad. 570: viae,vain, profitless,Stat. Th. 11, 449: labores,Plin. Ep. 8, 23, 6: manus,without effect,Stat...

castanetum.definition: castanea. A chestnut-grove, Col. 4, 30, 3; 4, 33, 3; Pall. Nov. 7, 21.

castellanus.definition: castellānus, a, um, castellum Of or pertaining to a fort or castle: triumphi, for the capture of a castle, * Cic. Brut. 73, 256: miles, Cod. Th. 7, 15, 2. As subst.: castellāni, ōrum, m., the occupants of a castle, Sall. J. 92, 7; Hirt. B. Alex. 42, 3; Liv 34, 27, 2; 38, 45, 9.

castellatim.definition: castellātim, id. Castle-wise: dissipati, scattered about, qs. in different fortresses, i. e. in separate detachments, Liv. 7, 36, 10: grumulis imponere allium, i. e. in clusters or hills, Plin. 19, 6, 34, § 112.

castellum.definition: dim.castrum A castle, fort, citadel, fortress, stronghold, Sisenn. ap. Non. p. 514, 7; Caes. B. G. 2, 30; id. B. C. 3, 36; Cic. Phil. 5, 4, 9; id. Caecin. 7, 20; Sall. J. 54, 6; Nep. Milt. 2, 1; id. Alcib. 7, 4; Liv. 10, 46, 11; 21, 11, 10; Verg. A. 5, 440; Hor. Ep. 2, 2, 34 al.; also of a single bulwark, bastion, Caes. B. G. 1, 8; 2, 8; 7, 69; id. B. C. 3, 44; and poet. of a dwelling in an elevated position, Verg. G. 3, 475. Trop., shelter, stro...

castifico.definition: castĭfĭco, āre, castificus To purify, make pure (eccl. Lat.), Tert. Pud. 19; Aug. Conf. 9, 9 al.

castigatio.definition: castigo A correcting, chastising, punishment, correction, etc. (in good prose). Trop.: loquendi,the tempering, moderating of the speech,Macr. S. 2, 4, 12.

castigator.definition: castigo One who corrects or chastises, a corrector, reprover (not in Cic.), Plaut. Trin. 1, 2, 150; 3, 1, 13: lacrimarum atque inertium querelarum,Liv. 1, 59, 4: castigator censorque minorum, * Hor. A. P. 174: tot saeculorum,Col. 8, 16, 6; cf. Sen. Ira, 1, 15, 3; Plin. Pan. 40, 1.

castigo.definition: castīgo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.castum-ago, as purgo = purum-ago To set right by word or deed, to correct, chastise, punish; to blame, reprove, chide, censure, find fault with (syn.: animadvertere, punire; more forcible than reprehendere and vituperare; weaker than culpare; class. in prose and poetry): pueros non verbis solum, sed etiam verberibus,Cic. Tusc. 3, 27, 64; so, verberibus,Plin. 8, 3, 3, § 6; cf. Liv. 26, 27, 8; Curt. 8, 6, 5: magnā clade,...

castimonia.definition: f. (, , n., App. M. 11. p. 266, 9; cf. castimonium ἁγνεία, Gloss. Philox.) [castus, like acrimonia, aegrimonia, etc.]. * Ingen., purity of morals, morality, Cic. Cael. 5, 11. Esp., purity, such as is requisite for religious services (abstaining from sexual intercourse, from delicate food, etc.), purity, chastity, abstinence (rare but class.): quae sacra per summam castimoniam virorum ac mulierum fiant, eadem per istius stuprum ac flagitium esse...

castimonialis.definition: castĭmōnĭālis, e, castimonia Pertaining to abstinence or continence: liquamen,Pall. Febr. 25, 12, p. 92 Bip.

castitas.definition: castus Purity. In gen., purity of morals, morality (postclass.): vitae,Gell. 15, 18, 2. Esp.

castor.definition: The castor, beaver; pure Lat. fiber: Castor fiber, Linn.; Plin. 32, 3, 13, § 26; cf. id. 8, 30, 47, § 109; Cic. ap. Isid. Orig. 12, 2, 21; Ov. Nux. 166; acc. castorem, App. M. 1, p. 106, 10: castora,Juv. 12, 34.

castoreum.definition: 1. castor Castor or castoreum, a secretion of the beaver having a strong odor, Plin. 8, 30, 47, § 109; Lucr. 6, 794; Cels. 6, 7, 8; Scrib. 3.—In plur., Verg. G. 1, 59; Plin. 32, 9, 31, § 101; Nemes. C. 224.

castorinatus.definition: castŏrīnātus, a, um, 1. castor Clothed in the fur of the beaver, Sid. Ep. 5, 7.

castorinus.definition: castŏrīnus, a, um, id. Pertaining to the beaver, beaver-: oleum,Marc. Emp. 35: pellis, Edict. Diocl. p. 23.

castrametor.definition: castră-mētor, āri, 1 To pitch a camp, Jornand. 4, 54 al.

castratio.definition: castro. An emasculating, castration of animals, Col. 6, 26; 7, 11, 1; Pall. Mai, 7, 3; Dig. 21, 1, 38. A pruning, Plin. 16, 40, 76, § 206.

castrator.definition: id. One who castrates (late Lat.), Tert. adv. Marc. 1, 1.

castratorius.definition: castrātōrĭus, a, um, id. Of or for castration: ferramenta,Pall. 1, 4, 3.

castratura.definition: id.. * An emasculalion, castration of animals, Pall. Mai, 7, 2. A pruning, cleansing of plants: siliginis,Plin. 18, 9, 20, § 86.

castrensiarius.definition: castrensĭārĭusNEGOTIATOR A purveyor for the camp, a suttler, Inscr. Orell. 4254.

castrensis.definition: castrensis, e, castra Of or per-taining to the camp, camp-: ratio ac militaris,Cic. Cael. 5, 11: arma,Prop. 3 (4), 9, 19. consilium,Liv. 44, 35, 4: triumphus,id. 7, 36, 8: corona, awarded to him who first entered the enemy's camp, acc. to Gell. 5, 6, 17; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 57 Müll. (also called vallaris, v. h. v.): jurisdictio,Tac. Agr. 9: ludi,Suet. Tib. 72 Oud.: jocus,id. Calig. 9: vigilia,Plin. 10, 21, 24, § 46: exsilium. sarcastically, for...

castro.definition: castro, āvi, ātum, 1, Sanscr. çastra, knife, sword. To deprive of generative power (both of male and female), to emasculate, castrate, geld: hircum,Plaut. Merc. 2, 2, 1 and 4: agnum,Varr. R. R. 2, 2, 18: gallos,id. ib. 3, 9, 3; Curt. 6, 3, 12; Val. Max. 6, 1, 13; Suet. Dom. 7: sues,Plin. 8, 51, 77, § 208; 10, 21, 25, § 50; 11, 51, 112, § 261 al. In gen., to shorten, cut off, curtail: caudas catulorum,Col. 7, 12, 14; cf. Plin. 8, 41, 63, § 153: al...

castrum.definition: castrum, i, n.kindred with casa, q. v.. In sing., any fortified place; a castle, fort, fortress (more rare than castellum): ei Grunium dederat in Phrygiā castrum, etc.,Nep. Alcib. 9, 3; Liv. 32. 29, 4; Dig. 27, 1, 17 fin. In plur.: castra, ōrum, n. (castra, ae, f.: castra haec vestra est, Att. ap. Non. p. 200, 30; Trag. Rel. p. 238 Rib.).

castus.definition: castus, a, um, i. e. cas-tus, partic., kindr. to Sanscr. çludh, to cleanse; Gr. καθ-αρός; Germ. keusch, heiter; cf. the opp. in-ces-tus, impure, Bopp, Gloss. 351, 6; Pott. 1, 252. In gen., morally pure, unpolluted, spotless, guiltless, = purus, integer (gen. in respect to the person himself, while candidus signifies pure, just, in respect to other men; v. Doed. Syn. p. 196 sq.; class. in prose and poetry): castus animus purusque,Cic. Div. 1, 53,...

casualis.definition: cāsŭālis, e, casus. Casual, fortuitous (post-class. and very rare): condicio,depending upon chance,Cod. Just. 6, 51, 1, § 7.—Adv.: cāsŭālĭter, accidentally, Sid. Ep. 9, 11; Fulg. Myth. 1, 5. In gram., relating to or declined with cases: Casuale, ut ab equo: equum,Varr. L. L. 8, § 52, p. 116 Bip.; cf. id. ib. 10, § 18, p. 164 Bip.: formae,Prisc. p. 672 P. al.

casula.definition: dim.casa A little cottage or hut, a small house, Petr. 44, 15; 46, 2; 77, 4; Juv. 11, 153. A sepulchre = hypogeum, Petr. 111, 5.

casus.definition: (Ciceronis temporibus paulumque infra s geminabatur: , etc., Quint. 1, 7, 20; cf.: causa, Juppiter al.; in inscr. also KASVS), ūs (dat. casu, Nep. Alcib. 6, 4), cado. Lit., a falling (acc. to cado, I. A. and C.). Trop.

cata.definition: cătă, , = , in distrib. sense By: faciet sacrificium super eo cata mane mane,morning by morning,Vulg. Ezech. 46, 15; cf. v. 14.

catabasis.definition: abl. A going down, descent, the name of a ceremonial at the festival of the Magna Mater, Macr. S. 1, 21, 10.

catachana.definition: (or ) A tree inoculated with buds of different fruit-trees, M. Aurel. ap. Front. 1, p. 77. Trop., of parodies, Spart. Had. 16, 2.

catachresis.definition: a rhet. figure An improper use of a word; in pure Lat. abusio, Paul. ex Fest. p. 58 Müll.; cf. Quint. 8, 6, 34; 8, 2, 5; and Don. p. 1775 P. (where, as in Cic. Or. 27, 94, it is written as Greek).

catadromus.definition: A rope for rope-dancers, Suet. Ner. 11; cf. Plin. 8, 2, 2, § 4 sq.; Dig. 19, 1, 54.

catagraphus.definition: cătăgrăphus, a, um, , = . Painted, colored, depicted: Thyni,Cat. 25, 7. Subst.: cătăgră-pha, ōrum, n., profile paintings, side views (pure Lat. obliquae imagines), Plin. 35, 8, 34, § 56.

catalepsis.definition: A sudden attack of sickness, catalepsy (pure Lat. apprehensio or oppressio), Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 10, 56.

catalepticus.definition: cătălēptĭcus, a, um Cataleptic, Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 10, 74 sq.

catalogus.definition: An enumeration (post-class.): virtutum, Hier. Ep. 83.—Esp., a list of names, a catalogue, Macr. S. 5, 15; Aus. Per. Iliad. 2.

cataphasis.definition: (acc. cataphasin) An affirmation (pure Lat. affirmatio, aientia; opp. apophasis or abnuentia), Aur. Aug. Rhet. 11; Isid. Orig. 2, 27, 3.

cataphractus.definition: cătăphractus, a, um Mailed, in mail (of soldiers and their horses), Sall. ap. Non. p. 556, 16 sq. (id. H. 4, 57 Dietsch).—As subst.: cătă-phracti, ōrum, m., mailed soldiers, Sisenn. ap. Non. 1. 1.: loricatos, quos cataphractos vocant,Liv. 35, 48, 3; 37, 40, 5 al.; Prop. 3 (4), 12, 12; Serv. ad Verg. A. 11, 770; Front. Princ. Hist. 5, p. 247 Nieb.; Inscr. Orell. 804.

cataplasma.definition: Veg. 2, 14 (abl. cataplasmatibus, Veg. 3, 25; access. form ; only Abl. sing. cataplasmo, Lucil. ap. Non. p. 311, 25, and dat. and abl. plur. cataplasmis, Cels. 7, 26, 5; 4, 4, 3; 4, 7, 2; Veg. 2, 3 b; 5, 2, 2; cf. Schneid. Gr. p. 267), = κατάπλασμα; in medicine,a poultice, plaster, cataplasm,Cels. 3, 19, and l. l.; Plin. 20, 17, 73, § 191; 36, 17, 28, § 133; Veg. 2, 14, 2.

cataplasmo.definition: cătăplasmo, āre, cataplasma To apply a poultice to: praecordia,Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 19, 120; cf. id. Tard. 5, 1: equum,Veg. 5, 2, 2; Macer. Flor. 18, v. 723.

cataplus.definition: κατάπλους ( The coming to shore of a fleet or ship; hence, abstr. pro concr.), the ship or fleet that comes to land: ille Puteolanus,Cic. Rab. Post. 14, 40 B. and K. dub.; Mart. 12, 74, 1; Aus. Urb. 13, 21; Sid. Ep. 6, 8; 7, 7.

catapotium.definition: (that which is swallowed down); In medicine,a pill,Cels. 4, 8; Plin. 28, 1, 2, § 7; Scrib. Comp. 89; cf. id. ib. 87.

catapulta.definition: A large engine of war for throwing arrows, lances, stones, etc., a catapult (cf. ballista): catapultis ballistisque per omnia tabulata dispositis,Liv. 21, 11, 7; 21, 11, 10: maximae formae,id. 26, 47, 5; Vitr. 10, 11, 1; 10, 11, 19; 10, 15 sq.; Veg. Mil. 4, 22; Naev., Lucil., Varr., and Sisenn. ap. Non. p. 552, 17 sq.; Caes. B. C. 2, 9 al.; cf. Dict. of Antiq. Meton., like ballista, for the missile itself, Plaut. Pers. 1, 1, 28; id. Curc. 3, 24; ...

cataracta.definition: (also ), , f. (, , m., Plin. and Sol.; V.the foll.), = ὁ καταρράκτης or καταράκτης. Lit., a waterfall, in gen.; the waterfalls of the Euphrates, Plin. 5, 24, 20, § 85.—Hence In milit. lang., a drawbridge, portcullis, Veg. Mil. 4, 4; Liv. 27, 28, 10 and 11.

catarrhus.definition: A flowing down, the catarrh, rheum, Marc. Emp. 5; Plin. Val. 1, 2; Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 17.

catasceua.definition: ; rhet. t. t. The confirmation of an assumption (opp. anasceua), Isid. Orig. 2, 12, 1 sq.; cf. Sulp. Vict. Inst. Or. § 3.

catasta.definition: κατάστασις (postAug.) A scaffold, stage On which slaves were exposed for sale, Tib. 2, 3, 60; Pers. 6, 77 Schol.; Plin. 35, 18, 58, § 200; Suet. Gram. 13; Stat. S. 2, 1, 72. For the public burning (of criminals, martyrs, etc.), Prud. στεφ. 1, 56; 2, 399 al. For delivering a lecture, Rutil. 1, 393; Cypr. Ep. 28.

catastalticus.definition: cătastaltĭcus, a, um, , = ; in medicine Restraining, checking: medicamentum,Veg. 3, 22, 2; also absol. catastalticum, id. 6, 28, 2.

catastema.definition: Position, situation, condition of a star: recursu catastematis (sc. solis et siderum),at the close of a cycle,Veg. 1, 17, 5.

catax.definition: cătax, only in nom. [cf. catena] Limping, lame, Paul. ex Fest. p. 45 Müll.; Lucil. ap. Non. p. 25, 18 sq.

catechismus.definition: A book of elementary Christian instruction, a catechism, Aug. de Fide et Oper. 13.

catechista.definition: A religious teacher, catechist, Hier. Ep. 50, 1.

catechizo.definition: cătēchīzo (-isso), āre, , = κατηχιζω To instruct in religion, to catechise, Tert. Cor. Mil. 11; id. adv. Marc. 4, 29; id. Idol. 10.

catechumenus.definition: m., and , , f. One who is receiving elementary instruction in religion, a catechumen, Tert. Praescr. 41 et saep.—In fem., Aug. Ep. ad Euseb. 169; Ambros. Ep. 34.

categoria.definition: (postclass.). An accusation, Hier. Ep. 82, 9; Macr. S. 7, 3 (where others write it as a Greek word). In logic, a predicament, category or class of predicables (pure Lat. praedicamenta): Aristotelicae,Isid. Orig. 2, 26, 1; Sid. Ep. 4, 1: Aristotelica quaedam, quas appellat decem categorias, Aug. Conf. 4, 16; Serg. Expl. in Art. Don. p. 487, 25 Keil.

categoricus.definition: cătēgŏrĭcus, a, um Relating to a category, categorical, Sid. Ep. 9, 9; Cassiod. de Dial. p. 513, A.

cateia.definition: Celt. or Germ. A kind of spear, probably barbed, Verg. A. 7, 741; Sil. 3, 277; Val. Fl. 6, 83; Gell. 10, 25, 2; cf. Serv. ad Verg. l. l.; Isid. Orig. 18, 7, 7.

catellus.definition: m., and , , f.dim.catulus, canis A little dog, puppy, whelp.

catena.definition: (once with Num. distrib. as piur. tantum: trinis catenis vinctus,Caes. B. G. 1, 53) [Sanscr. kat, to fall away; cf. catax]. A wooden bracket, brace, etc., for holding two beams together, Cato, R. R. 18, 9; Vitr. 7, 3; Pall. 1, 3, 1. A chain

catenarius.definition: cătēnārĭus, a, um, catena Of or pertaining to a chain: canis,a dog fastened by a chain,Sen. Ira, 3, 37, 2; Petr. 72, 7.

catenatio.definition: cătēnātĭo, ōnis F [cateno; lit. a binding; hence, abstr pro concr.],a band, clamp, clincher, pin,Vitr. 2, 9; 10, 1; Petr. 34, 9.

caterva.definition: A crowd, troop, a bandof men; in the sing. and plur. (class. in prose and poet.; syn.: turba, manus, agmen). In gen.: comitum,Lucr. 2, 628; cf. id. 2, 611; Verg. A. 1, 497; 11, 533; Ov. M. 12, 216: Postumius obviam cum bene magnā catervā suā venit,Cic. Mur. 33, 69; so id. de Or. 1, 40, 184; cf. Sall. C. 14, 1: catervae testium,Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 43, § 113: contra dicentium,id. Tusc. 1, 31, 77: pugilum,Suet. Calig. 18: infernae,Tib. 1, 2, 47 al.— Po...

caterua.definition: A crowd, troop, a bandof men; in the sing. and plur. (class. in prose and poet.; syn.: turba, manus, agmen). In gen.: comitum,Lucr. 2, 628; cf. id. 2, 611; Verg. A. 1, 497; 11, 533; Ov. M. 12, 216: Postumius obviam cum bene magnā catervā suā venit,Cic. Mur. 33, 69; so id. de Or. 1, 40, 184; cf. Sall. C. 14, 1: catervae testium,Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 43, § 113: contra dicentium,id. Tusc. 1, 31, 77: pugilum,Suet. Calig. 18: infernae,Tib. 1, 2, 47 al.— Po...

catervarius.definition: cătervārĭus, a, um, caterva Of or pertaining to a crowd or troop: pugiles,fighting in bands,Suet. Aug. 45 (cf.: catervae pugilum,id. Calig. 18); Inscr. Orell. 2530.

cateruarius.definition: cătervārĭus, a, um, caterva Of or pertaining to a crowd or troop: pugiles,fighting in bands,Suet. Aug. 45 (cf.: catervae pugilum,id. Calig. 18); Inscr. Orell. 2530.

catervatim.definition: cătervātim, id. In companies, in troops, Lucr. 6, 1144; Verg. G. 3, 556; Sall. J. 97, 4; Liv. 23, 27, 5; 44, 41, 8; Col. 3, 19, 3; Plin. 10, 24, 35, § 72.

cateruatim.definition: cătervātim, id. In companies, in troops, Lucr. 6, 1144; Verg. G. 3, 556; Sall. J. 97, 4; Liv. 23, 27, 5; 44, 41, 8; Col. 3, 19, 3; Plin. 10, 24, 35, § 72.

catharticum.definition: A means of purifying, a cathartic, Tert. Pall. 5 fin.; Hier. in Ezech. 7, 23.

cathedra.definition: A chair, a stool, esp. one furnished with cushions and supports for women, an arm-chair. In gen., Hor. S. 1, 10, 91; Phaedr. 3, 8, 4; Prop. 4 (5), 5, 37; Juv. 6, 91 al.; also, a sedan chair, Juv 1, 65; 9, 52 Rup. al.; cf. Dict. of Antiq. Esp., a teacher's or professor's chair, Juv. 7, 203; Mart. 1, 77 fin.—Hence

cathedralicius.definition: căthēdrālĭcĭus, a, um, cathedra Pertaining to an arm-chair: ministri,i. e. effeminate,Mart. 10, 13, 1.

cathedrarius.definition: căthēdrārĭus, a, um, id. Of or pertaining to an arm-chair: subsellia,Dig. 33, 10, 5: servi,who carry a chair,Sid. Ep. 1, 11. Esp., pertaining to the chair or office of a teacher: philosophi,teachers,Sen. Brev. Vit. 10, 1; cf. cathedra, II.; so, oratores,Sid. Ep. 4, 3.

catheter.definition: A surgical instrument for drawing off the urine, a catheter, Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 1, 13 al.

catheterismus.definition: The application of the catheter, Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 1, 23.

cathetus.definition: (that is sunk down) A perpendicular line, a perpendicular, Vitr. 3, 3; Cod. Just. 8, 10, 12.

catholicus.definition: căthŏlĭcus (catholicus, Prud. Apoth. 70), a, um Universal, relating to all (post - Aug.; in Quint. 2, 13, 14 as Greek, transl. by universalis and perpetualis; cf. Cael. Aur. Acut. 1, 5, 46): catholica et summa bonitas Dei,Tert. adv. Marc. 2, 17.—Adv.: căthŏlĭcē: in medium proferre. Tert. Praescr. 26.—More freq. subst.: căthŏlĭca, ōrum. n., the universe: anne caelestes dii catholicorum dominantur?App. Trism. 39, p. 100, 13: catholica siderum,gener...

catillo.definition: cătillo, ātum, āre, 1. catillus To lick a plate, Plaut. Cas. 3, 2, 22; Auct. ap. Fulg. 563, 7.

catillus.definition: m. (plur. heterocl. , n., Petr. 50, 6; cf. Prisc. p. 556 P.; an uncontr. access. form , Varr. ap. Charis. p. 61 ib.), dim. catinus. A small bowl, dish, or plate, Cato, R. R. 84 fin.; Asin. ap. Charis. p. 61 P.; Hor. S. 2, 4, 75; Col. 12, 57, 1; Val. Max. 4, 3, 5. Of objects in the form of a plate.

cato.definition: Căto, ōnis, m.1. catus A cognomen of several celebrated Romans in the gens Porcia, Valeria, Vettia al. M. Porcius Cato the elder, distinguished as a rigid judge of morals; hence with the appel. Censorius; whose most celebrated works were the Origines and De Re Rustica,Cic. de Or. 3, 33, 135; Liv. 31, 1 sqq.; Plin. 7, 27, 28, § 100; 7, 30, 31, § 112; cf., concerning him, Bernhardy, Röm. Litt. p. 521 sq.; 650; Bähr, Lit. Gesch. p. 515; 258; 354 al....

catocha.definition: A complete stupor, catalepsy, Cael. Aur. Ac. 2, 10.

catomidio.definition: cătōmĭdĭo, āre To lay one over the shoulders of another, and thus to flog him; acc. to others, to strike on the shoulders, Petr. 132 init.; Spart. Had. 18.

catomus.definition: κατ̓ ὤμους The shoulders (late Lat.): catomus cervix, Gloss.: catomis caedi, Schol. Juv. 2, 142; cf. catomidio.

catonium.definition: κάτω The Lower World, Laber. ap. Gell. 16, 7, 4; cf. Schol. Juv. p. 65 Cram.—Hence the play upon the word: vereor, ne in catonium Catoninos,Cic. Fam. 7, 25, 1 B. and K. (others read catomum; v. this word).

catulio.definition: cătŭlĭo, īre, catulus To desire the male, of dogs, Varr. R. R. 2, 9, 11; of the she-wolf, Laber. ap. Non. p. 90, 33.

catuloticus.definition: cătūlōtĭcus, a, um Good for healing over: medicamentum,Veg. 6, 28, 4.

catulus.definition: dim.2. catus The young of animals, a whelp; cf. Non. p. 457, 8 sq. In gen., of swine, Plaut. Truc. 2, 2, 13; of a panther,Lucr. 5, 1036; of a lion,Verg. G. 3, 245; Hor. C. 3, 20, 2; Ov. M. 13, 547; of a tiger,Plin. 8, 4, 5, § 10; of a cat,Phaedr. 2, 4, 24; of a wolf,Verg. A. 2, 357; of a bear,Ov. M. 13, 836; 15, 379; of a serpent,Verg. G. 3, 438 al.; cf. in gen.: catulos ferae Celent inultae,Hor. C. 3, 3, 41. Esp., a young dog, a puppy (in this s...

catus.definition: cătus, a, um, adj.root ka-; Sanscr. ça-, to whet, sharpen; cf. cos, cautes, cuneus; Sabine, = acutus, acc. to Varr. L. L. 7, § 46, p. 90 Bip.. * Sharp to the hearing, clear-sounding, shrill (cf. acutus, 2.): jam cata signa fere sonitum dare voce parabant, Enn. ap. Varr. l. l. (Ann. 447 Vahl.). Transf. to intellectual objects, in a good and bad sense.

caucula.definition: dim.from the unus. cauca, v. caucus A small dish, App. M. 5, 20, p. 62 Min. Vit. Debr.

cauculator.definition: A reckoner, ψηφιστής, Gloss. Lat. [ = calculator].

cauda.definition: (also , , etc., Varr. ap. Non. p. 86, 19; id. R. R. 2, 7, 5; Petr. 44, 12; Fest. p. 178, 29; Paul. ex Fest. p. 38, 17 Müll.) [etym. dub.; cf. codex] The tail of animals, Lucr. 2, 806; 3, 658; Cic. de Or. 3, 59, 222; id. Fin. 3, 5, 18; Plin. 11, 50, 111, § 264; Varr. R. R. 2, 2, 3; 2, 5, 8. Transf.: membrum virile,Hor. S. 1, 2, 45; 2, 7, 49. Trop., of the addition to the name Verres, making it Verrucius: videtis extremam partem nominis, codam illa...

caudex.definition: (more recent orthography ) [etym. dub.; cf. cauda]. The trunk of a tree, the stock, stem (rare). Inpartic.

caudicarius.definition: caudĭcārĭus (cōdĭc-), a, um, id. Of or pertaining to the trunks of trees: naves, made of rough, stout trunks of trees (cf. caudex, II.), Varr. and Sall. H. Fragm. ap. Non. p. 535, 15 sq.; Sen. Brev. Vit. 13, 4; cf. also Paul. ex Fest. p. 46 Müll.: caudicariae naves ex tabulis grossioribus factae.— Hence, patroni caudicarii, masters of such ships, Cod. Th. 14, 4, 9.—Subst.: caudĭ-cārĭi or cōdĭcārĭi, ōrum, m., those who sail on such ships (esp. tho...

cauliculatus.definition: caulĭcŭlātus, a, um, cauliculus Furnished with or having a stalk: rami,App. Herb. 90.

cauliculus.definition: or , , dim. caulis The small stalk or stem of a plant; form cauliculus, Cels. 2, 18; Plin. 23, 7, 63, § 119; Suet. Gram. 11; Scrib. Comp. 128; Veg. 2, 6, 2; form coliculus,Cato, R. R. 158, 1; Varr. R. R. 1, 31, 4; 1, 42, 4; Col. 11, 2, 10; 12, 7, 1; 12, 56, 1. In architecture, a stalk or stem as an ornament on the capitals of columns, Vitr. 4, 1, 12; 7, 5, 3.

caulis.definition: (, Cato, R. R. 35, 2; Varr. R. R. 1, 31, 2; 1, 41, 6; Col. 5, 6, 36; id. Arb. 9, 2; also in Hor. S. 2, 4, 15, the best MSS have colis; and , Cels. 6, 18, 2; cf. cauliculus), , , = καυλός The stalk or stem of a plant: brassicae,Cato, R. R. 157, 2: cepae,Col. 11, 3, 21 and 58: fabarum,Plin. 18, 12, 30, § 120 et saep.: dictamni,Verg. A. 12, 413.—Of the vine, the tendrils, Cato, R. R. 33, 4; Col. 4, 7, 2.— κατ̓ ἐξοχήν, a cabbage-stalk, a cabbage, ...

caupo.definition: (also and , Charis. p. 47 P.; cf. Isid. Orig. 20, 6, 7; The form copo,Cic. Clu. 59, 163; Inscr. Orell. 4169; Inscr. Momms. 5078), , m.root cap-, to take in, receive, v. capio; cf. κάπηλος, a petty tradesman, huckster, innkeeper, Plaut. Aul. 3, 5, 35; Cic. Div. 1, 27, 51; Hor. S. 1, 1, 29 K. and H.; 1, 5, 4; Mart. 1, 57; Dig. 4, 9, 1 al.—* Trop.: sapientiae atque facundiae,Tert. Anim. 3.

caupona.definition: (upon the form cf. Prisc. p. 684 P.) [caupo]. A female shopkeeper, huckster, a landlady, hostess (anteand post-class.), Lucil. ap. Prisc. l. l.; App. M. 1, p. 105, 23, p. 18 Bip. A retail shop, an inn, tavern (syn. taberna), Cic. Pis. 22, 53; Hor. S. 1, 5, 51; id. Ep. 1, 11, 12; 1, 17, 8; Gell. 7, 11, 4; Plin. 9, 47, 71, § 154: cauponam exercere,to keep an inn,Just. 1, 7, 12.

cauponius.definition: caupōnĭus, a, um, caupo Of or belonging to a retail shopkeeper, or to an innkeeper: puer, a shop or tavern boy, waiter, Plaut. Poen. 5, 5, 19: taberna,Dig. 23, 2, 43; 33, 7, 13: artes exercere,Just. 1, 7. Subst.: caupōnĭum, ii, n., tavern furniture, Dig. 33, 7, 15 pr.

cauricrepus.definition: caurīcrĕpus, a, um, caurus-crepo Blown through by the north-west wind, Avien. 869.

caurus.definition: or , , cf. Goth. skūra, the north wind The north-west wind; form Caurus, Gell. 2, 22, 12 and 22; Lucr. 6, 135; Vitr. 1, 6, 5; Verg. G. 3, 356; form Corus,Caes. B. G. 5, 7; Sen. Q. N. 5, 16, 5; Plin. 2, 47, 46, § 110.

causa.definition: (by Cicero, and also a little after him, , Quint. 1, 7, 20; so Fast. Praenest. pp. 321, 322; Inscr. Orell. 3681; 4077; 4698 al.; in Mon. Ancyr. 3, 1 dub.), , perh. root cav- of caveo, prop. that which is defended or protected; cf. cura That by, on account of, or through which any thing takes place or is done; a cause, reason, motive, inducement; also, in gen., an occasion, opportunity (opp. effectis, Quint. 6, 3, 66; 7, 3, 29: factis,id. 4, 2, 52...

causalis.definition: causālis, e, causa (rare and only late Lat.). Of or pertaining to a cause, causal: ratio,Aug. Gen. 7, 23.—Subst.: Causālĭa, a work on the causes of things, Arn. 5, p. 163. In gram.: conjunctiones. which annex a reason for what precedes (e. g. nam, enim, itaque, etc.), Charis. p. 199 P.; Diom. p. 410 ib.; Prisc. p. 16, p. 1027 ib. —Adv.: causālĭter, causally, Aug. l. l. 5 fin.; 6, 5.

causarius.definition: causārĭus, a, um, causa, II. D.. In medic. lang., sick, diseased, ill (not ante-Aug.): corpus,Sen. Q. N. 1 praef. § 4: partes, quibus adhibenda curatio est,id. Ep. 68, 7: dens,Marc. Emp. 12: dentes,Plin. 23, 3, 37, § 75.—Subst.: causarii vel latere vel faucibus,sick,Plin. 25, 5, 25, § 61: oculorum,Marc. Emp. 8. In milit. lang., discharged on account of ill health, invalid, Liv. 6, 6, 14.—Hence, missio, a discharge from military service on account...

causativus.definition: causātīvus, a, um, causa. Causative: vis,Mart. Cap. 7, § 731. Of or pertaining to a lawsuit; subst.: causativum litis,the matter in dispute, the gist of the action,Mart. Cap. 5, § 472; Fortun. Art. Rhet. 1, 2; Jul. Vict. Art. Rhet. 1, 2; 3, 8. In gram.: causativus casus = accusativus, the accusative, i. e. the arraigning case, Prisc. p. 671 P.; cf. persona,i. e. the first person,id. p. 821 ib.

causatiuus.definition: causātīvus, a, um, causa. Causative: vis,Mart. Cap. 7, § 731. Of or pertaining to a lawsuit; subst.: causativum litis,the matter in dispute, the gist of the action,Mart. Cap. 5, § 472; Fortun. Art. Rhet. 1, 2; Jul. Vict. Art. Rhet. 1, 2; 3, 8. In gram.: causativus casus = accusativus, the accusative, i. e. the arraigning case, Prisc. p. 671 P.; cf. persona,i. e. the first person,id. p. 821 ib.

causidicatus.definition: Forensic oratory, δικολογία, Gloss. Gr. Lat.

causidicus.definition: (), , causadico A pleader, advocate (in a contemptuous sense in distinction from orator; cf. Burm. Petr. 46, 7): in somnis videmur ... Causidici causas agere,Lucr. 4, 966: litium advocatus,Quint. 12, 1, 25 Spald.; connected with proclamator and rabula,Cic. de Or. 1, 46, 202; cf. id. Or. 9, 30; Suet. Claud. 15; Tac. Or. 1 al.; with praeco,Juv. 6, 439; Petr. 46, 7; App. Mag. p. 305, 20; Cod. Th. 2, 10, 1 sqq.

causificor.definition: causĭfĭcor, āri, causa-facio To allege a cause, to make a pretext or pretence, to pretend (very rare): haut causificor quin eam Ego habeam,I offer no pretext against keeping her,Plaut. Aul. 4, 10, 25: blaterans atque causificans,App. M. 10, p. 242.

causor.definition: causor (causs-), ātus, 1, and Trans. [causa]. In the ante-class. per., to plead, dispute concerning a subject, to discuss it for and against, to debate a question, Pac., Att., and Afran. ap. Non. p. 89, 11 sq. Since the Aug. per. (in Ciceronian Lat. the word is not used), to give as a reason (a real, and more freq. a feigned one) for something, to make a pretext of, to pretend, to plead.

caussa.definition: caussa, caussālis, caussārĭus, etc., v. causa, etc.

causula.definition: dim.causa. A petty lawsuit, Cic. Opt. Gen. 3, 9; Capitol. Macrin. 4, 3. A slight occasion, Auct. B. Afr. 54.

caute.definition: cautē, , v. caveo P. a. fin.

cautela.definition: cautus, caveo (mostly post - class.) Caution, precaution. In gen.: si minus cum curā aut cautelā locus loquendi lectus est,Plaut. Mil. 3, 1, 6 dub. (bracketed by Brix); App. M. 2, p. 117, 7; 5, p. 160, 36. Esp., in the jurists, = cautio, a surety, security, Dig. 3, 3, 15; 13, 7, 6; 16, 3, 14.

cauter.definition: (accessory form to cauterium, and only post-class.). A branding-iron, Pall. 1, 41, 2; 1, 43, 3; Prud. στεφ. 10, 490.—Trop.: cauterem adigere ambitioni,Tert. Pall. 5. A wound made by burning, Prud. στεφ. 5, 229.

cauterio.definition: cautērĭo, āre, cauterium To burn, and trop., to mark with a branding-iron, to brand (eccl. Lat.), Paul. ad Tim. 1, 4, 2 al.

cauterium.definition: . An instrument used for branding, a branding-iron, Veg. 1, 14, 3; 1, 1, 28; in medicine,a cautery,Plin. 25, 8, 39, § 80; 22, 23, 49, § 102; Scrib. Comp. 240. An instrument used in encaustic painting for burning in the wax, Dig. 33, 7, 17; Tert. adv. Herm. 1.

cauterizo.definition: cautērīzo, āre To burn with a hot iron, to brand, Veg. 5, 1.

cautes.definition: (e. g. Tib. 2, 4, 9: , Prud. στεφ. 10, 701), , kindr. with cōs, cōtis; Sanscr. s)ō, acuere, Bopp, Gloss. 353, 6 A rough, pointed rock: saxa et cautes timere,Caes. B. G. 3, 13: celsae,Enn. Ann. 402 Vahl. ex conj.: durae,Verg. A. 4, 366; Ov. M. 4, 672; 7, 418: praerupta,id. ib. 1, 719: solida,id. ib. 12, 124: inviae,Plin. 37, 2, 10, § 27. —As a symbol of insensibility, Ov. M. 11, 330.

cautim.definition: cautim, cautus, caveo Cautiously, warily, = caute, perh. only Non. p. 512, 11 and 12; Ter. Heaut. 4, 8, 29.

cautio.definition: (old uncontr. form , acc. to Paul. ex Fest. p. 61 Müll.), , caveo A guarding or taking care of one's self, wariness, precaution, caution, heedfulness, circumspection, εὐλάβεια (besides the comic poets, mostly in Cic.). In gen.: a malis natură declinamus: quae declinatio, si cum ratione fiet, cautio appelletur; quae autem sine ratione, nominetur metus,Cic. Tusc. 4, 6, 13: cautio et timiditas,id. de Or. 2, 74, 300: omnium horum vitiorum atque inc...

cautor.definition: caveo. * One who is on his guard or is wary, Plaut. Capt. 2, 2, 6. One who is surety or bail for any one, Cic. Sest. 7, 15.

cautroma.definition: cauter A wound made by branding (late Lat.), Plin. Val. 3, 47.

cautulus.definition: cautŭlus, a, um Adj. dim. [cautus], rather safe, Gell. 1, 3, 30.

cavamen.definition: cavo. A hollowing out: temonis,Amm. 23, 4, 2. A cavern, hollow, Sol. 9, § 9.

cauamen.definition: cavo. A hollowing out: temonis,Amm. 23, 4, 2. A cavern, hollow, Sol. 9, § 9.

cavannus.definition: κικκάβη The nightowl, Anthol. Lat. 5, 134, 29 Burm.

cauannus.definition: κικκάβη The nightowl, Anthol. Lat. 5, 134, 29 Burm.

cavator.definition: id. One who hollows or excavales: CABATORES (hollowing workmen), Inscr. Orell. 4155: arborum (aves),Plin. 10, 18, 20, § 40.

cauator.definition: id. One who hollows or excavales: CABATORES (hollowing workmen), Inscr. Orell. 4155: arborum (aves),Plin. 10, 18, 20, § 40.

cavatura.definition: id. A hollow, cavity (post-class.): temporum,Veg. 1, 25, 2: vulneris,id. 3, 26, 1: dentium,Marc. Emp. 12.

cauatura.definition: id. A hollow, cavity (post-class.): temporum,Veg. 1, 25, 2: vulneris,id. 3, 26, 1: dentium,Marc. Emp. 12.

cavea.definition: ( Gen. caveāï, Lucr. 4, 78) [cavus]. an excavated place, a hollow, cavity. In gen., Plin. 11, 2, 2, § 3.—Hence Esp.

cauea.definition: ( Gen. caveāï, Lucr. 4, 78) [cavus]. an excavated place, a hollow, cavity. In gen., Plin. 11, 2, 2, § 3.—Hence Esp.

cavealis.definition: căvĕālis, e, cavea Kept in a cave or cellar, Veg. 5, 53, 2; 6, 14, 1 dub.

cauealis.definition: căvĕālis, e, cavea Kept in a cave or cellar, Veg. 5, 53, 2; 6, 14, 1 dub.

cavefacio.definition: căvĕfăcĭo, cĕre, = caveo, Ven. Carm. 8, 6, 192.—Hence, in Pass.: CAVIFIERI,Inscr. Orell. 3678.

cauefacio.definition: căvĕfăcĭo, cĕre, = caveo, Ven. Carm. 8, 6, 192.—Hence, in Pass.: CAVIFIERI,Inscr. Orell. 3678.

S. 2, 3, 38; Prop. 1, 7, 25; v. Neue, Formenl. 2, p. 435; old sup. CAVITVM, C. I. L. 1, 200, 6 sq.), 3, v. n. and a. cavernatim.definition: căvernātim, caverna Through caverns: aqua eructata,Sid. Ep. 5, 14.

cauernatim.definition: căvernātim, caverna Through caverns: aqua eructata,Sid. Ep. 5, 14.

caverno.definition: căverno, āre, id. To make hollow: fistulam,Cael. Aur. Tard. 4, 3, 26.

cauerno.definition: căverno, āre, id. To make hollow: fistulam,Cael. Aur. Tard. 4, 3, 26.

cavillatio.definition: id. A jeering, raillery, scoffing, irony in jest or in earnest: cum duo genera sint facetiarum, alterum aequabiliter in omni sermone fusum, alterum peracutum et breve: illa a veteribus superior cavillatio, haec altera dicacitas nominata est,Cic. de Or. 2, 54, 218: cavillatio est jocosa calumniatio, Paul. ex Fest. p. 45 Müll.; Plaut. Stich. 1, 3, 75; id. Truc. 3, 2, 17; Suet. Vesp. 23; Gell. 5, 5, 2: inter consules magis cavillatio quam magna cont...

cavillator.definition: (, Plaut. Truc. 3, 2, 13), , id. A jester, jeerer, caviller: facetus,Plaut. Mil. 3, 1, 46: probus,id. Truc. 3, 2, 15; * Cic. Att. 1, 13, 2; Gell. 4, 20, 3. Meton., a sophist, Sen. Ep. 102, 20.

cauillator.definition: (, Plaut. Truc. 3, 2, 13), , id. A jester, jeerer, caviller: facetus,Plaut. Mil. 3, 1, 46: probus,id. Truc. 3, 2, 15; * Cic. Att. 1, 13, 2; Gell. 4, 20, 3. Meton., a sophist, Sen. Ep. 102, 20.

cavillatrix.definition: cavillator, II. (only twice in Quint.) She who seeks to take by sophistry: conclusio,Quint. 7, 3, 14; hence also sophistry, id. 2, 15, 25.

cauillatrix.definition: cavillator, II. (only twice in Quint.) She who seeks to take by sophistry: conclusio,Quint. 7, 3, 14; hence also sophistry, id. 2, 15, 25.

cavillor.definition: căvillor, ātus, 1, and A. [cavilla], to practise jeering or mocking; or (act.) to censure, criticise; to satirize in jest or earnest, to jest, etc. (syn.: jocari, ludere, illudere). Meton., to reason captiously, to use sophisms, to quibble, Liv. 3, 20, 4; Plin. 11, 51, 112, § 267; 35, 10, 36, § 85.

cavillosus.definition: căvillōsus, a, um, cavillor Full of raillery, irony, Firm. Math. 5, 8.

Ov. M. 4, 525: naves ex arboribus,Liv. 21, 26, 9: arbore lintres,Verg. G. 1, 262: buxum,id. ib. 2, 450: dentes cavantur tabe pituitae,Plin. 7, 16, 15, § 70: luna cavans cornua (in waning),id. 8, 17, 23, § 63: parmam galeamque gladio,i. e....

cavum.definition: căvum, i, v. cavus, I. B.

cedo.definition: cēdo, cessi, cessum, 3, v. n. and A. [perh. for cecado, redupl. from cado], to go, i. e. to be in motion, move, walk, go along. In gen. In partic.

cedria.definition: The pitch or resin from cedar, Col. 6, 32, 1; Plin. 29, 3, 11, § 47; 32, 7, 24, § 70 al.

cedrinus.definition: cēdrĭnus, a, um Of cedar-wood, cedar-: trabes,Plin. 16, 40, 79, § 213: Apollo,id. 13, 5, 11, § 53: oleum,id. 32, 7, 24, § 76.

cedrus.definition: The cedar, juniper-tree: Juniperus oxycedrus, Linn., which has a very fragrant wood, and furnishes an oil that protects from decay,Plin. 13, 5, 11, § 52; 16, 40, 76, § 203; Col. 9, 4, 3; Vitr. 2, 9, 13.—Of cedar-wood, Verg. G. 3, 414; id. A. 7, 13; 7, 178; Curt. 5, 7, 5; 8, 10, 8; Suet. Calig. 37.—Hence Meton., cedar-oil (with which the backs of books were usually anointed to preserve them from moths and decay): liber flavus cedro,Ov. Tr. 3, 1, 1...

celeber.definition: cĕlĕber, ēbris, ēbre, ( Masc. celebris, Auct. Her. 2, 4, 7; Tac. A. 2, 88 fin.; 13, 47; 14, 19; Curt. 5, 1, 18; Gell. 17, 21, 10; comp. very rare, but sup. freq.) [perh. Sanscr. çru-, audire; Gr. κλέος; v. Corss. Beitr. p. 368], that which contains a multitude, numerous; hence Where there is a multitude, or where a multitude comes together; of places, much frequented or resorted to, populous, abounding in, rich in (syn.: plenus, frequens; opp. d...

celebrabilis.definition: cĕlēbrābĭlis, e, celebro Commendable (late Lat.): favor,Amm. 29, 5, 56; Ambros. de Cain et Abel, 2, 3, 12 al.

celebratio.definition: id.. A numerous assemblage, concourse: hominum coetus et celebrationes,Cic. Off. 1, 4, 12: quae domus? quae celebratio cottidiana?id. Sull. 26, 73. The celebrating of a festival in great numbers, a festal celebration, a festival: ludorum,Cic. Att. 15, 29, 1; cf. Tac. A. 1, 15: epuli,Vell. 2, 56, 1: sacri,Plin. 30, 1, 3, § 12.—* An honoring, a commending, praising: celebrationem habere,to be valued, esteemed,Plin. 34, 5, 10, § 19.

celebritas.definition: id.. A great number, a multitude, a large assembly, a numerous concourse or gathering, a crowd (syn. frequentia; opp. solitudo; in good prose): in multitudine et celebritate judiciorum,Cic. Fam. 7, 2, 4; cf. Tac. A. 16, 29: odi celebritatem; fugio homines; esset mihi ista solitudo non amara,Cic. Att. 3, 7, 1; cf. id. ib. 12, 13, 1; id. Off. 3, 1, 3; Quint. 1, 2, 18: in celebritate versari, to live in society, Nep. praef. § 6: virorum ac mulierum,...

celebriter.definition: cĕlēbrĭter, id. Frequently; only in sup.: per noctes celeberrime acclamatum est,Suet. Tib. 52 Oud. (Roth, creberrime).

celebro.definition: cĕlēbro, āvi, ātum, v. a.id.. To go to a place or person in great numbers or often, to frequent, to fill (syn. frequento; class.): deūm delubra festis diebus,Lucr. 5, 1167: viam,Cic. Cael. 14, 34; id. Sest. 63, 131: domum alicujus,id. Mur. 34, 70: atria,Ov. M. 1, 172: silvas,id. ib. 10, 703: tecta,id. ib. 4, 444: forum,id. ib. 4, 144; cf.: forum maxime celebratum,Sall. J. 47, 1: Penates, i. e. domum redire,Tib. 1, 3, 33: me magistrum,id. 1, 4, 75...

celer.definition: cĕler, ĕris, e ( Masc.cĕleris, Cato ap. Prisc. p. 760 P.; fem. celer, Liv. Andron. ap. Prisc. l. l.; cf. acer; sup. celerissimus, Enn. and Manlius ap. Prisc. l. l.) [cello; cf. Doed. Syn. 2, pp. 123 and 93, urging, pressing forward; cf. also 1. cello], swift, fleet, quick, speedy (with the access. idea of energy, struggling, and even power; v. Doed. above cited; syn.: expeditus, promptus, velox, citatus; opp. tardus, segnis, lentus). Of corporeal...

celere.definition: cĕlĕrĕ, , v. 1. celer, II. B. a.

celeritas.definition: celer Swiftness, quickness, speed, celerity (in good prose; syn.: velocitas, pernicitas; opp. tarditas): velocitas corporis celeritas appellatur, quae eadem ingenii laus habetur, etc.,Cic. Tusc. 4, 13, 31: celeritas et vis equorum,id. Div. 2, 70, 144; cf. equitum,Caes. B. G. 1, 48 fin.: navis,Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 34, § 88: pedum,id. Ac. 1, 5, 19: in capiendis castris,Caes. B. G. 7, 46: veneni,the quick effect,Cic. Cael. 24, 60: incredibili celeritate...

celero.definition: cĕlĕro, āvi, ātum, 1, and n. id. (mostly poet., or in post-Aug. prose). Act., to quicken, hasten, accelerate; syn.: festinare, properare): casus,Lucr. 2, 231: fugam in silvas,Verg. A. 9, 378: gradum,id. ib. 4, 641: iter inceptum,id. ib. 8, 90: viam,id. ib. 5, 609: gressum,Sil. 1, 574: vestigia,id. 7, 720: opem,Val. Fl. 3, 251: haec celerans, hastening, executing this (message), Verg. A. 1, 656; cf.: imperium alicujus,to execute quickly,Val. Fl. 4...

celeusma.definition: (also ), , n. (, , f., Ven. Vita S. Mart. 4, 423), = ) A command or call given by the chief oarsman, which gave the time to the rowers, Mart. 3, 67, 4; Rutil. 1, 370; cf. Ascon. Cic. Div. in Caecil. 17, 55.

celia.definition: (), , Celtic A kind of beer made in Spain, Plin. 22, 25, 82, § 164; Flor. 2, 18, 12; Oros. 5, 7; Isid. Orig. 20, 3, 18.

cella.definition: cf. celo, oc-cul-o, clam, v. Varr. L. L. 5, 33, 45; Fest. p. 50 A storeroom, chamber. In agricult. lang., a place for depositing grain or fruits, or for the abode of animals, a granary, stall, etc.: olearia, vinaria, penaria, etc.,Cato, R. R. 3, 2; Varr. R. R. 1, 11, 2; Col. 1, 6, 9; 12, 18, 3; Cic. Sen. 16, 56; Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 2, § 5; 2, 3, 87, § 200 sq. al.; cf. id. Pis. 27, 67; Verg. G. 2, 96; Hor. C. 1, 37, 6; id. S. 2, 8, 46; Vitr. 6, 9: co...

cellariensis.definition: cellārĭensĭs, e, cella Belonging to a store-room: species, Cod. Th. 7, 4, 32; 11, 28, 16.

cellarius.definition: cellārĭus, a, um (access. form Acc. plur. cellares, perh. for the purpose of avoiding the os four times repeated, Col. 8, 8, 1), cella, of or pertaining to a storeroom: sagina,Plaut. Mil. 3, 2, 31.—Hence Subst.: cellārĭus, ii, m., one who keeps provisions, a steward, butler, Plaut. Capt. 4, 2, 115; Col. 11, 1, 19; 12, 3, 9; 12, 4, 2; Plin. 19, 12, 62, § 188 al.

cellula.definition: dim.cella A small store-room or apartment, Ter. Eun. 2, 3, 19; Col. 8, 9, 3; and acc. to cella, II. D.,Petr. 11, 1.

cellulanus.definition: cellula A hermit, recluse, Sid. Ep. 9, 3.

celo.definition: cēlo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. (contract. form of the Gen. plur. part. pass. celatum = celatorum, Plaut. Trin. 2, 1, 15 Ritschl N. cr.) [cf. caligo], to hide something from one, to keep secret, to conceal; constr. With a double acc., as in Gr κρύπτω τινά τι; cf. Zumpt, Gram. § 391 (class. in prose and poetry): neque enim id est celare, quicquid reticeas; sed cum, quod tu scias, id ignorare emolumenti tui causā velis eos, quorum intersit id scire, et...

celox.definition: cĕlox, ōcis, f.celer, cello (orig. adj., related to celer, as atrox to ater, ferox to ferus, etc.; cf. Doed. Syn. 2, p. 123; later Subst., sc. navis, ratis, etc.), a swift-sailing ship, a cutter, yacht, κέλης, Enn. ap. Isid. Orig. 19, 1, 22; Varr. and Turp. ap. Non. p. 533, 5 sq.; Liv. 21, 17, 3: celocem (celetem, Sillig),Plin. 7, 56, 57, § 208 et saep.; cf. Isid. Orig. l. l.: publica,a packet-boat,Plaut. Capt. 4, 2, 94; humorously for a full be...

celsitudo.definition: celsus. A lofty carriage of the body: corporis,Vell. 2, 94. In late Lat., a title; your Highness, Cod. Th. 1, 6, 6; 9, 1, 15 al.

celsus.definition: celsus, a, um, adj.P. a., of obsolete 2. cello, found in antecello, excello, etc., to rise high, tower; root kar-, in κάρη, κάρηνον, κόρυς; cerebrum, crista, pro-ceres; calamus, culmus, columna, etc. Raised high, extending upward, high, lofty (syn.: altus, erectus, sublimis, elatus, procerus). Physically: (deus homines) humo excitatos, celsos et erectos constituit,Cic. N. D. 2, 56, 140: celsissimo Germano procerior (Judaeus),Col. 3, 8, 2: stat...

celtis.definition: An African species of lotus, Plin. 13, 17, 32, § 104.

cena.definition: (not , ; old form ; cf. Casmena for Camena,Fest. p. 205, 15 Müll.), , f. Sanscr. khad-, eat; Umbr. çes-na; cf. Gr. κνίζω, the principal meal of the Romans in the early period, taken about midday, dinner, supper (Paul. ex Fest. p. 54, 4; Fest. p. 338, 4 and 368, 8 Müll.); subsequently, the prandium was taken at noon, and the cena was usually begun about the 9th hour, i. e. at 3 o'clock P. M. (v. Dict. of Antiq. s. v. coena; cf.: prandium, jentacu...

cenaculum.definition: ( and ), , cena, orig. A dining-room, usu. in an upper story; hence, an upper story, an upper room, a garret, attic (later, the dwelling of the poorer class of people): ubi cubabant cubiculum, ubi cenabant cenaculum vocitabant. Posteaquam in superiore parte cenitare coeperunt, superioris domūs universa cenacula dicta,Varr. L. L. 5, § 162 Müll.: cenacula dicuntur, ad quae scalis ascenditur (the Gr. ὑπερῶ̔ον), Paul. ex Fest. p. 54, 6 ib.; cf. Liv...

cenatio.definition: ( and ), , id. (lit. an eating, dining), meton. (like cena, II. C.) A dining-room, a dining-hall (post-Aug. prose), Plin. Ep. 2, 17, 10 and 12; Plin. 36, 7, 12, § 60; Sen. Prov. 4, 9; id. Cons. ad Helv. 9, 2; id. Ep. 90, 9; 115, 8; id. Q. N. 4, 13, 7; Col. 1, 6, 2; Petr. 77, 4; Suet. Ner. 31 bis.; Juv. 7, 183; Mart. 2, 59, 1.

cenator.definition: cēnātor (coen-) [ceno] A diner, guest, δειπνητής, Gloss. Gr. Lat.

cenatorius.definition: cēnātōrĭus (caen- and coen-), a, um, id. Of or pertaining to dinner, or to the table (only post-Aug.): fames,Sid. Ep. 2, 9 fin.: vestis,Capitol. Max. Jun. 4.— Subst.: cēnātōrĭa, ōrum, n., dinner dress, Petr. 21, 5; Mart. 10, 87, 12; 14, 135 tit.; Dig. 32, 2, 34.—In sing. also cēnātōrĭ-um, ii, n., = cenatio, a dining-room, Inscr. Orell. 2493; cf. cenatorium, οἴκημα, δειπνητήριον, Gloss. Cyr.

cenatus.definition: cēnātus (caen- and coen-), a, um, v. ceno Fin.

cenito.definition: cēnĭto (caen- and coen-), āre V. freq. [ceno], to dine often or much, to be accustomed to dine, to dine (rare but class.).

ceno.definition: cēno (caen- and coen-), āvi (e. g. Lucil. ap. Cic. Fin. 2, 8, 24: Plaut. Am. 1, 1, 154; Cic. Fam. 1, 2, 3; Suet. Aug. 64; id. Calig. 24 al.; acc. to Varr. ap. Gell. 2, 25, 7, also cenatus sum, but of that only the Part. cenatus is in use; v.infra, and cf. poto and prandeo), ātum, 1, and a. [cena]. Neutr., to take a meal, to dine, eat (class., and very freq.): libenter,Cato, R. R. 156, 1: cenavi modo, Plant. Am. 1, 1, 154: lepide nitideque,id. Cas...

cenotaphium.definition: An empty tomb, the monument of one whose body is elsewhere, a cenotaph, Dig. 11, 7, 2 and 6; Lampr. Alex. Sev. 63, 3; Vop. Flav. 15, 1; Hyg. Fab. 273 (pure Lat.: tumulus inanis,Verg. A. 3, 304; or honorarius,Suet. Claud. 1).

censeo.definition: cēnseo (on the long E, v. Corss. Ausspr. 1, p. 257 sq.), ui, cēnsum (late Lat. censitum, Cod. Just. 11, 47 tit.; 11, 49 tit.; 11, 47, 4 al.; but not in Monum. Ancyr.; cf. Neue, Formenl. 2, 557), 2, v. a. etym. dub.; often referred to root cas-, whence carmen, camoenus; but prob. from centum, orig. centere, to hundred or number the people; cf. Fischer, Gram. 1, p. 373. To tax, assess, rate, estimate. Of transactions in and by the Senate, to judge ...

censio.definition: 1. censeo (only anteand post-class.). An estimating, taxing, esp. censor's estimating, rating, appraising: capitis,Gell. 16, 10, 13: Servi Tulli,id. 10, 28, 2; cf. Varr. L. L. 5, § 81; Paul. ex Fest. p. 65, 9 Müll. A severe opinion, judgment: de nostris epistulis,Symm. Ep. 1, 3; Ambros. Abrah. 2, 1, 1.

censitio.definition: 1. censeo, censītus. * A taxing, tax, tribute: levare,Spart. Pescenn. Nigr. 7 fin. A declaration of the will, a command: Vespasiani censitione et jussu,Front. Colon. p. 146 Goes.

censitor.definition: id., in the provinces The magistrate presiding over the rating of citizens ( = censor), Dig. 41, 1, 30; 50, 15, 4; Cod. Th. 6, 3, 2; Inscr. Orell. 208 al.

censitus.definition: censītus, a, um, = census, v. 1. censeo.

censor.definition: 1. censeo; cf. also Umbr. censtur; Sanscr. canster, leader, governor A censor, a Roman magistrate, of whom there were two, chosen orig. every five, and afterwards every one and a half years, who at first only had the charge of the Roman people and their property, in respect to their division according to rank or circumstances; but gradually came to the exercise of the office of censor of morals and conduct, and punished the moral or political cri...

censorius.definition: censōrĭus, a, um, censor Of or pertaining to the censor, censorial: tabulae,the lists of the censor,Cic. Agr. 1, 2, 4: lex,a contract for leasing buildings,Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 55, § 143; public revenues, id. Prov. Cons. 5, 12; id. Q. Fr. 1, 1, 12, § 35 (the same: locatio,Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 6, § 12); sometimes, also, the order, decisions of the censor (concerning the divisions of the people, taxes, public buildings, etc.), id. Rab. Perd. 5, 15; Varr. R...

censualis.definition: censŭālis, e, census Of or pertaining to a census (in late and jurid. Lat.): forma,Dig. 50, 15, 4: vincula, ib.: professiones,ib. 50, 4, 18. Subst.: censŭ-āles, ium, m.

censura.definition: censor. The office of censor, censorship, Liv. 4, 8, 2; 4, 24, 3 sq.; 9, 34, 16 sq.; 9, 46, 10 et saep.; Cic. Inv. 1, 30, 48; Plin. 14, 4, 5, § 44; Ov. F. 6, 647 et saep.—Prov.: dat veniam corvis, vexat censura columbas,Juv. 2, 63. Trop.

census.definition: census, a, um, Part., from 1. censeo.

centaureum.definition: or , , n. (access. form , , f., App. Herb. 34 and 35), = κενταύρειον and κενταύριον Centaury, a plant of two kinds: majus, Centaurea centaurium, Linn.; and minus, Gentiana centaurium, id.; Plin. 25, 6, 30, § 66: ferum,Lucr. 2, 401: tristia,id. 4, 124: Thessala,Luc. 9, 918; Verg. G. 4, 270.

centaurus.definition: Κένταυρος A Centaur; the Centaurs were wild people in the mountains of Thessaly, who fought on horseback; acc. to the fable, monsters in Thessaly of a double form (the upper parts human, the lower those of a horse), sons of Ixion and of a cloud in the form of Juno (hence nubigenae, Verg. A. 7, 674), Lucr. 5, 876; 5, 889; Ov. M. 9, 191; 12, 219 sq.; Verg. G. 2, 456; id. A. 7, 675; Hor. C. 4, 2, 15 al.; Jul. Val. Rer. Gest. Alex. 1, 13 (21): nobil...

centenarius.definition: centēnārĭus, a, um, centeni Consisting of a hundred, relating to a hundred: numerus,Varr. L. L. 5, § 86 Müll., p. 26 Bip.: grex,id. R. R. 2, 4, 22; 3, 6, 6: pondera,Plin. 7, 20, 19, § 83: ballistae, throwing stones weighing a hundred pounds, Lucil. ap. Non. p. 555, 25: fistula,of a hundred inches,Vitr. 8, 7; Front. Aquaed. 29; 62; Pall. Aug. 12: basilicae,a hundred feet long.Capitol. Gord. 32: rosae,i. e. hundred-leaved,Tert. Cor. Mil. 14: libert...

centenionalis.definition: centēnĭōnālis nummus A small coin, Cod. Th. 9, 23, 1 and 2.

centiceps.definition: centĭceps, cĭpĭtis, centum-caput Hundred-headed: belua, i. e. Cerberus,Hor. C. 2, 13, 34.

centifidus.definition: centĭfĭdus, a, um, centum-findo Divided into a hundred parts, or, in gen., into a great many parts: iter,Prud. adv. Symm. 2, 888.

centimalis.definition: centĭmālisκέντημα fistula A surgical instrument, a trocar; Fr. trois quarts, Veg. 2, 15, 4; 2, 5, 24.

centimanus.definition: centĭmănus, ūs (cf. Prisc. p 718 P.; Lachm. ad Lucr. 2, p. 107), centum-manus Having a hundred hands, an epithet of Gyges, Hor. C. 2, 17, 14; of Typhoeus,Ov. M. 3, 303: infantes centimanos,Arn. 2, p. 97, acc. to Lachm. l. l. (al. centenarios).

centimeter.definition: centum-metrum He who employs a hundred, or, in gen., verymany metres: Terentianus,Sid. Carm. 9, 265.

centimetrum.definition: centum-metrum The title of a metrical writing of Servius in Putsch. p. 1817 sq.

centinodius.definition: centĭnōdĭus, a, um, centum-nodus With a hundred knots: herba (an unknown plant),Marc. Emp. 31.

cento.definition: κέντρων A garment of several bits or pieces sewed together, a rag-covering, patchwork, etc., Cato ap. Fest. s. v. prohibere, p. 234 Müll.; id. R. R. 2, 3; 10, 5; Lucil. ap. Non. p. 176, 1; Sisenn. ib. p. 91, 27; Caes. B. C. 2, 9; 3, 44 fin.; Dig. 33, 7, 12. The title of a poem made up of various verses of another poem, a cento; so the Cento Nuptialis of Ausonius (the thirteenth of his Idyls), etc., Isid. Orig. 1, 38, 25; Tert. Praescr. 39.

centoculus.definition: centum-oculus Hundred-eyed, or with a multitude of eyes: Argus,Hier. in Ezech. 1, 1.

centonarius.definition: centōnārĭus, a, um, 1. cento Of or pertaining to patchwork: mos,Tert. Praescr. 39: VESTIARIVS,Inscr. Orell. 4296. Subst.: centōnārĭus, ii, m., a maker of patchwork, a dealer in rags, Petr. 45; Cod. Th. 14, 8; 16, 10 al.

centratus.definition: centrātus, a, um, id. In the middle or centre, central, Fulg. Myth. 1, 11.

centrum.definition: (a prickle, sharp point). Centrum circini, the stationary foot of the compasses, around which the other is carried in making a circle, Vitr. 3, 1; 9, 5.—Hence Meton.

centumgeminus.definition: Centum -gĕmĭnus, a, um A hundreafoid, poet. epithet of the hundredarmed Briareus, Verg. A. 6, 287 Serv.; cf. Macr. S. 5, 14, 8; and of the hundred-gated Thebes,Val. Fl. 6, 118.

centumpondium.definition: or , , centum-pondus A weight of a hundred pounds, Plaut. As. 2, 2, 37; Cato, R. R. 13 fin.

centumviralis.definition: centumvĭrālis, e, centumviri Of or pertaining to the centumviri: judicium,Cic. Caecin. 18, 53; id. de Or. 1, 39, 177; Quint. 11, 1, 78; Suet. Vesp. 10: causae,Cic. de Or. 1, 38, 173; Quint. 5, 2, 1 Spald.; Gell. 16, 10, 8: hasta,Suet. Aug. 36: lis,id. Rhet. 6.

centumuiralis.definition: centumvĭrālis, e, centumviri Of or pertaining to the centumviri: judicium,Cic. Caecin. 18, 53; id. de Or. 1, 39, 177; Quint. 11, 1, 78; Suet. Vesp. 10: causae,Cic. de Or. 1, 38, 173; Quint. 5, 2, 1 Spald.; Gell. 16, 10, 8: hasta,Suet. Aug. 36: lis,id. Rhet. 6.

centunculus.definition: dim.1. cento. A small patch or patchwork, Sen. Ep. 80, 8; App. M. 1, p. 104 al. A plant, bind-weed, knotweed: Polygonum convolvulus, Linn.; Plin. 24, 15, 88, § 138; as fem., id. 26, 11, 66, § 105.

centuplico.definition: centūplĭco, 1, v. a.id. To increase a hundredfold: populum,Vulg. 2 Reg. 24, 3. —Hence, centŭplīcātus, a, um, Part., increased a hundredfold, centuple: fructus,Prud. Contr. Symm. 2, 1050.—Subst.: cen-tŭplīcāta, ōrum, n., a hundredfold: capere,Juvenc. Hist. Sacr. 3, 548.—And adv.: centŭplĭcātō vēnire, to be sold a hundred times dearer, Plin. 6, 23, 26, § 101.

centuplus.definition: centūplus, a, um, centum-plus Hundredfold, centuple (eccl. Lat.): fructus,Vulg. Luc. 8, 8: fenoris usus,Alcim. Avit. ad Sor. 365: augere populum suum centuplum,Vulg. 1 Par. 21, 3.—As subst.: centūplum, i, n., a hundredfold: accipere, Aug. Civ. Dei, 20, 7; Vulg. Matt. 19, 29: invenire,id. Gen. 26, 12: reddere alicui,Salv. adv. Avar. 3, 17.

centuria.definition: centum, orig. An assemblage or a division consisting of a hundred things of a kind; hence in gen., any division, even if it consists not of a hundred. In agricult., a number of acres of ground, Varr. L. L. 5, 4, 10, § 35; cf. id. R. R. 1, 10 fin.; 18, 5; Col. 5, 1, 7; Hyg. Lim. p. 154 Goes. In milit. lang., a division of troops, a century, company: centuriae, quae sub uno centurione sunt, quorum centenarius justus numerus,Varr. L. L. 5. 16, 26, §...

centurialis.definition: centŭrĭālis, e, centuria Pertaining to a century.

centuriatim.definition: centŭrĭātim, id.. By companies or centuries, Caes. B. C. 1, 76 Oud. N. cr.: centuriatim citare populum,Liv. 6, 20, 10: tributim et centuriatim descriptis ordinibus,Cic. Fl. 7, 15.—* Trop., in masses or crowds, by hundreds, Pompon. ap. Non. p. 18, 12 (Com. Rel. v. 153 Rib.).

centuriatio.definition: 1. centurio A dividing into centuries. only in the Agrimensores, Hyg. Lim. p. 206 Goes.

centuriatus.definition: centŭrĭātus, a, um, Part., from 1. centurio.

centurio.definition: centŭrĭo, āvi, ātum, 1, centuria To divide into centuries (acc. to centuria, I.). Of land: agrum,Hyg. Lim. p. 195 Goes.; cf. Fest. p. 53 Müll. Of the army (only of infantry; cf. decurio), to arrange in centuries, assign to companies: cum homines in tribunali Aurelio palam conscribi centuriarique vidissem,Cic. Red. Quir. 5, 13: rem gerit palam (Octavius); centuriat Capuae; dinumerat. Jam jamque vides bellum,id. Att. 16, 9 fin.: juventutem,Liv. 25,...

centurionatus.definition: 2. centurio The office of a centurion, Val. Max. 3, 2, ext. 23. An election of centurions, Tac. A. 1, 44.

centussis.definition: centum-as A hundred asses, Varr. L. L. 5, § 170; 9, § 81; gen. centussis, Varr. ap. Gell. 15, 19, 2.— Abl. centusse, Pers. 5, 191.—Plur.: centussibus, Fest. s. v. peculatus, p. 237 Müll.— Hence, in allusion to the law of Faunius, limiting the expenditure on games: Fauni centussis misellus, Lucil. ap Gell. 2, 24, 4.

cenula.definition: ( or ), , dim. cena A little dinner: hesterna,Cic. Tusc. 5, 32, 91: facere cenulas,id. Fam. 9, 24, 2; Suet. Claud. 21: parva,Mart. 5, 78 fin.

cephalaeota.definition: A collector of a capitation tax, Cod. Th. 11, 24, 6.

cephalalgia.definition: or euphon. A headache, Plin. Val. 1, 3; Aem. Mac. cap. de Acidula.

cephalalgicus.definition: cĕphălalgĭcus (euphon. cĕphăl-argĭcus), a, um Sick with a headache: equus,Veg. 1, 25, 2.

cephalicus.definition: cĕphălĭcus, a, um, , = ; in medicine Of or relating to the head, head-: emplastrum,Cels. 5, 19, 7; Veg. 6, 28, 1.

cepuricus.definition: cēpūrĭcus, a, um Of or pertaining to gardening: loca, Firm. Math. 2, 12.—Hence, in neutr. plur.: Cē-pūrĭca; gen. -cōn, a treatise on gardening, Plin. 19, 10, 57, § 177.

cera.definition: Sanscr. kar-, to scatter, throw away; cf. Gr. κρίνω; Lat. cerno; Gr. κηρός; cf. sincerus Wax, Lucr. 6, 516; 6, 966; Cic. de Or. 3, 45, 177: id. Tusc. 1, 45, 108; Col. 9, 15, 8; 9, 16, 1; Plin. 21, 14, 49, § 83 sq. et saep.; Verg. E. 2, 32.—In plur., the wax cells of the hives, Verg. G. 4, 57; 4, 162; 4, 241; Col. 9, 15; 9, 7 sq.; Plin. 11, 8, 8, § 118 al. Meton., acc. to its diff. uses.

ceras.definition: (a horn) A kind of wild parsnip, App. Herb. 80. Hesperion Ceras, = Ἑσπέριον κέρας, a mountain on the west coast of Libya, Plin. 6, 30, 35, § 197.

cerasus.definition: κέρασος The cherrytree, brought by Lucullus from Cerasus, in Pontus, to Italy, Varr. R. R. 1, 39, 2; Serv. ad Verg. G. 2, 18; Plin. 15, 25, 30, § 102; Col. 11, 2, 96; Ov. Nuc. 32 al. A cherry, Prop. 4 (5), 2, 15; in prose, instead of it, neutr.: , , Cels. 2, 24, 27; Pall. Oct. 12, 7 al.—Of doubtful gender: ceraso,Pers. 6, 36: cerasorum,Plin. 15, 25, 30, § 102; 15, 28, 34, § 112.

ceratina.definition: The sophistical argument concerning horns (quod non perdidisti habes; cornua non perdidisti: habes igitur cornua,Gell. 18, 2, 8; cf. Sen. Ep. 45, 7), Quint. 1, 10, 5 Spald.; Front. Eloq. p. 86 Nieb.

ceratum.definition: (, , Mart. 11, 98; Pall. 1, 41, 3; Veg. 3, 7, 2: , , Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 11; id. Tard. 2, 3; Marc. Emp. 35: , , Theod. Prisc. 1, 9), , = κηρωτόν A wax plaster, wax salve, wax pomatum, Cels. 4, 4, 2; 4, 4, 20; 4, 4, 24; Col. 7, 7, 4; Plin. 13, 22, 43, § 124; 22, 24, 56, § 117; 26, 14, 87, § 141; Scrib. Comp. 250.

ceratus.definition: cērātus, a, um, Part., from cero.

ceraula.definition: A hornblower, corneter, App. M. 8, p. 213; id. Flor. 4, p. 342.

ceraunius.definition: cĕraunĭus, a, um, , = (pertaining to thunder or lightning). Gemma (also cĕraunĭum, Claud. Laud. Ser. 77; and: cĕraunus, Prud. Psych. 470), a precious stone, perh. a kind of onyx, Plin. 37, 9, 51, § 134 sq.; or a meteoric stone, id. 37, 10, 65, § 176; Lampr. Elag. 21; Inscr. Orell. 2510: gemma,Mart. Cap. 1, §§ 67 and 75. Vites, of a red color, Col. 3, 2, 1: uvae,Isid. Orig. 17, 5, 17. Nom. propr.: Cĕraunĭi, m.

cerberus.definition: Cerbĕrus (-ros), i, m., = Κέρβερος The three- (acc. to others, the hundred-) headed monster Cerberus, Lucr. 3, 10; 3, 24; Verg. G. 4, 483; id. A. 6, 417; Prop. 3 (4), 5, 44; Hor. C. 2, 19, 29; 3, 11, 17; Ov. M. 4, 450; Hyg. Fab. 151 (cf. Verg. A. 6, 400; Hor. C. 2, 13, 34); Cic. Tusc. 1, 5, 10 al. —Hence Cerbĕrĕus, a, um, , of or pertaining to Cerberus: facies canum,Lucr. 4, 735: os,Ov. M. 4, 501: latratus,Stat. S. 5, 1, 249: portae,i. e. of the...

cercopithecus.definition: A monkey with a tail, Varr. ap. Non. p. 201, 26; Plin. 8, 21, 30, § 72; Mart. 14, 202; 14, 128; divine honors were paid to it by the Egyptians,Juv. 15, 4.—Acc. cercopithecon, Mart. 7, 87, 4. A proper name, Suet. Ner. 30.

cercops.definition: . A species of long-tailed apes, Manil. 4, 664; cf. Amm. 22, 14, 3. The name of a Pythagorean philosopher, Cic. N. D. 1, 38, 107. = Κέρκωπες, a cunning, trickish people on the island of Pithecusa, changed by Jupiter into monkeys, Ov. M. 14, 92.

cercurus.definition: () A kind of light vessel peculiar to the Cyprians, Plaut. Merc. prol. 86; id. Stich. 2, 2, 44; Lucil. ap. Non. p. 533, 27; Liv. 33, 19, 10; Plin. 7, 56, 57, § 208. A sea-fish, Ov. Hal. 102; Plin. 32, 11, 54, § 152.

cerdo.definition: ] Ahandicraftsman, Juv. 4, 153; 8, 182: sutor,a cobbler,Mart. 3, 59; cf. id. 3, 16. A proper name, esp. of slaves, Dig. 38, 1, 42; Inscr. Orell. 4161.

cerealis.definition: Cĕrĕālis (Cĕrĭālis; cf. Serv.ad Verg. A. 1, 177; so Cic. Att. 2, 12, 2 and 4 Orell.), e, Ceres. Pertaining to Ceres, devoted to her, and, meton., pertaining to the cultivation of land, grain, or agriculture: nemus,sacred to Ceres,Ov. M. 8, 741: sacrum,id. Am. 3, 10, 1: Eleusin,id. F. 4, 507; id. M. 7, 439 (cf. Mel. 2, 3, 4: Eleusin Cereri consecrata): papaver (as her symbolic attribute),Verg. G. 1, 212 Heyne; Col. 10, 314: cenae,i. e. splendid, l...

cerebellum.definition: dim.cerebrum A small brain, Cels. 2, 18; Plin. 29, 5, 32, § 100; 30, 13, 38, § 112; * Suet. Vit. 13.—Figuratively, Petr. 76, 1.

cerebrosus.definition: cĕrĕbrōsus, a, um, id. Having a madness of the brain, hare-brained, hotbrained, passionate, Lucil. ap. Non. p. 22, 8 sq.: unus, * Hor. S. 1, 5, 21 (but Plaut. Most. 4, 2, 36, ellebosus).—Of animals: boves,Col. 2, 11, 11.

cerebrum.definition: (per tmesin: saxo cerecomminuit-brum, Enn. ap. Don. p. 1777 P., and ap. Serv. ad Verg. A. 1, 412), , root kar- of κάρη, v. celsus init.; and root bharof φέρω, fero; cf. Corss. Beitr. p. 354 The brain, Plaut. Cas. 3, 5, 19; Ter. Ad. 4, 2, 32; 5, 2, 7; Verg. A. 5, 413; 9, 419; Lucr. 6, 804; Cic. Tusc. 1, 9, 19; Plin. 11, 37, 49, § 133 sq.; 33, 6, 34, § 102 et saep. Transf. to plants, the pith in the upper part, Plin. 13, 4, 8, § 36.

ceres.definition: (cf. Verg. G. 1, 96; Ov. F. 4, 615; Mart. 3, 58, 6), ĕris ( Gen. CERERVS, Inscr. Fabr. p. 626, 225; cf. Inscr. Orell. 1364), f. Sabini Cererem panem appellant, Serv. ad Verg. G. 1, 7; prop. the goddess of creation (cf. Serv. l. l.), from the stem cer, Sanscr. kri, to make, the daughter of Saturn and Ops, Ov. F. 6, 285, sister of Jupiter and Pluto, mother of Proserpine, goddess of agriculture, esp. of the cultivation of corn, and of the growth of ...

cereus.definition: cērĕus, a, um, cera Waxen, of wax. Prop., Cic. N. D. 3, 12, 30: effigies,Hor. S. 1, 8, 30: imago,id. ib. 1, 8, 43; id. Epod. 17, 76; cf. id. Ep. 2, 1, 265: castra,cells of wax, honey-comb,Verg. A. 12, 589; cf. regna,waxen realms,id. G. 4, 202: simul acra,Ov. H. 6, 91. Meton.

cerinus.definition: cērĭnus, a, um Waxcolored, yellow like wax: pruna. Plin. 15, 13, 12, § 41 sq.: berylli,id. 37, 5, 20, § 77. Subst.: cērĭna, ōrum, n., a wax-colored garment, Plaut. Ep. 2, 2, 51; cf. Non. p. 548, 33.

cernentia.definition: ae. , cernens, cerno The sight, seeing, opp. to caecitas, Mart. Cap. 4, §§ 384 and 386.

cerno.definition: cerno, crēvi, crētum ( Part. pass. cretus is apparently used only once: cineris bene creti,Pall. 12, 22, 3; but freq. in the compounds of cerno; for the simple part., the orig. form certus also is very rarely used: certā deinde sorte senatus consultum factum est,Liv. 36, 2, 2; v. under II. C., and cf. certus), 3, v. a. root car- for scar-, to separate; cf. κρίνω; hence, σκώρ, stercus, screo; cf. cera. To separate, sift (rare): per cribrum, Cato...

cernulus.definition: cernŭlus, a, um, id. Turning a somersault (late Lat.), App. M. 9, p. 235, 28.

cernuo.definition: cernŭo, āvi, ātum, 1, and n. cernuus To throw or fall head foremost (only ante- and post-class.), Varr. ap. Non. p. 21, 8; App. M. 1, 19, p. 111, 9; Front. Princ. Hist. 5.—In dep. form: tigres cernuantur,Sol. 17: equus de industriā cernuatus,id. 45.

cernuus.definition: cernŭus, a, um, root kar, v. celsus; cf. κάρηνον, cerebrum With the face turned towards the earth, inclined forwards, stooping or bowing forwards (very rare and only poet.): cernuus dicitur proprie inclinatus, quasi quod terram cernit,Non. p. 20, 33 sq.; Lucil. ib. p. 21, 1: ejectoque incumbit cernuus armo, * Verg. A. 10, 894 (v. Serv. ad h. 1.): cernuus inflexo sonipes effuderat armo,Sil. 10, 255 sq.; Arn. 7, p. 246.—Hence That turns a somersau...

ceroferarius.definition: cera-fero The waxlight bearer, an attendant at Christian ceremonial worship (eccl. Lat.), Isid. Orig. 7, 12, 29.

ceroma.definition: ( Abl. plur. ceromatis, Plin. 35, 13, 47, § 168; acc. plur. ceromas, Arn. 3, 114), = κήρωμα, an ointment for wrestlers, much used in the time of the emperors, Plin. l. l.; 28, 4, 13, § 51; Mart. 4, 19; 7, 32; 14, 50. Meton.

cerritulus.definition: cerrītŭlus, a, um Adj. dim. [cerritus], somewhat mad, Mart. Cap. 8, § 806.

cerritus.definition: cerrītus, a, um, contr. from cĕrĕbrītus, from cerebrum; cf. cerebrosus Having a crazed brain, frantic, mad: cerritus furiosus,Fest. p. 54 Müll. (rare and only poet.), Plaut. Fragm. ap. Non. p. 44, 31; id. Am. 2, 2, 144; id. Rud. 4, 3, 67; * Hor. S. 2, 3, 278.

cerrus.definition: A kind of oak, Turkey oak, Col. 7, 9, 6; Plin. 16, 5, 6, § 17; 16, 6, 8, § 19; Vitr. 2, 8; Pall. 1, 9, 3; id. Febr. 18, 3.

certamen.definition: id. A contest, struggle, strife, whether friendly or hostile, physical or intellectual; most freq. of a pugilistic contest of any kind; but also of contention in war. A contest, struggle in games or otherwise. Esp., a military strife, battle, engagement, contest, fight, combat.

certatim.definition: certātim, certatus, 2. certo Emulously, earnestly, eagerly (class. in prose and poetry): certatim de alicujus salute dicere,Cic. Sest. 34, 74; Liv. 1, 54, 3: mulieres puerique saxa et alia... certatim mittere,Sall. J. 67, 1: certatim alter alteri obstrepere,Liv. 1, 40, 6: hoc Cicero atque Asinius certatim sunt usi, * Quint. 6, 1, 21: currere,Cic. Phil. 2, 46, 118: ascendere,Liv. 26, 44, 9: exsurgere,Tac. A. 3, 65: erumpere curiā,id. ib. 12, 7: am...

certatio.definition: 2. certo A contending, striving, a combat, strife, contest, etc. (in good prose, most freq. in Cic.). Lit. Trop.: Medea nequaquam istuc istac ibit: magna inest certatio, Enn. ap. Cic. N. D. 3, 25, 65 (Trag. Rel. v. 304 Vahl.): relinquitur non mihi cum Torquato sed virtuti cum voluptate certatio,Cic. Fin. 2, 14, 44: haec inter eos (amicos) fit honesta certatio,id. Lael. 9, 32: ingenia exercere certationibus,Vitr. 2, 1, 3.—Of a judicial contest: ha...

certative.definition: certātīvē, id. In order to stir up strife, combatively (late Lat.), Cassiod. Hist. Eccl. 1, 11.

certatiue.definition: certātīvē, id. In order to stir up strife, combatively (late Lat.), Cassiod. Hist. Eccl. 1, 11.
