certator.definition: id. A disputant (rare and post-class.), Gell. 12, 10, 3; App. Dogm. Plat. p. 2.

certe.definition: certē, adv., v. certus, adv. B.

certim.definition: certim, certus, analog. to certatim, from certatus Certainly: scire,Jul. Val. Rer. Gest. Alex. M. 1, 31.

certioro.definition: certĭōro, āvi, ātum, 1, certior, = certiorem facere To inform, apprise, show (only in jurid. Lat., and most freq. used by Ulpian), Gai 2, 190; Dig. 13, 6, 5, § 8; 19, 1, 1 fin.: certioratus,ib. 29, 4, 1, § 4; 43, 29, 3, § 6.

certo.definition: certō, adv., v. certus, adv. A.

certus.definition: certus, a, umorig. P. a. from cerno; hence, adj. Determined, resolved, fixed, settled, purposed: non dubius. (Acc. to cerno, II. D.) Certum est (mihi), it is determined, it is my (thy, his, etc.) decision, resolution, will, I am resolved, I mean, etc. (mostly ante-class.; most freq. in Plaut.); with inf.: quorum virtuti belli Fortuna pepercit, Eorundem me libertati parcere certum est, Enn. ap. Cic. Off. 1, 12, 38 (Ann. v. 206 Vahl.): certum'st ho...

cerula.definition: dim.cera A small piece of wax: miniata,a kind of crayon,Cic. Att. 15. 14, 4 (with which the Romans were accustomed to strike out exceptionable passages in books): miniatula, the same,id. ib. 16, 11, 1 (al. miniata). Transf., = ceriolarium, a candlestick or stand for wax tapers: ARGENTEAE,Inscr. Orell. 2032.

cerussa.definition: ae. White-lead, ceruse (used by painters, and by women for making the skin white; also in medicine, and in large doses as a poison),Plin. 28, 9, 33, § 129; 34, 18, 54, § 175 sq.; Vitr. 7, 12, 1; Cels. 5, 27, 15; Plin. 28, 9, 33, § 129; 35, 6, 19, § 37; Plant. Most. 1, 3, 101; Ov. Med. Fac. 73; Mart. 10, 22, 2; Pall. Aug. 11, 3.

cerussatus.definition: cērussātus, a, um, cerussa Colored or painted with white-lead: buccae,Cic. Pis. 11, 25: cutis,Mart. 7, 25, 2: Sabella,id. 2, 41, 12: tabulae, Cod. Th. 11, 27, 1.

cerva.definition: cervus A hind, Plin. 11, 37, 45, § 123 sq.; Ov. M. 6, 636; 12, 34. Poet., for deer in gen., Ter. Phorm. prol. 7; Cat. 63, 72; Verg. A. 4, 69; Hor. C. 1, 1, 27; 3, 5, 32; Ov. M. 7, 546; 11, 772; id. A. A. 3, 670; Tib. 4, 3, 13.

cerua.definition: cervus A hind, Plin. 11, 37, 45, § 123 sq.; Ov. M. 6, 636; 12, 34. Poet., for deer in gen., Ter. Phorm. prol. 7; Cat. 63, 72; Verg. A. 4, 69; Hor. C. 1, 1, 27; 3, 5, 32; Ov. M. 7, 546; 11, 772; id. A. A. 3, 670; Tib. 4, 3, 13.

cervarius.definition: cervārĭus, a, um, id. Of or pertaining to deer: lupus,a lynx,Plin. 8, 22, 34, § 84; 11, 37, 79, § 202: venenum,an herb with which arrows were smeared,Plin. 27, 11, 76, § 101; Fest. s. v. toxicum, p. 355: cervaria ovis, quae pro cervā immolabatur (Dianae),Fest. p. 57.

ceruarius.definition: cervārĭus, a, um, id. Of or pertaining to deer: lupus,a lynx,Plin. 8, 22, 34, § 84; 11, 37, 79, § 202: venenum,an herb with which arrows were smeared,Plin. 27, 11, 76, § 101; Fest. s. v. toxicum, p. 355: cervaria ovis, quae pro cervā immolabatur (Dianae),Fest. p. 57.

cervical.definition: (, Cassiod. Orth. p. 2302 P.), , cervix A pillow or bolster, = pulvinus; sing., Mart. 14, 146; Juv. 6, 353; Petr. 56, 8; plur., Plin. Ep. 6, 16, 16; Petr. 32, 1; 78, 5; Suet. Ner. 6; Plin. 20, 20, 82, § 217; 28, 4, 12, § 47.

ceruical.definition: (, Cassiod. Orth. p. 2302 P.), , cervix A pillow or bolster, = pulvinus; sing., Mart. 14, 146; Juv. 6, 353; Petr. 56, 8; plur., Plin. Ep. 6, 16, 16; Petr. 32, 1; 78, 5; Suet. Ner. 6; Plin. 20, 20, 82, § 217; 28, 4, 12, § 47.

cervicatus.definition: cervīcātus, a, um, id. Stiffnecked, obstinate, Vulg. Ecclus. 16, 11.

ceruicatus.definition: cervīcātus, a, um, id. Stiffnecked, obstinate, Vulg. Ecclus. 16, 11.

cervicosus.definition: cervīcōsus, a, um, cervix Stubborn, obstinate, Eccl. Ambros. ap. Voss. Vit. L. L. 3, 4; cf.: cervicosus αὐχενίας, Gloss. Labb.

ceruicosus.definition: cervīcōsus, a, um, cervix Stubborn, obstinate, Eccl. Ambros. ap. Voss. Vit. L. L. 3, 4; cf.: cervicosus αὐχενίας, Gloss. Labb.

cervicula.definition: dim.id.. A small neck, * Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 19, § 49; App. Flor. p. 348: contracta,Quint. 11, 3, 180.—* In mechanics, the neck of a hydraulic machine, Vitr. 10, 8, 2.

ceruicula.definition: dim.id.. A small neck, * Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 19, § 49; App. Flor. p. 348: contracta,Quint. 11, 3, 180.—* In mechanics, the neck of a hydraulic machine, Vitr. 10, 8, 2.

cervinus.definition: cervīnus, a, um, cervus Of or pertaining to a deer: cornu, deer's horn, Varr. R. R. 3, 9, 14; Col. 8, 5, 18 al.: pellis,Hor. Ep. 1, 2, 66: vellera, * Ov. M. 6, 592: pilus,Plin. 28, 19, 77, § 246: color equi,Pall. Mart. 13, 4: senectus, i. e. great age (because the deer was said to live to a great age; cf. Cic. Tusc. 3, 28, 69; Plin. 8, 32, 50, § 119; Aristot. H. A. 9, 6),Juv. 14, 251. Subst.: cervīna, ae, f. (sc. caro), deer's meat, venison, Edic...

ceruinus.definition: cervīnus, a, um, cervus Of or pertaining to a deer: cornu, deer's horn, Varr. R. R. 3, 9, 14; Col. 8, 5, 18 al.: pellis,Hor. Ep. 1, 2, 66: vellera, * Ov. M. 6, 592: pilus,Plin. 28, 19, 77, § 246: color equi,Pall. Mart. 13, 4: senectus, i. e. great age (because the deer was said to live to a great age; cf. Cic. Tusc. 3, 28, 69; Plin. 8, 32, 50, § 119; Aristot. H. A. 9, 6),Juv. 14, 251. Subst.: cervīna, ae, f. (sc. caro), deer's meat, venison, Edic...

cervisia.definition: or , , Gallic Beer, Plin. 22, 25, 82, § 164; Dig. 33, 6, 9; Isid. Orig. 20, 3, 17; Edict. Diocl. 2, 11.

ceruisia.definition: or , , Gallic Beer, Plin. 22, 25, 82, § 164; Dig. 33, 6, 9; Isid. Orig. 20, 3, 17; Edict. Diocl. 2, 11.

cervix.definition: ( Gen. plur. cervicum, Cic. Or. 18, 59; Plin. 23, 2, 33, § 68: cervicium, acc. to Charis. p. 100), f. cer-vix; cf. Sanscr. s)iras, caput, and vincio, Bopp, Gloss. 348 b, the neck, including the back of the neck, the nape (in ante-Aug. prose usu. in plur.; so always in Cic. and Sall.; acc. to Varr. L. L. 8, § 14; 10, § 78 Müll.; and Quint. 8, 3, 35, Hortensius first used the sing.; it is, however, found even in Ennius and Pacuvius; v.the foll.). T...

ceruix.definition: ( Gen. plur. cervicum, Cic. Or. 18, 59; Plin. 23, 2, 33, § 68: cervicium, acc. to Charis. p. 100), f. cer-vix; cf. Sanscr. s)iras, caput, and vincio, Bopp, Gloss. 348 b, the neck, including the back of the neck, the nape (in ante-Aug. prose usu. in plur.; so always in Cic. and Sall.; acc. to Varr. L. L. 8, § 14; 10, § 78 Müll.; and Quint. 8, 3, 35, Hortensius first used the sing.; it is, however, found even in Ennius and Pacuvius; v.the foll.). T...

cervula.definition: dim.cerva A little hind, Aug. Serm. 215.

ceruula.definition: dim.cerva A little hind, Aug. Serm. 215.

cervulus.definition: dim.cervus, II. B. A little chevaux-de-frise, Front. Strat. 1, 5, 2.

ceruulus.definition: dim.cervus, II. B. A little chevaux-de-frise, Front. Strat. 1, 5, 2.

cervus.definition: (old orthogr. ; cf. Quint. 1, 7, 26), , kindr. with cornu and carina A stag, a deer, Plin. 8, 32, 50, § 112 sq.: alipedes,Lucr. 6, 765: fugax,Hor. C. 4, 6, 34; Ov. Tr. 3, 11, 11: fugientes,Hor. C. 3, 12, 11: pavidi,Ov. F. 5, 173: surgentem in cornua,Verg. A. 10, 725 al.—As a type of fleetness: vincere cervum cursu,Plaut. Poen. 3, 1, 27. Transf. (from resemblance to the horns of a stag; cf. Varr. L. L. 5, § 117 Müll.): cervi, forked stakes. *

ceruus.definition: (old orthogr. ; cf. Quint. 1, 7, 26), , kindr. with cornu and carina A stag, a deer, Plin. 8, 32, 50, § 112 sq.: alipedes,Lucr. 6, 765: fugax,Hor. C. 4, 6, 34; Ov. Tr. 3, 11, 11: fugientes,Hor. C. 3, 12, 11: pavidi,Ov. F. 5, 173: surgentem in cornua,Verg. A. 10, 725 al.—As a type of fleetness: vincere cervum cursu,Plaut. Poen. 3, 1, 27. Transf. (from resemblance to the horns of a stag; cf. Varr. L. L. 5, § 117 Müll.): cervi, forked stakes. *

cerycium.definition: or , , , = κηρύκιον or κηρύκειον, a pure Greek form for caduceus The herald's staff, Dig. 1, 8, 8; Mart. Cap. 4, § 331.

cespes.definition: cespes, cespitator, cespito, ce-sposus, v. caespes, etc.

cessatio.definition: cesso. A tarrying, delaying: non datur cessatio,Plaut. Poen. 4, 2, 103.—Hence Inactivity, idling, cessation, omission, idleness: furtum cessationis quaerere,Q. Cic. Fam. 16, 26, 2: cessatio libera atque otiosa,Cic. Leg. 1, 3, 10 Orell. N. cr.: pugnae,Gell. 1, 25, 8: Epicurus nihil cessatione melius existimat... deum sic feriatum volumus cessatione torpere, etc.,Cic. N. D. 1, 36, 102; 1, 37, 102.— So in jurid. lang.,a punishable delay,Dig. 37, 2, ...

cessator.definition: id. A loiterer, an idler, a dilatory person: non quo cessator esse solerem, praesertim in litteris,Cic. Fam. 9, 17, 3: de libris, Tyrannio est cessator,id. ad Q. Fr. 3, 5 (6), 6: nequam et cessator Davus, * Hor. S. 2, 7, 100; * Col. 11, 1, 16.

cessatrix.definition: cessator A (female) loiterer, idler, Tert. adv. Marc. 1, 24.

cessicius.definition: cessĭcĭus (-tĭus), a, um, cessus, 1. cedo; in jurid. lang. Of or pertaining to giving up, ceding: tutor, Gai Inst. 1, 169 sqq.; Ulp. Lib. Reg. tit. 11, 7: tutela, Gai Inst. 1, 171.

cessim.definition: cessim (cossim), cesso; cf. coxim Bending or turning in; hence, also, turned backwards, backwards (mostly anteand post-class.): cum domum ab Ilio cessim revertero, Varr. ap. Non. p. 247, 26; p. 276, 9: cessim ire,Dig. 9, 2, 52, § 2; Just. 2, 12, 7: lagena orificio cessim (obliquely) dehiscente patescens, App. M. 2, p. 121, 8.

cessio.definition: 1. cedo; only in jurid. lang. A giving up, surrendering: abalienatio est ejus rei, quae mancipi est, aut traditio alteri nexo aut in jure cessio,Cic. Top. 5, 28; Dig. 42, 3 tit.; Gai Inst. 3, 78; v. Dict. of Antiq., de cessione bonorum.— * Diei, the approach of a term, Dig. 36, 2, 7.

cesso.definition: cesso, āvi, ātum, 1 V. freq. n. and a. [1. cedo]; lit., to stand back very much; hence, to be remiss in any thing, to delay, loiter, or, in gen., to cease from, stop, give over (indicating a blamable remissness; while desinere, intermittere, requiescere do not include that idea: cessat desidiosus, requiescit fessus, Don. ad Ter. Eun. 3, 1, 15. Diff. from cunctari in this, that the latter designates inaction arising from want of resolution, but ce...

cesticillus.definition: () A small ring or hoop placed upon the head to support a burden, Fest. p. 45 [dim. from cestus; cf. Commod. p. 363].

cestus.definition: () or , , , = (lit. stitched, embroidered; hence Subst.; cf. Lidd. and Scott under κεστός), a girdle, tie, belt, girth, strap, Cato, R. R. 25 Schneid. N. cr.; Varr. R. R. 1, 8, 6.—Particularly, the girdle of Venus, Mart. 6, 138; 6, 14; 14, 206 sq.; Serv. ad Verg. A. 5, 69.

cetarius.definition: cētārĭus, a, um, cetus Of or pertaining to fish; only subst. Cētārĭus, ii, m., a fish-monger, Ter. Eun. 2, 2, 26 (also in Cic. Off. 1, 42, 150); Varr. ap. Non. p. 49, 15; Col. 8, 17, 12.—Cētārĭus, title of a book of C. Matius, Col. 12, 46, 1. Cētā-rĭum, ii, n., a fish-pond, Hor. S. 2, 5, 44.— Access. form cētārĭa, ae, f.; acc. plur. cetarias, Plin. 9, 15, 19, § 49; 37, 5, 17, § 66; an uncertain form, abl. plur. cetariis, Plin. 9, 30, 48, § 91; 31...

cetera.definition: cētĕra, cētĕro, cētĕrum, v. ceterus, II.

ceteroqui.definition: cētĕrōqui or -quīn ceterus-qui (like alioqui and alioquin; v. alioqui, and cf. Hand, Turs. I. p. 235) For the rest, in other respects, otherwise, = ἄλλως (rare): quem, nisi quod solum, ceteroquin recte quidam vocant Atticum,Cic. Or. 25, 83: ego ceteroqui animo aequo fero; unum vereor, ne hasta Caesaris refrixerit,id. Fam. 9, 10, 3; id. Att. 12, 3, 1; 14, 16, 1; 16, 4, 1; id. Fam. 6, 19, 1; id. N. D. 1, 22, 60; Dig. 28, 5, 35, § 3; Gell. 20, 1, ...

ceterus.definition: cētĕrus (caet-), a, um (the Nom. sing. masc. not in use; the sing., in gen., rare; in Cic. perh. only three times), adj. pronom. stem ki, and compar. ending; cf. ἕτερος, the other, that which exists besides, can be added to what is already named of a like kind with it; the other part (while reliquus is that which yet remains of an object, the rest; e. g. stipendium pendere et cetera indigna pati,and endured other indignities of the kind,Liv. 21...

cetosus.definition: cētōsus, a, um, cetus Of or pertaining to sea-fishes: viscera,Avien. Arat. 1300.

cetus.definition: m. (acc. to the Gr. , n., Plin. 32, 1, 4, § 10; and hence common in the plur. = κήτη, Verg. A. 5, 822; Plin. 9, 24, 40, § 78; 9, 50, 74, § 157; Sil. 7, 476), = κῆτος Any large sea-animal, a seamonster; particularly a species of whale, a shark, dog-fish, seal, dolphin, etc., Plin. l. l.; Plaut. Aul. 2, 8, 5; id. Capt. 4, 2, 72; Cels. 2, 18. As a constellation, the Whale, Vitr. 9, 7; Manil. 1, 612.

ceu.definition: ceu, contr. from ce-ve, like neu and seu, from neve and sive, a particle of equality or comparison As, like as, just as (in the ante-Aug. per., peculiar to more elevated poetry; later also in prose, in Seneca and Suet., and esp. freq. in Plin. H. N.): pars vertere terga, ceu quondam petiere rates,Verg. A. 6, 492: ceu talpae,Plin. 9, 6, 7, § 17: ceu notamus in muscis,id. 11, 48, 108, § 258; so id. 9, 37, 61, § 132; Suet. Vit. 17; Plin. 19, 12, 62,...

ceveo.definition: cēveo, ēre ( Perf. cevi, without voucher in Prob. p. 1482 P.), Sanscr. kju, to agitate one's self; cf. quatio. To move the haunches, Plaut. Fragin. ap. Non. p. 84, 18; Juv. 2, 21; 9, 40; Mart. 3, 95, 13; cf. criso.—* Trop. (the figure taken from the wagging of the tail of a dog), to fawn, flatter, Pers. 1, 87.

ceueo.definition: cēveo, ēre ( Perf. cevi, without voucher in Prob. p. 1482 P.), Sanscr. kju, to agitate one's self; cf. quatio. To move the haunches, Plaut. Fragin. ap. Non. p. 84, 18; Juv. 2, 21; 9, 40; Mart. 3, 95, 13; cf. criso.—* Trop. (the figure taken from the wagging of the tail of a dog), to fawn, flatter, Pers. 1, 87.

chalasticamen.definition: chalasticus An alleviating remedy, Theod. Prisc. 2, 10.

chalasticus.definition: chălastĭcus, a, um Of or pertaining to alleviating, soothing: aqua,Theod. Prisc. 1, 7 and 15: unctiones,Veg. 1, 28, 6.

chalatorius.definition: chălātōrĭus, a, um, chalo Pertaining to loosing or letting down: funes,Veg. Mil. 4, 15.

chalcis.definition: . A fish of the herring kind, Col. 8, 17, 12; Plin. 9, 47, 71, § 154; 9, 51, 74, § 162. A lizard with copper-colored spots on its back, Plin. 32, 3, 13, § 30; 32, 5, 17, § 46.

chalo.definition: chălo, no Perf., ātum, 1, , = χαλάω, to slacken, let down: cymbala,Vitr. 10, 13, p. 308 Bip.: culcitas,Veg. Mil. 4, 23.

chalybs.definition: Steel (cf. Plin. 34, 14, 41, § 142 sq.): vulnificus (because weapons were made of it),Verg. A. 8, 446; on account of its hardness: ferro durior et chalybe,Prop. 1, 16, 30; cf. Sen. Herc. Oet. 152; Sil. 1, 171; 2, 403. Meton., the things made of it.

chamaeleon.definition: . Masc., a kind of lizard that changes its color, the chameleon, Plin. 8, 33, 51, § 120; 10, 52, 73, § 143; Gell. 10, 12, 1 sq. Masc. and fem., a plant, the carline thistle; masc., Plin. 22, 18, 21, § 45; 27, 13, 118, § 143; fem., id. 30, 4, 10, § 30.

chamaemelinus.definition: chămaemēlĭnus, a, um, , = χαμαιμήλινος Of chamomile: oleum,Plin. Val. 3, 2; Theod. Prisc. p. 4, 1.

chamaepitys.definition: A plant, called in pure Lat. abiga, groundpine, said to have the power of producing abortion, Plin. 24, 6, 20, § 29; gen., id. 14, 16, 19, § 112; dat. chamaepityi, id. 21, 29, 103, § 175; acc. chamaepityn, id. 26, 8, 53, § 85.

chamelaea.definition: The dwarf olive, a shrub: Cneorum tricoccon, Linn.; Plin. 24, 15, 82, § 133; 15, 7, 7, § 24; Scrib. Comp. 133; 200.

chameunia.definition: A couch on the earth, Hier. Ep. 52, 3.

chanaan.definition: contr. The land of Canaan or Paiestine, Lact. 2, 13, 6; Vulg. Gen. 9, 22.—Form Chanan, Juvenc. 2, 129.

chanius.definition: chanĭus pēs = Molossus A foot consisting of three long syllables, ¯¯¯, Diom. p. 475 P.

character.definition: . An instrument for branding or marking, etc.: character est ferrum coloratum, quo notae pecudibus inuruntur, χαρακτήρ autem Graece, Latine forma dicitur, Isid. Orig. 20, 16, 7. Usu., the mark or sign burned or imprinted.

charadrius.definition: ïi A yellowish bird, Vulg. Lev. 11, 19; id. Deut. 14, 18.

charisma.definition: A gift, present, Prud. prooem. Apotheos. 11; id. στεφ. 13, 61.

charta.definition: (, , m., Lucil. ap. Non. p. 196, 19). f., = (cf. the letter A) A leaf of the Egyptian papyrus, paper, Plin. 13, 11, 21, § 68 sqq.; Lucr. 6, 112; 6, 114; Cic. Att. 5, 4, 4; Hor. Ep. 2, 1, 113: dentata,smooth,Cic. Q. Fr. 2, 14 (15), 1: emporitica inutilis scribendo involucris chartarum segestriumque mercibus usum praebet,Plin. 13, 12, 23, § 76: epistulares,Mart. 14, 11 in lemm.; Dig. 33, 9, 3, § 10: novae,ib. 37, 11, 4: purae,ib. 32, 1, 52, § 4: tr...

chartarius.definition: chartārĭus, a, um, id. Of or pertaining to paper, paper-: officinae,Plin. 18, 10, 20, § 89: calamus,App. Flor. 9. Subst.: chartārĭus, ii, m., a papermerchant, Diom. p. 313 P.; Inscr. Orell. 4159. Chartārĭum, i, n., archives, Hier. adv. Ruf. 3, 6.

chartularius.definition: chartula; in late Lat. A keeper of the archives of court, Cod. Th. 8, 1, 6 al.

charybdis.definition: Χάρυβδις A dangerous whirlpool between Italy and Sicily, opposite to Scylla, now Calofaro; personified, a monstrous female being, Mel. 2, 7, 14; Plin. 3, 8, 14, § 87: vasta,Lucr. 1, 723; Cat. 64, 156; Prop. 2 (3), 26, 54. implacata,Verg. A. 3, 420: Austro agitata,Ov. M. 8, 121: irrequieta,id. ib. 13, 730; acc. Charybdin, Hor. A. P. 145; Ov. M. 14, 75; so Cic. Phil. 2, 27, 67: Charybdim,Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 56, § 146 Zumpt N. cr.; abl. Charybdi, Hor....

chasma.definition: An opening of the earth, a chasm, abyss, Sen. Q. N. 6, 9, 2; Dig. 4, 4, 11; 50, 15, 4; 18, 6, 10. A kind of meteor: sunt chasmata, cum aliquod caeli spatium desedit et flammam velut dehiscens in abdito ostentat,Sen. Q. N. 1, 14, 1; Plin. 2, 26, 26, § 96; Serv. ad Verg. A. 9, 20.

chelidoniacus.definition: chĕlīdŏnĭăcus, a, um Pointed like a swallow's tail: gladius. Isid. Orig. 18, 6, 7.

chelidonius.definition: chĕlīdŏnĭus, a, um Pertaining to the swallow: lapilli,found in the crop of young swallows, swallow-stone,Plin. 11, 37, 79, § 203: ficus,a particular reddish species of fig,Col. 10, 415; Plin. 15, 18, 19, § 71: gemma,Plin. 37, 10, 56, § 154.

chelonium.definition: (lit. A tortoise-shell; hence); in mechanics, the similarly formed shield, cramp, or stay in which the axis of the crane or windlass moved, Vitr. 10, 2; 10, 4; 10, 8; 10, 15; 10, 18; 10, 21. A plant, also called cyclaminos, App. Herb. 17.

chelydrus.definition: A fetid serpent, living, for the most part, in water, Cels. 5, 27, 8; Verg. G. 3, 415; Ov. M. 7, 272; Luc. 9, 710; Sil. 3, 316; 8, 496; Prud. c. Symm. 1, 130.

chema.definition: A gaping mussel, a cockle, Plin. 32, 11, 53, § 147 Jan. (al. leg. chama).

cherub.definition: plur. Chĕrūbĭm (Cherubin), , plur. The name of a rank of angels mentioned in the Old Testament, Vulg. Ezech. 9, 3; id. Gen. 3, 24; Prud. Cath. 4, 4; cf. Hier. in Ezech. 9 and 28; Isid. Orig. 7, 5, 22 sq.; 14, 3, 4; Ven. Fort. Carm. 7, 3, 131.

chilo.definition: A cognomen, signifying having large lips, Fest. p. 43, 10 [χεῖλος, lip; cf. Charis. p. 78 P.; Vel. Long. p. 2234 ib.].

chiragra.definition: Gout in the hand, Cels. 1, 9 init.: podagra et chiragra et omnis vertebrarum dolor nervorumque interquiescit,Sen. Ep. 78, 8.—Poet. collat. form , , , Hor. S. 2, 7, 15; id. Ep. 1, 1, 31; Pers. 5, 58; Mart. 1, 99, 2; 9, 92, 9.

chiragricus.definition: chīrāgrĭcus, a, um, = χειραγρικός Having the gout in the hand; subst.: chī-rāgrĭci, ōrum, m., Cels. 4, 24; Petr. 132, 14; rarely : manus,Sid. Ep. 3, 13.

chirographum.definition: n. (access. form * , , m., sc. libellus or codex, Fulvius ap. Quint. 6, 3, 100 Spald., together with chirographum, Quint. ib. 5, 13, 8; and , , n., Sid. Carm. 16, 56), = . One's own handwriting, autograph; pure Lat. manus (in good prose; freq. in Cic.): extrema pagella pupugit me tuo chirographo,Cic. Fam. 2, 13, 3; Planc. ib. 10, 21, 3; Cic. Phil. 1, 7, 16; 2, 4, 8: neque utar meo chirographo neque signo,id. Att. 2, 20, 5: imitari,id. N. D. 3, 30...

chirurgia.definition: Surgery, Cels. 7 praef.; Scrib. Comp. 200; Veg. 3, 13, 1.—* Trop., a violent remedy: chirurgiae taedet, i. e. vim et arma detestor,Cic. Att. 4, 3, 3.

chirurgicus.definition: chīrurgĭcus, a um Surgical, chirurgical: medicina,Hyg. Fab. 274.

chirurgus.definition: A surgeon, a chirurgeon (pure Lat. medicus vulnerarius), Cels. 7 praef.; Mart. 1, 31; Scrib. Comp. 201; 209 al.; Auct. Priap. 38; Inscr. Orell. 4228 al.

chlamydatus.definition: chlămydātus, a, um, chlamys Dressed in a military cloak, Plaut. Ps. 4, 2, 8; 4, 6, 39; id. Rud. 2, 2, 9 al.; * Cic. Rab. Post. 10, 27; Val. Max. 2, 6, 2 and 3.

chlamys.definition: (, , as cassida = cassis, al., App. M. 10, p. 253, 31; 11, p. 269, 11; and perh. Varr. ap. Non. p. 539, 9, where, however, chlamyda may be acc. Gr. from chlamys) A broad, woollen upper garment worn in Greece, sometimes purple, and inwrought with gold, worn esp. by distinguished milit. characters, a Grecian military cloak, a state mantle, Plaut. Curc. 5, 2, 13; id. Ep. 3, 3, 51; id. Mil. 5, 30; id. Ps. 2, 4, 45; 4, 7, 88; Cic. Rab. Post. 10, 27; V...

choeras.definition: The scrofula (pure Lat. struma), Theod. Prisc. 1, 9; App. Herb. 2, n. 10.

choerogryllus.definition: χοιρόγρυλλος A kind of hare, Vulg. Lev. 11, 5; id. Deut. 14, 7.

choicus.definition: chŏĭcus, a, um, , = . Of earth or clay: homo,Tert. adv. Val. 24; id. Anim. 40; id. Res Carn. 49.

cholericus.definition: chŏlĕrĭcus, a, um Bilious, jaundiced, Plin. 24, 13, 72, § 116; Scrib. Comp. 256.

choliambus.definition: (the limping iambus) Iambic verse, whose last foot, instead of an iambus, is a spondee or trochee, Diom. p. 503 P.

choragium.definition: . The place where the chorus was trained and practised, Vitr. 5, 9; Inscr. Orell. 3209. ( = χορηγία; cf. Lidd. and Scott),the preparing and bringing out of a chorus,Plaut. Capt. prol. 61; App. Mag. p. 282, 1; cf. Fest. p. 52; in plur., Val. Max. 2, 4, 6.— Hence In mechanics, a spring, Vitr. 10, 8, 4.

choragus.definition: He who had the care of the chorus and the suppliesnecessary for it, the choragus, Plaut. Pers. 1, 3, 79; id. Trin. 4, 2, 16; id. Curc. 4, 1. Transf., he who pays the cost of a banquet, Poët. ap. Suet. Aug. 70 Ruhnk.

choraulicus.definition: chŏraulĭcus, a, um, choraules Of or belonging to the flute-players of the chorus: tibiae,Diom. p. 489 P.

chorda.definition: . * An intestine, as food, Petr. 66, 7 (al. leg. cord.).— Far more freq. Catgut, a string (of a musical instrument), Cic. de Or. 3, 57, 214; id. N. D. 2, 59, 149 fin.; Lucr. 2, 412; 2, 505; Tib. 2, 5, 3; 3, 4, 70; Hor. C. 4, 9, 4; id. S. 1, 3, 8; id. A. P. 348 al.

chordacista.definition: chorda A player on a stringed instrument, Mart. Cap. 9, § 924.

chordapsus.definition: χόρδαψος A disease of the intestines, Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 17, 144; Theod. Prisc. 4, 8 (in Cels. 4, 14 written as Greek).

chordus.definition: chordus (cordus V. the letter C), a, um, a very ancient word relating to husbandry, of unknown etym., lateborn, or produced late in the season: dicuntur agni chordi, qui post tempus nascuntur,Varr. R. R. 2, 1, 29; cf. Plin. 8, 47, 72, § 187; Varr. R. R. 2, 1, 19; 2, 2, 5: faenum, the second crop of hay or after-math, Cato, R. R. 5 fin.; Col. 7, 3, 21; Plin. 18, 28, 67, § 262: olus,Col. 12, 13, 2: frumenta, Paul. ex Fest. p. 65, 10.

chorea.definition: (chŏrĕa, Tib. 1, 3, 59; Prop. 2 (3), 19, 15; Verg. A. 6, 644), , , = χορεία (most freq. in plur.) A dance in a ring, a dance. Meton., of the circular motions of the stars: choreae astricae, Varr. ap. Non. p. 451, 11; Manil. 1, 668.

chorepiscopus.definition: A deputy of a bishop for a village, a suffragan bishop, Cod. Just. 1, 3, 42.

choreus.definition: or , , , = χορεῖος (sc. πούς, pes), in verse A foot, later called trochaeus,—˘, Cic. Or. 63, 212; Quint. 9, 4, 80; 9, 4, 82; 9, 4, 96; Marc. Vict. p. 2487 P. In later metrists, for the earlier tribrachys, ˘˘˘, Diom. pp. 261 and 475 P.

choricus.definition: chŏrĭcus, a, um Pertaining to the chorus: tibiae,Diom. 3, p. 489. —In metre: metrum, a kind of anapoestic verse, consisting of a hypercatalectic dipody, e. g. animus male fortis, Serv. Centim. p. 1821 P.

chorus.definition: χορός [cf. Lidd. and Scott under χορός]. A dance in a ring, a choral dance, a dance, = chorea: chorus et cantus,Tib. 1, 7, 44; cf. Prop. 4 (5), 6, 70. Nympharum leves chori,Hor. C. 1, 1, 31: ferre pedem choris,id. ib. 2, 12, 17; Tib. 2, 1, 56: choros agere,Prop. 2, 3, 18: agitare,Verg. G. 4, 533: ducere,Hor. C. 1, 4, 5; 4, 7, 6: exercere,Verg. A. 1, 499: indicere,id. ib. 11, 737: instaurare,Stat. Achill. 4, 145: ostentare,id. ib. 2, 148 sq.: ce...

chrisma.definition: in eccl. Lat. An anointing, unction, Tert. Bapt. 7; id. adv. Jud. 13; Prud. Cath. 6, 128; Psych. 361 al.

christianismus.definition: Χριστιανισμός Christianity, Tert. adv. Marc. 4, 33; Aug. Civ. Dei, 19, 23, 1; Hier. in Gal. 6, 4.

christianitas.definition: Christus. Christianity, = Christianismus, Cod. Th. 16, 7, 7; 12, 1, 112. Meton., the Christian clergy, Cod. Th. 12, 1, 123.

christianizo.definition: Christĭānīzo, āre To profess Christianity, Tert. adv. Marc. 1, 21.

christianus.definition: Christĭānus, a, um, Christus Christian: fides,Cod. Just. 16, 8, 18: lex,ib. 16, 8, 13: religio,ib. 9, 40, 16.—Hence, subst., a Christian, Tac. A. 15, 44; Suet. Ner. 16; Plin. Ep. 10, 97; very frequent in the Church fathers.—Absol., a Christian clergyman, Cod. Th. 5, 5, 2; 12, 1, 50.—Sup.: Christianissimus,the most Christian,Hier. Ep. 57, 12: princeps,Ambros. Ep. 1, 1.— Adv.: Christĭānē, in a Christian manner or spirit: regere,Aug. Ep. 89.

christicola.definition: Christus-colo A worshipper of Christ, a poet. designation for Christian, Prud. Cath. 3, 56; 8, 80; gen. plur. Christicolūm, id. contr. Symm. 2, 1002; id. στεφ. 3, 72.

christipotens.definition: Christĭ-pŏtens, entis, Christus Strong in Christ: juvenis,Prud. adv. Symm. 2, 709.

christus.definition: Χριστός (the Anointed, Heb. ; cf. Lact. 4, 7, 7) Christ, Tac. A. 15, 44 Rupert. ad loc.; Plin. Ep. 10, 97; and in the Church fathers very freq.

chromis.definition: m. or f. A seafish: immunda,Ov. Hal. 121; Plin. 10, 70, 89, § 193: chromin, qui, etc.,id. 32, 11, 54, § 153; 9, 16, 24, § 57. Nom. propr. m., of a satyr, Verg. E. 6, 13; of a Trojan, acc. Chromim, id. A. 11, 675; of a Centaur, acc. Chromin, Ov. M. 12, 333 al.

chronius.definition: chrŏnĭus, a, um, , = χρόνιος Chronic, Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 28, 148; 3, 16, 135.

chronographus.definition: A chronographer, annalist, Sid. Ep. 8, 6 fin.

chryseus.definition: chrȳsĕus, a, um Golden: basiliscus,i. e. gold - colored,App. Herb. 128.—Subst.: chrȳsĕa, ōrum, n., golden vessels, Mart. 9, 95, 4.

chrysocalis.definition: A plant, also called parthenium, App. Herb. 23.

chrysococcus.definition: chrȳsŏcoccus, a, um Having golden grains: flos,App. Herb. 28.

chrysocolla.definition: . Mountain - green, copper - green, borax. A precious stone, called also amphitane, Plin. 37, 10, 54, § 147.

chrysopastus.definition: A species of our topaz, Sol. 30 fin.

chrysoprasus.definition: The chrysoprase, a precious stone of a golden-yellow and a leek-green color, Plin. 37, 5, 20, § 77; Prud. Psych. 865; Isid. Orig. 16, 7, 7; 16, 14, 8; Ambros. in Psa. 118, Serm. 16, § 41 sq.; also called , Plin. 37, 8, 34, § 113.

chus.definition: A measure for liquids, = congius, Rhemn. Fann. Pond. 7, 70.

chylus.definition: The extracted juice of a plant, Veg. 5, 37 and 65.

chymus.definition: (juice) The fluid of the stomach, chyle, Ser. Samm. 48, 900.

chytropus.definition: A pot or chafing-dish with feet for coals, Vulg. Lev. 11, 35.

cibalis.definition: cĭbālis, e, cibus Pertaining to food: fistula, the oesophagus or gullet, Lact. Opif. Dei, 11, 5.

cibarius.definition: cĭbārĭus, a, um, cibus Pertaining to or suitable for food (class.): res,Plaut. Capt. 4, 3, 1: leges, i. e. sumptuary laws, laws restraining luxury, Cato ap. Macr. S. 2, 13: uva, suitable only for eating, not for wine, Plin. 14, 3, 4, § 37; cf.: uva vilitatis cibariae,id. 14, 2, 4, § 35. Meton. (in accordance with the fare given to servants), ordinary, common: panis,black bread,Cic. Tusc. 5, 34, 97 (cf. Isid. Orig. 20, 2, 15: panis cibarius est, q...

cibatio.definition: cibo A feeding; concr., a meal, repast (post-class.), Sol. 27, 13; Cael. Aur. Tard. 1, 1, 12; 1, 4, 3.

cibo.definition: cĭbo, no Perf., ātum, 1, cibus, to give food to animals, to feed or fodder (rare): genera avium,Col. 8, 10 fin.: locustae utiles cibandis pullis,id. 8, 11, 15: draconem manu suă,Suet. Tib. 72.—In pass.: cibari,to take food,Liv. Epit. 19. With men as objects (late Lat.), Vulg. Prov. 25, 21; id. Rom. 12, 20.

cibus.definition: perh. root of capio Food for man and beast, victuals, fare, nutriment, fodder (class. in prose and poetry, both in sing. and plur.; syn.: esca, epulae; opp. potio,Cic. Fin. 1, 11, 37; cf. id. N. D. 2, 54, 136; so, cibus potusque,Tac. A. 13, 16: cibus et vinum,Cic. Div. 1, 29, 60; Juv. 10, 203: unda cibusque,Ov. M. 4, 262): cibum capere,Plaut. Trin. 4, 2, 60; Ter. Eun. 2, 3, 77: petere,id. ib. 3, 2, 38; id. Heaut. 5, 2, 25: capessere (of animals),...

cicada.definition: The cicada, tree-cricket: Cicada orni, Linn.; Plin. 11, 26, 32, § 92 sq.; Lucr. 4, 56; 5, 801; Verg. E. 2, 13; 5, 77; id. G. 3, 328; id. Cul. 151 al.—Worn as an ornament in the hair of the Athenians, Verg. Cir. 128 Sillig; cf. Lidd. and Scott, under τέττιξ.—As a symbol of summer, Ov. A. A. 1, 271; Juv. 9, 69.

cicatricor.definition: cĭcātrīcor, ātus, 1, cicatrix To be scarred over, cicatrized (late Lat.), Fest p. 65, 14 Müll.; Cael. Aur. Tard. 4, 8, 118. Trop., Sid. Ep. 6, 7; 6, 1fin.

cicatricosus.definition: cĭcātrīcōsus, a, um, id. Full of scars, covered with scars: tergum,Plaut. Am. 1, 1, 290: facies,Quint. 4, 1, 61: Ira (personified),Sen. Ira, 2, 35, 5: vitis,Col. Arb. 11, 1: putatio,id. ib. 4, 27, 3. Trop., of a writing, amended or polished here and there, Quint. 10, 4, 3; v. the context.

cicatrix.definition: A scar, cicatrice (freq. and class.). Prop., Ter. Eun. 3, 2, 29; Cic. Phil. 7, 6, 17; Quint. 5, 9, 5; 6, 1, 21; 6, 3, 100; Suet. Aug. 65 al.; Hor. S. 1, 5, 60; id. C. 1, 35, 33; Ov. M. 12, 444; id. R. Am. 623 al.: cicatrices adversae, wounds in front (therefore honorable), Cic. de Or. 2, 28, 124; Sall. H. 1, 55 Dietsch: aversa,on the back,Gell. 2, 11, 2; cf.: cicatrices adverso corpore,Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 1, § 3; Sall. J. 85, 29; Liv. 2, 23, 4: cica...

cicer.definition: The chickpea: Cicer Arietinum, Linn. (used only in sing. acc. to Varr. L. L. 8, 25, 115; 9, 39, 142; 10, 3, 174); Col. 2, 10, 19; Plin. 18, 12, 32, § 124 sq.; Pall. Mart. 4; Plaut. Bacch. 4, 5, 7; Hor. S. 1, 6, 115; 2, 3, 182; id. A. P. 249; Mart. 1, 104; Pers. 5, 177; Petr. 14, 3.

cicercula.definition: dim.cicera; al. cicer; v. Plin. 18, 12, 32, § 124 A kind of small chickpea, Col. 2, 10, 19; Plin. 18, 12, 32, § 124; 18, 18, 73, § 304; 22, 25, 72, § 148; Pall. Jan. 5; id. Febr. 4.

cicero.definition: Cĭcĕro, ōnis, m., = Κικέρων A Roman cognomen in the gens Tullia. M. Tullius Cicero, the greatest of the Roman orators and writers; born on the 3d of January, 106 B.C. (648 A.U.C.), at Arpinum (hence Arpinae chartae, Mart. 10, 19, 17); assassinated, at the age of sixty-three years, by the soldiers of Antonius, 43 B.C. (711 A.U.C.): ille se profecisse sciat, cui Cicero valde placebit,Quint. 10, 1, 112; Juv. 10, 114 al.— Hence Q. Tullius Cicero, th...

cichorium.definition: or (, * Hor. C. 1, 31, 16), , , = κιχόρια (usu. κιχώριον) Chiccory, succory, or endive: Cichorium intybus, etc., Linn.; Plin. 20, 8, 30, § 74 sq.; 19, 8, 39, § 129.

cicindela.definition: candela A glowworm, Plin. 18, 26, 66, § 250; cf. Fest. p. 42, 13 Müll.

cicinus.definition: cīcĭnus, a, um, cici: Oleum,an aperient oil expressed from the fruit of the cici, castor-oil,Cels. 5, 24, 3; Plin. 23, 4, 41, § 83 al.

ciconia.definition: A stork, Plin. 10, 23, 32, § 63; Hor. S. 2, 2, 49; Ov. M. 6, 97; Juv. 14, 74 al.; at Praeneste called conia, Plaut. Truc. 3, 2, 23. Meton.

cicur.definition: cĭcur, ŭris, cf. cacula Tame (cf. mansuetus): quod a fero discretum id dicitur cicur,Varr. L. L. 7, § 91 Müll. (syn. mansuetus; opp. ferus, immanis; apparently not used after Cic.): cicurum vel ferarum bestiarum,Cic. N. D. 2, 39, 99; id. Lael. 21, 81: bestiae immanes, cicures,id. Tusc. 5, 13, 38: apes (opp. ferae),Varr. R. R. 3, 16, 19. Trop., mild: ingenium, Auct. ap. Varr. L. L. 7, § 91 Müll.: concilium, i. e. sapiens, Pac. ap. Fest. s. v. inci...

cicuro.definition: cĭcŭro, āre, cicur To tame ( = mansuefacio), Pac. ap. Varr. L. L. 7, § 91 Müll., p. 98 Bip.

cicuta.definition: The hemlock given to criminals as poison; prob. either Cicuta virosa or Conium maculatum, Linn.; Plin. 25, 13, 95, § 151; Cato, R. R. 27, 2; Lucr. 5, 897; Hor. S. 2, 1, 56 al.; plur., id. Ep. 2, 2, 53; drunk by Socrates; hence: magister sorbitio tollit quem dira cicutae,i. e. Socrates,Pers. 4, 1 sq.—To the extraordinary coldness produced by it, reference is made in Pers. 5, 145. Meton., a pipe or flute made from the stalks of the hemlock, a sheph...

cicuticen.definition: 1. cicuta, II. and cano A player upon a reed-pipe, Sid. Carm. 1, 15.

cieo.definition: cĭĕo, cīvi, cĭtum, 2 (from the primitive form cĭo, cīre, prevailing in the compounds accio, excio, etc. (cf. Prisc. pp. 865, 905, and 908 P.), are also found: Pres. cio, Mart. 4, 90, 4: cit,Verg. Cul. 201; Col. 6, 5, 1 Schneid.: cimus,Lucr. 1, 213; 5, 211: ciunt,Lact. Ep. 4 dub.: ciant,App. Flor. 2, n. 17, p. 358; Mart. Cap. 1, § 91: ciuntur, id. de Mundo, 22, p. 67), v. a. kindr. with κίω, to go; and by the addition of the causative signif. lik...

cignus.definition: A measure, = 8 scrupuli, Plin. Val. 2, 30 and 31.

ciliciolum.definition: dim.cilicium A small garment or coverlet of goats' hair, Hier. Ep. 71, 7; 108, 15.

cilicium.definition: Cĭlĭcĭum, Cĭlĭcĭus, and Cĭlissa, v. Cilicia.

cilio.definition: (a vulgar collat. form of caelum) A chisel, graver, Isid. Orig. 20, 4, 7.

cilium.definition: kindr. with Gr. κυλίς, κύλα. An eyelid, Paul. ex Fest. p. 43, 3 Müll.; Plin. 11, 39, 93, § 227; App. M. 10, p. 247, 10; Lact. Opif. Dei, 10 init. Transf., the lower eyelid (opp. supercilium): extremum ambitum genae superioris,Plin. 11, 37, 57, § 157.

cilliba.definition: A round dining-table, Varr. L. L. 5, § 118 Müll.; Paul. ex Fest. p. 43, 9 ib.

cillo.definition: cillo, ĕre To move, put in motion (only in mal. part.), Serv. ad Verg. G. 2, 389; Isid. Orig. 20, 14, 11.

cimeliarcha.definition: A treasurer, keeper of treasure, Cod. Just. 7, 72, 10.

cimeliarchium.definition: A place where jewels are deposited, a treasury, Cod. Just. 7, 72, 10, § 2; 11, 47, 19.

cimex.definition: (so always acc. to Neue, Formenl. 1, p. 619 sq.; but Fem., Plin. 32, 10, 47 § 136 Sillig and Jan.), a bug, Liv. Andron. ap. Fest. p. 210, 17; Varr. R. R. 1, 2 fin.; Col. 6, 18, 2; Plin. 30, 14, 45, § 131; 29, 4, 17, § 61; Veg. 2, 33, 2; 5, 14, 21; Cat. 23, 2; Petr. 98, 1; Mart. 11, 32 al.—As a term of reproach, * Hor. S. 1, 10, 78.

cimico.definition: cīmĭco, āre, = κορίζω To purify from bugs, Gloss. Gr. Lat.

cinaedicus.definition: cĭnaedĭcus, a, um, adj.cinaedus, 1. Pertaining to one who is unchaste; immodest, lewd (ante-class.): cantio,Plaut. Stich. 5, 5, 19.—Subst. = cinaedus, Plaut. Stich. 5, 7, 1 (769); Varr. ap. Non. p. 176, 19.

cinaedulus.definition: dim.id. A male wanton, Scip. Afric. ap. Macr. S. 2, 10.

cinaedus.definition: . He who practises unnatural lust, a sodomite, catamite, Plaut. As. 3, 3, 37; id. Aul. 3, 2, 8; id. Poen. 5, 5, 40; Scip. Afric. ap. Gell. 7, 12, 5; Cat. 16, 2; 25, 1; Petr. 21, 2; Juv. 2, 10; 14, 30 al. He who performs a wanton dance, Plaut. Mil. 3, 1, 73; Lucil. ap. Non. p. 5, 31. The name of a sea-fish, Plin. 33, 11, 53, § 146.

cincinnalis.definition: cincinnālis, e, cincinnus Curled: herba, a plant, also called polytrichon, App. Herb. 51.

cincinnatus.definition: cincinnātus, cincinnus With curled hair, having locks or ringlets of hair (as an indication of luxurious effeminacy), Plaut. Capt. 3, 4, 115: moechus,id. Mil. 3, 3, 49; id. Truc. 2, 7, 48: consul,Cic. Sest. 11, 26: ganeo,id. Red. in Sen. 5, 13; Cael. ap. Quint. 1, 5, 61. Transf., of comets: stellae, Schol. Juv 6, 207 (in Cic. N. D. 2, 5, 14, better crinitas).

cincinnus.definition: i. kindr. with Gr. κίκιννος and Lat. cirrus; Sanscr. cicura, crinis, Bopp, Gloss. 124 a Curled hair, a lock or curl of hair, Plaut. Truc. 2, 2, 32; Varr. R. R. 1, 31, 4; Cic. Pis. 11, 25. Trop., too artificial or elaborate oratorical ornament (cf. calamister, II.): in oratoris aut in poëtae cincinnis ac fuco offenditur, quod, etc.,Cic. de Or. 2, 25, 100; Aug. ap. Suet. Aug. 86.

cinctura.definition: 2. cinctus, cingo A nncture, a girdle (very rare), * Suet. Caes. 45; * Quint 11, 3, 139.

cinctus.definition: cinctus, a, um, Part., from cingo.

cinctutus.definition: cinctūtus, a, um, a lengthened form from cinctus, like astutus, actutum, versutus, etc., from astus, actus, versus, etc. Girded, girt (rare; perh. only in the foll. exs.): Luperci, * Ov F 5, 101 Cethegi, i. e. the ancients (who did not, like the more effeminate men of a later time, wear the tunic ungirded), * Hor. A. P 50.

cineraceus.definition: cĭnĕrācĕus, a, um, cinis Similar to ashes, ashy terra, Plin. 17, 5, 4, § 33: color,ash-colored,id. 27, 7, 27, § 44.

cinerarium.definition: cĭnĕrārĭum, ii, v. cinerarius, II. B.

cinerarius.definition: cĭnĕrārĭus, a, um, adj.cinis Pertaining to ashes. As adj. very rare: fines, boundaries of land bordering upon graves, Auct. Limit. p 296 Goes. More freq. subst.

cinereus.definition: cĭnĕrĕus, a, um, cinis Similar to ashes, ash-colored: color,Col. 2, 2, 16; Scrib. 23; Plin. 37, 10, 68, § 183 sq.: terra,id. 35, 16, 54, § 192 uva, id. 14, 3, 4, § 42.—Hence, subst.: cĭnĕrĕum, ĕi, n., a kind of salve, Scrib. Comp. 37; cf.: collyrium spodiacum a quibusdam cinereum dicitur,id. ib. 24 init.

cingetorix.definition: A Gaul, rival of his father-in-law Indutiomarus, in respect to dominion over the Treviri, Caes B. G. 5, 3; 5, 56 al A king of the region about Cantium, in Britain, Caes. B. G. 5, 22.

cingillum.definition: dim.cingulum A small girdle, Petr 67, 4; Not. Tir. p 158 Grut.; cf.: cingillus, στρόφιον, ζώνιον, Gloss.

cingo.definition: cingo, xi, nctum, 3, cf. Gr κυλλός, κυρτός; Lat. curvus, and clingo,Georg Curtius Griech. Etym. p. 545 sq. To go round in a circle, to surround, encompass, environ, gird, wreathe, crown, etc. (class. in prose and poetry). Prop

cingulum.definition: (access. form M, and , , ; v.infra, cf cingulum hominum generis neutri est, nam animailum feminino genere dicimus has cingulas, Isid. Orig 20, 16, 4; Serv. ad Verg A. 9, 360) [cingo, cf. Varr. L. L. 5, § 114 Müll.]. The girdle encircling the hips, a zone, belt (mostly poet.). Meton., a girdle of the earth, a zone: cingulus, i, * Cic. Rep. 6, 20, 21; Macr. S. Somn. Scip. 2, 5, 7.

cinifes.definition: or (), , , = σκνιπες or κνίπες A kind of stinging insect (eccl. Lat.), Aug Trin. 3, 7; Hier. in Joel, 2, 25; cf. Isid. Orig. 12, 8, 14.

cinis.definition: (in Sing. fem., Lucr. 4, 926; Cat. 68, 90; 101, 4; Caesar, acc. to Non. p. 198, 11; Calvus ap. Non. l. l. and ap. Charis; p. 78 p; App. M. 9, 12, p. 222; Scrib. c. 226; 230; 232; 245, Ser. c. 44; Aus. Parent 27, 3; Inscr. Orell 4479; cf. Neue, Formenl. 1, p. 657; access. form: hoc , Gloss. Labb.; Sicul. Flacc. p. 140, 17,Agrim. p. 308, 3; p. 308, 5; cf. Lachm. ad Lucr 2, p. 190, and a nom. is mentioned by Prisc. 5, p. 688: 6, p. 707) [kindr with ...

cinisculus.definition: dim.cinis A little ashes: arens,Prud. Cath. 10, 149.

cinnamomum.definition: or , , n. (post-class. access. form , , m., Sol. 33, in the signif. of ll.), = κινναμωμον or κίνναμον [] Cinnamon: Laurus cinnamomum, Linn. Meton. for twigs of cinnamon; plur.: cinnama,Ov. M. 15, 399; 10, 308; id. F. 3, 731; Stat. S. 2, 6, 88; Claud. Laud. Stil. 2, 420.

cinnus.definition: kindr. with κυκεών, κόγχος A mixed drink of spelt-grain and wine, Arn. 5, 174; cf. Non. p. 59, 30.

cinyphes.definition: corrupted from κνῖπες, σκνῖπες Very small flies, gnats, Isid. Orig. 12, 8, 14.

cinyra.definition: ; Gr. κινύρα The lyre, an instrument of ten strings, Vulg. 1 Macc. 4, 54; 13, 51.

cippus.definition: (), , kindr. with scipio; cf. σκήπτω A pale, stake, post, pillar, Lucil. ap. Fest. p. 258; and specif. A gravestone, tombstone, * Hor. S. 1, 8, 12; Pers. 1, 37; Prud. Apoth. 361; Inscr. Orell. 4524 al. In the Agrimensores, a landmark, boundary-stone or post, Simplic. ap. Goes. p. 88.—* In milit. lang., , , , a bulwark formed of sharpened stakes, Caes. B. G. 7, 73.

cipus.definition: () A fabled Roman proetor, upon whose head horns grew suddenly, Ov. M. 15, 565; Plin. 11, 37, 45, § 123; Val. Max. 5, 6, 3.

circa.definition: circā, a later access. form for circum; not freq. before the Aug. per., esp. in Livy and Quintilian [acc. to Klotz, circa = circum ea; cf: antea, interea, postea, praeterea, etc.]. Adv. Prep. with acc.

circellus.definition: dim.circulus A small ring, Apic. 2, 5, Schol Juv. 6, 379.

circensis.definition: Circensis, e, v. Circus, II. b.

circes.definition: circum-ire A circle (ante- and post-class.): ut parvi circuli Anuli, sic magni dicebantur circites Ani, Varr L. L. 6, § 8 Müll.; Sid. Carm. 22, 222. —So of the circumference of the circus, Sid. Carm. 23, 381.

circinatio.definition: circino (lit. the describing of a circle; hence, concrete) The circumference of a circle, a circle (a word of Vitr.): linea circinationis,Vitr. 1, 6, 6: circuli,id. 9, 7, 2; 3, 3; 10, 10 al.—Of the circular path of the planets, Vitr. 9, 4, pp. 264, 266 Bip.

circino.definition: circĭno, āvi, ātum, 1, circinus To make round, to round (perh. not anteAug.): arbores, quae in orbem ramos circinant,Plin. 17, 12, 17, § 88; 16, 38, 73, § 185: circinatum tympanum,id. 18, 34, 77, § 332: folia circinatae rotunditatis,id. 16, 23, 35, § 86—Poet.: (Cyllenius) inclinat cursus, et easdem circinat auras, flies through in a circular course, * Ov. M. 2, 721: utque suos arcus per nubila circinat Iris,vaults, arches,Manil. 1, 710.

circinus.definition: circĭnus, i M.. = κίρκινος, a pair of compasses' flumen Dubis. ut circino circumductum, paene totum oppidum cingit, Caes. B. G. 1, 38: diducere,Vitr. 9, 7, 2: circino spatia dimetiri, id ib.; id. 10, 4, 1: ratio circini,Plin. 2, 15, 13, § 63.

circiter.definition: circĭter, adv. and prep. circus. Adv. Prep. with acc. (orig. an adv. with acc. of time or of space traversed; cf. Hand, Turs. II. p. 71 sq.).

circitor.definition: (or , Petr. 53, 10), , for circumitor, from circumeo, lit. one who goes around, hence A watchman (of gardens. buildings, etc.; postclass.),Auct. Priap. 16, 1, Front. Aquaed. 117; Petr. 1 1. In milit. lang., plur., those who go the rounds and visit the posts of sentinels, patrols, Veg. Mil. 3, 8; Hier. Ep. 61, n. 7.—Sing.' CIRCITOR, Inscr. Murat. 540, 2. A pedler, Dig. 14, 3, 5, § 4.

circitorius.definition: circĭtōrĭus, a, umcircitor, II. Pertaining to patrols: dignitas, Cod. Th. 7, 22, 2, § 2.

circius.definition: (, Cato ap. Gell. 2, 22, 28 sq.), , perh. from circus, on account of its circular motion, but said to be a Gallic word A violent wind blowing in Gallia Narbonensis; to the Romans,a west-northwest wind,Plin. 2, 47, 46, § 121; Sen. Q. N. 5, 17, 5, Vitr. 1, 6, 10; Suet. Claud. 17; Favorin. ap. Gell. 2, 22, 20 sq.

circuitio.definition: (, Cic. Div. 2, 17, 40; 2, 61, 127; Liv. 3, 6, 9; Front. de Or. 3; Amm. 24, 2, 2), , circumeo. A going round; in milit. lang., the rounds: circuitio ac cura (vigiliarum) aedilium plebei erat. Liv. 3, 6, 9. Meton. (abstr. pro concr.), a place for going round something, a way, passage, corridor, Vitr. 4, 4; 6, 3; 10, 19.

circuitus.definition: circŭĭtus, a, um, Part., from circumeo.

circularis.definition: circŭlāris, e, circulus Circular, round (post-class.): flexus,Mart. Cap. 6, § 579; 8, § 814 init.

circulator.definition: id.. A pedler: auctionum, Asin. ap. Cic. Fam. 10, 32, 3. A mountebank, quack, Cels. 5, 27, 3; Petr 68, 6; Dig. 47, 11, 11; Sen. Ben. 6, 11, 2; App. M. 1, p. 103, 38.—Of noisy philosophers, Sen. Ep. 29, 5

circulatrix.definition: id. A female mountebank or stroller, Auct. Priap. 18, 1. —Adj.: lingua,of a mountebank,Mart. 10, 3, 2.

circulo.definition: circŭlo, āre, (post - class. collat. form of circulor) [circulus] To make circu lar or round, App. flor. 9, p. 346, 21. circulatus gressus, Cael. Aur Tard. 1, 1: digitos. bent in, App. Mag. 89, p. 330. Esp., to encircle, encompass: verticem varietatibus,Mart. Cap. 7, § 728: sideribus,id. 8, § 831; 4, § 333 al.; cf. Neue, Formenl. 2, p. 269.

circulor.definition: circŭlor, ātus, 1, id.. To form a circle (of men) about one's self, or to gather in a company or circle for conversation, * Cic. Brut. 54, 200: totis vero castris milites circulari et dolere, etc.,Caes. B. C. 1, 64.—Hence Of mountebanks, to collect people around one's self, Sen. Ep. 40, 3; 52, 7.

circulus.definition: (contr. , like vinclum = vinculum, Verg. G. 3, 166) [kindred with κίρκος, κύκλος, circinus] A circular figure, a circle: circulus aut orbis, qui κύκλος Graece dicitur, Cic. N. D. 2, 18, 47: muri exterior,Liv. 36, 9, 12: circulus ad speciem caelestis arcūs orbem solis ambiit,Suet. Aug. 95. Meton.

circum.definition: circumproperly acc. from circus = κίρκος, adv. and prep., designates either an entire encompassing or surrounding of an object, or a proximity only partially em. bracing or comprehending it Around, about, all around, περί, ἀμφί Adv. Prep. with acc.

circumactio.definition: circumago. Lit., a turning around, revolving (very rare): solis,Vitr. 9, 9, 15; Mart. Cap. 8, § 885.—* Trop., of discourse, a turning, turn, compass, Gell. 17, 20, 4.

circumactus.definition: circumactus, a, um, Part. and , from circumago, q. v. Fin.

circumaggero.definition: circum-aggĕro, no Perf., ātum, 1, , to heap up around (very rare): terram,Col. 5, 12, 3: fimo radices,Plin. 19, 5, 23, § 68.

circumago.definition: circum-ăgo, ēgi, actum, 3, v. a. To drive or turn in a circle, turn round (most freq. since the Aug. per.; not in Cic. or Quint.): impera suovetaurilia circumagi,Cato, R. R. 141, 1.—And with two acc. (on account of circum): terram fundumque meum suovetaurilia circumagi jussi,Cato, R. R. 141, § 2: (annus) qui solstitiali circumagitur orbe,Liv. 1, 19, 6: chamaeleonis oculos ipsos circumagi totos tradunt,Plin. 11, 37, 55, § 152.—Act. in mid. sense (...

circumamictus.definition: circum-ămictus, a, um, amicio Enveloped, invested (eccl. Lat.), Vulg. Apoc. 4, 4.

circumaro.definition: circum-ăro, āre To plough around, Liv. 2, 10, 12; Plin. 18, 3, 3, § 9.

circumcido.definition: circum-cīdo, cīdi, cīsum, 3, v. a.caedo To cut around, cut, clip, trim (orig. in agriculture; syn.: amputo, reseco): ars agricolarum, quae circumcidat, amputet, erigat, etc.,Cic. Fin. 5, 14, 39: gemmam acuto scalpello circumcidito... ejusdem spatii corticem circumcidito,Col. Arb. 26, 8; 12, 36: latera scrobis,id. 5, 9, 9: arbores ad medullam,Plin. 16, 39, 74, § 191: aciem,Lucr. 3, 412: caespitem gladiis,Caes. B. G. 5, 42: ungues,Cels. 7, 26, 2: v...

circumcingo.definition: circum-cingo, ĕre To enclose around, surround: quā Mons Apenninus regiones Italiae Etruriaeque circumcingit,Vitr. 2, 6, 5: eum zonā gloriae,Vulg. Ecclus. 45, 9: PORTICVS,Inscr. Orell. 4043.—In part. pres., Cels. 7, 15: telis circumcingentibus,Sil. 10, 2.

circumcirca.definition: circum-circā, , a strengthened circum or circa All around (cf. the Heb. , Vulg. Ezech. 40, 5; the Gr. ἀμφὶ τερί; and our round about—very rare, perh. only in the foll. exs.; and acc. to Serg. ap. Don. p. 1855 P. also in Cato): ubi erat haec defossa, occoepit scalpturire ibi ungulis circumcirca, * Plaut. Aul. 3, 4, 9: coepi regiones circumcirca prospicere, Sulp. ap. Cic. Fam. 4, 5, 4; Auct. B. Hisp. 41; App. M. 11, p. 258, 23; cf. Prisc. p. 989...

circumcirco.definition: circumcirco, āre, , = circumeo To go round: regiones,Amm. 31, 2, 23 Eyssenh.; dub. (al. circumcurrunt).

circumcise.definition: circumcīsē, , v. circumcido P. a. fin.

circumcisio.definition: circumcido A cutting around, circumcision, physical and moral (only in eccl. Lat.): carnis, cordis, spiritūs,Lact. 4, 17, 1 sqq.; Tert. adv. Jud. 2; 3 et saep.

circumcisorium.definition: id. An instrument for cutting around, Veg. Vet. 1, 26, 2; cf. id. ib. 2, 28, 31.

circumclamo.definition: circum-clāmo, āre To roar around, poet. of the raging waves: ora circumclamata procellis,Sid. Carm. 2, 506.

circumclaudo.definition: circum-claudo, ĕre, 3, (postclass. collat. form of circumcludo) To shut in: farinā circumclaudendus locus,Cael. Aur. Tard. 4, 7, 103.

circumcludo.definition: circum-clūdo, si, sum, 3, claudo To shut in, enclose on every side (in good class. prose): ne duobus circumcluderetur exercitibus,Caes. B. C. 3, 30; cf. * Suet. Tib. 20; Auct. B. Hisp. 6: cornua ab labris argento,to surround with a rim of silver,Caes. B. G. 6, 28 fin.; Plin. 18, 35, 78, § 344: SEPVLCRVM MACERIIS,Inscr. Orell. 4349. Trop.: L. Catilina consiliis, laboribus, periculis meis circumclusus ac debilitatus,hemmed in,Cic. Cat. 2, 7, 14: al...

circumcola.definition: circumcolo Dwelling around: gentes,Tert. adv. Gnost. 3 fin.

circumcolo.definition: circum-cŏlo, ĕre To dwell round about or near: sinum maris,Liv. 5, 33, 10: paludem,id. 31, 41, 4; absol., Dig. 43, 12, 1; cf. ib. 43, 13, 1: Amazones circumcolunt Tanain,Amm. 22, 8, 27: insulam,id. 22, 8, 43.

circumcordialis.definition: circum-cordĭālis, e Around the heart (post-class.): calor,Tert. Anim. 43: sanguis,id. ib. 15.

circumcurso.definition: circum-curso, āre, and n. To run round about, to run about in, at, or near something (ante- and post-class.; in Cic. Fam. 7, 1, 5, more recent editt. read concursare); act.: omnia, * Plaut. Rud. 1, 4, 4: aliquam hinc illinc, * Cat. 68, 133.— Absol.: hac illac, * Ter. Heaut. 3, 2, 1: atria versari et circumcursare columnae... uti pueris videantur,Lucr. 4, 400: per omnes portas,Lact. 6, 12 (in paraphr. of Cic.).

circumdatio.definition: circumdo The putting around: auri,Vulg. 1 Pet. 3, 3.

circumdo.definition: circum-do, dĕdi, dătum, dăre, , lit. To put, set, or place around, i. e. both to wrap around (e. g. a mantle). and also to enclose (e. g. a town with a wall; syn.: cingo, vestio, saepio, circumvallo al.), with a twofold construction (cf. Zumpt, Gr. § 418). Aliquid (alicui rei), to place something around something, to put, set around, etc. (class. in prose and poetry). Aliquem or aliquid (aliquā re), to surround some person or thing (with somethin...

circumdoleo.definition: circum-dŏlĕo, ēre To sufferon every side: spiratio circumdolens; acc. to Forcellini: circum, seu undique, vel ab omni parte angens,i.e. very painful,Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 14, 92.

circumduco.definition: circum-dūco, xi, ctum, 3, ( Imper. circumduce, Plaut. As. 1, 1, 83; id. Most. 3, 2, 159; id. Mil. 2, 2, 66), to lead or draw around (class.; esp. freq. in milit. lang.; in Cic. perh. only once). Prop.: circumduce exercitum,Plaut. Mil. 2, 2, 66; cf. Liv. 1, 27, 8; 8, 13, 8: miles aliquo circumducitur,Plaut. Truc. 4, 4, 21: quattuor cohortibus longiore itinere circumductis,Caes. B. G. 3, 26: alas ad latus Samnitium,Liv. 10, 29, 9: agmen per invia c...

circumductio.definition: circumduco. A leading or conducting around: aquarum,Vitr. 8, 6, 5 sq.: sphaerae,the circumference,Hyg. Astr. 1, 2; of a person, Cod. Th. 4, 8, 1. Trop. *

circumductor.definition: id. One who leads about, converts another, Tert. adv. Val. 10.

circumerro.definition: circŭm-erro, āre To wander round, stroll about: neque turba lateri circumerrat,Sen. Contr. 2, 9, 7: tempora (of the revolution of Saturn in his orbit), to pass through, App. de Mundo, p. 71, 11.

circumferentia.definition: circumfero A circumference (post-class.): sedilium,App. Flor. 18, p. 359; Mart. Cap. 8, § 817; Front. Expos. Form. p. 33 Goes.

circumfero.definition: circum-fĕro, tŭli, lātum, ferre V. a. to bear round, or, in gen., to move or carry round or about (class. in prose and poetry). Prop.: age circumfer mulsum,pass around,Plaut. Pers. 5, 2, 45: satiatis vino ciboque poculum... circumferetur,Liv. 26, 13, 18: circumferri vinum largius jubet,Curt. 7, 4, 7: hisce (poculis) etiam nunc in publico convivio potio circumfertur,Varr. L. L. 5, § 122 Müll.: sanguinem in pateris,Sall. C. 22, 1; Flor. 4, 1, 4 Duk...

circumfigo.definition: circum-fīgo, ĕre To fix or fasten round (very rare): columellam cuneis,Cato, R. R. 20, 1: duo scelesti circumfiguntur Christo,Tert. adv. Marc. 4, 42.

circumfingo.definition: circum-fingo, ĕre To form around: carnem alicui,Tert. Anim. 23.

circumfinio.definition: circum-fīnĭo, īre To complete a circle, to bring to an end: annum,Sol. 3.

circumflagro.definition: circum-flagro, āre To blaze or scorch all around: per immensum circumflagrantibus Austris,Avien. Arat. 274.

circumflecto.definition: circum-flecto, xi, xum, 3 To bend or turn about (Verg. and post-class. writers); prop. of the charioteer in the circus; hence, transf.' longos cursus,Verg. A. 5, 131; 3, 430. Trop.: circumflexa saecula,returning upon themselves,Claud. VI. Cons. Hon. 391: anceps labyrinthus et error circumflexus,full of windings and turnings,Prud. Apoth. 71.

circumflexibilis.definition: circumflexĭbĭlis, e, circumflecto Provided with a circumflex accent (late Lat.), Excerpt. ex Macr. Diff. p. 235 Jan.

circumflexio.definition: id. A bending or winding round: obliqua circuli,Macr. Somn. Scip. 1, 12, 1.

circumflo.definition: circum -flo, āre To blow round about; of the wind (very rare; in the class. per. only in the foll. exs.): circumflantibus Austris,Stat. Th. 11, 42. Trop.: ab omnibus ventis invidiae circumflari, to be assailed by every blast. of envy, * Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 41, § 98.

circumfluo.definition: circum-flŭo, xi, 3, and A., to flow round (class. in prose and poetry). Trop.

circumfluus.definition: circumflŭus, a, um, circumfluo (poet. or in post-Aug. prose). Act., flowing around, circumfluent: umor,Ov. M. 1, 30: amnis,id. ib. 15, 739: mare,Plin. 2, 66, 66, § 166.—More freq. Pass., flowed around, surrounded with water: insula,Ov. M. 15, 624: tellus Hadriaco ponto,Luc. 4, 407: Carthago pelago,Sil. 15, 220: urbs Ponto,Val. Fl. 5, 442: campi Euphrate et Tigre, * Tac. A. 6, 37: omnis circumfluo ambitu Pontus est,Amm. 22, 8, 46.

circumfodio.definition: circum -fŏdĭo, no Perf., fossum, ĕre (inf. pass.: circumfodiri,Col. 5, 9, 12; cf. fodio), and a., to dig around something, dig about (agricultural t. t.).

circumforaneus.definition: circum -fŏrānĕus, a, um, forum. * Of or around the forum or market-place: aes, debts due in the forum (because the bankers' shops were at the forum), Cic. Att. 2, 1, 11.—More freq. Strolling about from market to market, that attends markets: pharmacopola,Cic. Clu. 14, 40: lanista, * Suet. Vit. 12: medicabulum,App. M. 9, p. 218, 41.

circumfractus.definition: circum-fractus, a, um, Part. [frango] Broken off around: turbo, broken around (sc. scopulos), Amm. 22, 8, 15: colles,precipitous,id. 29, 4, 5.

circumfremo.definition: circum -frĕmo, ĕre, and A., to make a noise around something (post-Aug. and rare): nidos, of birds,Sen. Cons. ad Marc. 7, 2; Prud. Cath. 479.

circumfulcio.definition: circum-fulcĭo, īre To support, hold up around: togam,Tert. Pall. 5.

circumfundo.definition: circum-fundo, fūdi, fūsum, 3, , lit. To pour out around, i.e. as in circumdo, either with the acc. of that which is poured, to pour around; or, with the acc. of that around which something is poured, to surround with a liquid (class. in prose and poetry). Lit. Transf. to objects that do not flow, esp. if there is a great multitude, as it were, heaped upon a thing.

circumfusio.definition: circumfundo A pouring around (post-class.) spiritus ignei, Firm. Math. 1, 4: Oceani,id. ib. praef.

circumgarriens.definition: circum -garrĭens, entis, Part. [garrio] Blabbing or babbling about. falsiloquia, Claud Mam. Stat. An. 2, 9.

circumgesto.definition: circum-gesto, āre To bear or carry around' epistulam, * Cic. Q. Fr. 1, 2, 2, § 6; deam,App. M. 8, 213, 37.

circumgredior.definition: circum-grĕdĭor, gressus, grĕdi V dep [gradior], to go or walk around, travel about (esp. in a hostile manner; post-Aug., several times in Tac, elsewhere rare).

circumgressus.definition: circumgressus, a, um, Part., from circumgredior

circumhisco.definition: circum-hisco, ĕre V. n, to stare about with open mouth, Arn. 5, p 175 dub. (al. circumsciscere)

circumhumatus.definition: circum -hŭmātus, a, um Part [humo], buried around: corpora, Amm 22, 12, 8.

circumicio.definition: circum-ĭcĭo or circum-jĭcĭo (access. form circum-jăcĭo, Liv 33, 18, 17, where more recent editt. read circumagere), jēci, jectum, 3, v. a. To cast, throw, or place around (in good class. prose)' amic tum, Varr. L. L. 5, § 132: vallum, Liv 35, 4, 6: fossam quoque et alia munimenta verticibus iis... circumjecere,id. 38, 19, 5: pars urbis, cui brevior orbis munitionis circumjectus erat,id. 36, 9, 12 miles moenibus Cremonensium castra sua, castris va...

circuminvolvo.definition: circŭm-involvo, ĕre To involve all around, to enclose, envelop: singula puncta,Vitr. 10, 11 (al. circumvolvo).

circuminuoluo.definition: circŭm-involvo, ĕre To involve all around, to enclose, envelop: singula puncta,Vitr. 10, 11 (al. circumvolvo).

circumiaceo.definition: circum-jăcĕo, ĕre To lie round about, border upon (rare; not in Cic.). Trop., in rhet.: circumjăcentĭa, ĭum, n., the context, Qumt. 9, 4, 29.

circumiectio.definition: circumicio. A throwing around, casting about (postclass.) manuum, Cael. Aur Acut. 1, 2, 31. —* A putting on clothing, dressing: corporis,Arn. 2, p 73

circumiectus.definition: circumjectus, a, um, Part., from circumicio

circumlaticius.definition: circumlātĭcĭus or -tĭus, a, um, circumlatus That may be carried around, portable carcer, Sid. Ep 2, 2 fin.

circumlator.definition: id. One who carries about (post-class.), Tert. adv Marc. 1, 19; 1, 21 fin

circumlavo.definition: circum-lăvo, āre and ĕre V a., lit. to wash around, hence, of waters, to overflow all around (only in the foll. exs.): Aegyptus, quam Nilus circumlavat,Hyg. Fab 275: insula superjactis fluctibus circumlavitur, Sall. ap Non. p. 504, 1 (id. H. 2, 83 Dietsch).

circumlauo.definition: circum-lăvo, āre and ĕre V a., lit. to wash around, hence, of waters, to overflow all around (only in the foll. exs.): Aegyptus, quam Nilus circumlavat,Hyg. Fab 275: insula superjactis fluctibus circumlavitur, Sall. ap Non. p. 504, 1 (id. H. 2, 83 Dietsch).

circumlevo.definition: circum-lĕvo, āre V a., to raise up all around tegmina, Cael Aur Acut. 2, 37, 194.

circumleuo.definition: circum-lĕvo, āre V a., to raise up all around tegmina, Cael Aur Acut. 2, 37, 194.

circumligo.definition: circum-lĭgo, āvi, ātum, 1 Aliquid alicui rei, to bind something to something' natam mediae circumligat hastae, * Verg. A. 11, 555' spongias hydropicis, Plin 31, 11, 47, § 128.—More freq. Aliquid aliquā re, to bind something with something, to encompass, surround: stirpem salice,Cato, R. R. 40, 2: ferrum stuppā, Liv 21, 8, 10: totas (radices) caespite,Plin. 17, 11, 16, § 86' Roscius circumligatus angui, * Cic. Div. 2, 31, 66; Plin. 28, 2, 5, § 29....

circumlino.definition: circum-lĭno, lĭtum, 3 ( Perf. late Lat. circumlinisti, Vulg. Ezech. 23, 40), (access. form circumlĭnĭo, īre; cf. lino; so, circumliniunt,Quint. 12, 9, 8 Spald. N. er.: circumliniri,id. 1, 11, 6: circumliniendus,Col. 6, 16, 3; 6, 17, 9). Aliquid alicui, to smear, stick, or spread all over, to besmear: vulneribus aliquid circumlinitur,Plin. 22, 23, 49, § 103: Galbanum ramis ellebori circumlitum,id. 24, 5, 13, § 22: ciroumlita taedis sulfura,Ov. M. ...

circumlitio.definition: circumlino. A smearing or spreading over, anointing: oris,Plin. 24, 7, 24, § 40. In painting, an overlaying of color, the tint or hue given to marble by rubbing it with a mixture of oil and wax, Plin. 35, 11, 40, § 133; Sen. Ep. 86, 5; v O. Müll. Archaeol. § 310, 4.

circumlocutio.definition: circumloquor Circumlocution, periphrasis, = περίφρασις, * Quint. 8, 6, 61; Gell. 3, 1, 5; Arn. 6, p. 210.

circumloquor.definition: circum-lŏquor, lŏcūtus, lŏqui To make use of circumlocution or periphrasis (post-class.), Aus. Ep. 6, 7, and 146, 15.

circumluo.definition: circum-lŭo, ĕre To flow around or wash upon (rare): Rhenus tergum ac latera circumluit,Tac. H. 4, 12: pars arcis circumluitur mari,Liv. 25, 11, 1: litora subit et circumluit pelagus, Mel. prooem. 2: (Aegeum) mare laevā Imbrum et Tenedum circumluens,Amm. 22, 8, 2.

circumlustro.definition: circum-lustro, āvi, 1 To light all around; in tmesis: mundi templum, Lucr 5, 1437. Trop., to travel over or through: populos provinciae, Cod. Th. 4, 8, 5.

circummeo.definition: circum-mĕo, āvi, āre, and n. To go around: circum eam (sc. Taprobanen) isse, for circummeasse,Mel. 3, 7; Tert. Pall. 1.

circummitto.definition: circum-mitto, mīsi, missum, 3 To send around: legationes in omnes partes,Caes. B. G. 7, 63; id. B. C. 3, 55: praecones, id B. G. 5, 51; id. B. C. 1, 12: jugo circummissus Veiens,Liv. 2, 50, 10: post montes,id. 4, 18, 4: milites,id. 29, 33, 3; 36, 14, 13: scaphas,id. 29, 25, 7.

circummunio.definition: circum -mūnĭo (old orthog. cir-cummoenĭo, Plaut. Capt. 2, 2, 4), īvi, ītum, 4 To wall up around, to fortify, secure (freq. in the histt., elsewhere rare; but in MSS. constantly confounded with circumvenire; cf. Oud. ad Caes. B. C. 1, 18; 1, 81; 1, 84; 2, 16; 3, 97; Schneid. ad Col. 5, 9, 11; 5, 10, 1): plantas caveis,Col. 5, 9, 11: oppidum, Auct. B. Afr. 79: Thapsum operibus,id. ib. 80; cf. Auct. B. Hisp. 38: aliquos ut feras,Caes. B. C. 1, 84: (...

circummunitio.definition: circummunio; In milit. lang.,an investing of a town, circumvallation,Caes. B. C. 1, 19 fin.; Auct. B. Hisp. 38 fin.

circummuranus.definition: circum-mūrānus, a, um, murus Around (but beyond) the walls (perh. only in Amm.): bella,with the neighboring nations,Amm. 14, 6, 4: pericula,id. 21, 13, 2.

circumnecto.definition: circum-necto, no Perf., nexum, ĕre, , to wrap or bind around, surround, envelop (late Lat.): elephanti flammis conjectis undique circumnexi,Amm. 19, 7, 7: tenuis membrana illa perlucens, quā circumnectitur alvus, ac tegitur, Lact. Opif. Dei, 14, 2 (al. circumretitur).

circumornatus.definition: circum-ornātus, a, um Ornamented round about, Vulg. Psa. 143, 12.

circumpadanus.definition: circum-pădānus, a, um Found or situate around the Po: campi,Liv. 21, 35, 8: lanae,Plin. 8, 48, 73, § 190: musta,id. 14, 20, 25, § 125.

circumpendeo.definition: circum-pendeo (better written as two words), ēre To hang around: margaritis circum pendentibus,Curt. 8, 9, 24; Ov. F. 2, 529.

circumpes.definition: circum-pēs, pĕdis (that is round the feet). A kind of parasites (cf. antepes), Agroet. Orth. p. 2274 P. A covering of the foot, περισκελίς, Vulg. Ecclus. 45, 10.

circumplecto.definition: circumplecto, ĕre ( Act. collat. form of circumplector; cf. Neue, Formenl. 2, p. 312), to embrace, clasp around: meum collum circumplecte,Plaut. As. 3, 3, 106: circumplectito foramina laminis,Cato, R. R. 21, 2.—Part. pass. circumplexus: turris igni,Gell. 15, 1, 6: venter,App. Dogm. Plat. 1, p. 171 sq.

circumplector.definition: circum-plector, plexus, 3 V. dep. a., to clasp around, embrace, to surround, encompass (class. in prose and poetry): conjunctiones motu undique,Cic. Univ. 7 fin.: domini patrimonium quasi thesaurum draco,id. Phil. 13, 5, 12: arborem,Plin. 19, 4, 22, § 63; 13, 10, 19, § 65: pharetram auro,Verg. A. 5, 312: collem opere,to circumvallate,Caes. B. G. 7, 83: oppidum tragulis, Auct. B. Hisp. 32; Suet. Tib. 6: statuam pennis, of the eagle,id. Dom. 6; Sta...

circumplico.definition: circum-plĭco, āvi, ātum To wind, fold, or twine around: tum esset ostentum, si anguem vectis circumplicavisset,Cic. Div. 2, 28, 62: locum surculo,Gell. 17, 9, 14 (cf. id. 17, 9, 14, § 9): belua circumplicata serpentibus,Cic. Div. 1, 24, 49: puer serpentis amplexu,id. ib. 1, 36, 79. To bend around, Lact. Opif. Dei, 12, 5.

circumpono.definition: circum-pōno, pŏsui, pŏsĭtum, 3 To set, put, or place around (perh. not before the Aug. per.): ferulas,Cels. 8, 10, 1: stramenta, Plin. 17, 28, 47, § 263: armatos, * Suet. Caes. 30: piper catillis, * Hor. S. 2, 4, 75: nemus stagno,Tac. A. 14, 15; id. H. 2, 59.

circumpositio.definition: circumpono A setting or placing around (eccl. Lat.): auri,Aug. Ep. 199; Ambros. Ep. 38, 1.

circumpungo.definition: circum-pungo, ĕre To prick or puncture around: clavum pedis,Cels. 5, 28, 14 (cf.: clavi circum scarificati,Plin. 22, 23, 49, § 101).

circumrado.definition: circum-rādo, rāsi, rāsum, ĕre To scrape, shave, or pare around: tonsillas digito,Cels. 7, 12, n. 2: dentem,id. ib.: sarmentum circumrasum,Col. 4, 29, 14.

circumretio.definition: circum-rētĭo, īvi, ītum, 4 To enclose with a net, insnare. Prop.: Martem et Venerem Vulcani esse circumretitos arte,Arn. 5, p. 186; cf. id. 4, p. 181; cf. circumnecto fin. Trop.: aliquem,Lucr. 5, 1152: aliquem fraude,Sid. Ep. 5, 13: cum te implicatum severitate judicum, circumretitum frequentiă populi Romani esse videam, * Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 58, § 150.

circumrodo.definition: circum-rōdo, di, 3 To gnaw or nibble all round. Prop.: escam,Plin. 32, 2, 5, § 12. Trop.: dudum enim circumrodo, quod devorandum est, i. e. I have long hesitated to speak out, * Cic. Att. 4, 5, 1: qui Dente Theonino cum circumroditur, i. e. is slandered, calumniated, * Hor. Ep. 1, 18, 82.

circumroto.definition: circum-rŏto, āre To turn round in a circle: caeli orbem, C. German. Fragm. 3, 9: machinas,App. M. 9, p. 222, 7.

circumscribo.definition: circum-scrībo, psi, ptum, 3, v. a. Prop., to draw a line around, to circumscribe, enclose in a circle (in good prose; very freq. in Cic.): orbem,Cic. Fin. 5, 8, 23: lineas extremas umbrae,Quint. 10, 2, 7: virgulā stantem,Cic. Phil. 8, 8, 23: virgā regem,Liv. 45, 12, 5: aeneā fibulā pars auriculae latissima circumscribitur,Col. 6, 5, 4: terram surculo heliotropii,Plin. 22, 21, 29, § 60. Trop.

circumscripte.definition: circumscriptē, adv., v. circumscri, bo, P. a. 1. and 2.

circumscriptio.definition: circumscribo. * Prop. (acc. to circumscribo, I.), an encircling, and (concrete) a circle: ex circumscriptione excedere,Cic. Phil. 8, 8, 23. (Acc. to circumscribo, II. A.) A boundary, limit, outline, contour, circuit, compass (most freq. in Cic.): terrae situm, formam, circumscriptionem, Cic. Tusc. 1, 20, 45: aeternitas, quam nulla temporis circumscriptio metiebatur,id. N. D. 1, 9, 21: corporeae forma circumscriptionis,Arn. 2, 93; 3, 135.

circumscriptor.definition: circumscribo. * (Acc. to circumscribo, II. C.) A defrauder, deceiver, cheat, * Cic. Cat. 2, 4, 7; * Juv. 15, 136; Sen. Exc. Contr. 6, 3; Cod. Th. 10, 10, 27, § 4.—* (Acc. to circumscribo, II. D.) He who makes void, annuls: sententiae suae,Tert. adv. Marc. 1, 27.

circumscriptus.definition: circumscriptus, a, um, Part. and , from circumscribo, q. v. Fin.

circumseco.definition: circum-sĕco, no Perf., sectum āre, , to cut or pare around: radices vitium,Cato, R. R. 114, 1: ungulas,Col. 6, 6, 4: tuberculum ferro,id. 7, 5, 13: aliquid serrulā, to saw around, * Cic. Clu. 64, 180: circumsecta aluta,Scrib. Comp. 229.—* To circumcise, of the Jews (usu. circumcido), Suet. Dom. 12.

circumsedeo.definition: circum-sĕdĕo (sĭdĕo), sēdi, sessum, 2 To sit around a person or thing, to surround. In gen., absol.: inter tot milia populi circumsedentis,App. M. 3, p. 130, 2; Sid. Ep. 3, 13.—With acc.: florentes amicorum turba circumsedet: circa eversos ingens solitudo est,Sen. Ep. 9, 9.— Esp. To encamp around in a hostile manner, to besiege, blockade, invest, encompass, beset (in Cic. and Liv. several times; elsewhere rare): qui Mutinam circumsedent,Cic. Phil...

circumseparo.definition: circum-sēpăro, āre To separate around: gingivas a dentibus,Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 4, 74.

circumsido.definition: circum-sīdo, ĕre To set or place one's self around in a hostile manner, to besiege (several times in Livy; elsewhere rare): Plistiam,Liv. 9, 21, 6; 36, 13, 7; 41, 19, 10; 42, 56, 5: regem urbemque Philippopolim,Tac. A. 3, 38.

circumsigno.definition: circum-signo, āre To mark around: gemmam,Col. 5, 11, 19; id. Arb. 26, 8; Pall. Jun. 5, 3.

circumsilio.definition: circum-sĭlĭo, īre, salio To spring, leap, or hop around (rare): (passer) circumsiliens modo huc, modo illuc, * Cat. 3, 9.— Trop., to leap about, surround: morborum omne genus, * Juv. 10, 218.

circumsisto.definition: circum-sisto, stĕti (Caes. B. G. 3, 15 Oud. N. cr.; 4, 37; Curt. 15, 9, 10; Verg. A. 2, 559; Tac. A. 15, 15; id. H. 4, 79; cf. circumsto; rarely circumstiti,Tac. H. 3, 31), 3, , to place one's self or take one's stand around a person or thing, to surround, go or stand around (class.; most freq. in the histt.; in Cic. perh. only once).

circumsitus.definition: circum-sĭtus, a, um, sino Lying or situate around, neighboring: populi,Amm. 23, 6, 17, p. 358 Bip. al.

circumsocius.definition: circum-sŏcĭus, a, um Neighborly, in friendly neighborhood: nationes, Sext. Aur. Vict. Epit. 41.

circumsono.definition: circum-sŏno, āre, and A. (rare but class.). Neutr., to sound, resound (with something) on every side, to be filled with any sound: locus, qui circumsonat ululatibus cantuque symphoniae,Liv. 39, 10, 7; 27, 18, 16; Vitr. 5, 8, 1; Manil. 5, 582. Act.

circumsonus.definition: circum-sŏnus, a, um Sounding all around. * Act., filling with sounds: turba canum,barking around,Ov. M. 4, 723.—* Pass., filled with sounds, resounding around: Thisbe avibus,Stat. Th. 7, 261.

circumspectatrix.definition: spectator She who looks or spies around, a spy, Plaut. Aul. 1, 1, 2: juvenum,App. Mag. 76, p. 323, 10.

circumspecte.definition: circumspectē, , v. circumspicio P. a. fin.

circumspecto.definition: circum-specto, āvi, ātum, āre To look about with attention, precaution, desire, etc.; to cast a look around, to search around; and with acc., to look about one's self (attentively, anxiously, etc.) after something, to look all around upon something (class.) Prop. Trop.: dubitans, circumspectans, haesitans, tanquam rate in mari immenso nostra vehitur oratio,Cic. Tusc. 1, 30, 73: circumspectantes defectionis tempus,watching, waiting, on the look-ou...

circumspector.definition: circumspicio A watcher, watchman, spy (late Lat.): septem circumspectores sedentes in excelso ad speculandum,Vulg. Ecclus. 37, 18: Deus,i. e. all-seeing,id. ib. 7, 12.

circumspergo.definition: circum-spergo (-spargo, Apic. 8, 8, § 406; cf. aspergo), ĕre To sprinkle, strew, or scatter something around: quaternos modios stercoris caprini,Col. 11, 2, 87: impensam talem, Apic. l. l. To sprinkle with something all around: se purificantes aquā,Plin. 8, 1, 1, § 2.

circumspicio.definition: circum-spĭcĭo, exi, ectum, 3 ( Perf. sync. circumspexti, Ter. Ad. 4, 5, 55; inf. sync. circumspexe, Varr. ap. Non. p. 106, 16, or Sat. Men. 82), v. n. and a. (class.). Neutr., to look about one's self, to cast a look around; or, with an obj.-clause, to observe, see, look about: circumspicedum, numquis est, Sermonem nostrum quiaucupet,see whether there is any one,Plaut. Most. 2, 2, 41; 2, 2, 43; Ter. And. 2, 2, 20; Varr. l. l.: suus conjux ubi sit...

circumstagno.definition: circum-stagno, āre To be poured forth all around: lacrimae,Tert. Pud. 22.

circumstantia.definition: circumsto (post-Aug. and rare). A standing round, a surrounding: hostium,Gell. 3, 7, 5: aquae, aëris,Sen. Q. N. 2, 7, 2 (as transl. of the Gr. ἀντιπερίστασις).—* Trop., the state, condition, circumstances, attribute, quality: rerum negotiorumque,Gell. 14, 1, 15; 14, 2, 2; Tert. Bapt. 17: hoc genus argumentorum sane dicamus ex circumstantiā, quia περίστασιν dicere aliter non possumus, * Quint. 5, 10, 104.

circumsto.definition: circum-sto, stĕti, 1, and A. (the perf. and pluperf. having the same form with those of circumsisto, and a similar meaning, it is sometimes doubtful to which verb a form belongs), to stand around in a circle, to take a station round; and, with the acc., to stand around a person or thing, to surround, encircle, encompass. Prop. (very freq. and class.). Trop., to surround, encompass, occupy, take possession of (freq. in post-Aug prose); absol. or w...

circumstrepo.definition: circum-strĕpo, no Perf., pĭtum To make a noise around, to din with clamor, to cause to echo around (post-Aug.), (legatus) clamore seditiosorum circumstrepitur, Tac. H. 2, 44: fenestrae canticis circumstrepitae,App. Mag. 75, p. 322, 8; Sid. Ep. 7, 9; Manil. 1, 22. To cry or shout clamorously around (so only twice in Tac.): quidam atrociora circumstrepebant,Tac. A. 3, 36 fin.: ceteri circumstrepunt, iret in castra, etc.,id. ib. 11, 31.

circumstridens.definition: circum-strīdens, entis, Part. [strido] Shrieking or gibbering around: larvae,Amm. 14, 11, 17.

circumstringo.definition: circum-stringo, no Perf., strictum, 3, (post-class.). * To bind about, to put on: aliquid alicui rei: habitus cervicibus circumstrictus,Tert. Pall. 1. To tie around, to surround, clothe with: aliquid aliquā re: pallium,Tert. Pall. 5; id. Cor. Mil. 8.

circumstruo.definition: circum-strŭo, no Perf., ctum, 3, , to build round about, surround with buildings (post-Aug. and mostly in part. pass.).

circumsutus.definition: circum-sūtus, a, um, Part. [suo] Sewed together all around (post-Aug.): linamenta,Cels. 8, 5: navigia corio,Plin. 4, 16, 30, § 104; 34, 16, 47, § 156.

circumtego.definition: circum-tĕgo, ĕre To cover round about (post-class.): corpus veste,Dict. Cret. 3, 11: arca testamenti circumtecta ex omni parte auro,Vulg. Heb. 9, 4; v. also the spurious line,Lucr. 1, 1094 Lachm. and Munro ad loc.

circumteneo.definition: circum-tĕnĕo, ēre To keep around, to possess, Vulg. 4 Esdr. 16, 40.

circumtentus.definition: circum-tentus, a, um, Part. [tendo] Bound or covered with something that is stretched or drawn around, begirt (anteand post-class.): elephanti corio, * Plaut. Mil. 2, 2, 80: vasculum linteolis,Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 17, 174.

circumtermino.definition: circum-termĭno, āre, 1 To bound or limit round about, Isid. Orig. 7, 8, 39.

circumtextus.definition: Part. [texo] Woven all around: velamen,Verg. A. 1, 649. —Subst.: , , n., a garment inwoven with purple: et quod amictui habet purpuram circum, vocant circumtextum,Varr. L. L. 5, § 132; cf. Isid. Orig. 19, 24, 10.

circumtollo.definition: circum-tollo, ĕre To remove on every side: corticem,Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 4, 42.

circumtono.definition: circum-tŏno, ui, 1 To thunder around; or, poet., to make a noise or clamor around: virum armis,Sil. 4, 254: aulam strepitu,id. 6, 216: montem undā,Claud. in Rufin. 1, 274. Trop.: hunc circumtonuit gaudens Bellona cruentis (the figure taken from the clanging of the war-trumpets),Hor. S. 2, 3, 223.

circumtonsus.definition: circum-tonsus, a, um, Part. [tondeo] Shorn all around (rare). Prop., Varr. ap. Non. p. 179, 8; * Suet. Aug. 45: pinus,Petr. 131, 8, 3.—* Trop., of discourse: oratio circumtonsa et fucata et manu facta,elaborate, artificial,Sen. Ep. 115, 2.

circumundique.definition: circum-undĭque, v. circum, I. A. b.

circumvado.definition: circum-vādo, vāsi, 3 V.a., to assail or attack on every side, to encompass, beset (not ante-Aug.). Prop.: naves,Liv. 10, 2, 12: aliquem clamoribus turbidis, * Tac. A. 12, 43: redeuntem noctu,Plin. 9, 30, 48, § 92. —Pass., Amm. 20, 6, 3. Trop., ofterror falling upon one (so only a few times in Liv.): novus terror cum ex parte utrāque circumvasisset aciem,Liv. 9, 40, 13: barbaros,id. 34, 21, 5: urbem,id. 34, 38, 6.

circumuado.definition: circum-vādo, vāsi, 3 V.a., to assail or attack on every side, to encompass, beset (not ante-Aug.). Prop.: naves,Liv. 10, 2, 12: aliquem clamoribus turbidis, * Tac. A. 12, 43: redeuntem noctu,Plin. 9, 30, 48, § 92. —Pass., Amm. 20, 6, 3. Trop., ofterror falling upon one (so only a few times in Liv.): novus terror cum ex parte utrāque circumvasisset aciem,Liv. 9, 40, 13: barbaros,id. 34, 21, 5: urbem,id. 34, 38, 6.

circumvagus.definition: circum-văgus, a, um Wandering about, flowing around (very rare): oceanus, * Hor. Epod. 16, 41; cf. Auct. Pan. ad Pis. 19; Prud. Psych. 814.

circumuagus.definition: circum-văgus, a, um Wandering about, flowing around (very rare): oceanus, * Hor. Epod. 16, 41; cf. Auct. Pan. ad Pis. 19; Prud. Psych. 814.

circumvallo.definition: circum-vallo, āvi, ātum, 1 To surround with a wall, to circumvallate; in milit. lang., to blockade, invest, encompass in a hostile manner (class., esp. in the histt.): circumvallare loci natura prohibebat,Caes. B. G. 7, 17; 7, 11; id. B. C. 3, 43; Liv. 10, 35, 12 and 15; 28, 3, 4, and in part. perf. pass. Caes. B. G. 7, 44 fin.; Cic. Att. 9, 12, 1; Liv. 43, 19, 9. In gen., to surround, encompass: locum duobus sulcis,Col. 11, 3, 4; Claud. IV. Cons...

circumuallo.definition: circum-vallo, āvi, ātum, 1 To surround with a wall, to circumvallate; in milit. lang., to blockade, invest, encompass in a hostile manner (class., esp. in the histt.): circumvallare loci natura prohibebat,Caes. B. G. 7, 17; 7, 11; id. B. C. 3, 43; Liv. 10, 35, 12 and 15; 28, 3, 4, and in part. perf. pass. Caes. B. G. 7, 44 fin.; Cic. Att. 9, 12, 1; Liv. 43, 19, 9. In gen., to surround, encompass: locum duobus sulcis,Col. 11, 3, 4; Claud. IV. Cons...

circumvectio.definition: circumveho (only twice in Cic.). A carrying around (of merchandise), Cic. Att. 2, 16, 4. Solis, the circuit, revolution, Cic. Univ. 9, 26.

circumuectio.definition: circumveho (only twice in Cic.). A carrying around (of merchandise), Cic. Att. 2, 16, 4. Solis, the circuit, revolution, Cic. Univ. 9, 26.

circumvecto.definition: circum-vecto, āre To carry around: Penates,Sil. 3, 291.—Hence Esp., mid., to ride or sail around (rare): Ligurum oram,Liv. 41, 17, 7; cf. circumvectitor.—Poet., to go through, describe: +ugit irreparabile tempus, Singula dum capti circumvectamur amore,Verg. G. 3, 285 (dum speciatim cuncta describimus, Serv.).

circumuecto.definition: circum-vecto, āre To carry around: Penates,Sil. 3, 291.—Hence Esp., mid., to ride or sail around (rare): Ligurum oram,Liv. 41, 17, 7; cf. circumvectitor.—Poet., to go through, describe: +ugit irreparabile tempus, Singula dum capti circumvectamur amore,Verg. G. 3, 285 (dum speciatim cuncta describimus, Serv.).

circumvehor.definition: circum-vĕhor, vectus, 3 To ride around (in a carriage or on horseback), to sail around (class., but not in Cic.); constr. absol. or with acc. dependent on circum: in terras orasque ultimas,Plaut. Most. 4, 3, 4: mare superum omne Graeciamque exoticam... Sumus circumvecti,id. Men. 2, 1, 13: classe Pharon, Auct. B. Alex. 14; cf. Tac. Agr. 10: classe ad Romanum agrum,Liv. 8, 26, 1: circumvectus Brundisii promunturium,id. 10, 2, 4; cf. id. 44, 28, 5: ...

circumuehor.definition: circum-vĕhor, vectus, 3 To ride around (in a carriage or on horseback), to sail around (class., but not in Cic.); constr. absol. or with acc. dependent on circum: in terras orasque ultimas,Plaut. Most. 4, 3, 4: mare superum omne Graeciamque exoticam... Sumus circumvecti,id. Men. 2, 1, 13: classe Pharon, Auct. B. Alex. 14; cf. Tac. Agr. 10: classe ad Romanum agrum,Liv. 8, 26, 1: circumvectus Brundisii promunturium,id. 10, 2, 4; cf. id. 44, 28, 5: ...

circumvenio.definition: circum-vĕnĭo, vēni, ventum, 4, , lit. To come around something; hence (the coming being considered as accomplished; cf. advenio and adventus, II.). Lit. Trop.

circumuenio.definition: circum-vĕnĭo, vēni, ventum, 4, , lit. To come around something; hence (the coming being considered as accomplished; cf. advenio and adventus, II.). Lit. Trop.

circumventor.definition: id. A deceiver, defrauder, Lampr. Alex. Sev. 66.

circumuentor.definition: id. A deceiver, defrauder, Lampr. Alex. Sev. 66.

circumventorius.definition: circumventōrĭus, a, um, circumventor Deceitful, fraudulent: obsequia,Aug. Conf. 3, 3.

circumuentorius.definition: circumventōrĭus, a, um, circumventor Deceitful, fraudulent: obsequia,Aug. Conf. 3, 3.
