circumversio.definition: circumverto A turning round, moving around, revolving (post-Aug. and rare): manus (in gesturing), * Quint. 11, 3, 105 Spald.: cursus annui,Amm. 26, 1, 11.

circumuersio.definition: circumverto A turning round, moving around, revolving (post-Aug. and rare): manus (in gesturing), * Quint. 11, 3, 105 Spald.: cursus annui,Amm. 26, 1, 11.

circumverto.definition: circum-verto or circum verto (-vorto), ĕre To turn around (rare; not in Cic.): citius quam rotula circumvortitur,Plaut. Pers. 3, 3, 39; cf.: rota circumvertitur axem, turns or is turned around on its axis, Ov. M. 15, 522 (Merkel, circumvolvitur): ubi circumvortor, cado,turn myself around,Plaut. Ps. 5, 1, 32; cf.: circumvertens se, turning one's self to the right side, * Suet. Vit. 2; v. the commentt. in h. l.: mancipium,to declare free,Quint. Dec...

circumuerto.definition: circum-verto or circum verto (-vorto), ĕre To turn around (rare; not in Cic.): citius quam rotula circumvortitur,Plaut. Pers. 3, 3, 39; cf.: rota circumvertitur axem, turns or is turned around on its axis, Ov. M. 15, 522 (Merkel, circumvolvitur): ubi circumvortor, cado,turn myself around,Plaut. Ps. 5, 1, 32; cf.: circumvertens se, turning one's self to the right side, * Suet. Vit. 2; v. the commentt. in h. l.: mancipium,to declare free,Quint. Dec...

circumvestio.definition: circum-vestĭo, īre To clothe or cover over (very rare): arborem,Plin. 17, 23, 35, § 208.—In a figure: aliquem amictu prudentiae,Ambros. Virg. 12, 48.—* Poet., of one who uses language to conceal his thoughts: se circumvestire dictis, to wrap himself up in words, Poët. ap. Cic. de Or. 3, 39, 158 (Trag. Rel. inc. v. 113 Rib.).

circumuestio.definition: circum-vestĭo, īre To clothe or cover over (very rare): arborem,Plin. 17, 23, 35, § 208.—In a figure: aliquem amictu prudentiae,Ambros. Virg. 12, 48.—* Poet., of one who uses language to conceal his thoughts: se circumvestire dictis, to wrap himself up in words, Poët. ap. Cic. de Or. 3, 39, 158 (Trag. Rel. inc. v. 113 Rib.).

circumvincio.definition: circum-vincĭo, no Perf., vinctum, 4, , to bind around: juncis murteta, aliquem virgis,Plaut. Rud. 3, 4, 27; Avien. Perieg. 331.

circumuincio.definition: circum-vincĭo, no Perf., vinctum, 4, , to bind around: juncis murteta, aliquem virgis,Plaut. Rud. 3, 4, 27; Avien. Perieg. 331.

circumvolitabilis.definition: circumvŏlĭtābĭlis, e, circumvolito Flying round: aër,Mart. Cap. 6, § 584.

circumuolitabilis.definition: circumvŏlĭtābĭlis, e, circumvolito Flying round: aër,Mart. Cap. 6, § 584.

circumvolito.definition: circum-vŏlĭto or circum vŏlĭto, āvi, 1, and n. (mostly post-Aug.). Prop., to fly around something: lacus circumvolitavit hirundo, * Verg. G. 1, 377: thyma, * Hor. Ep. 1, 3, 21.—Absol.: circumvolitantium alitum,Tac. H. 2, 50. In gen., of men, to rove about a place, to hover around; absol.: et circumvolitant equites, * Lucr. 2, 329; Sil. 9, 420: limina potentiorum, Col. praef. 1, § 9: agmina infestorum equitum ad conquirendas proscriptorum latebras...

circumuolito.definition: circum-vŏlĭto or circum vŏlĭto, āvi, 1, and n. (mostly post-Aug.). Prop., to fly around something: lacus circumvolitavit hirundo, * Verg. G. 1, 377: thyma, * Hor. Ep. 1, 3, 21.—Absol.: circumvolitantium alitum,Tac. H. 2, 50. In gen., of men, to rove about a place, to hover around; absol.: et circumvolitant equites, * Lucr. 2, 329; Sil. 9, 420: limina potentiorum, Col. praef. 1, § 9: agmina infestorum equitum ad conquirendas proscriptorum latebras...

circumvolo.definition: circum-vŏlo, āvi, ātum, 1, (not ante-Aug.). Prop., to fly around: turba (Harpyiae) praedam circumvolat,Verg. A. 3, 233: seu (me) mors atris circumvolat alis,Hor. S. 2, 1, 58; so Verg. A. 2, 360: caput,id. ib. 6, 866; Ov. M. 2, 719; 14, 507: sedem,Quint. 2, 6, 7: aliquem, * Suet. Aug. 97.—Pass.: nave circumvolatā ab halcyone,Plin. 10, 32, 47, § 90. In gen., to run or hasten around: ordines exercitus,Vell. 2, 27, 2: jaculo campum,Sil. 17, 416.

circumuolo.definition: circum-vŏlo, āvi, ātum, 1, (not ante-Aug.). Prop., to fly around: turba (Harpyiae) praedam circumvolat,Verg. A. 3, 233: seu (me) mors atris circumvolat alis,Hor. S. 2, 1, 58; so Verg. A. 2, 360: caput,id. ib. 6, 866; Ov. M. 2, 719; 14, 507: sedem,Quint. 2, 6, 7: aliquem, * Suet. Aug. 97.—Pass.: nave circumvolatā ab halcyone,Plin. 10, 32, 47, § 90. In gen., to run or hasten around: ordines exercitus,Vell. 2, 27, 2: jaculo campum,Sil. 17, 416.

circumvolvo.definition: circum-volvo, no Perf., vŏlūtum, 3, , only with se or mid., to roll one's self around, to roll round, revolve, wind, or twine around (prob. not ante-Aug.): aliquid or alicui rei: magnum sol circumvolvitur annum,Verg. A. 3, 284: rota perpetuum circumvolvitur axem,Ov. M. 15, 522 Merkel: herba arboribus circumvolvens se,Plin. 16, 44, 92, § 244: serpentes circumvolutae sibi ipsae,id. 10, 62, 82, § 169; 11, 37, 88, § 217; Vitr. 10, 6, 2; Gell. 11, 9, ...

circumuoluo.definition: circum-volvo, no Perf., vŏlūtum, 3, , only with se or mid., to roll one's self around, to roll round, revolve, wind, or twine around (prob. not ante-Aug.): aliquid or alicui rei: magnum sol circumvolvitur annum,Verg. A. 3, 284: rota perpetuum circumvolvitur axem,Ov. M. 15, 522 Merkel: herba arboribus circumvolvens se,Plin. 16, 44, 92, § 244: serpentes circumvolutae sibi ipsae,id. 10, 62, 82, § 169; 11, 37, 88, § 217; Vitr. 10, 6, 2; Gell. 11, 9, ...

circus.definition: circus, i, m., = κίρκος [kindr. with κρίκος; Dor. κίρκος, and κορώνη; cf.: κυλινδέω, κυλλός, cirrus, curvus]. A circular line, circle, in astronomy (less freq. than circulus): quot luna circos annuo in cursu institit, Att. ap. Non. p. 20, 28: circus lacteus,the Milky Way,Macr. Somn. Scip. 1, 15, 2; cf.: candens circus, Lacteus hic notatur,Cic. Arat. 248 (492): illum incolunt locum ... erat autem is splendidissimo candore inter flammas circu...

ciris.definition: A bird (acc. to Hyg. Fab. 198, a fish = κίρρις, Etym. M.), into which Scylla, the daughter of Nisus, was changed, Ov. M. 8, 151; Verg. Cir. 488 sq.

cirratus.definition: cirrātus, a, um, cirrus. Curled, having ringlets (post-Aug.), Mart. 9, 30: feminae,Amm. 14, 6, 20.—Subst.: cir-rāti, Pers. 1, 29. Vestes, fringed, Capitol. Pert. 8.

cirrus.definition: (used mostly in plur.) A (natural) lock, curl, ringlet, or tuft of hair (rare): cirri, Varr. ap. Non. p. 94, 21; Mart. 10, 83.—Sing.: cirrus,Juv. 13, 165.—Also, the hair on the forehead of a horse, Veg. 2, 28, 34; 6, 2, 1. Transf.

cis.definition: cis, pronom. stem ki-, whence -ce; Gr. ἐ-κεῖ; cf.: hic, sic, etc. (far more rare than the kindr. citra) On this side (opp. uls, ultra, and trans; cf. Varr. L. L. 5, § 83 Müll.; Liv. 5, 35, 4; 5, 33, 9 al.); with acc. In space. In time, within (only in Plaut. and post-class. writers; in the former always in connection with pauci): cis dies paucos,Plaut. Truc. 2, 3, 27: paucos cis mensīs,id. Merc. 1, 2, 42 Lorenz ad loc.: cis paucas tempestates,i...

cisalpinus.definition: Cis-alpīnus, a, um Lying on this side of the Alps, Cisalpine (very freq.): Gallia,Cic. Imp. Pomp. 12, 35; Caes. B. G. 6, 1: Galli, Liv. 27, 38, 6: provincia,Suet. Caes. 29.

cisium.definition: A light two-wheeled vehicle, a cabriolet (vehiculi biroti genus, Non. p. 86, 30), Cic. Phil. 2, 31, 77; id. Rosc. Am. 7, 19; Vitr. 10, 1, 6; Aus. Ep. 8, 6; gen. cisi, Verg. Cat. 8, 3 Burm.; cf. Becker, Gall. 3, p. 9; Dict. of Antiq.

cista.definition: A wooden box or basket, often woven of slips or twigs, used for keeping money, clothes, books, fruit, etc. In gen., Plin. 15, 17, 18, § 60; 16, 40, 77, § 209; Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 85, § 197; * Hor. Ep. 1, 17, 54; Ov. M. 2, 554; Col. 12, 54, 2; Poët. ap. Quint. 8, 3, 19; Juv. 3, 206; 6, 44; Dig. 16, 3, 1. Esp.

cistella.definition: dim.cista A small chest or box, Plaut. Cist. 3, 7; 4, 1, 3 sq.; id. Rud. 4, 4, 65 sq.; Ter. Eun. 4, 6, 15; Auct. Her. 1, 12, 21 dub. (al. sitella).

cistellula.definition: dim.id. A little box or chest, Plaut. Am. 2, 2, 141 Ussing (Fleck. cistula); id. Rud. 2, 3, 60; 4, 4, 34.

cisterna.definition: cista A subterranean reservoir for water, a cistern, Varr. R. R. 1, 11, 2; Col. 1, 5, 2; Sen. Ep. 86, 3; Plin. 31, 3, 21, § 31; 36, 23, 52, § 173; Mart. 3, 56, 1; Tac. H. 5, 12 al.—For preserving wine, Dig. 47, 2, 21, § 5.

cisterninus.definition: cisternīnus, a, um, cisterna Of or pertaining to cisterns, cistern-: aqua,Col. 12, 43, 6; Cael. Aur. Tard. 5, 10; Veg. 2, 28, 18; 6, 8, 3.

cistifer.definition: cista-fero The bearer of a box or chest, Mart. 5, 17, 4.

cistophorus.definition: or , , , = . The bearer of the sacred box, Inscr. Orell. 2318. An Asiatic coin of the value of about four drachms, on which a cista was stamped, Cic. Att. 2, 6, 2; 2, 16, 4; 11, 1, 2; id. Dom. 20, 52.—Gen. plur. cistophorūm, Liv. 37, 46, 3; 39, 7, 1; Paul. ex Fest. p. 78.

cistula.definition: dim.cista A little box, chest, or basket, Plaut. Am. 1, 1, 264; id. Rud. 2, 3, 58; 4, 4, 38 sq.; Mart. 4, 46, 13; App. M. 9, p. 236, 40.

citate.definition: cĭtātē, , v. 2. cito P. a. fin.

citatio.definition: 2. cito. In law, the calling, proclaiming: edictorum sollemnium,Cod. Just. 1, 12, 6, § 4. Milit. t. t., the command, Hyg. Grom. § 43, p. 91.

citatorium.definition: 2. cito A summoning before a tribunal, Cod. Th. 6, 28, 5.

cite.definition: cĭtē, , v. cieo P. a. fin.

citeria.definition: An effigy or caricature carried in procession at the games, Paul. ex Fest. p. 59, 20 Müll.; Cato ib.

cithara.definition: The cithara, cithern, guitar, or lute (very freq. in the poets, esp. in Hor.), Lucr. 2, 28; 4, 981; Tib. 2, 3, 12; 2, 5, 2; Verg. A. 6, 120; 9, 776; Hor. C. 1, 15, 15; 2, 12, 4; Varr. L. L. S, § 61 Müll.; id. R. R. 2, 1, 3; Auct. Her. 4, 47, 60; Plin. 7, 56, 57, § 204; Quint. 1, 10, 3; 1, 10, 10; 2, 8, 15; Tac. A. 14, 14; 15, 65 al. Meton., the music of the cithara, or, in gen., of a stringed instrument, the art of playing on the cithara, Prop. 2...

citharista.definition: A player on the cithara (mostly in Cic.), Cic. Phil. 5, 6, 15; id. Div. 2, 64, 133.—Esp., a statue of a player on the cithara: etiam illum Aspendium citharistam, de quo saepe audistis id quod est Graecis hominibus in proverbio, quem omnia intus canere dicebant, sustulit, i. e. he was so skilfully represented that he seemed to be playing the music inwardly, though it was unheard,Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 20, § 53 Zumpt ad loc.

citharoedicus.definition: cĭthăroedĭcus, a, um Of or pertaining to the citharoedi: ars,Plin. 9, 8, 8, § 28; Suet. Ner. 40: habitus,id. ib. 25; Eutr. 7, 14: vestis,Dig. 50, 16, 127.

citharoedus.definition: One who plays on the cithara, accompanying it with the voice (diff. from citharista by the accompanying singing), Cic. Mur. 13, 29; id. de Or. 2, 80, 325; id. Tusc. 5, 40, 116; Varr. R. R. 2, 1, 3; * Hor. A. P. 355; Quint 1, 12, 3; 4, 1, 2; 11, 3, 88; Suet. Ner. 20, 21; 20, 22; 20, 41; id. Vit. 4; id. Dom. 4 al.—In fem.: CITHAROEDA, ae,she who plays on and sings to the cithara,Inscr. Orell. 2611.

citipes.definition: cĭtĭ-pēs, pĕdis, citus Swiftfooted, fleet: cursus, Diom, p. 472 P.

cito.definition: cĭtŏ, , v. cieo P. a. fin.

citrago.definition: (also in MSS.), , citrus The citrus-plant, lemon-balm, Pall. 1, 37, 2; 5, 8, 6.

citretum.definition: . , citrus An orchard of citrus-trees, Pall. Febr. 24, 14.

citreus.definition: cītrĕus, a. um, id.. Of or pertaining to the citrus-tree: mālus, the citrustree, Opp. ap. Macr. S. 2, 15: malum, citrusapple, Cloat. ib.: mensa, of citrus-wood (which was much prized by the ancients), Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 17, § 37: sub trabe citreā,Hor. C. 4, 1, 20 Zumpt; Petr. 119, 29; Mart. 14, 89: lecti,Pers. 1, 53: oleum,Plin. 23, 4, 45, § 88. Pertaining to the citron-tree; only subst. cĭtrĕ-um, i, n., the citron, Plin. 23, 6, 56, § 105; Pall. Ma...

citro.definition: cītrō, adv., v. citer, adv., B.

citrosus.definition: cītrōsus, a, um, citrus Smelling of citrus: vestis, Naev. ap. Macr. S. 2, 15, 5 (cf. εἵματα θυώδεα, Hom. Od. 5, 264 al.; in Paul. ex Fest. p. 42, 14 Müll. erron.: citrosa vestis appellata est a similitudine citri; so also Isid. Orig. 19, 22, 20).

citrum.definition: id. The wood of the citrus, q. v., citrus-wood, Plin. 16, 43, 84, § 231.

citrus.definition: cītrus, iprob. a mutilation of κέδρος, cedrus. The citrus, an African tree (hence Atlantis silva, Luc. 10, 144, and Massyla robora, Stat. S. 3, 3, 94), whose very fragrant wood (v. citrum) was used in making household furniture, and was prized very highly, Plin. 13, 15, 29, § 91 sq.; 13, 16, 30, § 100; Varr R. R. 3, 2, 4; Luc. 9, 428; cf. citreus, I. and citrum. The citrontree (also called malus Medica, Persica, etc.), Citrus Medica, Linn., whos...

Ep. 1, 3, 23: motus,id. C. 2, 1, 1: rabies,id. ib. 3, 24, 26; Flor. 3, 21, 5; cf. furor,id. 4, 2, 75: bella,Ov. civilis.definition: cīvīlis, e, adj.civis. Of or pertaining to citizens, civil, civic (class. in prose and poetry, and very freq.): sanguine civili rem conflant, by the blood of citizens, * Lucr. 3, 70; Cic. Fam. 15, 15, 1: conjuratio,id. ib. 5, 12, 2: bellum,id. Att. 7, 13, 1; id. Imp. Pomp. 10, 28: bella,Hor. Epod. 16, 1; Luc. 1, 1: genus belli,Cic. Att. 7, 13, 1; Sall. C. 47, 2; Quint. 12, 1, 16; Flor. 3, 22, 10; 3, 23, 7: facinus,Cic. Att. 7, 13, 1.—So De Bello ...

Of or pertaining to citizens, civil, civic (class. in prose and poetry, and very freq.): sanguine civili rem conflant, by the blood of citizens, * Lucr. 3, 70; Cic. C. 47, 2; Quint. 12, 1, 16; Flor. 3, 22, 10; 3, 23, 7: facinus,Cic. Att. 7, 13, 1.—So De Bello ...

civilitas.definition: civilis. (Acc. to civilis, I. B.) The art of government, politics, only three times in Quint. as transl. of the Gr. πολιτική, 2, 15, 25; 2, 15, 33; 2, 17, 14. (Acc. to civilis, II.) Courteousness, politeness, affability (post-Aug. and rare), Suet. Aug. 51; id. Claud. 35; Eutr. 7, 21; Lampr. Alex. Sev. 20.

ciuilitas.definition: civilis. (Acc. to civilis, I. B.) The art of government, politics, only three times in Quint. as transl. of the Gr. πολιτική, 2, 15, 25; 2, 15, 33; 2, 17, 14. (Acc. to civilis, II.) Courteousness, politeness, affability (post-Aug. and rare), Suet. Aug. 51; id. Claud. 35; Eutr. 7, 21; Lampr. Alex. Sev. 20.

civitatula.definition: dim.civitas. Citizenship in a small city, Sen. Apocol. 9, 3. A small city, App. M. 10, p. 238; Hier. in lsa. 8, 26, 5 sq.

ciuitatula.definition: dim.civitas. Citizenship in a small city, Sen. Apocol. 9, 3. A small city, App. M. 10, p. 238; Hier. in lsa. 8, 26, 5 sq.

clabulare.definition: clābŭlāre, is, n.clabula = clavula A large, open wagon, probably with sides of wicker-work, used in transporting soldiers, Cod. Th. 6, 29, 2, § 2.—Hence, clābŭlāris (clāv-), e, and clābŭlārius, a, um, , of or belonging to the transport wagons: clavularis cursus facultate permissā,Amm. 20, 4, 11; Cod. Th. 8, 5, 62.

clades.definition: ( Gen. plur. usu. cladium, Liv. 2, 63, 7; 5, 22, 8 et saep.: cladum,Sil. 1, 41; 7, 505; 9, 353; 16, 672; Amm. 29, 1, 14; 32, 2, 1), f. kindr. with Sanscr. klath, laedere; Gr. κλάω, to break, break in pieces; cf.: per - cello, clava, gladius. Prop., a breaking, beating, dashing to pieces; hence Transf.

clam.definition: clam (old access. form callim, or, acc. to Cod. Gu. 1, calam, Paul. ex Fest. p. 47, 3 Müll.) [root cal-; cf.: calix, celo, cella, occulo, caligo], adv. and prep. Secretly, privately; and in the predicate after sum and fore, hidden, secret, unknown (opp. palam; except once in Caes., v. II. infra; in class. prose only used as adv.). Adv. Prep., without the knowledge of, unknown to, constr. with abl. or acc.

clamator.definition: clamo A bawler, noisy declaimer (in oratory; prob. only in the foll. exs.): ut intellegi possit, quem existimem clamatorem, quem oratorem fuisse,Cic. Brut. 49, 182; id. de Or. 3, 21, 81; Mart. 12, 26, 11 (Schneid. clamatus, i. e. vocatus); * Gell. 19, 9, 7.

clamatus.definition: clamo A crying aloud, shouting, Paul. Nol. Carm. 15, 279.

clamito.definition: clāmĭto, āvi, ātum ( Part. pres. nom. plur. clamitantis, Varr. ap. Non. p. 356), 1, v. freq. n. and a. [clamo], to cry out violently or aloud, to bawl out, vociferate (class., esp. freq. since the Aug. per.; in Cic. only twice; not in Quint.; usu. of human beings). Neutr. (rare): ut illi clamitant,Cic. Caecin. 3, 9; of a bird: ipsum (passerem) accipiter ... vano clamitantem interficit,Phaedr. 1, 9, 7. Act.

clamo.definition: clāmo, āvi, ātum, 1, and A. [Sanscr. kar-, to celebrate; Gr. καλέω, κλητός; cf.: clarus, classis, nomenclator, concilium]. Neutr., to call, cry out, shout aloud, to complain with a loud voice, vociferari (class. and very freq.; mostly of human beings): populus convolat; Tumultuantur, clamant, pugnant de loco, Ter. Hec. prol. alt. 33: dic mihi, Non clamas? non insanis?id. Ad. 4, 7, 9; cf. id. ib. 5, 3, 3; id. Phorm. 4, 3, 59: clamare de pecuniā,...

clamor.definition: (old form , , etc., Quint. 1, 4, 13), , clamo. A loud call, a shout, cry; of men and (poet.) of animals (very freq. in all periods and species of composition): facere clamorem,Plaut. Bacch. 4, 8, 33: tollere,id. Curc. 2, 2, 27; Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 43, § 94; id. Q. Fr. 2, 1. 3; Liv. 3, 28, 2; Quint. 5, 10, 46; Verg. A. 3, 672 al.: tollere in caelum,id. ib. 11, 745: ad aethera,id. ib. 2, 338; cf.: clamorem mittere ad sidera,Stat. Th. 12, 521: edere,Ci...

clamosus.definition: clāmōsus, a, um, clamor (mostly post-Aug.) Full of clamor or noise, i. e. Act., clamoring or bawling continually or loudly, clamorous, noisy, bawling: turbidus et clamosus altercator,Quint. 6, 4, 15: pater,Juv. 14, 191: magister,Mart. 5, 84, 2.— * Adv.: clāmōsē, clamorously: clamose ne dicamus omnia,Quint. 11, 3, 45. Pass., filled with noise or clamor, noisy: urbs,Stat. S. 4, 4, 18: theatri turba,id. ib. 3, 5, 16: valles,id. Th. 4, 448: circus,Ju...

clanculum.definition: clancŭlum, and Prep. dim. [id.], secretly, privately (ante-class. but freq.).

clandestinus.definition: clandestīnus, a, um, for clamdies-tinus; cf. matutinus; v. Corss. Ausspr. 1, p. 461 sq. Secret, hidden, concealed, clandestine (class. in prose and poetry): suspitio,Plaut. Am. 1, 2, 28: nuptiae,id. Cas. 5, 3, 6: natura,Lucr. 1, 779: motus materiaï,id. 2, 127: scelere,Cic. Sull. 11, 33; cf. Liv. 42, 18, 1: introitus,Cic. Off. 2, 23, 81; cf. Suet. Ner. 48: colloquia cum hostibus,Cic. Sen. 12, 40: consilia, Crassus ap. Cic. Or. 66, 223; Caes. B. G....

clango.definition: clango, no Perf., ĕre, 3, kindred with crocio, glocio; cf. clamo and κλάζω, to clang, to sound, resound (rare; only in ante-class. and post-Aug. poets): crepitu clangente, Att. ap. Non. p. 463, 16: horrida clangunt signa tubae,Stat. Th. 4, 342; cf.: luctificum clangente tubā,Val. Fl. 3, 349: clangunt aquilae, Auct. Carm. Phil. 28.

clangor.definition: clango A sound, clang, noise (mostly poet. and in Aug. prose). Of wind instruments: tubarum,Verg. A. 2, 313; cf. id. ib. 8, 526; 11, 192; Luc. 1, 237; Sil. 2, 19; Stat. Th. 3, 651; Flor. 4, 2, 67; cf. Ov. M. 3, 707. Of birds (in crying or flying). clangorem fundere, Cic. poët. Tusc. 2, 10, 24: tremulo clangore volare, id. poët. Div. 2, 30, 63; Ov. M. 12, 528; 13, 611: cum magno clangore volitare,Liv. 1, 34, 8; 5, 47, 4; Col. 8, 13, 2; Plin. 18, 3...

clareo.definition: clārĕo, ēre, clarus. Prop., to be clear or bright, to shine (poet.): hoc lumen candidum claret mihi, Enn. ap. Non. p. 85, 25 (Trag. Rel. v. 367 Rib.); so of stars,Cic. Arat. 5 (240); 107 (348). Trop.

claresco.definition: clāresco, clārui, 2 V. inch. n. [clareo] (poet. or in post-Aug. prose), to become or grow bright or clear. Prop. Trop.

clarificatio.definition: clarifico A glorification (eccl. Lat.): Domini,Aug. Qu. 83, 62; Cypr. Ep. 77, 2.

clarifico.definition: clārĭfĭco, āre, clarus - facio To make illustrious or famous (eccl. Lat.): nomen suum grandi aliquo facinore,Lact. 3, 18, p. 213 Bip.; so Sedul. 4, 173; 5, 8; Paul. Nol. Carm. 26, 304 al.

clarigito.definition: clārĭgĭto (in the MSS. clārĭcĭto), āre V. freq. [clarigo], to recall, recollect; saecla ferarum, Lucr. 5, 947; v. Lachm. ad h. l.

clarissimatus.definition: clarissimus; v. clarus, II. B. The dignity of a Clarissimus (late Lat.), Cod. Th. 6, 24, 9; Amm. 21, 16, 2.

claritas.definition: clarus Clearness, brightness, splendor (in good prose, most freq. in the post-Aug. per.). Prop. Trop.

claritudo.definition: clarus Clearness, brightness (access. form of claritas; in lit. signif. very rare; trop. in Sall. a few times, in Tac. very freq., but not in Cic., Caes., Quint., or Suet.). Lit. Trop. (cf. claritas, II. B.), renown, celebrity, splendor, fame, reputation: inclitissima, Cato ap. Gell. 3, 7, 19; Sisenn. ap. Non. p. 82, 7: artes animi, quibus summa claritudo paratur,Sall. J 2, 4: in tantam claritudinem pervenire,id. ib. 7, 4: eminere claritudine,Vel...

claritus.definition: clārĭtus, , = clare (a form like, antiquitus, divinitus, humanitus, etc.), acc. to Cels. ap. Charis. p. 190 P.

clarividus.definition: clārĭvĭdus, a, um, clare-video Seeing clearly, clear-sighted: sensus,Marc. Emp. 18.

clariuidus.definition: clārĭvĭdus, a, um, clare-video Seeing clearly, clear-sighted: sensus,Marc. Emp. 18.

claro.definition: clāro, āvi, 1, clarus To make bright or clear, to illuminate (poet. and very rare). Lit.: Juppiter excelsā clarabat sceptra columnā, showed, exhibited, Cic. poët. Div 1, 12, 21: aestatis primordia,id. Arat. 39: iter longae limite flammae,Stat. Th. 5, 286. Trop.

clarus.definition: clārus, a, um, adj.kindr. with Germ. klar; Engl. clear; cf. clamo Clear, bright (opp. obscurus, caecus; very freq. in all periods, and in all kinds of composition). Lit. Trop.

classiarius.definition: classis, 1. B. 2. Pertaining to the navy: centurio,a captain of a ship,Tac. A. 14, 8; cf. Inscr. Orell. 3617. —More freq. as subst.: , , , marines, naval forces, Caes. B. C. 3, 100; Nep. Milt. 7, 3; id. Them. 3, 2; Tac. A. 4, 27; 12, 56; 15, 51; Suet. Tib. 62; id. Galb. 12; id. Oth. 8; id. Vesp. 8.

classicum.definition: classĭcum, i, v. classicus, II. B. 1.

classicus.definition: classĭcus, a, um, adj.classis Of or belonging to a classis. To a class or division of the Roman people; only transf., belonging to the first class, of the highest class: classici dicebantur non omnes qui in quinque classibus erant, sed primi tantum classis homines (opp. classem, infra), Cat. ap. Gell. 6 ($3), 13, 1; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 113, 12: testes classici,id. ib. p. 56, 15. To the military and naval forces (v. infra; and cf. classis, I. B....

classis.definition: (old orthog. CLASIS, Column. Rostr.; v. under I. B. 2.), is ( Acc. sing. usu. classem; classim, Auct. B. Afr. 9, 2; abl. usu. classe; classi,Verg. A. 8, 11; Liv. 23, 41, 8; Vell. 2, 79), f. root cal-, cla-, of clamo, καλέω; prop. the people as assembled or called together, hence After the division of the Roman people by Servius Tullius into six (or, the citizens who paid tribute alone being reckoned, into five) classes In the post-Aug. per., som...

claudeo.definition: claudeo, ēre, or claudo, no Perf., sum, ĕre, claudus, ground form of the more common claudico, to limp or halt, to be lame, to falter (mostly trop.).

claudicatio.definition: claudico A limping, Cic. N. D. 1, 30, 83; id. de Or. 2, 61, 249; Col. 6, 12, 1; Val. Max. 8, 11, ext. 3.

claudico.definition: claudĭco (clōdĭco, Cic. de Or. 2, 61, 249, like Claudius and Clodius, codex and caudex, etc., v. au), āre, claudeo; like albico, candico from albeo, candeo To limp, halt, be lame (class.). Prop.: Carvilio graviter claudicanti ex vulnere,Cic. de Or. 2, 61, 249; Ov. F. 3, 758; Col. 6, 12, 3; Suet. Aug. 80; Just. 6, 2, 6. Trop., to halt, waver, to be wanting, incomplete or defective: claudicat ingenium,Lucr. 3, 453: tota res vacillat et claudicat, C...

clauditas.definition: claudus A lameness, limping (post-Aug.), Plin. 8, 43, 68, § 169; 28, 4, 7, § 35; App. Flor. 16.—In plur., Plin. 28, 4, 6, § 33.

claudius.definition: Claudĭus (Clōdĭus, like claudo and clodo, codex and caudex, plostrum and plaustrum, etc.), Claudĭa, Clōdĭa The name of two very celebrated Roman gentes (one patrician, the other plebeian; cf. Suet. Tib. 1 and 2; Verg. A. 7, 708; Liv. 2, 16, 4). Hence

H. Germ. scliuzu; M. H. Germ. schliessen; also claudus, clavus, to shut. To shut something that is open, to close, shut up (opp. aperire; freq. in prose and poetry). (For the compounds includo, co...

claudus.definition: claudus (clūdus, Plaut. Ps. 2, 2, 64; and clōdus, Arat. Act. Apost. 266), a, um, root klu-; v. claudo; prop. shut in, hampered Limping, halting, lame. Prop.: sutor,Plaut. Aul. 1, 1, 34: deus,Cic. N. D. 1, 30, 83: claudus altero pede,Nep. Ages. 8, 1; Hor. Ep. 1, 17, 61: pes,id. C. 3, 2, 32: pars serpentis,Verg. A. 5. 278 al. Trop., wavering, crippled, imperfect, defective (rare; mostly poet.): clauda navigia aplustris, * Lucr. 4, 436; cf.: claudae...

claustralis.definition: claustrālis, eid. Of or pertaining to a fortress: munimen,Cassiod. Var. 11, 14.

claustrarius.definition: claustrārĭus, a, umclaustra Pertaining to locks: artifex,a locksmith,Lampr. Elag. 12.

clausula.definition: ae. claudo. A close, conclusion, end (cf. claudo, I. B.; in good prose; most freq. in Quint.): in quo (mimo) cum clausula non invenitur,a fitting end,Cic. Cael. 27, 65: tantum bonam clausulam inpone,Sen. Ep. 77, 20; Suet. Aug. 99: epistulae,Cic. Phil. 13, 21, 47; id. Fam. 2, 4, 2: edicti,Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 14, § 35: clausulam inponere disputationi,Col. 3, 19, 3: peracti operis,id. 12, 57, 5: summae nervorum,Plin. 11, 45, 101, § 247. Esp.

clausura.definition: or , , claudo. * (Cf. claustra, I. A.) A lock, bar, bolt, Inscr. Orell. 2510. (Cf. claustra, II. B.) A castle, fort (late Lat.), Cod. Just. 1, 27, 2, § 4; Cassiod. Var. 2, 5.

clausus.definition: clausus, a, um, Part. and , from claudo.

clava.definition: root cel- of percello; cf. Gr. κλάω and clades. A knotty branch or stick, a staff, cudgel, club: adfer duas clavas... probas,Plaut. Rud. 3, 5, 20; Lucr. 5, 968: sternentes agmina clavā,Verg. A. 10, 318; Curt. 9, 4, 3; Ov. F. 1, 575; Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 43, § 94; Plin. 19, 1, 3, § 18; a bar, lever, Cato, R. R. 13, 1.—As a weapon for exercising, used by young men, and esp. by soldiers, a foil, Cic. Sen. 16, 58; Veg. Mil. 1, 11.—As a badge of Hercules...

claua.definition: root cel- of percello; cf. Gr. κλάω and clades. A knotty branch or stick, a staff, cudgel, club: adfer duas clavas... probas,Plaut. Rud. 3, 5, 20; Lucr. 5, 968: sternentes agmina clavā,Verg. A. 10, 318; Curt. 9, 4, 3; Ov. F. 1, 575; Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 43, § 94; Plin. 19, 1, 3, § 18; a bar, lever, Cato, R. R. 13, 1.—As a weapon for exercising, used by young men, and esp. by soldiers, a foil, Cic. Sen. 16, 58; Veg. Mil. 1, 11.—As a badge of Hercules...

clavator.definition: clava One who carries clubs or foils, used in military exercises, a cudgel-bearer, Plaut. Rud. 3, 5, 25; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 62, 9 Müll.

clauator.definition: clava One who carries clubs or foils, used in military exercises, a cudgel-bearer, Plaut. Rud. 3, 5, 25; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 62, 9 Müll.

clavicarius.definition: clavis A locksmith (late Lat.), Cod. Just. 10, 64, 1.

clauicarius.definition: clavis A locksmith (late Lat.), Cod. Just. 10, 64, 1.

clavicula.definition: dim.id. * A small key, Caes. Germ. Arat. 195. A tendril, by which the vine clings to its props, Cic. Sen. 15, 52; id. N. D. 2, 47, 120; Col. 4, 6, 2; Plin. 23, prooem. § 5. A bar, bolt of the door, Hyg. Grom. 55.—Hence, , , , a key-keeper, jailer, Firm. Math. 3, 66.

clauicula.definition: dim.id. * A small key, Caes. Germ. Arat. 195. A tendril, by which the vine clings to its props, Cic. Sen. 15, 52; id. N. D. 2, 47, 120; Col. 4, 6, 2; Plin. 23, prooem. § 5. A bar, bolt of the door, Hyg. Grom. 55.—Hence, , , , a key-keeper, jailer, Firm. Math. 3, 66.

claviger.definition: clāvĭger, gĕra, gĕrum Clubbearing; as an epithet of Hercules [clavagero], the club-bearer (v. clava, 1.), Ov. M. 15, 22; 15, 284; id. F 1, 544; 4, 68.—Also of the robber Periphetes: clavigera proles,Ov. M. 7, 437: clavigerum numen,Sil. 3, 14.

clauiger.definition: clāvĭger, gĕra, gĕrum Clubbearing; as an epithet of Hercules [clavagero], the club-bearer (v. clava, 1.), Ov. M. 15, 22; 15, 284; id. F 1, 544; 4, 68.—Also of the robber Periphetes: clavigera proles,Ov. M. 7, 437: clavigerum numen,Sil. 3, 14.

clavis.definition: (, acc. to Pompon. Comment. p. 459), , (acc. commonly clavem, clavim, Plaut. Most. 2, 1, 78; Tib. 2, 4, 31; cf. Paul ex Fest. p. 56 Müll.; Don. p. 1750 P.,Charis. p. 101 ib.; abl. clavi and clave: clavi,Varr. R. R. 1, 22 fin., App. M. 1, 14, p. 108; Dig. 48, 8, 1, § 3; Serv. ad Verg. A. 10, 252; cf. Charis. l. l.: clave,Juv. 15, 158; App. M. 9, 20, p. 226; Dig. 21, 1, 17, § 15; cf. Neue, Formenl. 1, 199) [root klu-, v. claudo], a key: clavim cedo...

clauis.definition: (, acc. to Pompon. Comment. p. 459), , (acc. commonly clavem, clavim, Plaut. Most. 2, 1, 78; Tib. 2, 4, 31; cf. Paul ex Fest. p. 56 Müll.; Don. p. 1750 P.,Charis. p. 101 ib.; abl. clavi and clave: clavi,Varr. R. R. 1, 22 fin., App. M. 1, 14, p. 108; Dig. 48, 8, 1, § 3; Serv. ad Verg. A. 10, 252; cf. Charis. l. l.: clave,Juv. 15, 158; App. M. 9, 20, p. 226; Dig. 21, 1, 17, § 15; cf. Neue, Formenl. 1, 199) [root klu-, v. claudo], a key: clavim cedo...

clavo.definition: clāvo, no Perf., ātum, 1, clavus (rare; not ante-Aug.; mostly in part. perf.). To furnish or fasten with nails, to nail, Paul. Nol. 21, 103: clavata concha, i. e. furnished with points or prickles, Plin. 9, 36, 61, § 130. To furnish with a purple stripe (cf. clavus, II. D.): mantilia cocco clavata,Lampr. Alex. Sev. 37: clavata auro tunica,Vop. Bonos. 15; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 56, 9 Müll.

clauo.definition: clāvo, no Perf., ātum, 1, clavus (rare; not ante-Aug.; mostly in part. perf.). To furnish or fasten with nails, to nail, Paul. Nol. 21, 103: clavata concha, i. e. furnished with points or prickles, Plin. 9, 36, 61, § 130. To furnish with a purple stripe (cf. clavus, II. D.): mantilia cocco clavata,Lampr. Alex. Sev. 37: clavata auro tunica,Vop. Bonos. 15; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 56, 9 Müll.

clavulus.definition: dim.clavus. A small nail, a tack, Cato, R. R. 21, 3; Varr. R. R. 2, 9, 15.—* A small swelling (cf. clavus, II. B.), Marc. Emp. 33.

clauulus.definition: dim.clavus. A small nail, a tack, Cato, R. R. 21, 3; Varr. R. R. 2, 9, 15.—* A small swelling (cf. clavus, II. B.), Marc. Emp. 33.

clavus.definition: root klu-, v. claudo; prop. that which shuts or fastens. A nail, usually of metal. Meton. of objects of like form.

clauus.definition: root klu-, v. claudo; prop. that which shuts or fastens. A nail, usually of metal. Meton. of objects of like form.

clematitis.definition: A creeping plant, a species of Aristolochia, called also Cretica, Plin. 25, 8, 54, § 96.

clemens.definition: clēmens, entis (abl. usu. -ti; But -te,Liv. 1, 26, 8; Laber. ap. Macr. S. 2, 7, 3), etym. dub.; cf. lemures; and Germ. hold. Orig. (in the class. per. very rare), of the quiet, placid, pleasant state of the air, wind, or weather, mild, calm, soft, gentle ( = the class. placidus, quietus): undae clementi flamine pulsae, * Cat. 64, 272: clementior Auster vela vocat,Stat. Th. 5, 468: aura Favoni,Claud. Cons. Prob. Olyb. 272; cf. id. III. Cons. Hon. ...

clementia.definition: 1. clemens. A calm, tranquil state of the elements, calmness, mildness, tranquillity (like clemens in this signif. mostly post-Aug.): clementia ventorum, tranquillitas maris,App. de Deo Socr. p. 52, 1: soli caelique,Flor. 3, 3, 18; cf.: emollit gentes clementia caeli,Luc. 8, 366: aestatis,Plin. Ep. 5, 6, 5: hiemis,Col. 5, 5, 6: nascentis anni,id. 11, 3, 9: diei,id. 9, 13, 4: Nili,Stat. Th. 3, 527. (Acc. to clemens, II. B.) Indulgent, forbearing c...

cleopatra.definition: Clĕŏpātră (on the ā cf. Juv. 2, 109; Luc. 9, 1071; 10, 56; Stat. S. 3, 2, 120), ae, f., = Κλεοπάτρα. Queen of Egypt, and daughter of Ptolemy Auletes, notorious for her amorous intercourse with Coesar, and afterwards with Antony; conquered at Actium by Augustus, Caes. B. C. 3, 103; 3, 107; Suet. Caes. 35; Luc. 10, 354 sqq.; Val. Fl. 4, 464; Mart. 4, 22, 2; 4, 59, 5.—Hence A sister of Alexander the Great, and wife of Alexander, king of Epirus, Liv...

clepo.definition: clĕpo, psi, ptum (not clepi, v. Neue, Formenl. 2, 493; Madv. ad Cic. Fin. 5, 25, 74), 3, root klep- of κλέπτω, whence also clipeus; kindred with celo, cella, occul-o, clam To steal (rare, and mostly anteclass. for furor): sacrum qui clepsit rapsitve, old form. ap. Cic. Leg. 2, 9, 22: si quis clepsit, etc., old form. ap. Liv. 22, 10, 5; Att. ap. Cic. Tusc. 2, 10, 23; id. ap. Cic. N. D. 3, 27, 68; Plaut. Ps. 1, 2, 6; Lucil. ap. Varr. L. L. 7, § 94...

clepsydra.definition: κλεψύδρα An instrument for measuring time by water, similar to our sand-glasses, a water-clock, clepsydra, Sen. Ep. 24, 19; Veg. Mil. 3, 8; App. M. 3, p. 130, 19; used by speakers to measure the length of their discourse,Cic. Tusc. 2, 27, 67; Plin. Ep. 2, 11, 14; 6, 2, 5; 1, 23, 2.—Meton., the time measured by the clepsydra, and hence, petere clepsydram, to ask leave to speak; and dare clepsydram, to give leave to speak, Cic. de Or. 3, 34, 138; ...

clericalis.definition: clērĭcālis, e, clericus Clerical, priestly (eccl. Lat.): tirocinium,Sid. Ep. 6, 7: comitatus,id. ib. 7, 2 et saep.

clericatus.definition: id. The clerical office (eccl. Lat.), Hier. Ep. 60, n. 10; 125, n. 8 et saep.

clericus.definition: A clergyman, priest (eccl. Lat.), Hier. Ep. 60, n. 10 al.

clerus.definition: The clerical order, the clergy (eccl. Lat.), Tert. Monog. 12; Prud. στεφ. 4, 78 al.

clibanarius.definition: clibanus A soldier clad in mail, a cuirassier, Lampr. Alex. Sev. 56; Amm. 16, 10, 8; Eutr. 6, 7, 9.

clibanicius.definition: clībănĭcĭusid.: pānis Bread baked in a clibanus, lsid. Orig. 20, 2, 15 (cf. Plin. 18, 11, 27, § 105).

clibanus.definition: An earthen or iron vessel for baking bread, broader at the bottom than at the top, Plin. 18, 11, 27, § 105; 20, 9, 39, § 99; cf. Col. 5, 10, 4; id. Arb. 19, 2; Cels. 2, 17; 3, 21 al.—As a utensil of the rich, also of silver, Petr. 35, 6. Generally, an oven or furnace, Tert. adv. Marc. 4, 30; Sulpic. Sev. Dial. 1, 18.

cliens.definition: or , ( Gen. plur. usu. clientium; clientūm,Plaut. Men. 4, 2, 7; Hor. C. 3, 5, 53; Sen. Ep. 68, 9; Macr. S. 1, 2, 1), m. (comm. acc. to Charis. p. 77 P.; cf. Neue, Formenl. 1, 600, and v. clienta) [for cluens, from clueo, to hear; but acc. to Serv. ad Verg. A. 6, 609, from colens], one who hears, in relation to his protector (patronus), a client (Dion. Halic. 2, 9 and 10, pp. 83-85; cf. Nieb. Röm. Gesch. 1, p. 359 sq.; Gell. 5, 13, 2; Cato ap. Gel...

clienta.definition: cliens A female client, Plaut. Mil. 3, 1, 193; id. Poen. 5, 4, 12; id. Rud. 4, 1, 2; Afran. ap. Charis. p. 77 P.; * Hor. C. 2, 18, 8; Aus. Parent. 24; Pseudo scon. ad Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 46, § 120 Orell. N. cr.

clientela.definition: id. The relation of patron and client, clientship; patronage, protection; the intimate and reciprocal duties of attachment and interest, based on the private relations in Rome between a Roman of a lower grade (plebeian or freedman) or a foreigner, and the patron chosen by him (cf. Dion. Halic. 2, 9 and 10, pp. 83- 85; Gell. 5, 13; 20, 1): Thais patri se commendavit in clientelam et fidem, * Ter. Eun. 5, 8, 9; cf.: esse in fide et clientelā. to be...

clientulus.definition: dim.cliens A small or insignificant client, Tac. Or. 37.

clima.definition: ( Abl. plur. climatis, Firm. Math. 2, 13), n., = κλίμα (prop. the inclination, slope; hence, cf. Lidd. and Scott under κλίμα, II.) A clime, climate (late Lat.), App. Trism. p. 98, 23; Mart. Cap. 8, § 859; Tert. Anim. 49; Serv. ad Verg. G. 1, 246 (in Vitr. 1, 1, 10, used as Greek). A land measure of 60 feet square, Col. 5, 1, 5.* † , , f., = κλιμακίς, a small staircase or ladder, Vitr. 10, 11, 8.

climacter.definition: (gradation) A critical epoch in human life, a climacteric (in accordance with the ancient belief, the years 7, 14, 21, 28, etc.), Plin. 7, 49, 50, § 161; Gell. 3, 10, 9; Firm. Math. 4, 14; Censor. 14 (cf. κλιμακτήρ in Lidd. and Scott).

climax.definition: (a ladder) A rhetorical figure, consisting in a gradual increase in force of expression, a climax (pure Lat. gradatio), Mart. Cap. 5, § 536 (in Quint. 9, 3, 54, used as Greek, and transl. by gradatio).

clinatus.definition: clīnātus, a, um, Part. [clino = κλίνω] Inclined, bent, sunk (only in the foll. exs.), Cic. Arat. 53; 86 (but in Lucr. 6, 563, read inclinata; v. Lachm. ad h. l.).

clinicus.definition: κλινικός [κλίνη, the bed]. A physician who attends patients sick in bed, Mart. 9, 97; cf. MEDICVS,Inscr. Orell. 2983: deus,Prud. Apoth. 205. A patient confined to his bed, Hier. Ep. 105, n. 5. A bearer of the bier, sexton, grave-digger, Mart. 3, 93, 24 (al. archiclinico; cf. id. 1, 31). One who was baptized when sick or infirm, Cypr. Ep. 69 fin.

clipeus.definition: (in inscrr. and MSS. also and ), , m. (, , n., Verg. A. 9, 709; Liv. 1, 43, 2; 34, 52, 5; 35, 10, 12; 38, 35, 5; 40, 51, 3; Licin. et Laber. ap. Non. p. 196, 22 sq. al.) [root in clepo]. The round brazen shield of Roman soldiers (diff. from scutum, which was oval, and made of wood covered with bull's hide; cf. Dict. of Antiq. p. 268 sq.), Enn. ap. Varr. L. L. 7, § 93 Müll.; id. ap. Prisc. p. 838 P. (Enn. Ann. 364 Vahl.); Plaut. Trin. 2, 4, 195; 3...

clitellarius.definition: clītellārĭus, a, um, clitellae Of or pertaining to a pack-saddle, bearing a pack-saddle: asini,Cato, R. R. 10, 1: mulus,Col. 2, 21, 3; Plaut. Most. 3, 2, 93: homines,id. ib. 3, 2, 94.

clivius.definition: clivius, a, um, : auspicia Which forbid any thing to be done, Paul. ex Fest. p. 64, 10 Müll.: avis,Plin. 10, 14, 17, § 57.

cliuius.definition: clivius, a, um, : auspicia Which forbid any thing to be done, Paul. ex Fest. p. 64, 10 Müll.: avis,Plin. 10, 14, 17, § 57.

clivosus.definition: clīvōsus, a, um, clivus Hilly, full of hills, steep (poet. or in post-Aug. prose): rus,Verg. G. 2, 212: trames,id. ib. 1, 108: loci et aridi,Col. Arb. 4, 3; opp. planus,id. R. R. 2, 16, 1: solum,Plin. 18, 24, 55, § 200: Olympus,Ov. F. 3, 415: Ida,id. Am. 1, 14, 11. Trop.: tramite vitae,steep, difficult,Sil. 6, 120.

cliuosus.definition: clīvōsus, a, um, clivus Hilly, full of hills, steep (poet. or in post-Aug. prose): rus,Verg. G. 2, 212: trames,id. ib. 1, 108: loci et aridi,Col. Arb. 4, 3; opp. planus,id. R. R. 2, 16, 1: solum,Plin. 18, 24, 55, § 200: Olympus,Ov. F. 3, 415: Ida,id. Am. 1, 14, 11. Trop.: tramite vitae,steep, difficult,Sil. 6, 120.

clivulus.definition: dim.id. A little hill, Col. 6, 37, 10; App. M. 4, p. 144, 36.

cliuulus.definition: dim.id. A little hill, Col. 6, 37, 10; App. M. 4, p. 144, 36.

clivus.definition: m. (plur.: , , n., Cato ap. Non. p. 195, 2; Front. Limit. p. 43 Goes. dub.) [clino = κλίνω, to incline] A gently sloping height, a declivity, slope, an ascent, a hill, eminence, ascending road (class.): quā se subducere colles Incipiunt, mollique jugum demittere clivo,Verg. E. 9, 8; cf. id. G. 3, 293; Ov. M. 11, 151; 8, 191; so Plaut. As. 3, 3, 118; Ter. Ad. 4, 2, 36; Caes. B. C. 3, 46; Liv. 21, 32, 8; Hor. Ep. 1, 13, 10 et saep.—As antithet. to...

cliuus.definition: m. (plur.: , , n., Cato ap. Non. p. 195, 2; Front. Limit. p. 43 Goes. dub.) [clino = κλίνω, to incline] A gently sloping height, a declivity, slope, an ascent, a hill, eminence, ascending road (class.): quā se subducere colles Incipiunt, mollique jugum demittere clivo,Verg. E. 9, 8; cf. id. G. 3, 293; Ov. M. 11, 151; 8, 191; so Plaut. As. 3, 3, 118; Ter. Ad. 4, 2, 36; Caes. B. C. 3, 46; Liv. 21, 32, 8; Hor. Ep. 1, 13, 10 et saep.—As antithet. to...

cloaca.definition: 1. cluo = purgo; cf. Gr. κλύζω An artificial canal in Rome, constructed by Tarquinius Priscus, by which the filth was carried from the streets into the Tiber; in gen., a sewer, drain, Cic. Sest. 35, 77; id. Caecin. 13, 36; Hor. S. 2, 3, 242 al.; cf. Liv. 1, 38, 6; 1, 56, 2; 5, 55, 5; Plin. 36, 15, 24, § 104 sq.; Cassiod. Var. 3, 30; Dion. Halic. 3, 67; v. Dict. of Antiq. p. 269 sq.

cloacarium.definition: cloaca The duty paid for conducting the private sewers into the public ones or for maintaining and cleansing the sewers, Dig. 30, 1, 39, § 5; 7, 1, 27, § 3; cf. Becker, Antiq. II. 2, p. 121, n. 616.

cloacula.definition: dim.cloaca A small sewer, drain, Lampr. Elag. 17.

clueo.definition: clŭĕo, ēre (clŭo, ĕre, Aus. Prof. 21; Att. ap. Varr. L. L. 5, § 30 Müll.; Prud. ap. Symm. 2, 585; Symm. Ep. 1, 1; Mart. Cap. 6, § 571), and A. [root klu-; Sanscr. s)ru, hear; cf. Gr. ἀκροάομαι, κλέος; Lat. laus], like audio, 5., to hear one's self called in some way, to be named, called, spoken of, reputed, esteemed, or famed in some way, = dicor (only ante- and post-class.; most freq. in Plaut. and Lucr., but not in Ter.; mostly in mock-heroi...

clueor.definition: clŭĕor, ēri, 2, (collat. form of clueo, q. v.) To be named, called, reputed, esteemed: quippe ego te ni contemnam, Stratioticus homo qui cluear?Plaut. Ps. 4, 1, 13: sed hi cluentur hospitum infidissimi, Pac. ap. Non. p. 88, 3 (Trag. Rel. v. 194 Rib.); Varr. ib.

clunalis.definition: clūnālis, e, clunis Pertaining to the hinder parts, hind-: pedes,Avien. Arat. 361.

clunis.definition: (mostly Plur.; acc. clunem, Juv. 2, 21; 6, 334; Auct. Priap. 19, 2; abl. clune, Hor. S. 2, 8, 91; Juv. 11, 164; Mart. 9, 47, 6; 11, 100, 3; Plin. 10, 50, 71, § 140; 29, 6, 39, § 141; Petr. 23, 3), m. and f. (hence the grammarians vary in the designation of the gender; cf. Voss. Arist. 1, 29, p. 498; Rudd. 1, p. 25, n. 35) [Gr. κλόνις; Sanscr. s)rōni: nates, clunes, Bopp, Gloss. 358 a; cf. 1. cluo], a buttock, haunch.

cluo.definition: clŭo = purgo, acc. to Plin. 15, 29, 36, § 119; cf. Serv. ad Verg. A. 1, 720 (where, instead of pugnare, purgare should be read).

clusaris.definition: clūsāris, e, cludo = claudo Easily shutting or closing (post-class.): anguli, Hyg. ap. Goes. p. 181: portio quadrata,ib. p. 156.—Access. form * clūsārĭus, a, um: latus, Hyg. ap. Goes. p. 183.

clusor.definition: id. One who encloses or encompasses, Sid. Ep. 8, 6.

clutus.definition: clŭtus = Gr. κλυτός Famous, renowned; hence, inclitus, Paul. ex Fest. p. 55, 14 Müll.

clybatis.definition: A plant, also called helxine: Parietaria officinalis, Linn.; App. Herb. 81.

clyster.definition: (, Scrib. Comp. 179), ēris (abl. clystĕre, Aem. Mac. cap. de anetho), , = . A clyster, injection (pure Lat. lotio, Cels. 2, 12), id. 7, 27; Scrib. Comp. 154; 179 al.; Plin. 25, 5, 23, § 56; Suet. Ner. 20 al. A clyster-pipe or syringe, Suet. Claud. 44; Plin. 31, 6, 33, § 65; Dig. 9, 2, 9: oricularius,an ear-syringe,Cels. 7, 27; Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 1.

clysterium.definition: A clyster (late Lat.), Scrib. Comp. 114; 118; Paul. ex Fest. p. 78, 13 Müll.

clysterizo.definition: clystērīzo, āre To apply a clyster (late Lat.), Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 4; Veg. Vet. 2, 15, 5; 2, 17, 3 (in id. ib. 1, 42, clysterio is used).

cnecus.definition: () Safflower: Carthamus tinctorius, Linn.; Plin. 21, 15, 53, § 90; 21, 32, 107, § 184; Col. 7, 8, 1; Scrib. Comp. 135.

cnemis.definition: A greave; fig. of the end of the verse, Mall. Theod. Metr. 4, 12.

cnisa.definition: () The steam or odor of a sacrifice, Arn. 7, p. 212.

coacervatio.definition: coacervo. * A heaping together. A rhetorical figure, * Cic. Part. Or. 35, 122; * Quint. 9, 3, 53.

coaceruatio.definition: coacervo. * A heaping together. A rhetorical figure, * Cic. Part. Or. 35, 122; * Quint. 9, 3, 53.

coacervo.definition: cŏ-ăcervo, āvi, ātum, 1 To heap together, heap up, collect in a mass (class., esp. in prose; most freq. in Cic.). Prop.: pecuniae coguntur et coacervantur,Cic. Agr. 2, 27, 70; cf. id. ib. 1, 5, 14: quantum (argenti, etc.) in turbā et rapinis coacervari unā in domo potuit,id. Rosc. Am. 46, 133: tantam vim emblematum,Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 24, § 54: multitudinem civium,id. ib. 2, 5, 57, § 148: cadavera,Caes. B. G. 2, 27; cf.: hostium cumulos,Liv. 22, 7, ...

coaceruo.definition: cŏ-ăcervo, āvi, ātum, 1 To heap together, heap up, collect in a mass (class., esp. in prose; most freq. in Cic.). Prop.: pecuniae coguntur et coacervantur,Cic. Agr. 2, 27, 70; cf. id. ib. 1, 5, 14: quantum (argenti, etc.) in turbā et rapinis coacervari unā in domo potuit,id. Rosc. Am. 46, 133: tantam vim emblematum,Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 24, § 54: multitudinem civium,id. ib. 2, 5, 57, § 148: cadavera,Caes. B. G. 2, 27; cf.: hostium cumulos,Liv. 22, 7, ...

coacesco.definition: cŏ-ăcesco, ăcŭi, 3 V. inch. n., to become acid or sour (rare but in good prose). Prop.: genus uvae,Varr. R. R. 1, 65, 2; cf.: ut non omne vinum, sic non omnis aetas vetustate coacescit,Cic. Sen. 18, 65; Dig. 33, 6, 9 pr.: secunda mensa in imbecillo stomacho coacescit,Cels. 1, 2: si coacuit intus cibus aut computruit,id. 4, 5 fin. Trop (the fig. drawn from wine): quare cum integri nihil fuerit in hac gente plenā, quam valde eam putamus tot transfu...

coacte.definition: cŏactē, , v. cogo P. a. fin.

coactiliarius.definition: coactilis A maker of thick, fulled cloth: LANARIVS,Inscr. Orell. 4206.—Adj.: taberna,a fulling-mill,Capitol. Pert. 3; but v. coctilicius.

coactilis.definition: cŏactĭlis, e, coactus, cogo Made thick; hence subst.: cŏactĭlĭa, ium, n., thick, fulled cloth or felt, Dig. 34, 2, 26; cf. Edict. Diocl. p. 21.

coactim.definition: cŏactim, id. (of expression) Concisely, briefly, Sid. Ep. 9, 16.

coactio.definition: cogo (post-Aug. and rare). * A collecting, calling in: coactiones argentarias factitavit,Suet. Vesp. 1. An abridgment or epitome of a discourse, Inst. 4, 15. A disease of animals, Veg. Art. Vet. 2, 9, 1; 2, 10, 5; 2, 15, 5.

coactor.definition: id.. Prop. Trop., one who forces to something: adjutor, et, ut ita dicam, coactor,Sen. Ep. 52, 4.

coactus.definition: cŏactus, a, um, Part. and , v. cogo.

coadoro.definition: cŏ-ădōro, āre To worship or adore along with (late Lat.), Ambros. Spir. Sanct. 3, 12; Cod. Just. 1, 1, 4.

coadulesco.definition: cŏ-ădŭlesco, ēvi, 3 V. inch. n., to grow up along with (eccl. Lat.), Tert. Anim. 19; 16.

coadunatio.definition: coaduno A uniting into one, a summing up: totius calculi,Cod. Just. 5, 12, 31 fin.

coaduno.definition: cŏ-ădūno, āvi, ātum, 1 To unite, add, or join together, to collect into one (postclass.), Dig. 10, 4, 7; 2, 14, 9; Aur. Vict. Vit. 1; Dict. Cret. 4, 13.

coaedifico.definition: cŏ-aedĭfĭco, no Perf., ātum, 1, , to build up together, build upon (only in Cic.): Campum Martium,Cic. Att. 13, 33, 4: loci coaedificati an vasti,id. Part. Or. 10, 36: quarta pars (urbis),Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 53, § 119 Zumpt N. cr. (al. aedificata).

coaegresco.definition: cŏ-aegresco, ĕre, 3 V. inch. n., to become sick at the same time with, Tert. Anim. 5 dub. (al. cohaerescit).

coaegroto.definition: cŏ-aegrōto, āre To be sick at the same time with, Hier. adv. Jovin. 1, 47.

coaequalis.definition: cŏ-aequālis, e, adj. Of equal age, coeval (post-Aug.): sinciput,Petr. 136, 1.— Subst., a comrade, companion in age, Just. 23, 4, 9; Inscr. Orell. 4407 al.—Transf., of geese, Col. 8, 14, 8.

coaequo.definition: cŏ-aequo, āvi, ātum, 1 To make one thing equal or even with another, to even, level (rare but in good prose). Prop.: aream,Cato, R. R. 91 and 129: montes,Sall. C. 20, 11: pastinatum,Col. 3, 16, 1: sulcum,id. 11, 3, 48: glaebas,id. 2, 17, 4; cf. Pall. 1, 13 fin. Trop.

coaetaneo.definition: cŏaetānĕo, āre, coaetaneus To be of the same age, Tert. Res Carn. 45.

coaeternus.definition: cŏ-aeternus, a, um Coeternal (eccl. Lat.), Tert. adv. Herm. 11; Hier. Ep. 16, n. 4 al.

coaevus.definition: cŏ-aevus, a, um, aevum Of the same age, coeval (eccl. Lat.), Aug. Serm. 38; id. Verb. Dom. 7; Prud. Cath. 12, 137; Vulg. Dan. 1, 10.

coaeuus.definition: cŏ-aevus, a, um, aevum Of the same age, coeval (eccl. Lat.), Aug. Serm. 38; id. Verb. Dom. 7; Prud. Cath. 12, 137; Vulg. Dan. 1, 10.

coagito.definition: cŏ-ăgĭto, no Perf., ātum, 1, , to shake together (in late medic. lang.), Apic. 2, 1; 4, 3; Marc. Emp. 8.

coagmentarius.definition: coagmentum Joining together, ἁρμολόγος, Gloss. Gr. Lat.

coagmentatio.definition: coagmento A joining or connecting together; a connection, combination, union (several times in Cic.; elsewh. rare): corporis,Cic. Univ. 5 fin.: non dissolubilis,id. N. D. 1, 8, 20: naturae,id. ib. 2, 46, 119.—Plur., Vitr. 2, 9, 11; Plin. 36, 22, 51, § 172.

coagmento.definition: cŏagmento, āvi, ātum, 1, coagmentum, t. t. To join, stick, glue, cement, etc., together, to connect (in good prose; most freq. in Cic.). Prop.: opus ipsa suum eadem, quae coagmentavit, naturā dissolvit,Cic. Sen. 20, 72: nihil concretum, nihil copulatum, nihil coagmentatum,id. Tusc. 1, 29, 71; cf. id. Fin. 3, 22, 74: tubulum,Vitr. 8, 7: ancones,id. 8, 6: fissuram,Col. 4, 29, 8: allium nucleis,Plin. 19, 6, 34, § 111; Curt. 4, 7, 23. Trop. (only in ...

coagmentum.definition: cogo A joining together; in concr., a joint (in good prose; not in Cic.; mostly in plur.). Prop., Non. p. 42, 20 sq.; Cato, R. R. 18, 9; Plaut. Most. 3, 2, 143; Caes. B. C. 3, 105 fin.; Vitr. 2, 3, 4; 2, 8, 3; 4, 4, 4. Trop., a joining or connecting together: syllabarum,Gell. 17, 9, 2.

coagulare.definition: coagulo (sc. intestinum) The colon, Veg. 8, 16, 1 al.

coagulo.definition: cŏāgŭlo, āvi, ātum (contr. COAGLAVI, Inscr. ap. Anthol. Lat. 1177 Meyer), 1, coagulum To cause a fluid to curdle or coagulate (mostly in the elder Pliny): lac,Plin. 12, 25, 54, § 123; 20, 14, 53, § 147: picem,id. 16, 11, 22, § 53; v. Sillig N. cr.: aquam,id. 20, 23, 97, § 259: sudorem,id. 35, 15, 52, § 186: caseum,Pall. Mai, 9, 1 al.

coagulum.definition: cogo A means of coagulation, a coagulum or coagulator (the curdled milk in the stomach of a sucking animal, the stomach itself, etc.), rennet or runnet, Varr. R. R. 2, 11, 4; Col. 7, 8, 1; Plin. 11, 41, 96, § 237 sq.; 23, 7, 63, § 117; Ov. M. 13, 830; 14, 274; id. F. 4, 545 al.—Meton. (causa pro effectu), the curdled milk, Plin. 28, 10, 45, § 162. Trop., that which holds or binds together, a bond, tie (only anteand post-class. and rare): hoc (vin...

coalesco.definition: cŏ-ălesco, ălŭi, ălĭtum ( Part. perf. only in Tac. and subseq. writers; contr. form colescat,Varr. R. R. 1, 41, 2: colescere,Lucr. 6, 1068: coluerunt,id. 2, 1061 Lachm. N. cr.), v. inch. n. (most freq. since the Aug. per.; never in Cic.). To grow together with something, to unite. To grow firmly, strike root, increase, become strong.

coalitus.definition: cŏălĭtus, a, um, Part., from coalesco.

coalo.definition: cŏ-ălo, ĕre To sustain or nourish together with: fetus,Hier. in Jovin. 1, 36.

coambulo.definition: cŏ-ambŭlo, āre To go with, Claud. Mam. Stat. An. 1, 3.

coangusto.definition: cŏ-angusto, āvi, ātum To bring into a narrow compass, to confine, compress, contract, enclose, hem in (rare and mostly post-Aug.). Prop.: alvos, * Varr. R. R. 3, 16, 15: quo facilius fistula claudatur vel certe coangustetur,Cels. 7, 27 fin.; Auct. B. Hisp. 5; cf. Aur. Vict. Epit. 42: aditum aedium,Dig. 19, 2, 19.—Of a city, to invest, besiege: et coangustabunt te undique,Vulg. Luc. 19, 43. Trop., to limit, restrict: haec lex dilatata in ordinem c...

coaptatio.definition: coapto An accurate joining together (a word coined by Augustine for translating the Gr. ἁρμονία), Aug. Trin. 4, 2; id. Civ. Dei, 22, 24.

coaresco.definition: cŏ-āresco, ārui, 3 V. inch. n., to dry or become dry together, Vitr. 7, 11 (al. coaluerint).

coarguo.definition: cŏ-argŭo, ŭi, 3, , orig. To assail a person or thing in different directions (cf. arguo init.); hence, jurid. t. t. Aliquem, to overwhelm with reasoning, refute, silence, expose; convict of guilt or crime, prove guilty (class., most freq. in Cic.; syn. convinco): Graecus testis... vinci, refelli, coargui putat esse turpissimum,Cic. Fl. 5, 11: criminibus coarguitur,Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 47, § 104: ut illum natura ipsius consuetudoque defendat, hunc aut...

coargutio.definition: coarguo A convicting, refutation, Hier. Ep. 41, 4.

coarmo.definition: cŏ-armo, āvi, ātum, āre To arm together, Cassiod. Hist. Eccl. 5, 45 al.

coartatio.definition: (), , coarto A drawing or crowding together (rare): laxatio aut coartatio,Vitr. 9, 9: plurium in angusto tendentium,Liv. 27, 46, 2; so, militum eo loco, Auct. B. Alex. 74 fin.

coarticulo.definition: cŏ-artĭcŭlo, āre To cause to articulate: ora mutorum,Arn. 1, p. 31.

coarto.definition: cŏ-arto (cŏarcto), āvi, ātum, 1 To press together, compress, contract, confine (opp. laxo, dilato, etc.; class.). Prop.: faenum in struem,Col. 2, 19, 2; 8, 7, 2: alveum Tiberis (opp. laxo),Suet. Aug. 30: angustae fauces coartant iter,Liv. 28, 5, 8; so id. 33, 6, 7: viam,Dig. 43, 8, 2: forum,Tac. Or. 39; Front. Aquaed. 35: os et fauces sudario, to strangle one's self, Val. Max. 9, 12, 7 al.: Gnaeus in oppidis coartatus,Cic. Att. 7, 10 med.: in ter...

coassatio.definition: (), , coasso A joining of timber (boards or planks) together; hence in concr., a boarded floor, Vitr. 6, 3, 9; 7, 1, 1 sq.—In plur., Plin. 36, 25, 62, § 186.

coassumo.definition: cŏ-assūmo, sumpsi, sumptum, ĕre To assume together, Boëth. Arist. top. 6, 8.

cobio.definition: cobio and cobius, v. gobio and gobius.

coccinatus.definition: coccĭnātus, a, um, coccinus Clothed in scarlet: puerulus,Suet. Dom. 4; cf. Mart. 1, 97, 6; 5, 37, 2.

coccineus.definition: coccĭnĕus, a, um, coccum Scarlet-colored: pallium,Petr. 32, 2: tomentum,id. 38, 5: lacernae,Mart. 14, 131in lemm. Access. form coccĭnus, a, um: acini,Plin. 21, 31, 105, § 177: gausapa,Petr. 28, 4. laena, Juv. 3, 283: aluta,Mart. 2, 29, 8.

coccum.definition: (a berry, and specif.) The berry that grows upon the scarlet oak (Quercus coccifera, Linn.; acc. to modern botany a kind of insect, cochineal kermes), with which scarlet was colored, Plin. 16, 8, 12, § 32; 9, 41, 65, § 140.—Also used in medicine, Plin. 24, 4, 4, § 8 al. Coccum Gnidium, also called granum Gnidium, a grain of the shrub thymelaea cnestron, or cneoron, used in medicine, Plin. 13, 21, 35, § 114; 27, 9, 46, § 70; Cels. 5, 5; 5, 8; Scri...

cocetum.definition: perh. from κυκεών A kind of food prepared from honey and poppies, Tert. adv. Val. 12; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 39, 8 Müll.

cochlis.definition: A precious stone like a snail-shell in form, Plin. 37, 12, 74, § 194.

cocio.definition: or (, Paul. ex Fest. p. 20, 12, and 51, 3 Müll. N. cr.), , m.cf. cunctor, a broker, factor; acc. to Gell. more usu. called arilator (v. h. v. and cf. Fest. p. 20), Laber ap. Gell. 16, 7, 12.

cocionatura.definition: cocio, μετάπρασις Brokery, Gloss. Gr. Lat.

coclea.definition: (; cf. the letter C), , κοχλίας, ό A snail: quom caletur cocleae in occulto latent,Plaut. Capt. 1, 1, 12; Plin. 9, 56, 82, § 173 sq.; Varr. R. R. 3, 14; Cic. Div. 2, 64, 133; Auct. Her. 4, 49, 62; Hor. S. 2, 4, 59: nudae,without shells,Plin. 29, 6, 36, § 112; an emblem of slowness,Plaut. Poen. 3, 1, 29. Meton.

coclear.definition: (), (, , Scrib. Comp. 122; 96; Cels. 3, 22; , , Mart. 8, 71, 10; 8, 14, 121; and , , Plin. 20, 22, 89, § 242), coclea, of the form of a snail-shell A spoon, Mart. l. l.; Cels. 6, 14; Plin. 28, 2, 4, § 19; Petr. 33, 6 al.—As a measure for liquids, esp. in medicine, a spoonful, = half a cheme or 1/144 of a cotyla, Rhem. Fann. Pond.; Col. 12, 21, 3; Plin. 23, 4, 38, § 76; 27, 4, 5, § 17, and the above passages with coclearium.

coclearium.definition: (), , coclea. An enclosure or pen in which snails were kept and fed, Varr. R. R. 3, 12, 2; 3, 14, 1. A spoon; v. cochlear.

cocleatim.definition: coclĕātim (cochl-), id. Spirally, Sid. Ep. 4, 15 fin.

cocleatus.definition: coclĕātus (cochl-), a, um, id. Spiral or screw-formed: equuleus, Pomp. ap. Non. p. 105, 15, and 182, 14: aures,Cassiod. Anim. 9.

cocleola.definition: (), , dim. id. A small snail, Hier. Ep. 64, n. 19; id. in Jov. 2, 6.

cocles.definition: for scoculus; root ska-; cf. σκιά, σκότος, and oculus (cf. Fleck. in Rhein. Mus. 8, p. 231) Cognomen of a person blind with one eye, Plin. 11, 37, 55, § 150; so Enn. ap. Varr L. L. 7, § 71; Plaut. Curc. 3, 1, 23.

coco.definition: coco, acc. to others cocococo The sound naturally made by the hen, clucking, Petr. 59, 2.

cocolobis.definition: or A Spanish name for a kind of grape.—Form -ŭbis, Col. 3, 2, 19.—Form -ŏbis, Plin. 14, 2, 4, § 30.

coctilicius.definition: coctĭlĭcĭus, a, umcoctilis Of or pertaining to dried wood: taberna, in which dry wood is sold, Capit. Pert. 3; others less correctly coactiliaria.

coctilis.definition: coctĭlis, e, coquo Burned: lateres,Varr. R. R. 1, 14 fin.: laterculus,Plin. 7, 56, 57, § 193; Curt. 5, 1, 25: muri (Babylonis),built of burned bricks,Ov. M. 4, 58; cf. Curt. l. l., and Just. 1, 2, 7 (cocto latere). Subst.: coctĭlĭa, ium, n. (sc. ligna), very dry wood, that burns without smoke (cf. acapnos), Treb. Claud. 14; cf. Dig. 32, 55, § 7.

coctio.definition: id.. Lit., a cooking, burning: calcis,Cassiod. Var. 7, 17. A digesting of food, Plin. 20, 9, 39, § 101.

coctura.definition: id. A cooking; a melting; a manner or style of cooking, Col. 11, 3, 23, p. 453 Bip.: Apiciana,Plin. 19, 8, 41, § 143; 34, 8, 20, § 96; Apic. 6, 2 al.; Pall. Nov. 1, 3. Meton.

coctus.definition: coctus, a, um, Part., from coquo.

cocula.definition: (also ), , dim. coquus A female cook, Varr. ap. Non. p. 531, 32.

coculum.definition: coquo. * A vessel for cooking, Plaut. Fragm. ap. Isid. Orig. 20, 8, 1; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 39, 2 Müll. Acc. to some, small wood for cooking, Paul. ex Fest. l. l.; cf. Gloss. Isid. Plac. p. 448 Mai.

coelectus.definition: cŏ-ēlectus, a, umeligo Elected together, Vulg. 1 Pet. 5, 13.

coelementatus.definition: cŏ-ĕlĕmentātus, a, um, elementum Composed of elements, Tert. adv. Val. 23.

coeliacus.definition: coelĭăcus, a, um, , = . Relating to the abdomen or to the stomach: dolor,pain in the stomach,Cato, R. R. 125 (in Cels. 4, 12, written as Greek).— Subst.: coelĭăca, ae, f. (sc. medicina), stomach remedy, Plin. 20, 18, 76, § 201. Afflicted with a disease of the bowels: apes,Varr. R. R. 3, 16, 22; and subst., one diseased in the bowels, Plin. 20, 14, 53, § 148; 20, 18, 76, § 201; 28, 14, 58, § 204; 30, 7, 19, § 58; Scrib. Comp. 95 al.

coelicola.definition: coelĭcŏla, coelĭcŭlus, coelĭcus, coelĭfer, coelĭgĕnus, coelĭlŏquus, etc., v. cael-.

coelioticus.definition: coelĭōtĭcus, a, um Cleansing the stomach or bowels, Cael. Aur. Tard. 1, 5.

coemendatus.definition: cŏ-ēmendātus, a, um, Part. [emendo] Amended at the same time, Arn. 2, 18 fin.

coemesis.definition: A somniferous song, Mart. Cap. 9, p. 335 (by Kopp, § 996, written as Greek).

coemeterium.definition: (a sleeping - chamber; hence) A churchyard, cemetery, burying-ground (eccl. Lat.), Tert. Anim. 51 al.

coemo.definition: cŏ-ĕmo, ēmi, emptum, 3, (cf. the contracted form, 1. como) To purchase together, to buy up (class.): aliquid,Ter. Ad. 2, 2, 17; Caes. B. G. 1, 3; Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 59, § 133; Cassius ap. Cic. Fam. 15, 19, 3; Hor. S. 1, 2, 9; Quint. 11, 1, 80; Suet. Vesp. 16 al.: coemptarum rerum pretia,id. Ner. 5; Juv. 14, 293.

coemptio.definition: coëmo, jurid. t. t. A pretended purchase of an estate which was subjected to a mock sale for the purpose of divesting it of the burden of certain sacrifices attached to it, Cic. Mur. 12, 27 Moeb. Esp., a marriage, consisting in a mutual mock sale of the parties, by which the wife was freed from the tutela legitima and the family sacra, Gai Inst. 1, 110; 1, 113 sq.; Cic. Fl. 34, 84; id. de Or. 1, 56, 237; Varr. L. L. 6, § 43; cf. id. ap. Non. p. 5...

coemptionalis.definition: cŏëmptiōnālis (in MSS. also contracted cōmptiōnālis; cf. Lachm. ad Lucr. p. 135), e, coëmptio Pertaining to a sham sale or a sham marriage: senex, who was made use of in such a performance (cf. Cic. Mur. 12, 27); accordingly,poor, worthless,Plaut. Bacch. 4, 9, 52.—Of a low kind of slaves, Cur. ap. Cic. Fam. 7, 29, 1.

coenobita.definition: coenobium A cloister-brother, a monk, Hier. Ep. 22, n. 34 al.

coenobium.definition: A cloister, convent, Hier. Ep. 22, n. 36 al.

coenomyia.definition: The common fly, Vulg. Psa. 104, 31 al.; cf. Hier. Ep. 106 fin.

coepio.definition: coepĭo, coepi, coeptum, 3 (the Tempp. press. only a few times in the ante-class. period, and coepturus, Liv. 30, 5, 6; 42, 47, 3; Quint. 10, 1, 46; Plin. 16, 25, 41, § 98; Suet. Calig. 46; the tempp. perff., both in act. and pass. form, very freq.; a trisyl. coëpit,Lucr. 4, 619 Lachm. N. cr.), v. a. and n. contr. from co-ăpio = apo; hence coapias for coepias in Cod. Ambros.; Plaut. Trin. 4, 3, 46; v.in the foll., and cf. Lachm. ad Lucr. 2, p. 248...

coepiscopus.definition: An associate bishop, Hier. adv. Lucif. 9; Sid. Ep. 4, 25 et saep.

coepto.definition: coepto, āvi, ātum, 1, and n. coepio (mostly poet., and in Tac.; in Cic. in prose only once, apparently for a change with coepit and incipit). Act., to begin eagerly, to begin, undertake, attempt. Intr., to begin, commence, make a beginning (only post-Aug. and rare): coeptantem conjurationem disjecit,Tac. A. 4, 27; id. H. 3, 4: Olympiade septimā coeptante,Sol. 1: nocte coeptante,Amm. 20, 4, 14.

coeptum.definition: coeptum, i, v. coepio, I. B. Fin.

coeptus.definition: coeptus, a, um, Part., from coepio.

coepulor.definition: cŏ-ĕpŭlor, āri, 1 To feast together (late Lat.), Ambros. Ep. 19, 15.

coerceo.definition: cŏ-ercĕo, cui, cĭtum, 2, arceo To enclose something on all sides or wholly, to hold together, to surround, encompass: qui (mundus) omnia complexu suo coërcet et continet,Cic. N. D. 2, 22, 58; cf. id. ib. 2, 40, 101; Ov. M. 1, 31: quā circum Galli lorica coërcet,where the Gallic coat of mail encloses,Lucr. 6, 954; cf. of a band holding the hair together,Ov. M. 1, 477; 2, 413; Hor. C. 2, 19, 19; 1, 10, 18: est animus vitaï claustra coërcens,holding...

coercitio.definition: (in MSS. also ), , coërceo, II. A restraining, coercing; coercion, restraint, compulsion, chastisement, punishment (not ante-Aug.). Prop.: coërcitionem inhibere,Liv. 4, 53, 7: sine coërcitione magistratus,on the part of the magistrates,id. 26, 36, 12: quo modo judex doceri potest, si desit... interpellantis coërcitio, contentio? * Quint. 9, 2, 2: servorum,Sen. Brev. Vit. 3, 2: indignamur aliquā admonitione aut coërcitione nos castigatos, id. Ira,...

coercitor.definition: coërceo One who restrains: disciplinae militaris,an enforcer,Eutr. 7, 20; 7, 18 Bip.

cofanus.definition: A pelican, App. Fragm. p. 609 Oud.

cogitabilis.definition: cōgĭtābĭlis, e, cogito Conceivable, imaginable (post-Aug. and very rare), Sen. Ep. 58, 13: Deus,App. Mag. p. 315, 4.

cogitabundus.definition: cōgĭtābundus, a, um, id. Thinking, thoughtful: Socrates,Gell. 2, 1, 2.

cogitamentum.definition: id. A thought (late Lat.), Vulg. 4 Esdr. 7, 22; cf. cogitamentum, ἐνθύμημα, Gloss. Gr. Lat.

cogitatio.definition: cogito, i. e. co-agito; cf. Varr. L. L. 6, § 43; Cic. Off. 1, 6, 19; Paul. ex Fest. p. 66, 7 Müll.. Abstr., a thinking, considering, deliberating; thought, reflection, meditation (in good prose, and very freq.). Meton.

cogitatorium.definition: cogitatus A receptacle of thought (late Lat.): animae caro,Tert. Res Carn. 15; id. Anim. 11.

cogitatus.definition: cōgĭtātus, a, um, Part., from cogito.

cogito.definition: cōgĭto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.contr. from cŏ-ăgito, acc. to Varr. L. L. 6, § 43 Müll.; but more prob. from con and root of aio, Sanscr. ah; cf.: nego, adagium To pursue something in the mind (cf. agito, II.), i. e. To consider thoroughly, to ponder, to weigh, reflect upon, think (class. in prose and poetry); constr. absol., with aliquid, de aliquo, or de aliquā re, sic, ita, or a rel. -clause: cogitate cum animis vestris si quid, etc., Cato ap. Gell...

cognatio.definition: cognatus. Lit., blood relationship, kindred, connection by birth. Transf., concr., kindred, relations, persons, allied by descent: homo summae potentiae et magnae cognationis,Caes. B. G. 7, 32: hoc commune dedecus familiae, cognationis, nominis,Cic. Clu. 6, 16: cum tibi tota cognatio sarraco advehatur, id. ap. Quint. 8, 3, 21. Trop.

cognatus.definition: co-gnātus, a, um, natus, nascor Sprung from the same stock, related by blood, kindred; and subst.: cognātus, i, m., and cognāta, ae, f., a blood-relation, kinsman (on either the father's or the mother's side; a more comprehensive word than agnatus, q. v.; very freq. and class.). Trop., kindred, related, connected, like, similar: nihil est tam cognatum mentibus nostris quam numeri ac voces,Cic. de Or. 3, 51, 197: (deus mundo) formam et maxime sibi...

cognitio.definition: cognosco. In gen., a becoming acquainted with, learning to know, acquiring knowledge, knowledge as a consequence of perception or of the exercise of our mental powers, knowing, acquaintance, cognition (in good prose; esp. freq. in Cic. and Quint.). Specif., a legal t. t., a judicial examination, inquiry, cognizance, trial (very freq.): ne quod judicium, neve ipsius cognitio illo absente de existimatione ejus constitueretur,Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 25, § ...

cognitionalis.definition: cognĭtĭōnālis, e, cognitio, II. Pertaining to judicial inquiry: sententiae,Cod. Just. 7, 42, 1; 7, 45, 13.—* Adv.: co-gnĭtĭōnālĭter: introductus,by judicial investigation,Cod. Just. 7, 63, 5 fin.

cognitor.definition: cognosco, a judic. t. t. A witness, who testifies that he knows a person, a voucher, Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 65, § 167 sq.; cf. id. ib. § 168; 2, 1, 5, § 13.

cognitorius.definition: cognĭtōrĭus, a, um, cognitor Pertaining to an advocate, Gai Inst. 2, 39; 2, 52; 4, 82 al.

cognitura.definition: id. The office of a fiscal agent, who looks up the debtors to the treasury; a state's attorneyship, a state agency, Gai Inst. 4, § 124; Paul. Sent. 1, 2, § 2; Suet. Vit. 2.

cognitus.definition: cognĭtus, a, um, Part. and , from cognosco.

cognobilis.definition: cognōbĭlis, e, id. That can be understood, intelligible (only in the two foll. exs.): libri,Gell. 20, 5, 9, as a translation of the Aristotelian ξυνετοί, and in imitation of the Catonian cognobilior cognitio, Cato ib. fin.

cognomen.definition: co-nomen. A name added to the nomen (or name of the gens), usu. the third word in order in the full name of each citizen; sometimes followed by a fourth, the agnomen, but in the class. per. including the agnomen, a Roman surname, family name, epithet (e. g. Cicero, Scipio, etc., Africanus, Asiaticus, etc.; cf. Quint. 7, 3, 27; freq. and class.): T. Manlius, qui Galli torque detracto cognomen (sc. Torquati) invenit,Cic. Off. 3, 31, 112; cf. id. Fi...

cognomentum.definition: access. form of cognomen A surname (rare in class. prose; most freq. in Tac.; not used by Cic.; v. Madv. ad Cic. Fin. 2, 5, 15), Plaut. Mil. 4, 2, 47; id. Ps. 4, 2, 20; id. Pers. 1, 2, 8; Poët. ap. Cic. Fin. 2, 5, 15; Sall. Fragm. ap. Gell. 18, 4, 4; Messala ap. Sen. Suas. 2; Tac. A. 12, 55; 14, 27; Gell. 18, 7, 1. (Like cognomen in poets, v. cognomen, II.) In gen., a name (partic. of inanim. things or of persons to designate a peculiar quality),...

cognominis.definition: cognōmĭnis, e (abl. cognomine V.the foll.; cf.: bimestris, coelestis al.), cognomen, like - named, of the same name (mostly poet. or in post-Aug. prose); with gen., dat., or absol.: duae germanae meretrices cognomines,Plaut. Bacch. 1, 1, 5: cognomine Insubribus pago Haeduorum,Liv. 5, 34, 9 Weissenb. ad loc.: flumen Absarrum cum castello cognomine,Plin. 6, 4, 4, § 12: mox Asiacae cognomines flumini,id. 4, 12, 26, § 82: eorum,id. 6, 2, 2, § 5; Suet...

cognomino.definition: cognōmĭno, āvi, ātum, 1, id.. To furnish with a surname, to surname, denominate (mostly post-Aug.; only once in Cic.): amaracum Phrygium,Plin. 21, 11, 39, § 67; 21, 3, 7, § 10; * Quint. 4, 1, 2; Suet. Tib. 17.—In part. pass.: quo ex facto ipse posterique ejus Torquati sunt cognominati, Quadr. ap. Gell. 9, 13, 19; Suet. Aug. 7; Plin. 35, 10, 37, § 112; 33, 10, 17, § 133; Flor. 3, 5, 1: verba cognominata, i. e. synonyms, * Cic. Part. Or. 15, 53. Ra...

cognoscens.definition: cognoscens, entis, Part. and , from cognosco.

cognoscenter.definition: cognoscenter, adv., v. cognosco, P. a. 1.

cognoscibilis.definition: cognoscĭbĭlis, e, cognosco Recognizable, discernible (late Lat.), Boëth. Arist. Anal. Post. 1, 541.—Adv.: cogno-scĭbĭlĭter, recognizably: a magnitudine creaturae cognoscibiliter poterit creator videri,Vulg. Sap. 13, 5.

cognosco.definition: co-gnosco, gnōvi, gnĭtum, 3 ( Tempp. perff. contr. cognosti, Ter. And. 3, 4, 7: cognostis,id. Hec. prol. 8: cognoram,Cic. de Or. 1, 31, 143; Cat. 66, 26: cognoro,Cic. Att. 7, 20, 2; id. Fam. 2, 11, 2 fin.: cognorim, Cael. ap. Cic. Att. 10, 9, A, 1: cognoris,Ter. Phorm. 2, 1, 35; Lucr. 6, 534: cognorit,Ter. Eun. 5, 4, 11: cognosses,Cic. Fl. 21, 51; Cat. 91, 3: cognossent,Nep. Lys. 4 fin.: cognosse,Lucr. 1, 331; Cat. 90, 3; Ov. M. 15, 4 al.; v. Neu...

cogo.definition: cōgo, cŏēgi, cŏactum (COGVIT = cogit, Inscr Marin Fratr Arv. p. 170), 3, v. a. contr. from co-ago To drive together to one point, to collect, compress, crowd, bring, or urge together, to assemble, gather together (class. and very freq.; syn.: colligo, congrego) Lit. Trop.

cohabitatio.definition: cohabito A dwelling together, Aug. Ep. 137 fin.

cohabitator.definition: id. He who dwells with any one (late Lat.), Cassiod. Var. 3, 48; Aug. Serm. 1 al.

cohabito.definition: cŏ-hăbĭto, āre To dwell together (late Lat.), Hier. Ep. 101; Aug. Ep. 12 al.

cohaerentia.definition: cohaereo A cohering, coherence, connection (rare): mundi, * Cic. N. D. 2, 62, 155: regionum,Macr. S. 5, 15: mortis et vitae,Gell. 6, 13, 11: vocis,id. 15, 3, 6.

cohaereo.definition: cŏ-haerĕo, haesi, haesum, 2, v. n. To cling together, to be united, either of that whose parts cling together, to cohere, or of that which cleaves to something else, to adhere. Of a whole as composed of parts, or of the parts of a whole, to cling together, be united, to cohere, press or crowd together. To cling closely to something else, to adhere, be connected with, cleave to, be in contact with, etc.

cohaeresco.definition: cŏ-haeresco (-hēresco), si, 3 V. inch. n. [cohaereo], to hang together, cohere (very rare): atomi cohaerescunt inter se,Cic. N. D. 1, 20, 54; id. Fin. 1, 6, 17: pituita in gulā cohaerescens,Plin. 24, 15, 80, § 130; 20, 16, 64, § 172.

cohaesus.definition: cŏhaesus, a, um, Part. and , from cohaereo.

coheres.definition: () A coheir, fellow-heir, Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 48, § 127; id. Fam. 13, 46 init.; 7, 2, 1; Quint. 5, 14, 16.— Gen. plur. coheredum, Hor. S. 2, 5, 107: esse coheres alicui,id. ib. 2, 5, 54; Petr. 76, 2.— In the fem., Dig. 34, 9, 16.

cohibeo.definition: cŏ-hĭbĕo, ui ( Perf. subj. cohibessit, Lucr. 3, 444 Lachm.), ĭtum, 2, v. a. habeo. To hold together, to hold, contain, confine, embrace, comprise (class.; syn. contineo): omnes naturas ipsa (universa natura) cohibet et continet,Cic. N. D. 2, 13, 35; Lucr. 3, 441 sq.; 1, 517; 1, 536: (nubes) ut fumus constare nequirent, Nec cohibere nives gelidas et grandinis imbres,id. 6, 107: aliquid in se,id. 2, 1031; cf. Cic. Fat. 9, 19: at Scyllam caecis cohi...

cohonesto.definition: cŏ-hŏnesto, āvi, ātum, 1 To honor in common or abundantly, do honor to, to honor, grace (rare, but in good prose): exsequias,Cic. Quint. 15, 50: funus laudatione pro rostris ceterisque solennibus,Tac. A. 3, 76: statuas,Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 69, § 168: aliquam,id. Fam. 13, 11, 3: MEMORIAM PVELLAE,Inscr. Orell. 5037: victoriam,Liv. 38, 47, 3: aliquid virtute,id. 25, 16, 17: patrem deorum,Arn. 5, 172: res turpes,to call by honorable names,id. 5, 187. Met...

cohorresco.definition: cŏ-horresco, horrui, 3 V. inch. n., to shudder, shake, or shiver with fear or cold: nisi cohorrescit corpus meum, Aug. ap. Suet. Tib. 21.—In perf.: quem ubi agnovi, equidem cohorrui,Cic. Rep. 6, 10, 10; id. Att. 5, 21, 12; 7, 1, 1: ex quo (sudore) cum cohorruisset,id. de Or. 3, 2, 6.

cohors.definition: (or ; cf. Non. p. 83, 14 sq.; later aspirated orthog. of MSS. ; cf. the letter C, and Schneid. ad Varr. R. R. 1, 13, 3), , Sanscr. root har, rapio; cf. Gr. χορός. A place enclosed around, a court, enclosure, yard, pen, etc., esp. for cattle, poultry, etc. Meton. (cf. chorus).

cohortalinus.definition: cŏhortālīnus (cort-, Paul. Nol. Ep. 22, 2), a, um, cohortalis (late Lat.) Pertaining to an imperial body-guard: militia, Cod. Th. 16, 5, 48; cf. ib. 6, 35, 14.

cohortalis.definition: cŏhortālis (cort-), e, cohors. Pertaining to a cattle or poultry-yard (freq. in Col.; elsewhere very rare): aves,Col. 1, prooem. § 27; 6, 27, 4; 8, 1, 3: gallina,id. 8, 2, 1: pullus,Cels. 2, 18: officina,Col. 8, 3, 8: ratio,id. 8, 2, 6. Pertaining to an imperial body - guard (late Lat.): officium, Cod. Th. 12, 58, 13: condicio,ib. 16, 62, 3 al.

cohortatio.definition: cohortor An exhorting, inciting; exhortation, encouragement (rare, but in good prose): militum,Nep. Hann. 11, 1: legionis,Caes. B. G. 2, 25: Caesaris, Auct. B. Alex. 22: ducis,Tac. A. 14, 30: judicum,Cic. Clu. 50, 138: incredibiliter me commovet tua cohortatio,id. Att. 16, 13, C, 2; so id. Fam. 1, 7, 9; id. de Or. 1, 47, 204: his cohortationibus,id. ib. 1, 61, 262.

cohortatiuncula.definition: dim.cohortatio A short exhortation, Ambros. Ep. 4, 33.

cohorto.definition: cŏhorto, āre, 1, (rare collat. form of cohortor) To exhort, encourage: et dicerent castra capta esse, atque hos cohortarent uti maturarent, Quadrig. ap. Non. p. 472, 19: exercitus pransus, paratus, cohortatus, Cat. ap. Gell. 15, 13, 5; v. cohortor.

cohortor.definition: cŏ-hortor, ātus, 1 To animate or encourage by forcible language, to incite, exhort, admonish. Esp., of the general before a battle, or in other milit. proceedings: cohortatus suos proelium commisit,Caes. B. G. 1, 25: acies instruenda, milites cohortandi, signum dandum,id. ib. 2, 20: exercitum ad pugnam,id. B. C. 3, 90: militem ad proelium,Quint. 12, 1, 28. In gen., and without the sphere of military operations (in good prose).

cohospes.definition: A fellow-guest (late Lat.), Paul. Nol. Carm. 21, 385; 24, 438.

cohospitans.definition: cŏhospĭtans, antis, = cohospes, Paul. Nol. Ep. 32, 6.

cohum.definition: The strap by which the plough-beam was fastened to the yoke; so called, acc. to Paul. ex Fest. p. 39, 4, a cohibendo; cf. Varr. L. L. 5, § 135 Müll.

coillum.definition: () The inmost part of the house, where the Lares were worshipped, Tert. Spect. 5.

coimbibo.definition: cŏ-imbĭbo, ĕre To imbibe along with, or at the same time, Arn. 5, 178.

coinquinatio.definition: coinquino A polluting, Vulg. Esd. 1, 6, 21; Sulp. Sev. Ep. 2, 9; 2, 19.

coinquino.definition: cŏ-inquĭno (or contr. cōnquĭno, cf. Lachm. ad Lucr. 2, p. 135), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. To defile all over, to pollute wholly, to contaminate. Prop. (rare; not in Cic.): stercore conquinatae,Col. 8, 5, 19; 8, 7, 2. Trop. *

coitio.definition: coëo. * A coming or meeting together, a meeting: prima coitio est acerrima,Ter. Phorm. 2, 2, 32. Esp.

coitus.definition: cŏĭtus, a, um, Part., from coëo.

colaphizo.definition: cŏlăphīzo, āre To box one's ears, Tert. adv. Marc. 5, 12.

colaphus.definition: A blow with the fist, a cuff, a box on the ear: icere,Plaut. Pers. 5, 2, 65 Ritschl: ducere,Quint. 6, 3, 83.—In plur.: in cerebro colaphos abstrudere,Plaut. Rud. 4, 3, 68; cf.: infringere alicui,Ter. Ad. 2, 1, 45; Plin. 8, 36, 54, § 130: incutere alicui,Juv. 9, 5: perpeti,Plaut. Capt. 1, 1, 20; Ter. Ad. 2, 2, 37.

colatura.definition: 2. colo Filtration; concr., that which has been strained, Cael. Aur. Tard. 5, 3, 55.

colatus.definition: cōlātus, a, um, Part. and , from 2. colo.

colepium.definition: A knuckle of beef or pork, Petr. 70; Veg. 5, 17, 5.

colicus.definition: cōlĭcus, a, um Pertaining to the colic; suffering from or sick with the colic, Veg. Art. Vet. 4, 28 dub.

coliphium.definition: (in MSS. also ) A kind of nourishing food for athletoe, Plaut. Pers. 1, 3, 12; Mart. 7, 67; Juv. 2, 53; cf. colepium.

collabor.definition: col-lābor (conl-), lapsus (or labsus), 3 To fall together, to fall in ruins; esp. of buildings, to fall in, fall from age (in the ante-Aug. period very rare; not in Cic., Hor., or Quint.). Prop., Liv. 35, 9, 3: moenia subito collapsa ruinā sunt,id. 29, 18, 17; Suet. Aug. 30; id. Claud. 25; id. Calig. 21: fastigium domūs collabitur,id. Caes. 81: qui collapsā jacuere ruinā,Sil. 7, 727: succisis asseribus collapsus pons,Liv. 44, 5, 6. postquam conla...

collaboro.definition: col-lăbōro (conl-), āre To labor with or together, Tert. Poen. 10.

collacrimo.definition: col-lācrĭmo (conl- and -lacrŭmo), āvi, 1, and A., to weep together or very much, to bewail, deplore (rare).

collactaneus.definition: col-lactānĕus (conl-), a lacteo A brother or sister nourished at the same breast, a foster-brother or sister (post-class.); masc., Gai Inst. 1, 39; Dig. 40, 2, 13; Inscr. Orell. 2281 al.; fem., Dig. 34, 4, 30, § 1 al.

collacteus.definition: col-lactĕus (conl-), a A foster-brother, foster-sister; masc., Hyg. Fab. 224; Inscr. Orell. 678; fem., Juv. 6, 307; Mart. Cap. 1, § 6; 2, § 111.

collaetor.definition: col-laetor (conl-), āri To rejoice together, Tert. ldol. 14.

collapsio.definition: (), , collabor A falling together, precipitation: fulminum, Jul. Firm. Err. Prof. Relig. 21.

collare.definition: ( Nom. sing. first in Apic. 7, 5 sq.), is (, , acc. to Prisc. p. 590 P.), n. collum, a band or chain for the neck, a collar; abl. collari, Lucil. ap. Non. p. 36, 26; Plaut. Capt. 2, 2, 107; nom. plur. collaria, Varr. R. R. 2, 9, 15 fin.

collaris.definition: collāris, e, collum Pertaining to the neck: offa,Petr. 56, 8.

collatero.definition: col-lătĕro (conl-), āre, 2. latus To admit on both sides: C vocales utrimque collaterat,Mart. Cap. 3, § 249.

collaticius.definition: collātĭcĭus (conl-) or -tĭus, a, um, confero Brought together, raised by contribution, mingled (post-Aug.): instrumenta,Sen. Cons. ad Marc. 10, 1: stipe,App. M. 8, p. 213, 36: myrrha,Plin. 12, 16, 35, § 69: aere,Tert. adv. Val. 12: sepultura,effected by contributions,Quint. Decl. 6, 11: PECVNIA,Inscr. Orell. 3730.

collatio.definition: (), , confero A bringing together, collecting. Prop., of the standards in war for battle, a hostile meeting: signorum,Cic. de Or. 1, 48, 210: centuriarum, for voting, id. ap. Ascon. in Toga Cand. p. 85, 18 Baiter: hyacinthorum et auri,Plin. 37, 9, 42, § 126.—Of money, a contribution, collection, a gratuity collected together for the emperor: stipis aut decimae,Liv. 5, 25, 5; 4, 60, 6; 6, 14, 12; Tac. G. 29; Suet. Calig. 42; id. Ner. 38; 44; id. T...

collativus.definition: collātīvus (conl-), a, um, collatus, confero Brought or carried together, collected, combined (very rare): collativum sacrificium dicitur, quod ex collatione offertur, Paul. ex Fest. p. 37, 13 Müll.: collativum ventrem magnum et turgidum dixit Plautus (Curc. 2, 1, 16), quia in eum omnia edulia congeruntur, Paul. ex Fest. p. 58, 17 Müll.: favor,common, joint,Macr. Somn. Scip. 116: vis,Nazar. Pan. ad Const. 18 fin. Subst.: collātīvum, n., = collati...

collatiuus.definition: collātīvus (conl-), a, um, collatus, confero Brought or carried together, collected, combined (very rare): collativum sacrificium dicitur, quod ex collatione offertur, Paul. ex Fest. p. 37, 13 Müll.: collativum ventrem magnum et turgidum dixit Plautus (Curc. 2, 1, 16), quia in eum omnia edulia congeruntur, Paul. ex Fest. p. 58, 17 Müll.: favor,common, joint,Macr. Somn. Scip. 116: vis,Nazar. Pan. ad Const. 18 fin. Subst.: collātīvum, n., = collati...

collator.definition: (), , confero. He who bears, brings, places together, a contributor, etc. (ante- and post - class.): symbolarum,Plaut. Curc. 4, 1, 13.—Trop.: salutis,Fulg. Myth. 1, 1; also, one who pays a voluntary contribution to the state, Cod. Th. 7, 6, 5. One who compares, a comparer: et disputator,Aug. Ep. 147.

collaudabilis.definition: collaudābĭlis (conl-), e, collaudo Worthy of praise in every respect, Prud. Ham. 694.

collaudatio.definition: (), , id. Warm praise (perh. only in the foll. exs.; only in the abl.): scriptoris,Cic. Inv. 2, 43, 125; Auct. Her. 2, 9, 13.

collaudator.definition: (), , id. One who praises warmly: nullo collaudatore,Aug. Con. 4, 14 fin.
