collaudo.definition: col-laudo (conl-), āvi, ātum, 1 To praise or commend very much, extol highly (class.): quantis laudibus Suum erum servus collaudavit,Plaut. Capt. 2, 3, 61: collegam,id. As. 3, 2, 30: alios, se,id. Truc. 2, 6, 15: filium,Ter. Ad. 3, 3, 13: ab omnibus conlaudāri,Cic. Fam. 1, 7, 5: me, * Hor. S. 1, 6, 70: collaudati milites,Caes. B. G. 5, 2; Nep. Ages. 1, 1; Liv. 1, 52, 1; Suet. Caes. 16: aliquem multum,Curt. 7, 5, 38; Stat. Th. 6, 490: magis utrumq...

collectaculum.definition: (), , id. A place of assembling, a receptacle, reservoir: aquae, Innocent. Cas. Lit. p. 230 Goes. vesicae, Cassiod. Var. 10, 30.

collectaneus.definition: collectānĕus (conl-), a, um, id. Gathered or collected together, collectaneous (very rare): aes,Plin. 34, 9, 20, § 97: Dicta collectanea, the title of a work of Caesar, now lost,Suet. Caes. 56 (perh. his Ἀποφθέγματα, mentioned by Cic., Fam. 9, 16, 4).—Hence, subst.: Collectānĕa, ōrum, n., the title of the collected works of Jul. Solinus.

collectarius.definition: (), , id. A money-changer, banker, cashier, Cod. Just. 4, 2, 16; Symm. Ep. 10, 49 al.

collecticius.definition: collectĭcĭus (conl-), or -tĭus, a, um, colligo Collected, gathered together (very rare): exercitus, gathered hastily without selection, * Cic. Fam. 7, 3, 2: ignis,fed by fuel gathered here and there,Sen. Q. N. 7, 23, 2.

collectim.definition: collectim (conl-), id. Summarily, briefly: redigere aliquid,Claud. Mam. Stat. An. 3, 14.

collectio.definition: (), , id.. Abstr., a collecting together. Concr. in medic. lang., a swelling, tumor, abscess, Plin. 22, 25, 58, § 122; 24, 4, 7, § 13; 26, 12, 79, § 127; 27, 12, 87, § 110 et saep.; Sen. Ep. 68, 7; Scrib. Comp. 206.

collectivus.definition: collectīvus (conl-), a, um, colligo. * Collected, gathered together: umor,Sen. Q. N. 3, 7, 3. Trop.

collectiuus.definition: collectīvus (conl-), a, um, colligo. * Collected, gathered together: umor,Sen. Q. N. 3, 7, 3. Trop.

collectus.definition: collectus (conl-), a, um, Part. and , from 1. colligo.

collega.definition: (), , 1. lego. Lit., one who is chosen at the same time with another: collegae, qui una lecti,Varr. L. L. 6, § 66 Müll.—Hence Transf., of an associate in other than official position, a colleague, associate, companion, fellow: Metrodorus, Epicuri collega sapientiae,Cic. N. D. 1, 40, 114; a fellow-member of a club or sodalitia, Cic. Sull. 2, 7; a joint-guardian, Dig. 26, 7, 13 and 45; fellow-slaves, Plaut. As. 3, 2, 10 and 30; a fellow-actor, Juv....

collegatarius.definition: () A person to whom is bequeathed a legacy in common with others, a collegatary, joint-legatee, Gai Inst. 2, § 199; Dig. 7, 2, 10 and 30.

collegiarius.definition: collēgĭārĭus (conl-), a, um, id. Collegial: ministri,Tert. Spect. 11.

collegiatus.definition: (), , id. He who is with one in a society, college, corporation, etc., Cod. Just. 11, 17: De collegiatis, Cod. Th. 6, 30, 16; 7, 20, 12, § 3; so also Inscr. Orell. 3948 al.

collegium.definition: (); in inscrr. sometimes corrupted , m., Inscr. Orell. 2413; 4101 al.), , n. collega. Abstr., the connection of associates, colleagues, etc., colleagueship (rare): ita, quae nostra officia fuerunt, pro collegio et pro propinquitate et vivo et mortuo ei praestitimus,Serv. ad Cic. Fam. 4, 12, 3: Decium, expertum mihi concordi collegio virum, mecum consulem faciatis,Liv. 10, 13. 13; so id. 22, 3, and 24, 6: magister equitum ex collegio prioris anni,...

collema.definition: That which is glued or cemented together: fruticis Niloticae,Mart. Cap. 3, § 225.

colleticus.definition: collētĭcus, a, um Suitable for gluing or sticking together: clysteria,Veg. 1, 46.

collevo.definition: col-lēvo (con-, -laevo), āre Tomake entirely smooth, to smooth (post-class. and rare): plagam arboris falce,Plin. 17, 22, 35, § 192: asperitatem oculorum,Sen. Ep. 64, 7; cf.: interanea vesicae,Plin. 23, 1, 18, § 30.

colleuo.definition: col-lēvo (con-, -laevo), āre Tomake entirely smooth, to smooth (post-class. and rare): plagam arboris falce,Plin. 17, 22, 35, § 192: asperitatem oculorum,Sen. Ep. 64, 7; cf.: interanea vesicae,Plin. 23, 1, 18, § 30.

collibertus.definition: () A fellowfreedman, Plaut. Poen. 4, 2, 88; Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 59, § 154 dub.; Dig. 36, 3, 18 al.

collicellus.definition: dim.collis A very little hill, Agrim. p. 245; 272 Goes.

collido.definition: col-līdo (conl-), līsi, līsum, 3, laedo To clash, strike, dash, beat, or press together, etc. (rare; mostly post-Aug.; most freq. in Quint.). Prop.: umor ita mollis est, ut facile premi collidique possit,Cic. N. D. 3, 12, 31; Lucr. 1, 532: collidere manus,to clap,Quint. 2, 12, 10: dentes colliduntur,chatter,Sen. Ep. 11, 2: anulus ut fiat, primo colliditur aurum,Ov. A. A. 3, 221: mare inter se navigia collidit,Curt. 4, 3, 17; 9, 9, 16: amnis uterq...

colligatio.definition: (), , 2. colligo A binding together, connection (rare). Prop.: ex his colligationibus,Cic. Univ. 7, 21: tota operis colligatio,Val. Max. 8, 14, 6; cf.: inter quattuor (elementa),Macr. Somn. Scip. 1, 6, 28. Trop. (only in Cic.): causarum omnium,Cic. Div. 1, 56, 127: colligatione naturali omnia fiunt,id. Fat. 14, 31: artior societatis propinquorum,id. Off. 1, 17, 53.

colligo.definition: col-lĭgo (conl-), lēgi, lectum, 3 V.a. [2. lego, ĕre], to gather or collect together into a whole or to a point, to assemble, draw or bring together, collect (class. and very freq.) Prop. Trop.

collimitaneus.definition: col-līmĭtānĕus (conl-), a, um Bordering upon; with dat.: Phrygia Galatiae,Sol. 40, 9.

collimito.definition: col-līmĭto (conl-), āre, and collī-mĭtor, āri To border upon (post-class. and very rare); with dat., Amm. 31, 2, 14; Sol. 25.

collina.definition: collinus Hilly land, Innoc. de Cas. Litt. p. 224 Goes.

collineo.definition: col-līnĕo (conl-), āvi, ātum, āre, v. a. To direct something in a straight line, to aim (rare, and except in Cic. only postclass.). Prop.: hastam aut sagittam aliquo,Cic. Fin. 3, 6, 22: manum et oculos, Julian. ap. Gell. 9, 1, 6: oculos ad umbram,App. M. 9, p. 237; id. Flor. 23.—* To take a right aim, Cic. Div. 2, 59, 121; cf. Madv. Fin. p. 382.—Hence, collīnĕātē, adv., in a direct line; trop., skilfully, artistically; in sup., Jul. Val. Alex. M....

collino.definition: col-lĭno (conl-), lēvi, lĭtum, 3 To besmear, to cover over, defile, pollute: aliquid, aliquā re (rare; not in class. prose). Prop.: ora venenis,Ov. R. Am. 351: tabulas cerā,Gell. 17, 9, 17: crines adulteros pulvere, * Hor. C. 1, 15, 20 (cf. Verg. A. 12, 99: foedare in pulvere crines): caeno collitus,Plaut. Poen. 4, 2, 4. Trop.: pulchrum ornatum turpes mores pejus caeno collinunt,Plaut. Most. 1, 3, 133; id. Poen. 1, 2, 96.

collinus.definition: collīnus, a, um, adj.collis Of or pertaining to a hill, found or growing on a hill, hilly, hill- (class.). In gen.: genus agrorum (opp. to campestre and montanum),Varr. R. R. 1, 6, 2: vineae,id. ib. 1, 6, 5; Col. 12, 21, 1: loca,id. 3, 2, 6: aqua,id. 1, 5, 3: vina,id. 12, 21, 4: frumentum,Cels. 2, 18. Esp.: Collīnus, a, um, adj., pertaining to the hills in the northeastern part of Rome (the Quirinal and Viminal), Colline: regio urbis Collina,Varr...

colliquefactus.definition: col-lĭquĕfactus (conl-), a, um, Part. [liquefio] Made fluid, liquefied, dissolved, melted (very rare): glacies,Varr. R. R. 2, 4, 6: venenum in potione, * Cic. Clu. 62, 173.

colliquesco.definition: col-lĭquesco (conl-), lĭqui, ĕre V. inch. n., to become fluid, to liquefy, melt, dissolve (rare). Prop.: cum aurum colliquisset, Varr. ap. Non. p. 334, 27 sq.: cum aes colliquisset,id. ib. (but Neue, Formenl. 2, 486, would read collicuisset in both these passages): in pice colliquescere,Col. 12, 22, 2: igni,App. Mag. p. 306, 10. Trop.: lacrimis, to melt into tears, Fronto, Nep. Am. 2.

collis.definition: (abl. reg. colle, e. g. Ov. M. 1, 698; 14, 90; 14, 333; 14, 822; 14, 836; Caes. B. G. 1, 24; 2, 18; Sall. J. 52, 3: Aventino,Liv. 1, 3, 9 et saep.; colli,Lucr. 2, 317 and 322; Auct. Aetn. 466; gen. plur. collium, Tac. Agr. 37; Lact. Opif. Dei, 10), m. cel-, root of ex-cello, celsus; cf. calamus, high ground, a hill (opp. mons and campus), Lucr. 5, 1373; Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 18, § 47; Caes. B. G. 2, 8; 7, 19: altus,Ov. M. 15, 306: aperti,Verg. G. 2, 1...

collisus.definition: collīsus (conl-), a, um, Part., from collido.

collocatio.definition: (), , colloco A putting together, arrangement, a setting up, erecting, placing, collocation (except in rhet. use, very rare). In gen.: siderum,Cic. Univ. 9, 26: moenium,Vitr. 5, 3. Esp.: filiae, an endowing, giving in marriage (v. colloco, I. B.), Cic. Clu. 66, 190.

colloco.definition: col-lŏco (conl-), āvi, ātum, 1 To place together, to arrange, to station, lay, put, place, set, set up, erect, etc., a thing (or person) somewhere (class. in prose and poetry; cf.: statuo, pono, sisto). Lit. Trop. (in good prose; most freq. in Cic. and Quint.).

collocupleto.definition: col-lŏcŭplēto (conl-), āvi, 1 To make very rich, to enrich (prob. only in the foll. exs.). Prop.: se,Ter. Heaut. 2, 3, 17. Trop., to embellish, enrich, adorn: rei honestandae et collocupletandae causā,Auct. Her. 2, 18, 28.

collocutio.definition: (), , colloquor A (familiar or private) conversation, conference (very rare): hominum,Cic. Tusc. 1, 13, 30; id. Att. 12, 1, 2: venire cum aliquo in collocutionem,Auct. Her. 1, 15, 25.—In plur.: familiarissimae cum aliquo,Cic. Phil. 11, 2, 5: in sermonibus collocutionibusque aliquid videre,id. Fam. 1, 9, 4.

collocutor.definition: (), , id. He who talks with another (eccl. Lat.), Tert. adv. Prax. 5; Aug. Conf. 9, 6.

colloquium.definition: (), , id. A conversation, conference, discourse (class. in prose and poetry; not in Hor.): colloquium cum conveniunt in unum locum loquendi causā,Varr. L. L. 6, § 57 Müll.; Titin. ap. Non. p. 256, 16: eo ad colloquium venerunt,Caes. B. G. 1, 43: in colloquium venire,id. ib. 1, 35: in Antonii congressum colloquiumque veniendum est,Cic. Phil. 12, 11, 26: pervenire ad conloquium alicujus,id. ib. 9, 1, 2: denos ut ad colloquium adducerent,Caes. B. G....

colloquor.definition: col-lŏquor (conl-), cūtus, 3 To talk together, converse, to hold a conversation, a parley, or a conference (in good prose); constr. commonly cum aliquo, inter se, or absol.; in Plaut. several times as verb act. with acc.

colluceo.definition: col-lūcĕo (conl-), ēre To give light on every side, to shine brightly, to be wholly illuminated, to be bright or brilliant (class. in prose and poetry; not in Hor.). Prop. Trop., to shine, be resplendent: vidi collucere omnia furtis tuis,Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 22, § 58; id. N. D. 2, 39, 99: collucent floribus agri,Ov. F. 5, 363; cf. Col. 3, 21, 3; 10, 293.

colluco.definition: col-lūco (conl-), āre, lux To make light, to clear or thin a forest, etc.: collucare est succisis arboribus locum luce implere, Fest. s. v. sublucare, p. 348, 18 Müll. (explained in a different manner by Paul. ex Fest. p. 37, 12 ib.): lucum,Cato, R. R. 139: arborem,Col. 2, 21, 3.

colluctatio.definition: (), , colluctor A wrestling, struggling, contending with something (post-Aug. prose). Prop.: in colluctatione vel pancratio,Dig. 9, 2, 7; so of the fighting of oxen,Col. 6, 2, 4. Trop., the death struggle, Sen. Q. N. 3, 18, 1. —Of an embracing in love, App. M. 9, p. 219, 12; Lact. 1, 17.—Of a difficult utterance: est aliis concursus oris et cum verbis suis colluctatio,Quint. 11, 3, 56.

colluctor.definition: col-luctor (conl-), āri To struggle, contend, wrestle with (post-Aug. and rare); constr. with cum aliquo, alicui, or absol.: praedonibus,Prud. Ham. 523.—Absol., Just. 13, 8, 8; App. M. 2, p. 129.—Trop.: cum agro,Col. 1, 3, 9; cf.: cum solo,Plin. 27, 2, 2, § 5: cum petulantiā morbi,Gell. 12, 5, 9.

colludium.definition: (), , colludo (post-class.). A sporting, playing together: delphinorum,Sol. 12; so Symm. Ep. 3, 5. A secret, deceptive understanding, collusion, esp. in justice, Amm. 18, 5, 1; Cod. Th. 9, 42, 20; 11, 42, 7; Symm. Ep. 4, 20.

colludo.definition: col-lūdo (conl-), si, sum, 3 To play or sport together, play with (very rare). Prop., with dat.: (puer) gestit paribus colludere, * Hor. A. P. 159.—Poet.: aut summā nantes in aquā colludere plumas, * Verg. G. 1, 369: DIGITIS COLLVDENTIBVS TRADERE PECORA,Inscr. Orell. 3166. Jurid. t. t., to keep up false appearances with one to the injury of a third person, to have a secret understanding with one, to act collusively, * Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 24, § 58; D...

collugeo.definition: col-lūgĕo (conl-), ēre To lament, grieve together, Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 5, 88.

collum.definition: n. (ante-class. access. form , , m., Naev., Cato, Lucil., Att., Caecil., Varr. ap. Non. p. 200, 14 sq.; Plaut. Capt. 2, 2, 107; 4, 3, 2; and, acc. to Non. l. l., also id. Am. 1, 1, 289: Nec collos mihi Calvus persuaserit,Quint. 1, 6, 42; Front. Ep. ad M. Caes. 2, 16) [cf. Germ. Hals]. Prop., the neck, of men and animals: accipite si vultis hoc onus in vostros collos, Cato, l.l.: anseris, Lucil. l.l.: pavonis, Varr. l. l.: columbarum,Lucr. 2, 802;...

colluo.definition: col-lŭo (conl-), lŭi, lūtum, 3 To wash thoroughly, wash out, rinse (mostly post-Aug.; not in Cic.); constr. aliquid, or aliquid aliquā re; rarely aliquid de aliquā re: metretam amurcā,Cato, R. R. 100; Pers. 1, 18: os de oleo,Plin. 23, 4, 38, § 77: decocto,id. 23, 6, 56, § 105: dentes aquā,id. 20, 6, 23, § 53: gemma melle colluta,id. 37, 10, 56, § 155.—Poet.: ora, to moisten, wet, i. e. to quench thirst, * Ov. M. 5, 447 (cf.: abluere sitim,Lucr. 4...

collusio.definition: (), , colludo, II. A secret, deceptive understanding, collusion, * Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 13, § 33: inter raptae patrem et raptorem,Sen. Contr. 2, 11, 22: per collusionem,id. ib. 5, 31fin.: illa inter virum et uxorem nota collusio,App. Mag. p. 322, 13; Dig. 40, 16: de collusione detegendā,ib. 40, 4; 8, 5, 19; 17, 1, 8; 12, 2, 30, § 3.

collusor.definition: (), , colludo. A companion in play, playmate (in good prose), Cic. Phil. 2, 23, 56; 2, 39, 101; 5, 5, 13; * Suet. Calig. 41; Plin. Ep. 9, 33, 8; Dig. 11, 5, 1, § 1.—* (Acc. to colludo, II.) He who has a secret understanding with one to the injury of a third, in law, Cod. Th. 7, 20, 2.

collustrium.definition: collustro A corporation that procured the lustration of the fields of a district, Inscr. Orell. 1773.

collustro.definition: col-lustro (conl-), āvi, ātum, 1 To lighten on all sides, to illumine, brighten (rare but class.; most freq. in Cic.). Prop.: sol omnia clarissimā luce collustrans,Cic. N. D. 2, 36, 92; id. Div. 2, 43, 91; id. Rep. 6, 17, 17 (al. lustret).—* Trop., to consider a thing on all sides, to inspect, survey: omnia oculis, Cic. Tusc. 5, 23, 65: omnia,Verg. A. 3, 651: cuncta,Tac. A. 2, 45.

collutito.definition: col-lŭtĭto (conl-), āre, colluo; cf. Ritschl, prol. ad Plaut. p. 74 To soil, defile much; trop., Plaut. Trin. 3, 2, 67 Ritschl N. cr.; cf. Non. p. 84, 25 (al. collutulo).

colluvio.definition: (), , and , (the latter form not freq. before the Aug. per.; but exclusively used by Col., Pliny the elder, and Tac.; a third collat. form , acc. to Isid. Diff. Verb. 40), colluo A conflux or collection of filth, washings, sweepings, draff, swill. Prop. More freq. trop., the impure conflux of different objects, dregs, impurities, impure mixture, vile medley, offscourings.

colluuio.definition: (), , and , (the latter form not freq. before the Aug. per.; but exclusively used by Col., Pliny the elder, and Tac.; a third collat. form , acc. to Isid. Diff. Verb. 40), colluo A conflux or collection of filth, washings, sweepings, draff, swill. Prop. More freq. trop., the impure conflux of different objects, dregs, impurities, impure mixture, vile medley, offscourings.

collybista.definition: A money-changer, banker, Hier. in Matt. 21, 12.

collybus.definition: (), , , = [prob. of Phoenicio-Semitic origin, kindr. with the Heb. , to change] The exchange of coins of different kinds, or of different countries, agio. Prop., Cic. Att. 12, 6, 1; Cassiod. Parm. ap. Suet. Aug. 4. Meton., the rate or premium of exchange, Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 78, § 181.

collyra.definition: A kind of pastry of a round, elongated form, maccaroni, vermicelli, shred into broth, Plaut. Pers. 1, 3, 12.—Hence Of vermicelli, vermicelli soup, Plaut. Pers. 1, 3, 15 and 17.

collyriolum.definition: dim.collyrium A small collyrium, tent, pessary, etc., Macer. 4, 12.

collyris.definition: (, , Vulg. 2 Reg. 6, 19; id. Lev. 8, 26; cf.: cassida, chlamyda, etc.), , = . Lit., a roll or cake, Aug. in Gen. 8, 5 fin.; Vulg. Lev. 7, 12 (transl. of the Heb. ). Meton.

collyrium.definition: (a mass similar to the collyra-dough; hence, in medic. lang.) A tent, pessary, suppository, etc., Cels. 5, 28, 12; Col. 6, 6, 5; 6, 30, 8; Plin. 26, 12, 78, § 126; 28, 9, 37, § 139; Scrib. Comp. 142. Meton., a shaft, pillar, Sid. Ep. 2, 2.

colo.definition: cŏlo, colŭi, cultum, 3, v. a.from the stem ΚΟΛ, whence βουκόλος, βουκολέω; cf.: colonus, in-cola, agri-cola (orig. pertaining to agriculture) To cultivate, till, tend, takecare of a field, garden, etc. (freq. in all per. and species of composition). Prop. Trop. (freq. and class.).

colobathrarius.definition: κωλόβαθρον One who walks on stilts, Non. p. 115, 20.

colobicus.definition: cŏlŏbĭcus, a, um Mutilated, Firm. Math. 3, 14, 8.

colobium.definition: (, , Cod. Th. 14, 10, 1) An undergarment with short sleeves, Serv. ad Verg. A. 9, 616.

colocasia.definition: f. (plur.: , , n., * Verg. E. 4, 20; Mart. 8, 33, 13), = κολοκασία or κολοκάσιον An Egyptian bean; a magnificent plant of the lily kind, growing in the lakes and marshes of Egypt, whose beans, roots, and even the stalks and stems, were considered as luxuries, and from its large leaves drinking-cups (ciboria) were made, Plin. 21, 15, 51, § 87; Col. 8, 15, 4; Pall. Febr. 24, 14; id. Apr. 3, 5; cf. Voss ad Verg. l. l. (The colocasia of Virgil is s...

colona.definition: colonus A countrywoman, Ov. F. 4, 692; 2, 646; Dig. 19, 2, 54 fin.; Inscr. Orell. 4644.

colonarius.definition: cŏlōnārĭus, a, um, colonia Of or pertaining to the colonus, rustic (late Lat.): persona,Sid. Ep. 5, 19: condicio,Cod. Just. 1, 4, 24.

colonatus.definition: colonus The condition of a rustic (post-class.), Cod. Th. 12, 1, 33; 14, 18, 1.

colonia.definition: colonus. (Acc. to colonus, I.) A possession in land, a landed estate, a farm, Col. 11, 1, 23; Dig. 19, 2, 24, § 4; 33, 7, 20. (Acc. to colonus, II.) A colony, colonial town, settlement: colonia dicta est a colendo: est autem pars civium aut sociorum, missa ubi rem publicam habeant ex consensu suae civitatis aut publico ejus populi unde profecti sunt consilio. Hae autem coloniae sunt. quae ex consensu publico, non ex secessione sunt conditae,Serv....

coloniarius.definition: m., and , , f.colonia, II. Native of a colony, Gai Inst. 3, § 56; 1, § 28; Ulp. Sent. 19, 4.

colonicus.definition: cŏlōnĭcus, a, um, colonus, I.. Of or pertaining to agriculture or husbandry: leges,Varr. R. R. 1, 2, 17: genus ovium,found upon any farm, common,Plin. 8, 47, 72, § 189; 26, 10, 62, § 96. Pertaining to a colony: cohortes,levied from colonies,Caes. B. C. 2, 19: decuriones,Suet. Aug. 46.

colonus.definition: colo. A husbandman, tiller of the soil (opp. pastor), Cato, R. R. prooem. § 2; Varr. R. R. 2, prooem. § 5; id. L. L. 5, § 21 Müll.; Cic. de Or. 2, 71, 287; Hor. C. 1, 35, 6; 2, 14, 12; id. S. 2, 1, 35; 2, 2, 115; Verg. E. 9, 4; id. G. 1, 125; Ov. M. 1, 272; Sen. Ep. 114, 25. A colonist, inhabitant of a colonial town, ἄποικος, Cic. Agr. 2, 28, 75; id. Phil. 2, 40, 102; id. N. D. 3, 19, 48; Nep. Milt. 1, 1; Liv. 4, 11, 3 sq.; 9, 26, 3 and 5; Verg...

colophon.definition: Cŏlŏphon, ōnis (acc. -nem, Cic. Imp. Pomp. 12, 33; -na,Vell. 1, 4, 3; Tac. A. 2, 54), m., = Κολοφών, one of the twelve Ionian towns in Lydia, situated near the sea, and renowned for its cavalry, now perh. Zille or Altobosco, Mel. 1, 17, 2; Cic. Imp. Pomp. 12, 33; Liv. 37, 26, 5 sq.; Hor. Ep. 1, 11, 3. Hence

color.definition: (old form , , etc., Plaut. Mil. 4, 4, 43; Lucr. 6, 208; 6, 1073; Sall. C. 15, 5, acc. to Prob. II. pp. 1456 and 1467 P.; Plin. 13, 15, 30, § 98; 35, 11, 42, § 150), , root cal-, to cover; cf.: caligo, occulere, calyx Color, hue, tint. Lit. Trop.

colorabilis.definition: cŏlōrābĭlis, e, , = chromaticus, q. v., Mart. Cap. 9, § 942.

colorator.definition: A polisher, στιλβωτής et ινδικοπλάστης, Gloss. Lat.; Inscr. Murat. 887, 3.—Name of a comedy of Laberius, Gell. 6 ($3), 9, 4.

coloratus.definition: cŏlōrātus, a, um, v. coloro P.a.

coloreus.definition: cŏlōrĕus or -ĭus, a, um, color Colored, variegated (rare, mostly class.): gausapes coloriae, August. ap. Charis. p. 80 P.; so, vestis,Dig. 34, 2, 33 fin.: tunicae coloreae,Vop. Aur. 46.

coloro.definition: cŏlōro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.id.. To give a color to, to color, tinge (class.): corpora,Cic. N. D. 1, 39, 110: lignum sinopide,Plin. 35, 6, 13, § 31: lineas testa trita,id. 35, 3, 5, § 16: medicamentum rubricā vel atramento,Scrib. Comp. 228: coloratum Tithoni conjuge caelum,Ov. Am. 2, 5, 35. Trop. (cf. color, II.).

colosseus.definition: cŏlossēus (-ossiaeus, Plin. 36, 5, 4, § 26), a, um Colossal, huge, gigantic (post-Aug. prose): statuae,Plin. 34, 7, 18, § 39; cf. id. 36, 5, 4, § 26; Suet. Vesp. 23: colosseum se pingi Nero jussit,Plin. 35, 7, 33, § 51.

colossicus.definition: cŏlossĭcus, a, um Colossal, gigantic: Apollo,Vitr. 10, 6: signum colossicon,Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 54.— Comp. Gr. colossicoteros, -a, acc. -an, Vitr. 3, 5, 9, p. 98 Bip., and id. 10, 2, 4, p. 292 id. (prob. to be written with Greek letters).

colossus.definition: A gigantic statue, a colossus, Plin. 35, 11, 40, § 128; Suet. Ner. 31; Stat. S. 1, 3, 51.—In partic., the celebrated Colossus at Rhodes; it was dedicated to the sun, and was 70 ells high, Plin. 34, 7, 18, § 41; Suet. Vesp. 18; Paul. ex Fest. p. 58, 2 Müll.

colostra.definition: (), , f. (, , n., Mart. 13, 38, 2; in sing.: , Mart. l. l.; Serv. ad Verg. E. 2, 22) The first milk after delivery, the biestings, Plin. 28, 9, 33, § 123; 11, 41, 96, § 236; Col. 7, 3, 17; Pall. Nov. 13, 1.—As a dainty dish, Mart. l. l.—As a term of endearment, Plaut. Poen. 1, 2, 154; 1, 2, 177; Laber. ap. Non. p. 84, 13.

coluber.definition: akin to celer A serpent, snake (poet.), Verg. G. 2, 320; 3, 418; id. A. 2, 471 (an imitation of Hom. Il. 22, 93: ὡς δὲ δράκων, κ.τ.λ.); Ov. M. 4, 620; 11, 775; Col. 10, 231. Esp., as an attributive of the hair of Medusa, the Furies, the Hydra, etc., Lucr. 5, 27; Ov. M. 9, 73; 10, 21; Luc. 6, 664; Val. Fl. 6, 175.

colubra.definition: coluber A female serpent; and in gen., a serpent, snake, Lucil., Turp., and Varr. ap. Non. p. 201, 22 sq.; Hor. C. 1, 17, 8; id. S. 1, 8, 42; Ov. M. 6, 559; Juv. 5, 103; Cels. 5, 27, 3; Col. 10, 230; Plin. 32, 5, 19, § 53.—As an attributive of the hair of the Furies, Medusa, etc. (v. coluber), Ov. M. 4, 474; 4, 491; 4, 783; Luc. 9, 634.— Hence, prov.: quas tu edes colubras?i. e. art thou frantic?Plaut. Stich. 2, 1, 50 Ritschl N. cr.; and: colubra...

colubrimodus.definition: cŏlubrĭmŏdus, a, um, coluber-modus Serpent-like: capilli, Coripp. Fragm. 4.

colubrinus.definition: cŏlubrīnus, a, um, coluber Like a serpent; trop., cunning, wily (ante- and post-class.): ingenio esse,Plaut. Truc. 4, 3, 6: vis gestūs,Tert. Spect. 18. Subst.: cŏlubrīna, ae, f., a plant, also called bryonia and dracontea, App. Herb. 14.

colubrosus.definition: cŏlubrōsus, a, um, id. Serpentine, winding: actus (viae),Tert. adv. Val. 4.

colum.definition: A vessel for straining, a strainer, colander, Cato, R. R. 11, 2; Verg. G. 2, 242; Col. 11, 2, 70; 12, 19, 4; 12, 38, 7; Plin. 36, 23, 52, § 173; App. M. 3, p. 130, 20; Scrib. Comp. 156 al.: colum nivarium, for cooling wine,Mart. 14, 103 inscr.; cf. id. 14, 104; Dig. 34, 2, 2.—* Poet., a bow-net, a net of wicker-work for catching fish, a wear, Aus. Ep. 4, 57; cf. 2. colo.

columba.definition: columbus A dove, pigeon, Cic. Ac. 2, 25, 79; id. Fin. 3, 5, 18; Plaut. As. 3, 3, 103; Varr. R. R. 3, 7; Col. 8, 8; Plin. 10, 34, 52, § 104; Pall. 1, 24; Ov. M. 1, 506; 5, 605; id. Am. 2, 6, 56; Hor. C. 1, 37, 18; 4, 4, 32; id. Epod. 16, 32; as sacred to Venus: Cythereiades,Ov. M. 15, 386; cf. Hyg. Fab. 197.—As a term of endearment, my dove, Plaut. Cas. 1, 1, 50 al.; cf. Vulg. Cant. 2, 10.

columbar.definition: columba A kind of collar (so called from its similarity to the hole in a dove-cot), Plaut. Rud. 3, 6, 50.

columbinaceus.definition: cŏlumbīnācĕus, a, um, columbinus Pertaining to a dove: pullus,a young dove,Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 18, 111.

columbinus.definition: columba Pertaining to a dove or pigeon, dove-: pulli,Varr. R. R. 3, 7, 9; * Cic. Fam. 9, 18, 3; so also absol.: , , m., little doves, Mart. 13, 66: ovum, * Hor. S. 2, 4, 56: fimus,Plin. 17, 27, 47, § 259: stercora,id. 35, 6, 27, § 46.

columbus.definition: κόλυμβος; cf.: calvus, color A male dove or cock - pigeon (and transf., of male persons), Varr. L. L. 9, § 56; Plaut. Rud. 3, 6, 49; Cat. 29, 9; 68, 125; Hor. Ep. 1, 10, 5 A dove in gen. (very rare), Col. 8, 8, 1; Plin. 10, 9, 11, § 25.

columella.definition: (in MSS. often ), , dim. columna, columen A small column, a pillar, Cato, R. R. 20, 1; 22, 2; Cic. Leg. 2, 26, 66; id. Tusc. 5, 23, 65; Caes. B. C. 2, 10. Trop., a pillar, support, prop (cf. columen), Lucil. ap. Don. Ter. Phorm. 2, 1, 57.

columellaris.definition: cŏlŭmellāris, e Adj [columella], pillar-formed (rare): dentes,the grinders of horses,Varr. R. R. 2, 7, 2; Plin. 11, 37, 64, § 168; in vulg. Lat. colomelli, acc. to Isid. Orig. 11, 1, 48.

columen.definition: n., and contr. , , n.root cel- of excello; cf.: celsus, culmus, calamus, collis, lit. That which rises in height, is prominent, projects; hence the point, top, summit, ridge. Form , n. (only this form is used by Plautus, v. Ritschl, prol. ad Plaut. p. 65). An elevated object that supports, sustains something; in archit., the top of a gable-end, a gable pillar, a prop, Vitr. 4, 2, 1; 4, 7, 5.—Esp. freq.

columna.definition: root cel- of excello; v. columen, of which it is orig. a collat. form.

columnar.definition: for columnarium A stone-quarry, marble-quarry, Inscr. Orell. 4034.

columnaris.definition: cŏlumnāris, e, columna Rising in the form of a pillar: lux,a pillar of fire,Prud. Ham. 476 (in imitation of the Heb. , Exod. 13, 21); cf. columnifer.

columnarius.definition: cŏlumnārĭus, a, um, columna Of or pertaining to a column; only subst., * Cŏlumnārĭus, ii, m., one who was condemned at the Columna Maenia (v. columna, A.); therefore a criminal or debtor, Cael. ap. Cic. Fam. 8, 9, 4. Cŏlum-nārĭum, ii, n., a tribute for the pillars of a house, a pillar-tax, Cic. Att. 13, 6, 1; Caes. B. C. 3, 32; cf. columnar.

columnatus.definition: cŏlumnātus, a, um, id. Supported by posts or pillars (perh. only in the foll. exs.): tholus,Varr. R. R. 3, 5, 12: diversoria, Ambros. de Cain et Abel, 1, 5, 19: pons,Ampel. Lib. Mem. 8, 3.—Humorously: os,i. e. supported upon the hand,Plaut. Mil. 2, 2, 57; cf. id. ib. 2, 2, 54.

colurnus.definition: cŏlurnus, a, um, transp. for corulnus, from corulus = corylus Made of the hazel-bush: verna,Verg. G. 2, 396 Serv.; cf. Prisc. p. 595 P.: hastilia, Paul. ex Fest. p. 37, 7 Müll.

colurus.definition: cŏlūrus, a, um Mutilated; hence In astron.: coluri circuli, = κόλουροι, the colures, two circles passing through the equinoctial and solstitial points, and cutting each other at right angles at the poles, Macr. Somn. Scip. 1, 15. In metre: metrum, a syllable too short, Plotius, Metr. p. 2649 P.

colus.definition: (i and), ūs (cf. Prisc. pp. 654 and 719 P.; Rudd. 1, p. 166, n. 100), f. (m., Cat. 64, 311; Prop. 4, 1, 72; 4, 9, 48) [root prob. kar-, to be bent or round; cf.: corona, curvus, collum] A distaff; sing. nom. colus, Tib. 2, 1, 63; Ov. M. 4, 229; Plin. 8, 48, 74, § 194; Claud. IV. Cons. Hon. 594; gen. colus, Val. Fl. 2, 148; acc. colum, * Cat. 64, 312; Ov. H. 9, 116; abl. colo, Tib. 1, 3, 86; Prop. 4 (5), 1, 72; Verg. A. 8, 409 (quoted by Prisc. p....

colymbas.definition: (swimming; hence): olivae Prepared or put in brine, Col. 12, 47, 8; Plin. 15, 3, 4, § 16; 23, 3, 36, § 73; Pall. Nov. 22, 1.

colymbus.definition: A swimming-bath, Lampr. Elag. 23; Prud. στέφ. 12, 36.

coma.definition: cŏma, ae, f. The hair of the head (hence barba comaeque, Ov. M. 7, 288), considered as an ornament for the head: comae dicuntur capilli cum aliquā curā compositi, Paul. ex Fest. p. 63, 13 Müll. (class., esp. in poetry and post-Aug. prose; very rare in Cic.).—With : unguentis effluens calamistrata coma,Cic. Sest. 8, 18: madens,id. post Red. in Sen. 6, 13: fulva, ξανθή, Prop. 2, 2, 5: flava,Hor. C. 1, 5, 4; Tib. 1, 5, 44: myrtea,id. 3, 4, 28: long...

combibo.definition: com-bĭbo (conb-), bĭbi, 3, and A. Neutr., to drink with any one as a companion (very rare): aeque combibendi et convivandi peritissimus,Sen. Ep. 123, 15. Act., to drink completely up, to absorb, to imbibe (the most common signif., rare before the Aug. per., in Cic. only once trop.).

combinatio.definition: combino A joining two by two, ζεῦξις κατὰ δύο, Gloss. Gr. Lat.

combino.definition: com-bīno (conb-), no Perf., ātum, 1, bini, to unite, combine (late Lat.): combinat ζευγνὐει, συνάπτει, Gloss. Lat.; ζευγίζω combino, Gloss. Gr. Lat.; part. perf. combinatus, Aug. Conf. 8, 6; Sid. Ep. 9, 8.

comburo.definition: com-būro (conb-), ussi, ustum, ĕre, v. a. root bur-, pur-; cf. burrus, Gr. πυρρός, pruna, Gr. πίμπρημι, and Lat. bustum To burn up, consume (class.). Prop.: quae potuere Nec cum capta capi, nec cum combusta cremari, Enn. ap. Macr. S. 6, 1 (Ann. v. 360 Vahl.): fumo comburi nihil potest,Plaut. Curc. 1, 1, 54: flamma comburens impete magno,Lucr. 6, 153: is ejus (solis) tactus est, ut saepe comburat,Cic. N. D. 2, 15, 40: aedis,Plaut. Aul. 2, 6, 12:...

combustio.definition: comburo A burning, consuming, Firm. Math. 4, 12.

combustura.definition: combustūra, ae F [comburo], a burning (post-class.), Apic. 4, 4, § 179; Vulg. Lev. 13, 28; Macer de Rosa, 21.

comedo.definition: cŏm-ĕdo, ēdi, ēsum (comessum, Prol. ad Plaut. p 102 Ritschl), or estum, 3, (comesus, the more usual form, Cato, R. R. 58; Varr R. R. 1, 2, 11; Plaut. Trin. 2, 4, 5, Juv 1, 34; Valgius ap. Diom. p. 382 P—Hence, comessurus, Plaut. Ps. 4, 7, 25: Comestus,Cato, R. R 50; Cic. Clu. 62, 173, acc. to Prisc. p. 893; and Val. Max. 9, 12, ext. 6, and Didius ap. Diom. l. l.—Contr forms: comes,Plaut. Most. 1, 1, 11: comest,id. ib. 3, 1, 26; id. Trin. 2, 1, 20...

comes.definition: con and 1. eo (lit. one who goes with another) A companion, an associate, comrade, partaker, sharer, partner, etc. (whether male or female; class. and freq.). In gen. In partic.

comesor.definition: (, Gloss. Philox.), , 1. comedo An eater, a gourmand, Tert. adv. Marc. 1, 1; Dig. 21, 1, 18.

comestibilis.definition: cŏmestĭbĭlis, e, id. Eatable, Isid. Orig. 17, 7, 9.

comestio.definition: id. A consuming, Isid. Orig. 20, 2, 2; Anthol. Lat. 3, 90, 7.

comesus.definition: cŏmēsus, a, um, v. comedo Init.

comicus.definition: cōmĭcus, a, um Of or pertaining to comedy, comic: poëta,Cic. Or. 20, 67: artificium,id. Rosc. Com. 10, 18: levitates,id. N. D. 3, 29, 72: res,the material of comedy,Hor. A. P. 89: scaenae,Vitr. 5, 8: gestus,Quint. 11, 3, 125: senarius,id. 9, 4, 140: ad morem,id. 1, 8, 3: virtus (Terentii), C. Caes. ap. Suet. Vit. Ter. 5: persona,Quint. 11, 3, 79; Plin. 25, 11, 88, § 137: auctores,Quint. 2, 10, 13. Subst.: cōmĭcus, i, m.

comis.definition: cōmis, e, adj.etym. dub.; cf. concinnus Courteous, affable, kind, obliging, friendly, loving (class. in prose and poetry; on account of similarity of meaning, in MSS. very freq. interchanged with communis; hence the readings vary in the best edd.; cf. Liv. 25, 12, 9 Drak.; Suet. 2, p. 241 Wolf; Cic. Fin. 2, 25, 80 Madv.).

comissabundus.definition: cōmissābundus (cōmess-), a, um, comissor Holding a riotous procession, revelling, banqueting, carousing: comissabundus temulento agmine per Indiam incessit (Alexander Magnus; in regard to his imitation of the procession in honor of Bacchus through Asia; v. Curt. 9, 10, 26), Liv. 9, 17, 17; Curt. 5, 7, 10; 9, 10, 26: ubi (Athenis) comissabundi juvenes ante meridiem conventus sapientium frequentabant, decorated, crowned, etc., for a procession, Pli...

comissaliter.definition: cōmissālĭter (cōmess-), adv., from an adj. comissalis, not in use [id.] As in revelling processions, wantonly, jovially: cantare,Sid. Ep. 1, 5.

comissatio.definition: (), , id. A Bacchanalian revel, and the succeeding nocturnal procession with torches and music, a revelling, rioting, Cic. Mur. 6, 13; Liv. 40, 13, 3; Suet. Calig. 55; Mart. 12, 48, 11; Gell. 1, 9, 9.—In plur., Cic. Cael. 15, 35; id. Cat. 2, 5, 10; Varr. L. L. 7, § 89 Müll.; Liv. 1, 57, 5; Suet. Vit. 13; id. Tit. 7; Sen. Ben. 6, 32, 1; id. Cons. ad Helv. 10, 9; id. Ep. 51, 1.—The tropes tempestas comissationis and comissatio tempestatis are censu...

comissator.definition: (), , id. One who holds or joins in a festive procession, a reveller, Ter. Ad. 5, 2, 8; Cic. Cael. 28, 67; Liv. 40, 7, 8; 40, 9, 1; Quint. 3, 6, 26; Petr. 65, 3; Mart. 9, 62, 15; Gell. 4, 14, 4 al. Trop.: libellus, a book of songs used in a comissatio, Mart. 5, 16, 9: comissatores conjurationis, in contempt for the companions, participants, in the Catilinian conspiracy, Cic. Att. 1, 16, 11.

comissor.definition: cōmissor (on account of erroneous deriv. from comis, comedo, commensa, etc., often written cōmisor, commisor, commissor, cōmesor, cōmes-sor, commessor, commensor, etc.; v. Vel. Long. p. 2233; Liv. 40, 7, 5 Drak.; Quint. 11, 3, 57; Spald. and Zumpt), ātus, 1, , = (v. Lidd. and Scott in h. v.) To hold a festive procession, to revel, make merry; of young people, who went about with music and dancing, to celebrate a festival, and finally returned to ...

comitabilis.definition: cŏmĭtābĭlis, e, comitor Attending, accompanying, Paul. Nol. 10, 298.

comitas.definition: comis Courteousness, kindness, obligingness, friendliness, affability, gentleness (syn.: benignitas, facilitas, humanitas; opp. gravitas and severitas; in good prose; esp. freq. in Cic.): si illius (sc. Catonis) comitatem et facilitatem tuae gravitati severitatique asperseris,Cic. Mur. 31, 66; id. Or. 10, 34; id. Off. 2, 14, 48; id. de Or. 2, 43, 189: Crassus in summā comitate habebat etiam severitatis satis, Scaevolae multā in severitate non dee...

comitatensis.definition: cŏmĭtātensis, e, comitatus Of or pertaining to the dignity or office of courtiers (v. comes, II. D. and E.; postclass.): munus, Cod. Th. 12, 1, 38: legio,ib. 12, 36, 14: fabrica, i. e. machinatio,a court intrigue,Amm. 18, 4, 2.

comitatus.definition: cŏmĭtātus, a, um, Part. and , from comitor and comito; v. comitor.

comitialis.definition: cŏmĭtĭālis, e, comitium, II. Of or pertaining to the comitia: dies,on which the comitia were held,Cic. Q. Fr. 2, 2, 3; 2, 13, 3; Varr. L. L. 6, § 29 Müll.; Liv. 3, 11, 3; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 38, 12 Müll.; Macr. S. 1, 16; so, biduum,Caes. B. C. 1, 5: mensis,Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 52, § 130: homines,who were always at the comitia, and sold their votes,Plaut. Poen. 3, 2, 6: morbus, the epilepsy (so called because its occurrence on the day of the comitia...

comitianus.definition: cŏmĭtĭānus, a, um Of or pertaining to the Comes Orientis (a court officer), Cod. Th. 8, 4, 18 al.

comitio.definition: cŏmĭtĭo, āvi, ātum, 1, and A. [comitium]. To go into the comitium: quando rex comitiavit, fas (abridged, Q. R. C. F.), an old formula in Varr. L. L. 6, § 31 Müll.; cf. Fest. p. 278, 14 id.; Kalend. Praen. ap. Inscr. Orell. vol. 2, p. 386. —Hence Cŏmĭtĭātus, i, m., a military tribune elected at the comitia, Ps.-Ascon. Cic. Verr. 1, 10, 30.

comitium.definition: locus a coëundo, id est insimul veniendo, est dictus, Paul. ex Fest. p. 38, 12 Müll.; cf. Varr. L. L. 5, § 155 id.: comitium ab eo quod coibant eo comitiis curiatis, et litium causā. In sing., the place for the assembling of the Romans voting by the curioe situated near the Forum, and separated from it by the ancient Rostra, but sometimes considered as a part of the Forum in a more extended sense (hence, in Dion. Halic. ὁ κράτιστος and ό ἐπιφ...

comitivus.definition: cŏmĭtīvus, a, um, comes, II. E. Pertaining to a chief officer (post-class.): dignitas, Veg. Mil. 2, 9: sedes. Cod. Th. 11, 21, 3; also,subst., a chief,Cod. Just. 1, 33, 3 al.

comitiuus.definition: cŏmĭtīvus, a, um, comes, II. E. Pertaining to a chief officer (post-class.): dignitas, Veg. Mil. 2, 9: sedes. Cod. Th. 11, 21, 3; also,subst., a chief,Cod. Just. 1, 33, 3 al.

comito.definition: cŏmĭto, āre, 1, v. a. (poet. collat. form of comitor) To accompany, attend, follow: quod si Romanae comitarent castra puellae,Prop. 2, 7, 15; Ov. P. 2, 3, 43; id. M. 14, 259; 13, 55; 8, 692: funera,id. P. 1, 9, 47 (Att. ap. Non. p. 85, 139, is, on account of the corruption of the text, dub.).

comitor.definition: cŏmĭtor, ātus, 1 V. dep. a. [comes], to join one's self to any one as an attendant, to accompany, attend, follow (class.; esp. freq. after the Aug. per.); constr. with acc. or absol., with abstr. subjects by Cic. three times (qs. comitem esse) with dat. (v. B. β). In gen. In partic., to attend one to the grave: (Eumenem) comitante toto exercitu humaverunt,Nep. Eum. 13, 4; id. Att. 22, 4: juvenem exanimum vano honore,Verg. A. 11, 52; cf.: supremum...

comma.definition: . In gram. In verse, the coesura, Marc. Vict. p. 2519 P.

commaceratio.definition: commacero A dissolution, maceration (late Lat.): corporis,Ambros. In Psa. 37, § 59.

commacero.definition: com-măcĕro, āre To soften by steeping, to macerate: aliquid in aquā pluviali,Marc. Emp. 36 fin.; Ambros. in Luc. 5, 6.

commacesco.definition: com-măcesco, ĕre V. inch. n., to grow lean, Varr. ap. Non. p. 137, 3; cf. macesco.

commaculo.definition: com-măcŭlo, āvi, ātum, 1 Tospot, stain, pollute, defile on all sides (rare but class.). Lit.: sanguine manus,Verg. E. 8, 48: sanguine suo altaria deūm,Tac. A. 1, 39: commaculatus sanguine,Paul. Nol. 6, 164. Trop.: se isto infinito ambitu, * Cic. Cael. 7, 16: se cum Jugurthā miscendo,Sall. J. 102, 5: pia templa domosque occursu,Stat. Th. 11, 752: se consortiis aliquorum, Cod. Th. 3, 12, 3: vidnitatem stupri procacitate,ib. 3, 16, 2: flagitiis comm...

commando.definition: com-mando, no Perf., sum, ĕre, , to chew (late Lat.): frondes myrti,Ser. Samm. 36, 684: radix commansa,Marc. Emp. 8.

commanduco.definition: com-mandūco (conm-), no Perf., ātum, 1, v. a. (access. form commandū-cor, ātus, 1, v. dep., Lucil. ap. Non. p. 81, 26; p. 123, 27; p. 479, 2 sq.; in trop. signif.), to chew much, chew to pieces, masticate: linguam,Val. Max. 3, 3, ext. 4: acinos,Plin. 24, 4, 6, § 11; 25, 13, 105, § 165 sq.; Scrib. Comp. 9; 53; 165.

commaneo.definition: com-mănĕo, ēre To remain somewhere constantly (late Lat.): in domo,Macr. S. 6, 8 fin.; Cod. Th. 7, 8, 1: aliquo loco, Aug. Civ. Dei, 22, 8; Jul. Val. Rer. Gest. Alex. M. 1, 20 Mai.

commanifesto.definition: com-mănĭfesto, āre To manifest together, Boeth. Arist. Top. 6, 2, p. 707.

commanipularis.definition: A comrade who is in the same manipulus, Tac. H. 4, 46; Inscr. Orell. 3557.—So also ‡ COMMANIPVLARIVS, ii,Inscr. Rein. 8, 74.

commanipulatio.definition: commanipulo Companionship in a manipulus, Spart. Nig. 10, 6.

commanipulo.definition: A comrade of the same manipulus, Spart. Nig. 10, 5.— So also ‡ COMMANIPVLVS and COMMANIPLVS,Inscr. Orell. 3557; Inscr. Grut. 551, 1.

commarceo.definition: com-marcĕo, ēre V. n.; lit., to wither; trop., to become wholly faint or inactive (late Lat.): miles,Amm. 17, 10, 1; 31, 12, 13.

commargino.definition: com-margĭno, āre To furnish with a parapet or railing: pontes,Amm. 31, 2, 2.

commartyr.definition: A fellow-martyr, companion in martyrdom, Tert. Anim. 55.

commasculo.definition: com-mascŭlo, āre, masculus To make manly, firm, courageous, to invigorate, embolden (post-class.): animum,App. M. 2, p. 124, 32: frontem,Macr. S. 7, 11.

commastico.definition: com-mastĭco, no Perf., ātum, 1, , to chew (late Lat.), Aem. Mac. 2, 15; 4, 8.

commaticus.definition: commătĭcus, a, um Cut up, divided, short (eccl. Lat.): hymnus,Sid. Ep. 4, 3: rhythmi,id. Carm. 23, 450.

commeabilis.definition: com-mĕābĭlis, e, (perh. only in Arn.). Pass., that is casily passed through, permeable: venae,Arn. 2, p. 84, 3. Act., that easily passes through: aurae,Arn. 7, p. 233.

commeatalis.definition: commĕātālis, e, commeatus Pertaining to provisions or supplies: formula,Cassiod. Var. 7, 36: miles,accompanying the provisions,Cod. Just. 1, 27, 2, § 9; 12, 38, 16, § 2.

commeatus.definition: (), , id.. A going to and fro, passing freely, going at will: in eo conclavid ego perfodi parietem, Quā conmeatus clam esset hinc huc mulieri,Plaut. Mil. 2, 1, 65; cf.: commeatum vocis exercent fauces,Pall. 1, 3. Meton.

commeditor.definition: com-mĕdĭtor, āri To impress carefully on one's mind, to practise, imitate: sonitus chartarum,sounds like,Lucr. 6, 112 Munro ad loc. (but Auct. Her. 3, 18, 31 B. and K. read commode notare).

commeio.definition: commējo, āre, = κατουρῶ, Gloss. Gr. Lat.: Lectum,Charis. 5, p. 261 P.

commembratus.definition: com-membrātus, a, um, membro Grown up together, united; only trop., Paul. Nol. Ep. 44, 4.

commemorabilis.definition: commĕmŏrābĭlis (conm-), e, commemoro Worth mentioning, memorable (rare): clara et conmemorabilis pugna, * Plaut. Ps. 1, 5, 111: multa commemorabilia proferre,Cic. N. D. 2, 52, 131: pietas,id. Marcell. 4, 10.

commemoratio.definition: (), , id. A calling to mind, reminding, suggesting, commemorating, remembrance, mentioning (several times in Cic. and Quint.; elsewh. rare): istaec commemoratio Quasi exprobratio est immemoris benefici, * Ter. And. 1, 1, 16.—With obj.-gen.: antiquitatis,Cic. Or. 34, 120: nominis nostri,id. Arch. 11, 29: rei gestae,Quint. 5, 11, 6: frequens illorum, quae egerat in senatu,id. 11, 1, 18; Tac. A. 13, 3: fortitudinis,Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 78, § 192: (Verre...

commemorator.definition: id. One who mentions a thing, a commemorator: vetustatum,Tert. adv. Marc. 4, 26.

commemoratorium.definition: id. A means of remembrance: calliditatis,Ambros. Off. 25.

commemoro.definition: com-mĕmŏro (conm-), āvi, ātum, 1 To recall an object to memory in all its particulars. Rarely of one's self, to call to mind, be mindful of, keep in mind, remember; with acc. and inf. or rel. -clause: quid quoque die dixerim, audierim, egerim, commemoro vesperi,Cic. Sen. 11, 38.—With acc. and inf.: cottidie commemorabam te unum in tanto exercitu mihi fuisse adsensorem,Cic. Fam. 6, 21, 1: vitandi rumoris causā, quo patrem Caesarem vulgo reprehensu...

commendabilis.definition: commendābĭlis, e, commendo Worthy of praise, commendable (rare; perh. not ante-Aug.); with abl., Liv. 42, 5, 5: arbustum fructu,Col. 5, 6, 37: suco,Plin. 13, 9, 18, § 62: aviculae cantu,Val. Max. 9, 1, 2. —Absol., Liv. 37, 7, 15.—Comp., Treb. XXX. Tyrann. 16.

commendaticius.definition: commendātĭcĭus or -tĭus, a, um, commendatio Serving for commendation, commendatory (very rare): litterae, letters of recommendation or introduction, Cic. Fam. 5, 5, 1; cf. Dig. 41, 1, 65; so, tabellae,Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 66, § 148; and absol., commendaticiae, ārum, f., Aug. in Macr. S. 2, 4, 15.

commendatio.definition: commendo A commendation, recommending (in good prose, and very freq.). In abstr., as an act: amicorum,Cic. Fam. 1, 3, 1; 12, 26 ter; id. Fin. 5, 15, 41; Sall. C. 35, 1; Quint. 9, 2, 59; cf. id. 5, 10, 41; 4, 3, 17; Suet. Caes. 75; id. Aug. 46 al.—In plur., Cic. Fam. 13, 32, 1.—With gen. obj.: ad ceteros contempti hominis,Cic. Att. 8, 4, 1: sui,id. Or. 36, 124 (opp. offensio adversarii); Dig. 1, 16, 4, § 3: commendationes morientium,Cic. Fin. 3, 2...

commendativus.definition: commendātīvus, a, um, commendo Commendatory: casus, i. e. dativus,Prisc. p. 670 Putsch.

commendatiuus.definition: commendātīvus, a, um, commendo Commendatory: casus, i. e. dativus,Prisc. p. 670 Putsch.

commendatorius.definition: commendātōrĭus, a, um, commendator Serving for commendation, commendatory (for the class. commendaticius): litterae,Sid. Ep. 9, 10; Jul. Epit. Nov. 6, § 26.

commendatrix.definition: id. That which commends (rare): legem commendatricem virtutum, * Cic. Leg. 1, 22, 58: terra, * Plin. Ep. 8, 20, 2.

commendo.definition: com-mendo (conm-), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. 1. mando To commit to one for preservation, protection, etc., to intrust to one's charge, commit to one's care, commend to. Prop. In gen., to commend or recommend, i. e. to procure favor for, to make agreeable, to set off with advantage, to grace (class.): principes undique convenire et se civitatesque suas Caesari commendare coeperunt,Caes. B. G. 3, 27 fin.; Auct. B. G. 8, 50: P. Rutilii adulescentiam ad op...

commensurabilis.definition: commensūrābĭlis, e, mensuro Having a common measure, commensurable, Boëth. 1 Arithm. 18, p. 1000 al.

commensuratio.definition: id. Symmetry, uniformity, Boëth. Arist. Top. 2, 1, p. 680.

commensuratus.definition: commensūrātus, a, um, id. Equal: consonantiae, Boëth. 1 Mus. 29, p. 1084.

commensus.definition: commensus, a, um, Part., v. commetior.

commentariensis.definition: commentarius One who takes control, has the care of a thing; and specif. A registrar of public documents, a recorder, secretary, Dig. 49, 14, 45, § 7; Cod. Just. 1, 27, 1, § 8. One who makes out a list of prisoners, a keeper of a prison, Cod. Just. 9, 4, 4; Dig. 48, 20, 6; 48, 3, 8. One who forms a list of soldiers, Ps.-Ascon. Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 28, § 71.

commentariolum.definition: n. (, , m., Hier. Ep. 149, 1), dim. commentarius A short treatise, brief commentary: hoc,Q. Cic. Pet. Cons. 14 fin.; of dub. form,abl. plur.,Cic. Fin. 4, 4, 10; id. de Or. 1, 2, 5; id. Phil. 1, 7, 16; Quint. 1, 5, 7.

commentarius.definition: (sc. liber; Both together,Gell. 13, 20, 17); , , (sc. volumen, Varr. L. L. 6, § 90 Müll.; Cic. Brut. 44, 164; cf. commentariolum) [commentor]. Orig. a note-book, sketch-book, memorandum: diurni,a journal,Suet. Aug. 64. As the title of a book on any subject, but esp. historical, which is only sketched down or written without care (mostly in plur.), a sketch, a paper, memoirs, a commentary, etc., Cic. Fam. 5, 12, 10; Liv. 42, 6, 3; Quint. 2, 11, 7;...

commentatio.definition: id.. Abstr., a diligent meditation upon something, a studying, a careful preparation, μελέτη (so perh. only in Cic.): loci multa commentatione atque meditatione parati,Cic. de Or. 2, 27, 118.—In plur., Cic. de Or. 1, 60, 257; id. Brut. 71, 249; 27, 105: commentatio inclusa in veritatis lucem proferenda est,id. de Or. 1, 34, 157.—* Concr., a learned work, treatise, dissertation, description (so perh. not ante-Aug.): commentatio (de naturā animali...

commentator.definition: 2. commentor. An inventor, contriver (post-class. and rare): omnium falsorum,App. Mag. p. 321, 36: evangelii,i. e. the author,Tert. Res Carn. 33. An interpreter: legum,Cod. Just. 1, 17, 2, § 20; Serv. ad Verg. E. 6, 11.

commenticius.definition: commentĭcĭus or -tĭus, a, um, , commentus, comminiscor Thought out, devised, fabricated (most freq. in Cicero). Opp. to that already existing, invented, new: nominibus novis et commenticiis appellata,Cic. Fin. 5, 30, 90: spectacula (opp. usitata),Suet. Claud. 21; Dig. 48, 19, 20. Opp. to that which is actual.

commentior.definition: com-mentĭor, ītus, 4 To invent or devise a falsehood (post-class.), App. Mag. p. 314, 31; id. de Deo Socr. p. 50, 39: se virum bonum,id. M. 7, p. 188, 2.

commento.definition: commento, āvi, 1 V. act., collat. form of 1. commentor, q. v. (cf. Prisc. p. 797 P.), to delineate, sketch; only trop.: ora, humorously, qs. to demonstrate on the face, for to cudgel or beat, Plaut. Men. 5, 7, 30 dub. (Brix, commetavi; cf. 2. commeto).—Hence

commentor.definition: commentor, ātus sum, 1 V. freq. dep. [comminiscor]. Prop., to consider thoroughly, meditate, think over, study, deliberate, weigh, prepare one's self mentally, etc. (class.). Transf.

commentus.definition: commentus, a, um, Part., from comminiscor.

commeo.definition: com-mĕo (conm-), āvi, ātum, 1 To go and come, pass to and fro: remeare redire, ut commeare ultro citroque ire, unde commeatus (leave of absence; v. commeatus, II. B.) dari dicitur, id est tempus, quo ire et redire commode quis possit,Fest. p. 276, 5, and p. 277, 25.—Hence freq. with ultro and citro (in good prose; freq. in Cic. and the histt.; not in Quint.). In gen. With particular reference to the terminus ad quem, to go, come, travel somewhere...

commercior.definition: commercĭor, āri, 1, commercium To trade: commerciandi licentia,Cassiod. Var. 5, 39.

commercium.definition: (; ante-class.; sometimes ‡ ; cf. Vel. Long. p. 2236 P.), , merx. Commercial intercourse, trade, traffic, commerce: mare magnum et ignara lingua commercia prohibebant,Sall. J. 18, 5; Plin. 33, 1, 3, § 7; Plin. Pan. 29; Tac. Agr. 24; Liv. 4, 52, 6: salis,id. 45, 29, 13: commercium hominum in locum aliquem mutui usus contrahunt,id. 38, 18, 12: neque Thraces commercio faciles erunt,id. 40, 58, 1: jus commercii,Dig. 49, 5, 6. In gen., intercourse, co...

commercor.definition: com-mercor (con-m-), ātus, 1 To trade, traffic together, buy up, purchase (except in Sall., only ante - class.): captivos,Plaut. Capt. prol. 26; 1, 1, 32: cives, homines liberos,id. Pers. 4, 9, 12: arma, tela, etc.,Sall. J. 66, 1.—Hence, commercātus, a, um, Part. in pass. signif.: edulia, Afran. ap. Non. p. 28, 30.

commereo.definition: com-mĕrĕo, ŭi, ĭtum, 2 To merit fully, to deserve something; usu. in a bad sense. Prop.: interrogabatur reus, quam quasi aestimationem commeruisse se maxime confiteretur,Cic. de Or. 1, 54, 232: poenam,Ov. Tr. 2, 4: numquam sciens commerui merito ut caperet odium illam mei,Ter. Hec. 4, 2, 4. Meton. (with culpam, etc.; antecedens pro consequenti; prop. to earn, acquire, bring to or upon one's self), to err in something, to commit an offence or crim...

commereor.definition: commerĕor (conm-), ĭtus sum, 3, (ante- and post-class. collat. form of commereo). To commit, be guilty of: me culpam conmeritum scio,Plaut. Aul. 4, 10, 8: quae numquam quicquam erga me conmerita'st,Ter. Hec. 3, 5, 36. To earn, merit (post-class.): fidem sedulitatis et veritatis,Gell. 1, 6, 6: cultus et sacrificia,Arn. 2, p. 93.

commetior.definition: com-mētĭor (con-m-), mensus, 4 To measure (very rare): omnes porticus,Plaut. Most. 3, 3, 8: agros,Col. 5, 1, 2: siderum ambitus inter se numero,Cic. Univ. 9.—* Trop., to measure with or by something, to proportion: negotium cum tempore,Cic. Inv. 1, 26, 39.

commeto.definition: commēto (conm-), āre V. freq. n. [commeo, II.], to go frequently, Afran. and Novius ap. Non. p. 89, 30 sq.: ad mulierculam,Ter. Heaut. 3, 1, 35.—With acc. of distance: nam meus scruposam victus conmetat viam,Plaut. Capt. 1, 2, 82.

commictus.definition: commictus, a, um, Part., from commingo.

commigro.definition: com-mīgro (con-m-), āvi, ātum, 1 To go or remove somewhere with all one's effects, to migrate, enter (rare, but in good prose; esp. freq. after the Aug. per.): huc habitatum,Plaut. Trin. 4, 3, 77: huc,id. Pers. 1, 3, 58; Ter. Ad. 4, 5, 15: huc viciniae,id. And. 1, 1, 43: in tuam (domum), * Cic. Q. Fr. 2, 3, 7: Romam,Liv. 1, 34, 1; 5, 53, 7; 41, 8, 7; Suet. Tib. 1: Antium, deinde Alexandriam,id. Calig. 49: Athenas,Plin. 35, 11, 40, § 135: e German...

commilitium.definition: militia Companionship in war (prob. not in use before the Aug. period). Prop., Veil. 2, 29, 5; * Quint. 5, 10, 111; Tac. A. 1, 60; Flor. 4, 4, 2; Just. 5, 10, 3; 11, 5, 3; Plin. Ep. 10, 11, 2; 10, 18, 1. Transf., fellowship, companionship in gen. (very rare): (studiorum),Ov. P. 2, 5, 72; App. Flor. 3, p. 356, 1; Manil. 1, 780.

commilito.definition: A comrade, companion in war, fellow-soldier (in good prose; most freq. in the histt., esp. of the post-Aug. per.), * Cic. Deiot. 10, 28; Caesar ap. Suet. Caes. 67; August. ap. Suet. Aug. 25; C. Cassius ap. Quint. 6, 3, 90; Liv. 3, 50, 5 and 7; Vell. 2, 59, 4; Suet. Claud. 10; id. Galb. 20; id. Vit. 11; Flor. 2, 20, 2. Transf., in gen., a comrade: carissimus sibi,Petr. 80: di,Flor. 1, 11, 4; and for a prostitute, Elag. ap. Lampr. Elag. 26.

comminabundus.definition: commĭnābundus, a, um, comminor Threatening (with dat.): comminabundus nobilibus,Tert. adv. Marc. 4, 15.

comminatio.definition: id. A threatening, menacing (rare, but in good prose): orationis tamquam armorum, * Cic. de Or. 3, 54, 206 (cf. Quint. 9, 1, 33): taurorum,Plin. 8, 45, 70, § 181; Dig. 26, 7, 7, § 7.—In plur.: imperiosae, Tiro ap. Gell. 7, 3, 13: Hannibalis,Liv. 26, 8, 3: Tiberii,Suet. Tib. 37.

comminativus.definition: commĭnātīvus, a, um, id. Threatening, menacing: sensus,Tert. adv. Marc. 2, 25.

comminatiuus.definition: commĭnātīvus, a, um, id. Threatening, menacing: sensus,Tert. adv. Marc. 2, 25.

comminator.definition: id. A threatener: ignium,Tert. adv. Gnost. 9.

commingo.definition: com-mingo, minxi, minctum, 3 To pollute, defile: lectum potus (by vomiting), * Hor. S. 1, 3, 90: suavia comminxit spurcā salivā tuā,Cat. 78, 8; cf. id. 99, 10: commictum caenum, as a term of reproach, for a paltry, dirty fellow: commictum caeno stercilinium publicum,Plaut. Pers. 3, 3, 3.

comminiscor.definition: com-mĭniscor (con-m-), mentus, 3 V. a. dep. [miniscor, whence also reminiscor, stem men, whence mens, memini; cf. Varr. L. L. 6, § 44] (lit. to ponder carefully, to reflect upon; hence, as a result of reflection; cf. 1. commentor, II.), to devise something by careful thought, to contrive, invent, feign. (Class., of something untrue; esp. freq. in Plaut.) Reperi, comminiscere, cedo calidum consilium cito,Plaut. Mil. 2, 2, 71: fabricare quidvis, qu...

comminor.definition: com-mĭnor, ātus, 1 To threaten one with something, esp., in milit. lang., to threaten with an attack, to menace (in prose most freq. in the histt.; not in Cic.); constr. usu. alicui aliquid; rarely alicui aliquā re, aliquem, or absol.: comminando magis quam inferendo pugnam,Liv. 10, 39, 6: impetum, Auct. B. Afr. 71: obsidionem,Liv. 31, 26, 6; 42, 7, 5: necem alicui,Suet. Caes. 14: inter se,Liv. 44, 9, 7: alicui cuspide,Suet. Caes. 62: accusatione...

comminuo.definition: com-mĭnŭo, ŭi, ūtum, 3 To make small, either by breaking into many small parts, or by removing parts from the whole (class. in prose and poetry). To separate into small parts, to break or crumble to pieces, to crush, split, etc.: saxo cere comminuit brum, Enn. ap. Serv. ad Verg. A. 1, 412 (Ann. v. 586 Vahl.): fores et postes securibus,Plaut. Bacch. 5, 1, 31: ossa atque artua illo scipione,id. Men. 5, 2, 103: tibi caput,id. Rud. 4, 4, 74: illi sta...

comminus.definition: com-mĭnus (less correctly cōmĭ-nus), manus; cf. Beda, Orth. p. 2331 P.; Fronto, Diff. p. 2193 ib.; orig. belonging to milit. lang., of conflict In close contest, hand to hand (with the sword, etc.), Gr. συσταδόν; opp. eminus, also to missilia, sagittae, etc. (class.; most freq. in the histt.): quae mea comminus machaera atque hasta hostibit e manu, Enn. ap. Fest. p. 270, 29 Müll.: nec eminus hastis aut comminus gladiis uteretur,Cic. Sen. 6, 19; ...

comminutus.definition: commĭnūtus, a, um, Part., from comminuo.

commisceo.definition: com-miscĕo (con-m-), miscui, mixtum, or mistum, 2 To mix or mingle together, to intermingle (class.). Lit., constr. with cum, with abl., with in or inter, and absol. Transf., in gen., to unite, bring together, join, mingle: ego abeo a te, ne quid tecum consili conmisceam, Plaut Mil. 2, 5, 68: siquis cum eo (Neptuno) quid rei conmiscuit,id. Rud. 2, 6, 3: jus accusatoris cum jure testimonii,Auct. Her. 4, 35, 47: numquam temeritas cum sapientiā comm...

commiscibilis.definition: commiscĭbĭlis, e, commisceo That can be mingled: animus,Tert. Anim. 12.

commiscuus.definition: commiscŭus, a, um, id. Common, κοινός, Gloss Gr. Lat.

commiseratio.definition: commiseror; In rhetoric,a part of an oration intended to excite compassion,Cic. de Or. 2, 28, 125; 3, 58, 219; * Quint. 10, 1, 107; Auct. Her. 2, 31, 50.

commiseresco.definition: com-mĭsĕresco, ĕre, 3 V. inch. a., to commiserate, have sympathy with (anteclass.): servos, Enn. ap. Non. p. 472, 29 (Trag. v. 222 Vahl.): Priamus si adesset, ipse ejus commiseresceret, Pac. ap. Serv. ad Verg. A. 11, 259 (Trag. Rel. v. 391 Rib.): ut illius conmiserescas miserulae orbitudinis, Turp. ap. Non. p. 146, 18 (Com. Rel. v. 211 ib.).—Impers., with acc. pers. and gen. rei: Bacchidem ejus commiseresceret,Ter. Hec. 1, 2, 54.

commisero.definition: miser A companion in misfortune (post-class.), Tert. adv. Marc. 4, 9, as transl. of Gr. συνταλαίπωρος; id. ib. 4, 37.

commiseror.definition: com-mĭsĕror, ātus, 1 V. a. dep., to commiserate, pity, to bewail (class. but rare); aliquem or aliquid: aliquem, Att. ap. Non. p. 445, 11: fortunam Graeciae,Nep. Ages. 5, 2: in commiserandā re,Auct. Her. 4. 55, 69: interitum fratris,Gell. 1, 5, 6.— * In rhetoric, absol., of an orator, to excite compassion (cf. commiseratio): quid cum commiserari, conqueri coeperit, Cic. Div. in Caecil. 14, 46: cum commiserandum sit, * Quint. 11, 3, 58.

commissio.definition: committo. (Acc. to committo, I. B.) Lit., a setting or bringing together in contest; hence, the beginning of a contest (in the public games, etc.): tecum ago, ut jam ab ipsā commissione ad me... persequare, etc.,Cic. Att. 15, 26, 1; 16, 5, 1: ludorum,Suet. Aug. 43; id. Galb. 6; Plin. Ep. 7, 24, 6; id. Pan. 54, 1; Macr. S. 2, 7. (Acc. to committo, II. B. 4.) A perpetration, commission: piaculi,Arn. 4, p. 148.

commissor.definition: committo, II. B. 4. A perpetrator, Ennod. 1, 4.

commissorius.definition: commissōrĭus, a, um, committo; Lex, in jurid. lang. A clause in the condition of a sale or of a contract (by which a vendor reserved to himself the privilege of rescinding the sale if the purchaser did not pay his purchase-money at the time agreed on), Dig. 18, 3, 14.—So also absol.: com-missōrĭa, ae, f., Dig. 18, 3, 14; 43, 23, 11.

commissura.definition: committo. Prop., a joining or connecting together; hence, in concr., a band, knot, joint, seam, juncture, commissure (class.): commissura funis,Cato, R. R. 135, 4; cf. nodorum,Sen. Ben. 5, 12, 2: molles digitorum,Cic. N. D. 2, 60, 150: mirabiles ossium,id. ib. 2, 55, 139; id. Univ. 7 fin.: navium,Plin. 16, 36, 64, § 158: nucum,id. 17, 10, 11, § 64: colorum,a mingling,id. 35, 5, 11, § 29; Sen. Q. N. 1, 3, 4: Piscium,the knot in the constellation P...

commissuralis.definition: commissūrālis, e, commissura Of or pertaining to a juncture (only in Veg.): loca,Veg. Art. Vet. 3, 13, 4; 3, 3, 51.

commistim.definition: commistim (commixtim), commisceo In a mixed manner, jointly; opp. separatim, Hier. praef. in Isa.

committo.definition: com-mitto (con-m-), mīsi, missum, 3, v. a. Of two or more objects, to bring, join, combine into one whole; to join or put together, to connect, unite. To place a thing somewhere for preservation, protection, care, etc.; to give, intrust, commit to, to give up or resign to, to trust (syn.: commendo, trado, credo; very freq. and class.); constr. with aliquid (aliquem) alicui, in aliquid, or absol.

commixtio.definition: (), , commisceo A mixing, mingling (post-class.), Marc. Emp. 8; cf. Vet. Gloss.: commixtio χύμα.

commobilis.definition: commōbĭlis, e, commoveo Easily moving, Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 9, 48.

commodatio.definition: 2. commodo A rendering of service, accommodation: alternae,App. Trism. p. 81, 16.

commodator.definition: 2, commodo; In jurid. Lat.,a lender,Dig. 13, 6, 7; 47, 2, 14 and 55.

commode.definition: commŏdē, adv., v. 1. commodus, adv. B. 3.

commoderatus.definition: com-mŏdĕrātus, a, um Brought into the right measure, exact: dispositio, Cod. Th. 14, 17, 15.

commoditas.definition: commodus. Due measure, just proportion, symmetry (so very rare): commoditas et aequitas membrorum, * Suet. Aug. 79. (Acc. to commodus, II.) Easy, unrestrained, free action: corporis aliqua commoditas non naturā data, sed studio et industriā parta,i. e. dexterity, skill,Cic. Inv. 1, 25, 36.

commodo.definition: commŏdŏ, adv., v. commodus, adv. B. 2.

commodule.definition: commŏdŭlē Adv. dim. [commode, v. commodus, ], at one's convenience, conveniently, suilably; only Plaut., ludere, Rud. 2, 5, 11, and Arn. 2, p. 55.

commodulum.definition: dim.commodum A small advantage or profit, Arn. 1, p. 7.

commodus.definition: com-mŏdus, a, um, adj. That has a due or proper measure; hence Object., complete, perfect, of full weight or measure, fit, suitable, due, proper, etc. (mostly poet. or in post-Aug. prose; most freq. in Plaut.): statura,a tall stature,Plaut. As. 2, 3, 21: capillus,id. Most. 1, 3, 98: viginti argenti minae,full twenty,id. As. 3, 3, 134 (cf. id. ib. 3, 3, 144: minae bonae); id. Merc. 2, 3, 101: talentum argenti,id. Rud. 5, 2, 31; Lucil. ap. Non. p. ...

commolior.definition: com-mōlĭor (conm-), ītus, 4, (ante- and post-class. and very rare); prop. To set in motion: commoliri tempestas fulmina coeptat,Lucr. 6, 255.—Trop.: lamenta virum commoliri atque ciere,Lucr. 6, 242 Lachm. N. cr.: dolum aut machinam, Caecil. Stat. ap. Cic. N. D. 3, 29, 73. —Transf.: nimis moleste confabricatus commolitusque est originem vocabuli, has undertaken, Favorin. ap. Gell. 3, 19, 3.

commollio.definition: com-mollĭo, īre To soften: duritias palpebrarum,Marc. Emp. 8 fin.

commolo.definition: com-mŏlo, ŭi, ĭtum, 3 To grind thoroughly, to pound (post-Aug.): (grana) minutissime,Col. 12, 28, 1: olivam, bacam,id. 12, 50, 18; cf. also Commolenda.

commonefacio.definition: commŏnĕ-făcĭo (conm-), fēci, factum ( Pass. -fio, -factus sum, -fieri), 3, commoneo, to remind one forcibly (of something), to put in mind, to admonish, to impress upon (in good prose, most freq. in Cic.); constr. with acc. (personae or rei), a rel.clause, ut or acc. and inf.: te propter magnitudinem provinciae etiam atque etiam esse commonefaciendum,Cic. Fam. 13, 72, 1; cf. humorously: commonefacere aliquem monimentis bubulis,to give one a remem...

commoneo.definition: com-mŏnĕo (conm-), ŭi, ĭtum, 2 To remind one forcibly of something, to put in mind, to impress upon, to bring to recollection (in good prose); constr. (cf. admoneo).

commonitio.definition: commoneo An earnest reminding or putting in mind, an admonition, Quint. 4, 2, 51; 4, 4, 9; Cod. Th. 6, 35, 10 (in Q. Cic. Petit. Cons. 14, 54 dub.).

commonitor.definition: id. One who earnestly reminds, Symm. Ep. 7, 105 dub.

commonitorius.definition: commŏnĭtōrĭus, a, um, commonitor Suitable for reminding (late Lat.), Cod. Just. 1, 3, 33. Subst.: commŏ-nĭtōrĭum, ii, n., a writing for reminding, a letter of instructions, Amm. 28, 1, 1; Symm. Ep. 5, 21; Cod. Th. 2, 29, 2, § 3; 6, 29, 10; Aug. Ep. 129 fin.

commonstro.definition: com-monstro (conm-), āvi, ātum, 1 (old form conmonstrasso = commonstravero, Plaut. Ep. 3, 4, 5) To show, point out something fully or distinctly (perh. only in Plaut., Terence, and Cic.): si istunc hominem, quem quaeritas, Tibi conmonstrasso,Plaut. Ep. 3, 4, 5; id. Poen. 5, 2, 83: parentes meos mihi,Ter. Heaut. 5, 4, 4: hominem commonstrarier Mihi istum volo, aut ubi habitet demonstrarier,id. Phorm. 2, 1, 75: aurum alicui,Cic. de Or. 2, 41, 174: ...

commoratio.definition: commoror. A dwelling, tarrying, abiding, lingering, sojourning (so only in Cic.): villa et amoenitas illa commorationis est, non deversorii,is suitable for a place of residence,Cic. Fam. 6, 19, 1: tabellariorum,id. Q. Fr. 3, 1, 7, § 23 (and perh. urbana, id. Fam. 9, 15, 3). Transf., an abiding place, dwelling (late Lat.), Vulg. Act. 1, 20; id. 3 Esd. 1, 21; 9, 37.

commordeo.definition: com-mordĕo, ēre To bite sharply or eagerly (in post-Aug. prose, and very rare): tela ipsa,Sen. Contr. 4, 29, § 2.— Trop., of abusive lang., Sen. Vit. Beat. 21, 1.

commorior.definition: com-mŏrĭor (conm-), mortuus, 3 V. dep. n., to die with or at the same time with one (mostly post-Aug.; not in Cic.); constr. with cum, with the dat. or absol. Trop.: duo venena commoriuntur,i. e. their effects vanish together,Plin. 27, 2, 2, § 5.

commoror.definition: com-mŏror (conm-), ātus, 1 V. dep. n. and a. (act. access. form ‡ commŏro, āre, acc. to Prisc. p. 797 P.). Neutr. Act., to stop, detain, retard one (ante- and post-class.).— Prop.: an te auspicium conmoratum est?Plaut. Am. 2, 2, 58: me nunc conmoror, has foris quom non ferio,id. Ps. 4, 7, 35: cantharum,id. Men. 1, 2, 64; Sen. Contr. 2, 14, 10; Isid. Orig. 11, 3, 31.

commorsito.definition: com-morsĭto (-sico), āre To bite to pieces, App. M. 7, p. 195, 14.—Trop., App. M. 10, p. 249.

commotio.definition: commoveo A moving, motion. Lit. (only post-class.): vasorum,Pall. Oct. 14, 5: ventris,Cael. Aur. Acut. 1, 13; 2, 9: capitis,id. Tard. 1, 1, 41; Vulg. Psa. 43, 15. Trop., a rousing, exciting, agitation, commotion (cf. commoveo, II. B.) (class.): commotionem accipi volunt temporarium animi motum, sicut iram, pavorem, * Quint. 5, 10, 28: commotio suavis jucunditatis in corpore,Cic. Fin. 2, 4, 13: animi,id. Tusc. 3, 4, 8.—In plur.: animorum,Cic. Tusc...

commoto.definition: commōto, āre, commoveo To move very violently, to agitate: assidue,Theod. Prisc. 1, 8.

commotor.definition: id. One who sets in motion (late Lat.): Liber et Libera seminum commotores et emissores, Aug. Civ. Dei, 7, 3.

commotus.definition: commōtus, a, um, Part. and , from commoveo.

commoveo.definition: com-mŏvĕo (conm-), mōvi, mōtum, 2 (contr. forms: Commōrunt,Lucr. 2, 766; commōrat, Turp. ap. Non. p. 278, 2; Ter. Phorm. 1, 2, 51; commōrit, Cael. ap. Cic. Fam. 8, 15, 1; Hor. S. 2, 1, 45; commossem,Cic. Planc. 37, 90; commosset,Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 18, § 45; commosse,id. ib. 2, 5, 37, § 96; id. Fam. 7, 18, 3), v. a., to put something in violent motion, to move; both of removing from a place and backwards and forwards in a place; to shake, stir (freq...

commoueo.definition: com-mŏvĕo (conm-), mōvi, mōtum, 2 (contr. forms: Commōrunt,Lucr. 2, 766; commōrat, Turp. ap. Non. p. 278, 2; Ter. Phorm. 1, 2, 51; commōrit, Cael. ap. Cic. Fam. 8, 15, 1; Hor. S. 2, 1, 45; commossem,Cic. Planc. 37, 90; commosset,Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 18, § 45; commosse,id. ib. 2, 5, 37, § 96; id. Fam. 7, 18, 3), v. a., to put something in violent motion, to move; both of removing from a place and backwards and forwards in a place; to shake, stir (freq...

commulceo.definition: com-mulcĕo, ēre, (very rare, and mostly post-class.) To caress, coax, or soothe much. Prop.: puerum trepidantem,App. M. 9, p. 229, 34. Trop., to soothe, please, cajole: narium sensus,Arn. 7, p. 233: aures,id. 1, p. 35: sensus judicum honorificis sententiis, Tiro ap. Gell. 7, 3, 13.

commulco.definition: com-mulco, āre To beat violently, App. M. 8, p. 214, 30.

communalis.definition: commūnālis, e, commune Belonging to the community: loca,Aggen. p. 41 Goes.

commundo.definition: com-mundo, no Perf., ātum, 1, , to cleanse, purify wholly (very rare): vasa eluere et commundare,Col. 12, 18, 3: mulier ornata, sed non commundata,Dig. 34, 2, 25, § 10; Jul. Obseq. 115.

communicarius.definition: commūnĭcārius (dies), in quo omnibus dīs communiter sacrificabatur, Paul. ex Fest. p. 220, 19 Müll.

communicatio.definition: communico (several times in Cic., elsewh. rare) A making common, imparting, communicating. In gen.: largitio et communicatio civitatis,Cic. Balb. 13, 31: quaedam societas et communicatio utilitatum,id. Fin. 5, 23, 65: consilii,id. Fam. 5, 19, 2: sermonis,id. Att. 1, 17, 6: criminis cum pluribus, Tiro ap. Gell. 7, 3, 14: nominum,i. e. the like appellation of several objects,Plin. 24, 14, 80, § 129: juris,Dig. 23, 2, 1: damni,ib. 27, 3, 1, § 14. In...

communicator.definition: id. (postclass.). He who makes one a participant in a thing: rei familiaris,Arn. 4, p. 154 fin. He who has part in a thing, Tert. Pudic. 22.

communico.definition: commūnĭco (conm-), āvi, ātum, 1, ( Dep. access. form, communicati sint = communicaverint, Liv. 4, 24, 2) [communis]. To divide something with one, whether in giving or receiving. In Tertull., acc. to communis, II., to make common, i. e. low, base, to contaminate, defile, Tert. Spect. 17; id. Patient. 8.

communio.definition: com-mūnĭo, īvi or ii, ītum, 4 To fortify on all sides or strongly, to secure, barricade, intrench (class.). Prop.: castella,Caes. B. G. 1, 8; Nep. Alcib. 7, 4: castra,Caes. B. G. 5, 49; Liv. 2, 32, 4; 21, 32, 11; 42, 58, 1: loca castellis idonea,Nep. Milt. 2, 1: hibernacula,Liv. 22, 32, 1: praesidium,id. 2, 49, 8: tumulum,Caes. B. C. 1, 43.—Transf.: os arteriae,Gell. 17, 11, 5. Trop., to make sure, to strengthen: auctoritatem aulae,Cic. Fam. 15, ...

communis.definition: com-mūnis (comoinis, S. C. de Bacch.), e, con and root mu-, to bind; Sanscr. mav-; cf.: immunis, munus, moenia That is common to several or to all, common, general, universal, public (opp. proprius, that belongs to one: quod commune cum alio est, desinet esse proprium,Quint. 7, 3, 24; cf. id. 2, 4, 40; 7, 1, 28; 8, 5, 6; 10, 1, 16; 12, 10, 42; 12, 3, 7; v. also the foll.; freq. in all periods and every species of composition); constr. with cum, d...

communitas.definition: communis. Community, society, fellowship (very freq. in Cic.; elsewhere rare): nulla cum deo homini,Cic. N. D. 1, 41, 116: condicionis, aequitatis, legationis cum hoc gladiatore,id. Phil. 6, 2, 3: et conjunctio humana,id. Off. 1, 44, 157; cf. id. ib. 1, 44, 156: vitae atque victūs,id. Fam. 9, 24, 3; id. Off. 1, 14, 45. (Acc. to communis, II.) Courtesy, condescension, affability, Nep. Milt. 8, 4.

communitio.definition: 1. communio. Abstr., the making or preparing of a way; trop. = Gr. ὁδοποίησις: anne autem principium aut rei totius, quae agetur, significationem habere debebit, aut aditum ad causam et communitionem, etc.,Cic. de Or. 2, 79, 320. Concr., a fortification, Vitr. 10, 13, 1.

commurmuro.definition: com-murmŭro, āre, 1, v. n., or com-murmŭror, āri, 1, v. dep. To murmur to one's self or with others (very rare). Act. form: clauso commurmurat ore,Sil. 15, 821: (ciconiae) congregatae inter se commurmurant,Plin. 10, 23, 31, § 62. Dep. form: ut scriba secum ipse commurmuratus sit, Cic. Pis. 25, 61: commurmurantur αὐτοί, Varr. ap. Non. p. 178, 9 (Sat. Men. 64, 8).

commutabilis.definition: commūtābĭlis, e, commuto Subject to change, changeable (class.). In gen.: cera,Cic. N. D. 3, 12, 30: haec imbecilla et commutabilis pecunia,id. Par. 1, 1, 7: commutabilis, varius, multiplex animus,id. Lael. 25, 92: ratio vitae,id. Mil. 26, 69: principia verbi,Varr. L. L. 9. § 99 Müll. In rhet.: exordium quod ab adversario potest, leviter mutatum, ex contrariā parte dici, = commune,Cic. Inv. 1, 18, 26; so * Quint. 4, 1, 71.

commutatio.definition: id. A changing, change, alteration (in good prose). In gen.: annuae,Cic. Inv. 1, 34, 59; cf.: tempestatum atque caeli,id. Div. 2, 42, 89: temporum,id. Tusc. 1, 28, 68: crebrae aestuum,Caes. B. G. 5, 1: magnae rerum,id. B. C. 3, 68: ordinis,Quint. 9, 1, 6: subita,Nep. Dion, 6, 1: ventorum,Col. 11, 2, 94: morum aut studiorum,Cic. Lael. 21, 77: civiles,id. Fam. 5, 12, 4. Esp.

commuto.definition: com-mūto (conm-), āvi, ātum, 1 To alter wholly, change entirely (class.; most freq. in Cic.). To exchange something with another, to change, interchange, replace, substitute, barter, traffic.

como.definition: cōmo, mpsi (msi), mptum (mtum), 3, v. a. co- (i. e. con) and emo; cf.: demo, promo. To bring together, form, frame, construct (Lucretian): dum perspicis omnem Naturam rerum quā constet compta figurā,Lucr. 1, 950 Munro ad loc.: nunc ea quo pacto inter sese mixta quibusque compta modis vigeant,id. 3, 259: quibus e rebus cum corpore compta vigeret (animi natura), Quove modo distracta rediret in ordia prima,id. 4, 27. To care for, take care of. Trop....

comoedia.definition: ( Gen. comoediai, Plaut. Poen. prol. 51), = κωμὡδία, a comedy (cf. Varr. L. L. 9, § 99 Müll.; Paul. ex Fest. p. 39, 6 ib.), Plaut. Am. prol. 60; Cic. Off. 1, 29, 104; Quint. 6, 2, 20; 10, 1, 65; Hor. A. P. 281 al.: Plaut. As. prol. 13: facere,Ter. And. prol. 26: agere,id. Heaut. prol. 4: legere,Plin. Ep. 6, 21, 2: spectare, Ter. And. prol, 27: exigere, to hiss from the stage, id. ib.; cf. id. Hec. alt. prol. 4 and 7. The younger Pliny humorousl...

comoedus.definition: cōmoedus, a, um Of or pertaining to comedy, comic: natio,adapted to comedy, given to acting,Juv. 3, 100.—More freq. Subst.: cōmoedus, i, m., a comedian, comic actor (while histrio is a play-actor in gen.), Cic. Rosc. Com. 11, 30; Quint. 6, 2, 35; 1, 11, 1; 11, 3, 91; 11, 3, 181; Juv. 3, 94; 6, 73; Plin. Ep. 1, 15, 2; 3, 1, 9; Suet. Tib. 47; Gai Inst. 3, 212; Dig. 9, 2, 22, § 1.

comosus.definition: cŏmōsus, a, um, coma Hairy, with much or long hair (rare): frons,Phaedr. 5, 8, 2: Phoebus,Auct. Priap. 37.—Transf., of plants, leafy: genus tithymali comosissimum,Plin. 26, 8, 45, § 71; 16, 6, 8, § 22.

compaco.definition: com-pāco, āre To bring to peace (eccl. Lat.): Aegyptios,Cassiod. Hist. Eccl. 1, 20; 8, 13.

compacticius.definition: compactĭcĭus or -tĭus, a, um, = compactus Agreed upon: soter,Tert. adv. Val. 31.

compactilis.definition: compactĭlis, e, compactus, compingo. Pressed or joined together, compact: trabes,fitted one to another,Vitr. 4, 7: postes,id. 10, 14, 2: operimentum (of nuts),Plin. 15, 22, 24, § 88. Of form, thick-set, compact; of lions, Plin. 8, 16, 18, § 46; of bees,id. 11, 18, 19, § 59.

compactio.definition: compingo. In abstr., a joining together: membrorum,Cic. Fin. 5, 11, 33.—* In concr., the things that are joined together, a structure, frame, Vitr. 10, 15, 2 Schneid.

compactivus.definition: compactīvus, a, um, id. Suitable for joining: gummi,Isid. Orig. 17, 7, 10.

compactiuus.definition: compactīvus, a, um, id. Suitable for joining: gummi,Isid. Orig. 17, 7, 10.

compages.definition: (, ĭnis; nom., Stat. Th. 7, 43; acc. compaginem, Sen. Ep. 91, 12; abl. compagine, Ov. M. 1, 711; Cels. 4, 7; Manil. 1, 717; 1, 725; 1, 838), root pag-; v. pango A joining together, a connection, joint, structure (freq. and class.). Prop., Lucr. 6, 1070; Ov. M. 3, 30; Luc. 2, 487; 3, 491; Curt. 4, 3, 6; 4, 4, 12; Plin. 25, 3, 6, § 20; Suet. Aug. 43 et saep.—Gen. plur. compagum, Plin. 2, 2, 2, § 5 Sillig. Trop.: in Veneris compagibus haerent,i. e. ...

compagina.definition: compago A joining together, combination (peculiar to the agrimensores): litterarum, Baro ap. Goes. Agrim. p. 239, and Innoc. ib. pp. 245 and 246.

compaginatio.definition: A joining, joint, = compages, junctura. ἁρμογή, Vet. Gloss.; Ambros. in. Psa. 37, § 29; Cassiod. in. Psa. 17, 6.

compagino.definition: compāgĭno, āvi, ātum, 1, compago. To join together (late Lat.), Amm. 21, 2, 1; 28, 2, 3; Prud. στεφ. 10, 889; Aug. Conf. 13, 30 al. Neutr., to border upon: compaginantes agri,Agrim. p. 346 Goes.

compalpo.definition: com-palpo, āre To stroke, caress, Aug. Serm. Temp. 214.

compar.definition: com-par (conp-), păris, adj. (abl. compari, Liv. 36, 44, 7: Compare,Ov. Am. 3, 5, 38; id. A. A. 3, 359; gen. plur. comparum, Plaut. Ps. 1, 1, 64), like or equal to another (poet.; after the Aug. per. also in prose). Adj. Subst. comm., an equal, a companion, comrade, colleague, Plaut. Ps. 4, 3, 9; * Hor. C. 2, 5, 2.

comparabilis.definition: compărābĭlis, e, 1. comparo That may be compared, comparable (very rare): species,Cic. Inv. 1, 28, 42; cf. id. ib. 1, 30, 47 and 49: mors trium virorum,Liv. 39, 52, 7.

comparatio.definition: (), , 1. comparo A comparing, comparison (in good prose). In gen.: comparationis duo sunt modi; unus cum idemne sit an aliquid intersit quaeritur: alter, cum quid praestet aliud alii quaeritur,Cic. de Or. 3, 29, 117; cf. id. ib. § 116: potest incidere saepe contentio et comparatio, de duobus honestis utrum honestius,id. Off. 1, 43, 152: majorum, minorum, parium,id. Top. 18, 71: orationis suae cum scriptis alienis,id. de Or. 1, 60, 257: rerum,Quin...

comparativus.definition: compărātīvus, a, um, 1. comparo Of or pertaining to comparison, depending on comparison, comparative. In gen.: judicatio,Cic. Inv. 2, 25, 76 (cf. 1. comparatio, I.): genus causae (opp. simplex),Quint. 7, 4, 3: vocabulum,Gell. 5, 21, 13.—Subst.: compărātīva, ōrum, n., words in the comparative degree, comparatives, Quint. 9, 3, 19.—Adv.: compărā-tīvē, with comparison: dicere,Gell. 5, 21, 14; Ambros. de Fide, 5, 9, 71. Esp. in gram.

comparatiuus.definition: compărātīvus, a, um, 1. comparo Of or pertaining to comparison, depending on comparison, comparative. In gen.: judicatio,Cic. Inv. 2, 25, 76 (cf. 1. comparatio, I.): genus causae (opp. simplex),Quint. 7, 4, 3: vocabulum,Gell. 5, 21, 13.—Subst.: compărātīva, ōrum, n., words in the comparative degree, comparatives, Quint. 9, 3, 19.—Adv.: compărā-tīvē, with comparison: dicere,Gell. 5, 21, 14; Ambros. de Fide, 5, 9, 71. Esp. in gram.

comparco.definition: com-parco (conp-) or comperco (Sol. 22, 17), parsi or persi, 3 To save, husband well, lay up (ante- and post-class.). Prop.: quod ille compersit miser,Ter. Phorm. 1, 1, 10: cibum,Fronto, Laud. Neglig. 2, p. 371; Pacat. Pan. Theod. 32 fin. Trop., to abstain, forbear; with inf.: conperce, amabo, me attrectare,Plaut. Poen. 1, 2, 137; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 60, 5 Müll.

compareo.definition: com-pārĕo (conp-), ui, 2 To be perfectly evident or apparent, to appear, be visible (class.). Prop.: qui modo nusquam conparebas, nunc quom conpares peris,Plaut. Aul. 4, 4, 2: ita ego ad omnis conparebo tibi res benefactis frequens ( = in omnibus rebus),id. Mil. 3, 1, 68: nec tamen ulla Comparebat avis, * Lucr. 6, 1220: omnis suspitio in eos servos, qui non comparebant, commovebatur,Cic. Clu. 64, 180: repente comparuit incolumis,Suet. Aug. 14 et ...

comparilis.definition: com-părĭlis, e Equal, like: figurae,Aus. Ecl. 2, 38: ratio,Arn. 2, p. 68.

comparo.definition: compăro (conp-), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. compar To couple together in the same relation, to connect in pairs, to pair, match, unite, join; constr. aliquid cum aliquā re, alicui rei, aliqua inter se, or absol. Lit. (rare but class.). Trop.

comparticeps.definition: com-partĭceps, tĭcĭpis Partaking, participants together (late Lat.): promissionis,Vulg. Eph. 3, 6; Hier. in Eph. 3, 5 sqq.

comparturio.definition: com-partŭrĭo, īre, 4 To be associated in childbirth with any one, Ambros. Hexaem. 4, 8, 31; id. de Fide, 1, 14, 87.

compasco.definition: com-pasco (con-), no Perf., pastum, ĕre, and a. To feed together, feed in common: si compascuus ager est, jus est compascere,Cic. Top. 3, 12; Dig. 8, 5, 20. To feed, pasture, in gen.: Brundisiana (ostrea),Plin. 32, 6, 21, § 61.

compascuus.definition: com-pascŭus, a, um Of or pertaining to common pasturage: ager,a common pasture,Cic. Top. 3, 12; Lex Thor.; Inscr. Orell. 3121; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 40, 1 Müll.: jus compascui,Dig. 8, 5, 20; cf. Quint. 5, 10, 85.

compassibilis.definition: compassĭbĭlis, e, compatior Suffering with one, Tert. adv. Prax. 29.

compassio.definition: id. Fellow-suffering,fellow-feeling (eccl. Lat.), Tert. Res Carn. 4: sententiarum,sympathy, agreement,id. ib. 3 fin.

compatior.definition: com-pătĭor, passus, 3, (late Lat.). To suffer with one, Tert. adv. Prax. 29; Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 16, 98. To have compassion, to feel pity, Aug. Ep. 40, 29, 6; id. Conf. 3, 2.

compatronus.definition: A fellow-patron (Lat. of jurists), Dig. 26, 4, 3, § 4 sq.; 38, 5, 1.

compauper.definition: A companion in poverty, fellow-pauper (late Lat.), Aug. Serm. 25 ex 50 homil. c. 3.

compecco.definition: com-pecco, āre To err or commit a fault together (late Lat.), Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 12; id. Tard. 3, 1 fin.

compectum.definition: compectum and compectus, a, um, v. compaciscor.

compedio.definition: compĕdĭo (conp-), no Perf., ĭtum, 4, compes, to fetter, shackle (mostly anteand post-class.). Prop.: pedes corrigiis, Varr. ap. Non. p. 28, 9: servi conpediti,Cato, R. R. 56; Plaut. Capt. 5, 1, 24; Sen. Tranq. 10, 1; Dig. 4, 3, 7, § 7 al.—* Trop.: rebus immortalibus perniciosissime compediri,Aug. Ep. 39.

compellatio.definition: 2. compello. In gen., an accosting, Auct. Her. 4, 15, 22. Esp. with reproach, a reprimand, reproof, rebuke (rare), Cic. Phil. 3, 7, 17; in plur., id. Fam. 12, 25, 2; Gell. 1, 5, 2.
