compello.definition: com-pello (conp-), pŭli, pulsum, 3 To drive together to a place, to collect, assemble (opp. expello, Cic. Pis. 7, 16; to dispellere,Plaut. As. 3, 3, 149; and to aspellere,id. Trin. 3, 2, 46; class.). Lit. of herds, flocks: tum compellendum (agnos) in gregem ovium,Varr. R. R. 2, 2, 18: armentum in speluncam,Liv. 1, 7, 5; cf.: pecoris vim ingentem in saltum avium,id. 9, 31, 7: greges in unum,Verg. E. 7, 2: pecus totius provinciae,Cic. Pis. 36, 87: ...

compendiarius.definition: compendĭārĭus, a, um, adj.compendium Short, compendious, only a few times of ways or roads: via ad gloriam proxima et quasi compendiaria, * Cic. Off. 2, 12, 43; cf. Val. Max. 7, 2, ext. 1. Subst.

compendio.definition: compendĭo, āvi, ātum, 1, compendium (eccl. Lat.). To shorten, abridge: sermonem,Tert. adv. Marc. 4, 9; 4, 1. Compendiare alicui, lit., to shorten the way of life for one; hence, to kill him, Aug. Quaest. in Hept. 7 fin.

compendiosus.definition: compendĭōsus, a, um, compendium. Advantageous (opp. damnosus), Col. 1, 4, 5. Abridged, short, brief, compendious (post-class.): verba,App. M. 11, p. 268, 12: iter,id. ib. 6, p. 186, 12: exitus citae mortis, Prud. στεφ. 2, 334.—Adv.: compendĭōsē, compendiously, briefly, Cassiod. Var. 8, 29.—In comp., Sid. Ep. 7, 10.

compendium.definition: compendo, orig. belonging to the lang. of econ. That whichis weighed together, kept together, saved (cf. Varr. L. L. 5, § 183 Müll.; Paul. ex Fest. p. 72, 10 Müll.); a saving or gain, profit acquired by saving (opp. dispendium; class. in prose and poetry). Prop.: ego hodie compendi feci binos panes in dies,have saved two loaves,Plaut. Pers. 4, 3, 2; cf. id. Truc. 2, 4, 26: aliquem mercibus suppeditandis cum quaestu compendioque dimittere,Cic. Ver...

compensatio.definition: (), , compenso A weighing, balancing of several things together. Prop., in the lang. of business, a balancing of accounts, a rendering of an equivalent, equalizing: compensatio est debiti et crediti inter se distributio,Dig. 16, 2, 1; so ib. 24, 3, 15; Gai Inst. 4, 66 sq.: mercium, an exchange, barter (opp. pecunia), Just. 3, 2, 11. Trop (only in Cic.): hac usurum conpensatione sapientem, ut voluptatem fugiat, si ea majorem doiorem effectura sit,...

compensativus.definition: compensātīvus, a, um, id. Serving for compensating (late Lat.), Victor. Rhet. 1, p. 137; 2, p. 217.

compensatiuus.definition: compensātīvus, a, um, id. Serving for compensating (late Lat.), Victor. Rhet. 1, p. 137; 2, p. 217.

compenso.definition: com-penso (conp-), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. To poise, weigh several things with one another; hence, in the lang. of business, to equalize one thing with another by weighing, to balance with one another, to make good, compensate, balance against, lit. and trop. (class. in prose and poetry; most freq. in Cic.); constr. aliquid cum aliquā re, aliquā re, or absol. In gen. In post-Aug. poets, of a way, to shorten, spare, save: longum iter,Sen. Hippol. 83 (...

comperendinatio.definition: comperendino A deferring of the time (of trial) to the third day or later (post-Aug.), Sen. Ep. 97, 5; Plin. Ep. 5, 21, 1; 6, 2, 6; Gell. 14, 2, 1; Tac. Or. 38; cf. Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 9, § 26. Transf., in gen., delay: sine ullā comperendinatione,Ambros. in Luc. 1, 8.

comperendinatus.definition: id., i. q. comperendinatio, q. v., Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 9, § 26; id. Brut. 22, 87.

comperendino.definition: compĕrendĭno, āvi, ātum, 1, comperendinus, jurid. t. t.; prop. of the judge To cite a defendant to a new time of trial, appointed on the third following day or later: reum,Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 9, § 26; 2, 1, 7, § 20. Meton., of the party which demands the deferring: ut ante primos ludos comperendinem,Cic. Verr. 1, 11, 34 Klotz ad loc.

comperio.definition: com-pĕrĭo, pĕri, pertum, 4, v. a.root par-, of paro, pario; cf. 2. comparo, and aperio, operio, etc.; by others separated from these words and referred to root per-, of πειράω, peritus, periculum; but cf. Corss. Ausspr. II. 410, lit. To disclose wholly, lay open (a fact), without the access. idea of communicating the thing disclosed (which aperio expresses; v. aperio); to obtain a knowledge of a thing, to find out with certainty, to have or gain...

comperior.definition: compĕrĭor (conp-), īri, pertus sum, 4, , collat. form of comperio, q. v. To ascertain, learn, obtain certain knowledge that, etc. (rare); constr. mostly with acc. and inf.: dum ne ab hoc me falli comperiar,Ter. And. 5, 3, 31; Sall. J. 45, 1; 108, 3; Tac. A. 4, 20; Gell. 3, 3, 1: quid comperior?App. M. 2, p. 124, 11; perf., Tert. adv. Herm. 28.

compernis.definition: com-pernis, e, perna With the knees bent inwards, knock-kneed, Lucil. ap. Non. p. 26, 3; Plaut. Fragm. ap. Fest. p. 375, 20 Müll.; Varr. L. L. 9, § 10 Müll.

comperpetuus.definition: com-perpĕtŭus, a, um Coeternal, Prud. Apoth. 339.

compes.definition: (), , f. (m. acc. compedem meum, Vulg. Thren. 3, 7; plur. compedes parati, Lact. Mort. Persec. c. 21) A (wooden) fetter or shackle, for the feet (usu. in plur.). Prop., nom. and acc.: jubete huic crassas conpedis inpingier,Plaut. Capt. 3, 5, 76: ut istas conpedis Tibi adimam,id. ib. 5, 4, 30; id. Men. 1, 1, 4; id. Pers. 2, 3, 17; Ter. Phorm. 2, 1, 19; gen. conpedium, Plaut. Pers. 3, 3, 15, abl.: conpedibus levior filius,id. Capt. 5, 4, 28; Cato a...

compesco.definition: compesco, pescui (pescitum, Prisc. p. 887 P.), 3, compes To fasten together, to confine, hold in check, to repress, curb, restrain (mostly poet. or in post-Aug. prose; not in Cic.; the words quoted as from Cic. by Quint. 11, 3, 169: quin compescitis vocem istam? ap. Cic. himself, Rab. Perd. 8, 18, are: quin continetis vocem). Lit.: ramos fluentes,i. e. to clip, prune,Verg. G. 2, 370; Col. 5, 6, 11: spatiantia bracchia,Ov. M. 14, 630: ignibus igne...

competentia.definition: competo (postclass.) A meeting together, agreement: membrorum inter se,symmetry,Gell. 1, 1, 3; cf. Macr. Somn. Scip. 1, 19, 21. Esp., of the stars, conjunction, aspect: nasci ad eandem competentiam (sc. siderum),Gell. 14, 1, 26; Macr. Somn. Scip. 1, 6, 24 al.

competitio.definition: id. (late Lat.). An agreement, Sid. Ep. 2, 9. A judicial demand, Cod. Th. 2, 23, 1. Rivalry, Ambros. de Elia, 21, 79.

competitor.definition: id. A rival, competitor (in good prose); in gen.,Cic. Off. 1, 12, 38; id. Planc. 4, 9; id. Att. 1, 1, 1; Liv. 6, 41, 2; 37, 57, 15; Quint. 3, 7, 2; 7, 1, 29; 9, 2, 97; Suet. Caes. 13; 19; Dig. 50, 2, 3, § 2. Esp., a plaintiff, Cod. Th. 10, 9, 2.

competitrix.definition: competitor A female competitor, Cic. Mur. 19, 40.

competo.definition: com-pĕto (conp-), īvi or ii, ītum, 3, v. a. and n. (first common since the Aug. per.; very rare before that time; not found in Cic., and perh. not in the poets). Act., to strive after something in company or together (post-class. and very rare): unum locum,Just. 13, 2, 1: unam speciosam (puellam),Aur. Vict. Vir. Ill. 59: bona, Cod. Th. 10, 10, 27, § 6. Neutr., to meet or come together.

compilator.definition: id. A plunderer: veterum, an epithet of Virgil (on account of his imitation of Homer, Ennius, etc.), acc. to Hier. praef. Hebr. Quaest. in Genes., and Isid. Orig. 10, 44.

compilo.definition: com-pīlo, āvi, ātum, 1 To snatch together and carry off, to plunder, pillage, rob (rare but class.). Prop., with acc. of person or thing robbed: aedes,Plaut. As. 2, 2, 6: fana,Cic. N. D. 1, 31, 86: si malui compilari quam venire,id. de Or. 2, 66, 268: consulem, exercitum, provinciamque,Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 13, § 35: hortos,id. Phil. 3, 12, 30: templa omnibus ornamentis compilata,Liv. 43, 7, 10: totum oppidum ostiatim,Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 24, § 53: ne te ...

compingo.definition: com-pingo (conp-), pēgi, pactum, 3, v. a. con-pango. To join or unite several parts into one whole, to put together, frame, make by joining, compose (in verb. finit. mostly in post-Aug. prose). Compingere aliquem or aliquid aliquo, to confine, lock up, put, conceal (several times in Plaut. and Cic., elsewh. rare).

compinguesco.definition: com-pinguesco, ĕre V. inch. n., to thicken to a solid substance, Tert. Anim. 25.

compitalicius.definition: compĭtālĭcĭus or -tĭus, a, um, compitalis Of or belonging to the compitalia: dies,Cic. Att. 7, 7, 3: ludi,id. Pis. 4, 8; Suet. Aug. 31: ambulationes,Cic. Att. 2, 3, 3 fin.

compitalis.definition: compĭtālis, e, adj.compitum Of or pertaining to the cross-ways: Lares,Varr. L. L. 6, § 25 Müll.; Suet. Aug. 31 (qui compita servant, Ov. F. 2, 615; cf. id. ib. 5, 140 sq.). Subst.

compitum.definition: (, Varr. L. L. 6, § 25 Müll.), , n. (mostly in plur.; in sing., Cato, R. R. 5, 4; Varr. L. L. 6, § 43 Müll., and in Non. p. 94, 27; Liv. 27, 4, 12; Fest. p. 174, 7 Müll.; Dig. 8, 10, 12, § 3; Tert. Test. Anim. 1 fin.—Access. form , , m., Varr. and Caecil. ap. Non. p. 196, 9 sq.) [competo] A place where several ways meet, a cross - way, cross - road, Cic. Agr. 1, 3, 7; Liv. 34, 2, 12; Verg. G. 2, 382; Prop. 4 (5), 1, 23; 4 (5), 3, 57; Ov. F. 1, 14...

complaceo.definition: com-plăcĕo, plăcŭi and plăcĭtus sum, 2, v. n. (except in Col., only ante- and postclass.). To be pleasing at the same time, to please also: postquam me amare dixi, complacita'st tibi,Ter. And. 4, 1, 21: ut et tibi et Gallioni nostro complacuerat, * Col. 9, 16, 2; cf. Gell. 17, 9, 4. To be very pleasing to: Veneri haec complacuerunt,Plaut. Rud. 3, 4, 22: hoc deo complacitum'st,id. ib. 1, 3, 3; cf. Gell. 18, 3, 4: ejus sibi complacitam formam,Ter. ...

complano.definition: com-plāno, āvi, ātum, 1 To make even, level, or plain (rare). Prop.: terram tabulā, manibus, pedibus,Cato, R. R. 151, 3: montium juga,Suet. Calig. 37: lacum,id. Caes. 44: opera, Auct. B. Alex. 63: domum,to make even with the ground, to pull down, raze,Cic. Dom. 38, 101.—* Trop.: complanare et mollire aspera, dura,i. e. to render tolerable,Sen. Prov. 5, 9.

complanto.definition: com-planto, no Perf., ātum, 1, , to plant together (late Lat.); only trop.,Vulg. Rom. 6, 5; Ambros. Abrah. 2, 11, 80 fin.: virtutibus,id. Ep. 42 fin.

complaudo.definition: com-plaudo, ĕre To applaud together, Paul. Nol. 18, 8.

complector.definition: complector (conp-), plexus, 3, v. dep. (in signif. mostly coinciding with amplector), prop. To entwine around a person or thing (cf. amplector; class. in prose and poetry). Lit. Trop.

complementum.definition: compleo That which fills up or completes, a complement (rare; only fig.): numerorum (inania quaedam verba), * Cic. Or. 69, 230: omnium accusationum,that gives them their full weight,Tac. A. 3, 38: accusationis, Cod. Th. 9, 24, 3.

compleo.definition: com-plĕo (conp-), ēvi, ētum, 2 (contr. forms: complerunt, complerint, complerat, complesse, etc., for compleverunt, etc., very often), v. a. pleo, whence suppleo, plenus To fill up, fill full, fill out (class. in prose and poetry). Lit., of material objects. Trop.

completio.definition: compleo (postclass.). A filling, Paul. ex Fest. p. 105, 2 Müll.; Jul. Ep. Nov. c. 66, § 234. A filling up, fulfilment: sanctae prophetiae,Aug. Ep. 161.

completivus.definition: complētīvus, a, um, id. Serving for filling up, completive (late Lat.): particula,Prisc. p. 1026 P.

completiuus.definition: complētīvus, a, um, id. Serving for filling up, completive (late Lat.): particula,Prisc. p. 1026 P.

completor.definition: id. One who fills up, a fulfiller: legum (Jesus),Juvenc. in Matt. 2, 12, v. 574.

completorium.definition: id. A service containing prayers at the close of the day (eccl. Lat.): completorii hora, Hymn. de Pass. Domin.

complex.definition: complex, plĭcis, complico Closely connected with one, confederate, participant (late Lat.): dii consentes et complices,i. e. agreeing,Arn. 3, p. 123 (v. consentes).— With gen., Cod. Th. 6, 4, 21; Ambros. Off. 3, 4; Prud. Ham. 614.

complexio.definition: (), , complector (Ciceron.) A combination, connection. Prop. Trop.

complexo.definition: complexo, āvi, ātum, 1, complecto = complector To encompass, embrace closely, clasp around (post-class. and rare), Coripp. 1, 104: artissime complexatum aliquem recipere,App. M. 10, p. 249, 18.

complexor.definition: complexor, āri, 1 To embrace closely (late Lat.): eos,Vulg. Marc. 10, 16.

complexus.definition: complexus, a, um, Part., from complector.

complicabilis.definition: complĭcābĭlis, e, complico That may be folded together (late Lat.), Isid. Orig. 15, 7, 4.

complicatio.definition: id.. A folding together, enveloping, Cael. Aur. Tard. 4, 3, 26. A multiplication: denaria,Aug. Mus. 1, n. 19.

complico.definition: com-plĭco (conp-), āvi, ātum (postAug. ui, ĭtum; cf.: applico, explico, etc.), 1 To fold together, to fold up (rare but class.). Prop.: rudentem,Plaut. Rud. 4, 3, 1: armamenta,id. Merc. 1, 2, 83: epistulam,Cic. Q. Fr. 3, 1, 5, § 17; id. Att. 12, 1, 2: Diogenes se complicuit in dolio,Sen. Ep. 90, 11: pedibus complicitis,App. M. 9, p. 236; cf.: complicitus in genua,id. ib. 1, p. 111, 3. —* Trop.: si quis voluerit animi sui complicatam notionem evol...

complodo.definition: com-plōdo, si, sum, 3, plaudo: manus To strike or clap the hands together in applauding, from joy, pain, etc. (only in post-Aug. prose): complodere manus scaenicum est,Quint. 11, 3, 123; so Petr. 18, 7; 20, 5; Sen. Ira, 1, 1, 4; App. M. 9, p. 235, 33.

comploratio.definition: (), , comploro A loud, violent complaint, lamentation, esp. by several persons (several times in Liv., elsewhere rare; not ante-Aug.): lamentabilis mulierum,Liv. 3, 47, 6; cf. id. 1, 41, 6; 26, 29, 2; 40, 9, 7; 41, 11, 5; Just. 11, 9, 13; Gell. 10, 3, 7.—Of one person: sororis,Liv. 1, 26, 3.

comploratus.definition: (), , id., i. q. comploratio A loud, violent moaning, lamentation, etc., esp. of several persons (only in Liv.): familiarum,Liv. 22, 55, 7; 23, 42, 5: justo conploratu prosequi mortuos,id. 25, 26, 10.

comploro.definition: com-plōro (conp-), āvi, ātum, 1 To bewail, lament together loudly or violently (rare, and not ante-Aug.): penates,Ov. Tr. 1, 3, 95: cum vivi mortuique promiscue complorarentur,Liv. 22, 55, 3; cf. id. 5, 39, 4: desperata et complorata respublica,id. 22, 53, 4; 37, 7, 4; Gell. 7, 5, 6: nondum morte comploratā,Cic. Dom. 37, 98.—Impers.: comploratum publice est,Flor. 2, 15, 8.

compluriens.definition: complūrĭens (conp-, -ĭes), complures Several times, many times, often (only ante - class.), Cato ap. Paul. ex Fest. p. 59, 19 Müll.; id. ap. Gell. 5, 21, 15 sq.; id. ap. Non. p. 87, 15 sq.; Plaut. Pers. 4, 3, 65 (quoted by Gell. and Non. l. l.).

complutor.definition: compluit, II. He who gives rain, who waters, Aug. Serm. Div. 8, 3.

compluviatus.definition: complŭvĭātus, a, um, compluvium, ll. Fashioned like a compluvium, i.e. square (rare): species jugationis,Varr. R. R. 1, 8, 2: vites,Plin. 17, 21, 35, § 164.

compluuiatus.definition: complŭvĭātus, a, um, compluvium, ll. Fashioned like a compluvium, i.e. square (rare): species jugationis,Varr. R. R. 1, 8, 2: vites,Plin. 17, 21, 35, § 164.

compluvium.definition: compluit, I. A quadranguiar open space in the middle of a Roman house, which collected the rain-water flowing from the roofs and conducted it to a basin (impluvium) placed below, Varr. L. L. 5, § 161 Müll.; Paul. ex Fest. p. 108, 14 ib.; Varr. R. R. 1, 13, 3; Vitr. 6, 3, 1; * Suet. Aug. 92; cf. impluvium, II. A.— Hence Meton., a quadrangular support for vines, Col. 4, 24, 14 Schneid. N. cr.; 4, 26, 3; cf. compluviatus.

compluuium.definition: compluit, I. A quadranguiar open space in the middle of a Roman house, which collected the rain-water flowing from the roofs and conducted it to a basin (impluvium) placed below, Varr. L. L. 5, § 161 Müll.; Paul. ex Fest. p. 108, 14 ib.; Varr. R. R. 1, 13, 3; Vitr. 6, 3, 1; * Suet. Aug. 92; cf. impluvium, II. A.— Hence Meton., a quadrangular support for vines, Col. 4, 24, 14 Schneid. N. cr.; 4, 26, 3; cf. compluviatus.

componderans.definition: com-pondĕrans, antis, pondero Weighing: pari lance,App. Trism. p. 89, 11.

compono.definition: com-pōno (conp-), pŏsŭi (COMPOSEIVERVNT, C. I. L. 1, 199, 2), pŏsĭtum (compostus, Plaut. Mil. 4, 7, 21 Lorenz; Verg. A. 1, 249; Lucil. ap. Cic. de Or. 3, 43, 171; Varr ap. Sen. Ep. 56, 6), 3, v. a. To put, place, lay, bring or set together, to unite, join, connect, collect, aggregate, compose, to order, arrange, adjust, etc. (class. and very freq.). In gen., of different objects. In partic.

comportatio.definition: (), , comporto A bringing or carrying together, Vitr. 1, 5, 1.

comportionalis.definition: com-portĭōnālis, e, : comportionales termini The limits between the boundaries of possessions, Aggen. ap. Goes. p. 51; cf. ib. p. 254.

comporto.definition: com-porto (conp-), āvi, ātum, 1 To bear, carry, or bring together, to collect (class.): nobis opus est rebus exquisitis, undique collectis, arcessitis, comportatis,Cic. de Or. 3, 24, 92: eo frumentum ex Asiā,Caes. B. C. 3, 42: frumentum ad mare in Graeciam,Liv. 36, 2, 12: frumentum ex agris in loca tuta,Cic. Att. 5, 18, 2: huc frumentum,Sall. J. 47, 2: arma in templum Castoris,Cic. Pis. 10, 23; cf.: aquam in arcem,Caes. B. C. 3, 12: ad aggerem ca...

compos.definition: com-pŏs (conp-), pŏtis, potis Having the mastery, control, or power over a thing, master of, partaking of, possessing, participating or sharing in, guilty of, etc. (very freq. and class.); constr. usu. with gen., more rarely with abl., or absol. Transf., of the thing: compote voto,Sen. Agam. 364.

composcens.definition: com-poscens, entis, Part. [posco] Demanding at the same time, Mart. Cap. 5, p. 136 Grot. dub. (Kopp, § 425, Deliacos poscens artus); Not. Tir. p. 58.

composite.definition: compŏsĭtē, , v. compono P. a. fin.

compositio.definition: (), , compono. A putting together, compounding, connecting, arranging, composition, adjustment, etc. A laying together for preservation, a laying up of fruits, Col. 12, 26, 6; 12, 51, 1; in plur.: rerum auctumnalium,id. 12, 44, 1.

compositivus.definition: compŏsĭtīvus, a, um, compositus, compono Suitable for uniting, compositive, Mart. Cap. 9, § 945.

compositiuus.definition: compŏsĭtīvus, a, um, compositus, compono Suitable for uniting, compositive, Mart. Cap. 9, § 945.

composito.definition: compŏsĭtō, v compono P. a. fin.

compositor.definition: (), , compono An orderer, arranger, disposer, maker (rare): inventor aut compositor aut actor,Cic. Or. 19, 61: anni,id. Leg. 2, 12, 29 (al. compositio): operum,Ov. Tr. 2, 356: juris,Cod. Just. 6, 28, 4: historiae Cumanae,Fest. p. 266, 26 Müll.: melodiae,Cassiod. Hist. Eccl. 1, 2 fin.

compositura.definition: (contr. , Cato, R. R. 22, 3). , id. A joining together, connection (very rare, and only anteclass.). Prop.: olei, Cato, l. l.: oculorum,a connection, commissure,Lucr. 4, 327. Trop., of discourse, conneclion, syntax: partium orationis, Sinn. Capito ap. Gell. 5, 20, 2.

compositus.definition: compŏsĭtus, a, um, Part. and , from compono.

compostus.definition: compostus, a, um, v. compono Init.

compotatio.definition: A drinking together, as transl. of the Gr. συμπόσιον (perh. only in Cic.), Cic. Sen. 13, 45; id. Fam. 9, 24, 3.

compotator.definition: collat. form of compotor A drinking-companion (late Lat.), Ambros. de Job et Dav. 3, 5, 17.

compotens.definition: compŏtens, entis Having power with one, an epithet of Diana, Inscr. Grut. 41, 2.

compotio.definition: compŏtĭo (conp-), īvi, ītum, 4, compos To make partaker of (only anteand post- class.); constr. with acc. pers. and abl. or gen. rei.

compotrix.definition: (), , compotor A female drinking - companion, Ter. And. 1, 4, 5; Sid. Ep. 2, 9.

compraes.definition: A joint-surety, Paul. ex Fest. p. 39, 10 Müll.

comprecatio.definition: comprecor A common or public imploring of a deity: sollennis deorum,Liv. 39, 15, 2; plur.: deūm inmortalium,Gell. 13, 22, 1.

comprecor.definition: com-prĕcor (conp-), ātus, āri, (lit. to worship a deity with all the usages belonging thereto; hence, in gen.) To pray to, supplicate, implore (mostly ante-class. and rare; not in Cic.); constr. alicui, aliquem, aliquid, or absol.: Jovi molā salsā,Plaut. Am. 2, 2, 108: deos,Ter. Ad. 4, 5, 65 and 70: caelestūm fidem, * Cat. 64, 191.— Absol., to pray, supplicate: abi intro et conprecare,Plaut. Mil. 2, 4, 41: Cythereïa, comprecor, ausis Assit,Ov. M....

comprehendo.definition: com-prĕhendo (conp-; also com-prendo, very freq. in MSS. and edd.; cf. Quint. 1, 5, 21. In MSS. also comprae-hendo and compraendo, v. prehendo), di, sum, 3 V. a., to lay hold of something on all sides; to take or catch hold of, seize, grasp, apprehend; to comprehend, comprise (class. in prose and poetry). Prop. Trop.

comprehensibilis.definition: comprĕhensĭbĭlis (conp-), e, comprehendo That can be seized or laid hold of (very rare; prob. first used by Cic.). Prop.: comprehensibile et solidum corpus,Lact. 7, 12, 2.—As subst.: comprĕ-hensĭbĭle, is, n. (opp. incomprehensibile), Tert. Apol. 48. Trop. *

comprehensio.definition: (), , id. A seizing or laying hold of with the hands. Prop. Trop.

comprehensivus.definition: comprĕhensīvus, a, um, comprehendo Comprehensible, conceivable (late Lat.): definitione, Boëth. Defin. p. 660.

comprehensiuus.definition: comprĕhensīvus, a, um, comprehendo Comprehensible, conceivable (late Lat.): definitione, Boëth. Defin. p. 660.

compresse.definition: compressē, ; v. comprimo P. a. fin.

compressio.definition: (), , com primo A pressing together, compression. Prop. Trop., of diction, the compression of an expression, Cic. Brut. 7, 29; v. Ellendt. ad h. l.

compresso.definition: compresso, no Perf., ātum, 1, id., to press, oppress (late Lat.), Tert. contr. Gnost. 3; Porphyr. ad Hor. S. 2, 3, 173.

compressor.definition: (), , id. One who compresses (in mal. part.), Mythogr. Vatic. 1, 18; Plaut. Argum. Aul. 2, 7.

compressus.definition: compressus, a, um, Part. and , from comprimo.

comprimo.definition: com-prĭmo (conp-), pressi, pressum, 3, premo To press or squeeze together, compress (very freq and class.). In gen.: (corpora) inter se compressa teneri,Lucr. 6, 454: dentis,Plaut. Ps. 3, 1, 21: cum plane (digitos) compresserat pugnumque fecerat,Cic. Ac. 2, 47, 145; cf.: compressa in pugnum manus,Quint. 2, 20, 7; 11, 3, 104: (oculos) opertos compressosque,id. 11, 3, 76: compressā palmā,with the clinched hand,Plaut. Cas. 2, 6, 53: compressam forci...

comprobo.definition: com-prŏbo (conp-), āvi, ātum, 1 Subject., to approve wholly of something, to assent to, sanction, acknowledge (class and very freq., esp in prose): istam tuam sentent. am laudo vehementissimeque comprobo,Cic. Imp. Pomp. 24, 69: decretum consulum,id. Att. 16, 16, D, 14 sq.: orationem omnium assensu,Liv. 5, 9, 7; cf. Suet. Aug. 68; 53: consensu potius eruditorum quam puerorum amore comprobari,Quint. 10, 1, 130 et saep.: has comproba tabulas,Cic. Ca...

compromissarius.definition: comprōmissārĭus, a, um, compromissum Pertaining to arbitration: judex, an arbitrator, umpire, referee chosen by contending parties (jurid. Lat.), Dig. 4, 8, 41; 26, 5, 4.

compromissum.definition: A mutual promise to abide by the award of an arbiter, Cic. Rosc. Com. 4, 12; Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 27, § 66; id. Fam. 12, 30; Dig. 4, 8, 1 sq.—From

compromitto.definition: com-prōmitto (conp-), mīsi, missum, 3 (contr. form conpromesise = conpromisisse, S. C. Bacch. v. 14), , jurid. t. t. in lawsuits To promise mutually to abide by the decision of an arbiter: tribunicii candidati conpromiserunt,Cic. Q. Fr. 2, 14 (15, 6): de aliquā re,Dig. 4, 8, 13: in arbitrum,ib. 44, 4, 4; 4, 8, 21 al. To promise at the same time (very rare): eisque spolia peremptorum hostium compromittens,Cassiod. Hist. Eccl. 6, 1.

comprovincialis.definition: com-prōvincĭālis, e Adj., born in the same province, Sid. Ep. 7, 7.

comprouincialis.definition: com-prōvincĭālis, e Adj., born in the same province, Sid. Ep. 7, 7.

compte.definition: comptē, , v. 1. como P. a. fin.

comptor.definition: 1. como One who adorns; only trop.: fabricarum,Cassiod. Var. 4, 51.

compugnantia.definition: compugno A fighting together (late Lat.): inter se contrariorum aërum,Isid. Orig. 5, 35, 8.

compugno.definition: com-pugno, āre To fight or contend together (post-class.), Gell. 12, 5, 3; 14, 5, 4; 14, 5 fin.; Sulp. Sev. de Vita S. Mart. 14. To combat together: amaritudinem,Veg. Art. Vet. 1, 13, 6.

compulsamentum.definition: compulso An impelling; trop., an exhortation, Fulg. Myth. 3, 6.

compulsatio.definition: id. A (hostile) pressing together, a contest, contention (late Lat.), Tert. Apol. 21; 38; Fulg. Myth. praef. fin.

compulsor.definition: id. (late Lat.). Lit., a driver (of cattle), Pall. Jun. 2, 3. Transf., one who asks or forces to a payment, an exacter of money, Amm. 22, 6, 1; Cod. Th. 8, 10, 3 and 4; 11, 7, 15.

compulsus.definition: compulsus, a, um, Part., from compello.

compunctio.definition: compungo. Lit., a puncture: ligni,Ambros. in Psa. 118, Serm. 3, § 8. Trop., the sting of conscience, remorse (eccl. Lat.), Salv. adv. Avar. 4, 8 al.

compunctorius.definition: compunctōrĭus, a, um, id. Admonitory, hortatory (eccl. Lat.): sermo,Sid. Ep. 6, 6.

compunctus.definition: compunctus, a, um, Part., from compungo.

compungo.definition: com-pungo (conp-), nxi, nctum, 3 V. a., to prick or puncture severely, to sting. Prop. (rare but class.): collum dolone,Phaedr. 3, 6, 3: aculeis urticae,Col. 8, 14, 8: acu,Cels. 6, 18, 9: barbarus compunctus notis Threïciis,branded,Cic. Off. 2, 7, 25: (colores) qui compungunt aciem lacrumareque cogunt,dazzle,Lucr. 2, 420; cf. of heat and cold: sensus corporis,id. 2, 432 (for Sen. Ep. 88, 39, v. compingo). Trop.

compurgatio.definition: A complete purification (late Lat.): tres compurgationes, i. e. by fire, air, and water, Mythogr. Lat. 3, 6, 18.

compurgo.definition: com-purgo, āre V. a., to purify completely: visum,Plin. 20, 13, 50, § 127.

computatio.definition: id. A computing, reckoning; a computation (post-Aug.). In gen., Sen. Ep. 84, 7; id. Ben. 7, 10, 4; Plin. 2, 108, 112, § 247; 6, 33, 38, § 206; Plin. Pan. 38, 3; * Quint. 1, 10, 35 al. Specif., the reckoning of avaricious men, close reckoning, niggardliness, parsimony, Sen. Ben. 4, 11, 2; Plin. 17, 22, 35, § 192.

computo.definition: com-pŭto (conp-), āvi, ātum, 1 To sum up, reckon, compute. To reckon in with, or in addition to (in jurid. Lat.): fetus pecorum fructibus,Dig. 23, 3, 10; cf.: aliquid in fructum,ib. 24, 3, 7.

computresco.definition: com-pūtresco (conp-), trŭi, 3 V. inch. n., to become wholly putrid, to putrefy, rot (very rare; not in Cic.): Cass. Hem. ap. Plin. 13, 13, 27, § 86; Col. 5, 10, 7; Plin. 32, 7, 23, § 67 (Sillig, conputuere).—Per tmesin: artus pereunt conque putrescunt,Lucr. 3, 343.

computus.definition: computo A computation (late Lat.), Firm. Math. 1, 12 fin.; Auct. ap. Goes. Agrim. p. 236.

comte.definition: comtē = compte, v. 1. como P. a. fin.

comtus.definition: comtus, a, um, = comptus, a, um, v. 1. como

conabilis.definition: cōnābĭlis, e, conor Laborious, difficult (late Lat.): conabiles atque laboriosi vomitus, Cael. Aur Acut. 3, 1, 4.

conamen.definition: id. An effort, exertion, struggle (poet.): alarum,Lucr. 6, 836: eundi,id. 6, 326: magno conamine,Ov. M. 3, 60; cf. id. ib. 8, 366; id. F. 4, 325; Luc. 4, 287.—In plur.: conamina mortis,Ov. M. 10, 390; Lucr. 6, 1040. Concr., a support, prop: constitit (infans), adjutis aliquo conamine nervis,Ov. M. 15, 224.

conatus.definition: conor. Abstr., an effort, exertion, struggle, endeavor: ue ista hercle magno jam conatu magnas nugas dixerit, Ter. Heaut. 4, 1, 8: quo majore conatu studioque aguntur,Cic. Quint. 14, 47: omnem sui tribunatus conatum in meam perniciem parare,id. Fam. 5, 2, 6: Genucius ad hostes magno conatu profectus,Liv. 7, 6, 9: in ipso conatu rerum circumegit se annus,i. e. just as the affair was well begun,id. 9, 18, 15 Weissenb. ad loc.: vixdum inchoatis rebu...

concaco.definition: con-căco, āvi, ātum, 1 V. a., to defile with ordure, to fill with defilement: totam regiam,Phaedr. 4, 17, 11: se,Sen. Apoc. 4 fin.: catillus concacatus,Petr. 66.

concalefacio.definition: con-călĕfăcĭo, fēci, factum, 3 V. a., to warm thoroughly (rare but class.).

concalesco.definition: con-călesco, lŭi, 3 V. inch. n., to become or grow thoroughly warm, to glow. Prop. (rare but class.): corpora nostra ardore animi concalescunt, * Cic. Tusc. 1, 18, 42: frumenta non poterunt cito concalescere,Vitr. 6, 9; cf. Plin. 18, 30, 73, § 304; Col. 12, 52, 17.—In perf., Plaut. Am. 1, 3, 15; Varr. R. R. 3, 16, 38; Col. 2, 18, 1; 2, 50. Trop., to glow with love: concaluit, quid vis? * Ter. Heaut. 2, 3, 108 Don.

concallesco.definition: con-callesco, callui, 3 V. inch. [calleo]; lit., to become hard or callous; hence, trop., * Of the intellect, to become shrewd, practised (cf. calleo, I.): callidos eos appello, quorum, tamquam manus opere, sic animus usu concalluit,Cic. N. D. 3, 10, 25.—* Of the feelings, to become insensible, obtuse: locus ille animi nostri, stomachus ubi habitabat olim, concalluit, Cic. Att. 4, 16, 10.

concameratio.definition: concamero A vaulting; a vault, Vitr. 2, 4; 5, 10; Plin. 11, 10, 10, § 22; Dig. 32, 31 al.

concamero.definition: con-cămĕro, āvi, ātum, 1 V. a., to vault or arch over: templum,Plin. 34, 14, 42, § 148.—In part. pass.: sudatio,Vitr. 5, 11, 2; Suet. Aug. 90; Inscr. Orell. 3033: uvae pensili concameratae nodo, suspended from a vault or arch, Plin. 14, 1, 3, § 16.

concaptivus.definition: A fellow-captive, Hier. Ep. 119; Vulg. Rom. 16, 7.

concaptiuus.definition: A fellow-captive, Hier. Ep. 119; Vulg. Rom. 16, 7.

concarnatio.definition: concarno A uniting with flesh, incarnation, Tert. Mon. 9 fin.

concarno.definition: con-carno, āre V. a., to unite or clothe with flesh, to incarnate (post-class. and very rare), Tert. Carn. Christ. 20; Veg. Art. Vet. 2, 22, 3.

concastigo.definition: con-castīgo, āre V. a., to chastise severely, to punish (ante- and post-class.): hominem probe,Plaut. Bacch. 3, 3, 94; 5, 2, 56; id. Trin. 1, 1, 4; M. Aur. ap. Fronto Ep. ad M. Caes. 1, 9.

concatenatio.definition: concateno A connecting, joining (late Lat.). Lit., Cassiod. Var. 12, 19. Trop.

concateno.definition: con-cătēno, no Perf., ātum, 1, v. a., to link or bind together, to connect (late Lat.), Lact. 3, 17; Min. Fel. 17, 2.

concatervatus.definition: con-cătervātus, a, um, caterva Heaped or crowded together: copiae,Amm. 29, 5, 38: manipuli,id. 31, 13, 2.

concateruatus.definition: con-cătervātus, a, um, caterva Heaped or crowded together: copiae,Amm. 29, 5, 38: manipuli,id. 31, 13, 2.

concavitas.definition: concavus A hollow, cavity (late Lat.), Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 1, 14.

concauitas.definition: concavus A hollow, cavity (late Lat.), Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 1, 14.

concavus.definition: Adj., hollow, concave; arched, vaulted; bent, curved: cymbala,Lucr. 2, 619; cf.: concava aera,Ov. M. 4, 30: loca terrae,Lucr. 5, 1255: altitudines speluncarum,Cic. N. D. 2, 39, 98: saxa,Verg. G. 4, 49: vallis,Ov. M. 8, 334: bracchia Cancri,id. ib. 10, 127; 15, 369: jugula,Cic. Fat. 5, 10: manus (opp. plana),Sen. Ep. 56, 1: dentes,Plin. 11, 37, 61, § 162: folia,id. 16, 24, 38, § 92: aqua,swelling,Ov. Tr. 1, 11, 20: puppis,id. F. 4, 276: vela,id. H...

concauus.definition: Adj., hollow, concave; arched, vaulted; bent, curved: cymbala,Lucr. 2, 619; cf.: concava aera,Ov. M. 4, 30: loca terrae,Lucr. 5, 1255: altitudines speluncarum,Cic. N. D. 2, 39, 98: saxa,Verg. G. 4, 49: vallis,Ov. M. 8, 334: bracchia Cancri,id. ib. 10, 127; 15, 369: jugula,Cic. Fat. 5, 10: manus (opp. plana),Sen. Ep. 56, 1: dentes,Plin. 11, 37, 61, § 162: folia,id. 16, 24, 38, § 92: aqua,swelling,Ov. Tr. 1, 11, 20: puppis,id. F. 4, 276: vela,id. H...

concedo.definition: con-cēdo, cessi, cessum, 3, v. n. and A. (a strengthened cedo, and corresp. with it in most of its signiff.); lit., to go, walk; hence Neutr., with reference to the terminus a quo, to go or walk away from a place, to depart, retire, withdraw, remove from (in lit. signif. rare but class.). Neutr., in respect to the terminus ad quem, to go, walk, betake one's self somewhere, to retire, withdraw to, etc.; with ad, in, or adv.: tantisper hic ego ad j...

concelebro.definition: con-cĕlēbro, āvi, ātum, 1 V..a. (a strengthened celebro; rare but class.). To resort to in multitudes or frequently, to frequent: variae volucres loca aquarum Concelebrant,Lucr. 2, 345: convivia et passim et tributim,Q. Cic. Pet. Cons. 11, 44. Meton.

concellita.definition: cella He who dwells with one in a cell, a cell-mate, Sid. Ep. 8, 14.

concenatio.definition: () A supping together, companionship at table; transl. of σύνδειπνον (like compotatio of συμπόσιον), Cic. Sen. 13, 45; id. Fam. 9, 24, 3.

concentio.definition: concino A singing together, harmony (very rare): clarissima (catervae),Cic. Sest. 55, 118; id. Tim. 8, 24; App. de Mundo, p. 71, 20.

concentor.definition: id. One who sings with others in a chorus (late Lat.), συνῳδός, Gloss. Isid. 7, 12, 28.

concenturio.definition: con-centŭrĭo, āre V. a.; lit., to assemble by centuries; hence, humorously, in Plaut., to collect, bring together, to prepare in gen.: dum concenturio in corde sycophantias,Plaut. Ps. 1, 5, 159: epistulae illae mihi concenturiant metum In corde,id. Trin. 4, 2, 160 Brix ad loc.

concentus.definition: concino Sounds blending harmoniously together, symphony, harmony, harmonious music (class.). Prop. Trop., concord, agreement, harmony, unanimity (also class.): quā ex conjunctione naturae et quasi concentu atque consensu, quam συμπάθειαν Graeci vocant, etc., Cic. Div. 2, 14, 34; cf. actionum,id. Off. 1, 40, 145; and: omnium doctrinarum,id. de Or. 3, 6, 21: virtutis,Tac. G. 3: omnium laudum,Plin. Pan. 4, 6: nunc age, quid nostrum concentnm divida...

conceptaculum.definition: concipio That which receives something, a receptacle (post-Aug. and rare). Prop., Plin. 2, 45, 44, § 115: sanguinis,Gell. 18, 10, 9; Front. Aquaed. 22 al.—* Trop.: superbia aliubi conceptaculum, sed hic (sc. in superciliis) sedem habet,Plin. 11, 37, 51, § 138.

conceptionalis.definition: conceptĭōnālis, e, conceptio Pertaining to conception: fatum,Fulg. Myth. 2, 8; sol, Firm. Math. 7, 1.

conceptivus.definition: conceptīvus, a, um, concipio. * That is conceived: fides et dilectio non substantiva animae sed conceptiva,Tert. Res Carn. 40. That is ordered, directed; so only feriae, in the Roman ritual, those festivals that were not fixed for a certain day, but were celebrated annually on days appointed by the priests or magistrates, movable festivals. Such were the Compitalia, Paganalia, Sementivae, Latinae, etc., Varr. L. L. 6, § 26; Macr. S. 1, 16; cf. Pa...

conceptiuus.definition: conceptīvus, a, um, concipio. * That is conceived: fides et dilectio non substantiva animae sed conceptiva,Tert. Res Carn. 40. That is ordered, directed; so only feriae, in the Roman ritual, those festivals that were not fixed for a certain day, but were celebrated annually on days appointed by the priests or magistrates, movable festivals. Such were the Compitalia, Paganalia, Sementivae, Latinae, etc., Varr. L. L. 6, § 26; Macr. S. 1, 16; cf. Pa...

concepto.definition: concepto, āre, id. (late Lat.). To conceive, become pregnant, Arn. 4, p. 141. To conceive in mind: majora,Amm. 31, 10, 5.

conceptum.definition: v. concipio, I. B. Fin., and II. B. fin.

conceptus.definition: conceptus, a, um, Part., from concipio.

concerno.definition: con-cerno, ĕre V. a., to mix, mingle together (as in a sieve, in order to separate by sifting): carni,Aug. Conf. 5, 10 fin.

concerpo.definition: con-cerpo, psi, ptum, 3, carpo To pluck, pull, or tear in pieces, to rend (rare). Prop.: epistulas,Cic. Att. 10, 12, 3: librum,Liv. 38, 55, 11; cf. Gell. 4, 18, 12; cf. litteras,Suet. Ner. 47: folia coronae concerpta,Plin. 21, 3, 9, § 13: linteolum,lint,id. 28, 15, 61, § 216; 31, 9, 45, § 100.— * Trop. (acc. to carpo, II. B. b. α), to abuse, revile, censure: Curionem ferventissime, Cael. ap. Cic. Fam. 8, 6, 5.

concertatio.definition: concerto A strife of words, a disputation, dispute, controversy (several times in Cic.; elsewhere rare): contentiones concertationesque in disputando pertinaces,Cic. Fin. 1, 8, 27; cf.: concertationum plenae disputationes,id. de Or. 1, 43, 194: concertationis studium,id. Div. 1, 30, 62: imitatur disputandi prudentiam concertatio captatioque verborum, a love of disputation (the ἐριστική of the sophists), id. Part. Or. 23, 81: jejuna verborum,id....

concerto.definition: con-certo, āvi, ātum, 1 V. a., to contend with any one zealously or warmly (rare but class.; cf. aemulor). In gen.: te audio nescio quid concertasse cum ero,Ter. Ad. 2, 2, 3: pro explorato habebat, Ambiorigem proelio non esse concertaturum, * Caes. B. G. 6, 5: de regno,Suet. Aug. 21: aves nandi velocitate concertant,Col. 8, 15, 4.—Poet., with dat.: triclinia templis concertant,Manil. 5, 507. Esp., to dispute, debate (only so in Cic.): (Pompeius) ...

concertor.definition: concertor, āri, 1 V. dep.; collat. form of concerto, q. v. (late Lat.), Vulg. Sap. 15, 9; id. Ecclus. 38, 29.

concessio.definition: concedo, I. B. 3. An allowing, granting, conceding, permission, leave (rare, but in good prose). In gen.: agrorum,Cic. Agr. 3, 3, 11; Tac. A. 3, 73: praemiorum, Planc. ap. Cic. Fam. 10, 8, 3: concessio, ut peculiare aliquid in fundo pascere liceat,Varr. R. R. 1, 17, 7: vestra,Cic. Att. 3, 24, 1: competitorum,id. Tog. Cand. Fragm. 5 (8, 5, p. 21 B. and K.). Esp., in rhet., a figure of speech, concession: cum aliquid etiam iniquum videmur causae fi...

concessivus.definition: concessīvus, a, um, concedo Pertaining to concession, concessive (late Lat.), Serv. ad Verg. A. 10, 33; Diom. p. 390 P.

concessiuus.definition: concessīvus, a, um, concedo Pertaining to concession, concessive (late Lat.), Serv. ad Verg. A. 10, 33; Diom. p. 390 P.

concesso.definition: con-cesso, āvi, 1 V. a., to cease, leave off, desist (ante- and post-class., and very rare): lavari aut fricari,Plaut. Poen. 1, 2, 9: quid ego hic properans concesso pedibus, linguā largior?id. As. 2, 2, 24; Front. Ep. ad M. Antonin. Aug. 1, 2.—Of things as subjects: concessavit praeceptum,Tert. Fug. Pers. 6.

concessus.definition: concessus, a, um, Part., from concedo.

concha.definition: . A bivālve shell-fish, mussel, Plaut. Rud. 2, 1, 8; 2, 1, 15; Lucr. 2, 374; Verg. G. 2, 348; Plin. 9, 33, 52, § 102: legere,Cic. de Or. 2, 6, 22; Suet. Calig. 46: cavae,Ov. M. 4, 725: marinae,id. ib. 15, 264: viles,Hor. S. 2, 4, 28: unionum,Suet. Ner. 31. A mussel-shell, Lucr. 4, 937; Cic. N. D. 2, 48, 123: ostrea in conchis suis,Ov. F. 6, 174.—Hence

conchicla.definition: dim.contr. from conchicula, from conchis The boiled bean, Apic. 5, 4; cf. Petr. 66, 7.—Hence, , , adj., prepared with beans: pullus,Apic. 5, 4.

conchis.definition: A kind of bean boiled with the pods, Mart. 13, 7; Juv. 3, 293; 14, 131; cf. Apic. 5, 4.

conchula.definition: dim.concha A small shell-fish (very rare), Cels. 2, 29; Val. Max. 8, 8, 1 al.

conchyliarius.definition: conchylium A purple dyer, Inscr. Donat. 315, 8.

conchyliatus.definition: conchȳlĭātus, a, um, id.. Of a purple color: peristromata,Cic. Phil. 2, 27, 67: vestis,Plin. 9, 39, 64, § 138; Suet. Caes. 43: lana,Petr. 54, 4; Marc. Emp. 9. Clothed in purple: relictis conchyliatis cum illo seminudo loquor,Sen. Ep. 62, 3.

conchylilegulus.definition: id. A collector of shell-fish, Cod. Th. 11, 7, 15; 13, 1, 9.

conchylium.definition: κογχύλιον. A shell-fish, a testaceous animal, in gen., Plin. 9, 29, 46, § 86; Cic. Div. 2, 14, 33. Specif.

concido.definition: con-cĭdo, cĭdi, 3, cado To fall together, to fall down, to tumble to the ground (class. in prose and poetry). In gen., of buildings: conclave illud concidit,Cic. de Or. 2, 86, 353: navis veluti terrestre machinamentum,Tac. A. 14, 6: turris terrae motu,Suet. Tib. 74; cf.: urbs acerbissimo concidat incendio conflagrata,Auct. Her. 4, 8, 12.—Of other objects: omne caelum,Cic. Rep. 6, 25, 27: ipse et equus ejus ante signum Jovis concidit,id. Div. 1, 3...

conciliabulum.definition: concilium A place of assembly, a public place, esp. for public intercourse or traffic; a marketplace, an exchange, a place for courts, etc.: conciliabulum dicitur locus, ubi in conciliam convenitur, Paul. ex Fest. p. 38, 3 Müll.; so Liv. 7, 15, 13; 25, 5, 6; 34, 1, 6, and 34, 56, 2; 39, 14, 7; 40, 37, 3; 43, 14, 10; Tac. A. 3, 40: martyrum,where their memory is solemnly celebrated,Hier. Ep. 60, 12: spectaculorum, places for public exhibitions, as...

conciliatio.definition: concilio (in Cic. and Quint.). A connection, union. An acquiring, procuring: pecuniam dedit ad conciliationem gratiae,Cic. Clu. 31, 84; cf.: omnis conventio conciliatio nominatur, Don. ad Ter. Eun. 4, 4, 2.

conciliator.definition: id.. He who provides, prepares, or causes a thing; an author, founder, promoter, etc. (in good prose, but not in Cic.; cf. however: conciliatrix and conciliatricula): suillae carnis,who prepares it savorily, makes it palatable,Varr. R. R. 2, 4, 8: nuptiarum,Nep. Att. 12, 2: proditionis,Liv. 27, 15, 17: adfinitatis atque amicitiae,Suet. Aug. 48; cf. Tac. A. 1, 58: piscis conciliator capturae (piscium), by which other fishes are caught, a decoy, Pl...

conciliatrix.definition: conciliator. In gen., that which occasions, produces, procures: (omitto) orationis vim, quae conciliatrix est humanae maxime societatis,Cic. Leg. 1, 9, 27: conciliatrix amicitiae virtutis opinio,id. Lael. 11, 37. In partic., she who unites or conciliates, in a good and bad sense; a match-maker, a procuress, a bawd: conciliatrix dicitur, quae viris conciliat uxores et uxoribus viros, Paul. ex Fest. p. 62, 13 Müll.—In a bad sense in Lucil. ap. Non....

conciliciatus.definition: con-cĭlĭcĭātus, a, um, Cilicium Clothed in a garment of hair (of a penitent), Tert. Pud. 13.

concilio.definition: concĭlĭo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.concilium. To bring together several objects into one whole, to unite, connect (class. in prose and poetry, not in Hor.). With acc. and dat. (aliquid alicui) or absol., to procure, provide, prepare, produce something for one.

concilium.definition: con- and root cal- of calo; Gr. καλέω; cf. clamo A collection of people, an association, gathering, union, meeting, assembly, = coetus (class.). In gen.: videre ambas in uno concilio,Plaut. Mil. 2, 2, 96; id. Clst. 4, 2, 33: Camenarum cum Egeria,Liv. 1, 21, 3: ab sede piorum, coetu concilioque abigi,id. 2, 38, 4: pastorum,Cic. Off. 3, 9, 38: deorum,id. Tusc. 1, 30, 72; id. Div. 1, 24, 49; cf. caelestium,id. Off. 3, 5, 25: divinum animorum,id. Se...

concinentia.definition: concino (postclass. for concentus) Musical harmony, concord, Macr. Somn. Scip. 2, 2 fin.; 2, 3. Trop., in archit., symmetry: architectonica,Sid. Ep. 8, 4; Claud. Mam. Stat. Anim. 21.

concineratus.definition: con-cĭnĕrātus, a, um, cinis Sprinkled with ashes, Tert. Pud. 13.

concingo.definition: con-cingo, ĕre V. a., to gird, surround completely, Theod. Prisc. 4, 1.

concinnatio.definition: id. (post-class.). In economics, an adjusting, preparing: aquae marinae, Auct. Lemmat. ap. Cato, R. R. 106. Transf., a making, composing: epistulae,Aus. Ep. 17; cf. id. ib. 7 and 15: metrorum, Mar. Vict. p. 2547 P.

concinnator.definition: id. (post-Aug.). An arranger, disposer: capitum et capillorum,a hair-dresser,Col. 1, prooem. § 5. A maker, contriver, author, inventor: causarum,an advocate,Dig. 1, 16, 9: concinnatores atque inventores tantarum deformitatum (poetae),Arn. 4, 149: criminum,Sid. Ep. 3, 13.

concinnitas.definition: concinnus A neat, elegant, or skilful joining of several things (in good prose, but rare). In gen.: concinnitates colorum,Gell. 2, 26, 4: non est ornamentum virile concinnitas,a too carefully arranged dress,Sen. Ep. 115, 3: vitare concinnitatem,Suet. Aug. 86. Esp., in rhet., beauty of style, produced by a skilful connection of words and clauses, Cic. Or. 44, 149; 49, 164 sq.; id. Brut. 83, 287; 95, 325 (not in Quint.).

concinno.definition: concinno, āvi, ātum, v. a.id. To join fitly together, to order, arrange appropriately, to set right, adjust: concinnare est apte componere, Paul. ex Fest. p. 38, 1 Müll. (cf. compono, II. B.; mostly anteclass. and post-Aug.; most. freq. in Plaut.; not in Ter., Cic., or Quint.; in Cic. Oecon. Fragm. 7, p. 474 Orell., the words prob. belong to Col.; v. Col. 12, 2, 6). Prop.: vinum,Cato, R. R. 114; 115: et commodare trapetum,id. ib. 135 fin.: pallam...

concinnus.definition: con-cinnus, a, um, adj.etym. dub.; acc. to Non. p. 43, 21, and p. 59, 30, from cinnus Fitly, skilfully put together or joined, well adjusted, beautiful (class.; esp. freq. in Cic. of discourse). Object. Subject. ( = commodus, II.): concinnus alicui, suited to, fit, appropriate for; of persons, suiting one's self to, courteous, pleasing, etc. (rare): viris Venus ut concinnior esset, * Lucr. 4, 1276: concinnus amicis,Hor. S. 1, 3, 50.—*

concino.definition: con-cĭno, cĭnŭi, no Sup., 3, and a. [cano]. Neutr., to sing, play, or sound together, in concert or harmoniously (class.). Act., to cause to sound together, in concert or harmoniously, to make concordant sounds, to sound, sing of, celebrate in song, magnify, etc.

concipilo.definition: concĭpĭlo, āvi, 1, concipio To seize, take, catch (only in the foll. exs.): concipilavisti dictum a Naevio pro corripuisti et involasti, Paul. ex Fest. p. 62, 6: quem ego offatim jam jam concipilabo,Plaut. Truc. 2, 7, 61.

concipio.definition: con-cĭpĭo, cēpi, ceptum, 3, capio To take or lay hold of, to take to one's self, to take in, take, receive, etc. (class. in prose and poetry). Prop. Trop.

concise.definition: concīsē, , v. 2. concido P. a. fin.

concisor.definition: id. One who cuts down or fells: nemorum, Coripp. 4, 22.

concisorius.definition: concīsōrĭus, a, um, id. Suitable for cutting: ferramentum,Veg. Art. Vet. 1, 56, 31.

concisura.definition: id.. * A dividing, distributing: aquaram,Sen. Ep. 100, 6.—* A hollow, chink, cleft, Plin. 34, 8, 19, § 63.

concisus.definition: concīsus, a, um, v. 2. concido P. a.

concitate.definition: concĭtātē, , v. concito P. a. fin.

concitatio.definition: concito, lit. A hastening, quick movement: remorum,Liv. 44, 28, 10. Trop.

concitator.definition: id. One who excites or rouses, a mover, exciter (rare): belli,Hirt. B. G. 8, 38; Tac. H. 3, 2: turbae ac tumultūs,Liv. 25, 4, 10: concitator et instimulator seditionis,Cic. Dom. 5, 11: tabernariorum,id. ib. § 13; absol.: multitudo concitata ipsum concitatorem antecessit,Sen. Ira, 3, 2, 4.

concitatrix.definition: concĭtātrix, īcis, f.concitator That which excites or stirs up (very rare): Veneris (eruca),Plin. 19, 8, 44, § 154; and : concitatricem vim habet satyrion,id. 26, 10, 62, § 96.

concitatus.definition: concĭtātus, a, um, Part. and , from concito.

concito.definition: concĭto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. freq. a.concieo To move violently, to put in violent or quick motion, to stir up, rouse up, excite, incite, shake. Prop. (thus most freq. in the poets and histt.): artus,Lucr. 3, 292; 3, 301: equum calcaribus,Liv. 2, 6, 8; cf.: equum in aliquem,Nep. Pelop. 5, 4: concitant equos permittuntque in hostem,Liv. 3, 61, 8: equos adversos,id. 8, 7, 9; cf. also under P. a.: naves quantā maximā celeritate poterat,id. 36, 44, 4; cf...

concitor.definition: concieo He who rouses or excites, an exciter (rare; not in Cic.; in MSS. freq. interchanged with concitator): belli,Liv. 23, 41, 1; 29, 3, 3; 37, 45, 17; Tac. A. 4, 28; id. H. 1, 68; 4, 56; Just. 2, 9, 21: vulgi,Liv. 45, 10 10.

concitus.definition: concĭtus and concītus, a, um, v. concieo.

concivis.definition: A fellow-citizen, transl. of συμπολίτης (late Lat.), Tert. adv. Marc. 5, 17; id. Res Carn. 41.

conciuis.definition: A fellow-citizen, transl. of συμπολίτης (late Lat.), Tert. adv. Marc. 5, 17; id. Res Carn. 41.

conclamans.definition: conclāmans, ntis P. and of conclamo.

conclamatio.definition: conclamo A loud shouting or calling of many persons together, a shout (rare; not in Cic.): universi exercitūs,Caes. B. C. 2, 26: tot milium sub gladio gementium,Sen. Clem. 1, 12, 2; in plur., Tac. A. 3, 2; id. H. 4, 1.

conclamatus.definition: conclāmātus, a, um, Part. and , from conclamo.

conclamo.definition: con-clāmo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. n. and A., to cry or call out together. (Con subject.) To call or cry out together or in a body (hence often joined with omnes, universi, pariter, omnes pariter, Liv. 34, 61, 8; Curt. 5, 13, 5; 8, 11, 22; 10, 17, 3), to shout, esp. in approbation or assent (class. in prose and poetry). To call together, to call to one's help (very rare): socios,Ov. M. 13, 73: duros agrestes,Verg. A. 7, 504.

conclave.definition: ( Gen. plur. heterocl. conclaviorum, Vitr. 6, 3, 8: conclavium,id. 7, 9), n. clavis: conclavia dicuntur loca, quae unā clave clauduntur, Paul. ex Fest. p. 39, 9 Müll.; cf. Don. ad Ter. Eun. 3, 5, 35, a room, chamber, dining hall, cage for animals, stall, coop, etc., that may be locked up.

conclaue.definition: ( Gen. plur. heterocl. conclaviorum, Vitr. 6, 3, 8: conclavium,id. 7, 9), n. clavis: conclavia dicuntur loca, quae unā clave clauduntur, Paul. ex Fest. p. 39, 9 Müll.; cf. Don. ad Ter. Eun. 3, 5, 35, a room, chamber, dining hall, cage for animals, stall, coop, etc., that may be locked up.

conclavo.definition: conclāvo To nail together, συνηλῶ, Gloss. Gr. Lat.

conclauo.definition: conclāvo To nail together, συνηλῶ, Gloss. Gr. Lat.

conclericus.definition: A fellow-clergyman, Jul. Epit. Nov. c. 115, § 475.

concludo.definition: con-clūdo, si, sum, 3 ( Part. perf. solecist. conclausa semina, Col. 3, 12, 2), v. a., to shut up closely, to close up, enclose, confine. Prop. (class. in prose and poetry), constr. with in and acc., with and absol. (not with in and abl., for the true read., Cic. Univ. 3 fin., is inclusit): in vincla bestiam nequissimam,Plaut. Rud. 3, 1, 18; cf.: bestias delectationis causā,Cic. Fin. 5, 20, 56 Madv.: eos concludit, magnam hominum multitudinem,Cic...

conclusio.definition: concludo. A shutting up, closing (rare, not in Cic.). (Acc. to concludo, II. B. and D.; freq. in Cic. and Quint.) A conclusion, end: in extremā parte et conclusione muneris ac negotii,Cic. Q. Fr. 1, 1, 16, § 46.

conclusive.definition: conclūsīvē, concludo, II. D. In form of a conclusion, conclusively, Cassiod. Inst. Div. Litt. 1 med.

conclusiue.definition: conclūsīvē, concludo, II. D. In form of a conclusion, conclusively, Cassiod. Inst. Div. Litt. 1 med.

conclusus.definition: conclūsus, a, um, Part., from concludo.

concolona.definition: colonus She who inhabits the same town or house with one, a female fellow-citizen or fellow-inhabitant, Aug. Ep. 169.

concolor.definition: con-cŏlor, cŏlōris Adj. gen. omn. (postclass. access. form of the fem. concolora, Carystos, Mart. Cap. 6, § 659 fin.; cf. id. 1, § 80), of the same color (poet. and in postAug. prose; most freq. in Ov.; perh. first used by him). Like, similar, App. M. 5, p. 166, 10.

concolorans.definition: con-cŏlōrans, antis, color Of the same color, Tert. Pud. 8.

concolorus.definition: concŏlōrus, a, um, v. concolor Init.

concomitor.definition: con-cŏmĭtor, ātus, āri, 1 V. dep., to attend, accompany (late Lat., except in part. perf., v.infra): concomitando tuos, Ven. Carm. 8, 7, 183: Astris Caesario concomitante suo,id. ib. 8, 6, 157.—Part. perf. in pass. sense: * concŏmĭtātus, a, um, accompanied: quibus concomitata,Plaut. Mil. 4, 3, 10 Brix ad loc.

concoquo.definition: con-cŏquo, coxi, coctum, 3 To boil or seethe together (very rare): sal et nitrum sulphuri concoctum in lapidem vertitur,Plin. 31, 10, 46, § 122: odores,Lucr. 2, 853: (spondyli) perturbati concoctique,Sen. Ep. 95, 28: remedia,Macr. S. 7, 16, 23. To digest (class., esp. in prose).

concordabilis.definition: concordābĭlis, e, concordo Easily according, harmonizing, Censor. de Die Nat. 10, 4.

concordatio.definition: id., = concordia Concord, unanimity (late Lat.), Vulg. Ecclus. 22, 27; 27, 23.

concordia.definition: concors An agreeing together, union, harmony, concord (opp. discordia, Sall. J. 10, 6; Sen. Ep. 94, 46; opp. bellum,Lucr. 1, 457; opp. repugnantia,Plin. 29, 4, 17, § 61; freq. and class. in prose and poetry). Of persons: redigere aliquem in antiquam concordiam alicujus,Plaut. Am. 1, 2, 13; cf.: redire in concordiam,id. ib. 3, 3, 7: conjunctio atque concordia,Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 9, § 23: conspiratio atque concordia omnium ordinum ad defendendam liber...

concordialis.definition: concordĭālis, e, concordia Of or pertaining to concord or union (late Lat.): vincla, Firm. Math. 6, 32.

concorditas.definition: concors, = concordia Concord, Pac. ap. Non. 88, 20 (Trag. Rel. v. 188 Rib.).

concordo.definition: concordo, āvi, ātum, 1, and A. [concors]. Neutr., to agree together, to be united, be of one mind, to harmonize (rare but class.). Act., to bring into union: matrimonium bene concordatum dirimere,concordant,Dig. 48, 5, 11, § 11.

concorporalis.definition: Adj., of or belonging to the same body or company (late Lat.): gentes,Vulg. Eph. 3, 6.—Subst.: , m., a comrade, Amm. 21, 12, 15; 28, 5, 7.

concorporatio.definition: concorporo A union, harmony (eccl. Lat.), Tert. adv. Marc. 4, 4; id. Baptism. 8.

concorporificatus.definition: concorpŏrĭfĭcātus, a, um, concorporo-facio United in one body, incorporated, Tert. adv. Val. 23.

concorporo.definition: con-corpŏro, āvi, ātum, 1 V. a., to unite in one body, to incorporate (except in Pliny the elder, only in late Lat.): aliquid cum melle,Plin. 22, 24, 53, § 113: vitiligines,id. 27, 12, 90, § 112: scopuli concorporati,Amm. 22, 8, 15: concorporatus ecclesiae,Tert. Pud. 15: medicamen concorporatum,Marc. Emp. 36.

concors.definition: con-cors (ante-class. concordis, e, Caecil. Stat. ap. Prisc. p. 726 P.; cf. Prisc. p. 764 ib.), cordis (abl. usu. concordi, Cic. Univ. 5 med.; Prop. 4 (5), 5, 6; Ov. M. 1, 25; 5, 664; Sil. 16, 381; Suet. Caes. 19; Sen. Agam. 781 al.: concorde, acc. to Prisc. p. 764 P. Plur. neutr.: concordia,Verg. A. 3, 542; Sil. 13, 650; Pers. 5, 49), cor: aliis cor ipsum animus videtur: ex quo excordes, vecordes concordesque dicuntur, Cic. Tusc. 1, 9, 18, of th...

concrasso.definition: con-crasso, āre V. a., to thicken, make thick: liquida,Cael. Aur. Tard. 4, 3, 62.

concreatus.definition: con-crĕātus, a, um Adj., created together (eccl. Lat.): diabolus sanctis angelis,Claud. Mam. Stat. Anim. 3, 7; cf. Vulg. Eccl. 1, 16.

concredo.definition: con-crēdo, dĭdi, dĭtum, 3, (anteclass. form Pres.concrēdŭo, Plaut. Aul. 3, 6, 49; hence perf. concredui, id. Cas. 2, 8, 43; cf. credo), to intrust, consign, commit to, = commendo (class.; very freq. in Plaut.; in Cic. perh. only twice; never in Quint.).

concrematio.definition: concremo A burning up, conflagration, Fulg. Myth. 1, 15.

concremo.definition: con-crĕmo, āvi, ātum, 1 V. a., to burn up, consume (perh. not before the Aug. per.): vivos igni,Liv. 3, 53, 5; cf. id. 9, 12, 8: hostilia arma subdito igne,id. 8, 30, 8: urbem igni,id. 6, 33, 4: omnia tecta,id. 5, 42, 2: domos,id. 21, 14, 4: duas naves fulminis ictu,id. 41, 9, 5: commentarios,Suet. Calig. 15: epistulas,id. Oth. 10: quantum cinnamomi,Plin. 12, 18, 41, § 83: urbes,Sen. Ep. 9, 19: funebres rogos,Sen. Hippol. 1216.

concrepo.definition: con-crĕpo, pŭi, pĭtum, 1, and A. Neutr., to rattle, creak, grate, sound, resound, clash, make a noise, etc. (class.): foris concrepuit hinc a vicino sene,Plaut. Mil. 2, 1, 76: foris,id. Bacch. 2, 2, 56; 4, 2, 28: ostium,id. Men. 2, 2, 73; 3, 2, 57; * Ter. And. 4, 1, 58: scabilla concrepant, aulaeum tollitur, Cic. Cael. 27, 65: conclamat omnis multitudo et suo more armis concrepat,Caes. B. G. 7, 21.—Of the din or clashing of weapons (i. e. of the ...

concresco.definition: con-cresco, crēvi, crētum, 3 ( Inf. perf. sync. concresse, Ov. M. 7, 416), v. n., to grow together; hence with the prevailing idea of uniting, and generally of soft or liquid substances which thicken; to harden, condense, curdle, stiffen, congeal, etc. (very freq., and class. in prose and poetry). Prop.: concrescunt semina (opp. extenuantur),Lucr. 4, 1261; 6, 626; cf.: concrescunt subitae currenti in flumine crustae,Verg. G. 3, 360; opp. liquere,...

concretio.definition: concresco. Abstr., compacting, uniting, condensing, congealing (opp. liquor), Cic. Univ. 14 init.: individuorum corporum concretio,id. N. D. 1, 25, 71: prava corporis, Firm. Math. 1, 3: substantiarum,Tert. Anim. 52. Concr., materiality, matter: (deus) mens soluta quaedam et libera segregata ab omni concretione mortali,Cic. Tusc. 1, 27, 66; cf. Lact. 1, 5.

concretus.definition: concrētus, a, um, Part. and , from concresco.

concrispo.definition: con-crispo, no Perf., ātum, 1, (very rare, and only in part. pres. and perf.). To curl, to give a curling, undulatory motion to: concrispati cincinni,Vitr. 4, 1, 7: umores (se) concrispantes,id. 8, 1, 1.—* To brandish, of a weapon: tela,Amm. 16, 12, 36.

concrispus.definition: con-crispus, a, um Adj., curled (late Lat.), Isid. Orig. 19, 22, 20.

concrucifigo.definition: con-crŭcĭfīgo, āre V. a., to crucify together: aliquem alicui,Sid. Ep. 6, 1; Ambros. Sacram. 6, 2, 8.

concrustatus.definition: con-crustātus, a, um Adj., entirely covered with a crust, incrusted (late Lat.), Amm. 17, 7, 11; 30, 6, 5.

concubatio.definition: concubo A lying or reclining upon: dura lecti,Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 37, 193.

concubinalis.definition: concŭbīnālis, e Adj [concubinus], lascivious: illecebrae,Sid. Ep. 9, 6 fin.

concubinatus.definition: id.. Union of a man with an unmarried woman (usu. of a lower social grade than himself), concubinage (opp. matrimonium on the one hand, and adulterium or stuprum on the other; not in Cic.): emere aliquam in concubinatum sibi,Plaut. Poen. prol. 102: in concubinatum alicui dare (opp. in matrimonium),id. Trin. 3, 2, 64; cf. Dig. 25, 7, 1; 48, 5, 13.—* Adulterous intercourse: nuptarum,i.e. with the betrothed,Suet. Ner. 28.

concubinus.definition: m., and , , f.concubo One who lives in concubinage (cf. concubinatus), a concubine (male or female), a less reproachful designation than paelex (cf. Dig. 5, 16, 144).

concubitus.definition: id.. A lying together; in gen. (very rare), for sleeping. Varr. L. L. 7, § 78 Müll.; at dinner,reclining,Prop. 4 (5), 8, 36.(cf. concubo, I.): dentium,a firm, close shutting together of the teeth,Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 10; 3, 6.—Far more freq. Copulation, coition (in sing. and plur.): ficti (deorum) cum humano genere concubitus, Cic. N. D. 1, 16, 42; so Liv. 4, 2, 6; Ov. M. 4, 207; 6, 541 al.; * Hor. A. P. 398; Suet. Aug. 94; id. Tib. 44: concubitus...

concubius.definition: concŭbĭus, a, um, adj.concubo Of or belonging to lying in sleep, or to the time of sleep. As adj. only in the connection concubiā nocte (rarely: nocte concubiā, nocte in concubiā, noctu concubiā; v.the foll.), at the time of the first sleep, in the first sleep, Sisenn. ap. Non. p. 91, 22 (primi somni, Non.); Cic. Div. 1, 27, 57; Liv. 25, 9, 8; Tac. H. 3, 69; Just. 22, 8, 8: nocte concubiā,Tac. A. 1, 39: nocte in concubiā,Plin. 29, 6, 34, § 110: n...

conculcatio.definition: conculco A treading under foot, stamping upon, Plin. 8, 18, 26, § 68: fructuum in areā,Dig. 3, 34, 14, § 1.

conculco.definition: con-culco, āvi, ātum, 1, calco To tread under foot, to crush or bruise by treading. * Prop.: vinaceos in dolia picata,Cato, R. R. 25.—More freq. Trop. (cf. calco, I. B.).

concumbo.definition: con-cumbo, cŭbŭi, cŭbĭtum, 3 Lit., to lie together, lie in numbers (very rare): Evandri profugae concubuere boves,Prop. 4 (5), 1, 4. To lie with (for sexual intercourse).

concumulatus.definition: con-cŭmŭlātus, a, um, Part. [cumulo] Heaped up, accumulated: cena in verticem,Tert. Virg. Vel. 7 fin.

concupiscentia.definition: concupisco An eager desire, longing, concupiscence (late Lat.), Tert. Res Carn. 45, id. Anim. 16 al.; Hier. Ep. 63, 1; Paul. Nol. Ep. 30, 3.

concupiscentialis.definition: concŭpiscentĭālis, e, adj.concupiscentia Full of desire (late Lat.), Aug. Civ. Dei, 1, 25 fin.—Hence, adv.: concŭpi-scentĭālĭter, lustfully, Aug. Peccat. Mer. 2, 9; 2, 28.

concupiscentivus.definition: concŭpiscentīvus, a, um, concupisco Passionately desiring, transl. of ἐπιθυμητικός, Tert. Anim. 16.

concupiscentiuus.definition: concŭpiscentīvus, a, um, concupisco Passionately desiring, transl. of ἐπιθυμητικός, Tert. Anim. 16.

concupiscibilis.definition: concŭpiscĭbĭlis, e Adj., worthy to be longed for, very desirable (eccl. Lat.), Hier. Quaest. in Paral. 1, 1.

concupiscitivus.definition: concŭpiscĭtīvus, a, um, , = concupiscentivus Passionately desiring, Hier. in Ezech. 1, 1, 7.

concupiscitiuus.definition: concŭpiscĭtīvus, a, um, , = concupiscentivus Passionately desiring, Hier. in Ezech. 1, 1, 7.

concupisco.definition: con-cŭpisco, cŭpīvi or cŭpii, ītum, 3 V. inch. a. [cupio], to long much for a thing, to be very desirous of, to covet, to aspire to, strive after (class. in prose and poetry). Transf., of things (very rare): (faba) aquas in flore maxime concupiscit; cum vero defloruit, exiguas desiderat,Plin. 18, 12, 30, § 120.

concupitor.definition: concupisco One who longs eagerly for or covets something (late Lat.), Firm. Math. 8, 22 fin.

concurro.definition: con-curro, curri, cursum, 3 ( Perf. redupl. concucurrit, Flor. 4, 2, 33 Duker N. cr.: concucurrisse, Cato ap. Prisc. p. 901 P., and Suet. Caes. 15; cf. Liv. 1, 12 Oud., and Ind. Flor. s. h. v. Duker) To run together (of several persons), to come or assemble together in multitudes, to rush or flock together in crowds (very freq., and class.). To run upon one another, to meet or dash together (class.).

concursatio.definition: concurso. A running together, a disorderly meeting: cum multā concursatione (populi),Cic. Brut. 69, 242; Tac. A. 6, 17. A running upon, pushing against one another: concursatio in obscuro incidentium aliorum in alios incertum fecerat, an, etc.,Liv. 41, 2, 6. A running about, going to and fro, etc.: quid ego hujus lacrimas et concursationes proferam?Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 30, § 75 Zumpt ad loc.: et in Albaniā et Seplasiā quae concursatio percunctantium,...

concursator.definition: id. One who runs hither and thither; in milit. lang., a skirmisher (opp. statarius; rare, perh. only in Livy): concursator et vagus pedes,Liv. 31, 35, 6: levis et concursator hostis,id. 27, 18, 14.

concursatorius.definition: concursātōrĭus, a, um, concursator Of or pertaining to skirmishing: pugna,a skirmish,Amm. 16, 9, 1.

concursio.definition: concurro, II. A running or meeting together, a concurrence, concourse (several times in Cic.; elsewhere rare). In gen.: atomorum,Cic. Ac. 1, 2, 6: ut (corpora) concursionibus inter se cohaerescant,id. Fin. 1, 6, 17: stellarum,Gell. 14, 1, 29: crebra vocum,Cic. Or. 44, 151; cf.: crebrae vocalium,Auct. Her. 4, 12, 18: fortuitorum,Cic. Top. 20, 76. Esp., in rhet., a figure of speech, consisting of an emphatic repetition of the last words of a senten...

concurso.definition: con-curso, āre V. freq. n. and a. To come violently together, to rush together, clash: concursare, coire et dissultare vicissim (semina),Lucr. 3, 396.—Far more freq. and class. To go to and fro, run about, rush hither and thither, travel about (cf. commeo).

concursus.definition: concurro. A running or flocking together, a concourse, assembly: fit concursus per vias,Plaut. Ep. 2, 2, 27; cf. in plur.: incredibilem in modum concursus fiunt ex agris,Cic. Att. 5, 16, 3: magni domum concursus ad Afranium fiebant,Caes. B. C. 1, 53: magni concursus sunt facti,Nep. Phoc. 4, 1: concursus fit celeriter in praetorium,Caes. B. C. 1, 76: in forum a totā urbe,Liv. 2, 56, 13; Nep. Dat. 3, 3: ingens,Verg. A. 9, 454: undique concursus, * ...

concussibilis.definition: concussĭbĭlis, e, concutio That can be shaken, Tert. adv. Marc. 1, 25.

concussio.definition: id. (post-Aug.) A shaking, concussion. In gen.: vasorum,Col. 9, 14 fin.: assidua facium,Plin. Ep. 4, 9, 11: vasta concussio quae duas suppressit urbes,an earthquake,Sen. Q. N. 6, 25, 4. In jurid. Lat., an extortion of money by means of threats, Dig. 47, 13: de concussione, several times; also Tert. ad Scap. 4 sq.

concussor.definition: id. One who extorts money by threats (late Lat.), Tert. Fuga in Persec. 12 sq.

concussura.definition: id., = concussio, II. The extorting of money by threats (late Lat.), Tert. ad Scap. 13.

concussus.definition: concussus, a, um, Part. and , from concutio.

concustodio.definition: con-custōdĭo, īre V. a., to guard, watch carefully: NATOS,Inscr. Orell. 2486.

concutio.definition: con-cŭtĭo, cussi, cussum, 3, quatio, as cur = quāre. To strike one upon another, to strike together (rare): utrum cavae manus concutiantur, an planae, Sen. Q. N. 2, 28, 1: concussā manu dare signa,Ov. M. 11, 465: frameas,Tac. G. 11. To shake violently, to shake, agitate (freq. and class. in prose and poetry).

condalium.definition: (access. form more nearly related to the Greek: CONDULUS anulus, Paul. ex Fest. p. 38, 14 Müll.; cf. condylus) [κονδύλιον, κόνδυλος; cf. calix = κύλιξ, etc.] A little ring for slaves, Plaut. Trin. 4, 3, 7; 4, 3, 13.—Also, the title of a comedy not now extant, ascribed by Varr. (L. L. 7, § 77 Müll.) to Plaut., but denied to him by Attius (ap. Gell. 3, 3, 9).

condator.definition: con-dător Joint contributor, συντελεστής, Gloss. Lat. Gr.

condecerno.definition: con-dēcerno, ĕre V. a., to decide, determine together, Cassiod. Hist. Eccl. 2, 12 med.

condecoro.definition: con-dĕcŏro, āvi, ātum, 1 V. a., to ornament, decorate, adorn excessively or carefully (rare): ova parire solet genus pinnis condecoratum, Enn. ap. Varr. L. L. 5, § 59 Müll. (Ann. v. 10 Vahl.): ludos scenicos, * Ter. Hec. alt. prol. 37: loca picturis, Poët. ap. Plin. 35, 10, 37, § 115: actiones, amici. tias, domos,Sen. Ep. 66, 8; Vitr. 1, 1, 11; Cod. Th. 10, 22, 1 al.

condemnabilis.definition: condemnābĭlis, e, condemno Worthy of condemnation, Pall. Insit. 11.

condemnatio.definition: id. A condemning, condemnation (post-Aug.): pecuniaria,Dig. 2, 10, 5: condemnationem facere,to condemn,ib. 42, 1, 59; or,to bring about the condemnation of one,Cod. Just. 8, 14, 8: pati,to be condemned,Dig. 4, 2, 14: post condemnationem, Gai Inst. 3, 180; opp. absolutio,Ascon. ad Cic. Div. in Caecil. 7, 24.

condemno.definition: con-demno, āvi, ātum, 1, damno. To sentence, condemn, convict (in good prose; rare in the poets). To urge the condemnation of a person, to effect it, to prosecute (rare): ego hoc uno crimine illum condemnem necesse est,Cic. Div. in Caecil. 10, 30; Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 69, § 177; id. Rosc. Com. 9, 25 al.: tanto apud judicem hunc argenti condemnabo facilius,Plaut. Most. 5, 1, 50: Fannium Caepionem ... reum majestatis apud judices fecit et condemnavit,S...

condensatio.definition: condenso A condensing, condensation, Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 18, 187.

condenso.definition: condenso, āre (access form *con-densĕo, ēre: Quia se condenseat aër,Lucr. 1, 392; cf. denseo = denso), condensus, to make very dense, to condense, to press close together (rare; not in Cic.): oves se congregant ac condensant in locum unum,Varr. R. R. 2, 3, 9: aciem, Auct. B. Afr. 13; Col. 2, 18, 6: condensari,id. 7, 8, 4: humus condensata subsidit,id. 4, 1, 7; 4, 17, 8.

condensus.definition: con-densus, a, um Adj., very dense, close, thick (mostly poet.; most freq. in Lucr.; not in Cic.): condensa contextaque magis (corpora),Lucr. 4, 57: condensa atque arta nubila,id. 6, 466; cf. id. 6, 102: conciliatu,id. 1, 575; 2, 100: agmine,id. 1, 606: acies,Liv. 26, 5, 13: puppes litore,Verg. A. 8, 497: columbae,id. ib. 2, 516: arbor,Plin. 10, 73, 94, § 202; cf.: vallis arboribus,thickly covered,Liv. 25, 39, 1: condensi ruunt,Sil. 14, 639: arma...

condescendo.definition: con-dēscendo, ĕre, no Perf., 3, v. n., to stoop, let one's self down, to condescend (eccl. Lat.): alicui,Cassiod. Var. 11, 16; id. Amic. 8, 4: ad alicujus inscitiam,Ambros. Cant. Cantic. 6, 9.

condescensio.definition: Condescension (late Lat.): seu demissio Jesu Christi,Cod. Just. 6, c. de S. Trinit.

condicio.definition: condĭcĭo (in many MSS. and edd. incorrectly condĭtĭo, and hence falsely derived from condo; cf. 2. conditio), ōnis, f. condico An agreement, stipulation, condition, compact, proposition, terms, demand. Prop. In gen., the external position, situation, condition, rank, place, circumstances (very freq. and class.).

condicionabilis.definition: condĭcĭōnābĭlis, e, condicio Conditional: persecutio,Tert. adv. Gnost. 9.

condicionalis.definition: condĭcĭōnālis (condit-), e, id. With a condition attached, conditional, with conditions (freq. in the jurists): datio,Dig. 34, 4, 9: creditores,ib. 50, 16, 54: servi,Cod. Just. 10, 1, 7 et saep.: criminatio,Tert. adv. Jud. 13 fin.—condĭcĭōnālĭter, adv., conditionally (opp. pure, simpliciter): conceptā causā,Dig. 25, 1, 17; cf. ib. 46, 3, 98, § 5 al.

condico.definition: con-dīco, xi, ctum, 3 To talk a thing over together, to agree upon, to concert, to promise (most freq. as publicists' t. t.): condixit pater patratus populi Romani Quiritium patri patrato priscorum Latinorum, etc., old form ap. Liv. 1, 32, 11: status condictusve dies cum hoste, Cincius ap. Gell. 16, 4, 4; Plaut. Curc. 1, 1, 5; cf.: quoniam pactum atque condictum cum rege populi Romani perfide ruperat,Gell. 20, 1, 54: sic constituunt, sic condicun...

condicticius.definition: condictīcĭus- or tĭus, a, um, condictio Of or pertaining to a demand of restitution: actio,Dig. 12, 1, 24; 12, 2, 13, § 2 al.

condictio.definition: condico. In the lang. of religion, the proclamation of a festival, acc. to Serv. ad Verg. A. 3, 117 (without voucher); cf.: condictio, in diem certum ejus rei quae agitur denuntiatio, Paul. ex Fest. p. 66 Müll. In jurid. Lat., a formal claim of restitution, Gai Inst. 4, 18 sq.; Dig. 12, 6, 30 al.

condignus.definition: con-dignus, a, um Adj., wholly deserving, very worthy (very rare; mostly anteand post-class.).

condimentarius.definition: condīmentārĭus, a, um, condimentum Of or pertaining to spices or seasoning: caepae,Plin. 19, 6, 32, § 105: genus,id. 19, 8, 50, § 165. Subst.: condī-mentārĭus, ii, m., one who prepares or sells spices; trop.: omnium haereticorum (Platonem),Tert. Anim. 23.

condimentum.definition: condio (rare; Most freq. in Plaut. and Cic.),spice, seasoning,Plaut. Cas. 2, 3, 3 sq.; id. Ps. 3, 2, 31 sq.: cibi,Cic. Fin. 2, 28, 90: arida,Col. 12, 51, 2: viridia,green herbs used in seasoning,id. 12, 8, 1. Trop.: condimentum postremum Fabulae plausus,Plaut. Poen. 5, 6, 33: optumum aerumnae est animus aequus,id. Rud. 2, 3, 71 (but the verse Plaut. Trin. 2, 2, 87, is prob. spurious; cf. Ritschl N. cr.): amicitiae suavitas quaedam sermonum atque ...

condio.definition: condĭo, īvi or ĭi, ītum, 4, v. a.an access. form from condo, q. v. II., and cf. compono, II. B. 2. (orig. belonging to econ. lang.). To put fruit in vinegar, wine, spices, etc., to preserve, pickle: oleas albas,Cato, R. R. 117: lactucam (corresp. with componere),Col. 12, 9, 3; 12, 7, 5: corna, pruna,id. 12, 10, 2: caules vitium in aceto et muriā,Plin. 14, 19, 23, § 119 al. Of food, to make savory, to season, spice: cenam,Plaut. Ps. 3, 2, 21: meas...

condiscipula.definition: condiscipulus A female school-fellow, Mart. 10, 35, 15; App. M. 9, p. 224 al.

condiscipulatus.definition: id. Companionship in school (very rare), Nep. Att. 5, 3; and Just. 12, 6, 17 fin.; Inscr. Orell. 7392.

condiscipulus.definition: A school-mate, companion at school, Cic. Tusc. 1, 18, 41; id. Att. 5, 19, 3; Nep. Att. 1, 3; Sen. Ep. 66; Quint. 1, 2, 26; 2, 2, 12; Suet. Ner. 22; id. Vit. 14; Plin. Ep. 1, 19, 1.

condisco.definition: con-disco, dĭdĭci, 3, * To learn with or in company with one: ex his, qui mihi Athenis condidicere,App. Flor. 3, n. 18, p. 362, 8. To learn carefully, eagerly, or well, to learn thoroughly (rare but class. in prose and poetry).

conditicius.definition: condĭtĭcĭus or -tĭus, a, um, condo Laid up, preserved: cibaria,Col. 8, 8, 2 (Schneid. conditiva).

conditivus.definition: condĭtīvus, a, um, condo Suitable for laying up or preserving, laid up, preserved (rare; not in Cic.): olea,Cato, R. R. 6, 1; Macr. S. 2, 16: mala,Cato, R. R. 7, 3; Varr. R. R. 1, 59, 1: cibi,Col. 7, 9, 9; cf. also conditicius.—Subst.: condĭtīvum, i, n., a tomb, Sen. Ep. 60, 4; 82, 2; Inscr. Orell. 4511.

conditiuus.definition: condĭtīvus, a, um, condo Suitable for laying up or preserving, laid up, preserved (rare; not in Cic.): olea,Cato, R. R. 6, 1; Macr. S. 2, 16: mala,Cato, R. R. 7, 3; Varr. R. R. 1, 59, 1: cibi,Col. 7, 9, 9; cf. also conditicius.—Subst.: condĭtīvum, i, n., a tomb, Sen. Ep. 60, 4; 82, 2; Inscr. Orell. 4511.

conditor.definition: id. A maker, builder, framer, establisher, founder, author, compiler, etc. Prop. (class.; most freq. in the poets and prose writers after the Aug. per.). Nom. propr., a rural deity who presided over the laying up of fruits, acc. to Serv. ad Verg. G. 1, 21.

conditorium.definition: condo A place where any thing is laid up, a repository (post-Aug.). In gen.: tormentorum muralium,Amm. 18, 9, 1. Specif.

conditrix.definition: 1. conditor. She who lays to rest (late Lat.): luna mortalium corporum et auctor et conditrix, Macr. Somn. Scip. 1, 11. A female builder, founder, etc. (post-class.): Romae, Poët. ap. Philarg. Verg. E. 1, 20; Tert. Spect. 7: Karthaginis,id. Apol. 50: Athenarum, Eum. Pan. pro Instaur. Schol. 9, 4. Trop., of things: paupertas omnium civitatum,App. Mag. 18, p. 285: praestantissima potentia caeli ac terrae conditrix,Lact. 1, 5, 6.

conditura.definition: condo A preparing, making: vitreorum (vasorum),Petr. 51, 5; cf. Isid. Orig. 16, 16, 6.

conditus.definition: condĭtus, a, um, Part., from condo.

condo.definition: con-do, dĭdi, dĭtum, 3, v. a.con- = cum, and 2. do, lit. To bring, lay or put together (very freq. in all periods and species of composition). With the access. idea of uniting, to put or join together into a whole, to form, fashion, produce, make by joining together. With the access. idea of carefulness, to put away, to lay, put, or place somewhere for preservation, etc.; to lay up, store or treasure up (opp. promo).

condocefacio.definition: condŏcĕ-făcĭo, fēci, factum, 3, condoceo To train, teach, instruct, discipline (rare): beluas,Cic. N. D. 2, 64, 161; cf. elephantos, Auct. B. Afr. 27: tirones gladiatores,id. 71: animum, ut, etc.,Cic. Tusc. 5, 31, 87.

condoctor.definition: A fellow-teacher (eccl. Lat.), Aug. Conf. 1, 9 fin.

condoctus.definition: condoctus, a, um, Part. and , v. condoceo.

condoleo.definition: con-dŏlĕo, ēre V. n., to feel severe pain, to suffer greatly (eccl. Lat.). Universum corpus, Tert. Poen. 10. To suffer with another, to feel another's pain; with dat.: qui non condolent proximis suis, sed potius eos irrident, Aug. in Job, 19, 13; Vulg. Ecclus. 37, 5; ib. Heb. 5, 2.

condolesco.definition: con-dŏlesco, lŭi, 3 V. inch. n. [doleo], to feel severe pain, to suffer much, to be in pain or distress, to ache. Prop. (rare, but class. in prose and poetry; most freq. in temp. perf.): mihi de vento miserae condoluit caput,Plaut. Truc. 2, 8, 2; so in perf.: latus ei dicenti,Cic. de Or. 3, 2, 6: pes, dens,id. Tusc. 2, 22, 52: homines, quorum alter ne condoluisse quidem umquam videtur,id. ib. 1, 18, 41: tentatum frigore corpus, * Hor. S. 1, 1, 80...

condomo.definition: con-dŏmo, āre V. a., to tame completely, to curb, check; trop., Prud. Cath. 7, 98.

condonatio.definition: condono A giving away: bonorum possessionumque,Cic. Verr. 1, 4, 12.

condono.definition: con-dōno, āvi, ātum, 1 Aliquid (aliquem) alicui, to give something to one, to present, deliver up (in good prose; most freq. in Cic.; not in Quint.). Aliquem aliquid or absol., to present one with something (only in the foll. exs.): si quam (rem) debes, te condono,Plaut. Bacch. 5, 2, 24; so id. Pers. 5, 2, 36: argentum, quod habes, condonamus te,Ter. Phorm. 5, 8, 54: aurum aliquem, Afran. ap. Non. p. 497, 29.—Pass. impers., with acc. of thing: ha...

condormio.definition: con-dormĭo, īre V. n., to fall quite asleep (very rare), * Suet. Aug. 78; Curt. 6, 10, 14 (acc. to Madv. ad Cic. Fin. 5, 4, 11); Hyg. Fab. 125; Capitol. Ver. 4.

condormisco.definition: con-dormisco, dormīvi, 3 V. inch. [dormio], to go entirely to sleep, to fall asleep; only in Plaut. Curc. 2, 3, 81; id. Rud. 2, 7, 13; id. Mil. 3, 2, 13; in perf., id. Most. 2, 2, 55.

conducibilis.definition: condūcĭbĭlis, e, conduco, II. Advantageous, profitable, expedient (several times in Plaut., elsewhere rare): (consilium) ad eam rem,Plaut. Ep. 2, 2, 76: reperiamus aliquid calidi conducibilis consili,id. ib. 2, 2, 71: istuc facinus mihi,id. Bacch. 1, 1, 18; id. Cist. 1, 1, 80: conducibile et utile,id. Trin. 1, 1, 3; cf. id. ib. 1, 1, 14.— *Comp., Auct. Her. 2, 14, 21; Sid. Ep. 6, 1.

conduco.definition: con-dūco, xi, ctum, 3, and n. Act., to draw, bring, or lead together, to assemble, collect (class. in prose and poetry). Neutr., to contribute to something by being useful, to be of use or profitable, to profit, serve, etc. (syn.: convenit, utile est; class.; used only in the 3d pers. of the sing. and plur.); constr. with in, ad aliquid, the dat., or absol.

conducticius.definition: conductīcĭus or -tĭus, a, um, conduco Of or pertaining to hire, hired, rented (rare): fidicina,Plaut. Ep. 2, 3, 8; 5, 2, 41: alia,id. ib. arg. 2: exercitus,Nep. Iphicr. 2, 4; cf. catervae,id. Chabr. 1, 2: domus, Porcius, poët. ap. Suet. Vit. Ter. 1: operae,Varr. R. R. 1, 17, 2.

conductio.definition: id.. A bringing together, uniting. A hiring, farming (rare): (fundi),Cic. Caecin. 32, 94: (vectigalium), Liv. 43, 16, 2: tota renuntiata est,Cic. Verr. 1, 6, 16 Zumpt (B. and K. condicio).

conductor.definition: conduco One who hires a thing, a lessee, farmer, tenant, a contractor (rare, and mostly absol.): (histrionum),Plaut. As. prol. 3: (pecoris),Cato, R. R. 150, 2: (agri),Caes. B. C. 3, 21; Col. 3, 13, 12; cf. Plin. Ep. 7, 30, 3: (aedificii),Cato, R. R. 14, 3: operis,Cic. Q. Fr. 3, 1, 2, § 5: sacrae arae,Val. Max. 8, 12, ext. 1: Dig. 40, 7, 40, § 5; Inscr. Orell. 46; 4324; cf. Gai. Inst. 3, 145.

conductrix.definition: conductor She who hires or rents a thing, Cod. Just. 3, 3, 10; 4, 65, 24; 5, 12, 18.

conductus.definition: Part., and , , , v. conduco, I. B. 2. a. Fin.

condulco.definition: con-dulco, āre V. a., to sweeten, Vulg. Ecclus. 27, 26; 40, 18.

conduplicatio.definition: conduplico A doubling (very rare); humorously, for embracing, * Plaut. Poen. 5, 5, 18 (cf. id. Ps. 5, 1, 16).—As a figure of speech, a repetition of the same word, = ἐπαναδίπλωσις, Auct. Her. 4, 28, 38.

conduplico.definition: con-dūplĭco, āvi, 1 V. a., to double (ante-class.): cibum,Varr. R. R. 2, 4, 15: divitias,Lucr. 3, 71: primordia rerum,id. 1, 712: quod boni promeritus fueris, conduplicaverit, * Ter. Phorm. 3, 2, 31: tenebrae conduplicantur, Pac. ap. Cic. Div. 1, 14, 24 (Trag. v. 412 Rib.).—Humorously: corpora, of a loving embrace (cf. conduplicatio),Plaut. Ps. 5, 1, 16.

condyloma.definition: A swelling in the parts about the anus, Cels. 6, 18, 8; 7, 30, 2; Scrib. Comp. 224 and 225 al.; Plin. 21, 20, 83, § 143 al.

condylus.definition: (‡ , Paul. ex Fest. p. 38, 14 Müll.), , , = . * The knob or knuckle of a joint; esp. plur., the fist: complicatis in condylos digitis,Mart. Cap. 1, § 88.—* (A joint of a reed; hence meton.) A reed, Mart. 5, 78, 30 dub.—* = anulus, Paul. ex Fest. l. l.

conecto.definition: cōnecto (less correctly, connecto, v. Ritschl, Opusc. II. 448 sq.; Gell. 2, 17, 8), nexŭi, nexum, 3, v. a. necto To tie, bind, fasten, or join together, to connect, entwine, link together (class.; most freq. in part. pass. and the trop. signif.); constr. with cum, inter se, the dat., or absol. Lit.: id (palliolum) conexum in umero laevo,folded, gathered,Plaut. Mil. 4, 4, 42: omnia inter se conexa et apta,Cic. N. D. 2, 38, 97: omnia omnimodis,Lucr...

conexio.definition: (), , conecto, t. t. A binding together, close union, etc.: scutorum, armorum (in a testudo),Isid. Orig. 18, 12, 6; Serv. ad Verg. A. 9, 517. Esp. In gram., a syllable, Charis. p. 1 P.

conexus.definition: cōnexus, a, um, Part. and , from conecto.

confabulatio.definition: confabulor A conversation, a discoursing together (eccl. Lat.), Symm. Ep. 9, 84; Tert. ad Uxor. 2, 3 al.
