consonantia.definition: consono An agreement, harmony, consonance (postAug. and rare): vocis,Vitr. 5, 5, 7: vocum proximarum,Gell. 13, 20, 5: scripturarum,Tert. adv. Jud. 11 and 14.

consonatio.definition: id. Resemblance of sound (late Lat.), Cassiod. Anim. 12 med.

consono.definition: con-sŏno, ŭi, 1 V. n., to sound at the same time or together, to sound aloud, to resound (class., but rare till the Aug. period; not in Cic.). Lit. Trop., to agree, accord, harmonize (postAug.): quomodo inter se acutae ac graves voces consonent,Sen. Ep. 88, 9: quomodo animus meus secum consonet, id. ib: sibi in faciendis ac non faciendis,Quint. 2, 20, 5: sibi (tenor vitae),Sen. Ep. 31, 8: Capricorno (Virginis astrum),Manil. 2, 281; 2, 622: hoc et...

consonus.definition: Adj., sounding together in harmony, harmonious (rare, mostly poet.). Lit.: clangor,Ov. M. 13, 610: fila lyrae,id. Am. 1, 8, 60: vox,Sil. 17, 448. Trop., accordant, fit, suitable: fila telae,Claud. Rapt. Pros. 2, 42: credo Platonem vix putasse satis consonum fore, si, etc., * Cic. Att. 4, 16, 3; App. M. 2, p. 114. —With dat.: consona regno juvenem docere,Claud. Laud. Stil. 2, 69.—* Adv.: , harmoniously: clamitare,App. M. 1, p. 106, 34.

consopio.definition: con-sōpĭo, no Perf., ītum, 4, v. a., to bring into an unconscious state, to put fast asleep, lull to sleep, to stupefy (rare but class.). Lit.: somno consopiri sempiterno,Cic. Tusc. 1, 49, 117: Endymion a Lunā consopitus putatur,id. ib. 1, 38, 92; cf. id. Div. 2, 66, 135: inter initia (veneni) consopitus, * Suet. Claud. 44.—Absol.: (exstinctum lumen) consopit, benumbs the senses, * Lucr. 6, 793. Trop., of laws; pass., to become obsolete: cum omni...

consors.definition: Adj. m. and f. Sharing property with one (as brother, sister, relative), living in community of goods, partaking of in common: consortes, ad quos eadem sors,Varr. L. L. 6, § 65 Müll.; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 296, 7 ib.: consortes tres fratres,Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 23, § 57: frater,Plin. Ep. 8, 18, 4: consortem socium fallere,Hor. C. 3, 24, 60.—Hence, subst.: , , m. and f., a sharer, partner: consors censoris,Liv. 41, 27, 2; Vell. 1, 10, 6: de consortibu...

consortio.definition: consors, II. Fellowship, community, partnership, association (rare, but in good prose): omnis humana dissolvetur,Cic. Off. 3, 6, 26: sociabilis inter binos Lacedaemoniorum reges,Liv. 40, 8, 12; cf.: tribuniciae potestatis,Vell. 2, 99, 1; 2, 103, 2; and wholly absol.: quaenam ista societas, quaenam consortio est?Liv. 6, 40, 18 (v. the passage in connection): fati,Val. Max. 4, 6, 3: (animalia terrestria) hominum quādam consortione degentia,Plin. 9,...

consortium.definition: consors (not anteAug.). Community of goods, Suet. Claud. 28: voluntarium inter fratres,Dig. 17, 2, 52, § 8. Fellowship, participation, society, Liv. 4, 5, 5; Quint. 12, 1, 4; Col. 4, 16, 1; Tac. A. 4, 3; Plin. Pan. 7, 3; Flor. 1, 26, 4; Sen. Ep. 90, 3; id. Ben. 6, 13, 1; 7, 12, 2; id. Ep. 48, 2; 73, 7; Dig. 14, 2, 5; Petr. 101, 2; Lact. 4, 27, 11; 5, 19, 4; id. Epit. 42, 3; 53, 11.— In plur., Tac. A. 3, 34; Col. 9, 9, 1.

conspargo.definition: conspargo, consparsĭo, etc., v. conspergo, conspersio, etc.

conspectio.definition: conspicio A look, sight, view (late Lat. and rare for conspectus), Jul. Epit. Nov. 57, § 201.

conspectus.definition: conspectus, a, um, Part. and , from conspicio.

conspergo.definition: conspergo (in MSS. also conspar-go; cf. 1. aspergo), si, sum, 3, spargo. To sprinkle, moisten, besprinkle, bespatter, strew (very freq. and class.). To scatter, sprinkle: vinum vetus,Col. 12, 39, 3 dub.

conspersio.definition: (), , conspergo (late Lat.). Abstr., a scattering, strewing, sprinkling: crebra salis,Pall. Nov. 13, 3. Concr., paste, dough, Tert. adv. Marc. 4, 24 al.

conspicabilis.definition: conspĭcābĭlis, e, conspicor (eccl. Lat.). Visible: ore, Prud. στεφ. 10, 631. Remarkable, notable: thermae,Sid. Ep. 8, 4 al.

conspicabundus.definition: conspĭcābundus, a, um, conspicor Considering attentively: Pallas virginem,Mart. Cap. 8, § 803.

conspiciendus.definition: conspĭcĭendus, a, um, Part. and , from conspicio.

conspicientia.definition: conspicio The faculty of considering: rerum conspicien tiam habere,Cassiod. An. 3.

conspicillum.definition: (, Plaut. Fragm ap. Non. p. 84, 7), , id. A place to look from, and, transf., a watching: conspicillo consecutu'st me,Plaut. Cist. 1, 1, 92; cf. unde conspici possis, Plaut. ap. Non. 1. 1.

conspicio.definition: con-spĭcĭo, spexi, spectum, 3, v. a. and n. To look at attentively, to get sight of, to descry, perceive, observe (class. in prose and poetry). Lit. Trop., to perceive mentally, to understand, comprehend: satis in rem quae sint meam ego conspicio mihi,Plaut. Trin. 3, 2, 10: quantum ego nunc corde conspicio meo,id. Ps. 3, 1, 3; cf.: ut conspiciatis eum mentibus, quoniam oculis non potestis,Cic. Balb. 20, 47: nullus error talis in L. Aemilio Paulo ...

conspicor.definition: conspĭcor, ātus, 1 V. dep. a. [id.], to get sight of, to descry, see, perceive (very freq. in Plaut. and Caes.; several times in Ter.; elsewh. rare; never in Lucr., Cic., Virg., or Hor.).

conspicuus.definition: conspĭcŭus, a, um, 1. conspicio (poet. or in post-Aug. prose, esp. in Tac.; not in Quint.). Lit., that is or comes in view, visible; opp. occultus: quot inter Occultum stellae conspicuumque polum,Ov. Tr. 4, 10, 108: rebus ab auditis conspicuisque,id. P. 3, 4, 22: late vertex, * Hor. C. 3, 16, 19: signum in proeliis,Phaedr. 4, 6, 6: acies barbarorum,Tac. H. 4, 29: tabernaculum undique,Curt. 9, 6, 1: sidus omnibus e terris, Augustus ap. Plin. 2, 25...

conspiratio.definition: 1. conspiro, prop. A blowing or breathing together. * Lit., of unison in wind instruments: canentium,Col. 12, 2, 4.—Far more freq. Trop., an agreement in feeling or opinion, union, unanimity, concord, harmony.

conspiro.definition: V. n., to blow or breathe together, to sound together. * Lit.: aereaque adsensu conspirant cornua rauco,Verg. A. 7, 615 (et tubae simul inflabantur, Serv.).—Far more freq. and in good prose Trop.

conspissatio.definition: spisso A pressing together, a thickening: sordium,an accumulation,Theod. Prisc. 1, 18.

conspissatus.definition: con-spissātus, a, um, Part. [id.] Pressed together, thickened, condensed, dense (very rare): solum conspissatum et herbis colligatum,Col. 2, 18, 5: vinacea,id. 12, 45, 3: creta,Plin. 35, 6, 18, § 36.

consplendesco.definition: con-splendesco, ĕre V. n., to shine very much: tecta,Jul. Val. Rer. Gest. Alex. M. 3, 66.

conspolio.definition: con-spŏlĭo, āvi, 1 V. a., to rob (late Lat.), Hier. Ep. 98, 21 fin.

conspolium.definition: A kind of sacrificial cake, acc. to Arn. 7, 230.

conspondeo.definition: con-spondĕo, ndi, nsum (old orthog. consposum, acc. to Paul. ex Fest. p. 41, 14 Müll.), 2, and n. To engage or promise something mutually (ante- and postclass. and very rare): NEVE. CONSPONDISE. NEVE. CONPROMESISE. VELET., S. C. Bacch.; Wordsworth, Fragm. and Spec. p. 172: consponsi, Naev. ap. Varr. L. L. 6, § 70 Müll.; cf. Paul. l. l.: consponsa factio,App. M. 5, p. 168, 8; so, foedus,Aus. Ep. 10, 11.

consponsata.definition: sponso The betrothed, the bride (late Lat.), Ambros. in Luc. 3, 3.

consponsor.definition: A joint surety, Cic. Fam. 6, 18, 2; id. Att. 12, 17. One who binds or obligates himself to something ( = conjurator), acc. to Fest. p. 59, 7 Müll.

conspuo.definition: con-spŭo, no Perf., ūtum, 3, and n. Act., to spit upon (rare; most freq. in Petr.): me immundissimo basio,Petr. 23, 4.—Esp., to spit upon in contempt, Plaut. Curc. 4, 2, 17; Petr. 132, 3; Hier. Ep. 50, n. 4; cf. Barth. Advers. 23, 24.—Of an epileptic: faciem tuam,App. Mag. 44, p. 303, 1: conspuere sinus, as a charm to prevent the gods from being provoked by proud words, Juv. 7, 111 Mayor ad loc.; cf. spuo, I. Neutr., to spit out much, to spit: fa...

conspurco.definition: con-spurco, no Perf., ātum, 1, v. a., to defile, pollute (rare): omnia taetro sapore, * Lucr. 6, 22: (juvenem) per vim,Suet. Ner. 35; Col. 8, 3 fin.; Tert. Idol. 1.

constabilio.definition: con-stăbĭlĭo, īvi, 4 V. a., to confirm, establish, make firm (ante- and post-class. for stabilio, 2. fundo, and rare); only trop.: rem meam, * Plaut. Capt. 2, 3, 93; so * Ter. Ad. 5, 1, 9; Tert. adv. Valent. 39.

constagno.definition: con-stagno, āre, , of fluids, = congelo To cause to stand, to congeal, Fronto, p. 2198 P.

constans.definition: constans, antis, Part. and , from consto.

constanter.definition: constanter, , v. consto P. a. fin.

constantia.definition: 1. constans. A firm standing, steadiness, firmness, immutability, unchangeableness, constancy, perseverance (in good prose; esp. freq. in Cic.): (stellarum) perennes cursus atque perpetui cum admirabili incredibilique constantiā,Cic. N. D. 2, 21, 55; cf. id. ib. § 56, and 3, 9, 23: dictorum conventorumque,id. Off. 1, 7, 23; cf. promissi,id. Att. 4, 19 (17), 1: tantā constantiā vocis atque voltūs,Nep. Att. 22, 1: perseverantia constantiaque oppugn...

constantinopolis.definition: Κωνσταντίνου πολις The city Constantinople, previously called Byzantium; Turkish Stamboul, Amm. 22, 8, 8; 31, 16, 4; Eutr. 6, 6; Aur. Vict. Epit. 35; Aus. Urb. 2; id. Parent. 3, 11 al.—Hence, , , adj., of Constantinople: urbs,i. e. Constantinople,Cod. Just. 1, 2, 6: cives, Cod. Th. 11, 16, 6.

constantinus.definition: C. Flavius Vaferius Claudius Constantinus Constantine, a well-known Roman emperor, born A. D. 274, died A. D. 323, Eutr. 10, 2 sqq.; Lact. Mort. Pers. 18 sqq.; Amm. 21, 10, 8.—Hence, , , adj., of or pertaining to Constantine: genus,Amm. 27, 5, 1: lavacrum,id. 27, 3, 8.

constantius.definition: The name of a Roman emperor who reigned from 292 A. D. to 306 A. D., Eutr. 10, 6 sqq.; Lact. Mort. Pers. 15, 6; Aur. Vict. Caes. 40.—Hence, the adjj.: , , um: legiones,Amm. 21, 11, 2: , , um: thalamus,id. 22, 3, 12; and , , of or pertaining to Constantius: bellum, Sext. Ruf. Brev. 27.

constellatio.definition: stella A collection of stars supposed to exert an influence upon human affairs, a constellation (late Lat.), Amm. 29, 2, 27; Capitol. Gord. 20; Spart. Ver. 4 al.

constellatus.definition: con-stellātus, a, um Adj., starred, studded with stars: baltei, Treb. Gall. 2.

consternatio.definition: 2. consterno (not ante-Aug.; mostly in histt.) Confusion, dismay, consternation, alarm, disquietude, disturbance. In gen.: pavor et consternatio mentis,Tac. A. 13, 16: quae causa irae consternationisque subitae foret,Liv. 28, 25, 5 Weissenb. ad loc.: muliebris,id. 34, 2, 6: creditorum,Val. Max. 9, 7, 4: populi,id. 9, 15, 4; Suet. Calig. 51; id. Claud. 12.—* In partic., mutiny, tumult, disorder, sedition, Liv. 34, 2, 6; Tac. A. 1, 39: neque plures...

consterno.definition: con-sterno, strāvi, strātum, 3 To strew over, cover by strewing, bestrew, to thatch, floor, pave, spread, cover (class. in prose and poetry). To throw down, prostrate, level (very rare). *

constipatio.definition: constipo (postclass.) A crowding together; in concr., a dense crowd: exercitūs,Vop. Aur. 21: militum,Amm. 26, 6, 14.

constipo.definition: con-stīpo, āvi, ātum, 1 V. a., to press or crowd closely together (very rare): tantum numerum hominum in agrum Campanum, * Cic. Agr. 2, 29, 79: se (hostes) sub ipso vallo,Caes. B. G. 5, 42; Prud. στεφ. 11.

constituo.definition: con-stĭtŭo, ŭi, ūtum, 3, v. a.statuo To cause to stand, put or lay down, to set, put, place, fix, station, deposit a person or thing somewhere (esp. firmly or immovably), etc. (the act. corresponding to consistere; class.). In gen. Esp.

constitutio.definition: constituo. In gen., a constitution, disposition, nature: firma corporis,Cic. Off. 3, 33, 117 (as transl. of the Gr. εὐστάθεια τῆς σαρκός); so Sen. Ep. 121, 10 and 14: prima naturae,Cic. Fin. 4, 6, 15. In partic.

constitutionarius.definition: constitutio He who presides over the copying of the imperial constitutions, Gest. ap. Sen. Recip. Th. Cod.

constitutor.definition: constituo An orderer, arranger (mostly post-class.): legis,Quint. 3, 6, 43: rerum omnium Deus,Lact. 3, 9, 10: Deus machinator constitutorque rerum,id. 4, 6, 1: moderatorque cunctorum,Arn. 3, p. 101: SACRI CERTAMINIS,Inscr. Grut. 254, 4: CONSTITVTORES COLLEGII NVMINIS DOMINORVM,Inscr. Orell. 2389.

constitutum.definition: constĭtūtum, i, n., v. constituo, , B.

constitutus.definition: constĭtūtus, a, um, Part. and , from constituo.

consto.definition: con-sto, stĭti, stātum (constātūrus, Sen. Clem. 1, 19, 3; Plin. 18, 5, 6, § 30; Luc. 2, 17; Mart. 10, 41, 5; Lact. Opif. Dei, 7, 11), 1, v. n. To stand together, stand with some person or thing. With the access. idea of firmness, to stand firm, to remain immovable, unchanging, steadfast, to abide, last, endure, persevere, etc. (very freq. in all perr. and styles).

constratus.definition: constrātus, a, um, Part., from 1. consterno.

constrepo.definition: con-strĕpo, ĕre V. n., to resound, sound loudly or boisterously, to make a noise (post-class.). Lit.: domus tota constrepebat hymenaeum,App. M. 4, p. 154, 23; cf. id. ib. 11, p. 261, 34. Trop., of a vivid speech: horum omnium et testimoniis et exemplis constrepebat,Gell. 4, 1, 4.

constricte.definition: constrictē, , v. constringo P. a. fin.

constrictivus.definition: constrictīvus, a, um, id. Drawing together, contracting, astringent (in later medic. writers): cibi,Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 3 fin.: virtutis esse,id. Acut. 2, 18 al.—Adv.: constrictīvē, astringently: tractare aliquid,Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 4, 38.

constrictiuus.definition: constrictīvus, a, um, id. Drawing together, contracting, astringent (in later medic. writers): cibi,Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 3 fin.: virtutis esse,id. Acut. 2, 18 al.—Adv.: constrictīvē, astringently: tractare aliquid,Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 4, 38.

constricto.definition: constricto, āre V. freq. [id.], to draw together; of a physician (with inurere, amputare, etc.), Tert. adv. Marc. 2, 16.

constrictura.definition: id. A drawing together, Cael. Aur. Acut. 1, 9, 69.

constringo.definition: con-stringo, strinxi, strictum, 3 V. a., to draw together, bind together, to bind, tie up (class. in prose and poetry). Lit. Trop.

constructio.definition: construo A putting or placing together, a joining together (in good prose; most freq. in Cic.; not in Quint.). Lit. (rare): lapidum,Sen. Cons. Polyb. 18 (37), 2. Transf., an erecting, building, construction: hominis,Cic. Ac. 2, 27, 86: ejus (gymnasii), Traj. ap. Plin. Ep. 10, 40 (49), 2.—In plur., Pall. Nov. 22, 1. Trop.

construo.definition: con-strŭo, struxi, structum, 3 ( Part. fut. constrŭĭtūra, Ven. Carm. 2, 10 fin.) To heap, bring, or gather together, to heap or pile up (class.): acervos nummorum apud aliquem,Cic. Phil. 2, 38, 97; cf.: omnibus rebus et modis constructā et coacervatā pecuniā,id. Agr. 1, 5, 14; and acervum,Hor. S. 1, 1, 44: divitias,id. ib. 2, 3, 96: carros, to make a barricade, Sisenn. ap. Non. p. 195, 29: has omnes multas magnificasque res,Cic. de Or. 1, 35, 161...

constupeo.definition: con-stŭpĕo, ŭi, 2 V. n., to be very much astonished, Juvenc. 1, 179.

constupro.definition: con-stūpro, āvi, ātum, 1 V. a., to violate, ravisn, debauch, defile (rare, but in good prose). Prop.: matronas, virgines, ingenuos, raptos, etc.,Liv. 29, 17, 15: virginem,Curt. 10, 1, 5: praetextatos liberos,Q. Cic. Pet. Cons. 3, 10; Suet. Vit. 12 al. Trop.: afflicta res publica est empto constupratoque judicio,purchased by debauchery,Cic. Att. 1, 18, 3: aër scelestis vocibus constupratus,polluted,Tert. Spect. 27: pudicitiam,Hier. adv. Jovin. 2, ...

consuadeo.definition: con-sŭādĕo, ēre V. a., to advise or counsel strongly (Plautin.; cf. however, consuasor): id consuadeo,Plaut. Merc. 1, 2, 32: consuadet homini,id. Trin. 2, 4, 126: qui consuadet, vetat,id. ib. 3, 2, 46.—Of favorable auspices: picus et cornix ab laevā consuadent, etc.,Plaut. As. 2, 1, 13.

consubigo.definition: con-sŭbĭgo, ēre To work, knead, or mix together (late Lat.): cineres, lixiva, etc., Garg. Mart. de Cura Boum med.

consubstantialis.definition: con-substantĭālis, e Adj., of like essence, nature, or substance, consubstantial (eccl. Lat.), Tert. adv. Herm. 44 al.—Hence

consubstantialitas.definition: consubstantialis A like quality (late Lat.), Cassiod. Hist. Eccl. 2, 7 med.

consubstantivus.definition: con-substantīvus, a, um, ( = consubstantialis) Of like essence, nature, etc. (eccl. Lat.), Tert. adv. Val. 12 fin. and 18.

consubstantiuus.definition: con-substantīvus, a, um, ( = consubstantialis) Of like essence, nature, etc. (eccl. Lat.), Tert. adv. Val. 12 fin. and 18.

consudo.definition: con-sūdo, āvi, 1 V. n., to sweat much or profusely (very rare), Cato, R. R. 96, 1; Plaut. Ps. 2, 2, 71; Col. 12, 7, 2.

consuefacio.definition: consŭē-făcĭo, fēci, factum, 3 (in Ter. Ad. 1, 1, 29; 1, 1, 49, and 3, 3, 60, consue feci, consue facere, consue facio, acc. to Lachm. ad Lucr. p. 409), consueo To accustom one to a thing, to inure, habituale (rare, and mostly ante-class. for the class. assuefacio).

consueo.definition: con-sŭĕo, ēre V. a., to be accustomed, be wont, acc. to Charis. p. 224 P.; Prisc. p. 885 ib. (for consuemus in Prop.; v. consuesco init.).

consuesco.definition: consŭesco, suēvi, suētum, 3 (in the Tempp. perff. the sync. forms prevail: consuesti, consuestis, consuerunt; consueram, etc.; consuero, etc.; consuerim, etc.; consuessem, etc.; consuesse. Thus also consuēmus = consuevimus,Prop. 1, 7, 5), v. a. and n. Act., to accustom, inure, habituate a person or thing (ante-class. and postAug.): tum bracchia consuescunt firmantque lacertos,Lucr. 6, 397: juvencum plostro aut aratro,Col. 6, 2, 9: vitem largo umo...

consuetio.definition: consuesco, II. B. Carnal intercourse: clandestina,Plaut. Am. 1, 2, 28; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 61, 4 Müll.; Don. ad Ter. Ad. 4, 5, 32.

consuetudinarius.definition: consŭētūdĭnārĭus, a, um, consuetudo Customary, ordinary, usual (late Lat.): portitor. Sid. Ep. 7, 11: carnes,Salv. Gub. Dei. 6, p. 219 al.—Adv.: consŭētū-dĭnārĭē, in the usual manner, Cassiod. Var. 12, 2 fin.

consuetudo.definition: consuesco. A being accustomed, custom, habit, use, usage. Social intercourse, companionship, familiarity, conversation (freq. and class; in an honorable sense most freq. in Cic.).

consuetus.definition: consŭētus, a, um, Part. and , v. consuesco Fin.

consul.definition: (in the oldest inscrr. CONSOL, COSOL; abbrev. COS., also in plur. COSS., not before the time of the emperors), , prob. from root sal- of salio; Sanscr. sar-, go; hence also exsul, praesul, v. Corss. Ausspr. II. p. 71 A consul, one of the two highest magistrates of the Roman state, chosen annually, after the expulsion of the kings; cf. concerning his election, administration, duties, etc., Dict. Antiq., and the authors there cited (freq. in all pe...

consularis.definition: consŭlāris, e, adj.consul Of or pertaining to a consul, consular (very freq.): aetas, the age required by law for the consular office, viz. the 43d year, Cic. Phil. 5, 17, 48; cf. annus, II.: comitia,for the choice of consul,id. Mur. 26, 53; id. Att. 9, 9, 3: officium,id. Rab. Perd. 1, 2; cf. imperium,id. Pis. 16, 38; Sall. C. 55, 6: fasces,Liv. 2, 54, 4: lictor,Hor. C. 2, 16, 9: insignia,Vell. 2, 58, 3; Tac. A. 13, 10; id. H. 4, 4: ornamenta,Sue...

consularitas.definition: consularis, II. B. The dignity or office of consul or imperial governor (late Lat.), Cod. Th. 6, 19, 1; 6, 27, 10; 9, 26, 4 al.

consularius.definition: consŭlārĭus, a, um, , = consularis (late Lat.): dignitas, Jul. Epit. c. 98, § 359.

consulatus.definition: consul The office of consul, the consulate or consulship (very frq. in all periods): honorum populi finis est consulatus,Cic. Planc. 25, 60: consulatus ille antiquus,id. Tusc. 2, 17, 41: quo pluris est universa respublica quam consulatus aut praetura, etc.,Sall. J. 85, 2; 63, 2 et saep.—In plur. (not ante-Aug.): quinque consulatus eodem tenore gesti,Liv. 4, 10, 9; Tac. Or. 7.—Esp. in the phrases: consulatum petere,Cic. Mur. 3, 8; Sall. C. 16 fin....

consulo.definition: consŭlo, lŭi, ltum, 3, v. n. and A. [from con and root sal-; cf. consul and consilium]. To consider, reflect, deliberate, take counsel, reflect upon, consult. Sometimes meton. (causa pro effectu).

consultatio.definition: 2. consulto. A mature deliberation, consideration, consultation. An asking of advice, inquiry (rare).

consultator.definition: id. One who asks advice, consults (post-Aug. and rare, for the class. consultor, III.), Quint. 6, 3, 87; Dig. 1, 2, 2, § 35.

consultatorius.definition: consultātōrĭus, a, um, consultator Of or pertaining to consultation: hostiae (hostiarum genus, in quo voluntas dei per exta disquiritur), opp. animales,Macr. S. 3, 5.

consulte.definition: consultē, , v. consulo P. a. fin.

consulto.definition: consultō, , v. consulo P. a. fin.

consultor.definition: consulo. * One who maturely considers, reflects, takes counsel upon a thing, etc., Afran. ap. Non. p. 5, 6, 8 (Com. Rel. v. 332 Rib.). One who gives counsel, a counsellor, adviser. He who asks counsel of one, a consulter; esp. used of him who consults a lawyer in reference to a suit at law, a client (several times in Cic.; elsewh. rare),Cic. Balb. 19, 45; id. Mur. 9, 22 bis; id. Tusc. 5, 38, 112; * Hor. S. 1, 1, 10: dei,Luc. 5, 187 (i. e. qui con...

consummatio.definition: id. (postAug.). A casting up or reckoning together, a summing up, a summary view. Afinishing, completing, accomplishing, consummation: susceptae professionis,Col. 9, 2, 2: habet res minime consummationem,id. 1, prooem. § 7: maximarum rerum,Sen. Brev. Vit. 1, 3: operis,Quint. 2, 18, 2; 6, 1, 55: liberalitatis,Plin. Ep. 5, 12, 1; Vulg. Jer. 30, 11 (for the Heb. ) et saep.: alvi,i. e. a digestion of food,Plin. 26, 8, 28, § 43: gladiatorum,i. e. the ...

consummator.definition: consummo A completer, finisher (eccl. Lat.): novi testamenti (opp. initiator veteris),Tert. adv. Marc. 4, 22 al.

consummatus.definition: consummātus, a, um, Part. and , from consummo.

consummo.definition: con-summo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.summa (not in use before the Aug. per.; most freq. in Quint.). To cast or sum up. To bring about, accomplish, complete, finish, perfect, consummate.

consumo.definition: con-sūmo, sumpsi, sumptum, 3 ( Perf. sync. consumpsti, Prop. 1, 3, 37; inf. consumpse, Lucr. 1, 234), v. a., to take wholly or completely, i. e. Lit. Transf.

consumptibilis.definition: consumptĭbĭlis, e, consumo That can be consumed or destroyed, transient (late Lat.): vigor,Cassiod. An. 3.

consumptio.definition: id.. * A consuming, wasting, consumption, Cic. Univ. 6.—* An employing, bestowing, application, use: operae,Auct. Her. 4, 22, 32 (al. sumptione).

consumptor.definition: id. A consumer, destroyer (very rare): omnium ignis (connected with confector), * Cic. N. D. 2, 15, 41.—Of fire, Ambros. in Luc. 7, § 132.—Of the wasters of their property, spendthrifts, Sen. Exc. Controv. 3, 1, § 3.

consumptrix.definition: consumptor She who wastes, consumes (late Lat.): terra omnium corporum,Serv. ad Verg. A. 6, 395.

consuo.definition: con-sŭo, sŭi, sūtum, 3 To sew, stitch, or join together (very rare; mostly ante- and post-class.). In gen.: consuere aliquid aliquā re, to stuff, stop up, fill with something: pinacothecas veteribus tabulis,Plin. 35, 2, 2, § 4. —Hence, * consūtum, i, n., a garment stitched together, Gai Inst. 3, § 192.

consupplicatrix.definition: supplico She who supplicates with (rare), Claud. ap. Varr. L. L. 7, § 66 Müll.; Inscr. Orell. 1501.

consurgo.definition: con-surgo, surrexi, surrectum, 3 V. n., to raise one's self, to rise (esp. of a multitude), to rise up together, stand up, arise (class. in prose and poetry). Lit. Meton.

consurrectio.definition: consurgo A standing up (as a sign of assent in public transactions) (rare; perh. only in the foll. exs.): judicum,Cic. Att. 1, 16, 4: omnium vestrum,id. Har. Resp. 1, 2.

consus.definition: perh. from condo A very ancient deity of Italy, a god of the earth and of agriculture, giver of fertility, presiding over counsels and secret plans: CONSVS. CONSILIO. MARS. DVELLO. LARES. COMITIO. POTENTES., old. inscr. in Tert. Spect. 5; cf. Serv. ad Verg. A. 8, 636; Ascon. Cic. Verr. 1, 10, 31; Mart. Cap. 1, § 54.—Hence Romulus consecrated to him the games instituted with the purpose of attracting the Sabine women, Liv. 1, 9, 6, where this deit...

consutilis.definition: consūtĭlis, e, consuo Sewed together: crate praecinctus,Cassiod. Var. 5, 42.

contabesco.definition: con-tābesco, tābŭi, 3 V. inch. n., to waste away gradually, to be consumed, pine away (very rare). Lit.: cor guttatim contabescit, * Plaut. Merc. 1, 2, 92: Artemisia luctu confecta contabuit, * Cic. Tusc. 3, 31, 75.—* Trop.: o perfidiosae Fregellae, quam facile scelere vestro contabuistis,Auct. Her. 4, 15, 22.

contabulatio.definition: contabulo A joining of boards together, a flooring, planking; a floor or story, a covering of boards (very rare), Caes. B. C. 2, 9 (four times); Vitr. 10, 15, 3: proscenii,App. Flor. 4, 18. Transf., of garments, folds, tucks, App. M. 11, p. 258, 26.

contabulo.definition: con-tăbŭlo, āvi, ātum, 1 V. a., to furnish or cover with boards (several times in the histt.; elsewh. rare): turres,Caes. B. G. 5, 40: turres contabulatas machimentaque alia quatiendis muris portabant,i. e. built in stories,Liv. 24, 34, 7: pomaria,Plin. 15, 16, 18, § 59: totum murum ex omni parte turribus,Caes. B. G. 7, 22: pavimentum quernis axibus,Plin. 36, 25, 62, § 187: mare molibus,to furnish with a bridge, to bridge over,Curt. 5, 7, 8; cf. ...

contactus.definition: contactus, a, um, Part., from 1. contingo.

contages.definition: id. Contact, touch (Lucretian), Lucr. 3, 734; 4, 337; in plur., id. 6, 280 and 1242.

contagio.definition: f., , , n., and , , n. (contagium only in poets—and in plur.—and in postAug. prose writers; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 59, 12; Non. p. 199, 2; Marc. Vict. 1, p. 2469 P.; cf. also colluvio: contamen only in late Lat.) [id.] A touching, contact, touch, in a good or bad sense. In gen. Freq., in a bad sense, a contacl with something physically or morally unclean, a contagion, infection.

contagiosus.definition: contāgĭōsus, a, um, contagio, II. Contagious (perh. only in Veg.): passio,Veg. Art. Vet. 1, 14, 2: scabies,id. ib. 5, 70, 1.

contaminatio.definition: contamino (post-class.). A polluting, contamination, defilement: mulieris,Dig. 48, 5, 2: expositionis,Arn. 5, 168.—* Corruption, disease: ventris, Jul. Obseq. Prodig. 89.

contaminator.definition: id. A defiler, polluter (late Lat.): honorum,Lampr. Alex. Sev. 6: paterni tori,Tert. Pudic. 13.

contaminatus.definition: contāmĭnātus, a, um, Part. and , v. contamino.

contamino.definition: con-tāmĭno, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.from stem tag, tango. Orig., to bring into contact, touch. To deteriorate by mingling, corrupt, contaminate, defile, stain, pollute (something by something; very freq., esp. in the trop. signif., and in Cic.; not in Quint.).

contego.definition: con-tĕgo, xi, ctum, 3 V. a., to cover, to cover up or over (freq. and class.). In gen. In partic.

contemero.definition: con-tĕmĕro, āvi, 3 V. a., to stain, pollute, defile (very rare): torum dominae,Ov. Am. 2, 7, 18: manus,Mart. Spect. 10, 2.

contemnenter.definition: contemnenter Adv., in a contemptuous manner, Non. p. 515, 33.

contemno.definition: con-temno (also contempno; cf. Ritschl Prol. ad Plaut. p. 103), tempsi (-temsi), temptum (-temtum), 3 V. a., to consider a person or thing as unimportant or of small value, to value little, esteem lightly, contemn, despise, disdain, defy, not to fear, etc. (very freq. in connection with irridere, despicere, non curare, pro nihilo ducere, etc.; opp.: expetere, efferre, timere, metuere, etc.; v.the foll. and cf. aspernor; freq. and class. in prose ...

contemperatio.definition: contempero A proper or suitable mixture, Aug. Doctr. Chr. 2, 30.

contemplabilis.definition: contemplābĭlis, e, contemplor Aiming, taking aim (only in Amm.): dextera,Amm. 30, 5, 16: artifex,id. 23, 4, 2.— * Adv.: contemplābĭlĭter: ferire aliquid,taking aim,Amm. 20, 7, 9.

contemplabundus.definition: contemplābundus, a, um, contemplor Considering or contemplating attentively, Tert. adv. Marc. 4, 40.

contemplatio.definition: id. An attentive considering, a viewing, surveying, contemplation (in good prose). Physical. Mental.

contemplativus.definition: contemplātīvus, a, um, id. Contemplative, speculative: philosophia (opp. activa), theoretical (formed after the Gr. θεωρητικός), Sen. Ep. 95, 10: sapientiae pars, Aug. Civ. Dei, 8, 4: vita,Fulg. Myth. 2, 1.

contemplatiuus.definition: contemplātīvus, a, um, id. Contemplative, speculative: philosophia (opp. activa), theoretical (formed after the Gr. θεωρητικός), Sen. Ep. 95, 10: sapientiae pars, Aug. Civ. Dei, 8, 4: vita,Fulg. Myth. 2, 1.

contemplator.definition: id.. * An observer, surveyor: peritissimus,a marksman,Amm. 19, 1, 7. A contemplator, an observer (very rare): caeli ac deorum, * Cic. Tusc. 1, 28, 69: mundi animus,Sen. Cons. ad Helv. 8, 4: astrorum,App. Flor. 4, n. 18, p. 361, 4.

contemplatrix.definition: contemplator She who observes or contemplates (very rare): medicina, Cels. praef. 1, prooem. § 91; App. Dogm. Plat. 2, p. 16, 25.

contemplo.definition: contemplo, āvi, ātum, 1, (anteand post-class.; collat. form of contemplor) To survey, behold, observe, consider, contemplate, etc.; freq. in imper.: adspecta et contempla, Epidice,Plaut. Ep. 5, 1, 16: contempla et templum Cereris ad laevam aspice, Enn. ap. Varr. L. L. 7, § 9 Müll.; id. ap. Non. p. 470, 5; Att. and Titin. ib. p. 469, 31, and 470, 2; Plaut. Mil. 4, 2, 38 al.: contemplo placide formam et faciem virginis, Naev. ap. Non. p. 469, 33; P...

contemplor.definition: con-templor, ātus, 1 (arch. Inf. contemplarier, Plaut. Poen. 5, 3, 10), templum, I. A. (orig. pertaining to the lang. of augury; cf. Varr. L. L. 7, § 9 Müll.), to look at, view attentively, to survey, behold, gaze upon, give attention to, observe, consider, contemplate, = considero (class. in prose and poetry). Physically. Mentally (several times in Cic.): propone tibi duos reges, et id animo contemplare, quod oculis non potes,Cic. Deiot. 14, 40:...

contemporalis.definition: con-tempŏrālis, e Adj., contemporary; subst., a contemporary (late Lat.), Tert. adv. Herm. 6 sq. al.

contemporaneus.definition: con-tempŏrānĕus, a, um, tempus Contemporary; subst., a contemporary: M. Varro et Nigidius Caesari et Ciceroni,Gell. 19, 14 inscr.

contemporo.definition: con-tempŏro, āre, id. To be at the same time, to be contemporary, Tert. Res. Carn. 45.

contempte.definition: contemptē (-temtē), , v. contemno P. a. fin.

contemptim.definition: contemptim (-temt-), contemno Contemptuously, with contempt, scornfully (a favorite word of Livy; elsewhere rare): superbiter contemptim conterit legiones, Naev. ap. Non. p. 516, 1; imitated: ne nos tam contemptim conteras,Plaut. Poen. 3, 1, 34: magnifice de se ac contemptim de Romanis loquentes,Liv. 9, 41, 9: superbe quaedam et contemptim in se contionantem,id. 37, 10, 2; 2, 35, 3; 2, 56, 12: morte consulis succedentes ad castra Romana,id. 7, 7,...

contemptio.definition: (), , id. A despising; disregard, contempt, scorn, disdain (in good prose): omnium rerum humanarum contemptio ac despicientia,Cic. Tusc. 1, 40, 95: fortitudo est dolorum laborumque contemptio,id. Off. 3, 33, 117; id. Rep. Fragm. ap. Non. p. 201, 30; Hortens. Fragm. ib. p. 202, 1: mortis perpetua,Curt. 10, 8, 29: fortunae,Cic. Par. 4, 1, 27: pecuniae,id. Phil. 3, 6, 16: deorum inmortalium,Liv. 6, 41, 4: ut jam non solum hostibus in contemptionem S...

contemptor.definition: contemptor (-temt-), ōris, m. id. He who puts small value upon or makes light of a thing, a contemner, despiser (freq. after the Aug. per.; not in Cic. or Hor.): divum Mezentius,Verg. A. 7, 648; cf. superūm,Ov. M. 3, 514: magni Olympi cum dis,id. ib. 13, 761: religionum, * Suet. Ner. 56: gratiae, divitiarum (Cato),Liv. 39, 40, 10: famae,id. 44, 22, 7: suae infamiae,Tac. A. 6, 38: opum,id. H. 4, 5; cf. sui (opp. prodigus alieni),id. G. 31: Amulius...

contemptrix.definition: (), , contemptor She who puts small value upon a thing, a despiser, contemner (rare; not in Cic.): mea, * Plaut. Bacch. 3, 6, 2: superūm propago, * Ov. M. 1, 161. Of inanimate and abstract subjects: contemptrix frigorum eruca,Plin. 19, 8, 44, § 154; 37, 4, 15, § 59: fortitudo contemptrix timendorum est,Sen. Ep. 88, 29: turba periculi,Sil. 17, 411.

contemptus.definition: contemptus (-temt-), a, um Part. and P. a., from contemno.

contendo.definition: con-tendo, di, tum, 3, v. a. and n. To stretch, stretch out vigorously, to draw tight, strain. Lit. (rare and mostly poet.): arcum,Verg. A. 12, 815; Ov. M. 6, 286; id. R. Am. 435: tormenta, Sisen. ap. Non. p. 258, 27; Cic. Tusc. 2, 24, 57: muscipula, Lucil. ap. Non. p. 181, 31: tenacia vincla,Verg. G. 4, 412: ilia risu,Ov. A. A. 3, 285: pontem in alto, Enn. ap. Varr. L. L. 7, § 21 Müll. (Ann. v. 358 Vahl.): oculi contendunt se,Lucr. 4, 810.— Of s...

contenebro.definition: con-tĕnēbro, āvi, ātum, 1, id. To make very dark, to darken (eccl. Lat.), Tert. adv. Haer. 12; id. Jejun. 10; id. Apol. 2.

contente.definition: contentē, , v. contendo P. a. fin.

contentio.definition: contendo (acc. to contendo, II.) An eager stretching, a straining, exertion of the powers of body or mind, tension, effort, a vigorous struggling or striving for something, a struggle after (very freq. and in good prose). In gen. In partic.

contentiosus.definition: contentĭōsus, a, um, contentio Pertaining to contention, contentious, disputatious, headstrong, obstinate, pertinacious (mostly post-class.): contentiosa et pugnax oratio,Plin. Ep. 2, 19, 4: jurisdictio,Dig. 1, 16, 2.—Comp.: quid contentiosius, quam, etc.,Aug. Ep. 174: pernicies,obstinate,App. M. 8, p. 202, 23.—Adv.: con-tentĭōsē, pertinaciously, obstinately: dicere,Hier. ad Jovin. 2, 10.—Comp.: loqui,Quint. Decl. 18, 6.—Sup., Aug. Civ. Dei, 20, ...

contentus.definition: contentus, a, um Stretched, strained, exerted; v. contendo

conterebro.definition: con-tĕrēbro, āre V. a., to pierce or bore through (late Lat.): ossa,Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 3.

contermino.definition: contermĭno, āre, conterminus: alicui To be a borderer, to border upon; perh. only Amm. 14, 2, 5; 23, 6, 45.

conterminus.definition: Adj., bordering upon, neighboring, having a common border (not ante-Aug.; perh. first used by Ovid). Prop. Trop.: virtus morti,Stat. Th. 7, 702.

contero.definition: con-tĕro, trīvi (rarely conterui, App. M. 8, p. 212, 12; Ven. Fort. C. 6, 4, 33), trītum, 3 V. a., to grind, bruise, pound, to crumble, separate into small pieces. Prop. (so freq. in medic. lang.): medium scillae cum aquā ad mellis crassitudinem,Varr. R. R. 2, 7, 8: cornua cervi,Ov. Med. Fac. 60: horrendis infamia pabula sucis,id. M. 14, 44: radicem aridam in pulverem,Plin. 26, 11, 70, § 113: fracta, contrita,Lucr. 4, 697.—Far more freq. and clas...

conterreo.definition: con-terrĕo, ŭi, ĭtum, 2 V. a., to terrify greatly, to frighten (not freq. before the Aug. per.; esp. freq. in Livy); constr. with abl. or absol.

conterrito.definition: conterrĭto, āre, conterreo To frighten much or greatly, Coripp. 2, Joann. 54; 88.

conterritus.definition: conterrĭtus, a, um, Part. of conterreo.

contesseratio.definition: contessero The contracting of friendship, Tert. adv. Haeret. 20.

contessero.definition: con-tessĕro, āre, tessera To contract friendsnip by means of the tesserae, Tert. adv. Haeret. 36.

contestatio.definition: contestor. A jurid. t. t., an attesting, proving by witness, testimony: suprema testamenti,Dig. 28, 1, 20, § 8; cf.: verbum (testamentum) compositum a mentis contestatione,Gell. 6, 12, 2: litis, a formal entering of a suit in law, by calling witnesses, Gai inst. 3, 180 sq.; Dig. 3, 3, 40, § 3; 24, 3, 22, § 5; Cod. Just. 3, 9: de litis contestatione. An earnest entreaty: petivit tamen a me pater maximā contestatione, ut, etc., * Cic. Corn. 1 Fragm...

contestatiuncula.definition: contestatio A short speech, Sid. Ep. 7, 3.

contestificans.definition: con-testĭfĭcans, antis, Part. [testificor] Attesting at the same time, Tert. Testim. Anim. 1.

contestor.definition: con-testor, ātus, 1 V. dep., to take or call to witness. Prop. Trop., part. perf.: contestatus, in pass. signif., proved by witness, tried: ab hac perenni contestataque virtute majorum,proved,Cic. Fl. 11, 25.

contexo.definition: con-texo, xŭi, xtum, 3, and n. Act., to weave, entwine, braid, join together; to interweave, unite, connect (class. in prose and poetry). Neutr.: contexere de aliquā re, to treat of: de sili,Plin. 20, 5, 18, § 36.—Hence, contextus, a, um, P. a., cohering, connected: contexta condensaque corpora (opp. diffusa),Lucr. 4, 57: oratio alia vincta atque contexta, soluta alia,Quint. 9, 4, 19: tropos ille (corresp. with continua μεταφορά), id. 9, 2, 46.—...

contextim.definition: contextim, contexo In a connected manner, connectedly (very rare): luto nidificantes paene contextim, * Plin. 10, 53, 74, § 147; Aug. Ep. 112, 15.

contextio.definition: contexo (postclass.). A joining, putting together (opp. resolutio), Macr. Somn. Scip. 1, 5, 18. A preparing, composing: classis, Aus. prooem. Per. lliad: libri, Aug. Civ. Dei, 7, 2: narrationis,Macr. Somn. Scip. 1, 2.

contextor.definition: id. One who puts a writing together, a composer, author: codicis, Cod. Th. 1, 1, 6, § 2.

contextus.definition: contextus, a, um, Part. and , from contexo.

contheroleta.definition: vox hybr., θηρολέτης A fellow-destroyer of wild beasts, Fulg. Myth. 3, 2.

conticesco.definition: contĭcesco (contĭcisco, Plaut. Bacch. 4, 5, 28; id. Mil. 2, 4, 56; Arn. 5 init.), tĭcŭi, 3 V. inch., to become still, to cease speaking or sounding (class. in prose and poetry). Lit.: sed conticiscam: nam audio aperiri foris,Plaut. Bacch. 4, 5, 28; id. Mil. 2, 4, 56: ad quod ille quidem conticescit, sed sermonem suscipit Polus,Quint. 2, 15, 28: ad hos casus,i. e. in such cases,id. 6, 1, 42: conscientiā convictus repente conticuit,Cic. Cat. 3, 5, ...

conticinium.definition: conticesco, the time when all becomes still; cf. Varr. L. L. 6, § 7, and 7, § 79 Müll.; also , Macr. S. 1, 3, 12 The first part of the night, the evening, Plaut. As. 3, 3, 95 (quoted in Varr. l. l.); cf. Serv. ad Verg. A. 2, 268.

contiger.definition: contus-gero A spear-bearer, a lancer, Paul. Nol. Carm. 20, 188.

contignatio.definition: contigno, a joining together of beams; hence, concrete A floor composed of joists and boards; a story, floor, Caes. B. C. 2, 9; 2, 15; Auct. B. Alex. 1; Vitr. 2, 9; Liv. 21, 62, 3; Pall. 1, 9, 2 al.

contigno.definition: con-tigno, no Perf., ātum, 1, tignum, to join together with beams, to furnish with beams, joists, or rafters (rare), Caes. B. C. 2, 15; Vitr. 1, 5; Plin. 9, 3, 2, § 7.

contiguus.definition: contĭgŭus, a, um, contingo (not ante-Aug.). Act. (lit. touching; hence), bordering upon, neighboring, contiguous, near; absol. or with dat.: (Pyramus et Thisbe) contiguas tenuere domos,Ov. M. 4, 57: Cappadoces,Tac. A. 2, 60: luna montibus (opp. admota caelo),Plin. 2, 9, 6, § 43: perit Valens quinquagesimo anno contiguus,Amm. 31, 14, 1: tibi,Ov. A. A. 3, 410.— * Pass., that may be touched, within reach: hunc ubi contiguum missae fore credidit hast...

continenter.definition: contĭnenter, adv., v. contineo, P. a., 1. Fin.

continentia.definition: contineo. A holding back, repressing. * (Acc. to contineo, I. B. 3., and continens, C.) The contents of a work (only late Lat.): operis,Macr. Somn. Scip. 2, 12, § 2; Hier. in Isa. 5, 20 init.; 5, 23, 11; so the title of the work of Fulgentius: De Expositione Vergilianae Continentiae, etc.— * (Acc. to contineo, II., and continens, A. 1.) Contiguity, proximity: regionum (just before: cohaerentia regionum),Macr. S. 5, 15, 5.

contineo.definition: con-tĭnĕo, tĭnŭi, tentum, 2, v. a. and n. teneo. Act., to hold or keep together. Neutr., to hold together in itself, to hang together (in the verb. finit. very rare; but freq. as P. a.; cf. also the deriv. continuus): per hortum utroque commeatus continet,Plaut. Stich. 3, 1, 43.—Hence

contingo.definition: con-tingo, tĭgi, tactum, 3, and n. tango To touch on all sides. to touch, take hold of, seize (very freq. in all periods and species of composition). Lit. Trop.

continuanter.definition: contĭnŭanter and contĭnŭātē Advv., v. 2. continuo fin., 1. and 2.

continuatim.definition: contĭnŭātim, 2. continuo Continuously, συνημμένως, συνεχῶς, Vet. Gloss.; Aug. Ep. 112, 20.

continuatio.definition: id. A following of one thing after another, an unbroken series, a connection, continuation, succession (in good prose). In gen., with gen.: continuatio seriesque rerum,Cic. N. D. 1, 4, 9: continuatio immutabilis ordinis sempiterni,id. Ac. 1, 7, 29: imbrium,an uninterrupted succession,Caes. B. G. 3, 29: laborum, * Suet. Tib. 21; Flor. 4, 2, 79 al.: causarum,Cic. N. D. 1, 20, 55: sermonis,Quint. 8, 2, 14; cf. id. 9, 3, 23 al.—Absol.: in quibus (reb...

continuativus.definition: contĭnŭātivus, a, um, continuo Serving to connect the discourse, copulative: conjunctiones,Prisc. 16, p. 1027 P.

continuatiuus.definition: contĭnŭātivus, a, um, continuo Serving to connect the discourse, copulative: conjunctiones,Prisc. 16, p. 1027 P.

continuitas.definition: continuus A connected series, continuation (very rare), Varr. L. L. 8, § 107 Müll.: spinae,Plin. 8, 30, 44, § 105.

continuor.definition: contĭnŭor, ātus, āri, 1 Dep. collat. form of continuo (rare and mostly post-class.), to unite one's self to, to join: Marius ostio Liris evehitur, adque Aenariam suos continuatur, Sisenn. ap. Non. p. 93: inde me commodum egredientem continuatur Pytheas,App. M. 1, p. 113, 17: eam,id. ib. 5, p. 172, 34; 6, p. 180, 24; 11, p. 259, 26; Enar. Pan. Const. Aug. 8, 5; Symm. Ep. 1, 53; 4, 44; cf. continuo, I. A. α fin. and β fin.

continuus.definition: contĭnŭus, a, um, contineo, II. Joining, connecting with something, or hanging together, in space or time, uninterrupted, continuous. Of space (so mostly Aug. and post-Aug.; cf., however, continue); with dat. or absol. Of time and objects relating to it, following one after another, successive, continuous (class. in all periods and species of composition): auferet ex oculis veniens Aurora Boöten; continuāque die sidus Hyantis erit,the next day,Ov...

contionabundus.definition: contĭōnābundus, a, um, contionor Proposing something or haranguing in a public assembly (several times in Livy; elsewh. very rare).

contionalis.definition: contĭōnālis, e, contio Belonging to or suitable for an assembly of the people: contionalis prope clamor senatūs,Cic. Q. Fr. 2, 5, 1: genus dicendi,Quint. 8, 4, 1: officium,id. 3, 8, 14: hirudo aerarii,Cic. Att. 1, 16, 11: senex,who went about in the assemblies of the people for the purpose of exciting the multitude,Liv. 3, 72, 4; cf. comitialis.

contionarius.definition: contĭōnārĭus, a, um, id. Of or suited to an assembly of the people (very rare): populus,Cic. Q. Fr. 2, 3, 4: oratio,Amm. 27, 6, 5: tibia,Gell. 1, 11, 10: fistula,id. 1, 11, 10 in lemm.

contionatorius.definition: contĭōnātōrĭus, false read. for contionarius, Gell. 1, 11, 10.

contionor.definition: contĭōnor, ātus, 1, contio. * To be convened or united in an assembly, to form an assembly: nunc illi vos, singuli universos contionantes timent,Liv. 39, 16, 4.— Far more freq. (Acc. to contio, II.) To deliver an oration before an assembly of the people, to harangue, address: Dionysius contionari ex turri altā solebat,Cic. Tusc. 5, 20, 59; cf.: superiore e loco contionari,id. ib. 1, 49, 117: pro tribunali,Tac. A. 1, 61 fin.: apud milites,Caes. B....

contiuncula.definition: dim.contio A short harangue, a trifling speech (only in the foll. passages): oratorem excludi ab omni doctrina, ac tantum in judicia et contiunculas tamquam in aliquod pistrinum detrudi,Cic. de Or. 1, 11, 46; id. Att. 2, 16, 1.

contollo.definition: con-tollo, ĕre, 3 V. a., to bring together: contollam gradum, will go to meet him ( = contra tollam, Wagn. ad loc.), Plaut. Aul. 5, 6 (ap. Non. p. 82, 1).

contorqueo.definition: con-torquĕo, torsi, tortum (also -torsum, acc. to Prisc. 9, p. 871 P.), 2 V. a., to turn, twist, twirl, swing, whirl or brandish, etc. (class. in prose and poetry). Lit. Trop. (mostly in Cic. and of rhet. matters; the metaphor taken from missiles which are brandished, that they may be discharged with greater force): (auditor) tamquam machinatione aliquā tum ad severitatem, tum ad remissionem animi est contorquendus,Cic. de Or. 2, 17, 72.—So of di...

contorreo.definition: con-torrĕo, ŭi, 2 V. a., to dry up entirely, to parch, scorch: herbas,Amm. 18, 7, 4.

contorte.definition: contortē, , v. contorqueo P. a. fin.

contortio.definition: contorqueo. * A whirling round: dexterae,Auct. Her. 4, 19, 26 fin. An intertwining, involving; intricacy, complication; of discourse, in the plur.: contortiones orationis, * Cic. Fat. 9, 17; Aug. Retract. 1, 50.

contortus.definition: contortus, a, um, Part. and , from contorqueo.

contra.definition: contrā, adv. and prep. stem con, i. e. cum, through a comparative form conter; cf.: alter, uter, inter, praeter, etc.; in abl. fem. form like the locative adverbs eā, quā, etc.; cf.: ultrā, intrā, extrā, citrā, orig. In comparison with; hence, over against, fronting, in front, opposite, in opposition to, against, contrary to, opposed to, etc. Adv. (referring to an opposed object often with the force of a preposition with ellipsis of a pronoun, = ...

contrabium.definition: con-trabs A framework of beams, a flooring, Cassiod. Var. 12, 18.

contractio.definition: contraho A drawing together, contraction (in good prose; most freq. in Cic.). Lit.: contractio et porrectio digitorum,Cic. N. D. 2, 60, 150: bracchii (opp. projectio),id. Or. 18, 59: superciliorum (opp. remissio),id. Off. 1, 41, 146: frontis,id. Sest. 8, 19: umerorum (opp. allevatio),Quint. 11, 3, 83: nervorum,a contraction, cramp,Scrib. Comp. 255; without nervorum,Plin. 20, 17, 73, § 191: bonorum, i. e. consolidation, Gai Inst. 2, 155.—Hence Tro...

contractor.definition: contraho, I. B. 2. One who makes a contract, a contractor, Cod. Just. 5, 5, 8; cf. Cod. Th. 10, 6, 3.

contractura.definition: id.; lit. a drawing together; hence, t. t. in architecture A lessening, contracting (of pillars), Vitr. 3, 3, 12; 5, 1, 3 al.

contractus.definition: contractus, a, um, Part. and , from contraho.

contradicibilis.definition: contrādīcĭbĭlis, e, contradico That may be contradicted or spoken against: signum,Tert. de Carn. Christ. 23.

contradico.definition: contrā-dīco, xi, ctum, 3, , until the post-Aug. per. always written as two words, v. contra, I. B. 9.

contradictio.definition: contradico A reply, answer, objection, counter-argument (post-Aug.; most freq. in Quint. of judicial replications): ubi contradictioni locus non erit,Quint. 3, 8, 34; so id. 3, 8, 27; 5, 13, 48 sq.; 7, 3, 20; Sen. Prov. 1, 1, 1; id. Q. N. 1, 5, 11: sumere,to anticipate the objection of an antagonist,Quint. 11, 3, 163; Dig. 46, 3, 72, § 1 et saep.—In plur., Quint. 5, 13, 36; 5, 13, 42; Dig. 2, 17, 36; 7, 1, 38; Tac. A. 14, 43 al.

contradictor.definition: id.; in jurid. Lat. One who objects or replies, an opponent, Dig. 40, 11, 27, § 2; 40, 16, 3; Amm. 31, 14, 3.

contradictorius.definition: contrādictōrĭus, a, um, contradictio Containing an objection or contradiction (late Lat.), Cassiod. Hist. Eccl. 8, 1.

contrado.definition: con-trādo, dĭdi, dĭtum, 3 V. a., to deliver together or wholly (late Lat.), Cassiod. Var. 8, 23; Jornand. 11 al.

contrafactio.definition: A setting in opposition, contrast (late Lat. and rare), Cassiod. Complex. Apoc. 3.

contraho.definition: con-trăho, xi, ctum, 3 V. a., to draw or bring several objects together, to collect, assemble (freq. and class.). In gen. In partic., with the prevailing idea of shortening or diminishing by drawing together (cf.: cogo, colligo, etc.), to draw close or together, to draw in, contract, shorten, narrow, lessen, abridge, diminish (freq. and class.; opp. porrigo, dilato, tendo).

contrapono.definition: contrā-pōno No perf., pŏsĭtum, 3, v. a., to place opposite, to oppose to (several times in Quint.; elsewh. only in late Lat., and rare): non semper quod adversum est contraponitur,Quint. 9, 3, 84; Tert. ad Mart. 4. As subst.: contrā-pŏ-sĭtum, i, n., antithesis, Quint. 9, 3, 32; 9, 3, 81; 9, 3, 102 al.

contrarietas.definition: contrarius Opposition, contrariety (late Lat.), Macr. Somn. Scip. 2, 14, 26; 2, 15, 30; Sid. Ep. 4, 12.

contrarius.definition: contrārĭus, a, um, contra Lying or being over against, opposite. In gen. In partic.

contrascribo.definition: contra-scrībo, psi, ptum, 3 V. a., to countersign, App. Mag. p. 324, 10.

contravenio.definition: contrā-vĕnĭo, īre V. n., to oppose (late Lat.); with dat.: humanis ratiunculis falsis, Aug. Civ. Dei, 20, 1, 1.

contrauenio.definition: contrā-vĕnĭo, īre V. n., to oppose (late Lat.); with dat.: humanis ratiunculis falsis, Aug. Civ. Dei, 20, 1, 1.

contraversus.definition: contrā-versus, a, um, Part. [verto] (post-class.) Turned opposite, lying over against; with dat.: Africa promontorio Apollinis Sardiniae,Sol. 27: spiranti Zephy. ro contraversa (urbs) Gumathenam contingit,Amm. 18, 9, 2.—Adv.: contrāver-sum, on the contrary, on the other hand, = contra, Sol. 10.

contrauersus.definition: contrā-versus, a, um, Part. [verto] (post-class.) Turned opposite, lying over against; with dat.: Africa promontorio Apollinis Sardiniae,Sol. 27: spiranti Zephy. ro contraversa (urbs) Gumathenam contingit,Amm. 18, 9, 2.—Adv.: contrāver-sum, on the contrary, on the other hand, = contra, Sol. 10.

contrectabilis.definition: contrectābĭlis (contract-), e, contrecto That may be felt or handled (except in Lucr., only in late Lat.): contractabile et solidum corpus,Lact. 2, 8 al.—* Adv.: contrectābĭlĭter (contract-), so as to be felt, Lucr. 4, 660.

contrectatio.definition: (), ōnis. id. A touching, touch, contact (very rare). Prop.: equae, vaccae,Cic. N. D. 1, 27, 77: quam contrectationes et amores soluti et liberi,id. Rep. 4, 4, 4; cf. Dig. 41, 2, 3, § 18. In the jurists, an illegal appropriation of a thing to one's self, stealing, theft, Dig. 47, 2, 1, § 2; Paul. Sent. 2, 31, 29.

contrecto.definition: con-trecto (contracto), āvi, ātum, 1, tracto To touch, handle, come in contact with, feel (class.; most freq. after the Aug. per.). Lit. Trop., to contemplate, look at, consider, dwell upon: nudare corpus et contrectandum vulgi oculis permittere,Tac. A. 3, 12: mente varias voluptates,Cic. Tusc. 3, 15, 33; cf. id. de Or. 3, 6, 24: studia et disciplinas philosophiae,to apply one's self to,Gell. 17, 19, 3.

contremisco.definition: con-trĕmisco, mŭi, 3 V. inch. n. and a. Neutr., to tremble all over, to shake, quake (rare but class.): totā mente atque omnibus artubus,Cic. de Or. 1, 26, 121; cf.: toto corpore contremisco, Caecin. ap. Cic. Fam. 6, 7, 4: contremuere,Lucr. 3, 835; Cic. Div. 1, 28, 58; Verg. A. 7, 515; Ov. M. 8, 761. Act., aliquid, to shake on account of something, to tremble at a thing, be afraid of (perh. not ante-Aug.): non contremiscamus injurias, non vulnera...

contremo.definition: con-trĕmo, ŭi, 3 V. n., to tremble greatly, to quake (rare): caelum tonitru contremit, Pac. ap. Cic. de Or. 3, 39, 157 (Trag. Rel. v. 413 Rib.): fulminis horribili cum plagā torrida tellus Contremit,Lucr. 5, 1220.

contribulatio.definition: contribulo Anguish: spiritus,Tert. adv. Jud. 13 ex Isa. 65, 14.

contribulis.definition: Of the same tribus (very rare), Inscr. Fratr. Arv. Marin. p. 43; Inscr. Grut. 873, 4; Hier. in Gal. 2, 10; Ambros. Ep. 6, 14 fin.—* Transf., of the same religion, Sid. Ep. 8, 13.

contribulo.definition: con-trībŭlo, no Perf., ātum, 1, v. a., to crush, bruise (eccl. Lat.): capita draconum,Vulg. Psa. 73, 13: dorsum ipsorum,id. Ecclus. 35, 22 sq. Trop., to afflict much, to crush: sacrificium Deo spiritus contribulatus,Vulg. Psa. 50, 18: rogationem contribulati abicere,id. Ecclus. 4, 4.

contribuo.definition: con-trĭbŭo, trĭbŭi, trĭbūtum, 3 V. a., to throw together, bring together, unite, incorporate, impart. Of a part added to or united with a whole. Of several objects united in one whole.

contributio.definition: contribuo (postclass.). A dividing, distributing: debiti et crediti,Dig. 16, 2, 1: in contributionem venire,ib. 24, 3, 7, § 4; 35, 2, 30, § 8. A contribution: omnium,Dig. 14, 2, 1.

contristatio.definition: contristo An afflicting, affliction, grief (eccl. Lat.), Tert. adv. Marc. 2, 11; id. Pud. 7 al.

contristo.definition: con-tristo, āvi, ātum, 1, tristis To make sad or sorrowful, to sadden, afflict (except in Caelius, perh. not ante-Aug.). Lit.: contristavit haec sententia Balbum, Cael. ap. Cic. Fam. 8, 9, 5: prudens ... non perturbatur nec contristatur nec timet,Sen. Ep. 85, 14.—Of animals, Col. 8, 8, 4; of bees,id. 9, 14, 11. Transf.

contritio.definition: contero A grinding. Prop., Ennod. 3 med. Trop., contrition, grief, = θλίψις (eccl. Lat.), Lact. 7, 18; Aug. Conf. 7, 7; Vulg. Jer. 30, 15; id. Psa. 13, 3; 59, 2 al.

contritus.definition: contrītus, a, um, Part. and , from contero.

controversia.definition: ( Dat. plur. CONTROVORSEIS, C. I. L. 1, 199, 1), f. controversus, lit., a turning against. * Lit.: si controversia aquae insulam subverterit,the turning of the water against it,Dig. 39, 2, 24, § 5. Trop., controversy, contention, quarrel, question, dispute, debate (so in good prose, and very freq., esp. in jurid. and rhet. lang.; in Quint. more than sixty times): nulla controversia mihi tecum erit,Plaut. Aul. 2, 2, 83: apage! controversia'st,id. ...

controuersia.definition: ( Dat. plur. CONTROVORSEIS, C. I. L. 1, 199, 1), f. controversus, lit., a turning against. * Lit.: si controversia aquae insulam subverterit,the turning of the water against it,Dig. 39, 2, 24, § 5. Trop., controversy, contention, quarrel, question, dispute, debate (so in good prose, and very freq., esp. in jurid. and rhet. lang.; in Quint. more than sixty times): nulla controversia mihi tecum erit,Plaut. Aul. 2, 2, 83: apage! controversia'st,id. ...

controversialis.definition: contrōversĭālis, e, controversia Pertaining to controversy or dispute, controversial (late Lat.), Sid. Ep. 7, 9 al.

controuersialis.definition: contrōversĭālis, e, controversia Pertaining to controversy or dispute, controversial (late Lat.), Sid. Ep. 7, 9 al.

controversiola.definition: dim.id. A little controversy, Hier. in Rufin. 1, 30; cf. Diom. p. 313 P.

controuersiola.definition: dim.id. A little controversy, Hier. in Rufin. 1, 30; cf. Diom. p. 313 P.

controversiosus.definition: contrōversĭōsus, a, um, id. Very much controverted (very rare): res,Liv. 3, 72, 5; Sen. Ep. 85, 24.

controuersiosus.definition: contrōversĭōsus, a, um, id. Very much controverted (very rare): res,Liv. 3, 72, 5; Sen. Ep. 85, 24.

controversus.definition: contrō-versus, a, um, from the same root with contra; q. v. init.. * Lit., turned against, in an opposite direction (cf. controversia, I.; very rare): perticae,Cato, R. R. 43, 1: litora Isauriae scopulis,lying opposite,Amm. 14, 2, 3; cf. id. 22, 8, 2; 22, 15, 7 (al. contra versus).—Hence Trop.

controuersus.definition: contrō-versus, a, um, from the same root with contra; q. v. init.. * Lit., turned against, in an opposite direction (cf. controversia, I.; very rare): perticae,Cato, R. R. 43, 1: litora Isauriae scopulis,lying opposite,Amm. 14, 2, 3; cf. id. 22, 8, 2; 22, 15, 7 (al. contra versus).—Hence Trop.

contrucido.definition: con-trŭcīdo, āvi, ātum, 1 V. a., to hew or cut to pieces, to cut down, to put to the sword, slay (rare, but in good prose). Prop.: debilitato corpore et contrucidato se abjecit exanimatus (cf., shortly after, concisum vulneribus),Cic. Sest. 37, 79; so, plebem immisso milite,Sen. Ira, 1, 2, 3: universos,Suet. Calig. 28; cf. id. ib. 48; id. Ner. 43 al.: taurorum opima corpora,Sen. Ep. 115, 5: bestias ad munus populi comparatas,Suet. Caes. 75.—* Tro...

contrudo.definition: con-trūdo, si, sum, 3 To thrust or crowd together (mostly anteclass.): nubes (vis venti),Lucr. 6, 510; cf. id. 6, 211 and 734: penitusque casa contrusa jacebant Corpora,crowded together,id. 6, 1254. To press, thrust, push, or crowd in: uvam in dolia,Varr. R. R. 1, 54, 2: stantis equi corpus ... videtur vis in adversum flumen contrudere, aliquos in balneas,Cic. Cael. 26, 63; Varr. L. L. 8, § 31 Müll. —Rarely of a single person: Florentius ... cont...

contrunco.definition: con-trunco, āvi, ātum, 1 V. a., to cut down or to pieces (ante- and post-class. and very rare): filios,Plaut. Bacch. 4, 9, 51; cf.: inermes et obsistentes, Lampr. Alex. Sev. 61.—Facete: cibum,Plaut. Stich. 4, 1, 48: offulam grandiorem,App. M. 1, p. 103, 35: moles palearum,id. ib. 9, p. 222, 37.

contubernalis.definition: (abl. contubernale. Pomp. ap. Charis. p. 99 P., or Com. Rel. v. 73, where Rib. reads contubernaleio; Usu. -nali,Macr. S. 2, 4, 29; Dig. 40, 7, 31, § 1; 50, 16, 220, § 1) [contubernium]. Milit. t. t. Transf. from military affairs.

contubernium.definition: taberna. Abstr. Concr. (acc. to I. A. and B.).

contueor.definition: con-tŭĕor, ŭĭtus, 2 (ante-class. and poet.; access. form Pres.contŭor, Plaut. As. 2, 3, 23; Stat. Achill. 1, 131: contuimur,Lucr. 4, 35; inf. contui, Plaut. As. 1, 1, 111; 3, 1, 20; id. Most. 3, 2, 152; Pompon. ap. Non. p. 470, 31; cf. tueor and intueor; and in act. form contuo, Enn. ap. Macr. S. 6, 2, or Fragm. v. 95 Vahl.) To look on, gaze upon, behold, survey, to consider attentively (syn. conspicio; rare but class.; most freq. in Cic.). Incho...

contuitus.definition: contŭĭtus, a, um, Part., from contueor.

contumacia.definition: contumax Perseverance in one's purpose or opinion, generally in a bad sense, arrogance, inflexibility, contumacy, obstinacy, stubbornness. Prop. Transf., of animals: contumacia pervicax boum,Col. 6, 2, 11.—Of inanim. things: arborum (with fastidium),obstinacy in growth,Plin. 16, 32, 58, § 134.

contumax.definition: con-tŭmax, ācis, adj.from the root tem, whence also temno; cf. contemno, and contumelia Insolent, unyielding, obstinate, stiff-necked, stubborn, contumacious. Prop. Transf., of animals: boves,Col. 6, 2, 10: gallina ad concubitum,id. 8, 2, 8.—Of inanimate things, not yielding, furnishing opposition: lima,Phaedr. 4, 7, 5: cardamum frianti,Plin. 12, 13, 29, § 50: syllaba,not fitting into measure,Mart. 9, 12.—Hence, adv.: contŭmācĭter, obstinately, s...

contumelia.definition: (post-class. access. form , Mart. Cap. 4, § 424; cf.: contumia contumelia, Gloss. Isid.), , from a root tem, whence also temno, contemno, and contumax; cf. Dig. 47, 10, 1 Abuse, insult, affront, reproach, invective, contumely (cf.: injuria, ὕβρις; very freq. and class. in sing. and plur.): contumelia a contemptu dicta est, quia nemo nisi quem contempsit, tali injuriā notat,Sen. Const. 11, 2: patior facile injuriam, si est vacua a contumeliā, Pa...

contumeliosus.definition: contŭmēlĭōsus, a, um, contumelia Full of abuse, reproachful, insolent, abusive (in good prose): partim te superbum esse dicunt, quod nihil respondeas, partim contumeliosum, quod male respondeas,Cic. Fam. 1, 10: uti beneficio Antonii contumelioso,id. Att. 15, 12, 1: quam contumeliosus in edictis!id. Phil. 3, 6, 15: litterae in aliquem,id. Q. Fr. 1, 2, 3, § 9; id. Balb. 9, 24; Sall. J. 65, 2: contumeliosum id militibus,Tac. H. 2, 27: dicta,Sall. J....

contumesco.definition: con-tŭmesco, ĕre V. n., to swell greatly: gingivae,Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 4, 71.

contumulo.definition: con-tŭmŭlo, āre, * To heap up like a mound: ovis stragulum molle pulvere,Plin. 10, 33, 51, § 100. To furnish with a mound, to inter, bury: saucium ingestā humo,Ov. Ib. 460; cf. id. Tr. 3, 3, 33; Mart. 8, 57, 4.

contundo.definition: (tunsum, Plin. 21, 27, 101, § 174; 28, 16, 62, § 221 al.), 3 ( Perf. contūdit, Enn. ap. Prisc. p. 891 P., or Ann. v. 482 Vahl.; but contŭdit, id. ap. Prisc. l. l., or Ann. v. 387 Vahl.), v. a., to beat, bruise, grind, crush, pound, break to pieces (syn.: confringo, debilito; very freq. and class. in prose and poetry; not in Quint.; for in 11, 2, 13, confudit is the better reading). Lit. Trop., to break, lessen, weaken, destroy, subdue, put down, ...

conturbatio.definition: conturbo Disorder, confusion. * Lit.: oculorum, confused, indistinct vision, as a disease, Scrib. Comp. 19. Trop., confusion, disquiet, perturbation of mind (rare): conturbatio metus excutiens cogitata,a fear that drives away all thought,Cic. Tusc. 4, 8, 19; id. Top. 12, 52: mentis,id. Tusc. 4, 13, 30.

conturbator.definition: id. That brings disorder or ruin (cf. conturbo, II.), poet. for ruinous, expensive, or costly (very rare): aper,Mart. 7, 27, 10: macellus,id. 10, 96, 9.

conturbo.definition: con-turbo, āvi, ātum, 1 V. a., to throw into disorder or confusion, to confuse, derange, disorder, confound (rare, but class. in prose and poetry; most freq. in Lucr. and Cic.; not in Verg., Hor., or Quint.). In gen. In partic., t. t. in the lang. of business: conturbare rationes or rationem, or absol. conturbare, to bring one's pecuniary affairs into disorder, to become bankrupt.

conturmo.definition: con-turmo, āre V. a., to arrange in squadrons (turmae). se, Amm. 16, 12, 37.

contus.definition: A pole, pike (perh. not ante-Aug.), as an implement of a boat or ship, Verg. A. 5, 208; 6, 302; Tac. A. 14, 5; Suet. Calig. 32; as a weapon,Verg. A. 9, 510; Tac. A. 6, 35; id. H. 1, 44.—Prov.: non contis et remulco ferri, ut aiunt, sed velificatione plenā,Amm. 18, 5, 6: pedalis, i. q. membrum virile,Auct. Priap. 10, 3.

contusio.definition: contundo A crushing, breaking, battering, bruising (rare). In gen.: olivae,Col. 12, 47, 3: falcis hebetioris,Plin. 17, 24, 37, § 227. In medic. language, a bruise, contusion, Scrib. Comp. 101; 165 et saep.

conubialis.definition: cōnūbĭālis (less correctly connū-bĭālis; in the poets gen. to be read as four syll.; cf. conubium; only in Claud. Ep. 2, 18, cōnŭbiālis), e, conubium Pertaining to wedlock, connubial, conjugal (poet.; perh. first used by Ov.): jura,Ov. H. 6, 41: vincla,Stat. Th. 5, 112: carmen,Claud. IV. Cons. Hon. 651: vectigal,id. Epist. 2, 18: foedus,Salv. Gub. 7, p. 244.—* Adv.: cō-nūbĭālĭter, in a conjugal manner, connubially: procum allegaret,Mart. Cap. 6, ...

conubium.definition: (less correctly ; cf. Rib. prol. Verg. p. 393), ii (m the poets often trisyl., thus: Conubio,Verg. A. 1, 73; 4, 126; 7, 253; Ov. M. 6, 428: conubia,Lucr. 3, 777: conubiis,Verg. A. 3, 136; 4, 168; v. Wagn. and Forbig. ad Verg. A. 1, 73; and cf. conubialis), n.nubo, marriage, wedlock (considered as a civil institution; while conjugium had regard to the physical union, cf. Dict. of. Antiq.). Prop. (very freq. in prose and poetry), Cic. de Or. 1, 9, ...

conus.definition: A cone. In gen., Lucr. 4, 430 and 432; Cic. N. D. 1, 10, 24; 2, 18, 47 al. Esp., of conical bodies

convalescens.definition: convălescens, ntis, and Subst., v. convalesco, I. fin.

conualescens.definition: convălescens, ntis, and Subst., v. convalesco, I. fin.

convalescentia.definition: convalesco Convalescence, a regaining of health, Symm. Ep. 3, 11 fin.

conualescentia.definition: convalesco Convalescence, a regaining of health, Symm. Ep. 3, 11 fin.

convalesco.definition: con-vălesco, lŭi, 3 V. inch. n., to recover from a disease, to regain health, to grow strong, gain strength, etc. (very freq., and class.). Lit., with ex, de, ab, or absol.: ex morbo,Cic. Fat. 12, 28 sq.; so id. Fam. 13, 29, 4; Suet. Aug. 59; cf.: de vulnere,Ov. H. 21, 211: nec omnes, qui curari se passi sunt, continuo etiam convalescant,Cic. Tusc. 3, 3, 5: eum sustulere (defatigatum vulneribus), isque convaluit, Cat. ap. Gell. 3, 7, 19: ne aegri...

conualesco.definition: con-vălesco, lŭi, 3 V. inch. n., to recover from a disease, to regain health, to grow strong, gain strength, etc. (very freq., and class.). Lit., with ex, de, ab, or absol.: ex morbo,Cic. Fat. 12, 28 sq.; so id. Fam. 13, 29, 4; Suet. Aug. 59; cf.: de vulnere,Ov. H. 21, 211: nec omnes, qui curari se passi sunt, continuo etiam convalescant,Cic. Tusc. 3, 3, 5: eum sustulere (defatigatum vulneribus), isque convaluit, Cat. ap. Gell. 3, 7, 19: ne aegri...

convallis.definition: (abl. regularly convalle, e. g. Caes. B. G. 3, 20 fin.; Liv. 1, 12, 10; Verg. G. 2, 186; id. A. 6, 679 al.: Convalli,Varr. R. R. 1, 12, 3; gen. plur. convallium, Plin. 36, 15, 23, § 100). f. (plur. post-class. access. form , , n., sc. loca, Prud. στεφ. 10, 331 al.), a valley enclosed on all sides; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 42, 6 Müll.; Varr. L. L. 5, § 20 ib. (freq. and class. in prose and poetry); Lucr. 5, 1374; Cic. Agr. 2, 35, 96; Caes. B. G. 5, 3...

conuallis.definition: (abl. regularly convalle, e. g. Caes. B. G. 3, 20 fin.; Liv. 1, 12, 10; Verg. G. 2, 186; id. A. 6, 679 al.: Convalli,Varr. R. R. 1, 12, 3; gen. plur. convallium, Plin. 36, 15, 23, § 100). f. (plur. post-class. access. form , , n., sc. loca, Prud. στεφ. 10, 331 al.), a valley enclosed on all sides; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 42, 6 Müll.; Varr. L. L. 5, § 20 ib. (freq. and class. in prose and poetry); Lucr. 5, 1374; Cic. Agr. 2, 35, 96; Caes. B. G. 5, 3...

convario.definition: con-vărĭo, āre, and n. (post-class.). Act., to variegate: cutim maculationibus,App. Mag. p. 306, 14. Neutr., to be different, to vary, Cael. Aur. Tard. 1, 1, 7.

conuario.definition: con-vărĭo, āre, and n. (post-class.). Act., to variegate: cutim maculationibus,App. Mag. p. 306, 14. Neutr., to be different, to vary, Cael. Aur. Tard. 1, 1, 7.

convectio.definition: conveho A carrying or bringing together: annonae,Amm. 14, 10, 4.

conuectio.definition: conveho A carrying or bringing together: annonae,Amm. 14, 10, 4.

convecto.definition: convecto, āre, id. To bear, carry, or bring together in abundance (very rare): recentes praedas,Verg. A. 7, 749; cf. praedam,id. ib. 4, 405: ligones, dolabras, etc., e proximis agris,Tac. H. 3, 27: paleas, ligna, Cod. Th. 7, 4, 9; 13, 5, 10.

conuecto.definition: convecto, āre, id. To bear, carry, or bring together in abundance (very rare): recentes praedas,Verg. A. 7, 749; cf. praedam,id. ib. 4, 405: ligones, dolabras, etc., e proximis agris,Tac. H. 3, 27: paleas, ligna, Cod. Th. 7, 4, 9; 13, 5, 10.

convector.definition: conveho One who carries or brings together; hence, Convector, the deity who presided over the gathering in of grain, Fab. Pict. ap. Serv. ad Verg. G. 1, 21.

conuector.definition: conveho One who carries or brings together; hence, Convector, the deity who presided over the gathering in of grain, Fab. Pict. ap. Serv. ad Verg. G. 1, 21.

conveho.definition: con-vĕho, vexi, vectum, 3 V. a., to carry, bear, or bring together (in good prose). In gen.: frumentum ex finitimis regionibus in urbem,Caes. B. C. 1, 34 fin.; cf. Liv. 25, 13, 2; 24, 39, 11 al.: lintribus in eam insulam materiem, calcem, caementa, arma, * Cic. Mil. 27, 74; cf. Liv. 4, 60, 6: tus collectum Sabota camelis,Plin. 12, 14, 32, § 63: flores (apes),id. 11, 17, 18, § 58: cibos,id. 11, 18, 20, § 64.—Absol.: undique convehunt apes,Plin. 11...

conueho.definition: con-vĕho, vexi, vectum, 3 V. a., to carry, bear, or bring together (in good prose). In gen.: frumentum ex finitimis regionibus in urbem,Caes. B. C. 1, 34 fin.; cf. convello.definition: con-vello, velli (convulsi, Sen. Q. N. 2, 6, 4), vulsum (volsum), 3 To draw violently hither and thither something that is firm or quiet (esp. a tree, house, and the like); hence, to tear up, wrest from its position, to tear loose or away, to separate from, pull or pluck up (freq. and class.). To tear or rend to pieces, to cleave, dismember, shatter, break (perh. first in the poets of the Aug. per.).

conuello.definition: con-vello, velli (convulsi, Sen. Q. N. 2, 6, 4), vulsum (volsum), 3 To draw violently hither and thither something that is firm or quiet (esp. a tree, house, and the like); hence, to tear up, wrest from its position, to tear loose or away, to separate from, pull or pluck up (freq. and class.). To tear or rend to pieces, to cleave, dismember, shatter, break (perh. first in the poets of the Aug. per.).

convelo.definition: con-vēlo, āvi, ātum, 1 V. a., to veil, to cover over (very rare). Lit.: caput,Gell. 19, 9, 10. Trop.: ἐπαγωγήν multis argumentis, Gell. 7, 3, 44.

conuelo.definition: con-vēlo, āvi, ātum, 1 V. a., to veil, to cover over (very rare). Lit.: caput,Gell. 19, 9, 10. Trop.: ἐπαγωγήν multis argumentis, Gell. 7, 3, 44.

convena.definition: Adj. comm. [convenio], coming together, meeting: ego, qui amantis unā inter se facerem convenas,Plaut. Mil. 2, 1, 61: aquae,Amm. 23, 3, 8; 23, 6, 57; Sol. 37: serpentes,id. 47: convenā undique multitudine,Amm. 15, 5, 25.—Hence, subst. plur.: , , comm., a multitude collected together, assembled strangers, refugees, tramps, etc.: eodem convenae complures ex agro accessitavere, Cato ap. Gell. 18, 12, 7: Romulus pastores et convenas congregasse videt...

conuena.definition: Adj. comm. [convenio], coming together, meeting: ego, qui amantis unā inter se facerem convenas,Plaut. Mil. 2, 1, 61: aquae,Amm. 23, 3, 8; 23, 6, 57; Sol. 37: serpentes,id. 47: convenā undique multitudine,Amm. 15, 5, 25.—Hence, subst. plur.: , , comm., a multitude collected together, assembled strangers, refugees, tramps, etc.: eodem convenae complures ex agro accessitavere, Cato ap. Gell. 18, 12, 7: Romulus pastores et convenas congregasse videt...

conveniens.definition: convĕnĭens, entis, Part. and , from convenio.

conueniens.definition: convĕnĭens, entis, Part. and , from convenio.

convenienter.definition: convĕnĭenter, , v. convenio P. a. fin.

conuenienter.definition: convĕnĭenter, , v. convenio P. a. fin.

convenientia.definition: convenio, II. A. 2. A meeting together, agreement, accord, harmony, symmetry, conformity, suitableness, fitness (a Ciceronian philosoph. word).

conuenientia.definition: convenio, II. A. 2. A meeting together, agreement, accord, harmony, symmetry, conformity, suitableness, fitness (a Ciceronian philosoph. word).

convenio.definition: con-vĕnĭo, vēni, ventum, 4 ( Fut. convenibo, Plaut. Cas. 3, 2, 18), v. n. and a. To come together, meet together, assemble (class. and freq.). Pregn.

conuenio.definition: con-vĕnĭo, vēni, ventum, 4 ( Fut. convenibo, Plaut. Cas. 3, 2, 18), v. n. and a. To come together, meet together, assemble (class. and freq.). Pregn.

conventiculum.definition: dim.conventus (rare). An assembly, meeting, association: conventicula hominum, quae postea civitates nominatae sunt, Cic. Sest. 42, 91: plebei urbanae,id. Dom. 28, 74. A place of assembly, Tac. A. 14, 15: ritus Christiani,Amm. 15, 5, 31; 27, 3, 13; Arn. 4, 152; Lact. 5, 11, 10.

conuenticulum.definition: dim.conventus (rare). An assembly, meeting, association: conventicula hominum, quae postea civitates nominatae sunt, Cic. Sest. 42, 91: plebei urbanae,id. Dom. 28, 74. A place of assembly, Tac. A. 14, 15: ritus Christiani,Amm. 15, 5, 31; 27, 3, 13; Arn. 4, 152; Lact. 5, 11, 10.

conventio.definition: convenio A meeting, assembling. In gen. (very rare), Cod. Th. 8, 8, 3; 16, 2, 14 al. Esp.

conuentio.definition: convenio A meeting, assembling. In gen. (very rare), Cod. Th. 8, 8, 3; 16, 2, 14 al. Esp.

conventiuncula.definition: dim.conventio, I. A small assembly, Aug. Ep. 56 fin.

conuentiuncula.definition: dim.conventio, I. A small assembly, Aug. Ep. 56 fin.

conventus.definition: conventus, a, um, Part. of convenio.

conuentus.definition: conventus, a, um, Part. of convenio.

convenusto.definition: con-vĕnusto, āre V. a., to ornament, adorn (late Lat.): ecclesiam cultu,Sid. Ep. 7, 12: aliquid oratione,id. ib. 8, 6: Aurora primo convenustans habitu fenestras, Mart. Cap. poët. 2, § 219 al.

conuenusto.definition: con-vĕnusto, āre V. a., to ornament, adorn (late Lat.): ecclesiam cultu,Sid. Ep. 7, 12: aliquid oratione,id. ib. 8, 6: Aurora primo convenustans habitu fenestras, Mart. Cap. poët. 2, § 219 al.

converbero.definition: con-verbĕro, āvi, ātum, 1 V. a., to strike severely, to beat, bruise (post-Aug.). Lit.: faciem,Plin. 13, 22, 43, § 126: os,Curt. 7, 2, 5. Trop.: vitia,to chastise,Sen. Ep. 121, 4; cf. id. Ira, 3, 20, 1.

conuerbero.definition: con-verbĕro, āvi, ātum, 1 V. a., to strike severely, to beat, bruise (post-Aug.). Lit.: faciem,Plin. 13, 22, 43, § 126: os,Curt. 7, 2, 5. Trop.: vitia,to chastise,Sen. Ep. 121, 4; cf. id. Ira, 3, 20, 1.

convergo.definition: con-vergo, ĕre, 3 V. n., to incline together (late Lat.): punctus quo cuncta convergunt,Isid. Orig. 3, 12, 1.

conuergo.definition: con-vergo, ĕre, 3 V. n., to incline together (late Lat.): punctus quo cuncta convergunt,Isid. Orig. 3, 12, 1.

converro.definition: con-verro (or -vorro), verri, versum, 3 V. a., to sweep or brush together, to sweep, clear away (mostly ante- and post-class.). Lit., Cato, R. R. 143, 2: hoc egomet, tu hoc convorre,Plaut. Stich. 2, 2, 27: capiam scopas atque hoc convorram,id. ib. 2, 2, 51; 2, 2, 64; Publ. Syr. ap. Prisc. p. 900 P.: stabulum,Col. 7, 6, 6: locum,id. 8, 6, 6: limina templorum osculis,Arn. 1, p. 36 al. Meton.: hereditates omnium, to scrapetogether, * Cic. Off. 3, 19...

conversatio.definition: converso (not ante-Aug.). * Frequent use, Sen. Ben. 3, 2, 2; cf. Cod. Th. 11, 21, 1 al. Frequent abode in a place, Plin. 10, 33, 51, § 100; Dig. 11, 7, 12, § 1. Intercourse, conversation (so most freq.): licentiosior cum viris,Sen. Exc. Contr. 6, 8: hominum,Vell. 2, 102, 3: multorum,Sen. Ep. 7, 1; Quint. 6, 3, 17; Tac. A. 12, 49; id. Or. 9: inter servos,Quint. 1, 2, 4.

conuersatio.definition: converso (not ante-Aug.). * Frequent use, Sen. Ben. 3, 2, 2; cf. Cod. Th. 11, 21, 1 al. Frequent abode in a place, Plin. 10, 33, 51, § 100; Dig. 11, 7, 12, § 1. Intercourse, conversation (so most freq.): licentiosior cum viris,Sen. Exc. Contr. 6, 8: hominum,Vell. 2, 102, 3: multorum,Sen. Ep. 7, 1; Quint. 6, 3, 17; Tac. A. 12, 49; id. Or. 9: inter servos,Quint. 1, 2, 4.

conversio.definition: id. A turning round, revolving, revolution (class.). Lit. Trop.

conuersio.definition: id. A turning round, revolving, revolution (class.). Lit. Trop.

conversiuncula.definition: conversio A slight change or alteration (eccl. Lat.), Salv. Ep. 4, p. 320.

conuersiuncula.definition: conversio A slight change or alteration (eccl. Lat.), Salv. Ep. 4, p. 320.

converso.definition: con-verso, āvi, ātum, 1 V. freq. * Act., to turn round: animus se ipse conversans, * Cic. Univ. 8 med.—More freq. In medial form conversor, ātus, 1 (post-Aug.; a favorite word of Seneca; not in Quint.)

conuerso.definition: con-verso, āvi, ātum, 1 V. freq. * Act., to turn round: animus se ipse conversans, * Cic. Univ. 8 med.—More freq. In medial form conversor, ātus, 1 (post-Aug.; a favorite word of Seneca; not in Quint.)

conversus.definition: conversus, a, um, Part. of converro.

conuersus.definition: conversus, a, um, Part. of converro.

convertibilis.definition: convertĭbĭlis (convers-), e, id. Changeable (post-class.): propositiones,App. Dogm. Plat. 3, p. 33, 1 and 2 (al. conversibilis): deus convertibilis et demutabilis,Prud. Apoth. 344.—Hence, con-vertĭbĭlĭter, adv., changeably (late Lat.), Aug. Music. 5, 13.

conuertibilis.definition: convertĭbĭlis (convers-), e, id. Changeable (post-class.): propositiones,App. Dogm. Plat. 3, p. 33, 1 and 2 (al. conversibilis): deus convertibilis et demutabilis,Prud. Apoth. 344.—Hence, con-vertĭbĭlĭter, adv., changeably (late Lat.), Aug. Music. 5, 13.

converto.definition: con-verto (-vorto), ti, sum, 3, v. a. and n. Act., to turn or whirl round, to wheel about, to cause to turn, to turn back, reverse; and with the designation of the terminus in quem, to turn or direct somewhere, to direct to or towards, to move or turn to, etc. (very freq. in all perr. and species of composition). Neutr., to relurn (rare).

Am. 1, 1, 83; but the explanation is not satisfactory, and Fleck. reads: in fugam set tamen nemo convortitur, acc. to converto, I. A.; cf. Neue, Formenl. II. p. 330, and Ussing ad Plaut. 1. 1.

convestio.definition: con-vestĭo, īvi, ītum, 4 (arch. Inf. pass. convestirier, Poët. ap. Cic. Tusc. 1, 28, 69), v. a., to clothe, cover with clothing (rare, and mostly in ante-class. poetry). * Lit.: cruenta corpora, Enn. ap. Macr. S. 6, 2. Transf.: prata herbis, Poët. ap. Cic. Tusc. l. l.; cf.: Topiarium laudavi: ita omnia convestivit hederā,Cic. Q. Fr. 3, 1, 2, § 5: domum lucis,to surround,id. Dom. 38, 101: omnia suā luce sol, * Lucr. 2, 147.

cophinus.definition: A basket, Col. 11, 3, 51; Juv. 3, 14; 6, 542 al.; cf. Isid Orig. 20, 9, 9.

Eun. 2, 2, 26; Varr. R. R. 3, 14, 3; Cic. Rosc. Am. 46, 134; Liv. 39, 6, 9; Mart. 14, 220, 1 sq.; Dig. 40, 4, 24 et saep.—In ancient times the cook baked also the bread; cf. Naev. ap. Paul. ex Fest. p. 58, 14 Müll.—From the ancient writing, quoquus for cocus, originates the pun upon th...

cor.definition: (ŏ, e. g. Ov. Tr. 5, 8, 28; id. P. 1, 3, 32), cordis ( Gen. plur. cordium, Vulg. Jer. 4, 4, and 1 Cor. 4, 5; acc. to Fragm. Bob. Nom. et Pron. p. 132, also cordum, but without example), n. kindr. with Sanscr. hrid; Gr. καρδία; Germ. Herz; Engl. heart, the heart (very freq. in all periods and species of composition). Lit., the heart, as the chief source of the circulation of the blood, and so of life, Cels. 4, 1; cf. Plin. 11, 37, 69. §§ 181 and ...

cora.definition: (v. Lidd. and Scott in h. v. III.) The pupil of the eye, Aus. Ep. 16, 59.

coracino.definition: cŏrăcĭno, āre, id. To caw, croak, κρίιζειν, Isid. Orig. 12, 7, 43.

coracinus.definition: cŏrăcĭnus, a. um Raven-black: color,Vitr. 8, 3, 14; so absol., coracinum, Dig. 32, 1, 78, § 5 (al. croconum).

coralium.definition: or (, Sid. Carm. 11, 110), , , = κοράλλιον; Ion. κουράλιον Coral, esp. red coral, Plin. 32, 2, 11, § 21 sq.: curalium,id. 32, 2, 11, §§ 21 and 22: coralium,Ov. M. 4, 750; 15, 416; plur.: coralia, Claud. Nupt. Hon. et Mar. 169.—In the form , , , Plin. 37, 10, 56, § 153; masc., Isid. Orig. 16, 8, 1.

corallinus.definition: cŏrallĭnus, a, um, κοράλλιον Coral-red: labra, Poëta in Anth. Lat. 1, p. 651 Burm.

coralliticus.definition: cōrallītĭcus, a, um, : Lapis,a kind of white marble found in Asia Minor,Plin. 36, 8, 13, § 62; Isid. Orig. 16, 5, 9.

coram.definition: cōram, adv. and prep. prob. kindred with ōs, ōris. Object., in the presence of, before the eyes of, in the face of, before (freq. and class.). Subject. adv., present in one's own person or presence, personally (very freq. and class.): quia ted ipsus coram praesens praesentem videt,Plaut. Ps. 4, 7, 43: istos rastros ... faoito coram ut tradas in manum,id. Merc. 2, 2, 7: sine me expurgem atque illum huc coram adducam,Ter. And. 5, 3, 29: velut si co...

coranus.definition: Cŏrānus, a, um, v. 3. Cora, II.

corbicula.definition: dim.corbis A little basket, Pall. Febr. 10, 6.

corbis.definition: (abl. regularly corbe: Corbi,Cato, R. R. 136 twice), comm. corbes dicti quod curvatis virgis contexuntur, Isid. l. l.; but more prob. kindr. with κόλπος, a basket (esp. for use in gathering fruits, etc.).

corbona.definition: Syrian A treasurechamber, Hier. Ep. 27, 14; Vulg. Matt. 27, 6.

corbula.definition: dim.corbis A little basket, Cato, R. R. 11, 5; Varr. R. R. 1, 15; id. L. L. 5, § 139; Col. 12, 50, 8; Plaut. Aul. 2, 7, 4; Caecil. ap. Non. p. 197, 29; Suet. Ner. 19 al.

corculum.definition: dim.cor A little heart, Plaut. Most. 4, 2, 70; as a term of endearment,id. Cas. 4, 4, 14.—As a surname of Scipio Nasica, on account of his sagacity, Cic. Tusc. 1, 9, 18; id. Brut. 20, 70; Aur. Vict. Vir. Ill. 44, 6; and as masc. in plur.: Corculi cognominati,Plin. 7, 31, 31, § 118; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 61, 5 Müll.

corcus.definition: i. A disease of the chest, Marc. Emp. 21 dub.

cordatus.definition: cordātus, a, um, cor, II. B. Wise, prudent, judicious, sagacious (mostly anteand post-class.): egregie cordatus homo, Enn. ap. Cic. Tusc. 1, 9, 18 (Ann. v. 335 Vahl.); cf. Cic. Rep. 1, 18, 30; Sen. Lud. Mort. Claud. 12, 2, v. 7; Vulg. Job, 34, 10.—Comp.: cordatior,Lact. 3, 20, 2.—Adv.: cordātē, with prudence, wisely (with docte and cate), Plaut. Mil. 4, 2, 97; id. Poen. 1, 1, 3.
