cordax.definition: The extravagant dance of Grecian comedy, distinguished by lively movement and wanton gesture, and by the rope which was kept passing through the hands of the dancers; the imitation of this dance was regarded as a mark of drunkenness or licentiousness: ducere, to dance it (κόρδακα ἕλκειν), Petr. 52, 9 (cf. Ter. Ad. 4, 7, 34).—Adject.: cordaces sententiae, i. e. tinnulae, staggering (together with modulatae), Fronto de Or. 2, p. 240 Mai. Transf....

cordicitus.definition: cordĭcĭtus, cor From the heart, deep in the heart, Sid. Ep. 4, 6.

cordolium.definition: dolor Sorrow at heart, grief (ante- and post-class.), Plaut. Cist. 1, 1, 67; id. Poen. 1, 2, 86; App. M. 9, p. 226, 28.

corduba.definition: Κορδύβη A town in Hispania Baetica, on the river Baetis, now Caes. B. C. 2, 19 al.—, , adj., of Corduba, Plin. 3, 1, 3, § 7; 34, 2, 2, § 4; Auct. B. Alex. 57.—Hence. , , , the inhabitants of Corduba, Auct. B. Alex. 59.

cordyla.definition: The fry of the tunny-fish, Plin. 9, 15, 18, § 47; Mart. 3, 2, 4.

coriaceus.definition: cŏrĭăcĕus, a, um, corium Of leather: naves,made of leather,Amm. 24, 3, 11.

coriaginosus.definition: cŏrĭāgĭnōsus, a, um, coriago Afflicted with the coriago (late Lat.; perh. only in Veg.): equi,Veg. Art. Vet. 2, 10, 2; 2, 16, 1.

coriandrum.definition: or , , n.; also , , f. κορίαννον Coriander: Coriandrum sativum, Linn.; Cato, R. R. 157, 6 sq.; Col. 6, 33, 2; 11, 3, 29; Plin. 19, 7, 35, § 117 sq.; Varr. L. L. 5, § 103 Müll.; Plaut. Ps. 3, 2, 25; Apic. 4, 3, § 174 sq.

coriarius.definition: cŏrĭārĭus, a, um, corium Of or pertaining to leather frutex, i. e. useful for tanning leather, Plin. 24, 11, 54, § 91.— Hence Subst.: cŏrĭārĭus, ii, m., a tanner, currier, Plin. 17, 9, 6, § 51; Inscr. Orell. 4074 al.

corinthus.definition: (nom. Gr. Corinthos, Ov. M. 6, 416; acc. Gr. Corinthon, id. F. 4, 501; Mart. 9, 60; 10, 68), ( Masc., Inscr. Fratr. Arval. p. 30 Marin.: CORINTO DELETO), = Κόρινθος, Corinth, a celebrated commercial city in the Peloponnesus, pillaged and destroyed by Mummius, now the village Corinto or Gereme; it was situated on the Isthmus (hence, bimaris, Hor. C. 1, 7, 2; Ov. M. 5, 407; id. F. 4, 501; and: bimaris terra,Sen. Oedip. 282), Mel. 2, 3, 7; Plin. 4,...

corium.definition: n. (ante-class. , , m., Plaut. Poen. 1, 1, 11; id. Fragm. ap. Paul. ex Fest. p. 60, 7; Sillig reads caros in both places; Varr. ap. Non. p. 199, 16) [for scorium, kindr. with scortum; Sanscr. kar; old Germ. sceran; Gr. χόριον] Skin, hide, leather. Meton.

cornetum.definition: 1. cornus A grove of cornel-trees, Varr. L. L. 5, § 152 Müll.; cf. id. ib. § 146.

corneus.definition: cornĕus, a, um, cornu. Of horn, horny, horn- (rare but class.): corneo proceroque rostro (ibes), * Cic. N. D. 1, 36, 101: ora,Ov. M. 8, 545: arcus,id. ib. 1, 697: pyxis,Plin. 29, 6, 39, § 142: laterna,Mart. 14, 61: crater,id. 12, 32, 12: ungula (equi),Luc. 6, 83; cf. solum,Varr. R. R. 2, 9, 4: porta Somni,Verg. A. 6, 894; cf. Stat. S. 5, 3, 288. Hard as horn, horny (very rare): corpora piscatorum,Plin. 31, 9, 45, § 102; 7, 19, 18, § 80. Of the co...

cornicen.definition: cornu-cano; cf.: tibicen, tubicen, etc. A horn-blower, corneter, Liv. 2, 64, 10; Cic. Rep. 2, 22, 40; Juv. 2, 118; 3, 34 al.

cornicor.definition: cornīcor, āri, cornix To caw like a crow (very rare): quid grave secum inepte,Pers. 5, 12; cf. Prisc. p. 828 P.; Hier. Ep. 125, n. 16.

corniculans.definition: cornĭcŭlans, antis, 1. corniculum Horn-shaped, horned (late Lat.): luna,i. e. the new moon,Sol. 32, 17; Amm. 20, 3, 1; cf. corniculatus.

cornicularius.definition: 1. corniculum. In milit. lang. (prop. one who had been presented with a corniculum, and thereby promoted), an adjutant of a centurion, tribune, propraetor, etc. (post-Aug.), Val. Max. 6, 1, 11; Front. Strat. 3, 14, 1; Suet. Dom. 17; Inscr. Orell. 3465; Ascon. ad Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 28, § 71 al. Transf. to civil offices, an assistant, aid, secretary, Cod. Th. 1, 15, 11; 7, 4, 32; 8, 4, 10; Firm. Math. 3, 6.

corniculum.definition: dim.cornu A little horn. Prop., Plin. 9, 42, 67, § 143; 11, 28, 34, § 100. Meton.

corniculus.definition: 1. corniculum The civil office of a cornicularius, Cod. Th. 1, 15, 11; 8, 7, 8.

corniger.definition: cornĭger, gĕra, gĕrum, cornugero Having or bearing horns, horned (poet.): cervi,Lucr. 3, 751; Ov. M. 7, 701: matres haedi,Lucr. 2, 368: Taurus, Cic. poët. N. D. 2, 43, 110; Ov. M. 15, 511: juvencae,id. ib. 13, 926: Ammon,id. ib. 5, 17; 15, 309; cf. Stat. Th. 8, 201: fluvius Hesperidum,Verg. A. 8, 77; cf. Numicius,Ov. M. 14, 602: Lyaeus,id. Am. 3, 15, 17; v. Bacchus, I.—Subst.: cornĭgĕra, ōrum, n. (sc. animalia), horned animals, horned cattle, Pli...

cornipes.definition: cornĭ-pēs, pĕdis, cornu Hornfooted, hoofed (poet.): capella,Cat. 19, 16: equi,Verg. A. 6, 591: Faunus,Ov. F. 2, 361: planta (Panis),Sil. 13, 338.—Also subst.: cornĭpēs, pĕdis, m. (so most freq. in Claud.), a horn-footed animal; of the horse, Sil. 3, 361; 7, 684; Claud. Fesc. 11, 11 al.; of the centaur Chiron, Claud. in Rufin. 2, 180 et saep.

cornix.definition: kindred with corvus and κορώνη A crow, Lucr. 5, 1083: rauca,id. 6, 753: garrula,Ov. M. 2, 548: loquax,id. F. 2, 89; Plin. 10, 12, 14, § 30 al.; renowned as being long lived,Lucr. 5, 1083; Cic. Tusc. 3, 28, 69; Hor. C. 3, 17, 13; Ov. M. 7, 274; Plin. 7, 48, 49, § 153 et saep.; its appearance on the left side was considered as a favorable omen,Plaut. As. 2, 1, 12; Cic. Div. 1, 39, 85; Verg. E. 9, 15; Phaedr. 3, 18, 12; cf. Suet. Dom. 23; and its c...

cornu.definition: (so Caes. B. C. 3, 68 Dint.; Luc. 7, 217; Plin. 28, 11, 46, § 163 et saep.; Curt. 4, 12, 11 al.; ū in the connection cornu bubuli and cornu cervini; also Cael. Aur. Tard. 3, 5, 76; Veg. Art. Vet. 1, 20, 1 al.; cf. esp. Neue, Formenl. 1, p. 355), n. (access. form , , n., Varr. R. R. 3, 9, 14; Ter. Eun. 4, 7, 5 Fleck.; Lucr. 2, 388; Ov. M. 2, 874; Scrib. Comp. 141; Gell. 14, 6, 2 al.; Gen. plur. cornorum, Scrib. Comp. 60. —An access. form , , has b...

cornualis.definition: cornŭālis, e, cornu Of or pertaining to horns: concertatio,with the horns,Cassiod. Var. 1, 37.

cornulum.definition: dim.cornu A little horn, = corniculum (late Lat.), Apic. 8, 1.

cornum.definition: 1. cornus The cornelcherry, Verg. G. 2, 34; id. A. 3, 649; Hor. Ep. 1, 16, 9; Ov. M. 1, 105; 8, 665; 13, 816; Col. 12, 10, 3.—* = 1. cornus, II., Ov. M. 8, 408.

cornupeta.definition: cornupĕta, ae Adj. comm., pushing or goring with the horns, Vulg. Exod. 21, 29; 21, 36.

cornus.definition: f. (cornus, , f., Sil. 4, 552; Stat. Th. 7, 647) A cornel cherry-tree: Cornus mascula, Linn.; Plin. 16, 25, 42, § 103 sq.; Verg. G. 2, 448; Col. 5, 7, 1 al. Meton., a javelin made of cornelwood, Verg. A. 9, 698; Sil. 10, 122; Stat. l. l. al.; cf. 1. cornum, II.

cornutus.definition: cornūtus, a, um, cornu Horned: animalia,Varr. R. R. 2, 7, 2: aries,Col. 7, 3, 4. Trop.: syllogismus, a horned syllogism, a sophistical conclusion, sophism, = ceratina, Hier. Ep. 69, n. 2; cf.: cornuta interrogatio,id. adv. Helvid. 16.

corolla.definition: dim.corona A little crown or garland (mostly poet.), Plaut. Bacch. 1, 1, 37; Cat. 63, 66; Prop. 1, 16, 7; Plin. 8, 5, 5, § 13; Paul. ex Fest. p. 63, 14 Müll.

corollarium.definition: id.. Money paid for a garland of flowers; cf. Varr. L. L. 5, § 178; Plin. 21, 2, 3, § 5.—Hence In gen., a gift, present, douceur, gratuity: hic tamquam festivum acroama, ne sine corollario de convivio discederet, ibidem emblemata evellenda curavit,Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 22, § 49; 2, 3, 50, § 118; 2, 3, 79, § 184; Phaedr. 5, 7, 34; Sen. Ben. 6, 17, 1; Plin. 9, 35, 58, § 120.

corona.definition: (in the ante-Aug. per. sometimes written chorona, acc. to Quint. 1, 5, 20; cf. the letter C) A garland, chaplet, wreath. Lit., of natural or artificial flowers, etc. (very freq. used for personal adornment at festivals, when sacrificing, or as a gift for friends, etc., for ornamenting the images of the gods, edifices, victims, the dead, etc.), Lucr. 5, 1399; Lex XII. Tab. ap. Plin. 21, 3, 5, § 7; Plaut. Men. 3, 1, 16; Cic. Fl. 31, 75; id. Leg. 2,...

coronamentum.definition: id. Flowers for crowns or garlands, Cato, R. R. 8, 2; Plin. 21, 1, 1, § 1; 21, 9, 28, § 52 sq.; 22, 21, 26, § 53. The garland or crown itself, Tert. Cor. Mil. 1; 7.

coronarius.definition: cŏrōnārĭus, a, um, adj.corona Of or belonging to a wreath: anemonae,suitable for garlands,Plin. 21, 23, 94, § 164: aes,id. 33, 9, 46, § 131: lusus naturae,i. e. presenting a garland-like growth,id. 14, 3, 4, § 42: opus,stucco-work,Vitr. 7, 4 and 6; but also,the making of a golden crown,id. 9, praef. 10.—Esp. freq.: coronarium aurum, a present of gold collected in the provinces for a victorious general (orig. expended for a golden crown; cf. Liv. ...

corono.definition: cŏrōno, āvi, ātum, 1, corona To furnish with a garland or crown, to crown, wreathe (class., esp. freq. in the poets). Lit., aliquid or aliquem: templa,Ov. M. 8, 264; cf.: postes lauro,Quint. 8, 6, 32: aras,Prop. 3 (4), 10, 19.deos fragili myrto,Hor. C. 3, 23, 15: puppim,Ov. F. 4, 335: cratera,Verg. G. 2, 528 (cf.: magnum cratera coronā Induit,id. A. 3, 525); so, crateras magnos statuunt et vina coronant,id. A. 1, 724; 7, 147 Forbig. ad loc. (cf. ...

coronula.definition: dim.corona, II. D.. The ornament on a mitre, Vulg. Exod. 39, 26. The rim or border of the base of a laver, Vulg. 3, Reg. 7, 29. A little crown above the horse's hoof, Veg. Art. Vet. 3, 55, 2.

corporalis.definition: corpŏrālis, e, corpus Corporeal, pertaining to the body (post-Aug.; most freq. in the jurists): voluptates,Sen. Ep. 78, 22: sapientiam Stoici corporalem dicunt,id. ib. 117, 2: pignora,Dig. 1, 1, 15: possessio,ib. 13, 7, 40: dicimus quaedam corporalia esse, quaedam incorporalia,Sen. Ep. 58, 11.—Adv.: corpŏrālĭter, corporally, bodily, Petr. 61, 7; Dig. 41, 2, 1; Arn. 5, p. 168.

corporalitas.definition: corporalis Corporality (late Lat.), Tert. adv. Herm. 36.

corporasco.definition: corpŏrasco, ĕre V. inch. n. [corpus], to assume a body, become incarnate (eccl. Lat.): Deus,Claud. Mam. Stat. Anim. 1, 14.

corporativus.definition: corpŏrātīvus, a, um, corporatus Of or pertaining to the forming of a body (late Lat.): adjutoria,Cael. Aur. Tard. 1, 6, 183.

corporatiuus.definition: corpŏrātīvus, a, um, corporatus Of or pertaining to the forming of a body (late Lat.): adjutoria,Cael. Aur. Tard. 1, 6, 183.

corporatura.definition: id. The corporeal nature or structure (very rare): pecoris,Col. 6, 2, 15.—In plur.: ampliores,Vitr. 6, 1, 3.

corporeus.definition: corpŏrĕus, a, um, corpus Corporeal. In gen. (rare but class.; most freq. in Lucr.): corporeum et aspectabile itemque tractabile,Cic. Univ. 4: res,id. Fin. 3, 14, 45; Lucr. 2, 186: ignis,Cic. N. D. 2, 15, 41: natura,Lucr. 1, 303; 1, 330: e principiis,id. 4, 536: tela,id. 3, 177: vox,id. 4, 527; 4, 542; opp. incorporeus,Mart. Cap. 6, § 607. In partic.

corporo.definition: corpŏro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.corpus To make or fashion into a body, to furnish with a body. Prop.: semen tempore ipso animatur corporaturque,Plin. 7, 15, 13, § 66; cf. id. 10, 53, 74, § 148.—In part. perf.: corporatus Christus et veste carnis indutus,Lact. 4, 26; Tert. Pall. 2: undique mundus, * Cic. Univ. 2 B. and K. Transf.

corporosus.definition: corpŏrōsus, a, um, corpus Corpulent, gross, Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 17.

corpulentia.definition: corpulentus Corpulence, grossness or fleshiness of body (very rare), Plin. 11, 53, 118, § 283; Sol. 40. Corporeity (late Lat.), Tert. Carn. Chr. 3 al.

corpulentus.definition: corpŭlentus, a, um, corpus Corpulent, fleshy, fat (rare, and only anteclass. and post-Aug.): corpulentior atque habitior,Plaut. Ep. 1, 1, 8: litigator,Quint. 6, 1, 47: homo corpulentus et pinguis,Gell. 7, 22, 1: pecus,Col. 6, 3, 5. Physical, corporeal (late Lat.), Tert. adv. Herm. 19.

corpus.definition: cf. Sanscr. kar-, to make; Lat. creo Any object composed of materials perceptible by the senses, body, substance (opp. anima and animus; cf. the definition in Dig. 41, 3, 30 pr.). Lit. (very frequent in every period and species of composition). Meton., a whole composed of parts united, a body, frame, system, structure, community, corporation, etc.; of ships,the framework,Caes. B. C. 1, 54.—Of fortifications: totum corpus coronā militum cingere,Ca...

corpusculum.definition: dim.corpus A little body, most freq. of atoms, Lucr. 2, 152; 2, 530; 4, 199; Cic. N. D. 1, 24, 66 sq.: quantula hominum,Juv. 10, 173. As a term of endearment: melliculum,Plaut. Cas. 4, 4, 23.

corrado.definition: cor-rādo (conr-), si, sum, 3 V. a., to scrape or rake together (rare; mostly anteand post-class.). Lit.: corpora,Lucr. 6, 304; cf. id. 6, 444.—Esp., of money, Plaut. Poen. 5, 6, 26; Ter. Ad. 2, 2, 34; Dig. 26, 7, 4 al.; and of the collecting together of one's effects for sale,Ter. Heaut. 1, 1, 89. —* Trop., to procure with difficulty: fidem dictis nostris,Lucr. 1, 402.

correctio.definition: (), , corrigo An amendment, improvement, correction. In gen. (rare, but in good prose): correctio et emendatio philosophiae veteris,Cic. Fin. 4, 9, 21; cf.: veteris Academiae,id. Ac. 1, 12, 43: quādam adhibita,id. Off. 3, 2, 7: morum,Suet. Tib. 42; id. Dom. 8: delicto dolere, correctione gaudere,Cic. Lael. 24, 90. Esp., as a rhet. figure, the recalling of a word in order to use a stronger or more significant one in its place, Gr. ἐπανόρθωσις, C...

corrector.definition: (), , id. A corrector, improver. In gen. (rare but class.): corrector atque emendator nostrae civitatis,Cic. Balb. 8, 20: asperitatis et invidiae et irae,Hor. Ep. 2, 1, 129: unus legum usus,Liv. 45, 32, 7: peccantium,Sen. Ira, 2, 10, 7 al.—Absol., Ter. Ad. 4, 7, 24: corrector Bestius,i. e. a preacher of morals,Hor. Ep. 1, 15, 37: pessimus quisque correctorem asperrime patitur,Sen. Ira, 3, 36, 4. In the time of the emperors, the title of a kind of...

correctura.definition: (), , corrector, II. The office of a corrector, Aur. Vict. Caes. 35; 39; Aus. Parent. 24, 11.

correctus.definition: correctus (conr-), a, um, Part. and , from corrigo.

correcumbens.definition: cor-rĕcumbens (conr-), entis, Part. [recumbo] Lying down with any one, Tert. Test. An. 4.

corregno.definition: cor-regno (conr-), āre V. n., to reigntogether with one (late Lat.), Tert. adv. Jud. 8; Paul. Nol. Carm. 25, 227.

correpo.definition: cor-rēpo (conr-), psi, 3 V. n., to creep or slink to a place, to creep (rare but class.): intra murum,Varr. R. R. 2, praef. § 3; Col. 1, praef. § 15: in aliquam onerariam,Cic. Att. 10, 12, 2: correpunt membra pavore, creep, * Lucr. 5, 1218.—Fig.: in dumeta,Cic. N. D. 1, 24, 68 (v. Schoemann ad h. l.).

correpte.definition: correptē (conr-), corripio Shortly: dicere aliquid,Gell. 6, 9.—Comp., Ov. P. 4, 12, 13.

correptio.definition: (), , id. (not ante-Aug., and rare). A laying hold of, seizing: manus,Gell. 20, 10, 8: (morbi),Scrib. Comp. 171. A shortening, decreasing: dierum (opp. crescentia),Vitr. 9, 9: syllabae (opp. productio),Quint. 7, 9, 13; cf. vocum,id. 9, 3, 69.

correpto.definition: correpto, āre, 1 V. n. freq. [correpo], to creep (late Lat.): rursum matris in alvum,Juvenc. 2, 192.

correptor.definition: (), , corripio A reprover, censurer (cf. correptio, I. B.); the reading of some editions of Sen. Ira, 2, 10, 7, and 3, 36, 4, for which Haase has corrector, q. v.

correptus.definition: correptus (conr-), a, um, Part., from corripio.

corresupinatus.definition: cor-rĕsŭpīnātus (conr-), a, um, Part. [resupino] Bent backwards at the same time, Tert. Anim. 48.

corresuscito.definition: cor-rĕsuscĭto (conr-), āvi, ātum, 1 V. a., to raise from the dead together (eccl. Lat.), Tert. Res Carn. 23; Hier. adv. Jov. 1, 38 al.

corrigia.definition: (), , corrigo. A shoe-tie, shoe-latchet, Varr. ap. Non. p. 448, 26; Cic. Div. 2, 40, 84; Plin. 30, 4, 12, § 35. A rein for a horse, Edict. Diocl. p. 26.

corrigo.definition: cor-rĭgo (conr-), rexi, rectum, 3, rego To make straight, set right, bring into order. Lit. (rare): catenas,Cato, R. R. 18 fin.: alicui digitum,Plin. 7, 20, 19, § 83: verbaque correctis incidere talia ceris,smoothed out, erased,Ov. M. 9, 529: corpus informe gibbo, Aug. ap. Macr. S. 2, 4: vulvas conversas,Plin. 24, 5, 13, § 22; cf.: malas labentes,Suet. Aug. 99: cursum (navis),Liv. 29, 27, 14; cf.: se flexus (fluminum),Plin. 3, 1, 3, § 16. Trop., ...

corripio.definition: cor-rĭpĭo (conr-), rĭpŭi, reptum, 3, rapio To seize or snatch up, to collect, to seize upon, take hold of (very freq., and class. in prose and poetry). Lit. Trop.

corrivo.definition: cor-rīvo (conr-), āvi, ātum, 1 V. a., to conduct streams of water together, to draw together into one stream (post-Aug.): venas aquarum,Sen. Q. N. 3, 19, 4; cf. aquam,Dig. 39, 3, 3; Plin. 31, 4, 30, § 53: liquorem salis,id. 6, 14, 17, § 43: Tiberim piscinis,id. 3, 5, 9, § 53; with in aliquid, id. 6, 16, 18, § 47.

corriuo.definition: cor-rīvo (conr-), āvi, ātum, 1 V. a., to conduct streams of water together, to draw together into one stream (post-Aug.): venas aquarum,Sen. Q. N. 3, 19, 4; cf. aquam,Dig. 39, 3, 3; Plin. 31, 4, 30, § 53: liquorem salis,id. 6, 14, 17, § 43: Tiberim piscinis,id. 3, 5, 9, § 53; with in aliquid, id. 6, 16, 18, § 47.

corroboramentum.definition: (), , corroboro A means of strengthening; trop.: exercitia et corroboramenta virtutis,Lact. 3, 12, 35.

corroboro.definition: cor-rōbŏro (conr-), āvi, ātum, 1 V. a., to strengthen or invigorate, to make strong, to corroborate (in good prose; most freq. in Cic.). Lit.: (puerilis tua vox) se corroboravit,Cic. Sest. 4, 10: cum is jam se corroboravisset ac vir inter viros esset,i. e. had become stronger, greater, was grown up,id. Cael. 5, 11; cf. id. ib. 17, 41; Suet. Tib. 11: cerebrum,Plin. 11, 37, 49, § 134: stomachum,id. 20, 23, 99, § 263: torpentis membrorum partis,id. ...

corroco.definition: A kind of fish, now unknown, Aus. Ep. 4, 60.

corrodo.definition: cor-rōdo (conr-), si, sum, 3 V. a., to gnaw, gnaw to pieces (very rare): Platonis Politiam (mures),Cic. Div. 2, 27, 59 ter: ossa, * Juv. 15, 80.

corrogatio.definition: (), , corrogo A bringing together, Vulg. Ecclus. 32, 3.

corrogo.definition: cor-rŏgo (conr-), āvi, ātum, 1 V. a., to bring together by entreaty, to bring together, collect (rare, but in good prose): suos necessarios ab atriis,Cic. Quint. 6, 25; so of personal objects,id. Phil. 3, 8, 20; Quint. 10, 1, 18; Plin. Ep. 2, 14, 9: auxilia ab sociis,Liv. 43, 9, 7: pecuniam ad necessarios sumptus,Caes. B. C. 3, 102: nummulos de nepotum donis,Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 79, § 184: vela cum antennis ex navibus,Liv. 33, 48, 5 al.

corrotundo.definition: cor-rŏtundo (conr-), āvi, ātum, 1 V. a., to make round, to round off (postAug.). Prop.: cometarum corpus,Sen. Q. N. 7, 26, 2; 4, 3, 5; Petr. 39, 15. Transf., of money (cf. rotundo, and our phrase, a round sum), to make up a sum of money: centies sestertium,Petr. 76, 8.

corruda.definition: () Wild asparagus, Cato, R. R. 6, 3; Varr. R. R. 1, 24, 4; Col. 11, 3, 43; Plin. 19, 8, 42, § 145.

corrugo.definition: cor-rūgo (conr-), no Perf., ātum, 1, v. a., to make full of wrinkles, to wrinkle, corrugate (very rare): olivam,Col. 12, 50, 19; cf. acina,id. 12, 39, 3.—Poet.: ne sordida mappa Corruget nares,i. e. produce loathing, cause disgust,Hor. Ep. 1, 5, 23 (cf. Quint. 11, 3, 80).

corrumpo.definition: cor-rumpo (conr-), rūpi, ruptum (rumptum), 3, (orig. To break to pieces; hence) To destroy, ruin, waste, bring to naught (class., but less freq. than in the signif. II.]. With regard to the physical or moral quality of an object, to corrupt, mar, injure, spoil, adulterate, make worse, etc. (very freq., and class. in prose and poetry).

corruo.definition: cor-rŭo (conr-), ŭi, 3, and A. Neutr. Act., to bring to the ground, to heap together, overthrow, ruin (very rare).

corrupte.definition: corruptē (conr-), , v. corrumpo P. a. fin.

corruptela.definition: (), ante-class. also , , corrumpo That which corrupts, a corrupting, corruption, seduction, bribery, etc. Prop. (freq. and class. in sing. and plur.): mores hac (sc. cantūs) dulcedine corruptelaque depravati,Cic. Leg. 2, 15, 38: collapsus est hic in corruptelam suam,Plaut. Truc. 3, 2, 3: quem (adulescentulum) corruptelarum illecebris irretisses,Cic. Cat. 1, 6, 13: stupra dico et corruptelas et adulteria,id. Tusc. 4, 35, 75; cf. Suet. Claud. 16: v...

corruptibilis.definition: corruptĭbĭlis (conr-), e, id. Liable to decay, corruptible, perishable (eccl. Lat.), Lact. 6, 25; Arn. 2, 68 al.—Comp., Aug. de Vera Relig. 41.

corruptibilitas.definition: (), , corruptibilis Corruptibility, perishableness (eccl. Lat.), Tert. adv. Marc. 2, 16.

corruptio.definition: corruptĭo (conr-), ōnis F [corrumpo]. Act., a corrupting, spoiling, seducing: militum,bribery,Tac. A. 11, 2: judicii,Ascon. ad Cic. Verr. 1, 6, 15, p. 131 Bait. —Absol.: eo usque corruptionis provectus est, ut, etc.,Tac. A. 2, 55. Pass., a corrupt condition, corruption (very rare): totius corporis,Cic. Tusc. 4, 13, 29.

corruptivus.definition: corruptīvus (conr-), a, um, adj. id. Corruptible, perishable (eccl. Lat.), Tert. Res Carn. 50.—corruptīvē, adv., Boëth Arist. Top. 7, 2, p. 721.

corruptiuus.definition: corruptīvus (conr-), a, um, adj. id. Corruptible, perishable (eccl. Lat.), Tert. Res Carn. 50.—corruptīvē, adv., Boëth Arist. Top. 7, 2, p. 721.

corruptor.definition: (, Plaut. Trin. 2, 1, 14 Ritschl), , id. A corrupter, misleader, seducer, briber: latebricolarum hominum (amor),Plaut. Trin. 2, 1, 14: civium,id. Poen. 3, 6, 21: juventutis,Cic. Cat. 2, 4, 7: estne in corruptorem marito justior potestas? Hor. S. 2, 7, 63; cf.: virginum Vestalium,Suet. Dom. 8: nostri,Cic. Rab. Post. 3, 6; cf.: tribus venditor et corruptor,id. Planc. 16, 38.

corruptorius.definition: corruptōrĭus (conr-), a um, corrumpo Destructible, corruptible, perishable (eccl. Lat.), Tert. adv. Marc. 2, 16: sensus in homine,id. ib.

corruptrix.definition: (), , corruptor She that corrupts or seduces; or adj., corrupting (very rare): tam depravatis moribus, tam corruptrice provinciā,Cic. Q. Fr. 1, 1, 6, § 19: licentia, rerum corruptrix et morum,Amm. 25, 3, 18.

corruptus.definition: corruptus (conr-), a, um, Part. and , from corrumpo.

corruspor.definition: cor-ruspor (conr-), āri V. dep., to search carefully after, = conquiro, Plaut. Fragm. ap. Paul. ex Fest. p. 62 Müll.

corsica.definition: (, , Prisc. Perieg. 470), (among the Greeks, Κύρνος, Κορσίς) The island Corsica, in the Mediterranean Sea, renowned in ancient times for the honey and wax of wild bees; the place of banishment of Seneca the philosopher, Liv. Epit. 17; Sen. Cons. Helv. 6, 2; Tac. H. 2, 16; Mel. 2, 7, 19; Plin. 3, 6, 12, § 80; Monum. Scip. ap. Inscr. Orell. 552; Cic. N. D. 3, 20, 52 al. Hence adjj.

cortex.definition: m. and rar. f. (cf. Quint. 1, 5, 35) [Sanscr. kart, to cut, split; Gr. κείρω; cf. culter] The bark, rind, shell, hull. Prop., of plants: obducuntur libro aut cortice trunci,Cic. N. D. 2, 47, 120. Transf., of other shells than those of vegetables: ovi,Vitr. 8, 3.

corticeus.definition: cortĭcĕus, a, um, id. Of bark or cork, Varr. R. R. 1, 40; 3, 16; Plin. 11, 21, 24, § 71 (cortice, Sillig); Aus. Mos. 246 al.

cortina.definition: A round vessel, a kettle, caldron (for cooking, liquids, etc.), Cato, R. R. 66, 1; Plin. 15, 6, 6, § 22 al.; 36, 26, 65, § 191; Plaut. Poen. 5, 5, 12. Meton., of any thing caldron-shaped, an arch, a circle (very rare); the cault of heaven, Enn. ap. Varr. L. L. 7, § 48 Müll. N. cr. (Ann. v. 9 Vahl.); the circle of a theatre, Auct. Aetn. 295; and prob. also a circle of hearers, Tac. Or. 19 dub. (v. Andresen in h. l.).

cortinipotens.definition: Cortīnĭ-pŏtens, entis, id. Powerful on the tripod, an epithet of Apollo, Lucil. ap. Non. p. 258, 33.

cortinula.definition: dim.id. A small kettle, Amm. 29, 1, 31 dub. (v. Wagner ad h. l.).

cortumio.definition: cortumio, an old word of the augurial lang., perh. equiv. to contumio, from contueor, Varr. L. L. 7, § 9 Müll.

coruscatio.definition: id. A glittering, a flash, coruscation (post-class.): (margaritarum),Sol. 53 fin.: immanis,Vop. Car. 8.

corusco.definition: cŏrusco, āre, and n. (the access. form conisco is found in some copies of Lucr. 2, 320, and Cic. Fragm. ap. Quint. 8, 3, 21) [root scar-, to leap; Gr. σκαίρω; cf. also κορύσσω; v. Lidd. and Scott, s. v.]. To thrust or push with the horns (very rare): agni ludunt blandeque coruscant,Lucr. 2, 320: frontem,Juv. 12, 6: caput opponis cum eo coruscans, Cic. Fragm. ap. Quint. 8, 3, 21. Transf., to move quickly, to vibrate, shake, brandish, wave, tremb...

coruscus.definition: cŏruscus, a, um, corusco, II. (poet.). In waving motion, waving, vibrating, tremulous: silvae,Verg. A. 1, 164: ilices,id. ib. 12, 701.—Humorously: omnia corusca prae tremore fabulor,i. e. trembling,Plaut. Rud. 2, 6, 42. Flashing, gleaming, glittering: fulgura,Lucr. 5, 296.—So of lightning: ignis,Lucr. 6, 203; Hor. C. 1, 34, 6: lumina,Lucr. 6, 283.—Also: vis fulminis, Poët. ap. Cic. Tusc. 2, 9, 21: sol,Verg. G. 1, 234; cf.: radii (solis),Ov. M. 1,...

corvinus.definition: corvīnus, a, um, corvus Cf or pertaining to the raven, raven-: ovum,Plin. 10, 12, 15, § 32: nigredo,App. M. 2, p. 118, 31.

coruinus.definition: corvīnus, a, um, corvus Cf or pertaining to the raven, raven-: ovum,Plin. 10, 12, 15, § 32: nigredo,App. M. 2, p. 118, 31.

corvus.definition: root kar-, kal-, to sound; cf.: καλέω, κόραξ, etc. A raven, Plin. 10, 43, 60, § 121 sq.; acc. to the fable, orig. white, changed to a black bird in punishment for treachery,Ov. M. 2, 541 sq.; on account of its gift of prophecy (oscen,Hor. C. 3, 27, 11), consecrated to Apollo, Ov. M. 5, 329 (hence, Phoebeïus ales, id. ib. 2, 545: Delphicus ales,Petr. 122; cf. also Stat. Th. 3, 506); its flight to the right indicated good fortune,Plaut. As. 2, 1,...

coruus.definition: root kar-, kal-, to sound; cf.: καλέω, κόραξ, etc. A raven, Plin. 10, 43, 60, § 121 sq.; acc. to the fable, orig. white, changed to a black bird in punishment for treachery,Ov. M. 2, 541 sq.; on account of its gift of prophecy (oscen,Hor. C. 3, 27, 11), consecrated to Apollo, Ov. M. 5, 329 (hence, Phoebeïus ales, id. ib. 2, 545: Delphicus ales,Petr. 122; cf. also Stat. Th. 3, 506); its flight to the right indicated good fortune,Plaut. As. 2, 1,...

corycomachia.definition: The exercise of the athletae with the corycus (v. 1. corycus), Cael. Aur. Tard. 5, 11, 134.

corydalus.definition: The crested lark, Serv. ad Verg. E. 2, 1.

corylus.definition: or A hazel or filbert shrub, Cato, R. R. 18, 9; Verg. E. 1, 14; id. G. 2, 65; Ov. M. 10, 93 al.

corymbiatus.definition: cŏrymbĭātus, a, um, corymbus Set round with clusters of ivy-berries, corymbiated: discus, Gall. ap. Treb. Claud. 17, § 5.

corymbus.definition: A cluster of fruit, a cluster of flowers of different plants; so esp. freq. of a cluster of ivyberries, Verg. E. 3, 39; Ov. M. 3, 665; Juv. 6, 52; for the crowning of Bacchus,Prop. 2, 30 (3, 28), 39; 3 (4), 17, 29; of Osiris,Tib. 1, 7, 45: ferulae,Plin. 19, 9, 56, § 175: elaphobosci,id. 22, 22, 37, § 79 al. Meton.

cos.definition: Sanscr. ça, to whet, sharpen; cf. cautes Any hard stone, flintstone, Cic. Div. 1, 17, 33; Liv. 1, 36, 4 and 5; Curt. 4, 6, 8; 5, 3, 8; 8, 11, 23; Verg. E. 8, 43. In partic., a whetstone, hone, grindstone, Plin. 36, 22, 47, § 164; Hor. C. 2, 8, 16; Quint. 2, 12, 8.

coscinomantia.definition: κοσκινομαντεία A divination by the sieve, Aug. 5, p. 426.

cosmographia.definition: A description of the universe, Cassiod. Inst. Div. Litt. 25.

cosmographus.definition: One who describes the world, a cosmographer, Auct. Progen. Aug. 2; Mythogr. Lat. 3, 6, 35.

cosmus.definition: A celebrated maker of, and dealer in unguents at Rome, Juv. 8, 86; Mart. 11, 8, 9; 1, 89, 2; 14, 110, 1.—Hence, , , adj., named or derived from Cosmus: ampullae,Mart. 3, 82, 26; and subst.: , , (sc. unguentum), an unguent made by him, Mart. 12, 55, 7; 11, 15, 6.

cossus.definition: A kind of larva under the bark of trees, Plin. 11, 33, 38, § 113; 17, 24, 37, § 220; 30, 13, 39, § 115.

costa.definition: A rib, Cels. 8, 1; Plin. 11, 37, 82, § 207; Plaut. Ps. 1, 2, 4; Lucr. 5, 1297; Verg. G. 1, 273; id. A. 1, 211; Ov. H. 9, 111; Stat. Th. 2, 9; Mart. 9, 48, 10. Transf., a side, a wall: aheni,Verg. A. 7, 463: ratis,Pers. 6, 31; cf. navium,Plin. 13, 9, 19, § 63: corbium,id. 16, 18, 30, § 75.— Absol., Verg. A. 2, 16 al.

costabilis.definition: costābĭlis, e, costa Riblike (late Lat.), Cassiod. Var. 3, 48.

costamomum.definition: costum - amomum An aromatic plant, similar to the costum and amomum, Dig. 39, 4, 16, § 7.

costum.definition: n. (access. form, like the Greek, , , f., Luc. 9, 917) An Oriental aromatic plant: Costus Arabicus, Linn.; Plin. 12, 12, 25, § 41; Ov. M. 10, 308; Hor. C. 3, 1, 44 al.; freq. used in the preparation of costly unguents,Plin. 13, 1, 2, § 15 sq.; 13, 1, 2, § 18; in offerings,Prop. 4 (5), 6, 5.for the preservation of fruits,Col. 12, 20, 5 al.

cothurnatio.definition: cothurnatus A tragic representation, Tert. adv. Val. 13.

cothurnatus.definition: cŏthurnātus, a, um, adj.cothurnus Of or pertaining to the cothurnus, lit. buskined; hence, elevated, lofty, tragic (opp. excalceatus, comic, Sen. Ep. 8, 8; 76, 31; not ante-Aug.): Maronis grande opus,Mart. 5, 5, 8: Lycophron, Ov. lb. 529: vates,id. Am. 2, 18, 18: deae,id. F. 5, 348: sermo,Macr. S. 7, 5 fin.: scelera,Lact. 6, 20.—* adv.: cŏ-thurnātē, loftily, tragically; only comp. (late Lat.): cothurnatius,Amm. 28, 1, 4.

cothurnus.definition: A high Grecian shoe. In gen., Cic. Fin. 3, 14, 46; id. Phil. 3, 6, 16; Vell. 2, 82, 4 al. Esp.

cottidianus.definition: cottīdĭānus and cōtīd- (less correctly quŏtīd-), a, um (cŏtīd-, Mart. 11, 1, 2; But cōtĭd-,Cat. 68, 139), cottidie. Prop. Meton., every day, daily, usual, ordinary, common: formae,Ter. Eun. 2, 3, 6: verba,Cic. Fam. 9, 21, 1: sindon,Mart. 11, 1, 2.

cottidie.definition: cottī-dĭē or cŏtīdĭē (v. Osann ad Cic. Rep. p. 475; less correctly quŏtīdĭē, v. Neue, Formenl. I. p. 676 sq.), quotdies Daily (class.; cf. in dies): ibatne ad Bacchidem? Pa. Cotidie, Ter. Hec. 1, 2, 82: minari,Cic. Phil. 1, 2, 5: cotidie vel potius in dies singulos breviores litteras ad te mitto: cotidie enim magis suspicor te in Epirum profectum,id. Att. 5, 7 init.: cotidie augere,id. Mil. 13, 34; Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 8, § 18; id. Or. 34, 120: te co...

cottidio.definition: cottīdĭō (cotīd-), , for cottidie Daily, Q. Caepio ap. Charis. p. 174 P.

cotula.definition: () A small vessel, as a measure, equal to a hemina or half a sextarius, Fann. Pond. 12; Mart. 8, 71, 8; Veg. Art. Vet. 3, 6, 8 al.

coturnix.definition: (ō, * Lucr. 4, 641; Ŏ,Ov. Am. 2, 6, 27; Juv. 12, 97), , f.a sono vocis, Paul. ex Fest. p. 37, 4 Müll., a quail, Plin. 10, 23, 33, § 64 sq.; Plaut. Capt. 5, 4, 6; Varr. R. R. 3, 5, 7 al.—As a term of endearment, Plaut. As. 3, 3, 76.

cotyledon.definition: A plant, navelwort: Cotyledon umbilicus, Linn.; Plin. 25, 13, 101, § 159.

cous.definition: Cŏus, i, and Cōus, a, um, v. 2. Cos.

coutor.definition: cŏ-ūtor, ūti V. n.: aliquo, to associate with, have dealings with, = συγχρῆσθαι, Vulg. Joan. 4, 9.

coxa.definition: The hip. Prop, Cels. 4, 22, 1; 8, 1 fin.; 8, 10, 5; Cael. Aur. Tard. 4, 3, 38; cf. also coxendix.—Hence Transf., in the Agrimensores: agrorum, a bend inwards (with angulus), Sic. Fl. p. 6 Goes.

coxendix.definition: (ī, Plaut. Bacch. 5, 2, 40; Lucil. ap. Non. p. 94, 6; I,Ser. Samm. 702; 968), f.kindr. with coxa, the hip. Prop., Varr. R. R. 1, 20; Lucil. ap. Non. p. 94, 6; Plaut. Bacch. 5, 2, 40; Suet. Aug. 8. The hip-bone, Plin. 10, 61, 81, § 168; 28, 11, 49, § 179.

coxim.definition: coxim, coxa; cf.: cessim, cossim On the hips (late Lat.): insidens,App. M. 3, p. 129, 19.

crabro.definition: A hornet: Vespa crabro, Linn.; Plin. 11, 21, 24, § 71 sq.; Ov. M. 11, 335; Verg. G. 4, 245 al.—Prov.: irritare crabrones,to stir up a hornet's nest,Plaut. Am. 2, 2, 84.

crapula.definition: Excessive wine-drinking, intoxication, inebriation, Plaut. Most. 5, 2, 1; id. Ps. 5, 1, 46; Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 11, § 28; id. Phil. 2, 12, 30; Liv. 9, 30, 9; Plin. 21, 20, 83, § 142 et saep. Meton., a resin producing intoxication, which was sometimes mingled with wine, Plin. 14, 20, 25, § 124 sq.; 23, 1, 24, § 46.

crapulatio.definition: id. An intoxicating (late Lat.), Cassiod. An. 11.

crapulatus.definition: crāpŭlātus, a, um, id. Drunken with wine, inebriated, Vulg. Psa. 77, 65.

crapulentus.definition: crāpŭlentus, a, um, id. Very much intoxicated, Amm. 29, 5, 54.

crapulosus.definition: crāpŭlōsus, a, um, id. Inclined to drunkenness (late Lat.): libidines, Firm. Math. 8, 20.

cras.definition: crās, root ka-, ku-, to lighten, burn; Gr. καίω; cf. Sanscr. cvas, the same To-morrow, αὔριον (freq. and class.). Poet., in gen., the future, hereafter: quid sit futurum cras, fuge quaerere,Hor. C. 1, 9, 13: credula vitam Spes fovet et melius cras fore semper ait,Tib. 2, 6, 20; Ov. M. 15, 216 al.

crassamentum.definition: id. (post-Aug.) The thickness of an object. In gen.: portarum,Plin. 16, 40, 77, § 210: surculi,Gell. 17, 9, 7. Esp., the thick sediment of a liquid, the dregs, grounds, Col. 12, 12, 1.

crassesco.definition: crassesco, ĕre V. inch., to grow thick, to thicken, grow dense or hard, grow large or fat (post-Aug.; most freq. in Pliny the elder): turtures milio, etc.,Col. 8, 9, 2: sues,Plin. 13, 18, 32, § 110: ceparum capita,id. 19, 6, 32, § 103: pili quadrupedibus senectute,id. 11, 39, 94, § 231: mel (opp. dilutum),id. 11, 13, 13, § 32; cf.: vinum vetustate,id. 23, 1, 22, § 40: aër in nubes,id. 2, 43, 44, § 114: crassescente limo,id. 33, 5, 26, § 86.

crassificatio.definition: crassifico A making thick or fat; hence, thickness: viscosa,Cael. Aur. Tard. 5, 3, 56; id. Acut. 1, 14, 115.

crassitudo.definition: crassus Thickness, density. Abstr. (in good prose): postes ...Quantā firmitate facti et quantā crassitudine,Plaut. Most. 3, 2, 135: parietum,Caes. B. C. 2, 8: libramentum, in quo nulla omnino crassitudo sit,Cic. Ac. 2, 36, 116: columnarum,Vitr. 4, 4, 2: fornicum,Liv. 44, 11, 5 al.: stipites feminis crassitudine,Caes. B. G. 7, 73; cf. id. ib. 3, 13: aëris,Cic. Div. 1, 42, 93: cerae,Plin. 27, 9, 47, § 71: mellis,id. 28, 12, 50, § 187: (ostrea) cras...

crassus.definition: crassus, a, um, adj.Sanscr. kart-, to spin; cf.: crates, cartilago, etc.; as opp. to flowing, thin, lean, delicate, etc. Solid, thick, dense, fat, gross, etc. (freq. and class. in prose and poetry). Lit.: semina (opp. liquida),Lucr. 4, 1259; cf.: crassius semen,id. 4, 1244: corpus,id. 6, 857: unguentum,Hor. A. P. 375: paludes,Verg. G. 2, 110: cruor,id. A. 5, 469: aquae,greatly swollen,Ov. Am. 3, 6, 8: ager,Varr. R. R. 1, 24, 1; Cic. Fl. 29, 71; c...

crastinus.definition: crastĭnus, a, um, cras. Of to-morrow; to-morrow's (freq. and class. in prose and poetry): dies,Plaut. Stich. 4, 2, 55; Cic. Att. 15, 8, 2; Prop. 2 (3), 15, 54.al.: Titan,Verg. A. 4, 118: Cynthius,Ov. F. 3, 345: Aurora,Verg. A. 12, 76: lux,id. ib. 10, 244; cf.: stella diurna,Plaut. Men. 1, 2, 62: hora. Verg. G. 1, 425: tempora, * Hor. C. 4, 7, 17: dapes,Mart. 3, 58, 42: egestas,id. 3, 10, 3: quies,Luc. 7, 26 al.—In Gr. constr., of the person: cras...

cratera.definition: (acc. to Paul. ex Fest. p. 53, 10, and Non. p. 547, 25 sq., sometimes ; cf. Naev. Trag. Rel. v. 45 Rib.), , f., and (mostly poet.) , , m., = κρατήρ, Ion. κρητήρ A vessel in which wine was mingled with water, a mixing-vessel or bowl (mostly poet.). Prop. Meton.

craticius.definition: crātĭcĭus or -tĭus, a, um, cratis Composed of wicker-work, wattled: parietes,lattice-work,Vitr. 2, 8 fin.; Dig. 17, 2, 15; Pall. 1, 19, 2.

craticula.definition: dim.id., prop. Fine hurdle - work; hence, a small gridiron, Mart. 14, 221, 1; Cato, R. R. 13, 1; Petr. 31, 11; 70, 7.

cratis.definition: ( Nom. sing. only Veg. Art. Vet. 1, 56, 5; acc. sing. cratim, Plaut. Poen. 5, 2, 65), f. Sanscr. kart, to spin; cf. crassus, wicker-work, a hurdle. Lit. Transf., a joint, rib, etc.: pectoris,Verg. A. 12, 508: laterum,Ov. M. 12, 370; cf. spinae,the joints of the backbone,id. ib. 8, 806: favorum,honey-comb,Verg. G. 4, 214: cratem facit vitis,grows confusedly,Col. 4, 2, 1 al.

creabilis.definition: crĕābĭlis, e, creo That can bemade or created (post-class. and rare): materia,App. Trism. 85, 12; Aug. Conf. 12, 19 al.

creagra.definition: A fleshhook (late Lat.), Mart. Cap. 9, § 997; Vulg. 2 Par. 4, 11 al.

creamen.definition: creo The elements of which created things consist (late Lat.), Prud. Ham. 505.

creatio.definition: id. (very rare). A creating, producing, begetting: liberorum,Dig. 1, 7, 15, § 2.—Absol.: non hujus creationis,i. e. not of man's building,Vulg. Heb. 9, 11. An electing to an office, a choice: magistratuum,Cic. Leg. 3, 3, 10: tutoris,Dig. 26, 7, 39, § 6.

creator.definition: id.. A creator, author, begetter, founder. One who elects or appoints to an office, Cod. Just. 10, 31, 59; Dig. 50, 8, 2, § 7 al.

creatrix.definition: creator She who brings forth or produces, a mother (poet.): natura rerum,Lucr. 1, 630 al.: mea, patria (with genetrix),Cat. 63, 50: diva (of a mother),Verg. A. 8, 534; cf.: Alexandri Magni, Olympias,Aur. Vict. Epit. 40: dira bellorum (tellus),Sil. 15, 184; Ambros. Fid. 4, 30, 3.

creatura.definition: creo, only concr. A creature, thing created (late Lat.), Tert. Apol. 30; Prud. Ham. 508: omnes creaturae tuae,Vulg. Tob. 8, 7. The creation: Deus caelorum et Dominus totius creaturae,Vulg. Jud. 9, 17: Dei,id. Apoc. 3, 14 al.

crebresco.definition: crēbresco (in MSS. and edd. sometimes euphon. crēbesco, bŭi, like rubesco, from ruber), brŭi, 3 V. inch. [creber], to become frequent, to increase, grow strong; of a rumor, report, to spread abroad (perh. not ante-Aug.; most freq. in Tac.): crebrescunt optatae aurae,Verg. A. 3, 530: gestus cum ipsā orationis celeritate,Quint. 11, 3, 111: horror,Verg. A. 12, 407: bellum,Tac. H. 2, 67: tum crebescere fragor,Plin. Ep. 7, 27, 8: seditio,Tac. H. 1, 39...

crebritas.definition: creber Thickness, closeness, frequency: spissae venarum,Vitr. 2, 10, 2: caeli,id. 9, 8, 3: fluctuum, Sall. H. Fragm. ap. Serv. ad Verg. A. 1, 116 (3, 42 Dietsch): litterarum,Cic. Att. 13, 18 init.: crebritas et magnitudo officiorum,id. Fam. 3, 1, 1: sententiarum (with concinnitas),id. Brut. 95, 327.

crebritudo.definition: creber, for crebritas, Sisenn. ap. Non. p. 91, 30 dub.

credibilis.definition: crēdĭbĭlis, e, credo Worthy of belief, credible: credibile est quod sine ullo teste auditoris opinione firmatur,Cic. Inv. 1, 30, 48 (class. in prose and poetry): tametsi verissimum esse intellegebam, tamen credibile fore non arbitrabar,Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 61, § 158: narrationes,id. Or. 36, 124; cf. Quint. 4, 2, 52: imago rerum,id. 4, 2, 123: ratio,id. 5, 12, 13: suspicio,id. 9, 2, 90 et saep.: magnum narras, vix credibile, * Hor. S. 1, 9, 52; cf.: v...

credito.definition: crēdĭto, āre, credo To believe firmly, Fulg. Myth. 1, p. 6.

creditor.definition: credo, I. A creditor. Prop., Dig. 50, 16, 10 sq.; Cic. Phil. 6, 4, 11; id. Quint. 23, 74; Liv. 6, 14, 5; Sen. Ep. 87, 6; 119, 1; Quint. 3, 6, 84; * Hor. S. 2, 3, 65 et saep. Trop., of the belly, Plin. 26, 8, 28, § 43.

creditrix.definition: creditor A female creditor, Dig. 20, 5, 16; 42, 6, 38 al.

credo.definition: crēdo, dĭdi, dĭtum, 3 ( Pres. subj. creduam, Plaut. Poen. 3, 5, 2: creduas,id. Bacch. 3, 3, 72; id. Trin. 3, 1, 5: creduat,id. Bacch. 3, 4, 5; 4, 7, 6: creduis,id. Am. 2, 2, 49; id. Capt. 3, 4, 73: creduit,id. Truc. 2, 2, 52; inf. credier, id. Poen. 2, 43; crevi for credidi,id. Cist. 1, 1, 1), Sanscr. crat, crad, trust, and dha-; v. 2. do. Orig. belonging to the lang. of business, to give as a loan, to loan, lend, make or loan to any one: (vilicu...

credulitas.definition: credulus Easiness of belief, credulity (first freq. after the Aug. per.; never in Cic.): credulitas error est magis quam culpa, Plancus ap. Cic. Fam. 10, 23, 1; Quint. 5, 3, 7; Tac. A. 2, 40; Curt. 7, 7, 8; Ov. M. 15, 498; id. P. 1, 1, 44.—Of fishes trusting themselves to the hook, Ov. M. 13, 934; 15, 101; cf. credulus.—As a person, together with Error,Ov. M. 12, 59.

credulus.definition: crēdŭlus, a, um, credo, II. C. 2. That easily believes a thing, credulous, easy of belief, confiding. Prop. (freq. and class.). Transf., of inanimate subjects: aures regis,Curt. 10, 1, 28: credula res amor est,Ov. H. 6, 21; id. M. 7, 826: spes animi mutui,Hor. C. 4, 1, 30: convivia,full of confidence, confiding, trusting,Just. 2, 10, 10: fama ( = facile credens),Tac. H. 1, 34 fin.; cf. Roth ad Tac. Agr. p. 210.

crematio.definition: cremo A burning, consuming by fire, cremation (post-Aug. and rare), Plin. 23, 2, 31, § 64; Prud. στεφ. 6, 88.

cremator.definition: id. A burner, consumer by fire (eccl. Lat.): Deus,Tert. adv. Marc. 5, 16.

crementum.definition: cresco. Growth, increase (very rare): corporum, Varr. ap. Non. p. 169, 14: lunae,Plin. 11, 37, 55, § 149 (incrementum, Sillig). Crementum est semen masculi, Isid. Orig. 9, 5, 5; 11, 1, 15.

cremo.definition: crĕmo, āvi, ātum, 1, Sanscr. çar, çri, to boil, roast; cf. carbo To burn, consume by fire (freq. and class.; cf. comburo). In gen.: ignis silvas cremarat,Lucr. 5, 1242; cf.: poëtam igni,Suet. Calig. 27 fin.: omnes collegas suos vivos,Val. Max. 6, 3, 2; Curt. 4, 8, 9: damnatum poenam sequi oportebat, ut igni cremaretur,Caes. B. G. 1, 4; Curt. 8, 9, 32; 5, 6, 7: urbem incendiis,Plin. 17, 1, 1, § 5: cremare et diruere urbem,Liv. 28, 19, 12: Ilium,Ho...

cremor.definition: kindr. with cremo The thick juice obtained from animal or vegetable substances, thick broth, pap, etc., Cato, R. R. 86; Plaut. Pers. 1, 3, 15; Cels. 3, 7, 2; 6, 6, 26; Ov. M. Fac. 95.

creo.definition: crĕo (old form cerĕo, in Varr. L. L. 6, § 81 Müll.), āvi, ātum, 1, kindred with Sanscr. kar, kri, to make To bring forth, produce, make, create, beget (very freq. in every period and species of composition). Lit. Trop., to produce, prepare, cause, occasion: voluptatem meis inimicis,Plaut. Cas. 2, 7, 3: commoditatem mihi,id. Poen. 4, 2, 94: lites,id. ib. 3, 2, 9: omnis has aerumnas,id. Mil. 1, 1, 33: capitalem fraudem tuis cruribus capitique,id. i...

crepatura.definition: crepo A fissure, crack (late Lat.): parietum, Schol. Juv. 3, 196.

crepida.definition: The sole which served the Greeks, and the Romans who adopted Grecian habits, as a shoe, a sandal (pure Lat. solea; cf. Gell. 13, 21, 5 sq.), Cic. Rab. Post. 10, 27; Liv. 29, 19, 12; Suet. Tib. 13; id. Calig. 52; Hor. S. 1, 3, 127; Pers. 1, 127 al.—Prov.: ne sutor supra crepidam (judicaret),let the cobbler stick to his last,Plin. 35, 10, 36, § 85; Val. Max. 8, 12, ext. 3.

crepidarius.definition: crĕpĭdārĭus, a, um, crepida Of or pertaining to the sole or sandal: sutor, a sandal-maker, shoemaker, Sempr. Asell. ap. Gell. 13, 21, 8: culter, Gell. ib.

crepidatus.definition: crĕpĭdātus, a, um, id. Wearing sandals, Cic. Pis. 38, 92 and 93; Suet. Dom. 4: fabula, a kind of Graeco-Roman tragedy, Don. Ter. Ad. prol. 7; cf. Neukirch. Fab. Tog. pp. 15 and 57.

crepido.definition: κρηπίς. Prop., a ground, basis, foundation, a socle, pedestal, base, Plin. 36, 9, 14, § 66; Stat. S. 1, 1, 58: altaris,Vulg. Lev. 1, 15. Transf., an elevated enclosure, a high projection, an edge, brim, brink, border, dam, dike, pier, shore, bank, etc., Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 37, § 97; Varr. R. R. 3, 11, 2; Verg. A. 10, 653; Liv. 27, 18, 6; Curt. 5, 1, 28; Sen. Contr. 3, 17; Vitr. 4, 6, 3 et saep.

crepidula.definition: dim.crepida A small sandal, Plaut. Pers. 4, 2, 3; cf. Gell. 13, 21, 5.

crepitaculum.definition: crepito A rattle, Quint. 9, 4, 66; Mart. 14, 54; Mart. Cap. 1, § 7; 9, §§ 909, 927.

crepito.definition: crĕpĭto, āre V. freq. n. [crepo], to rattle much, to creak, crackle, clatter, rustle, rumble, chatter, murmur, etc. (poet. or in post-Aug. prose): dentibus,Plaut. Rud. 2, 6, 52; Lucr. 5, 746: tenui rostro,Ov. M. 11, 735; cf. id. ib. 6, 97: lapillis unda,id. ib. 11, 604: multā grandine nimbi,Verg. A. 5, 459; cf. id. G. 1, 449: leni vento brattea,id. A. 6, 209: duris incudibus enses,to ring,id. G. 2, 540; cf. arma,Tib. 2, 5, 73; Ov. M. 1, 143; 15, ...

crepitus.definition: crepo A rattling, creaking, clattering, clashing, rustling, a noise, etc. (in good prose). In gen.: cardinum,Plaut. Curc. 1, 3, 1; cf. claustrorum (with sonitus),id. ib. 1, 3, 47: carbasi,Lucr. 6, 110: e motu frenorum,Varr. R. R. 2, 7, 12: dentium,a chattering,Cic. Tusc. 4, 8, 19: pedum,id. Top. 12, 52: armorum,Liv. 25, 6, 21; 38, 17, 5: alarum (anserum). id. 5, 47, 4: plagarum,Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 62, § 162: inlisae manus umeris,Sen. Ep. 56, 1: tibi...

crepo.definition: crĕpo, ŭi, ĭtum, 1, and A. [Sanscr. krap, to lament; cf. crabro] (mostly poet. or in post-Aug. prose; in class. prose, concrepo). Neutr., to rattle, crack, creak, rustle, clatter, tinkle, jingle, chink, etc. Act., to make something sound, make a noise with, cause to resound or rattle.

crepulus.definition: crĕpŭlus, a, um, crepo Rattling, resounding, crashing (late Lat.): buccae,Sid. Ep. 9, 13, 2: fragor,id. ib. 4, 15.

crepusculascens.definition: crĕpuscŭlascens, entis, Part. [crepusculum] Growing dusk, dusky: hora,Sid. Ep. 8, 3.

crepusculum.definition: creper Twilight, dusk (cf. Varr. L. L. 6, § 5 Müll.); and in partic., evening twilight, the dusk of the evening (opp. diluculum, the morning twilight, dawn; poet. or in post-Aug. prose). Prop., Plaut. Cas. prol. 40; Ov. M. 1, 219; 15, 681; id. F. 4, 735; Plin. 18, 25, 58, § 219; Suet. Ner. 26 al. In gen., darkness: iter per opaca crepuscula,Ov. M. 14, 122; cf. id. ib. 11, 596.

cresco.definition: cresco, crēvi, crētum, 3 ( Inf. perf. sync. cresse, Lucr. 3, 683), v. inch. n. [1. creo]. Orig., of things not previously in existence, to come forth, grow, to arise, spring, be born, become visible, appear (so mostly poet.) Of things already in existence, to rise in height, to rise, grow, grow up, thrive, increase, etc.

creta.definition: Crēta, ae (nom. Crētē, Mel. 2, 7, 12; Ov. M. 8, 118; 9, 668; 9, 735; acc. Creten, id. ib. 8, 99; Hor. C. 3, 27, 34 al.; On the contrary, Cretam,Verg. A. 3, 129 al.), f., = Κρήτη, Crete, an island in the Mediterranean Sea, distinguished in ancient times by its fruitfulness and very early cultivation, now Candia, Mel. l. l.; Plin. 4, 12, 20, § 58; Verg. A. 3, 104; Hor. Epod. 9, 29; Cic. Fl. 13, 30; id. Phil. 2, 38, 97; Vell. 2, 34, 1; Varr. R. R. ...

cretarius.definition: crētārĭus, a, um, 2. creta Of or pertaining to chalk: ARS,Inscr. Grut. 641, 3. Subst.: crētārĭa, ae, f. (sc. taberna), a shop for Cretan earth, Varr. L. L. 8, § 55 Müll.

cretatus.definition: crētātus, a, um, id. Marked with chalk. Prop.: fasciae,Cic. Att. 2, 3, 1: pedes,Plin. 35, 18, 58, § 201: bos (decorated as an offering),Juv. 10, 66: Fabulla,whitened,Mart. 2, 41, 11. Transf.: ambitio, i. e. of the candidates for office, clothed in white (candidatorum), Pers. 5, 177.

cretifodina.definition: 2. creta A chalk- or clay-pit, Dig. 7, 1, 13, § 5 al.

cretio.definition: cerno, II.; jurid. t. t. The format declaration by the heir of his intention to enter upon his inheritance. Prop., Gai Inst. 2, § 7; 2, 164 sqq.; 2, 171 sqq.; Ulp. Fragm. 22, 25 sqq.; Varr. L. L. 6, § 81 Müll.: simplex, fruitless, i. e. where there is no property, Cic. Att. 11, 12, 4: libera,without restrictions by the testator,id. ib. 13, 46, 3; id. de Or. 1, 22, 101 al. Meton., an inheritance, Plin. 2, 26, 24, § 95 fin.

cretosus.definition: crētōsus, a, um, 2. creta Abounding in chalk or clay: locus,Cato, R. R. 8, 1; Plin. 15, 18, 19, § 72: terra,Varr. R. R. 1, 9, 3; Plin. 18, 19, 49, § 175: rura Cimoli,Ov. M. 7, 463.

cretula.definition: dim.id. White clay, used for sealing, = terra sigillata, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 26, § 58; Plin. 35, 7, 31, § 49.

cretura.definition: cerno; concr. The siftings of corn, bran, chaff (late Lat.), Pall. 1, 24, 3.

cretus.definition: crētus, a, um, Part., from cerno.

cribello.definition: crībello, no Perf., ātum, 1, cribellum, to pass through a sieve, to sift (late Lat.), Pall. 1, 41, 3; Theod. Prisc. 1, 17 al.

cribellum.definition: dim.cribrum A small sieve (late Lat.), Pall. Febr. 24; id. Jun. 11.

cribro.definition: crībro, āvi, ātum, 1, id. To pass through a sieve, to sift (perh. not anteAug.), Col. 12, 51, 1; Plin. 17, 11, 15, § 76 al.

cribrum.definition: from root cer, whence cerno A sieve, searce, riddle, Cato, R. R. 25, 76, 3; Plaut. Rud. 1, 2, 14; Cic. Div. 2, 27, 59; Col. 8, 5, 16; Plin. 18, 11, 28, § 108 sq.; Ov. M. 12, 437; Pers. 3, 112 et saep.— Facete, of a slave whose back was pierced by goads: carnificum cribrum, Plant. Most. 1, 1, 52.—Prov.: imbrem in cribrum gerere,i. e. to labor in vain,Plaut. Ps. 1, 1, 100.

crimen.definition: contr. for cernimen, from cerno, II. C.; lit. A judicial decision, verdict, judgment; hence, transf., like the Gr. κρῖμα, of the subject of such a decision, and with partieular reference either to the accuser or to the accused. Subject., or with reference to the accuser, a charge, accusation, reproach; esp. when unfounded, a calumny, slander (very freq. in every period and species of composition): criminin' me habuisse fidem?Plaut. Bacch. 4, 3, ...

criminatio.definition: criminor An accusation, complaint, calumny (in good prose): criminatione in me absentem uti,Cic. Agr. 3, 1, 3: criminatio tua quae est? Roscium cum Flavio pro societate decidisse,id. Rosc. Com. 13, 37; id. de Or. 2, 79, 321; Liv. 1, 54, 8 al.—In plur., Cic. Lael. 18, 65; Liv. 7, 5, 1; 9, 26, 19; Tac. A. 6, 25; Suet. Caes. 55; Just. 12, 14, 3 al.

criminator.definition: id. An accuser, a calumniator (very rare): meus,Plaut. Bacch. 4, 7, 28: in alios (opp. sui obtegens),Tac. A. 4, 1.—Of the devil, Lact. 2, 8, 6; 6, 4, 2.

criminatrix.definition: criminator A female accuser, calumniator, Vulg. Paul. ad Tit. 2, 3.

crimino.definition: crīmĭno, āre, 1 V. a.; collat. form of criminor, to accuse, make an accusation: aliquem apud aliquem,Plaut. Ps. 1, 5, 78.— Absol.: apud aliquem, Enn. ap. Non. p. 470, 16 (Sat. v. 9 Vahl.).

criminosus.definition: crīmĭnōsus, a, um, crimen, I. Full of reproaches, reproachful, accusalory, calumniating, slanderous (class.): ne cum me nimium gratum illi esse dicant, id mihi criminosum esse possit,Cic. Planc. 2, 4; Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 67, § 162; cf.: in hunc,id. Sull. 13, 36: nomen,id. Planc. 19, 46: orationes,Liv. 8, 12, 14: iambi,Hor. C. 1, 16, 2: criminosissimus liber,Suet. Caes. 75; cf. Quint. 9, 2, 23: ille acerbus, criminosus, popularis homo ac turbulentus,...

crinalis.definition: crīnālis, e, crinis Of or pertaining to the hair, hair- (poet., or in post-Aug. prose): vitta,Verg. A. 7, 403; Ov. M. 4, 6; 5, 617: aurum,Verg. A. 11, 576; Stat. Achill. 2, 97: acus,a hair-pin,App. M. 8, p. 207, 4; for which subst.: crīnāle, is, n., Ov. M. 5, 53: dentes,i. e. of a hair-comb,Claud. B. Gild. 137: corpore polypus,i. e. furnished with hair-like feelers,Ov. Hal. 30; cf. Plin. 9, 29, 46, § 86 (s. v. crinis, II. B.).

crininus.definition: crĭnĭnus, a, um Made of lilies, lily-: unguentum,Dig. 34, 2, 21; cf. crinon.

crinio.definition: crīnĭo, no Perf., ītum, 4, crinis, to provide or cover with hair; as verb. finit. rare, and only transf. of leaves of plants: frondibus crinitur arbos,Stat. S. 4, 5, 10; id. Th. 4, 217.—But freq. In part. perf.: crīnītus, a, um, covered with hair, hairy; esp., having long hair or locks, long-haired.

crinis.definition: ( Fem., Atta ap. Non. p. 202, 29; acc. to the latter also Plaut. Most. 1, 3, 69; and so in Ritschl) [kindr. with crista; cf. κόρυς, κορυφή], the hair. Prop. (class.; esp. freq. in the poets),Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 33, § 76; Caes. B. G. 1, 51; id. B. C. 3, 9; Liv. 1, 13, 1; 3, 7, 8 et saep.; Verg. A. 1, 480; Cat. 64, 391; Hor. C. 2, 5, 24; 2, 19, 20 et saep.: capere crines, i. e. to marry (since the matrons distinguished themselves from maidens by the...

crinitus.definition: crīnītus, a, um, v. crinio, II.

crisimus.definition: crĭsĭmus, a, um Decisive, critical: dies, the day of a crisis, in disease, Cael. Aur. Acut. 1, 14, 108; Censor. 14, 9.

crisis.definition: medic. t. t. A decision, crisis, Sen. Ep. 83, 4.

criso.definition: crīso or crisso, āvi, 1 V. n., to move the haunches (in mal. part.; of a female, as ceveo of a male), Lucil. ap. Non. p. 19, 26; Juv. 6, 322; Mart. 14, 203; Auct. Priap. 19, 4 Büch.; cf. Charis. p. 260 P.; Diom. p. 293 ib.; v. Lachm. ad Lucr. vol. 2, p. 276 sq.

crispitudo.definition: crispus A tremulous or vibratory motion, Arn. 2, p. 73.

crispo.definition: crispo, no Perf., ātum, 1, and n. id.. Act., to curl, crisp, crimp (poet. or in post-Aug. prose). Neutr., only in part. pres. crispans.

crispulus.definition: crispŭlus, a, um Adj. dim. [id.], curled, having curled hair, crisped, crimped (post-Aug.). Prop.: comatus et crispulus,Sen. Ep. 66, 25; cf. id. ib. 95, 24; Mart. 5, 61, 1.—* Trop., of discourse, elaborate, artificial, Fronto, Or. Ep. 3, p. 248.

crispus.definition: crispus, a, um, kindred with crinis, crista; cf. cresco. Originally of the hair, curled, crisped, crimped: cincinni,Plaut. Truc. 2, 2, 32; cf. coma,Sil. 16, 120; and: leo crispioribus jubis,Plin. 8, 16, 18, § 46.—Of persons, having curled hair, curlyheaded, Plaut. Capt. 3, 4, 115; id. Rud. 1, 2, 37; Ter. Hec. 3, 4, 26.—* Transf.

crista.definition: cf. cer- in cerebrum, pro-ceres, = cel- in excello. Prop., a tuft on the head of animals; most freq. of the comb of a cock, Varr. R. R. 3, 9, 4 and 5; Plin. 10, 56, 77, § 156; Juv. 13, 233 al.; of a lapwing,Ov. M. 6, 672; Plin. 10, 29, 44, § 86; of a serpent,Ov. M. 7, 150; 15, 669; Plin. 11, 37, 44, § 122.—Prov.: illi surgunt cristae, his crest rises, he carries his head high, i. e. he is conceited, Juv. 4, 70. Transf.

cristatus.definition: cristātus, a, um, crista That has a tuft or crest, tufted, crested. Lit.: ales,Ov. F. 1, 455; cf.: cristati oris ales,id. M. 11, 597: aves, i. e. galli,Mart. 14, 223: draco,Ov. M. 4, 599; Plin. 8, 13, 13, § 35. Transf., crested, plumed: cassis pennis,Ov. M. 8, 25: galeae,Liv. 9, 40, 3: jubar,Stat. Th. 3, 223: Achilles,Verg. A. 1, 468.

crithologia.definition: A gathering of barley, Cod. Just. 11, 27, 1; Cod. Th. 14, 26, 1.

criticus.definition: crĭtĭcus, a, um, adj. Fit or suitable for deciding, capable of judging. Adj., only as a medic. t. t. (cf. crisimus), decisive, critical: accessio morbi,Aug. Conf. 6, 1 fin.—More frequent Subst.: crĭtĭ-cus, i, m., a critic, Cic. Fam. 9, 10, 1 (also ap. Suet. Gram. 14); Quint. 2, 1, 4; Hor. Ep. 2, 1, 51.

crocatus.definition: crŏcātus, a, um, crocus Saffronyellow: semen,Plin. 16, 34, 62, § 147: vestis,Fronto, Ep. ad M. Caes. 2, 1.

croceus.definition: crŏcĕus, a, um, id. Of or pertaining to saffron, saffron-. Prop.: odores,Verg. G. 1, 56: flores,id. ib. 4, 109: tinctus,saffron-sauce,Plin. 10, 48, 68, § 134: color,id. 27, 10, 59, § 83. Transf., saffron-colored, yellow, golden: lutum,Verg. E. 4, 44: cubile,id. G. 1, 447: acanthus,id. A. 1, 649: chlamys,id. ib. 11, 775 al.: comae,Ov. A. A. 1, 530: honor,a saffron-tint,Sil. 8, 444.

crocidismus.definition: ; of the sick A picking off of flocks (of wool, etc.), Cael. Aur. Acut. 1, 3, 34; 1, 6, 48; cf. carphologia.

crocino.definition: crŏcĭno, āre, crocum To anoint with saffron-ointment: jumenta, Gargil. Mart. de Cura Boum, p. 457 Bip.

crocinus.definition: crŏcĭnus, a, um Of or pertaining to saffron, saffron-. Adj.: semen,Plin. 21, 19, 73, 124: unguentum,Cels. 3, 18: color,Scrib. Comp. 173: tunica,saffron-colored,Cat. 68, 134. Subst.: crŏcĭnum, i, n. (sc. oleum), saffron-oil, Prop. 3 (4), 10, 22.

crocio.definition: crōcĭo, īre To cry or croak as a raven [cf. glocio, clango], Plaut. Aul. 4, 3, 2; App. Flor. 23, p. 366, 19.

crocitus.definition: crocio The croaking of the raven, Non. p. 45, 18.

croco.definition: crŏco, āre V. a., to dye saffron-yellow, Isid. Orig. 6, 11, 4; cf. crocatus.

crocodilus.definition: A crocodile, Plin. 8, 25, 37, § 89 sq.; 28, 8, 28, § 107 sq.; Cic. N. D. 2, 48, 124; 2, 52, 129; 1, 29, 82; Sen. Q. N. 4, 2, 13.—In the metathesis , Phaedr. 1, 25, 4 and 6; Mart. 3, 93, 7 Schneid.; cf. Ritschl in Rhein. Mus. vol. 9, p. 478 sq.

crocomagma.definition: The residuum of saffron, after the extraction of the oil, Plin. 21, 20, 82, § 139; Cels. 5, 18, 9 al.

crocota.definition: (sc. vestis), ὁ κροκωτός (sc. χιτών) A saffron-colored court-dress (for women), Naev. and Nov. ap. Non. p. 548, 26 sq.; Plaut. ib. 538, 13; App. M. 11, p. 261, 2; Auct. Har. Resp. 21, 44; cf. crocotula.

crocotta.definition: () or An unknown witd animal in Ethiopia, perh. the hyena, Plin. 8, 21, 30, § 72; 8, 30, 45, § 107; Capitol. Anton. 10.

crocum.definition: n., and , , m. ( Fem., App. M. 10, p. 255, 30), = κρόκος, saffron: Crocus sativus, Linn.; masc. usu. of the plant, neutr. of the essence, etc., but the distinction is not closely observed. Meton.

crosmis.definition: A kind of sage, App. Herb. 101.

crotalisso.definition: crŏtălisso, āre, 1, , = κροταλίζω To rattle or sound with the castanet, Macr. Diff. 21, 8.

crotalistria.definition: κροταλίζω A (female) castanet dancer, Prop. 4 (5), 8, 39. Poet., transf., a (rattling) stork, P. Syrus ap. Petr. 55 (cf. Ov. M. 6, 97).

crotalum.definition: A rattle, a bell, castanet, used to accompany wanton dances, P. Scip. ap. Macr. S. 2, 10; Cic. Pis. 9, 20 al.

cruciabilis.definition: crŭcĭābĭlis, e, crucio Tormenting, torturing, painful, excruciating, miserable (rare; not in Cic.): cruciabilem me accipito,Plaut. Ps. 4, 1, 40 Ritschl: exitu periit,Gell. 3, 9, 7; cf. mors,Arn. adv. Gent. 2: silentio fatigatus,App. M. 10, p. 239, 20. Susceptible of torture: animae,Lact. 7, 20, 9.—Adv.: crŭcĭābĭlĭter, with torture, Plaut. Ps. 4, 1, 40 Fleck., Lorenz: interfecti, Auct. B. Afr. 46.

cruciabundus.definition: crŭcĭābundus, a, um, crucio Torturing, tormenting, Cypr. Ep. 55.

cruciamen.definition: id. Torture, torment, pain: leti,Prud. Cath. 10, 90.

cruciamentum.definition: id. Torture, torment, pain (very rare): vidi ego multa saepe picta quae Acherunti fierent Cruciamenta,Plaut. Capt. 5, 4, 2; id. As. 2, 2, 52: carnificum (with tormenta morborum),Cic. Phil. 11, 4, 8: ut orbitatis cruciamenta sentiret,Arn. 7, p. 43.

cruciarius.definition: crŭcĭārĭus, a, um, crux Of or pertaining to the cross, or, in gen., to torture. Adj.: exitus,full of torture,Tert. Praescr. Haeret. 2 dub. (al. cruciatorios): poenae,Sid. Ep. 8, 6. Subst., one who is crucified, Petr. 112; Sen. Contr. 3, 21.—Hence

cruciator.definition: crucio A tormenter, torturer, Arn. 1, p. 23; Firm. Math. 3, 13, 6.

cruciatus.definition: Torture, torment, a torturing, execution, etc. (often syn. with supplicium; freq. and class. in sing. and plur.). Lit., of the body: dedisti hodie in cruciatum Chrusalum,Plaut. Bacch. 4, 4, 36; id. Ep. 5, 1, 5; id. Ps. 3, 1, 12; Ter. And. 4, 4, 47; id. Hec. 5, 2, 7; Caes. B. G. 1, 31, 12; Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 4, § 9; 2, 5, 63, § 163; id. Rosc. Am. 41, 119; Sall. C. 51, 15; id. J. 24, 10; Liv. 29, 18, 14 Drak. N. cr.; Quint. 5, 4, 2; Ov. M. 9, 179 et ...

crucifer.definition: crux-fero The crossbearer, i. e. Christ, Prud. Cath. 3, 1.

crucifigo.definition: crŭcĭfīgo, ēre, better separated, cruci figo; v. crux.

crucifixor.definition: crux-figo A crucifier (eccl. Lat.), Paul. Nol. Ep. 18, 7.

crucio.definition: crŭcĭo, āvi, ātum, 1, crux. Orig., to put to death on the cross, to crucify (only in eccl. Lat.), Lact. Mort. Pers. 2, 1. In gen., to put to the rack, to torture, torment (freq. and class., esp. in the signif. B.).

crudelis.definition: crūdēlis, e, adj.cf. Gr. κρύος; Lat. crudus, cruor, caro Morally rude or unfeeling, with exclusive reference to conduct towards persons or things, hard, unmerciful, hard-hearted, cruel, severe, fierce (freq. and class. in prose and poetry). Of living subjects. Of inanimate subjects: crudele et exitiosum bellum,Cic. Att. 9, 6, 7: o rem cum auditu crudelem tum visu nefariam,id. Planc. 41, 99: poena in cives crudelis,id. Phil. 11, 1, 1: in tam crud...

crudelitas.definition: crudelis Harshness, severity, cruelty, barbarity (in good prose and very freq.): crudelitas est atrocitas animi in exigendis poenis,Sen. Clem. 2, 4, 1: crudelitas est inclinatio ad asperiora,id. ib. 2, 4, 3: ista in nostros homines crudelitas,Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 88, § 150; id. Off. 2, 8, 27; 3, 11, 46; id. Sest. 65, 135; id. Phil. 11, 3, 8; id. Rep. 1, 3, 5; Caes. B. G. 7, 77; Sall. C. 51, 14; Nep. Alcib. 4, 4; Liv. 3, 53, 7; 42, 8, 5 et saep.; Prud...

crudesco.definition: crūdesco, dŭi, 3 V. inch. n. [crudus], to grow harsh or violent, to increase, grow worse (poet. and in post-Aug. prose; perh. not before Virg.): coepit crudescere morbus,Verg. G. 3, 504; so, pugnae,id. A. 7, 788: ferrum magicā linguā,Sil. 1, 431: irae,Stat. Th. 2, 680; cf.: crudescente irā,Just. 8, 4, 4: seditio,Tac. H. 3, 10: noxa,Symm. Ep. 8, 57.

cruditas.definition: id. (lit. Indigestion; hence, meton.) (Effectus pro causa.) An overloading, repletion of the stomach, Cic. Sen. 13, 44; id. Fam. 9, 18, 4; id. Fat. 15, 34; Quint. 2, 21, 19; 5, 9, 11; Col. prooem. § 16; 6, 6, 1 al. (Abstr. pro concr.) Undigested food: cruditates digerunt daucum, plantago, etc.,Plin. 26, 7, 25, § 41; cf.: cruditas fructuum,i. e. bitterness,Pall. Febr. 9, 13.

cruditatio.definition: crudito, i. q. cruditas An overloading of the stomach, indigestion, Cael. Aur. Tard. 5, 2, 29.

crudito.definition: crūdĭto, āre, crudus To suffer from indigestion, Tert. Jejun. 16; id. Apol. 9.

crudus.definition: crūdus, a, um, root kru-, of Gr. κρύος; cf. cruor, crudelis Bloody, bleeding, trickling with blood, etc. Prop. (so rare): vulnus,Plin. Ep. 5, 16, 11: vulnera,Ov. Tr. 3, 11, 19; id. P. 1, 3, 16. Transf.

cruentatio.definition: cruento A staining with blood: altaris,Tert. adv. Marc. 4, 39.

cruento.definition: crŭento, āvi, ātum, 1, cruentus To make bloody, to spot with blood (class.). Lit.: vigiles, Enn. ap. Macr. S. 1, 4: manus suorum sanguine,Nep. Epam. 10, 3; cf. Liv. 23, 9, 4, and Tac. H. 1, 58 fin.: cornipedem ferratā calce,Sil. 17, 541: gladium,Cic. Inv. 2, 4, 14; cf. tela,Ov. M. 8, 424: ōs,id. ib. 4, 104: dextras,id. ib. 11, 23: cruentati redeunt,id. ib. 3, 572: ut sequenti die Luna se in Aquario cruentaret,would appear to be stained with blood...

cruentus.definition: crŭentus, a, um, cruor Spotted, covered, or stained with blood, bloody. Prop. (freq. and class.): cruentus sanguine civium Romanorum,Cic. Phil. 4, 2, 4; cf.: sanguine fraterno,Hor. S. 2, 5, 15: caede filii,Just. 38, 8, 4: cadaver Clodii,Cic. Mil. 13, 33: vehiculum,Liv. 1, 48, 8: gladius,Quint. 4, 2, 13; 6, 1, 30: praetexta C. Caesaris,id. ib. § 31: vestis,id. 5, 9, 1: busta,Prop. 2, 13 (3, 5), 38: sputa,id. 4 (5), 5, 68 et saep.: victoria,Sall. C...

crumena.definition: (), , for scrumena; root scru-, of scrutor, scrotum A small money-purse or bag (usually hanging from the neck). Prop., Plaut. Truc. 3, 1, 7 sq.; id. As. 3, 3, 63; 3, 3, 71; id. Ps. 1, 2, 37. Transf., like our purse, for money: non deficiente crumenā,Hor. Ep. 1, 4, 11; Juv. 11, 38.

crumino.definition: crŭmīno, āre, id. To fill like a purse, Ven. Vit. S. Mart. 2, 350.

cruor.definition: cf. κρέας, κρύος, caro, crudus. Blood (which flows from a wound), a stream of blood (more restricted in meaning than sanguis, which designates both that circulating in bodies and that shed by wounding): e nostro cum corpore sanguis Emicat exsultans alte spargitque cruorem,Lucr. 2, 194; Tac. A. 12, 47; and: cruor inimici recentissimus,Cic. Rosc. Am. 7, 19 (cf.: sanguis per venas in omne corpus diffunditur,id. N. D. 2, 55, 138 al.; v. sanguis; cf...

cruralis.definition: crūrālis, e, crus Of or belonging to the legs, crural: fasciae,Petr. 40, 5; Dig. 34, 2, 25.

crus.definition: etym. dub.; prob. kindr. with curro, currus; cf. celer, and -cello in recello, etc. The leg, shank, shin. Prop., Cels. 8, 1 fin.: perque fabam repunt (grues) et mollia crura reponunt, Enn. ap. Serv. ad Verg. G. 3, 76 (Ann. v. 545 Vahl.); imitated by Verg. G. 3, 76, and Sil. 16, 444; so Lucr. 3, 478; 3, 652; Cic. N. D. 1, 36, 101; Caes. B. G. 6, 27; Plin. 10, 46, 63, § 129; Quint. 11, 3, 139; Ov. M. 1, 306; 4, 580 et saep. The legs of criminals we...

crusmaticus.definition: crusmătĭcus, a, um Suitable for playing on a musical instrument: pars musicae,Censor. Fragm. 11.

crusta.definition: cf. crudus The hard surface of a body, the rind, shell, crust, bark, etc. In gen.: luti,Lucr. 6, 626; cf. soli,Dig. 39, 2, 9: panis,Plin. 19, 8, 53, § 168: glandis,id. 15, 28, 34, § 112: piscium,id. 9, 28, 44, § 83: locustarum,id. 9, 30, 50, § 95: ulcerum,the scab,Cels. 5, 9; cf. id. 5, 10: fluminis, a covering or crust of ice, Verg. G. 3, 360 et saep. In partic., t. t. of plastic art, inlaid, chased, or embossed work on walls or vessels, plaster...

crustarius.definition: crustārĭus, a, um, crusta, II. Pertaining to embossed work. Adj.: tabernae, Paul. ex Fest. p. 53, 6. Subst.: crustārĭus, ii, m., one who makes embossed or chased figures, on plate, etc., Plin. 33, 12, 55, § 157.

crusto.definition: crusto, āvi, ātum, 1, crusta To cover with a rind, shell, incrustation, plaster-work, embossed figures, etc. (post-Aug.): mala gypso,Plin. 15, 17, 18, § 64: domum marmoribus,to incrust,Luc. 10, 114; cf. Isid. Orig. 19, 3: portam crasso ferro,Amm. 24, 2, 14: vasa potoria crustata, Paul. ex Fest. p. 53, 6 Müll.: crustata crassities pectoris et ventris,incased with fat,App. M. 7, p. 189, 18.—Subst.: crustāta, ōrum, n. (sc. animalia), crustaceous ani...

crustula.definition: dim.id. A little rind, shell, or crust, Arn. 2, p. 84.

crustularius.definition: crustulum One who makes pastry, a confectioner, Sen. Ep. 56, 3.

crustulum.definition: dim.crustum Small pastry, confectionery, Varr. L. L. 5, § 107 Müll.; Hor. S. 1, 1, 25; 2, 4, 47; Juv. 9, 5; Sen. Ep. 99, 27; Inscr. Grut. 100, 5 al.

crustum.definition: access. form to crusta Pastry, any thing baked, Hor. Ep. 1, 1, 78; Verg. A. 7, 115; Inscr. Grut. 173, 4; 373, 8.

crux.definition: f. (m., Enn. ap. Non. p. 195, 13; Gracch. ap. Fest. s. v. masculino, p. 150, 24, and 151, 12 Müll.) [perh. kindred with circus]. Lit. Transf.

crypta.definition: A concealed, subterrunean passage, a vault, cavern, cave, grotto, pit, Varr. ap. Non. p. 169, 11; Suet. Calig. 58; Juv. 5, 106 al.—As a place of deposit, Vitr. 6, 8. Esp.: crypta Neapolitana, a dark grotto in the neighborhood of Naples, through which was a shorter passage to Puteoli, now Grotta di Napoli, Sen. Ep. 57, 1.

crypticus.definition: cryptĭcus, a, um Covered, concealed: arcus,Sid. Ep. 1, 5.

crystallinus.definition: crystallĭnus, a, um Made of crystal, crystalline, crystal. Adj.: calices,Capitol. Ver. 5: pila,Plin. 37, 2, 10, § 28: centra in sapphiris,id. 37, 9, 39, § 120. Subst.: crystallĭ-num, i, n. (sc. vas), Sen. Ira, 3, 40, 2.— Mostly plur, Juv. 6, 155; Mart. 1, 53, 6; 9, 59, 13; Plin. 37, 2, 11, § 30: PRAEPOSITVS A CRYSTALLINIS,Inscr. Orell. 2953.

crystallum.definition: n. (analog. to the Gr. , m., Sol. 15 fin.), = . Ice, Auct. Priap. 63, 6. A crystal, mountain- or rock-crystal, Plin. 37, 2, 9, § 23; Sen. Q. N. 3, 25, 12; Plin. 36, 26, 66, § 192; Curt. 3, 3, 8; Stat. S. 1, 2, 126.

cubator.definition: cubo He who lies down, Paul. Nol. Ep. 21, 4.

cubicularius.definition: cŭbĭcŭlārĭus, a, um (cŭbĭcŭlāris, e; Gen., Cic. Div. 2, 65, 134; dat., id. Tusc. 5, 20, 59; but ap. Suet. Aug. 7, the better read. is cubiculi Lares; v. cubiculum, I.), cubiculum, of or pertaining to a sleepingchamber. Adj.: lucerna,Mart. 14, 39in lemm.: gausapina,id. 14, 147in lemm.: stragula,Plin. 8, 58, 83, § 226. Subst.: cŭ-bĭcŭlārĭus, ii, m., a chamber-servant, valet-de-chambre: hunc vestri janitores, hunc cubicularii diligunt,Cic. Verr. 2, ...

cubiculum.definition: (, per sync., Mart. 10, 30, 17 dub.), , cubo An apartment for reclining or (more freq.) for sleeping (cf. cubo), a resting- or sleepingchamber, a bedchamber. Prop., Plaut. Most. 3, 2, 7; Serv. Galba ap. Cic. de Or. 2, 65, 263; Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 23, § 56; Plin. Ep. 1, 3, 1; Quint. 10, 3, 25; Tac. A. 14, 44; Suet. Caes. 49: Lares cubiculi,Suet. Dom. 17; id. Aug. 7 Roth ex conj. Lips.; v. cubicularius init. Transf.

cubile.definition: cubo A place of rest, a couch, bed. Lit. Trop.: avaritiae non jam vestigia, sed ipsa cubilia videre, the very den or lair, Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 77, § 190; cf. id. Clu. 30, 82: quas (stragis) nos non vestigiis odorantes ingressus tuos, sed totis volutationibus corporis et cubilibus persecuti sumus,id. Pis. 34, 83 al.

cubital.definition: id. A cushion for leaning on, an elbow-cushion, Hor. S. 2, 3, 255 (quoted in Fronto Ep. ad M. Caes. 1, 1).

cubitalis.definition: cŭbĭtālis, e, cubitum Pertaining to the elbow; hence, as a measure, a cubit long, Liv. 24, 34, 9; Plin. 12, 12, 26, § 45; Pall. Febr. 18, 6 al.: simulacrum cubitali majus,Suet. Galb. 4.

cubitio.definition: 1. cubitus A lying down, Aug. Ep. 151.

cubito.definition: cŭbĭto, āvi, 1 V. freq. n. [cubo], to lie down often, to be accustomed to lie down (rare): anus hic solet cubitare,Plaut. Curc. 1, 1, 76; Cic. Cael. 15, 36: humi (pavones),Col. 8, 11 fin.: super pedes cubitantis reclinis,Tac. A. 14, 5.—Of sexual intercourse: cum aliquā (aliquo),Plaut. Curc. 1, 1, 57; id. Stich. 4, 1, 41; Quint. 8, 3, 22.

cubitum.definition: n. (, , m., Cels. 8, 1; 8, 16; Non. p. 201, 16) [id.] The elbow (serving for leaning upon). Prop., Cels. 1. 1.; Plin. 11, 45, 102, § 249; Plaut. Stich. 2, 1, 13; Verg. A. 4, 690; Ov. M. 7, 343; Hor. C. 1, 27, 8; id. S. 2, 4, 39; Quint. 11, 3, 93 al. Meton.

cubitus.definition: id. A lying down (very rare). Prop.: supini, proni, in latera,Plin. 28, 4, 14, § 54. Meton. (abstr. pro concr.), a bed, couch: foliis cubitus sibi sternunt,Plin. 24, 9, 38, § 59.

cubo.definition: cŭbo, ŭi, ìtúm, 1 ( Perf. subj. cubaris, Prop. 2 (3), 15, 17; perf. inf. cubasse, Quint. 8, 2, 20; cf. also Neue, Formenl. II. p. 478), cf. κύπτω, to lie down. Of persons. Of inanim. objects.

cubus.definition: A die, cube, Vitr. 5, praef. 4. A cubic number, Gell. 1, 20, 6.

cucullatus.definition: cŭcullātus, a, um, cucullus Hooded, having a hood (late Lat.): vestis,Isid. Orig. 19, 24, 17.

cucullus.definition: m. (, , f., in eccl. Lat., Paul. Nol. 21, 389; Hier. Vit. Hil. 46; Ennod. Ep. 9, 14) [root kal-, of cella, clam, καλύπτω; cf. culleus] A covering. Of the head, a cap, hood, fastened to a garment, Col. 1, 8, 9; Mart. 11, 98, 10; Juv. 3, 170; as a disguise,id. 8, 145 al. Of the feet, Capitol. Pert. 8 dub. Of merchandise, a conical wrapper or case, Mart. 3, 2, 5.

cuculus.definition: (cŭcŭlus, Auct. Carm. Philom. 35), , Sanscr. ku-, to cry; cf. κωκύω A cuckoo, Plin. 18, 26, 66, § 249; as a term of reproach,Plaut. As. 5, 2, 73; id. Ps. 1, 1, 94; esp. of foolish men,id. Trin. 2, 1, 18; and of dilatory husbandmen, who are not through with their pruning until the cuckoo is heard (after the vernal equinox),Plin. 1. 1.; Hor. S. 1, 7, 31; cf. Plin. 18, 26, 66, § 249; Voss ad Verg. G. 2, 403.

cucuma.definition: coquo. A cookingvessel, a kettle, Petr. 135, 4; Dig. 48, 8, 1. Perh., a small private bath (opp. thermae), Mart. 10, 79, 4.

cucumeraceus.definition: cŭcŭmĕrācĕus, a, um Adj., cucumber-like, of cucumber, Theod. Prisc. p. 2, 3.

cucumerarium.definition: cucumis A cucumber-field (eccl. Lat., transl. of the Heb. , Isa. 1, 8), Tert. adv. Jud. 3; Hier. in Isa. 1, 1, 8.

cucumis.definition: (is, sometimes in the Nat. Hist. of Pliny; e. g. acc. cucumim, Plin. 9, 2, 1, § 3; 20, 1, 2, § 3; abl. cucumi, id. 20, 9, 40, § 103 al.; Together with cucumeris,id. 19, 5, 23, § 68; 19, 12, 61, § 186: cucumeres,id. 19, 5, 24, § 69 (cucumis, Sillig): cucumerum,id. 19, 5, 23, § 68 al.), m. A cucumber, Col. 11, 3, 48; Plin. 19, 5, 23, § 64 sq.; Pall. Mart. 9, 7; Varr. R. R. 1, 2, 25; Verg. G. 4, 122 al. A sea-plant, similar in color and odor to the ...

cucurbita.definition: A gourd. Prop., Col. 11, 3, 48 sq.; Plin. 19, 5, 24, § 69 sq.; Pall. Mart. 9, 16. Transf., in medic. lang., a cup, cupping-glass (of similar form), Scrib. Comp. 46; 67; Juv. 14, 58: cucurbitae medicinales,Plin. 32, 10, 42, § 123 al. Trop., a blockhead, Petr. 39.

cucurbitarius.definition: cucurbita A gourd planter, Hier. Ep. 112, n. 22.

cucurbitatio.definition: cucurbita, II. A cupping, Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 1, 32.

cucurbitinus.definition: cŭcurbĭtīnus, a, um, cucurbita Like or similar to a gourd: pira,the gourdpear,Cato, R. R. 7, 4; Plin. 15, 15, 16, § 56: ficus, Cloatius ap. Macr. S. 2, 16, 1; 2, 15, 6.

cucurbitula.definition: dim.id.. Silvestris, the bitter gourd, Scrib. Comp. 106. A cupping-glass, Cels. 2, 11; 3, 18.

cucurbitularis.definition: cucurbitula The field cypress, = chamaepitys, Isid. Orig. 17, 9, 86.

cucutium.definition: cf. cucullus A kind of hood, Treb. Poll. Claud. 17, 6.

cudo.definition: cūdo, ĕre V. a., to strike, beat, pound, knock (rare and only ante-class., and in postAug. prose). Prop.: aurum pilis,Plin. 33, 4, 21, § 69 (v. Sillig N. cr.): semina,to beat out, thresh,Col. 2, 10, 14; Lucr. 1, 1044; 4, 187.—Prov.: istaec in me cudetur faba,i. e. I must smart for that,Ter. Eun. 2, 3, 90 Don. Transf. (of metals), to prepare by beating or hammering, to forge; of money, to stamp, coin: plumbeos nummos,Plaut. Most. 4, 2, 11: argentu...

cuicuimodi.definition: cuicuimŏdi (ante-class. quoiquoi mŏdi) [quisquis-modus], euphon. form for cujuscujusmodi (very rare in MSS., but vouched for by the ancient grammarians; v. Kuhner, Gram. I. p. 398; 405 sq.) Of what sort, kind, or nature soever: sisne necne ut esse oportet, malus, bonus quoiquoi modi,Plaut. Bacch. 3, 2, 16: velim omnia quam diligentissime, cuicuimodi sunt, scribas,Cic. Att. 3, 22, 4; Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 41, § 107 Zumpt and Halm ad loc.; cf. Madv. ad ...

cuimodi.definition: cuimŏdiquis-modus for cujusmodi = qualis Of what kind or nature soever: cuimodi esset,Gell. 9, 13, 4; 12, 2, 2; 12, 15, 1; 13, 29, 1 al.

cuias.definition: cūjas (archaic quōjas), ātis, or (anteand post-class.) uncontr. cūjātis, is Pron. interrog. [pronom. stem quo-; cf.: quis, qui], whence originating? of what country, family, or town? whence? from what place? = ποδαπός; nom. cujatis (quoj-), Enn. ap. Cic. Balb. 22, 51; Att. ap. Non. p. 426, 24; Plaut. Curc. 3, 37; id. Men. 2, 2, 66; id. Poen. prol. 109; 5, 2, 33; App. M. 1, p. 104, 16; 8, p. 212, 31: quem cum percunctaretur Scipio, quis et cujas ...

cuius.definition: cūjus (archaic quōjus), a, um Pron. interrog. [pronom. stem quo-], pertaining to whom? of whom? whose? (most freq. in Plaut. and Ter.): quoja vox sonat procul?Plaut. Curc. 1, 2, 18; id. Ps. 2, 4, 11; id. Rud. 2, 3, 2; id. Trin. 1, 2, 7: illa mulier,id. Merc. 4, 3, 20; cf. id. ib. 1, 2, 87: fidicina,id. Ep. 2, 2, 109: virgo,Ter. Eun. 2, 3, 29: puer,id. ib. 4, 4, 24: navis,Plaut. Stich. 2, 2, 46: cujum pecus? an Meliboei?Verg. E. 3, 1; 5, 87.—Absol...

cuiuscemodi.definition: cūjuscĕmŏdi (quōj-) or cūjuscĕ mŏdi quisce-modus Of what kind or nature soever (late Lat.): voces,App. M. 8, p. 209, 9.

cuiusdammodi.definition: cūjusdammŏdi, better cūjusdam mŏdi Of some sort, Cic. Fin. 5, 12, 36; id. Div. 2, 14, 34.

cuiusmodi.definition: cūjusmŏdi (quōj-), also cūjus mŏdi quis-modus = qualis Of what kind: cupio cognoscere iter tuum cujusmodi sit,Cic. Fam. 15, 20, 3; Auct. B. Afr. 31; Plaut. Most. 3, 2, 132. Of whatever kind, Cic. Fam. 4, 7, 4 (al. leg. cuicuimodi); id. Tusc. 5, 41, 121 (al. cuicuimodi); Plaut. Bacch. 3, 2, 16.

culcita.definition: (in MSS. also ), , etym. dub.; acc. to Varr. L. L. 5, § 167 Müll.; Paul. ex Fest. p. 50, 8, from calco A sack filled with feathers, wool, hair, etc., for lying upon, warming, etc.; a bed, cushion, mattress, pillow, Cato, R. R. 10 fin.; 11fin.; Varr. ap. Non. p. 86, 5 sq.; Cic. Tusc. 3, 19, 46; Sen. Ep. 87, 2; 108, 23; Suet. Tib. 54 al. —Of a little cushion or patch for the eye, Plaut. Mil. 4, 4, 42.—Of a resting-place in a conservatory of birds, ...

culcitarius.definition: culcita A cushion-maker, acc. to Diom. p. 313 P.

culcitula.definition: dim.id. A small cushion or mattress, Lucil. ap. Non. p. 35, 20; cf. Diom. p. 326, 20 K.

culex.definition: m. (f., Plaut. Cas. 2, 3, 22) A gnat, midge (comprising very many species), Plin. 11, 2, 1, § 2 sq.; 11, 35, 41, § 118; 17, 27, 44, § 255; Plaut. Curc. 4, 2, 14; Lucr. 3, 391; Hor. S. 1, 5, 14; Col. 11, 3, 60; Mart. 3, 93, 9 al.—Also the title of a writing of Verg.; cf. Heyn. Verg. tom. iv. prooem.—As a term of reproach for a wanton lover,Plaut. Cas. 2, 3, 22.

culigna.definition: A small drinking-vessel, a cup, Cato, R. R. 132, 1; Fragm. ap. Paul. ex Fest. p. 55, 2 Müll.

culina.definition: (old orthogr. , acc. to Non. p. 55, 18 sq.), , Sanscr. çar, çri, to cook, mix A kitchen. Prop., Plaut. Most. 1, 1, 1; id. Truc. 2, 7, 53; Varr. R. R. 1, 13, 2; Cic. Fam. 15, 18, 1; Sen. Ep. 114, 26; Petr. 2; Hor. S. 1, 5, 73; 2, 5, 80; cf. of a portable kitchen, Sen. Ep. 78, 23; Juv. 3, 250. Transf.

culinarius.definition: cŭlīnārĭus, a, um, culina Pertaining to the kitchen, culinary, kitchen-. Adj.: operae,Fronto, B. Parth. p. 201. Subst.: cŭlīnārĭus, ii, m., a kitchen servant, Scrib. Comp. 230.

cullearis.definition: cullĕāris (cūl-), e, culleus, II. A. Of the measure of a culleus: labrum,Cato, R. R. 154: dolia,Vitr. 6, 9.

culleus.definition: (, and in the signif. II. B., ), ( Nom. plur. cullea, neutr., Cato ap. Varr. R. R. 1, 2, 7; Non. p. 197; gen. plur. culleūm, Cato, R. R. 11, 1), m., = κολεός, Ion. κουλεός (a sheath; hence), a leather bag, a sack for holding liquids. Prop.: Te ipsam culleo ego cras faciam ut deportere in pergulam,Plaut. Ps. 1, 2, 78; Nep. Eum. 8, 7; Plin. 7, 20, 19, § 82.—Parricides were sewed up in bags and drowned, Cic. Rosc. Am. 25, 70; id. Inv. 2, 50, 149; ...

culmen.definition: culmen, ĭnis, contr. form of columen, q. v.

culmeus.definition: culmĕus, a, um, culmus Of siraw: tecti culmina,Paul. Nol. Carm. 13, 387.

culmosus.definition: culmōsus, a, um, culmus Stalklike, poet.: fratres,sprung from the dragonteeth,Sid. Carm. 6, 72.

culmus.definition: kindr. with culmen A stalk, stem, esp. of grain, straw, Varr. R. R. 1, 48, 3 (Cod. Vindob. culmen); Cic. Sen. 15, 51; Verg. G. 1, 111; 1, 317 al.—Of other plants: milii, panici,Plin. 18, 7, 10, § 52: holci,id. 27, 10, 63, § 90: lilii,Stat. S. 3, 3, 128.

culpa.definition: kindr. in root with scelus; cf. Sanscr. skhal-, errare Crime, fault, blame, failure, defect (as a state worthy of punishment; on the contr. delictum, peccatum, etc., as punishable acts; diff. from scelus, which implies an intentional injury of others; but culpa includes in it an error in judgment). Prop. Meton., any thing mischievous or injurious, mischief: continuo culpam (sc. ovem aegram) ferro compesce,Verg. G. 3, 468: sedula (i. e. meretrix),...

culpabilis.definition: culpābĭlis, e, culpa Worthy of blame, culpable, criminal (post-class.): aliquid (opp. laudabile),App. Mag. p. 223: opinio de diis (opp. digna),Arn. 7, p. 222. —Comp.: tanto culpabilius est, non observare quod possis,Tert. ad Uxor. 2, 1.—Adv.: culpābĭlĭter, culpably, Symm. Ep. 9, 40. —Comp., Paul. Nol. Ep. 39, 4; Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 17, 172.

culpo.definition: culpo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.culpa. To reproach or blame a person or thing as wrong or faulty, to censure, reprove, disapprove, condemn (syn.: reprehendo, vitupero; opp. laudo, probo, etc.; rare; mostly post-Aug.; never in the Cic. per.). Culpare aliquid, to declare something as a crime, to impute a fault to, to complain of, find fault with: arbore nunc aquas Culpante, etc.,Hor. C. 3, 1, 31; cf.: agrorum infecunditatem,Col. 1, prooem. § 1: culpantur...

culte.definition: cultē, , v. colo P. a. fin.

cultello.definition: cultello, no Perf., ātum, 1, cultellus. To make in the shape of a knife: spinam dorsi,Plin. 8, 25, 38, § 91; 32, 2, 5, § 13 Sillig N. cr. To level land by the coulter, Front. Limit. p. 43 Goes.

cultellus.definition: dim.culter A small knife. Prop., Varr. R. R. 1, 69, 2; id. Fragm. ap. Non. p. 195, 18; Hor. Ep. 1, 7, 51; Plin. 12, 25, 54, § 115 al. Lignei, wooden pegs or pins, Vitr. 7, 3.

culter.definition: kindr. with Sanscr. kar, to wound, kill; cf. per-cello, clades. Orig. a plough-coulter, ploughshare, Plin. 18, 18, 48, § 171 sq.
