In gen., a knife; so a vintner's knife, Col. 4, 25, 2; 12, 45, 4; a butcher's knife, Plaut. Rud. 1, 2, 46; Liv. 3, 48, 5: qui ad cultrum bovem emunt,i. e. for slaughter,Varr. R. R. 2, 5, 11; Suet. Tib. 25; Scrib. Comp. 13; a razor: cultros metuens tonsorios,Cic. Off. 2, 7, 25: cultrum tonsorium super jugulum meum posui,...

cultor.definition: id.. Prop., one who bestows care or labor upon a thing, an elaborator, cultivator, etc.: agrorum,Liv. 2, 34, 11; 4, 25, 4: agri,id. 40, 29, 3; cf. agricultor: virentis agelli,Hor. A. P. 117: terrae,Cic. N. D. 2, 39, 99: vitis,a vine-dresser,id. Fin. 5, 14, 40: alveorum,a bee-master, apiarist,Col. 9, 3, 1.—Poet., of a bullock: pauperis agri,Ov. F. 5, 515. Trop. (acc. to colo, II. A. and B.).

cultrarius.definition: culter A slayer of the victim (for sacrifice), Suet. Calig. 32; Inscr. Orell. 4175.

cultrix.definition: cultor. Prop., she who labors at or cares for a thing: earum rerum quas terra gignit ... augendarum et alendarum quandam cultricem esse, quae sit scientia atque ars agricolarum,Cic. Fin. 5, 14, 39. Trop., a female worshipper: deorum montium,Lact. Mort. Pers. 11.

cultura.definition: 1. colo. A cultivating, care, cultivation: agri,Varr. R. R. 2, praef. § 4; Cic. Sen. 15, 54; Suet. Aug. 42 al.: agelli,Lucr. 5, 1366; cf. Cic. Agr. 2, 30, 83; 2, 35, 94; id. Fl. 29, 71, and agricultura: vitis,id. Fin. 5, 14, 39.—In plur.: agri culturas docuit usus,Lucr. 5, 1447. Trop.

cultus.definition: cultus, a, um, Part. and , from 1. colo.

culullus.definition: (acc. to Acro upon Hor. C. 1, 31, 11, orig. a sacrificial vessel for liquids; later, in gen.) A drinking-vessel, beaker, goblet, cup, bowl, Hor. l. l.; id. A. P. 434.

culus.definition: perh. kindr. with κοῖλος, of a curving form; cf. 1. anus The posteriors, fundament, Cat. 23, 19; 33, 4; 97, 2; Mart. 3, 98, 1.

cum.definition: cum (archaic form COM, found in an inscr., COM PREIVATVD; in MSS. sometimes quom or quum), with abl. [for skom, Sanscr. root sak, together; cf. sequor, and Gr. κοινός, σὐν], designates in gen. accompaniment, community, connection of one object with another (opp. sine, separatim, etc.) With, together, together with, in connection or company with, along with; sometimes also to be translated and. In gen., Plaut. Am. prol. 95: qui cum Amphitruone a...

cumatilis.definition: cūmātĭlis (cȳm-), e, from κῦμα, with the Lat. ending ilis. Adj., of the waves: deus,i. e. Neptune,Commod. 10, 1. Subst.: cūmātĭle, is, n., a bluish garment, Plaut. Ep. 2, 2, 49.

cumera.definition: f. (, , n., Varr. L. L. 7, § 34 Müll.; Paul. ex Fest. p. 50, 7 ib.) [cf. Gr. καμάρα, Lat. camera] A chest, box, or basket, to keep grain in, Hor. S. 1, 1, 53 Acro; id. Ep. 1, 7, 30; for the utensils of a bride, Paul. ex Fest. p. 63, 12; Varr. l. l.

cuminatus.definition: cŭmīnātus (cym-), a, um, cuminum Seasoned or mixed with cumin, Pall. Nov. 22, 5. Subst.: cŭmīnātum, i, n., cumin-spice, Apic. 1, 29.

cumininus.definition: cŭmīnīnus (cym-), a, um, id. Of cumin: oleum,App. Herb. 74.

cuminum.definition: () Cumin, a plant: Cuminum (Cyminum), Linn.; said to produce paleness,Plin. 20, 14, 57, § 159 sq.; Pall. Mart. 9, 17: exsangue,Hor. Ep. 1, 19, 18: pallens,Pers. 5, 55.

cummis.definition: cummis, is, and cummi, indecl., v. gummi.

cumque.definition: cumquĕ (quomquĕ or cunquĕ), cum-que, serves for the generalizing of any action, event, time, etc. However, whenever, howsoever, whensoever, -ever, -soever. Usu. with pronn. and pronom. advv.: quicumque, qualiscumque, etc., ubicumque, quotienscumque, etc. Very rarely standing alone: quae demant cumque dolorem,which remove pain in general, any pain,Lucr. 2, 21: cum solis lumina cumque Inserti fundunt radii per opaca domorum,in whatever manner,id. 2...

cumulate.definition: cŭmŭlātē, , v. cumulo P. a. fin.

cumulatim.definition: cŭmŭlātim, cumulatus Abundantly, in heaps, in abundance (ante- and post-class., and very rare): positum in doliis,Varr. R. R. 3, 15, 2; Prud. Apoth. 717; 739.

cumulatus.definition: cŭmŭlātus, a, um, Part. and , from cumulo.

cumulo.definition: cŭmŭlo, āvi, ātum, 1 V. a., to form into a heap, to accumulate, heap, or pile up (class.). In gen. With special access. ideas (class.).

cumulus.definition: Sanscr. çva, to swell; Gr. κυέω, κύω; cf. κῦμα A heap, as coming to a point, a pile, a mass piled up (class.; esp. freq. in the signif. II.): in hoc immenso aliarum super alias acervatarum legum cumulo,Liv. 3, 34, 6; cf.: hostium coacervatorum,id. 22, 7, 5; 5, 48, 3: corpus obrutum superstratis Gallorum cumulis,id. 9, 29, 19; and: armorum cumulos coacervare id. 5, 39, 1: caesorum corporum,id. 22, 59, 3: saxei,Plin. 31, 10, 46, § 111: eminens (...

cunctabundus.definition: cunctābundus (cont-), a, um, cunctor Lingering, loitering, delaying (very rare): (milites) cunctabundosque et resistentes egressos castris esse,Liv. 6, 7, 2: nusquam cunctabundus nisi cum in senatu loqueretur,Tac. A. 1, 7: verba,Mamert. in Jul. 18, 6: amnis,Eum. Pan. Const. 18, 3.

cunctalis.definition: cunctālis, e, cunctus General, Mart. Cap. 1, § 34.

cunctamen.definition: (), , cunctor A delaying, hesitating, Paul. Nol. 24, 416.

cunctanter.definition: cunctanter (cont-), adv., v. cunctor, P. a., 2. Fin.

cunctatio.definition: (), , cunctor A delaying, lingering, in a good or (more freq.) in a bad sense, a tarrying, delay, hesitation, doubt (subject., while mora is object.; freq. and in good prose): danda brevis cogitationi mora ... in hac cunctatione, etc.,Quint. 11, 3, 157: studium semper adsit, cunctatio absit,Cic. Lael. 13, 44: boni nescio quo modo tardiores sunt ... ita ut non numquam cunctatione ac tarditate ... otium atque dignitatem amittant,id. Sest. 47, 100: ...

cunctator.definition: (), , id. One who acts with hesitation or tardiness, a delayer, loiterer, lingerer (not in Cic.); in a bad sense, Cael. ap. Cic. Fam. 8, 10, 3: cunctato ex acerrimo bellatore factus,Liv. 6, 23, 5.—In a good sense, a considerate or cautious person (magister equitum Fabium) pro cunctatore segnem, pro cauto timidum compellabat, Liv. 22, 12, 12; so with cautus,Tac. H. 2, 25: non cunctator iniqui Labdacus,Stat. Th. 3, 79; cf.: Atheniensium populum cel...

cunctatrix.definition: cunctator One who hesitates, acts deliberately (late Lat.): lenta virtus omnis et diuturna cunctatrix,Ambros. Ep. 67, 5.

cuncticinus.definition: cunctĭcĭnus, a, um, cunctuscano, prop. Sounding all together; hence, concordant, harmonious (opp.simplex), Mart. Cap. 9, § 905.

cunctiparens.definition: id. Parent of all, Prud. στεφ. 14, 128.

cunctipotens.definition: cunctĭ-pŏtens, entis, m.id. All-powerful, omnipotent: Jesus (i. e. omnipotens), Prud. στεφ. 7, 56.

cuncto.definition: cuncto, āre, 1, (ante-class. collat. form of cunctor) To delay, hesitate, Enn. ap. Non. p. 469, 27 (Com. Rel. v. 3 Vahl.): cunctas? intus alii festinant,Plaut. Cas. 4, 2, 13: cunctant subferre laborem, Att. ap. Non. p. 469, 24 (Trag. Rel. v. 72 Rib.).

cunctor.definition: cunctor (in many MSS. and edd. also contor), ātus, 1 (archaic Inf. cunctarier, Lucr. 3, 67), v. dep. cf. Sanscr. çank, to be anxious; Gr. ὄκνος, to delay action (from deliberation or indolence), to linger, loiter, hesitate, doubt (freq. and class.); constr. absol., with the inf. or a subj.-clause. Of personal subjects. Poet. transf., of things as subjects: tardum cunctatur olivum,runs slowly,Lucr. 2, 392: refrigescit cunctando plaga,id. 4, 703:...

cunctus.definition: cunctus, a, um, and more freq. in plur.cuncti, ae, a, contr. from conjunctus All in a body, all together, the whole, all, entire (cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 50, 15 Müll.: cuncti significat quidem omnes, sed conjuncti et congregati; very freq. and class.).

cuneatim.definition: cŭnĕātim, cuneo In the form of a wedge, wedge-shaped (rare): constiterunt hostes,Caes. B. G. 7, 28; App. M. 8, p. 165 Bip.

cuneatus.definition: cŭnĕātus, a, um, Part. and , from cuneo.

cuneo.definition: cŭnĕo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.cuneus (rare, and not ante-Aug.; cf. cuneatim). To fasten with wedges, to wedge up: si quid cuneandum sit in ligno clavisve figendum,Plin. 16, 40, 76, § 206: unus lapis facit fornacem, ille, qui latera inclinata cuneavit et interventu suo vinxit,the key-stone,Sen. Ep. 118, 16.—* To make wedge-shaped; of places: (Britannia) iterum se in diversos angulos cuneat triquetra,is in the form of a wedge,Mel. 3, 6, 4 (cf. cuneus, ...

cuneolus.definition: dim.id. A little wedge, a small gore, Cic. Univ. 13; Col. 4, 29, 10; Pall. Febr. 17, 3.

cuneus.definition: cf. Sanscr. çā, çān, to sharpen; Lat. cos, cautes A wedge. Prop., Cato, R. R. 10, 3; 11, 4; Att. ap. Cic. Tusc. 2, 10, 23; Verg. G. 1, 144; Hor. C. 1, 35, 18: jamque labant cunei, i. e. the plugs or wedges by which the ship's hull was made tight, Ov. M. 11, 514: Britannia in cuneum tenuatur,is shaped like a wedge,Tac. Agr. 10; cf. cuneo, II.—* Meton.

cunicularis.definition: cŭnīcŭlāris, e, cuniculus Of or pertaining to the rabbit, rabbit-: herba,Marc. Emp. 14 fin.

cunicularius.definition: cuniculus, II. B.; In milit. lang.,a miner,Veg. Mil. 2, 11; Amm. 24, 4, 22.

cuniculator.definition: ( = cunicularius) A miner, Lact. ad Stat. Th. 2, 418.

cuniculus.definition: Spanish A rabbit, cony, Gr. κόνικλος or κύνικλος. Prop., Varr. R. R. 3, 12, 6; Plin. 8, 55, 81, § 217; Mart. 13, 60. Transf. (from their habit of burrowing in the ground; cf. Varr. l. l.; collat. form, , , , acc. to Paul. ex Fest. p. 50, 4, but perh. an acc.; v. Müll. ad loc.), a passage under ground, a hole, pit, cavity, canal, etc.

cunila.definition: () A plant, a species of origanum; form cunila,Plaut. Trin. 4, 2, 93; Col. 6, 13, 1; Plin. 19, 8, 50, § 165; 20, 16, 61, § 169; form conila,Arn. 6, 17 fin.; App. Herb. 122.

cunnilingus.definition: i. q. cunnum lingens, Mart. 12, 59, 10; Auct. Priap. 78, 2 al.

cunnus.definition: cf. Sanscr. çushi, ditch; Gr. κυσός The female pudenda. Prop., Mart. 1, 90, 7; 3, 72, 6; 3, 81, 4; Auct. Priap. 28, 5.—Also of animals: mulae,Cat. 96, 6. Transf., of the person, an unchastefemale, Hor. S. 1, 2, 36; 1, 3, 107; Auct. Priap. 69, 1 al.—As an obscene word, avoided acc. to Cic. Or. 45, 154; id. Fam. 9, 22, 3.

cupa.definition: cf. κύπτω A tub, cask, tun, vat, etc., for holding liquids, esp. wine, Varr. ap. Non. p. 83, 24 sq.; Pall. 1, 18, 2; 1, 38, 1; Cic. Pis. 27, 67 (but acc. to Ernesti, a female vintner; cf. copa); Caes. B. C: 2, 11; Luc. 4, 420; also for grain,Dig. 19, 2, 31; and for the ashes of the dead,a niche,Inscr. Orell. 2697; 4550.

cupedia.definition: cūpēdĭa, cūpēdĭnārĭus, cūpēdĭ-um, cūpēdo, v. cupp-.

cupella.definition: dim.1. cupa A small vat or cask, Pall. Febr. 25, 12; Apic. 1, 2.

cupiditas.definition: ( Gen. plur. rarely -tatium, Cic. Sest. 66, 138; Sen. Ep. 5, 7), f. cupidus, a desire, wish, longing, in a good and (more freq.) in a bad sense. In a good sense, a longing, desire. In a bad sense, a passionate desire, lust, passion, cupidity.

cupido.definition: ( or , Lucr. 1, 1082; 4, 1090; 5, 45), , f. (m., Plant. Am. 2, 2, 210; Hor. C. 2, 16, 15; 3, 16, 39; 3, 24, 51; id. S. 1, 1, 61; id. Ep. 1, 1, 33; Ov. M. 8, 74; 9, 734; Sil. 4, 99; and personified in all authors; V.the foll.) [cupidus], access. form of cupiditas, desire, wish, longing, eagerness, in a good and (more usu.) in a bad sense (very freq. in the poets and histt., esp. in Sall.; twice in Quint., but in Cic. only as personified). In gen. ...

cupidus.definition: cŭpĭdus, a, um, cupio Longing, desiring, desirous, eager, in a good and bad sense, wishing, loving, fond, etc. (very freq. and class.); constr. with gen., abl., inf., in, or absol. In a good sense. In a bad sense, passionately desiring or longing for, eager, greedy, lustful, passionate.

cupiens.definition: cŭpĭens, entis, Part. and , from cupio.

cupienter.definition: cŭpĭenter, , v. cupio P. a. fin.

cupio.definition: cŭpĭo, īvi or ĭi, ītum, 3 ( Imperf. subj. cŭpīret, Lucr. 1, 72; quoted ap. Non. p. 506 fin., and ap. Prisc. p. 879 P.), v. a. Sanscr kup, to be in active motion, to be angry; cf. recupero, to long for a thing, to desire, wish (designating a natural, involuntary inclination, or an unbridled or passionate desire, while volo indicates an energetic will, and opto a deliberate wish or choice, Cic. Mil. 12, 32; Sen. Ep. 116, 2; cf. Klotz in Jahn's Neue...

cupisco.definition: cŭpisco, ĕre, 3 V. inch. [cupio], to wish, desire (late Lat.): Deum videre,Aug. de Music. 4, 4; cf. Prisc. p. 824 P.

cupitor.definition: id. One who desires or wishes (very rare; perh. only in the foll. exs.): incredibilium,Tac. A. 15, 42: matrimonii,id. ib. 12, 7: amicitiae,App. Flor. 3, p. 807.

cupitus.definition: cŭpītus, a, um, v. cupio, I. A. α.

cuppedia.definition: (), , cuppes. * Fondness for dainties, daintiness, lickerishness, Cic. Tusc. 4, 11, 26; cf. Non. p. 85. Plur., dainty dishes, delicacies (late Lat.): conjectabamus ad cenulam non cuppedias ciborum, sed argutias quaestionum,Gell. 7 (6), 13, 2; 7 (6), 16, 6; Amm. 25, 2, 2; 26, 7, 1; 30, 1, 20; cf. cuppedium.

cuppedinarius.definition: () Adj., of or pertaining to dainty dishes or delicacies. Adj.: Forum,a place in Rome,Symm. Ep. 8, 19; cf. 2. cuppedo, and cuppes, II. Subst.: , , m., he who prepares delicacies or tidbits, a confectioner, Ter. Eun. 2, 2, 25; Lampr. Heliog. 30.

cuppedium.definition: (), , cuppes A tidbit, Varr. L. L. 5, § 146 Müll.; mostly plur.: , , (a later form , , , Apic. 5, 1; 7, 6; 8, 6), dainty dishes, tidbits, delicacies (anteand post-class.): nil moror cuppedia,Plaut. Stich. 5, 4, 32; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 48, 15 Müll.; cf. cuppes, II.

cuppes.definition: () Adj., fond of delicacies, dainty: blandiloquentulus, harpago, mendax, cuppes, etc.,Plaut. Trin. 2, 1, 13. Cuppes et cuppedia antiqui lautiores cibos nominabant; inde et macellum forum cupedinis appellabant, etc., Paul. ex Fest. p. 48, 15 Müll.; cf. 2. cuppedo.

cupressetum.definition: cupressus A grove or plantation of cypress - trees, a cypress wood, Cato, R. R. 151, 1; Cic. Leg. 1, 5, 15.

cupresseus.definition: cūpressĕus, a, um, id. Of cypress, cypress.: signa Junonis,Liv. 27, 37, 12: foliatura,Vitr. 2, 9.

cupressinus.definition: cūpressĭnus (cȳpress-, Vulg. Cant. 1, 16), a, um Of cypress, cypress-: frondes,Col. 2, 2, 11: coni,id. 6, 7, 2: oleum,Plin. 23, 4, 45, § 88.

cupressus.definition: and less freq. (m. acc. plur. rectosque cupressos, Enn. ap. Gell. 13, 20, 13, and ap. Non. p. 195; rare collat. form , , , Verg. A. 3, 680; cf. infra B.; and in late Lat. , , , Vulg. Ecclus. 24, 17; Isid. Orig. 17, 7, 34), = κυπάρισσος, the cypress, an evergreen tree sacred to Pluto and used at funerals: Cupressus sempervirens, Linn.— Sing. nom., Hor. C. 4, 6, 10; Plin. 16, 33, 60, § 142; 16, 40, 78, § 212; Ov. M. 10, 106.—Gen. cupressi, Cato, R...

cupreus.definition: cūprĕus (cȳpr-), a, um, cuprum Of copper, copper-: bidentes, Pall. Jul. 5: acus, Treb. Claud. 14 (for Plin. 23, 3, 37, § 74, v. Cyprius, s. v. Cyprus).

cuprinus.definition: cūprĭnus (cȳpr-), a, um, cuprum Of copper, copper-: clavus,Pall. Jan. 15, 18: cauterium,Veg. Art. Vet. 1, 14, 3 al.

cupula.definition: dim.1. cupa A little tub or cask, Dig. 33, 6, 3. A small burying-vault: Renier, Inscr. Afric. 3373; 3584 al.—Sync. form CVPLA, Inscr. Afric. 3172.

cur.definition: cūr (old orthog. quor; cf. Vel. Long. p. 2236 P.; and in MSS. sometimes cor, v. Lachm. ad Lucr. II. p. 171 sq.), contr. from quare; cf. Vel. Long. p. 2231 P. and the letter C; acc. to Voss, Etym. s. h. v.; Analog. 4, 21, and Hand, Turs. II. p. 175, from cui rei; cf.: quoi rei,Plaut. Poen. 2, 33, = quam ob rem For what reason, wherefore, why, to what purpose, from what motive. Rel.: duae causae sunt, cur tu frequentior in isto officio esse debeas ...

cura.definition: caveo; cf. curo init. Care, solicitude, carefulness, thought, concern. Trouble (physical or mental), bestowed on something; solicitude, care, attention, pains (syn.: diligentia, opera, studium, labor, etc.; opp. neglegentia, etc.; v.the foll.; very freq. in every per. and species of composition). Anxiety, solicitude, concern, disquiet, trouble, grief, sorrow; syn.: sollicitudo, metus, etc.; cf. φροντίς (very freq. in every per. and species of co...

curagendarius.definition: cura, I. A. 2. b., -ago A manager, overseer, Cod. Th. 6, 29, 1.

curans.definition: cūrans, ntis, , v. curo, II. B. β.

curate.definition: cūrātē, , v. curo P. a. fin.

curatio.definition: curo A taking care of something, administration, oversight, care, management, charge (rare but class.). In gen.: me sinas curare ancillas, quae mea est curatio,Plaut. Cas. 2, 3, 45; cf. id. Poen. 1, 2, 144: cultus et curatio corporis,Cic. N. D. 1, 34, 94; cf. id. ib. 2, 63, 158: curatio et administratio rerum,id. ib. 1, 1, 2: corporum,Liv. 25, 38: frumenti,Cic. Att. 15, 11, 1: vini,Col. 12, 25, 4: quid tibi hanc curatiost rem? (for hujus rei; cf....

curator.definition: (old orthog. COERATOR V.the foll.), , m.id., he who cares for or takes charge of a thing, a manager, overseer, superintendent, keeper. In gen.: ludorum,Plaut. Poen. prol. 36: suntoque aediles coeratores urbis annonae ludorumque solemnium,Cic. Leg. 3, 3, 6: viae Flaminiae,id. Att. 1, 1, 2: aviarii,a bird-keeper,Varr. R. R. 3, 5, 5; cf. apum,Col. 9, 9, 1: pavonini gregis,id. 8, 11, 2; and gallinarius,Varr. R. R. 3, 9, 7: fidus negotiorum,Sall. J. 7...

curatoria.definition: curatorius Guardianship, = ἐπιτροπή, several times in Dig. 27, 1, 1 and 2, always written as Greek, κουρατορία, etc.

curatoricius.definition: cūrātōrīcĭus or -tĭus, a, um, curator, I. Of or belonging to an overseer: equi, the horses of a provincial commissary, Cod. Th. 11, 1, 29.

curatorius.definition: cūrātōrĭus, a, um, curator, II. Pertaining to guardianship: STIPENDIA VETERANORVM,Inscr. Orell. 4968. Of or pertaining to a guardian: nomen, Gai Inst. 4, 82.

curatrix.definition: curator, II. A female guardian, Non. p. 150, 29.

curatura.definition: curo Management, care, attendance, Ter. Eun. 2, 3, 25 Ruhnk.

curatus.definition: cūrātus, a, um, Part. and , of curo.

curculio.definition: (, Plaut. Trin. 4, 3, 9 Ritschl, Fleck.; Pall. 1, 19, 2; id. Jun. 3; also in some MSS. of the authors cited infra), , kindr. with circulus, circus A corn-worm, weevil, Cato, R. R. 92; Varr. R. R. 1, 57, 63; Col. 1, 6, 15 sq.; Plin. 18, 11, 73, § 302; Serv. ad Verg. G. 1, 186. The name of a comedy of Plautus.

cures.definition: m. (parvi, Ov. F. 2, 135) and f. (Tatiae, Prop. 5, 9, 74), = Κύρεις or Κύρις [curis, Sabine word, = hasta, Ov. F. 2, 477] The ancient chief town of the Sabines, Varr. L. L. 5, § 51 Müll.; Cic. Fam. 15, 20, 1; Verg. A. 6, 811; 8, 638; Ov. M. 14, 778 al.; Liv. 1, 13, 5; 1, 18, 1; Flor. 1, 2, 1; cf. Quirites. Hence, , , adj., of Cures: turba,Ov. F. 3, 94.

curia.definition: kindr. with Quiris, Quirites; cf. the letter C A curia or court, one of the thirty parts into which Romulus divided the Roman people, ten for each of the three tribes; each curia contained ten gentes, Varr. ap. Dion. Hal. 2, 83; Liv. 1, 13, 6; Aur. Vict. Vir. Ill. 2, 12; Dig. 1, 2, 2; Paul. ex Fest. p. 49, 1 Müll. Meton. Curia Saliorum, the official building of the Salii on the Palatine Hill, consecrated to Mars, in which the sacred lituus was ke...

curialis.definition: cūrĭālis, e, curia Of or pertaining to a curia, i. e. Belonging to the same curia, district, or division of the people; subst.: cūrĭālis, is, m., a member of the same curia, = δημότης: neque quisquam curialium Venit,Plaut. Aul. 2, 2, 2: Cimonem etiam in suos curialis hospitalem fuisse,Cic. Off. 2, 18, 64; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 49, 13 Müll.: curiales ejusdem curiae ut tribules et municipes. Pertaining to the religious services of the curioe: curi...

curiatim.definition: cūrĭātim, curia By curiae (very rare): populum consuluit, *Cic. Rep. 2, 17, 31 (but in Gell. 15, 27, 2, the better read. is curiatum).

curiatus.definition: cūrĭātus, a, um, curia Of or pertaining to the curiae: comitia, in which the people voted according to curiae (orig. the only ruling assembly; later limited by the comitia centuriata to cases of arrogation (adoption), the choice of priests, the conferring of the chief command; cf. comitium, II.; Dict. of Antiq.), Lael. Felix ap. Gell. 15, 27, 2; Cic. Agr. 2, 11, 26 sq.; Liv. 5, 52, 15 al.: lex,passed in such comitia,Cic. Agr. 2, 10, 26; 2, 11, 28...

curio.definition: curia. The priest of a curia, Varr. L. L. 5, § 83; 6, § 46 Müll.: maximus,he who presided over all the curiae,Liv. 27, 8, 1; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 126, 17 Müll. Post-Aug., a crier, herald, = praeco, Mart. lib. 2 praef.; Treb. Gall. 12.

curionatus.definition: 1. curio, I. The office of priest of a curia, Paul. ex Fest. p. 49, 9 Müll. (cf. curionius).

curionius.definition: cūrĭōnĭus, a, um, 1. curio, I. Of or pertaining to the priest of a curia: curionium aes dicebatur quod dabatur curioni ob sacerdotium curionatus, Paul. ex Fest. p. 49, 19 Müll.: curionia sacra, quae in curiis fiebant,id. ib. p. 62, 11.

curiositas.definition: curiosus Desire of knowledge, curiosity, inquisitiveness (very rare), Cic. Att. 2, 12, 2; Macr. S. 1, 11, 45; Tert. adv. Haeret. 17; id. Apol. 25.

curiosus.definition: cūrĭōsus, a, um, cura. (Acc. to cura, I.) Bestowing care or pains upon a thing, applying one's self assiduously, careful, diligent, thoughtful, devoted (class.; esp. freq. in Cic.). (Acc. to cura, II.) Lit., that injures himself by care; hence, transf., emaciated, wasted, lean: belua,Plaut. Aul. 3, 6, 26 (v. the passage in connection); cf.: nempe ille vivit carie curiosior, Afran. ap. Non. p. 21, 28 (Com. Rel. v. 250 Rib.).—Adv.: cūrĭŏsē.

curis.definition: or , , Sabine A spear, Ov. F. 2, 477; cf. Macr. S. 1, 9, 16; Paul. ex Fest. p. 49, 10 Müll.; v. Quirites.—Hence, (), , , a surname of Juno as protector of spearmen, Mart. Cap. 2, § 149; Inscr. Orell. 1303 sq.; 8659.

curo.definition: cūro (old orthog. COERO and COIRO, Inscr. Orell. 31; 560; 570: Coeret, coerari, coerandi,Cic. Leg. 3, 4, 10), āvi, ātum, 1 (perf. subj. curassis, Plaut. Most. 2, 2, 93; id. Ps. 1, 3, 3; id. Poen. 3, 1, 50; inf. pass. curarier, id. Capt. 3, 5, 79), v. a. cura, to care for, take or have care of, to be solicitous for, to look or attend to, trouble one's self about, etc. (very freq. in every period and species of composition); constr. with the acc., ...

currax.definition: currax, ācis, curro Running fast, quick, swift (post-class. and rare): servus,Dig. 21, 1, 18.—Poet.: laquei,which are bound on the feet of running animals,Grat. Cyn. 89.

curriculum.definition: id. A running, course, race. Lit. Meton.

currilis.definition: currīlis, e, currus Of or for a chariot (late Lat.): praesepia equorum currilium,Vulg. 3 Reg. 4, 26: certamina,chariot-races,Ambros. Cant. Cantic. 7, 12: currilis equus, σὺν ἅρματι ἀγωνιζόμενος ἵππος, Gloss. Labb.; cf. also curulis.

curro.definition: curro, cŭcurri (old form cĕcurri, acc. to Gell. 7, 9, 14: curri, Varr. Imp. ap. Front. Ep. 2 Mai; Tert. Fug. in Pers. 12; Arn. 4, 4), cursum, 3, kindr. with celer, coruscus To run, to move quickly (on foot, on a horse, ship, etc.), to hasten, fly (very freq. in every period and species of composition). Lit. Trop.: non quo multa parum communis littera currat,not but that they have many letters in common,Lucr. 2, 692: proclivi currit oratio, venit ...

currulis.definition: currūlis, e, currus Of or belonging to a chariot, or a chariot-race: rabies equorum (post-class. and rare),App. M. 9, p. 221: strepitus (opp. equester fremitus),Fronto Ep. 3 Mai; cf. curulis.

currus.definition: curro A chariot, car, wain. Lit. Poet. transf. *

cursatio.definition: curso A running, Don. ad Ter. Hec. 3, 1, 35.

cursilitas.definition: curro A running about, Fulg. Myth. 3, 3; cf. Auct. Class. 3, p. 81 Mai.

cursim.definition: cursim, id. Quickly, swiftly, hastily, speedily (class.): currere,Plaut. Ps. 1, 3, 124; Afran. ap. Charis. p. 186 P.: hoc cito et cursim est agendum,Plaut. Poen. 3, 1, 64: rapi ad carnuficem,id. ib. 1, 2, 156: agmine acto,Liv. 27, 16, 9: dicere aliena (opp. sensim dicere quod causae prodesset),Cic. Phil. 2, 17, 42: arripere aliquid,id. de Or. 2, 89, 364: pergere ad aliquid,id. Tusc. 5, 5, 13 et saep.

cursitatio.definition: cursito A running about hither and thither, Sol. 42, 2.

cursito.definition: cursito, āre V. freq. n. [curso], to run about, run hither and thither (rare). In gen.: sursum deorsum, * Ter. Eun. 2, 2, 47; cf.: huc et illuc,Hor. C. 4, 11, 10; id. S. 2, 6, 107: modo ad Celsum modo ad Nepotem,Plin. Ep. 6, 5, 5; Suet. Tib. 38: excalciatos,id. Vesp. 10. In partic.

curso.definition: curso, āre V. freq. n. [curro], to run hither and thither, to and fro (rare but class.): ultro et citro,Cic. Rosc. Am. 22, 60: huc illuc,id. Att. 9, 9, 2; Tac. A. 15, 50; id. H. 5, 20: ad aliquem,Ter. Eun. 2, 2, 56 Bentl. N. cr.: per foros,Cic. Sen. 6, 17: per urbem,Tac. A. 2, 82: in omnes vias,Val. Fl. 4, 108.—Impers.: cursari rursum prorsum,Ter. Hec. 3, 1, 35. Act. (late Lat.), to run over, traverse: nunc jam compactis cursanda syllaba est form...

cursor.definition: id. A runner, and partic. Trop.: cursor iambus,Rufin. Rhet. p. 355 Capperon.

cursorius.definition: cursōrĭus, a, um, adj.id. Of or pertaining to running or to a race-course (late Lat.). Adj.: terminus,Front. Colon. p. 141 Goes. Subst.

cursualis.definition: cursŭālis, e, cursus Of or pertaining to a course, running (late Lat.): equi,post-horses,Cod. Just. 12, 51, 19: raeda, a stage-coach, Cod. Th. 12, 12, 9: sollicitudo,i. e. speed in running,ib. 6, 29, 7. Hasty, speedy: ministerium,Cassiod. Var. 5, 5.

cursura.definition: curro A running (ante-class.), Plaut. Bacch. 1, 1, 34; id. Merc. 1, 2, 10; id. As. 2, 2, 61; id. Most. 4, 1, 5; id. Trin. 4, 2, 164; Varr. R. R. 2, 7, 15 al.

cursus.definition: id. A running (on foot, on a horse, chariot, ship, etc.), a course, way, march, passage, voyage, journey, etc. (very freq.). Lit. Trop. (freq. in Cic. and Quint.), a course, progress, direction, way: qui cursus rerum, qui exitus futurus sit,Cic. Fam. 4, 2, 3; cf. Tac. H. 4, 34; id. Agr. 39: implicari aliquo certo genere cursuque vivendi,Cic. Off. 1, 32, 117: vitae brevis cursus, gloriae sempiternus,id. Sest. 21, 47: reliquus vitae cursus,id. Phil...

curto.definition: curto, āvi, ātum, 1, curtus To shorten, diminish (not ante-Aug., and very rare): aliquid,Cels. 7, 9: radices,Pall. Feb. 10, 3. Trop., to diminish: rem,Pers. 6, 34; cf.: Quantulum enim summae curtabit quisque dierum,Hor. S. 2, 3, 124.

curtus.definition: curtus, a, um, root in Sanscr. kart, to cut; cf. Germ. kurz Shortened, mutilated, broken, short (class.; most freq. in the poets). Lit.: dolia, pots (chamber vessels), Lucr. 4, 1026; cf. vasa,Juv. 3, 271: pergula,Prop. 4 (5), 5, 70. testa,Mart. 3, 82, 3; cf. testu,Ov. F. 2, 645 al.. calix, Mart. 1 92, 6, : curtum temone jugum,Juv. 10, 135: latus,Mart. 12, 32, 13: Judaei,i. e. circumcised,Hor. S. 1, 9, 70; cf. equus,castrated,Prop. 4 (5), 1, 20. b...

curulis.definition: cŭrūlis (curr-), e, currus Of or pertaining to a chariot. In gen.: equi,the four horses provided at the public cost for the games of the circus,Liv. 24, 18, 10; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 49, 14 Müll.; Cod. Th. 15, 5, 3; 15, 10, 1: ludi,Min. Fel. Oct. 37 fin.: triumphus, i. e. upon a chariot (in opp. to an ovatio, on horseback or on foot), Suet. Aug. 22: Juno curulis, in an ancient form of prayer in Serv. ad Verg. A. 1, 17. Esp.: sella curulis, the cu...

curvabilis.definition: curvābĭlis, e, curvo That may be bent, flexible: ulmus et fraxinus,Pall. Nov. 15, 2.

curuabilis.definition: curvābĭlis, e, curvo That may be bent, flexible: ulmus et fraxinus,Pall. Nov. 15, 2.

curvamen.definition: id. A bending, bend, vaulting (not ante-Aug.; perh. first used by Ov.): patriae curvamina ripae,Ov. M. 9, 450; 2, 130; 3, 672: haec (villa) unum sinum molli curvamine amplectitur,Plin. Ep. 9, 7, 4: caeli,of the climate,Gell. 14, 1, 10.

curuamen.definition: id. A bending, bend, vaulting (not ante-Aug.; perh. first used by Ov.): patriae curvamina ripae,Ov. M. 9, 450; 2, 130; 3, 672: haec (villa) unum sinum molli curvamine amplectitur,Plin. Ep. 9, 7, 4: caeli,of the climate,Gell. 14, 1, 10.

curvatura.definition: id. A bending, rounding, bend (not ante-Aug.). Abstr., Vitr. 2, 8, 11; Plin. 2, 17, 14, § 72; 10, 19, 21, § 42 al. Concr., a vault: camerae,an arched ceiling,Vitr. 7, 3: rotae,i. e. the rim,Ov. M. 2, 108.

curuatura.definition: id. A bending, rounding, bend (not ante-Aug.). Abstr., Vitr. 2, 8, 11; Plin. 2, 17, 14, § 72; 10, 19, 21, § 42 al. Concr., a vault: camerae,an arched ceiling,Vitr. 7, 3: rotae,i. e. the rim,Ov. M. 2, 108.

curvesco.definition: curvesco, ĕre V. n., to be crooked, curved, to make a curve (late Lat.): mare curvescens,Amm. 22, 8, 5; Ambros. in Luc. 9, 9; id. de Isaac et An. 7, 60; id. in Psa. 118, 26.

curuesco.definition: curvesco, ĕre V. n., to be crooked, curved, to make a curve (late Lat.): mare curvescens,Amm. 22, 8, 5; Ambros. in Luc. 9, 9; id. de Isaac et An. 7, 60; id. in Psa. 118, 26.

curvo.definition: curvo, āvi, ātum, 1, id. To crook, bend, bow, curve (not ante-Aug.; v. Orell. ad Cic. N. D. 1, 24, 66). Lit.: curvari manus et aduncos crescere in ungues,Ov. M. 2, 479: bimā cornua fronte (vitulus),Verg. G. 4, 299: trabes,Ov. M. 7, 441; Prop. 3 (4), 22, 38. flexile cornu,Ov. M. 5, 383; 11, 324; cf.: ingentem arcum manu,Stat. Achill. 1, 487: rotundas Curvat aper lances,i. e. by its weight,Hor. S. 2, 4, 41: Calabros sinus (Hadria),id. C. 1, 33, 16:...

curuo.definition: curvo, āvi, ātum, 1, id. To crook, bend, bow, curve (not ante-Aug.; v. Orell. ad Cic. N. D. 1, 24, 66). Lit.: curvari manus et aduncos crescere in ungues,Ov. M. 2, 479: bimā cornua fronte (vitulus),Verg. G. 4, 299: trabes,Ov. M. 7, 441; Prop. 3 (4), 22, 38. flexile cornu,Ov. M. 5, 383; 11, 324; cf.: ingentem arcum manu,Stat. Achill. 1, 487: rotundas Curvat aper lances,i. e. by its weight,Hor. S. 2, 4, 41: Calabros sinus (Hadria),id. C. 1, 33, 16:...

curvus.definition: curvus (-vŏs), a, um, root kar-, whence κορώνη; cf.: circus, varus Crooked, curved, bent (opp. rectus; mostly poet.). Prop.: aratrum,Lucr. 5, 933; 6, 1253; Verg. G. 1, 170: rastri,Cat. 64, 39: culter,Sen. Hippol. 53: falces,Verg. G. 1, 508: calamus,Cat. 63, 22: arbor,Ov. M. 5, 536: arcus,id. ib. 9, 114: dens,id. Am. 3, 10, 14: ungues,Varr. R. R. 2, 9, 4; Hor. Epod. 5, 93: lyra,id. C. 1, 10, 6; 3, 28, 11: crinale,Ov. M. 5, 53: (equi) alvus,Verg. ...

curuus.definition: curvus (-vŏs), a, um, root kar-, whence κορώνη; cf.: circus, varus Crooked, curved, bent (opp. rectus; mostly poet.). Prop.: aratrum,Lucr. 5, 933; 6, 1253; Verg. G. 1, 170: rastri,Cat. 64, 39: culter,Sen. Hippol. 53: falces,Verg. G. 1, 508: calamus,Cat. 63, 22: arbor,Ov. M. 5, 536: arcus,id. ib. 9, 114: dens,id. Am. 3, 10, 14: ungues,Varr. R. R. 2, 9, 4; Hor. Epod. 5, 93: lyra,id. C. 1, 10, 6; 3, 28, 11: crinale,Ov. M. 5, 53: (equi) alvus,Verg. ...

cusio.definition: cudo A stamping of money, Cod. Th. 11, 16, 18.

cuso.definition: cūso, āre V. freq. [id.], acc. to Prisc. p. 890 P.

cuspis.definition: etym. dub. A point, the pointed end of any thing (freq., esp. in the poets). Prop.: asserum, * Caes. B. C. 2, 2: vomeris,Plin. 18, 18, 48, § 172. acuta contorum, Verg. A. 5, 208: acuta teli,Ov. M. 1, 470: hastae,id. ib. 5, 9; 6, 78: jaculi,id. ib. 7, 673: medicata,Sil. 13, 197: aquilae, the pointed end of the standard; Gr. στύραξ, Suet. Caes. 62 et saep. Meton. (pars pro toto).

custodela.definition: custos (ante-class. form for custodia; in later Lat. preserved only in the vulgar lang.; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 51, 5 Müll.) A watch, guard, care, etc.: qui more antiquo in custodelam suom conmiserunt caput,Plaut. Rud. 3, 2, 10: in custodelam nos tuam ut recipias et tutere,id. ib. 3, 3, 34: (capram) in custodelam simiae concredere,id. Merc. 2, 1, 9: familiam pecuniamque tuam endo mandatelā tutelā custodelāque meā (esse aio), an ancient judicial fo...

custodia.definition: id. A watching, watch, guard, care, protection (freq. and class.). In gen. With the access. idea of hindering free motion, a watching, guarding, custody, restraint, confinement.

custodiarium.definition: custos A watchhouse (late Lat.), Tert. ad Martyr. 2; Inscr. Orell. 1391.

custodio.definition: custōdĭo, īvi, or ĭi, ītum, 4 ( Fut. pass. custodibitur, Plaut. Capt. 3, 5, 71), v. a. id., to watch, protect, keep, defend, guard (freq. and class.). In gen. With the access. idea of hindering free motion, in a good or bad sense.

custos.definition: root sku-, to cover, hide, etc.; cf. scutum, κεύθω, Germ. Haut, Haus, Corss. Ausspr. I. p. 353 A guard, watch, preserver, keeper, overseer, protector, defender, attendant, etc., protectress, etc., in a friendly or hostile sense (freq. and class.). In gen. In a hostile sense.

cutio.definition: A small insect, milleped, Marc. Emp. 8.

cutis.definition: (acc. cutem, App. Mag. p. 306, 14), kindr. with κύτος; Sanscr. gudh; Germ. Haut The skin. Prop., Planc. ap. Cic. Fam. 10, 18, 3; Cels. 2, 8; Plin. 28, 12, 50, § 183 sq.; Quint. 11, 3, 78; Hor. C. 1, 28, 13; id. A. P. 476; Sen. Ep. 95, 16; 123, 7 al.—In plur., Plin. 6, 31, 36, § 200; 11, 37, 45, § 128. Trop., the external appearance, surface, outside: tenerā quādam elocutionis cute,Quint. 5, 12, 18: imaginem virtutis effingere et solam ut sic dix...

cyathus.definition: A small ladle for transferring the wine from the mixing-bowl (crater) to the drinking-cup (cf. Becker, Gall. 3, p. 221). Prop., Varr. L. L. 5, § 124 Müll.; Plaut. Stich. 5, 4, 24; id. Ps. 4, 2, 2; Hor. S. 1, 6, 117; Juv. 9, 47; Suet. Caes. 49 al. As a measure, both dry and liquid (particularly for wine), the twelfth part of a sextarius, Hor. C. 3, 8, 13; 3, 19, 12; Plin. 14, 9, 11, § 85; or ten Greek drachmae, Plin. 21, 34, 109, § 185; cf. Rhemn....

cybaeus.definition: cybaeus, a, um, κύπη, κυβή, cupa Pertaining to a kind of merchantship: navis maxima,Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 17, § 44.—Absol.: cybaea, ae, f., a transport or merchant-ship, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 8, § 17.

cybiarius.definition: cybium A dealer in salt fish, Arn. 2, p. 70 dub.

cybium.definition: or , , , = . A tunny-fish, Varr. L. L. 5, § 77 Müll.; Mart. 11, 27, 3; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 52, 15 Müll. Meton., a dish made of pieces of the tunny-fish salted and chopped, Plin. 9, 15, 18, § 48; 32, 11, 53, § 151; Mart. 5, 79, 3.

cyceon.definition: A drink made of barley-grits, grated goats'-cheese, and wine, Arn. 5, p. 174 sq.

cyclas.definition: (circular; hence as in Greek; cf. Liddell and Scott in h. v. l.),a state-robe of women, with a border running round it,Prop. 4 (5), 7, 40.Juv. 6, 259; Vop. Sat. 9; Lampr. Alex. Sev. 41, 1; Serv. ad Verg. A. 1, 649 al. = Κυκλάδες, the Cyclades, islands lying in a circle round Delos, in the Aegean Sea, off the coast of the Peloponnesus, Mel. 2, 7, 11; Plin. 4, 12, 22, § 65 sq.; Caes. B. C. 3, 3; Nep. Milt. 2, 5; Liv. 34, 26, 11; Verg. A. 3, 127; O...

cyclophoreticus.definition: cȳclŏphŏrētĭcus, a, um Moved in a circle, circular: cyma,Mart. Cap. 8, p. 275 (written as Greek by Kopp, § 814).

cyclops.definition: Cȳclops, ōpis (acc. -ōpem or -ōpa), m., = Κύκλωψ (a round eye) A Cyclops; in plur.: Cyclopes, um,the Cyclopes, a fabulous race of giants on the coast of Sicily; said to have each but one eye, and that in the middle of the forehead; to them were ascribed the walls called Cyclopean; plur.,Cic. Div. 2, 19, 43; Plin. 7, 56, 57, §§ 195-198; Verg. A. 6, 630; 8, 424; Hor. C. 1, 4, 7; Ov. M. 3, 305 et saep.; sing. κατ̓ ἐξοχήν, the Cyclops Polyphemus, ...

cyclus.definition: A circle. Lit.: cycli axium,Isid. Orig. 3, 36. Transf.

cycneus.definition: cȳcnēus (cȳgn-), a, um, , = . Of or belonging to a swan, swan's-: tamquam cycnea vox et oratio,i. e. the last speech,Cic. de Or. 3, 2, 6: plumae,Ov. Tr. 4, 8, 1. Cȳcnēa (al. Cygnaea) Specula, a hill near Brixia, now still Cigneo, Cat. 67, 32.

cycnus.definition: (in MSS. and edd. freq. also ; Y,Hor. C. 4, 3, 20; Aus. Ep. 20, 8), , m., = κύκνος, the swan; celebrated for its singing, esp. for its dying song; consecrated to Apollo,Cic. Tusc. 1, 30, 73; Plin. 10, 23, 32, § 63; Lucr. 4, 181; 4, 910; Verg. E. 7, 38; id. A. 1, 393; Ov. M. 5, 387; Hor. C. 4, 3, 20 et saep.; attached to the chariot of Venus,Ov. M. 10, 708; id. A. A. 3, 809.

cydonia.definition: or , , , = Κυδωνία An ancient and celebrated town on the north coast of Crete, now Canea, Mel. 2, 7, 12; Plin. 4, 12, 20, § 59 Sillig N. cr.; Flor. 3, 7, 4. Hence

cylindrus.definition: A cylinder. Prop., Cic. N. D. 1, 10, 24; id. Fat. 19, 41. Meton.

cyma.definition: (), , n., and , f. A young sprout of a cabbage; neutr., Lucil. ap. Non. p. 195, 5; Col. 10, 129; fem., id. 11, 3, 24; 12, 54, 3; Plin. 19, 8, 41, § 137 sq.; 20, 9, 35, § 90 al. A hollow sphere, spherical layer, stratum: quarum (naturarum) circa ... centron, aquae primum, aërisque sequens, tertium ignis cyma commemorant,Mart. Cap. 8, § 814 Kopp ad loc.; cf. the context.

cymatium.definition: () or , , , = (a small wave); in architecture The volute of an Ionic column, Vitr. 3, 5, 7; 4, 1, 7. A channel, a waved moulding, an ogee, Vitr. 3, 5, 10; 4, 3, 6; 4, 3, 8; 4, 6, 2; Tert. Idol. 8.

cymba.definition: () A boat, skiff, first used by the Phoenicians, Plin. 7, 55, 57, § 208; Afran. in Non. p. 535, 31; Cic. Off. 3, 14, 59; Ov. M. 1, 293; id. F. 6, 777 al.—In partic., the boat of Charon which transported the dead, Verg. A. 6, 303; Hor. C. 2, 3, 28; Prop. 3 (4), 18, 24; Stat. S. 2, 1, 186. Trop.: non est ingenii cymba gravanda tui,i. e. meddle not with themes above your powers,Prop. 3, 3 (4, 2), 22; cf. Ov. A. A. 3, 26; Quint. 12, 10, 37.

cymbalaris.definition: A plant, also called cotyledon, App. Herb. 43.

cymbalicus.definition: cymbălĭcus, a, um Pertaining to a cymbal: voces, Ven. Carm. 2, 10 fin.

cymbalista.definition: A cymbal-player, App. de Deo Socr. p. 49, 18.

cymbalistria.definition: A female cymbal-player, Petr. 22 fin.; Inscr. Orell. 2449 sq.

cymbalum.definition: ( Gen. plur. cymbalum, Cat. 63, 21), = κύμβαλον, a cymbal. Prop., an instrument consisting of two hollow plates of brass, which emit a ringing sound when struck together. They were used in the festivals of Cybele and Bacchus, and on other festive occasions; also to hinder the flight of bees, etc. (usu. in plur.), Lucr. 2, 619; Cat. 63, 21; 63, 29; Ov. F. 4, 213; Verg. G. 4, 64; Liv. 39, 8; Cic. Pis. 9, 20 sq.; Plin. 5, 1, 1, § 7; Quint. 11, 3, 5...

cymbium.definition: A small drinking-vessel, a cup, bowl, Varr. ap. Non. p. 545, 28; Verg. A. 3, 66; 5, 267; Mart. 8, 6, 2; cf. Macr. S. 5, 21; Paul. ex Fest. p. 51, 10 Müll. A lamp in the same form, App. M. 11, p. 261. 40.

cynicus.definition: Cynĭcus, i, m., = (doglike). Subst., a Cynic philosopher, a Cynic, Cic. de Or. 3, 17, 62; id. Fin. 3, 20, 68; Hor. Ep. 1, 17, 18; Juv. 13, 121: nudi dolia,i. e. of Diogenes,id. 14, 309.—Hence, adj.: Cynĭcus, a, um, Cynic: institutio,Tac. A. 16, 34: cena,Petr. 14; and in * adv.: Cynĭcē, after the manner of the Cynics, Plaut. Stich. 5, 4, 22. Suffering byσπασμὸς κυνικός, spasmodic distortion, Plin. 25, 5, 24, § 60; cf. Cels. 4, 2, 2.

cyniola.definition: A kind of lettuce, Veg. Art. Vet. 3, 4, 29.

cynismus.definition: Cynical philosophy or conduct, Cassiod. Hist. Eccl. 7, 2.

cynocephalea.definition: (), , f. (, , n., App. Herb. 87) Dog's-head, a magical plant, called also osiritis, Plin. 30, 2, 6, § 18.

cynocephalus.definition: . An ape with a dog's head (in Africa): Simia inuus, Linn.; Plin. 6, 30, 35, § 190; 8, 54, 80, § 216; 37, 9, 40, § 124; Cic. Att. 6, 1, 25. The dog-headed Anubis, Tert. Apol. 6. A kind of wild man, Isid. Orig. 11, 3, 15; 12, 2, 32.

cynodon.definition: cynŏdon, ontis Adj., having pairs of projecting teeth, Isid. Orig. 11, 3, 7 al.

cynosura.definition: Κυνόσουρα (hound's-tail). The constellation at the north pole, the Cynosura, or Lesser Bear, Cic. Ac. 2, 20, 66; id. poët. N. D. 2, 41, 105 and 106; Caes. Germ. Arat. 187; Ov. F. 3, 107 al.—Hence A town in Arcadia, Stat. Th. 4, 295.

cyparissus.definition: cypărissus and Cypărissus, i, v. cupressus.

cyphi.definition: An Egyptian perfuming powder, Scrib. Comp. 70; Hier. in Jovin. 2, 8.

cyprianus.definition: Cyprian, a celebrated Church father of the third century, bishop at Carthage, Lact. 5, 1, 24; Hier. Ep. 58, n. 10; Sulp. Sev. Dial. 1, 3.

cyprinum.definition: A fragrant oil, made from the blossoms of the cyprus (κύπρος), cyprus-oil, cyprus-ointment, Plin. 15, 7, 7, § 28; 13, 1, 2, § 5 sq.; 28, 8, 28, § 109; Cels. 2, 33; 4, 20 al.

cypris.definition: Cȳpris, ĭdis, v. Cyprus, II. D.

cyprius.definition: Cȳprĭus, a, um, v. Cyprus, II. A.

cyprus.definition: Cȳprus (-ŏs), i, f., = Κύπρος An island in the Mediterranean Sea, on the coast of Asia Minor, renowned for its fruitfulness, its rich mines, especially of copper, and for the worship of Venus, Mel. 2, 7, 5; Plin. 5, 31, 35, § 129; Cic. Att. 9, 9, 2; id. Fam. 15, 4, 15; Hor. C. 1, 3, 1; 1, 19, 10; Ov. M. 10, 270 et saep. Hence

cytisus.definition: comm. (, , n., Varr. R. R. 2, 1, 17; 2, 2, 19) A shrubby kind of clover much valued by the ancients, perh. the shrubby snail-clover: Medicago arborea, Linn.; Varr. R. R. 2, 1, 17; Col. 5, 12: Plin. 13, 24, 47, § 130; Verg. E. 1, 79; 2, 64 al.

d.definition: (n. indecl., sometimes f. sc. littera), the flat dental mute, corresponding in character and sound to the English d and the Greek Δ, was the fourth letter of the Latin alphabet, and was called de: Ter. Maur. p. 2385 P., Auson. Idyll. 12, de Litt. Monos. 14. But at the end of a syllable, or after another consonant, its sound was sharpened, so that the grammarians often discuss the question whether d or t should be written, especially in conjunctio...

dactylicus.definition: dactylĭcus, a, um Dactylic: numerus,Cic. Or. 57: pes, Prud. στεφ. 3, 209: metra,Serv. Centim. p. 1820 P.; versus,Diom. p. 494 P. al.

dactylus.definition: ( A finger, hence meton.). A sort of muscle: "ab humanorum unguium similitudine appellati," Plin. 9, 61, 87, § 184. A kind of grape, Col. 3, 2, 1; called also , Plin. 14, 3, 4, § 40. A sort of grass, Plin. 24, 19, 119, § 182.

daduchus.definition: Gr. δᾳδοῦχος The torch - bearer.—Plur.: , the priests of Ceres (Demeter) at Eleusis, who guided the initiated with torches to the temple on the fifth day of the Mysteries, Front. Ep. ad Verr. 1; Fabrett. Inscr. 676, no. 29.

daedalus.definition: ( Acc. Gr. Daedalon, Ov. M. 8, 261; Mart. 4, 49), Δαίδαλος. The mythical Athenian architect of the times of Theseus and Minos, father of Icarus, and builder of the Cretan labyrinth, Ov. M. 8, 159; 183; id. Tr. 3, 4, 21; Verg. A. 6, 14 Serv.; Mel. 2, 7, 12: Plin. 7, 56, 57; Hyg. Fab. 39; Cic. Brut. 18, 71; Hor. Od. 1, 3, 34; Mart. 4, 49, 5; Sil. 12, 89 sq., et saep. A later sculptor of Sicyon, son and pupil of Patrocles: et ipse inter fictores la...

daemon.definition: a spirit, genius, lar (post-class.). In gen.: App. de Deo Socr. p. 49, 5: bonus = ἀγαθοδαίμων, in astrology, the last but one of the twelve celestial signs, Firm. Math. 2, 19: melior, Jul. Val. Res gest. A. M. 1, 27. In eccl. writers: κατ̓ ἐξοχήν, an evil spirit, demon, Lact. 2, 14; Vulg. Levit. 17, 7; id. Jacob. 2, 19; Tert. Apol. 22 init., et saep.

daemoniacus.definition: daemŏnĭăcus, a, um Pertaining to an evil spirit, demoniac, devilish (eccl. Lat.). Adj.: ratio,Tert. Anim. 46: potentia,Lact. 4, 15. Subst.: daemoniacus, i, m., a demoniac, one possessed by an evil spirit, Firm. Math. 3, 6; Sulpic. Sever. Vit. S. Mart. 18.

daemonicola.definition: daemon-colo A worshipper of devils, a heathen, Aug. Conf. 8, 2.

daemonicus.definition: daemŏnĭcus, a, um Belonging to an evil spirit, demoniac, devilish (eccl. Lat.): impetus,Tert. Res. Carn. 58: aras coli, Prud. στεφ. 36: fraudes,Lact. 4, 13, 16.

damalio.definition: δάμαλος A calf, Lampr. Alex. Sever. 22, 8.

damascus.definition: (-os, Luc 3, 215; cf. Prob. II. p. 1462 Fin. P., p. 121 Lindem.), , f., Δαμασκός, Heb. Dammesek or Darmesek, the very ancient capital of Coelesyria, on the Chrysorrhoas, celebrated for its terebinths, and, since the time of the Emperor Diocletian, for its fabrics in steel, now Dameshk, Curt. 3, 12 sq.; Plin. 5, 18, 16, § 74; 13, 6, 12, § 54; Flor. 3, 5, 29; Stat. S. 1, 6, 14; Vulg. Gen. 14, 12.—Hence Adj., of Damascus (eccl. Lat.), Vulg. Gen. 15...

damium.definition: : sacrificium, quod fie bat in operto in honorem Bonae Deae. Dea quoque ipsa DAMIA et sacerdos ejus DAMIATRIX appellabatur, Paul. ex Fest. p. 68, 8 Müll [δᾶμος = δῆμος]; cf. "damium, θυσίαι ὑπαίθριοι γινόμεναι," Gloss. Lab.

damma.definition: (), , f. (m., Verg. Ec. 8, 28; Georg. 3, 539; A. 8, 641; Stat. Ach. 2, 408; cf. Quint. 9, 3, 6) [R. dam-, v. domo], a general name for beasts of the deer kind; A fallow deer, buck, doe, antelope, chamois, Plin. 8, 53, 79, § 214; 11, 37, 45, § 124; Verg. G. 1, 308; 3, 410; Hor. Od. 1, 2, 12; Ov. M. 1, 442; 10, 539; 13, 832; id. F. 3, 646; Juv. 11, 121; Sen. Hippol. 62; Sid. Ep. 8, 6. Transf., venison: nil damma sapit,Juv. 11, 121; Ov. M. 13, 832.

damnabilis.definition: damnābĭlis, e, damno Worthy of condemnation, damnable (late Lat. for damnandus, or dignus qui damnetur): invidia, Treb. XXX. Tyrann. 17: res (with turpes),Salv. 6: ad mea ipsa verba,i. e. by my own rule,Sid. Ep. 6, 1 fin. Comp.: facinus,Salv. 4.—Adv.: damnābĭlĭter, culpably, Aug. Ep. 23.

damnas.definition: damnas, indecl.do, v. damnum Bound to make a gift or contribution, hence an old legal t. t., condemned, sentenced to do any thing (esp. to pay a fine).

damnaticius.definition: damnāticĭus (or -tius), a, um, damno Condemned, sentenced: "Κατάκριτον damnaticium," Gloss. Gr. Lat. (late Lat.): etsi nihil de damnaticiis participarent,Tert. Praescr. Haeret. 34 fin.

damnatio.definition: id. Condemnation (good prose). Prop. Transf., of inanimate things: apiastrum in confessa damnatione est venenatum,Plin. 20, 11, 45, § 116.

damnator.definition: id. One who condemns (late Lat.), Tert. ad Nat. 1, 3; id. adv. Marc. 1, 7: damnator Christi frater iniquus,Sedul. Hymn. 1, 10 al.

damnatorius.definition: damnātōrĭus, a, um, damnator Damnatory, condemnatory (rare, but good prose): judicium, * Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 22: d. et absolutoria tabella, * Suet. Aug. 33: ferrum,Amm. 28, 1 fin.

damnaustra.definition: damnaustra and ‡ dannaustra, words of a charm to cure a dislocated joint, Cato R. R. 160.

damnifico.definition: damnĭfĭco, āre V. a., to injure: (eccl. Lat.) aliquem pecuniis,to fine,Cassiod. Hist. Eccl. 7, 29.

damnificus.definition: damnĭfĭcus, a, um, damnumfacio Injurious, hurtful, pernicious: bestia,Plaut. Cist. 4, 2, 62: damnificum est aliquid facere,Pall. 3, 9 fin.

damno.definition: damno (in vulg. lang. and late Lat. sometimes dampno), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. damnum. Gen., to occasion loss or damage to, to harm, damage = damno afficere: pauperibus parcere, divites damnare atque domare,Plaut. Trin. 4, 1, 10. Esp. [cf. damnum, II.] a judicial t. t., to condemn, doom, sentence one to any punishment = condemno, v. Cic. Or. 49, 166 (opp. to absolvere, liberare, dimittere; cf. also condemno, culpo, improbo; common and classical).—Con...

damnosus.definition: damnōsus, a, um, damnum Full of injury; and hence Act., that causes injury, injurious, hurtful, destructive, pernicious (very freq. since the Aug. period, not in Cicero or Caesar): quid tibi commerci est cum dis damnosissimis?Plaut. Bac. 1, 2, 9; cf. Venus,Hor. Ep. 1, 18, 21: libido,id. ib. 2, 1, 107: canes, the worst cast of the tali (v. canis), Prop. 4, 8, 46; cf. Isid. Orig. 18, 65 al.: et reipublicae et societatibus infidus damnosusque,Liv. 2...

damnum.definition: (late Lat. sometimes dampnum), , for daminum, neut. of old Part. of dare, = τὸ διδόμενον, v. Ritschl, Opusc. Phil. 2, 709 sq. Less correctly regarded as akin to δαπάνη. Cf. Varr. L. L. 5, § 176 Müll.; Dig. 39, 2, 3 Hurt, harm, damage, injury, loss; opp. to lucrum (syn. jactura, detrimentum, incommodum, dispendium. Freq. and class.). In gen.: hauscit, hoc paullum lucri quantum ei damni adportet,Ter. Heaut. 4, 4, 25; cf.: si in maximis lucris pa...

damula.definition: (), , dim. damma A little fallow-deer, App. M. 8, p. 202, 26; Vulg. Isa. 13, 14.

daniel.definition: The Hebrew prophet, Vulg. Dan. passim, Ezek. 14, 14.

danista.definition: dănīsta, ae, m. A money-lender, usurer: fenerator (only in Plautus),Plaut. Epid. 1, 1, 51; 2, 2, 67; id. Most. 3, 1, 6; id. Ps. 1, 3, 53; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 68, 14.—Hence, dănīstĭcus, a, um, , = δανειστικός, money-lending, usurious: genus hominum,Plaut. Most. 3, 1, 129.

dapalis.definition: dăpālĭs, e, daps Belonging to a sacrificial feast (ante and post-class.): cena, Titin. ap. Non. 95, 5 (v. 136 Ribbeck); Aus. Ep. 9, 13: Juppiter, to whom such a cena was offered,Cato, R. R. 132.

daps.definition: or , (nom. daps obsol. Paul. Diac. p. 68, 3: dapis, Juvenc. ap. Auct. de gen. nom. p. 78.—The Gen. pl. and dat. sing. do not occur, but are supplied by epulae, cena, convivium, q. v.), f. stem, dap-, Gr. δαπάνη, expense: cf. δεῖπνον; R. da-, Gr. δαίω, to distribute; Sanscr. dapajami, to cause to divide, a solemn feast for religious purposes, a sacrificial feast (before beginning to till the ground; the Greek προηρόσια, made in honor of some d...

dapsile.definition: dapsĭle Adv., sumptuously, bountifully, v.the foll. art., Adv., no. β fin.

dapsilis.definition: dapsĭlis, e ( Abl. plur. dapsilis, Plaut. Ps. 1, 4, 3), δαψιλής, daps, sumptuous, bountiful, richly provided with every thing, abundant (mostly ante- and post-class.; in the class. period perhaps only in Colum. and Suet.): sumptus,Plaut. Most. 4, 2, 66: dotes,id. Aul. 2, 1, 45: corollae,id. Ps. 5, 1, 21: lectus,id. Truc. 1, 1, 34; lubentiae,id. Ps. 1, 4, 3: proventus (vitis),Col. 4, 27, 6: copia facundiae,App. M. 11, p. 258, 12.

dardanarius.definition: A speculator in corn, forestaller (law Lat.), Dig. 47, 11, 6; 48, 19, 37.

dasea.definition: (), , , Gr. δασεῖα, sc. προσῳδία The rough-breathing or spiritus asper, Pomp. Com. Art. Don. p. 80 Lind.; Prisc. p. 1287 P.

datarius.definition: dătārĭus, a, um, do To be given away (a comic word): nulla est mihi salus dataria,I have no salutation to give away,Plaut. Ps. 4, 2, 13.

datio.definition: do The act of giving, allotting, distributing; giving up, surrender (good prose, but rare). Prop.: in datione,Varr. R. R. 3, 9 fin.: legum ( = latio), * Cic. Agr. 2, 22, 60: signi dationem Palamedes invenit,Plin. 7, 56, 57, § 202: legati, opp. ademptio legati,Dig. 34, 4, 14: partis,ib. 45, 1, 2. Transf.

dativus.definition: dătīvus, a, um, do Of or belonging to giving, given, appointed. In jurid. Lat.: dativi tutores "qui nominatim testamento dantur," Gai. Inst. 1, § 149. In gram.: dativus casus, or absol. da-tivus, i, m., the dative, Quint. 1, 7, 18; 7, 9, 13; Gell. 4, 16, 3 et saep. (cf. casus dandi, Varr. L. L. 8, 18, 112; 10, 2, 165; Nigid. ap. Gell. 13, 25, 4; Gell. 4, 16, 4 al.).

datiuus.definition: dătīvus, a, um, do Of or belonging to giving, given, appointed. In jurid. Lat.: dativi tutores "qui nominatim testamento dantur," Gai. Inst. 1, § 149. In gram.: dativus casus, or absol. da-tivus, i, m., the dative, Quint. 1, 7, 18; 7, 9, 13; Gell. 4, 16, 3 et saep. (cf. casus dandi, Varr. L. L. 8, 18, 112; 10, 2, 165; Nigid. ap. Gell. 13, 25, 4; Gell. 4, 16, 4 al.).

dato.definition: dăto, āvi V. a. frequent. [id.], to give away, administer (mostly ante-class. and post-Aug., and very rare): evectionem, Cato ap. Front. Ep. ad Antomn. 1, 2 fin.: argentum fenore,Plaut. Most. 3, 1, 73: tributum annuum,Sid. Ep. 5, 13: binas non amplius drachmas (hellebori),Plin. 25, 5, 23, § 58. Obscenè, Plaut. Aul. 4, 4, 10; cf. datatim.

dator.definition: id. A giver (except in Plant. rare). In gen., Plaut. Truc. 2, 1, 33; 2, 7, 18; fragm. ap. Prisc. p. 616 P.: assit laetitiae Bacchus dator,Verg. A. 1, 734: hilarem enim datorem diligit Deus,Vulg. 2 Cor. 9, 7. Esp. in playing ball, the slave who hands the ball to the player, opp. factor, the player himself, Plaut. Curc. 2, 3, 18.

daucum.definition: (), , n., also , , m., Scrib. Comp. 167; 170; 177 A plant of the parsnip or carrot kind, much used in medicine, Plin. 19, 5, 27, § 89: probatissimus in Creta,id. 25, 9, 64, § 110 al.; Cels. 5, 23, 3 al. In App. Herb. 80, called daucion and daucites.

david.definition: or vīdis ( Gen. David, Aus. Ephem. 3, 84: Davidis,Juvenc. 1, 151; acc. -vīda, Juvenc. 2, 577: David,Vulg. 2 Reg. 23, 16), the second king of the Jews, and principal author of the Book of Psalms, Tert. adv. Jud. 9 et 12; Vulg. Ruth 4, 17 et saep.—Hence, , , adj., of or belonging to David: urbs,Sedul. Carm. 4, 42: lyra,Cassiod. Var. 2, 20.

dauid.definition: or vīdis ( Gen. David, Aus. Ephem. 3, 84: Davidis,Juvenc. 1, 151; acc. -vīda, Juvenc. 2, 577: David,Vulg. 2 Reg. 23, 16), the second king of the Jews, and principal author of the Book of Psalms, Tert. adv. Jud. 9 et 12; Vulg. Ruth 4, 17 et saep.—Hence, , , adj., of or belonging to David: urbs,Sedul. Carm. 4, 42: lyra,Cassiod. Var. 2, 20.

de.definition: dē, : of place Down, only in the phrase susque deque, q. v.

dea.definition: (dat. and Abl. plur.: diis,Varr. R. R. 3, 16, 7; Ins. Orell. 2076: deabus, Cn. Gell. ap. Charis. p. 39 P.; Aug. C. D. 7, 24; 3, 3; Apul. M. 4, p. 156: dis deabusque,Cic. Rab. Perd. 2, 5; id. fragm. ap. Prisc. p. 733 P., IV. 2, p. 451 ed. Orell.; cf. DIVIS DIVABVSQVE, Inscr. ap. Voss. Arist. 4, 4 fin.), f. deus, a goddess: Juno sancta dearum, Enn. ap. Serv. ad Verg. A. 4, 576 (Annal. v. 65 Vahl.): his diis (i. e. the Muses) Helicona atque Olympon ...

dealbatio.definition: dealbo A whitewashing, Aug. Civ. D. 3, 14.

dealbo.definition: dĕ-albo, āvi, ātum, 1, albus To whiten over, to whitewash, to parget, plaster (good prose, but rare): columnas,Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 55 fin. (twice): parietes,Pall. 1, 24, 1; Suet. Gall. 9; Vitr. 7, 4.—Prov.: duo parietes de eadem fidelia, Curius ap. Cic. Fam. 7, 29; v. fidelia.—In eccl. Lat., to purify, cleanse: in sanguine Agni,Vulg. Apoc. 7, 14.—Pass., to be white, Vulg. Psa. 50, 8 al.—Hence, dĕalbātus, a, um, P. a., whitewashed, plastered: sepulch...

deambulacrum.definition: deambulo A place to walk in, a promenade, walk, Mamert. Grat. act. ad Julian. 9; Vulg. 3 Reg. 7, 2.

deambulatio.definition: [id.) A walking abroad, promenading, Ter. Heaut. 4, 6, 2; Cael. Aur. Tard. 3, 8, 141; Vulg. Ezech. 12, 4.

deambulatorium.definition: id. A gallery for walking, Capitol. Gord. 3, 32.

deambulo.definition: dĕ-ambŭlo, āvi, ātum, l V. n., to walk abroad, walk much, to take a walk, to promenade (rare): aegrotus saliat decies et deambulet,Cato R. R. 127 fin.; 156, 4: eamus deambulatum, id. ap. Cic. de Or. 2, 63, 256; so in the supine, * Ter. Heaut. 3, 3, 26; deambulanti in litore,Suet. Aug. 96; 83; Vulg. Gen. 3, 8; id. Dan. 13, 7 (ambulatum is the true reading, Cic. Leg. 1, 3, 14).

deamo.definition: dĕ-ămo, āvi, ātum, 1 V. a., to be desperately in love with, to love dearly or passionately (ante-class.), "vehementius amare," Non. 97, 21 (cf. depereo). Prop.: illa, quam tuus gnatus annos multos deamat, deperit,Plaut. Epid. 2, 2, 35; id. Poen. 4, 2, 72; Afran. ap. Non. l. l. (v. 357 Ribbeck): Laber. ap. Charis. l, p. 84 P. (v. 41 Ribbeck). Transf.

deargumentor.definition: dĕ-argūmentor, āri V. dep. n., to decide finally (late Lat.): super aliqua re,Claud. Mamert. de Statu An. 2, 7.

dearmo.definition: dĕ-armo, āvi, ātum, l Aliquem, to disarm (except in particip., late Lat. for armis spoliare): dearmatus exercitus,Liv. 4. 10, 7. Aliquid, to deprive of power, blunt: pharetram expilet, sagittas dearmet,App. M. 5, p. 172, 25.

deascio.definition: dĕ-ascĭo, āvi, ātum, 1, 1, ascio To hew or cut with an axe, to smoothe. Lit. (late Lat.): deasciato stipiti, wrought, smoothed, Prud. στεφ. 10, 381. Trop.: aliquem, to cheat, to chouse (cf. abrado), Plaut. Mil. 3, 3, 11.

deauro.definition: dĕ-auro, āvi, ātum, 1 V. a., to gild, to gild over (late Lat. for inaurare): cassidas et tegerent argento et deanrarent, Cod. Theod. 10, 22, 1; Tert. Idol. 8: columnas,Vulg. Exod. 36, 36: vestitus,id. Psa. 44, 9: SIGNVM DEAVRATVM, Inscr. Orell. no. 3173 (of the year 162 post-Chr.).

debacchatio.definition: debacchor Passionate raving, fury: libidinis,Salv. Gub. D. 7 init.

debacchor.definition: dē-bacchor, ātus, 1 V. dep. n., to rave like the Bacchantes, to rage without control, revel wildly (rare): si satis jam debacchatus es, leno,Ter. Ad. 2, 1, 30 sq.; Hier. in Ies. 11, 37, 26. Poet., of inanimate things, to rage: qua parte debacchentur ignes, * Hor. Od. 3, 3, 55.

debellator.definition: debello A conqueror, subduer (rare; mostly poet.): ferarum, * Verg. A. 7, 651; * Stat. Th. 9, 545: Vespasianus Judaeorum debellator,Tert. Apol. 5: durus,Vulg. Sap. 18, 15.

debellatrix.definition: debellator A conqueress, she that conquers (late Lat.). Prop.: Phrygiac Graecia,Tert. Apol. 25. Trop.: pudoris et famae libido,Lact. 1, 9.

debello.definition: dē-bello, āvi, ātum, 1, and A. (not ante-Aug.; esp. freq. in Livy). Neutr., to bring a war to an end, to finish a war. So rare in the act. form: Aulius cum Ferentanis uno secundo proelio debellavit,Liv. 9, 16; cf. id. Epit. 33; id. 44, 39 fin.; 35, 35. But exceedingly common as an impersonal: debellari eo die cum Samnitibus potuisse,Liv. 8, 36; cf. id. 4, 58: ne absente se debellaretur,id. 41, 18: proelioque uno debellatum est,id. 2, 26; 31, 48fi...

debeo.definition: dēbĕo (dehibeo, Plaut. Trin. 2, 4, 24 Infra, cf. Ritschl, Opusc. Phil. 2, 590), ŭi, ĭtum, 2, de-habeo, (lit., to have or keep from some one: "qui pecuniam dissolvit, statim non habet id quod reddidit, qui autem debet, aes retinet alienum," Cic. Planc. 28, 68 Wund.; hence), to owe (Gr. ὀφείλω; opp. reddo, solvo, dissolvo, persolvo, freq. and class.). Lit., of money and money's worth. Trop., to owe something, i. e. to be under obligation, both to...

debibo.definition: dē-bĭbo, ĕre V. a., to drink of: flumen,Sol. 7, 27.

debilis.definition: dēbĭlis (old shortened form Debil, v. Ritschl, Opusc. Phil. 2, 331), e, de-habilis; cf. Dig. 49, 16, 4, § 12: lit. unmanageable, wanting in flexibility or activity; hence, lame, disabled, crippled, infirm, debilitated, feeble, frail, weak, etc. For syn. cf.: imbecillus, infirmus, invalidus (freq. and class.). Lit. Trop., disabled, weak, in mind, character, authority, etc.

debilitas.definition: debilis Lameness, debility, infirmity, weakness (good prose). Lit.: linguae,Cic. Pis. 1: membrorum,Liv. 33, 2: pedis, Labeo ap. Gell. 4, 2, 4: pedum,Tac. H. 1, 9: aliqua corporis, * Suet. Calig. 26 fin. et saep.—Absol.: bonum integritas corporis, miserum debilitas,Cic. Fin. 5, 28, 84; so id. Tusc. 3, 34; id. de Inv. 1, 25, 36; Liv. 2, 36; Cels. 5, 26, 28; Juv. 14, 156; Quint. 5, 12, 19; Plin. Ep. 8, 18, 9 al.— In plur.: a se dolores, morbos, debi...

debilitatio.definition: id. A laming, maiming; weakness (rare). Lit.: praemium debilitationis consecutus, i. e. of mutilation of nose and ears,App. M. 2, p. 128, 15. Trop.: animi, * Cic. Pis. 36, 88.

debilito.definition: dēbĭlĭto, āvi, ātum, 1, debilis To lame, cripple, maim; to debilitate, unnerve, disable, weaken (freq. and class.). Lit. Trop.

debitio.definition: debeo An owing, indebtedness (extremely rare): pecuniae et gratiae,Cic. Planc. 28, 68; cf. Gell. 1, 4, 2 sq.: torquetur debitione dotis,Cic. Att. 14, 13, 5.—Transf., the debt, Ambros. de Tobia, 7, 25.

debitor.definition: id. A debtor; cf.: nexus, obaeratus. Lit. (quite class.), Cic. Off. 2, 22, 78; id. Flacc. 20, 48; id. Pis. 35, 86; Caes. B. C. 3, 1; 3, 20; Quint. 3, 6, 84; * Juv. 16, 40 et saep.: aeris, * Hor. S. 1, 3, 86. Trop. (mostly poet., and perh. not ante-Aug.).

debitrix.definition: debitor A female debtor (post-class.). Lit.: mulier,Dig. 16, 1, 24: fisci,ib. 49, 14, 47. Trop.: omnium delictorum debitrix anima est,the guilty cause,Tert. Anim. 35.

deblatero.definition: dē-blătĕro, āvi, ātum, 1 V. a., to prate of a thing, to babble, blab out (ante and post-class.): versuum multa milia,Gell. 9, 15, 10; id. 1, 2, 6.—With acc. and inf., Plaut. Aul. 2, 3, 1; Lucil. ap. Non. 96, 10.

debucino.definition: dē-būcĭno (debuccino), āre V. a., to trumpet forth (eccl. Lat.), trop., Tert. virg. vel. 13.

decachinno.definition: dē-căchinno, āre V. a., to deride, laugh to scorn (eccl. Lat.), Tert. Apol. 47.

decachordum.definition: δεκάχορδον A musical instrument of ten strings (eccl. Lat.), Vulg. Psa. 91, 4.

decachordus.definition: dĕcăchordus, a, um, , = δεκάχορδος Ten-stringed (late Lat.): cithara,Fulg. Myth. 1, 14 al.

decacumino.definition: dē-căcūmĭno, āre V. a., to cut the top off, to top and lop (t. t. of agriculture): pampinum,Col. 4, 7, 3: ulmum,id. 5, 6, 12.

decalco.definition: dēcalco To plaster with lime, to whitewash = albo, κονιῶ, Gloss. Vet.

decalesco.definition: dēcălesco To become warm, ἐκθερμαίνομαι, Gloss. Cyrill.

decalvatio.definition: decalvo The making bald, Hieron. Ep. 122, 1.

decaluatio.definition: decalvo The making bald, Hieron. Ep. 122, 1.

decalvo.definition: dē-calvo, āvi, ātum, 1, (calvus] To make bald, to remove the hair (late Lat.): locum corporis,Veg. A. V. 2, 48, 3: Sampson a muliere decalvatus,shorn,Hier. adv. Jov. 1, 23: pueros David decalvavit,Vulg. 1 Par. 19, 4; 1 Cor. 11, 6.

decaluo.definition: dē-calvo, āvi, ātum, 1, (calvus] To make bald, to remove the hair (late Lat.): locum corporis,Veg. A. V. 2, 48, 3: Sampson a muliere decalvatus,shorn,Hier. adv. Jov. 1, 23: pueros David decalvavit,Vulg. 1 Par. 19, 4; 1 Cor. 11, 6.

decanicum.definition: id. A building belonging to the church, Cod. Theod. 16, 5, 30.

decano.definition: dē-căno, ĕre, 3 V. a., to celebrate by singing: Cererem, Prob. Cath. 1492 P.

decantatio.definition: decanto Talkativeness, as transl. of ἀδολεσχία, Hier. Ep. 106, no. 49.

decanto.definition: dē-canto, āvi, ātum, 1, (in the class. per. freq. in Cic.; elsewh. rare). To sing a thing off, to repeat in a singing manner (v. cano and canto). Intr.

decanus.definition: decem. A chief of ten, one set over ten persons (late Lat.). A kind of officer at the imperial court, Cod. 12, 27, 1. In astrology, the chief of ten parts of a zodiacal sign, Firm. Math. 2, 4.

decaprotia.definition: The office and dignity of the decaproti, Dig. 50, 4, 18, § 26.

decargyrum.definition: A large silver coin ( = majorina), Cod. Theod. 9, 23, 1.

decarmino.definition: dēcarmĭno, avi, 1, de-carmen To make prose of verse, to disarrange the order of the words in a verse: sed hic ordo nobis verborum faciendus est, ut versus hujus decarminata contextio ipsa se magis exponere videatur,Cassiod. in Psa. 130, 3, 4.

decarno.definition: dē-carno, āre, 2, caro To take off the flesh (late Lat.), Veg. A. V. 2, 27, 2; 2, 42, 1; 3, 6, 1; Apic. 7, 9.

decas.definition: A decade, Tert. de Praescr. 49 al.; Mart. Cap. 7, § 734.

decedo.definition: dē-cēdo, cessi, cessum, 3 ( Inf. sync. decesse, Ter. Heaut. prol. 32; Cic. Fam. 7, 1, 2; Neue Formenl. 2, 536. The part. perf. decessus perh. only Rutil. Nam. 1, 313), v. n., to go away, depart, withdraw. (For syn. cf.: linquo, relinquo, desero, destituo, deficio, discedo, excedo. Often opp. to accedo, maneo; freq. and class.)—Constr. absol. with de, ex, or merely the abl.; rarely with ab. Lit. Trop.

decello.definition: dē-cello, ĕre, , = declino To turn aside, deviate, Lucr. 2, 219 Lachm. ex conj. (better depellere, with the MSS. v. Munro ad loc.).

december.definition: decem and -ber, = fer, Sanscr. bhar, to carry, bear: cf. Septem-ber, etc. The tenth month of the Roman year, reckoned from March, and consequently our twelfth, December (containing, as now, 31 days): "dehinc quintus (mensis) Quintilis et sic deinceps usque ad Decembrem a numero," Varr. L. L. 6, § 34 Müll.; Cic. Leg. 2, 21 fin.: acceptus Geniis December (on account of the Saturnalia celebrated in this month),Ov. F. 3, 58; cf. Sen. Ep. 18: canus,Ma...

decemiugis.definition: jugum.—Lit. Adj., ten-yoked; hence (with currus understood), a ten-horse chariot (very rare), Suet. Ner. 24; Inscr. ap. Buleng. de Circo, 55.

decemmestris.definition: dĕcem-mestris, e, mensis; cf.: bimestris, trimestris Of ten months: annus, Censorin. 11; 20.

decempeda.definition: pes A ten-foot measuring rod, Cic. Mil. 27, 74; id. Phil. 14, 4, 10; id. Ac. 2, 41, 126; * Hor. Od. 2, 15, 14 al.

decempedalis.definition: dĕcempĕdālis, e, decem-pes Ten feet long: spatium, Cod. 11, 42, 6.

decemplex.definition: dĕcem-plex, ĭcis, plico Tenfold, Varr. L. L. 10, § 43 Müll: numerus hostium,Nep. Milt. 5.

decemplicatus.definition: dĕcemplĭcātus, a, um, decem-plex Multiplied by ten, ten times over, Varr. L. L. 6, § 38 Müll.

decemviralis.definition: dĕcemvĭrālis, e, decemviri Decemviral, of or belonging to the decem viri: leges,i. e. of the Twelve Tables,Liv. 3, 57 fin.; Gell. 20, 1, 3: potestas,Liv. 3, 55; Tac. A. 1, 1: annus,Cic. Rep. 2, 37 invidia, id. Brut. 14, 54; Liv. 3, 42: certaminibus,id. 3, 54: odio,id. 3, 42: ex collegio (sacerdotes),Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 49: pecunia (referring to the decemviri agris dividundis),id. Agr. 1, 5; cf.: auctis,ib. 2, 22, 58.— * Adv., dĕcemvĭrālĭter: loqui, ...

decemuiralis.definition: dĕcemvĭrālis, e, decemviri Decemviral, of or belonging to the decem viri: leges,i. e. of the Twelve Tables,Liv. 3, 57 fin.; Gell. 20, 1, 3: potestas,Liv. 3, 55; Tac. A. 1, 1: annus,Cic. Rep. 2, 37 invidia, id. Brut. 14, 54; Liv. 3, 42: certaminibus,id. 3, 54: odio,id. 3, 42: ex collegio (sacerdotes),Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 49: pecunia (referring to the decemviri agris dividundis),id. Agr. 1, 5; cf.: auctis,ib. 2, 22, 58.— * Adv., dĕcemvĭrālĭter: loqui, ...

decemviratus.definition: decemviri The decemvirate, the rank or office of a decemvir; with regard to the decemv. agr. divid., Cic. Agr. 2, 22, 60; with regard to the decemv. legib. scrib.,Liv. 4, 15 al.

decemuiratus.definition: decemviri The decemvirate, the rank or office of a decemvir; with regard to the decemv. agr. divid., Cic. Agr. 2, 22, 60; with regard to the decemv. legib. scrib.,Liv. 4, 15 al.

decennalis.definition: dĕcennālis, e, decem-annus Of ten years, decennial (late Lat.; cf. decennis): bellum, i. e. Caesar's in Gaul,Amm. 15, 12, 6; of the Trojan war,Hier. adv. Jovin. 1, 48. Subst.: DECENNALIA (ium, n.), a festival celebrated every ten years after the time of Augustus, Trebell. Gallien. 21, 5; Inscr. Grut. 116, 4; v. decennis fin.

decennis.definition: dĕcennis, e, id. Of ten years (post-Aug.): bellum, of the Greeks before Troy,Quint. 8, 4, 22; also proelium,Petr. 89, 2, 8: obsidio (Veiorum),Flor. 1, 12, 8: equae,ten years old,Plin. 8, 44, 69; cf.: decenni major asinus,Pall. Mart. 14, 1. Subst.: decennia, ium, n., = decennalia, a festival under the emperors, held every ten years, Treb. Gall. 5 fin.; cf.: decennalis, no. II.

decennium.definition: decennis. A period of ten years (post-class.), App. de Deo. Socr. p. 52, 7 al. I. q. decennalia, Trebell. Gallien. 7 fin.

decennovalis.definition: dĕcennŏvālis, e, decem novem Of nineteen years: cyclus, Cassiod., comp. pasch.

decennoualis.definition: dĕcennŏvālis, e, decem novem Of nineteen years: cyclus, Cassiod., comp. pasch.

decenter.definition: dĕcenter, v. decet P. a. fin.

deceptio.definition: decipio A deceiving, deception (late Lat.), Mart. Cap. 4 fin. al.; Cod. 11, 47, 6; Vulg. 1. Macc. 16, 17. Deceitfulness: vitae,Vulg. Sap. 14, 21: divitiarum,id. Marc. 4, 19.

deceptor.definition: id. A deceiver (late Lat. for fraudator), Sen. Thyest. 140; Lact. de Ira, 4, 8; August. Serm. 362, 18.

deceptrix.definition: deceptor She that deceives: perniciosa adulatio,Lact. Epit. 6 fin.

deceptus.definition: dēceptus, a, um, Part. of decipio.

deceris.definition: δεκήρης (sc. ναῦς) A ten-oared ship, i. e. a ship having ten banks of oars: Liburnicas,Suet. Calig. 37 (acc. to a conject. of Turneb. Adv. 22, 30; lect. vulg. de cedris).

decerno.definition: dē-cerno, crēvi, crētum, 3 (the syncop. forms decreram, etc., decrerim, etc., decresse are freq. in Cicero and Liv., also Plaut. Curc. 5, 3, 25; Ter. Hec. 1, 2, 73; 2, 1, 15, but not in Caes., where is only decreverat, B. G. 4, 17; 5, 5 Fin.; 5, 53, 2), and n. (acc. to cerno, no. II. 3.) To decide, determine any thing disputed or doubtful. For syn. cf.: scisco, jubeo, statuo, constituo, dico, sancio, consilium capio, destino, obstino, definio, de...

decerpo.definition: dē-cerpo, psi, ptum, 3, carpo To pluck off, to tear, pull, or break off, to crop, gather (class.; most freq. in the poets.—Constr., usually aliquid ex aliqua re; less freq. aliquid de aliqua re). Lit.: acina de uvis decerpito,Cato R. R. 112, 3: novos flores,Lucr. 1, 927; 4, 3; cf.: undique decerptam fronti praeponere olivam,Hor. Od. 1, 7, 7: arbore pomum,Ov. M. 5, 536; cf. id. Pont. 3, 5, 19; and auricomos fetus arbore,Verg. A. 6, 141: praetenuia...

decertator.definition: id. He who goes through a decisive contest, a champion: veritatis,Cassiod. Hist. Eccl. 3, 16 and 34.

decerto.definition: dē-certo, āvi, ātum, 1, and A., to go through a decisive contest, to fight it out (but certare, to fight, without reference to the result. But the difference was not strictly observed. Thus Caesar uses often —15 times—decertare, but never certare; Sallust only the latter; and Cicero the two indifferently; cf.: decerno, I. B. and no. II. inf.). In the milit. sphere. Beyond the milit. sphere, to contend: erat non jure, non legibus, non disceptando ...

decervicatus.definition: dē-cervīcātus, a, um, cervix Decollated, beheaded: cadavera,Sid. Ep. 3, 3 med.

deceruicatus.definition: dē-cervīcātus, a, um, cervix Decollated, beheaded: cadavera,Sid. Ep. 3, 3 med.

decessio.definition: decedo A going away, departure (opp. accessio—good prose). Lit. Trop.: verborum, the transition, transferring of words from their primary to a derivative meaning, Gell. 13, 29, 1.

decessor.definition: decedo, no. I. B. 2 One who retires from a province he has governed; hence, with reference to his successor, a retiring officer (rare): successori decessor invidit, Cic. Scaur. Fragm. § 33, p. 187 ed. Beier; so Tac. Agr. 7; Dig. 1, 16, 4, § 4. In gen., a predecessor in office (late Lat.), August. in Psal. 43, 16 al.

decessus.definition: decedo A going away, departure (opp. accessus—good prose). In gen.: post Dionysii decessum,Nep. Tim. 2, 3. Esp.

decido.definition: dē-cĭdo, cĭdi, 3, cado To fall off, fall down (class.). Trop., to fall, drop, fall away, fail, sink: quanta de spe decidi!Ter. Heaut. 2, 3, 9; for which quanta spe decidi!id. ib. 4, 8, 11; Suet. Oth. 5; and a spe societatis Prusiae,Liv. 37, 26: ex astris,Cic. Att. 2, 21, 4 (cf.: astrum, no. II. B. fin.): ego ab archetypo labor et decido,Plin. Ep. 5, 10, 1: eo decidit ut exsul de senatore fieret,has fallen so low,id. ib. 4, 11, 1: oculis captus in...

deciduus.definition: dēcĭdŭus, a, um, 1. decĭdo Falling down or off, deciduous (chiefly in Pliny: folia, Laber. ap. Non. 100, 10; Plin. 18, 25, 60, § 226; 16, 24, 38, § 92 (where Freund assumes decīdua, cut off, cf. Cato R. R. 5, 7, but without necessity): (ignes) decidui ad terras fulminum nomen habent,Plin. 2, 20, 18, § 82: sidera,falling, shooting stars,id. 2, 8, 6, § 28: cornua cervis,id. 11, 37, 45, § 127: testes pecori ad crura decidui, subus annexi,id. 11, 49,...

decima.definition: v. decimus No. I. B. and II. B.

decimanus.definition: dĕcĭmānus or dĕcŭmānus (v. decimus), a, um, decimus Of or belonging to the tenth part. Prop. Meton., considerable, large, immense (cf.: decimus, decem, decies, etc.): accipensere, Lucil. ap. Cic. Fin. 2, 8, 24: DECUMANA ova' dicuntur et DECUMANI fluctus, quia sunt magna, Paul. ex Fest. p. 71, 5; cf. ib. 4, 7 Müll.

decimarius.definition: dĕcĭmārĭus, a, um Adj., pertaining to tithes: leges, Cod. 8, 58. Paying tithes, subject to tithes, Ambros. in Psa. 128, Serm. 8, 4 al.

decimatio.definition: decimo The taking of a tenth. A tithing: omnis,Vulg. Tobiae, 1, 7. A selecting by lot of every tenth man for punishment, decimation, Capitol. Macr. 12. A tenth: adhuc in ea decimatio,Vulg. Isa. 6, 13.

decimo.definition: dĕcĭmo or dĕcŭmo, āvi, ātum, 1, decimus. To select by lot every tenth man for punishment, to decimate (postAug., although the practice itself occurs as early as 283 A. U. C.; v. Liv. 2, 59 fin.), Suet. Galb. 12: cohortes,id. Aug. 24: cohortium militem, Frontin. Strat. 4, 1, 37 al.— Absol., Suet. Calig. 48. To cause to pay tithes, to collect tithes from a person. —Pass.: et Levi decimatus est,Vulg. Hebr. 7, 9. To select the tenth part as an offeri...

decimus.definition: dĕcĭmus or dĕcŭmus (the latter form prevailed in the later law lang.; hence, decumanus), a, um, adj. decem with superl. ending The tenth. Prop.: mensis,Plaut. Am. 1, 2, 19; cf. Ter. Ad. 3, 4, 29: legio,Caes. B. G. 1, 40; cf. ib. 41; 42 al.: decima hora,Cic. Phil. 2, 31; and without hora,Auct. Her. 4, 51: annus,Verg. A. 9, 155: septuma (dies) post decumam,i. e. the seventeenth,id. G. 1, 284 Voss.: cum decumo efficit ager,i. e. tenfold,Cic. Verr. 2...

decineratus.definition: dēcĭnĕrātus, a, um, de-cinis Wholly turned to ashes (late Lat.), Tert. adv. Valent. 32.

decineresco.definition: dē-cĭnĕresco, ĕre V. n., to be wholly reduced to ashes (late Lat.): ut nullo igni decinerescat,Tert. Apol. 48 fin.

decipio.definition: dē-cĭpĭo, cēpi, ceptum, 3, capio, primarily signifies to catch away, catch up, seize an animal while running, fleeing, etc. (whence decipula, a snare, trap); but occurs only in the trop. sense (acc. to capio No. II. B.), to catch, ensnare, entrap, beguile, elude, deceive, cheat (for syn. cf.: fraudo, emungo, circumscribo, circumvenio, frustror, verba do, impono, fallo): fiunt transennae ubi decipiuntur dolis, etc.,Plaut. Rud. 4, 7, 9 sq.: ita dec...

decipula.definition: f., and , , n.decipio A snare, gin, trap. Lit. (late Lat.): plena avibus,Vulg. Jerem. 5, 27; Job 18, 10. Trop. (ante- and post-class.).

decircino.definition: dē-circĭno, āre V. a., to make of a circular form, to round off (only in Manil.): arcum,Manil. 1, 296: orbem,id. 3, 352.

decisio.definition: 2. decīdo. (Acc. to decīdo, no. II. B.) A diminishing: luminis, App. de Mundo, p. 71, 4.—Far more freq., and in good prose. (Acc. to decīdo, no. II. A.) A decision, settlement, agreement: nostra de aequitate,Cic. Caecin. 36 fin.: dicat decisionem factam esse, quae facta non est,id. Rosc. Com. 13, 48; id. Flacc. 36, 89; Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 54: quaestionis,Dig. 5, 3, 25.

decitans.definition: dēcĭtans, antis, de-cĭto Causing to glide down, App. M. 2, p. 116, 4.

declamatio.definition: declamo. Exercise in oratorical delivery, exercise or practice in speaking, declamation (class.; most freq. in Quint.): cum sit declamatio forensium actionum meditatio, etc.,Quint. 4, 2, 29; cf. id. 2, 10, 4; 12 et saep.: in quotidiana declamatione utilis, etc.,Cic. Fam. 16, 21, 6; cf. id. Tusc. 1, 4, 7; 2, 11, 26. In a bad sense, loud, eager talking, bawling (so several times in Cic.): desinamus aliquando vulgari et pervagata declamatione conten...

declamator.definition: declamo One who practises set speaking, a rhetorician, declaimer (diff. from orator, a practical speaker, Quint. 10, 2, 21): non enim declamatorem aliquem de ludo aut rabulam de foro, sed doctissimum et perfectissimum quaerimus,Cic. Or. 15, 47; cf. id. Planc. 34, 83; Quint. 3, 8, 44; 51; 5, 13, 42; Juv. 16, 23 et saep.

declamatorius.definition: dēclāmātōrĭus, a, um, adj.declamator Of or belonging to the exercise of speaking, declamatory, rhetorical (good prose): opus,Cic. de Or. 1, 16 fin.: illo genere duci et delectari,id. Q. Fr. 3, 3 fin.; ef.: genus dicendi,Quint. 2, 10, 9: consuetudo,id. 5, 13, 46: licentia,id. 8, 3, 76: res,id. 4, 2, 128: studium,Tac. Or. 14.—Hence, adv.: dēclāmātōriē, in a rhetorical manner (late Lat.), Hieron. al.

declamito.definition: V., freq. n. and a. [declamo], to practise rhetorical delivery or declamation, to declaim (good prose; most frequent in Cic.). In a good sense. In a bad sense, to talk violently, to bluster: de aliquo,Cic. Phil. 5, 7, 19; cf. id. ib. 2, 17.

declamo.definition: dē-clāmo, āvi, ātum, 1, and A.— Rhetor. t. t., to exercise one's self in rhetorical delivery, to practise speaking, to declaim. For syn. cf.: dictito, concionor, pronuntio, palam dico, praedico, recito, declamito. (Class., most freq. in Cic. and Quint.) In a good sense. In a bad sense, to speak as an orator with violence, to declaim, to bluster, bawl: ille insanus, qui pro isto vehementissime contra me declamasset,Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 66 fin.; so in ...

declaratio.definition: declaro A making clear or evident, a disclosure, exposition, declaration (very rare): animi tui,Cic. Fam. 10, 5, 2: amoris tui?id. ib. 15, 21, 3: sub eadem declaratione,App. Dogm. Plat. 3, p. 30 fin.; Vulg. Ps. 118, 130.

declarativus.definition: dēclārātīvus, a, um, id. Serving for explanation, explanatory (postclass.): pars,App. Dogm. Plat. 3, p. 30 and 33; Mart. Cap. 4, § 341.—Adv.: dēclārā-tīvē, by way of explanation, Mart. Cap. 4, § 393.

declaratiuus.definition: dēclārātīvus, a, um, id. Serving for explanation, explanatory (postclass.): pars,App. Dogm. Plat. 3, p. 30 and 33; Mart. Cap. 4, § 341.—Adv.: dēclārā-tīvē, by way of explanation, Mart. Cap. 4, § 393.

declaro.definition: dē-clāro, āvi, ātum, 1 V. a., to make clear, plain, evident (by disclosing, uncovering), to show, manifest, declare, etc., ἀποφαίνω (class.; most freq. in the trop. sense). For syn. cf.: monstro, demonstro, probo, confirmo, ostendo, ostento, significo, indico, defero; exsisto, appareo, eluceo. Lit. Trop., to make clear to the mind, to manifest, demonstrate, prove, show, explain: cum tot signis eadem natura declaret quid velit, tamen, etc.,Cic. ...

declinabilis.definition: dēclīnābĭlis, e, declino That can be (grammatically) inflected, Prisc. p. 670 P.

declinatio.definition: id. A bending from a thing, a bending aside; an oblique inclination or direction (good prose). Lit.: lanceam exigua corporis declinatione vitare,Curt. 9, 7 fin.; cf.: quot ego tuas petitiones parva quadam declinatione effugi,Cic. Cat. 1, 6, 15: declinare dixit (Epicurus) atomum perpaulum, et ipsa declinatio ad libidinem fingitur, etc.,id. Fin. 1, 6, 19; so of the oblique motion of atoms, id. Fat. 10, 22; 22, 47. Trop.

declinatus.definition: id. Variation, inflection of words (cf. the prec. art. II. B. 2), Varr. L. L. 9, § 34; 51; 53. But in Cic. Fin. 5, 7, 17, the best reading is: declinatum dolorem, v. Madvig ad h. l.).

declinis.definition: dēclīnis, e, id. Turning aside (perh. only in the two foll. places): declinia juga,Stat. Th. 5, 297 (quae declinarent et fugerent, Schol.). So of the retreating motion of the sea in ebb and flood: undae,ebbing,Luc. 4, 427 dub. (al. declivibus).

declino.definition: dē-clīno, āvi, ātum, 1, and n. CLINO = κλίνω, orig. To bend from the straight path; to turn aside or away (freq. and class.). Lit. Trop.

declivis.definition: dē-clīvis, e ( Nom. n. declivum, Cassiod. in Psal. 16, 5; neutr. plur. once heterocl. decliva, Ov. M. 2, 206; also declivia,id. ib. 1, 39 et saep.; cf. acclivis and aplustre), clivus, inclining downwards, sloping (for syn. cf.: devexus, praeruptas, abruptus, abscisus, proclivis, acclivis, propensus, praeceps, pronus.—Class. and freq., esp. in histt. and poets; perh. not in Cic. and Verg.). Prop.: collis ab summo aequaliter declivis ad flumen Sabi...

decliuis.definition: dē-clīvis, e ( Nom. n. declivum, Cassiod. in Psal. 16, 5; neutr. plur. once heterocl. decliva, Ov. M. 2, 206; also declivia,id. ib. 1, 39 et saep.; cf. acclivis and aplustre), clivus, inclining downwards, sloping (for syn. cf.: devexus, praeruptas, abruptus, abscisus, proclivis, acclivis, propensus, praeceps, pronus.—Class. and freq., esp. in histt. and poets; perh. not in Cic. and Verg.). Prop.: collis ab summo aequaliter declivis ad flumen Sabi...

decoctio.definition: decoquo (postclass.) A boiling down. Prop. Trop., of an association, a decoction, mixture: unius decoctioni universi respondere cogentur,Cod. Just. 11, 9, 5; cf. Cod. Theod. 4, 9, 3.
