demonstrativus.definition: dēmonstrātīvus, a, um, demonstro Pointing out, designating. In gen. (very rarely): digitus,the indexfinger, forefinger,Cael. Aur. Tard. 5, 1, 21. In rhetor., demonstrative, = ἐγκωμιαστικόν: genus (orationis), a branch of rhetoric employed in praising or censuring, i. e. laudatory or vituperative (usuually the former), Cic. Inv. 1, 5, 7; Quint. 3, 4, 14; 2, 10, 11: causa,Cic. Inv. 2, 4: materia,Quint. 3, 8, 53; 11, 1, 48: pars orationis,id. 2, 2...

demonstratiuus.definition: dēmonstrātīvus, a, um, demonstro Pointing out, designating. In gen. (very rarely): digitus,the indexfinger, forefinger,Cael. Aur. Tard. 5, 1, 21. In rhetor., demonstrative, = ἐγκωμιαστικόν: genus (orationis), a branch of rhetoric employed in praising or censuring, i. e. laudatory or vituperative (usuually the former), Cic. Inv. 1, 5, 7; Quint. 3, 4, 14; 2, 10, 11: causa,Cic. Inv. 2, 4: materia,Quint. 3, 8, 53; 11, 1, 48: pars orationis,id. 2, 2...

demonstrator.definition: id. One who points out or indicates; an indicator, exhibiter (very rare): uniuscujusque sepeliendi, * Cic. de Or. 2, 86, 353: hujus rationis,Col. 3, 10, 20: medicinarum Aesculapius,Tert. Apol. 23.

demonstro.definition: dē-monstro, āvi, ātum, 1 ( Arch. inf. pass.: demonstrarier,Ter. Ph. 2, 1, 76), v. a., to point out, as with the finger; to indicate, designate, show (freq. and class.). Lit. Trop., to designate, indicate, by speech or writing; to show, prove, demonstrate; to represent, describe; also simply to mention (in this signif. often in Caes. —for syn. cf.: monstro, commonstro, comprobo, probo, declaro).

demoratio.definition: demoror A lingering, abiding, remaining: in vini demorationibus,Vulg. Prov. 12, 11.

demorior.definition: dē-mŏrĭor, mortuus, 3 V. dep. n., to die off, to die, depart, decease (i. e. from an office, out of a circle of associates, etc., cf. Fabri ad Liv. 23, 21, 7. In the class. per. only in the perf. or part. perf.; not found in Caes. and the Aug. poets). Lit.: paene sum fame demortuus,Plaut. Stich. 1, 3, 62: cum esset ex veterum numero quidam senator demortuus,Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 50, § 124; cf.: tantum hominum demortuum esse, ut, etc.,Liv. 40, 19; 26, ...

demoror.definition: dēmŏror, ātus, 1 V. dep. n. and a. Act., to retard, detain, delay one: diu me estis demorati,Plaut. Epid. 3, 2, 40; cf.: ne diutius vos demorer, *Cic. de Or. 2, 58, 235: detinere aliquem et demorari, Lentul. in Cic. Fam. 12, 15: nullo hoste prohibente aut iter demorante,Caes. B. G. 3, 6 fin.; so, repentinas eorum eruptiones,id. B. C. 1, 81, 5: novissimum agmen,id. ib. 3, 75, 3; Tac. A. 12, 68.—Poet.: Teucros quid demoror armis?restrain from battl...

demorsito.definition: dē-morsĭto, no Perf., ātum, 1, v. int. a. [demordeo], to bite off (only in Apuleius): ora mortuorum, Ap. M. 2, p. 124: rosas,id. ib. 3, p. 140.

demosthenes.definition: ( Gen. i, Cic. Opt. Gen. 5, 14), m., Δημοσθένης, the most celebrated of the Grecian orators, Cic. de Or. 1, 13; 20; id. Brut. 9; Prop. 3 (4), 21, 27; Quint. 10, 1, 76; 12, 10, 23 sq.; Juv. 10, 114 et saep.—Hence Adj., Demosthenic: Demosthenicum, quod ter primum ille vocavit (i. e. action), Aus. Prof. 1, 19.

demoveo.definition: dē-mŏvĕo (often confounded in MSS. and edd. with di-moveo, q. v.), mōvi, mōtum, 2 V. a., to move or turn away; to put away, remove (freq. and good prose). Lit.: demoveri et depelli de loco necesse est eum qui deiciatur ... neminem statui detrusum, qui non adhibita vi manu demotus et actus praeceps intelligatur,Cic. Caecin. 17, 49: ex sua sede,id. Par. 1, 15; id. Leg. Agr. 2, 29, 81.—With abl. alone, id. Planc. 22, 53: hostes gradu,to compel to gi...

demoueo.definition: dē-mŏvĕo (often confounded in MSS. and edd. with di-moveo, q. v.), mōvi, mōtum, 2 V. a., to move or turn away; to put away, remove (freq. and good prose). Lit.: demoveri et depelli de loco necesse est eum qui deiciatur ... neminem statui detrusum, qui non adhibita vi manu demotus et actus praeceps intelligatur,Cic. Caecin. 17, 49: ex sua sede,id. Par. 1, 15; id. Leg. Agr. 2, 29, 81.—With abl. alone, id. Planc. 22, 53: hostes gradu,to compel to gi...

demulcatus.definition: dē-mulcātus, a, um, Part. [mulco] Beaten, cudgelled soundly: aliquis asperis verberibus,Mart. Cap. 8, § 807.

demulceo.definition: dē-mulcĕo, lsi, mulctum, 2 V. a., to stroke down, to stroke caressingly (rare). Prop.: caput tibi,Ter. Heaut. 4, 5, 14: dorsum,Liv. 9, 16 fin.: aures, Lact. de Ira, 7, 9: crura,Gell. 5, 14, 12. Trop., to soften, allure: aures omnium mentesque demulsit,Gell. 16, 19, 6; cf.: ita motus et demulctus et captus est, ut, etc.,id. 3, 13 fin.: eum,id. 18, 2, 1.

demum.definition: dēmum (also demus, like prorsus, quorsus, rursus, deorsus, Liv. Andr. ap. Paul. ex Fest. p. 70, 8 Müll.; Plaut. Trin. 3, 3, 51 Ritschl and Brix), a sup. form from de, downmost; cf.: sub, summus, used to give prominence to an idea in opposition to or restriction of another At length, at last, not till then; just, precisely; only, etc. In Latin of every period and description of writing (for syn. cf.: tandem, denique, postremum, primo). In postAug....

demuneror.definition: dē-mūneror, āri, 1 V. dep., to fee, reward: demunerarier ancillas,Ter. Heaut. 2, 3, 59 (dub. Umpf. and Fleck. munerarier).

demussatus.definition: dē-mussātus, a, um, Part. [musso] Borne silently (post-class. and rare): contumelia, Ap. M. 3, p. 140, 26: injuriis omnibus demussatis,Amm. 30, 1, 15.

demutabilis.definition: dēmūtābĭlis, e, demuto Changeable (eccl. Lat.), Prud. Apoth. 344; Tert. Anim. 2, 1.

demutator.definition: id. A changer, transmuter: ossium, Tert. Res. carn. 32.

demuto.definition: dē-mūto, āvi, ātum, 1, and n. Act., to change, alter, and sometimes to alter for the worse, to make worse (repeatedly in Plaut. and in post-Aug. prose; otherwise rare; not in the Ciceronian period): voces demutat, Cato ap. Macr. S. 2, 10 med.; cf.: orationem meam,Plaut. Mil. 4, 7, 8: imperium tuum,id. Men. 5, 2, 118: sententiam nostram in iis,Gell. 17, 1, 6: caro demutata, Tert. Res. carn. 55 al.: placitum instituto flaminum nihil demutari,Tac. A...

demuttio.definition: dē-muttĭo, īre V. n., to speak very softly, Isid. 10, 76.

denarismus.definition: denarius A sort of tax, Cod. Theod. 12, 1, 107 and 123.

denarius.definition: dēnārĭus, a, um, deni Containing ten. In gen.: numerus digitorum,Vitr. 3, 1: fistula,ten inches in circumference,Plin. 31, 6, 31, § 58; Vitr. 8, 7: DENARIAE caerimoniae dicebantur et TRICENARIAE, quibus sacra adituris decem continuis rebus vel triginta certis quibusdam rebus carendum erat, Paul. ex Fest. p. 71, 10.— Freq. Esp. nummus, or absol., de-narius, ii, m. (gen. plur., denarium, Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 55; id. Off. 3, 23 fin.; cf. Varr. L. L. 8, ...

denarro.definition: dē-narro, āre V. a., to tell, relate, recount, narrate (very rare; in the class. per. only once in Hor.): haec adeo ego illi jam denarrabo,Ter. Ph. 5, 7, 51: matri denarrat, ut, etc.,Hor. S. 2, 3, 315: puer, quid ipse matri dixisset, rem sicuti fuerat denarrat,Gell. 1, 23, 12.

denascor.definition: dē-nascor, nasci V. dep., to perish, die (ante-class. and rare), opp. nasci, Varr. L. L. 5, § 70 Müll.; 21; Cass. Hem. ap. Non. 101, 29 ( = decrescere, Non.).

dendrophorus.definition: (tree-bearer). An epithet of Sylvanus: SILVANO DENDROPHORO SACRVM,Inscr. Orell. 1602.—Hence A college of priests who carried about branches of trees in procession, in honor of a divinity, Inscr. Orell. 1602; 2385; 3741; Cod. Th. 16, 10, 20, § 2. A carpenter, Cod. Th. 14, 8, 1; Inscr. Grut. 45, 8.

denego.definition: dē-nĕgo, āvi, ātum, 1 To deny a thing, to say it is not so (very rare): datum denegant, quod datum est,Plaut. Men. 4, 2, 12: objecta,Tac. A. 15, 57.—Far more freq. and class. (cf., on the contrary, abnego). To reject, refuse, deny a request, entreaty, etc. (for syn. cf.: nego, infitias eo, infitior, diffiteor, recuso, abnuo, renuo, detrecto).

denicalis.definition: dē-nĭcālis (in MSS. also written denec-), e, nex Purifying from death; feriae or dies, a funeral solemnity among the Romans for the purification of the family of the deceased: nec vero tam denicales, quae a nece appellatae sunt, quia resident mortui, quam ceterorum celestium quieti dies feriae nominarentur, nisi, etc,Cic. Leg. 2, 22, 55; Cinc. ap. Gell. 16, 4, 4; Col. 2, 22, 5; Paul. ex Fest. p. 70, 9, and Fest. p. 242, 29 Müll. (v. Wordsworth Fr...

denigro.definition: dē-nīgro, āre V. a., to blacken utterly, dye or color very black (very rare; in the Ciceron. per. not at all). Lit.: terram (amurca),Varr. R. R. 1, 55 fin.: lanam,Plin. 33, 6, 35, § 109: capillum,id. 23, 5, 53, § 99: faciem super carbones,Vulg. Thren. 4, 8.— * Trop.: honorem famamque alicujus, to blacken, i. e. to asperse, defame, Firm. 5, 10 fin.

denique.definition: dēnĭquē, etym. dub.; perh. dēnĭ, locative of de, and que. Orig. denoting succession in time, and thereupon, and then, in the sequel. Transf., in enumerations.

denominatio.definition: denomino, rhetor. t. t. The substitution of the name of an object for that of another to which it has some relation, as the name of the cause for that of the effect, of the property for that of the substance, etc.; a metonymy, Auct. Her. 4, 32; cf. Quint. 8, 6, 23 sq., and immutatio.

denominativus.definition: dēnōmĭnātīvus, a, um Adj., pertaining to derivation, formed by derivation, derived: nomina,Prisc. p. 619 P.— Adv.: dēnōmĭnātīvē, by derivation: dicere aliquid,Mart. Cap. 4, § 381.

denominatiuus.definition: dēnōmĭnātīvus, a, um Adj., pertaining to derivation, formed by derivation, derived: nomina,Prisc. p. 619 P.— Adv.: dēnōmĭnātīvē, by derivation: dicere aliquid,Mart. Cap. 4, § 381.

denomino.definition: dē-nōmĭno, āvi, ātum, 1 V. a., to name, to designate specifically, to denominate (not ante-Aug.; most freq. in Quint.): hinc (sc. ab Lamo) Lamiae denominati, * Hor. Od. 3, 17, 3; cf. Auct. Her. 4, 32; Quint. 1, 5, 71: multa sunt et Graece et Latine non denominata,id. 8, 2, 4: etiam in iis, quae denominata sunt (opp. res plurimae carent appellationibus),id. 12, 10, 34: de re denominata (opp. de communi appellatione),id. 3, 6, 41; Gell. 2, 26, 6; 3...

denotatus.definition: id. A marking or pointing out; only denotatui, Tert. Pall. 4 med.

denoto.definition: dē-nŏto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. Lit., to mark, set a mark on, with chalk, color, etc.: pedes venalium creta,Plin. 35, 17, 58, § 199: lineam conspicuo colore,Col. 3, 15. Transf. Trop., to stigmatize, scandalize, brand with reproach or infamy: mollem et effeminatum omni probro,Suet. Cal. 56 fin.: turpia legata, quae denotandi legatarii gratia scribuntur,Dig. 30, 54 init.: qui gaudet iniquitate denotabitur,Vulg. Sir. 19, 5 sq.—Hence, P. a., dēnŏtātus, ...

dens.definition: ( Gen. plur. usually dentium, but dentum is approved by Varr. L. L. 7, 38, 67), m. root in Sanscr. dantas, Gr. ὀδούς, Goth. tunthus, Germ. Zahn, and Engl. tooth; cf. edo, Engl. eat, a tooth. Prop.: cui auro dentes juncti escunt, XII. Tab. 10, 9; Plin. 11, 37, 61, § 160 sq.; Cels. 8, 1; Cic. N. D. 2, 54; Isid. 11, 1, 52: primores,the front teeth,Plin. 7, 16, 15, § 68; also called adversi acuti,Cic. N. D. 2, 54: praecisores,Isid. 11, 1, 52; and i...

densabilis.definition: densābĭlis, e, denso Binding, astringent (late Lat.): cibus,Cael. Aur. Tard. 5, 7: vaporatio,ib. 3, 3.

densativus.definition: densātīvus, a, um, id. Binding, astringent (late Lat.): virtutis esse,Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 37.

densatiuus.definition: densātīvus, a, um, id. Binding, astringent (late Lat.): virtutis esse,Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 37.

dense.definition: densē Adv., thickly, frequently, etc. v. densus fin.

densitas.definition: densus Thickness, density (perh. not ante-Aug.). Lit.: limus spissatur et in densitatem coit,Plin. 35, 15, 51, § 178: chartae,id. 13, 12, 24, § 78: umoris,id. 11, 3, 2, § 6; Vulg. Isa. 9, 18 al. Trop.: sententiarum,Quint. 8, 5, 26: figurarum,id. 9, 2, 72.

denso.definition: denso, āvi, ātum, 1, and (less freq.) denseo, no Perf., ētum, 2 (cf. Prisc. p. 837 P.; Charis. p. 233 ib. The MSS. often confound the two forms; densare appears to be critically certain in Liv. and Quint.; densere act. only denset, Verg. A. 11, 650; imp. densete, id. ib. 12, 264: densebant,Lucr. 5, 491: denserent,Tac. A. 2, 14; also active forms, Apul. Mund. p. 61, 13; Prud. Cath. 5, 53 al.; Sil. 4, 159; gerund, densendo,Lucr. 6, 482; pass. inf. ...

densus.definition: densus, a, um, kindred with δασύς, δαυλός (i. e. δασυλός); cf. Lat. dumus, old form dusmus, and dumetum Thick, dense, i. e. consisting of parts crowded together. opp. to rarus (on the contrary, crassus, thick, is opp. to thin, fluid; and spissus, close, compact, with the predominant idea of impenetrability; cf. also: angustus, artus, solidus—class. and freq., esp. in poets and historians; in Cic. very rare). Lit. Trop. of speech, condensed, co...

dentale.definition: and , (only the Plural class.; sing. post-class.), n. dens, no. I. B., the share-beam, to which the vomer or ploughshare was attached. Prop., plur., Verg. G. 1, 172; Col. 2, 2, 24.—Sing.: genus vomerum toto porrectum dentali,Plin. 18, 18, 48, § 171.—* Meton.: sulco terens dentalia,a ploughshare,Pers. 1, 73.

dentaneus.definition: dentānĕus, a, um Adj., threatening: dentanea (fulgura) quae speciem periculi sine periculo adferunt,Sen. N. Q. 2, 49, 1 fin.

dentarius.definition: dentārĭus, a, um, dens Pertaining to the teeth (in the later medic. lang.): herba, i. e. that cures the toothache, Ap. Herb. 4, 8, 66.

dentarpaga.definition: vox hibr. from dens and ἅρπαξ An instrument for drawing teeth, Varr. ap. Non. 99, 24.

dentatus.definition: dentātus, a, um, dens. Toothed, having teeth. Charta, polished with a tooth, Cic. Q. Fr. 2, 15, 6; cf. Plin. 13, 12, 25, § 81.

denticulatus.definition: dentĭcŭlātus, a, um, denticulus Furnished with small teeth, denticulated (post-Aug.): falces,Col. 2, 20, 3: forfices,Plin. 9, 31, 51, § 97: conchae,id. 9, 33, 52, § 102: olus,id. 26, 15, 93, § 164.

denticulus.definition: dim.dens A little tooth (not ante-Aug.). Lit., Pall. 1, 28, 6; Ap. Mag. p. 278, 9. Meton.

dentiducum.definition: (sc. instrumentum) [dens-duco] An instrument for drawing teeth, as transl. of the Gr. ὀδονταγωγόν, Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 4 fin. (in Varro, dentarpaga q. v.).

dentifricium.definition: dens - frico Tooth-powder, dentifrice, Plin. 28, 11, 49, § 178 sq.; 29, 3, 11, § 46 al.; Scrib. Comp. 59 et saep.

dentio.definition: dentĭo, īre, dens To get or cut teeth, to teeth. Prop.: propria dentientium,Cels. 2, 1 med.: pueros tarde dentientis,Plin. 30, 3, 8, § 22; cf. id. 21, 20, 83, § 140 al.: auribus perhauriunda haec sunt, ne dentes dentiant (the words of a parasite who fears to have nothing for his teeth to chew upon),lest the teeth grow,Plaut. Mil. 1, 1, 34 Lorenz ad loc.

denubo.definition: dē-nūbo, psi, ptum, 3 V. n., to marry off (sc. from the paternal home; cf. deduco), to marry (rare; perhaps not ante-Aug.). Prop.: nec Caenis in ullos Denupsit thalamos,Ov. M. 12, 196; Ap. M. 9, p. 231, 29; 5, p. 166, 6: Claro fratri denupta,id. Mag. p. 319, 6. Transf.: plantis, Col. poët. 10, 158.

denudatio.definition: A laying bare, uncovering, Vulg. Sir. 11. 29. From

denudo.definition: dē-nūdo, āvi, ātum, 1 V. a., to lay bare, make naked, denude. I. q., nudo, to uncover (rare but class.). I. q., spolio, to strip, plunder. *

denuntiatio.definition: (), , denuntio An indication, intimation, announcement, declaration.

denuntiativus.definition: dēnuntĭātīvus, a, um, id. Monitory, indicatory, Cael. Aur. Tard. 1, 4, 67.

denuntiatiuus.definition: dēnuntĭātīvus, a, um, id. Monitory, indicatory, Cael. Aur. Tard. 1, 4, 67.

denuntio.definition: dē-nuntĭo (-cĭo), āvi, ātum, 1, Orig. t. t. in the lang. of pub. law, relig., and jurispr. To give an official intimation, to make an official announcement or declaration of one's intentions (by means of a messenger, herald, etc.); to announce, intimate, declare, = nuntiando declarare; and with a foll. ut or merely the subjunctive, to intimate, order, command (for syn. cf.: edico, indico, narro, nuntio, refero, defero, renuntio, enuntio, dico). P...

denuo.definition: dēnŭō, contr. from dē nŏvo, which never occurs; v. Ruhnk. Ter. And. prol. 26; Oud. App. M. 3, p. 225.; cf.: Fr. de nouveau Anew, afresh, again (most freq. in Plaut. and Ter.; elsewh. rare; not in Caes. or the Aug. poets—for syn. cf.: iterum, rursus, ab integro). Of the restoration of a thing which has been destroyed, = de integro, anew, afresh, ἐκ καινῆς: aedificantur aedes totae denuo,Plaut. Most. 1, 2, 36; cf.: urbes terrae motu subversas den...

deorsum.definition: dĕorsum (dissyll. Per synaeresin, Lucr. 1, 362; 2, 205 al.; cf., on the contrary, trisyll.,id. 2, 202.—Also deorsus, like prorsus, quorsus, rursus, adversus, Cic. N. D. 1, 25, 69; Ap. M. 8, p. 207, 18; id. ib. 9, p. 236, 40; id. de Deo Socr. p. 47, 35; id. Flor. no. 15), contr. from devorsum, turned down, downwards, κάτω, opp. to sursum (class.). To indicate motion: ego me deorsum duco de arbore, Plaut. Aul. 4, 8, 8: deorsum cuncta feruntur (opp...

deosculor.definition: dĕ-oscŭlor, ātus, 1 V. dep. a., to kiss warmly, affectionately (very rare). Prop.: vix reprimo labra, Ob istam rem quin te deosculer, etc.,Plaut. Cas. 2, 8, 17 sq.: Casinam,id. ib. 31: tuos oculos,id. ib. 1, 1, 48: Scipionis dexteram,Val. Max. 2, 10, 2; Vulg. 1 Reg. 10, 1; id. Cant. 8, 1.— * Transf., to praise, laud highly: fidem atque ingenium pueri,Gell. 1, 23, 13.!*? Deosculatus in pass. sense: rursum me deosculato, Ap. M. 2, p. 119; 121.

depalator.definition: id. One who marks out the bounds; hence, trop., a founder: disciplinae divinae (coupled with architectus),Tert. adv. Marc. 5, 6.

depalo.definition: dē-pālo, āvi, ātum, 1 V. a., to mark off or bound with palings (late Lat.). Prop.: jugera agri..ita uti depalatum est,Inscr. Orell. 3688. Transf., to found, establish: quodammodo mundum,Tert. adv. Herm. 29: civitatem,id. Apol. 10; cf. depalator.

depango.definition: dē-pango, no Perf., pactum, 3, v. a., to drive down, drive in, fix into the ground (rare). Lit.: malleolum,Col. 3, 16, 1; cf. id. 3, 21, 11; Plin. 16, 26, 46, § 110: quercus et olea in scrobe depactae,id. 24, 1, 1, § 1: in terram depacta,id. 2, 96, 98, § 211. —* Trop.: vitae depactus terminus alte tam manet, etc.,Lucr. 2, 1087.

depasco.definition: dē-pasco, pāvi, pastum, 3, , and dē-pascor, ci, 3 V. depon., to feed down, feed off. Lit. Trop.

depavitus.definition: dē-păvītus, a, um, Part. [pavio] Beaten down, trampled down, trop., Sol. 2.

depauitus.definition: dē-păvītus, a, um, Part. [pavio] Beaten down, trampled down, trop., Sol. 2.

depeciscor.definition: dēpĕciscor, -pectus, or dēpăciscor, pactus, 3 V. dep. a. [de-paciscor], to bargain for, agree upon; and absol., to make an agreement. Lit. (repeatedly in Cic., elsewh. rare): ipse tria praedia sibi depectus est,Cic. Rosc. Am. 39 fin.: cum illo partem suam depecisci,id. ib. 38, 110: aliquid cum aliquo,id. ib. 38, 110; cf.: depectus est cum eis, ut arma et impedimenta relinqueret,id. Inv. 2, 24, 72: ad condiciones alicujus,Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 24 fin. ...

depectio.definition: depeciscor A bargain, contract, agreement (late Lat.), Cod. Theod. 2, 10, 1.

depecto.definition: dē-pecto, no Perf., xum, ĕre, v. a., to comb off, comb down, to comb (very rare): crines buxo,Ov. F. 6, 229; cf. jubas,id. A. A. 1, 630: Liber depexus crinibus,id. F. 3, 465: ars depectendi digerendique lini,Plin. 19, 1, 3, § 18: vellera foliis,Verg. G. 2, 121; cf. Plin. 12, 14, 32, § 58; 6, 17, 20, § 54.— Jocosely, i. q. to curry one's hide, i. e. give him a beating, Ter. Heaut. 5, 1, 78; cf.: fusti pectito,Plaut. Capt. 4, 2, 116.

depeculator.definition: depeculor A plunderer, embezzler: aerarii,Cic. Verr. 1, 1, 2; id. de Or. 3, 27, 106; id. Pis. 40, 96.

depeculor.definition: dē-pĕcūlor, ātus (and old Act. fut. infin. depeculassere, Lucil. ap. Non. 97, 9; cf. Neue, Form. 2, 421, and v.infra), 1, v. dep. a. [peculium], to despoil, pillage, rifle, plunder, embezzle (very rare). Prop.: Apollonium omni argento spoliasti ac depeculatus es,Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 17. Trop.: laudem honoremque alicujus,i. e. to detract from, diminish,Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 36.!*? In pass. signif.: ubi senatus intellexit populum depeculari (ἀποσυλοῦσθαι)...

depello.definition: dē-pello, pŭli, pulsum, 3 V. a., to drive out, drive away, remove, expel; to drive, thrust, or cast down (class. and very freq.). Lit. Trop., to deter, divert, dissuade from: aliquem de suscepta causa propositaque sententia,Cic. Lig. 9; id. Fam. 1, 7, 7; for which, aliquem sententiā,id. Tusc. 2, 6, 16; Liv. 23, 8: aliquem de spe conatuque,Cic. Cat. 2, 7, § 14; for which, aliquem spe,Liv. 31, 25, 11; 41, 23, 13: te ex illa crudeli actione meo cons...

dependeo.definition: dē-pendĕo, ēre V. a., to hang from or on, to hang down (not freq. till the Aug. period; not in Cic. and Caes.—for syn. cf.: pendeo, impendeo). Lit.: (anellus) unus ex uno,Lucr. 6, 915; cf.: sordidus ex umeris nodo dependet amictus,Verg. A. 6, 301: dependente a cervicibus pugione,Suet. Galb. 11: dependent lychni laquearibus aureis,Verg. A. 1, 726: galea ramis,id. ib. 10, 836: parma laevo lacerto,id. ib. 11, 693: hasta umero,Quint. 11, 3, 130: sert...

dependo.definition: dē-pendo, di, sum, 3, and n. Act. (orig., to weigh out; hence), to pay (rare but class.). Transf., to spend, expend, lay out, bestow upon a thing (postAug.): plus in operis servorum avocandis quam in pretio rerum hujusmodi dependitur,Col. 11, 1, 20; incassum impenditur opera,id. 4, 22, 7: tempora Niliaco amori,Luc. 10, 80; cf.: caput felicibus armis,to give up, abandon,id. 8, 101.

depennatus.definition: dē-pennātus, a, um, penna Winged, trop.: depennato orationis eloquio, Varr. ap. Fulg. 561, 12.

depensio.definition: dependo The expenditure, outlay: theatralis,Cod. Theod. 6, 4, 29; lustralis auri,ib. 13, 1, 11.

deperdo.definition: dē-perdo, dĭdi, dĭtum, 3 V a. To destroy, ruin (so only in the part. perf., and rare): sator inopia deperditus,i. e. impoverished,Phaedr. 1, 14, 1: ut est deperditus Io,i. e. desperately in love,Prop. 2, 30, 29 (3, 28, 29 M.); cf. amore,Suet. Dom. 3: deperditum intelligitur, quod in rerum natura esse desiit,Gai. Dig. 5, 3, 21.—More freq. and class. To lose: qui non solum bona sed etiam honestatem miseri deperdiderunt,Cic. Prov. Cons. 5, 11: nihil...

depetigo.definition: petigo A leprosy, scab, spread over the whole body (v. de, no. II. 2. c.), Cato R. R. 157 fin.; cf.: scabies deque petigo, Lucil. ap. Non. 160, 18.

depictio.definition: depingo A description, delineation, Boeth. Geom. 1, p. 1210 al. Rhet. t. t., a characterization, = characterismus, Auct. Carm. de Fig. 148, p. 68 Halm.

depilis.definition: dē-pĭlis, e, 1. pilus Without hair (very rare): genae, Ap. M. 7, p. 191: pueri (with glabri), Varr. ap. Non. 530, 25.

depilo.definition: dē-pĭlo, no Perf., ātum, 1, id., to pull out the hair, pluck out the feathers. Prop. (ante-class. and post-Aug., and rare): depilari magis quam amiciri,Tert. Pall. 4: perdicem,Apic. 6, 3; Mart. 9, 28: struthiocamelum,Sen. Cons. Sap. 17: amygdalae,Apic. 2, 2. Transf., dēpĭlātus, plucked, i. e. plundered, cheated, Lucil. ap. Non. 36, 28.

depingo.definition: dē-pingo, pinxi, pictum, 3 ( Perf. syncop. depinxti, Plaut. Poen. 5, 2, 154) To depict, portray, paint, draw, represent by painting (rare but class.). To embroider: depictas gemmatasque indutus paenulas,Suet. Calig. 52: auro depicta chlamys,Val. Fl. 6, 226.

depinnatus.definition: dē-pinnātus, a, um Adj., feathered, winged, only trop.: orationis eloquium,Varr. Sat. Menip. 58, 1.

deplaco.definition: dē-plāco, āvi, ātum, 1 V. a., to appease, propitiate: aliquem sibi hostiis, Mythogr. Vatic. 1, 231, p. 71 ed. Bod.; Fulg. Myth. 3, 6 dub.

deplango.definition: dē-plango, nxi, 3 V. a., to express grief by beating the breast; to bewail, lament (poet. and very rare): Cadmeida palmis Deplanxere domum,Ov. M. 4, 546; 14, 580; Sen. Herc. Oet. 1852: antiqua peccata,Hier. Jes. 1, 1, 1.

deplano.definition: dē-plāno, āvi, ātum, 1 V. a., to level off, to make level or even (post-class.): montes,Lact. 4, 12, 18: vulnus,Veg. A. V. 3. 19.

deplanto.definition: dē-planto, āvi, ātum, 1 To take off a twig or shoot. = demitto, to set in the ground, to plant, Plin. 17, 16, 26, § 121; 17, 20, 33, § 146; cf. Voss. ad Verg. G. 2, 65.

depleo.definition: dē-plĕo, ēvi, 2 V. a., to empty out, to draw off (very rare): oleum,Cato R. R. 64 fin.; Col. 12, 50, 8, and 10: sanguinem,to let blood, to bleed,Plin. 18, 16, 43, § 148; for which, d. animal,Veg. A. V. 1, 13, 4.— Poet., to exhaust, haustu fontes, Stat. Ach. 1, 8: vitam querelis,Manil. 4, 13.

deplexus.definition: dē-plexus, a, um, plector Clasping, grasping any thing, Lucr. 5, 1321.

deploro.definition: dē-plōro, āvi, ātum, and A. Neutr., to weep bitterly, to moan, wail, lament, complain. Act., to weep for bitterly, bewail, lament, deplore.

depluo.definition: dē-plŭo, ŭi, ūtum, ĕre V. n., to rain down (poet. and very rare): multus in terras deplueretque lapis,Tib. 2, 5, 72; (in Prop. 2, 20, 8 (3, 13, 8 M.), the true reading is defluit; so Col. 10, 206 poet.): depluta terra, drenched, Boëth. Arist. analyt. post. 2, 13.

depolio.definition: dē-pŏlĭo, no Perf., ītum, 4, v. a., to smooth off, polish off (very rare). Prop.: aliquid cote,Plin. 36, 25, 63, § 188. —Comic.: dorsum meum virgis,to cudgel,Plaut. Ep. 1, 1, 85. Trop.: DEPOLITUM perfectum, quia omnes perfectiones antiqui politiones appellabant, Paul. ex Fest. p. 71, 20 Müll.; cf. the foll. art.

depompatio.definition: depompo. Lit., a depriving of ornament; hence A dishonoring: Christianorum,Hier. adv. Rufin. 31.

depompo.definition: dē-pompo, āre, Lit., to deprive of ornament; hence To dishonor, Hier. in Nahum. c. 3.

depondero.definition: dē-pondĕro, āre V. n., to press down by its weight, to weigh down, Petr. Fragm. 26, 3.

deponens.definition: dēpōnens, entis V.the foll. art. fin.

depono.definition: dē-pōno, pŏsŭi, pŏsĭtum, 3 ( Perf. deposivi, Plaut. Curc. 4, 3, 4: deposivit,id. Most. 2, 1, 35; Catull. 34, 8; inf. perf. deposisse, Verg. Cat. 8, 16; part. sync. depostus, Lucil. ap. Non. 279, 19, v. pono), v. a., to lay away, to put or place aside; to lay, put, or set down; to lay, place, set, deposit (freq. in all periods and sorts of writing).—Constr. with acc. alone; or acc. and locative or abl. with or without a prep.; or acc. and adv. of ...

depopulator.definition: id. One who lays waste, a marauder, spoiler, pillager: fori,Cic. Dom. 5, 13; Caecil. ap. Non. 118, 33 (v. 191 Rib.); Vulg. Isa. 21, 2.

depopulatrix.definition: depopulator She who spoils, destroys: generis humani (luxuries),Cassiod. Var. 11, 3 med.

depopulo.definition: dēpŏpŭlo, āre, v. the follg. Fin.

depopulor.definition: dē-pŏpŭlor, ātus, 1 V. dep. a., to lay waste, ravage, plunder, pillage (class.). Prop.: ut Ambiorigis fines depopularentur,Caes. B. G. 6, 42 fin.; cf.: ad fines depopulandos,id. ib. 7, 64, 6; Hirt. B. G. 8, 24, 4; Liv. 10, 12 al.: agros,Caes. B. G. 2, 7, 3; Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 36; Liv. 5, 4 fin. et saep.; cf.: extrema agri Romani,Liv. 4, 1: eam regionem,Caes. B. G. 6, 33, 2: vicinam humum late,Ov. Tr. 3, 10, 56 et saep.: multas domos, plurimas urbes...

deportatio.definition: deporto (rare) A carrying or conveying away, a transportation. In gen., Cato R. R. 144, 3. In partic., a perpetual banishment, transportation, deportation, exile, Dig. 48, 13, 3; 48, 22, 6 al.; cf. deporto, no. II. B.

deportatorius.definition: dēportātōrĭus, a, um, id. Belonging to removal or transportation: personale vel deportatorium onus, Cod. 12, 47, 1.

deporto.definition: dē-porto, āvi, ātum, 1 ( Arch. inf. pass. deportarier, Ter. Ph. 5, 7, 85), v. a., to carry or convey down; to carry off, to convey away (freq. and good prose). In gen.: de fundo tigna et oleam ne deportato,Cato R. R. 144, 3: arma Brundisium jumentis, Pomp. ap. Cic. Att. 8, 12 A. fin.: frumentum in castra. Caes. B. C. 1, 60, 3: ossa ejus in Cappadociam ad matrem,Nep. Eum. 13 fin.: corpus Augusti Romam,Suet. Claud. 6; cf. id. Aug. 100: aliquem per ...

deposco.definition: dē-posco, pŏposci, 3 V. a., to demand, require, request earnestly (freq. and class.). In gen.: unum ab omnibus sociis et civibus ad id bellum imperatorem deposci atque expeti,Cic. de Imp. Pomp. 2, 5; cf. id. 15, 44: id non modo non recusem, sed etiam appetam atque deposcam,id. Phil. 3, 13, 33; so opp. recusare,id. Fl. 38 fin.: sibi naves,Caes. B. C. 1, 56, 3: pugnam,Suet. Oth. 9; Front. Strat. 1, 11, 1; 2, 1, 3: pericula (opp. detrectare),Tac. Ag...

depositarius.definition: depono, no. I. B.; prop. pertaining to a deposit; hence, in jurid. Lat. One who receives a deposit, a trustee, depositary, Dig. 16, 3, 1, § 36; 16, 3, 7, § 2 (twice). One who makes a deposit, a depositor, Dig. 16, 3, 7 fin.

depositio.definition: depono (post-Aug.; most freq. in jurid. Lat.). Lit., a laying down, putting off. Trop.

depositivus.definition: dēpŏsĭtīvus, a, um, id. Of or belonging to a deposit: pecuniae,given in deposit,Cassiod. Var. 6, 8.

depositiuus.definition: dēpŏsĭtīvus, a, um, id. Of or belonging to a deposit: pecuniae,given in deposit,Cassiod. Var. 6, 8.

depositor.definition: id. (post-Aug. and very rare). One who deposits a thing for safe-keeping, a depositor, Dig. 16, 3, 1, § 37. One who disowns or disclaims: patris natique,Prud. Apoth. 179.

depositum.definition: dēpŏsĭtum, v. depono P. a. fin.

depositus.definition: dēpŏsĭtus, a, um, Part., from depono.

depostulator.definition: depostulo One who demands a person, sc. for punishment, torture, etc.: Christianorum,Tert. Apol. 35; cf. ib. 50 fin.

depraedatio.definition: depraedor A plundering (late Lat.), Cod. 2, 6, 5; Lact. Epit. 11; Vulg. Judith, 10, 12.

depraedator.definition: id. A plunderer (late Lat.), Aug. Ep. 199.

depraedor.definition: dē-praedor, ātus, 1 V. dep. a. (act. collat. form depraedaverunt, Ambros. de Fide, 2, 3), to plunder, pillage, ravage (postclass.; for praedor, depopulor): agros,Just. 24, 6, 3; Ap. M. 8, p. 215; Vulg. Job, 24, 9; id. Isa. 33, 1.—In pass. signif.: agri, depraedati, Dict. Cretens. 2, 16 Deder. N. cr.

deprandis.definition: dē-prandis, e, prandeo Fasting: leo, Naev. ap. Fest. p. 182, 24 Müll.

depravatio.definition: depravo A perverting, distorting, corrupting, vitiating (freq. in Cic.; elsewh. rare). Lit.: distortio et depravatio quaedam (membrorum),Cic. Fin. 5, 12, 35; cf.: pedum, manuum, articulorum omnium depravationes,Sen. Ep. 24 med.: oris,Cic. de Or. 2, 62, 252. Trop.: depravatio et foeditas animi (c. c. deformitas corporis),Cic. Off. 3, 29, 105: verbi,id. Part. Or. 36, 127: consuetudinum,id. Leg. 1, 10, 29.—Absol.: nostra (c. c. superstitio),perversi...

deprauatio.definition: depravo A perverting, distorting, corrupting, vitiating (freq. in Cic.; elsewh. rare). Lit.: distortio et depravatio quaedam (membrorum),Cic. Fin. 5, 12, 35; cf.: pedum, manuum, articulorum omnium depravationes,Sen. Ep. 24 med.: oris,Cic. de Or. 2, 62, 252. Trop.: depravatio et foeditas animi (c. c. deformitas corporis),Cic. Off. 3, 29, 105: verbi,id. Part. Or. 36, 127: consuetudinum,id. Leg. 1, 10, 29.—Absol.: nostra (c. c. superstitio),perversi...

depravo.definition: dē-prāvo, āvi, ātum, 1, pravus To pervert, distort, disfigure (opp. dirigere, corrigere; good prose). Lit.: depravata corrigere crura,Varr. L. L. 9, § 11 Müll.; cf. opp. corrigere,Cic. Fin. 1, 6; id. Div. 2, 46: (oculi) uni animalium homini depravantur, unde cognomina Strabonum et Paetorum,Plin. 11, 37, 55, § 150. Trop., to pervert, seduce, corrupt, deprave (for syn. cf.: corrumpo, vitio, adultero, perdo, pessum do, illicere, pellicere, adducere)...

deprauo.definition: dē-prāvo, āvi, ātum, 1, pravus To pervert, distort, disfigure (opp. dirigere, corrigere; good prose). Lit.: depravata corrigere crura,Varr. L. L. 9, § 11 Müll.; cf. opp. corrigere,Cic. Fin. 1, 6; id. Div. 2, 46: (oculi) uni animalium homini depravantur, unde cognomina Strabonum et Paetorum,Plin. 11, 37, 55, § 150. Trop., to pervert, seduce, corrupt, deprave (for syn. cf.: corrumpo, vitio, adultero, perdo, pessum do, illicere, pellicere, adducere)...

deprecabilis.definition: dēprĕcābĭlis, e, deprecor Thatmay be entreated, exorable (eccl. Lat.), Vulg. Psa. 90, 13.

deprecaneus.definition: dēprĕcānĕus, a, um, id. Exorable: fulmina, quae speciem periculi sine periculo afferunt, Caecinna ap. Sen. Q. N. 2, 49 (dub.—al. dentanea).

deprecatio.definition: id. A warding off or averting by prayer; a deprecating, deprecation. Prop. Transf., a prayer for pardon, deprecation: ejus facti,Cic. Part. Or. 37 fin.; cf. inertiae,Hirt. B. G. 8 prooem. § 1; Plaut. Capt. 3, 3, 7: assidua,Vulg. Jacob. 5, 16.—So in rhetoric, like the Gr. προπαραίτησις or συγγνώμη, Cic. Inv. 2, 34; id. de Or. 3, 53 fin.; Auct. Her. 1, 14; Quint. 9, 1, 32 al.

deprecatiuncula.definition: dim.deprecatio A little deprecation, a trifling plea for pardon, Salv. adv. Avar. 3, 2.

deprecativus.definition: dēprĕcātīvus, a, um, deprecor Deprecative: qualitas,Mart. Cap. 5, § 457: venia,Fortun. Art. Rhet. 1, 16: sententiae,Isid. 2, 21, 18.

deprecatiuus.definition: dēprĕcātīvus, a, um, deprecor Deprecative: qualitas,Mart. Cap. 5, § 457: venia,Fortun. Art. Rhet. 1, 16: sententiae,Isid. 2, 21, 18.

deprecator.definition: id. One who averts by praying; an interceder, intercessor: hujus periculi,Cic. Balb. 18: miseriarum,id. Fl. 1: causae suae,Tac. H. 3, 31: non solum sui deprecator, sed etiam accusator mei,Cic. Att. 11, 8, 2; for which: ego apud consulem deprecator defensorque vobis adero,Liv. 36, 35: fortunarum alicujus,Cic. Planc. 42, 102; cf.: salutis meae,id. Sest. 12, 27: deprecatorem me pro illius periculo praebeo,id. Fam. 2, 13, 2: legatos deprecatoresque a...

deprecatorius.definition: dēprĕcātōrĭus, a, um, deprecator Deprecatory: verba,Vulg. 1 Macc. 10, 24.

deprecatrix.definition: deprecator A female intercessor (late Lat.), Tert. adv. Marc. 4, 12.

depreciator.definition: dēprĕcĭātor and dēprĕcĭo, v. depretiator and depretio.

deprecor.definition: dē-prĕcor, ātus, 1 V. dep. a. To avert, ward off (from one's self or others) by earnest prayer; to deprecate; also to pray, to intercede for the averting of any evil, or to obtain pardon for any transgression (cf. Gell. 6, 16, 3). To pray for, intercede in behalf of (that which is in danger): vitam alicujus ab aliquo,Cic. Sull. 26; cf. vitam sibi, Auct. B. Afr. 89, 3; paucos dies exsolvendo donativo deprecatum,Tac. H. 1, 41: quos senatus non ad p...

deprehendo.definition: dē-prĕhendo or dēprendo (v. prehendo; cf. Quint. 9, 4, 59), di, sum, 3 To take or snatch away, esp. any thing which is in motion; to seize upon, catch (freq. and class.—For syn. cf.: invenio, reperio, nanciscor; offendo, aperio, patefacio, detego; incido, consequor, assequor, etc.). In a wider sense, to catch, overtake, surprise, apprehend, detect, find out, discover any one, esp. in doing any thing wrong.

deprehensio.definition: deprehendo, no. II. A catching, seizing, surprising; a discovery (very rare): deprehensione fieri manifestum furem,Dig. 47, 2, 7; cf. ib. 23, 2, 43, § 12: manifesta veneni, * Cic. Clu. 18, 50.

deprensa.definition: deprehendo A species of military punishment, more severe than castigatio, but milder than ignominia, Paul. ex Fest. p. 71, 15 Müll.

depressio.definition: deprimo A pressing or sinking down, a depression (not ante-Aug., and very rare), Macr. S. 1, 20: fundamentorum ad solidum,Vitr. 1, 3, 2: Socratica nasi, i. e. flat nose (opp. curva erectio), Macr. S. 7, 3, § 11.

depressus.definition: dēpressus, a, um, Part. and , from deprimo.

depretiator.definition: (), , depretio One who depreciates, a depreciator: operum,Tert. adv. Marc. 4, 29.

depretio.definition: dēprĕtĭo (deprec-), āvi, ātum, 1, pretium To lower the price of, to undervalue, to depreciate (post-class.). Prop.: vetera corpora depretiata sunt,Dig. 9, 2, 22; cf. Gai. Inst. 3, § 212: vilescit pretio depretiatus homo, Paul. Nol. carm. 22, 56. Trop. (eccl. Lat.), to disregard, make light of: Epicurus omnem dolorem depretiat,Tert. Apol. 45; Sid. Ep. 2, 10 fin.

deprimo.definition: dē-prĭmo, pressi, pressum, 3, v. a.premo To press down, weigh down, sink down, to depress (freq. and class.). Lit. Trop.

depromo.definition: dē-prōmo, prompsi (-msi), promptum (-mtum), 3 V. a., to draw out, draw forth; to bring, to fetch from anywhere, esp. out of any place (rare but class.).—Constr., usu. abl. w. ex or de of things, with a of persons; poet. and late Lat. with abl. alone, but domo depromere, Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 66, § 155. Lit.: pecuniam ex arca,Cic. Off. 2, 15; cf.: pecuniam ex aerario, id. de imp. Pomp. 13, 37, and v.infra, no. II.: tela pharetris,Verg. A. 5, 501; cf. 1...

depropero.definition: dē-prŏpĕro, āre, and A. Neutr., to make great haste, to hasten: cito introite, et cito deproperate,Plaut. Cas. 3, 6, 17. Act., to hasten or accelerate greatly, to prepare hastily (very rare): coronas, * Hor. Od. 2, 7, 24: miserabile humandi munus,Sil. 2, 265.—With inf. as object: sacruficare,Plaut. Poen. 1, 2, 108.

deproperus.definition: dē-prŏpĕrus, a, um, , = de-properans Making great haste, hastening, Cod. Th. 7, 1, 13 (cf. Cod. 12, 36, 12).

depso.definition: depso, sui, stum, 3, , = δεψέω, to Knead. Prop.: id ubi excoxeris, depsito bene,Cato, R. R. 90; cf. id. ib. 76: lu tum, id. ib. 40, 4: coria,to dress, to curry,id. ib. 135: tibi fortasse alius molit et depsit, Varr. ap. Non. 99, 14. Transf., in an obscene sense, to dishonor, acc. to Cic. Fam. 9, 22, 4.

depudesco.definition: dē-pŭdesco, ĕre V. inch. n., to become shameless (post-class. and rare): infamiā, Ap. M. 10, p. 253.—With gen.: non depudesco infelicitatis meae, am not ashamed, Hier. ad Eustoch.

depudico.definition: dē-pŭdīco, āre, pudicus To violate, dishonor: stupro, Laber. ap. Gell. 16, 7.

depugno.definition: dē-pugno, āvi, ātum, 1, and A. To fight eagerly, fight out; to contend, combat violently. To fight to the end, stop fighting: depugnato proelio, "the day after the fair," Plaut. Men. 5, 6, 31.

depulpo.definition: dēpulpo To grow lean, άποσαρκῶ, Gloss. Lat. Gr. [de-pulpa].

depulsio.definition: depello. A driving off, driving away, repelling, warding off. A lowering, sinking down of the eyes: luminum,Cic. Univ. 14, 42.

depulsor.definition: id. One who drives away, removes, repels (rare): dominatus, * Cic. Phil. 2, 11, 27: malorum,Lact. 2, 14, 13: alius vel servator honorum vel malorum depulsor, Boëth. Cons. Phil. 4, 6.—In inscriptions, an epithet of Jupiter, as the averter of evil (cf. Averruncus), Inscr. Orell. 2232 al.

depulsorius.definition: dēpulsōrĭus, a, um, id. Serving to avert, sc. evil: sacra,Plin. 28, 2, 3, § 11; Amm. 25, 2, 4.

depurgatio.definition: depurgo A cleansing by purgatives: ventris,Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 4; id. ib. 3, 21.

depurgo.definition: dē-purgo, no Perf., ātum, 1, v. a., to clean out, cleanse (rare): prata,Cato R. R. 50, 1: acina,id. ib. 112, 2: terram ab herba,id. 151: caules lactucae,Col. 12, 9, 1: sordes,id. 9, 14, 13: pisces,Plaut. Stich. 2, 2, 35. Esp. as med. t. t., to cleanse, clear, purge: eas partes ex quibus sputa feruntur,Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 18, 110; so absol.: aquae genus, quod potionibus depurgat,Vitr. 8, 3, 5.

deputo.definition: dē-pŭto, āvi, ātum, 1 In agriculture, to cut off, prune: vineam,Cato R. R. 49, 1; 50, 1: arbores,Col. 11, 2, 32: palmites falce,id. 4, 7, 1: malleolum,id. 3, 10, 19.—Poet.: umbras (i. e. ramos), Ov. de Nuce, 63. Ante- and post-class., to esteem, consider, count as; and alicui or ad aliquid, in late Lat., to destine, allot to any one or any thing: operam alicujus parvi preti,Ter. Hec. 5, 3, 1: cum iniquis deputari,to be classed among,Vulg. Luc. 22...

depuvio.definition: dē-pŭvĭo, īre, from pavio; cf. contubernium, from taberna To strike, beat: palmis misellam depuvit me, Lucil. ap. Paul. ex Fest. p. 70, 3 Müll.

depuuio.definition: dē-pŭvĭo, īre, from pavio; cf. contubernium, from taberna To strike, beat: palmis misellam depuvit me, Lucil. ap. Paul. ex Fest. p. 70, 3 Müll.

dequestus.definition: dē-questus, a, um, Part. [queror] Having deeply deplored, bitterly complained of (in post-Aug. poetry): secum dequesta labores,Val. Fl. 5, 448: imbres,Stat. Th. 1, 404; cf. talia,id. 11, 627.

derado.definition: dē-rādo, si, sum, 3 V. a., to rub or scrape off, to smooth off, shave off (anteclass. and post-Aug.): de virga lauri deradito,Cato R. R. 121: atramentum scalpro,Cels. 8, 4; 5, 26, 35; cf. ceram,Gell. 17, 9, 17; and: nomen urbis ex carmine,id. 7, 20: umorem specillis,Plin. 32, 7, 24, § 75: corticem,id. 20, 2, 6, § 12: cunctis margo derasis,id. Ep. 8, 20, 5: capillum ex capite omni,to cut off,Gell. 17, 9, 22, for which also caput, id. ib. § 25: der...

derbiosus.definition: derbĭōsus, a, um Adj., scabby ( = impetiginosus): oculi,Theod. Prisc. 1, 10.

dercea.definition: A plant, called also herba Apollinaris, a species of the solanum, Ap. Herb. 22.

derelictor.definition: derelinquo One who abandons (late Lat.): legis,Hier. in Psa. 88.

derelictus.definition: dērĕlictus, a, um, Part., from derelinquo.

derelinquo.definition: dē-rĕlinquo, līqui, lictum, 3 In the class. lang., to forsake wholly, to abandon, desert (good prose): cf.: Ti. Gracchum a Q. Tuberone derelictum videbamus,Cic. Lael. 11, 37: ut aratores agros latos ac fertiles desererent totasque arationes derelinquerent,Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 51, § 120: serere aliquid in inculto et derelicto solo,id. Brut. 4, 16: naves ab aestu derelictae, * Caes. B. G. 3, 13 fin.: castra,Liv. 39, 50, 5; cf. 37, 8, 5; 10, 17, 5: in a...

derepente.definition: dē-rĕpentĕ, (qs. departing from the regular course of time) Suddenly, on a sudden (mostly ante-class—for syn. cf.: desubito, subito, repente, statim, continuo, confestim, actutum, extemplo, etc.): derepente contulit sese in pedes, Enn. ap. Non. 518, 20; so id. ib. 6; Att. Afran. Turpil., Novius, Varro,Pompon. ib. 5-22; Plaut. Most. 2, 2, 57; Ter. Hec. 4, 1, 3 and 39; Poëta ap. Cic. Div. 1, 31, 66; Suet. Tib. 23; id. Vesp. 23; Tac. H. 1, 63 (in Li...

derepo.definition: dē-rēpo, psi, 3 V. n., to crawl down, sneak down (very rare): derepit ad cubile setosae suis,Phaedr. 2, 4, 12: ad hominum fana, Varr. ap. Non. 544, 29; Ap. M. 4, p. 145.—*

derideo.definition: dē-rīdĕo, si, sum, 2 V. a., to laugh at, laugh to scorn; to scoff at, deride (class.).

deridiculus.definition: dērīdĭcŭlus, a, um, derideo Very laughable, ridiculous (not in Cic. and Caes.): is deridiculu 'st omnibus,Plaut. Mil. 2, 1, 14: pueri,Gell. 13, 30, 9: versus,id. 12, 2, 3: quod est deridiculum,Varr. R. R. 1, 18, 5; so Liv. 39, 26.—And subst.: dērīdĭcŭ-lum, i, n., ridicule (subject.), or (object.) a mockery, game, an object of derision: quid tu me deridiculi gratia sic salutas?Plaut. Am. 2, 2, 50; id. Ps. 4, 5, 7; cf. Tac. A. 6, 2: deridiculo esse...

derigeo.definition: dē-rĭgeo, ēre V. a., to remove hardness, to soften, Commod. 73, 8.

derigesco.definition: dē-rĭgesco, gŭi, 3 V. inch. n. (occurring only in the perf.), to become stiff or rigid; to curdle (a poet. word): formidine sanguis deriguit,Verg. A. 3, 260: deriguere oculi,were fixed,id. ib. 7, 447; so, oculi,Ov. M. 14, 754: hirsutae comae,id. F. 3, 332: manus,Luc. 3, 613: cervix,Ov. M. 5, 233: Niobe malis,id. ib. 6, 303 (al. diriguit).

deripio.definition: dē-rĭpĭo (-rupio), rĭpŭi, reptum, 3, v. a. rapio To tear off, tear away, snatch away, remove violently; to pull down (class., esp. freq. in poets). Lit. constr., with abl. with or without a prep., or rarely with dat.: aliquem de ara,Plaut. Rud. 3, 6, 2; so with de, id. ib. 3, 5, 5; id. Men. 5, 2, 117; Tib. 1, 2, 82 al.; with ab, Plaut. Rud. 3, 3, 10: vestem a pectore,Ov. M. 9, 637: ferrum a latere,Tac. A. 1, 35; with ex: velamina ex humeris,id. i...

derisio.definition: derideo A laughing to scorn, mockery, derision (late Lat. for irrisio, illusio), Arn. 7, p. 239; Lact. 4, 18.

derisor.definition: id. A mocker, scoffer, satirical person (rare; not in Cic.): ut tu semper eris derisor,Hor. S. 2, 6, 54; id. A. P. 433; Quint. 3, 8, 51: Anubis derisor populi,Juv. 6, 534; Vulg. Prov. 9, 7 al. Applied to a (jeering) parasite, Plaut. Capt. 1, 1, 3; Hor. Ep. 1, 18, 11; to a stage mimic,Mart. 1, 5, 5; Orell. Inscr. 4926.

derisorius.definition: dērīsōrĭus, a, um, derisor Serving for laughter, ridiculous: condiciones,Dig. 28, 7, 14.

derisus.definition: dērīsus, a, um, Part., from derideo.

derivatio.definition: derivo A leading off, turning off, turning away. Lit.: derivationes fluminum, * Cic. Off. 2, 4, 14: sollemnis (sc. lacus Albani),Liv. 5, 15 (cf. shortly before, priusquam ex lacu Albano aqua emissa foret). Trop.

deriuatio.definition: derivo A leading off, turning off, turning away. Lit.: derivationes fluminum, * Cic. Off. 2, 4, 14: sollemnis (sc. lacus Albani),Liv. 5, 15 (cf. shortly before, priusquam ex lacu Albano aqua emissa foret). Trop.

derivativus.definition: dērīvātīvus, a, um, id., in the later grammat. lang. Derivative: nomina,Prisc. p. 593 P.: species verborum,id. p. 824 ib. et saep.

deriuatiuus.definition: dērīvātīvus, a, um, id., in the later grammat. lang. Derivative: nomina,Prisc. p. 593 P.: species verborum,id. p. 824 ib. et saep.

derivo.definition: dē-rīvo, āvi, ātum, 1, rivus To lead, turn, or draw off a liquid, from or to a place. Prop.: de fluvio aquam,Plaut. Truc. 2, 7, 12 sq.: aqua ex flumine derivata, * Caes. B. G. 7, 72, 3: flumen,Hirt. ib. 8, 40, 3; Liv. 5, 15, 12; 5, 16, 9: derivata in domos flumina,Sen. N. Q. 1 praef. 7; 4, 2, 8; cf.: umorem in conliquias,Col. 2, 8, 3. Trop.

deriuo.definition: dē-rīvo, āvi, ātum, 1, rivus To lead, turn, or draw off a liquid, from or to a place. Prop.: de fluvio aquam,Plaut. Truc. 2, 7, 12 sq.: aqua ex flumine derivata, * Caes. B. G. 7, 72, 3: flumen,Hirt. ib. 8, 40, 3; Liv. 5, 15, 12; 5, 16, 9: derivata in domos flumina,Sen. N. Q. 1 praef. 7; 4, 2, 8; cf.: umorem in conliquias,Col. 2, 8, 3. Trop.

derogator.definition: id. A detractor, depreciator (late Lat.), Sid. Ep. 3, 13.

derogo.definition: dē-rŏgo, āvi, ātum, 1, , jurid. t. t. To repeal a part of a law, to restrict or modify it. Prop.: huic legi nec obrogari fas est, neque derogari ex hac aliquid licet, neque tota abrogari potest,Cic. Rep. 3, 22; cf.: de lege aliquid derogare aut legem abrogare,id. Inv. 2, 45, 134; id. Cornel. I. Frag. 11: derogatur legi, cum pars detrahitur,Dig. 16, 102. Transf., beyond the legal sphere, to take away, detract from, to diminish, to remove, withdraw...

derosus.definition: dē-rōsus, a, um, Part. [derodo, not in use] Gnawed away, nibbled: clipeos a muribus, * Cic. Div. 1, 44, 99: vitis a cochleis,Plin. 11, 37, 62, § 164: ficus a locustis,id. 17, 25, 38, § 241.

deruncino.definition: dē-runcĭno, no Perf., ātum, 1, runcina, to plane off; hence, in the lang. of comedy, to deceive, cheat; to shave (only in the foll. passages): militem,Plaut. Mil. 4, 4, 6: ego deruncinatus, deartuatus sum miser,id. Capt. 3, 4, 108.

deruo.definition: dē-rŭo, rŭi, 3, and n. (a very rare word). Act., to throw or cast down. Neutr., to fall down: Ap. M. 2, p. 128; 7, p. 196.

deruptus.definition: dē-ruptus, a, um, Part. [derumpo, not in use] Broken; hence, like abruptus, of localities, precipitous, steep (not before Lucret.): dextra pars (maceriae) in aliquantum altitudinis,Liv. 42, 15; so, saxa,Lucr. 6, 539: ripae,Liv. 37, 39: angustiae (with praecipites),id. 21, 33: collis (with arduus),Tac. A. 2, 80: spatia terrae (with prona),Gell. 7, 2, 11.—Comp.: in deruptiorem tumulum,Liv. 38, 2.—Sup. and appear not to occur.

desaevio.definition: dē -saevĭo, ĭi (the Pluperfect subj. contr. desaevisset, Suet. Ner. 29), 4 To rave furiously, to rage (not anteAug., and very rare): toto Aeneas desaevit in aequore,Verg. A. 10, 569: pelago hiems,id. ib. 4, 52: omnes in artus,Luc. 6, 540; cf. Suet. Ner. 29: tragica in arte, * Hor. Ep. 1, 3, 14: belli Punici procella,Flor. 2, 6, 12: ira tua desaeviet,Vulg. Num. 16, 22.—* To cease raving or raging: nec dum desaeviat ira, Exspectat,Luc. 5, 304.

desaeuio.definition: dē -saevĭo, ĭi (the Pluperfect subj. contr. desaevisset, Suet. Ner. 29), 4 To rave furiously, to rage (not anteAug., and very rare): toto Aeneas desaevit in aequore,Verg. A. 10, 569: pelago hiems,id. ib. 4, 52: omnes in artus,Luc. 6, 540; cf. Suet. Ner. 29: tragica in arte, * Hor. Ep. 1, 3, 14: belli Punici procella,Flor. 2, 6, 12: ira tua desaeviet,Vulg. Num. 16, 22.—* To cease raving or raging: nec dum desaeviat ira, Exspectat,Luc. 5, 304.

descendo.definition: ( Perf. redupl.: descendidit, Valer. Antias ap. Gell. 7, 4 fin.; and, descendiderant, Laber. ib.; perf.: desciderunt, Inscr. Frat. Arv. 13 Henzen.), v. n., to come down; and of inanimate subjects, to fall, sink down, to descend, opp. to ascendo (class. and freq.). Lit. Trop.

descensio.definition: descendo (postAug.) A going down, descending. Prop.: balinearum,into the bath,Plin. 20, 17, 69, § 178: Tiberina,the sail down the Tiber,Cic. Fin. 5, 24, 70: grando in descensione saltus,upon the thickets,Vulg. Isa. 32, 19.—Hence, * Meton., the bath itself, Gr. ἐμβάσεις, Plin. Ep. 5, 6, 26.

descensorius.definition: dēscensōrĭus, a, um, descendo Descending, coming downwards: motus,Ambros. de Spir. Sanc. 1, 10, 118.

descensus.definition: dēscensus, a, um, Part., v. descendo Fin. !*?.

descisco.definition: dē-scisco, īvi or ĭi, ītum, 3, , orig. a publicist's t. t. To free one's self from a connection with any one, to withdraw, leave, revolt from, = sciscendo deficere; and with an indication of the terminus, to desert to, go over to any one (class. prose). Prop.: multae longinquiores civitates ab Afranio desciscunt,Caes. B. C. 1, 60 fin.; so, ab aliquo,id. ib. 2, 32, 2; Cic. Phil. 11, 9, 21; Liv. 6, 36; Nep. Alc. 5, 1; id. Dat. 5, 5; Just. 5, 1 fin....

descobino.definition: dē-scŏbīno, āvi, ātum, 1, scobina To file or scrape off (ante- and postclass., and very rare): supercilia, Varr. ap. Non. 492, 11; id. ib. 99, 28; Arn. 6, p. 200.

describo.definition: dē-scrībo, psi, ptum (in MSS. and edd. often confounded with discribo, q. v.), 3, v. a. To copy off, transcribe any thing from an original (freq. in Cic.; elsewh. rare): scripsit Balbus ad me, se a te (i. e. e tuo exemplo) quintum de Finibus librum descripsisse,Cic. Att. 13, 21; cf. id. Ac. 2, 4, 11: epistolam,id. Att. 8, 9; id. Fam. 12, 17, 2; 12, 7, 22: legem,Suet. Cal. 41; id. Dom. 20; so, to write down, write out: carmina in foliis,Verg. A. 3...

descriptio.definition: (in MSS. and edd. often confounded with discriptio V.infra), f.describo (freq. in Cic.), a marking out, delineation, copy, transcript: in concreto. Lit. (rare): eadem caeli descriptio,Cic. Rep. 6, 22; cf. id. ib. 1, 14: explicate descriptionem imaginemque tabularum,Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 77 fin. In plur.: numeris aut descriptionibus aliquid explicare,id. Tusc. 1, 17: volutarum,sketches, drawings,Vitr. 3, 3: orbis terrarum,maps,id. 8, 2 et saep. —Far mo...

descriptor.definition: describo A describer, delineator: morum,Lact. 5, 9, 19: descriptores gentium,ethnographers,Amm. 23, 6, 1.

descrobo.definition: dē-scrŏbo, āre, scrobs To set, enchase (late Lat.): gemmas auro, Tert. Res. carn. 7.

desculpo.definition: dē-sculpo, ĕre V. a., to carve out, to copy by carving or graving (late Lat.): simulacrum ligno,Tert. ad Nat. 1, 12.

desecatio.definition: A cutting off: ramorum,Cassiod. in Psa. 130: unus ensis, sed duas desecationes habet,edges,id. ib. 149, 7. From

deseco.definition: dē-sĕco, cŭi, ctum, 1 V. a., to cut off, cut away (class.): vitem,Varr. R. R. 1, 41, 3: partes ex toto,Cic. Univ. 7: uvas a vite,Col. 12, 43, 1: segetes et prata,id. 11, 1, 8: spicas fascibus,Liv. 42, 64: particulam undique, * Hor. Od. 1, 16, 15; and poet.: saxa metallis,to carve out,Stat. S. 2, 2, 85: hordeum, pabulum, herbas,Caes. B. C. 3, 58, 5; cf. segetem,Liv. 2, 5: aures,Caes. B. G. 7, 4 fin.; cf. cervicem,Liv. 31, 34: spicas fascibus,id. 3...

desero.definition: dē-sĕro, no Perf., sĭtum, 3, v. a., to sow, plant: desitis seminibus,Varr. R. R. 1, 23, 6.

deserpo.definition: dē -serpo, ĕre V. n., to creep down (post-Aug. and very rare): genis lanugo,Stat. Th. 6, 586; cf. Ap. Mag. p. 315.

desertio.definition: 2. desero A forsaking, deserting (rare; perh. not ante-Aug.).— Milit. t. t. (acc. to 2. desero, no. I. B.), desertion: peccatum desertionis,Dig. 49, 16, 3, § 6; 5, § 2 al.

desertor.definition: id. One who forsakes, abandons, deserts any one. Prop. Trop.: usus corporis desertor animi,a forsaker,Stat. Th. 8, 739.

desertrix.definition: desertor She that forsakes, neglects: divinae legis, Tert. de hab. mulier. 1.

desertus.definition: dēsertus, a, um, Part. and , from desero.

deservio.definition: dē-servĭo, īre V. n., to serve zealously, be devoted to, subject to (rare, but class.): valetudini tuae, dum mihi deservis, servisti non satis,Cic. Fam. 16, 18: cuivis,id. Off. 1, 30, 109: amicis,id. Sull. 9: grammatico soli deserviamus, deinde geometrae?Quint. 1, 12, 6: (Epicurei) sibi indulgentes et corpori deservientes,Cic. Leg. 1, 13, 39: studiis,Plin. Ep. 7, 7, 3: honoribus,id. Pan. 77, 6: Deo meo,Vulg. Act. 24, 14.

deseruio.definition: dē-servĭo, īre V. n., to serve zealously, be devoted to, subject to (rare, but class.): valetudini tuae, dum mihi deservis, servisti non satis,Cic. Fam. 16, 18: cuivis,id. Off. 1, 30, 109: amicis,id. Sull. 9: grammatico soli deserviamus, deinde geometrae?Quint. 1, 12, 6: (Epicurei) sibi indulgentes et corpori deservientes,Cic. Leg. 1, 13, 39: studiis,Plin. Ep. 7, 7, 3: honoribus,id. Pan. 77, 6: Deo meo,Vulg. Act. 24, 14.

deses.definition: dēses, ĭdis ( Nom. sing. appears not to occur), desideo, inactive, indolent, idle (syn.: iners, segnis, piger, ignavus, socors, tardus—rare, perh. not ante-Aug., nor in Aug. poets). Prop.: sedemus desides domi,Liv. 3, 68; so of persons,id. 1, 32; 3, 7; Col. 12, 1, 2: longa pace desides,Tac. H. 1, 88; 2, 21; Gell. 13, 8 fin. (with ignavus); with ab: desidem ab opere suo,Col. 7, 12, 2. Transf. of inanimate things: nec rem Romanam tam desidem umquam...

desideo.definition: dē-sĭdĕo, sēdi, 2, sedeo To remain or continue sitting, to sit long; and with the accessory idea of inactivity, to sit idle, to remain inactive (rare; not in Cic.). In gen.: tam diu Ibi desidere neque redire filium,Plaut. Bac. 2, 3, 4; id. Ps. 4, 4, 7: frustra ibi totum desedi diem,Ter. Hec. 5, 3, 2: aquila ramis,Phaedr. 2, 4, 21; cf.: amoenioribus locis,Quint. 5, 8, 1: apud Nicomedem,Suet. Caes. 2: in aliquo spectaculo,Sen. Ep. 7: in discrimine ...

desiderabilis.definition: dēsīdĕrābĭlis, e, desidero Desirable (rare): desiderabilia (anteponantur) iis, quibus facile carere possis,Cic. Top. 18, 69; id. Fin. 1, 16, 53: velut suis vitiis,Liv. 24, 5: princeps,Tac. H. 2, 76: terra,Vulg. Psa. 105, 24; and in the Comp. Suet. Tib. 21.—Sup. does not occur.—* Adv., dēsī-dĕrābĭlĭter, with ardent desire: concupiscere,Aug. Ep. 143, 2.

desideranter.definition: dēsīdĕranter Adv., eagerly, v. desidero, 1 fin.

desiderativus.definition: dēsīdĕrātīvus, a, um, id., in the late gram. lang. Desiderative: verba (e. g. esurio, coenaturio, etc.),Aug. p. 2006 P.

desideratiuus.definition: dēsīdĕrātīvus, a, um, id., in the late gram. lang. Desiderative: verba (e. g. esurio, coenaturio, etc.),Aug. p. 2006 P.

desiderium.definition: desidero A longing, ardent desire or wish, properly for something once possessed; grief, regret for the absence or loss of any thing (for syn. cf.: optio, optatio, cupido, cupiditas, studium, appetitio, voluntas—freq. and class.). Prop. Trop., of a person, as the object of longing: nunc desiderium, curaque non levis,Hor. Od. 1, 14, 18: desiderio meo nitenti, Catull. 2, 5; and as a term of endearment: mea lux, meum desiderium ... valete, mea desid...

desidero.definition: dē-sīdĕro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.etym. dub.; cf. considero To long for, greatly wish for, to desire something not possessed (freq. and class.—for syn. cf.: opto, requiro, expeto, appeto, affecto, cupio, concupisco, aveo, gestio, capto, volo). In gen., with acc.: Dies noctesque me ames, me desideres,Ter. Eun. 1, 2, 113: quam tu filium tuom, tam pater me meus desiderat,Plaut. Capt. 2, 2, 66: natura quid velit, anquirat, desideret,Cic. Lael. 24: nec si...

desidia.definition: desideo A sittinglong, remaining in a place. Prop. (rare), Prop. 1, 15, 6. A sitting idle, idleness, inactivity, slothfulness (class.; for syn. cf.: inertia, languor, otium, pax, feriae, justitium, dies fasti, etc., and v. deses): in portum confugere non inertiae neque desidiae,Cic. Brut. 2, 8; so with inertia,id. Sest. 10, 22; with languor,id. Off. 1, 34, 123; id. Tusc. 5, 27, 78; with socordia,Sall. C. 4, 1; with segnities,Suet. Galb. 9 et saep...

desidiosus.definition: dēsĭdĭōsus, a, um, desidia, qs. full of idleness, i. e. Slothful, indolent, lazy (for syn. cf.: piger, segnis, iners, deses, ignavus, socors, lentus, tardus, otiosus). Prop. (rare): qui in oppido sederent quam qui rura colerent, desidiosiores,Varr. R. R. 2 praef.: si comparer illi, sum desidiosissimus,Plin. Ep. 3, 5, 19; Col. 12, 1, 1: desidiosior in professione grammatica habebatur,Suet. Gramm. 8: qui nolet fieri desidiosus, amet,Ov. Am. 1, 9, 4...

desido.definition: dē-sīdo, sēdi (de-sīdi, Cic. l. l. infra, Lampr id. Alex. Sev. 39, 7), 3, , v. consido. —Of inanimate things, esp. of places To sink, fall, or settle down. Prop.: tantos terrae motus factos esse, ut multa oppida corruerint, multis locis labes factae sint terraeque desiderint,Cic. Div. 1, 35 fin.; 1, 43, 97; Liv. 32, 9; and poet. of the apparent sinking of mountains to one flying aloft: Gargara desidunt surgenti,Stat. Th. 1, 549: ovum inane natat,...

designatio.definition: or (the latter form better in sense II. Brambach S. v. Lex Jul. Munic. ap. Corp. Inscr. Lat. p. 206), , f. id.. A marking out, describing, designating: cellarum,Vitr. 5, 5: undarum,id. 5, 3: quadrata,id. 3, 1, 3. —Transf., a specification: personarum et temporum,Cic. de Or. 1, 31, 138; Lact. 4, 15, 5. A disposition, arrangement: totius operis,Cic. N. D. 1, 8 fin.: librorum meorum,id. Att. 4, 46.

designator.definition: or (the latter form freq. in inscrr., and preferred by Brambach; so Keller, ad Hor. Ep. 1, 7, 5; Corp. Inscr. Lat. pp. 597, 768), , id. One who regulates or arranges; a regulator.—As a t. t. An officer whose duty it was to assign seats in the theatre, Plaut. Poen. prol. 19. A master of ceremonies at funerals; an undertaker, Hor. Ep. 1, 7, 5; Sen. Ben. 6, 38; Tert. Spectac. 10; Inscr. Orell. 934; cf. Don. Ter. Ad. 1, 2, 7. An umpire at public spec...

designo.definition: dē-signo or dissigno (the latter form preferred by Brambach in sense II. B. 2. infra; so Keller, ad Hor. Ep. 1, 5, 16; cf. Roby, L. G. 2, p. 384), āvi, ātum, 1 V. a., to mark out, trace out (freq. in the Aug. per.); to describe, designate, define (for syn. cf.: nomino, appello; voco, dico; facio, coöpto, evoco, prodo, declaro, renuntio, seligo). Lit.: Aeneas urbem designat aratro,Verg. A. 5, 755; cf.: moenia fossā,id. ib. 7, 157: moenia sulco,Ov....

desilio.definition: dē-sĭlĭo, ĭlŭi (desului, Plaut. Rud. prol. 75: Desilivi,Col. 6, 24, 3: desilii,id. 8, 5, 14; Curt. 4, 12, 3 al.), ultum, 4, salio, to leap down. Prop. (class.). Constr. with abl. of the place whence, after de, ex, poet. and in later prose with ab or without a prep.: de navi in scapham,Plaut. Rud. prol. 75: de navibus,Caes. B. G. 4, 24, 2: de reda,Cic. Mil. 10, 29: de muro,Suet. Ner. 23: in terram e scapha,Plaut. Rud. 1, 2, 84: ex navi,Caes. B. G....

desino.definition: dē-sĭno, sĭi (rarely īvi, Sol. 35, 4, v. Neue, Form. II. 404; also Sync. perf.: desit,Mart. 6, 26, 3: desisse,Cic. Fam. 9, 24, 2; Suet. Ner. 33; 46; Gell. 15, 16, 2: desissem, Catull. 36, 5 al.: DESI, dissyl.,Inscr. Orell. 71), sĭtum, 3, and n.—Prop., to put or set down; hence, to leave off, give over, cease, desist (opp. coepi, the construction of which it for the most part follows; cf. for syn.: cesso, cunctor, tergiversor, defugio, haesito, mo...

desioculus.definition: desino-oculus One who has lost an eye, Mart. 12, 59, 9.

desipio.definition: dē-sĭpĭo, ĕre ( Perf. desipui, Lact. 2, 4, 4), and n. sapio. * Act., to render insipid (late Lat. and rare), Tert. Pudic. 13. Neutr., to be void of understanding, to be silly, foolish; to act foolishly (class.): summos viros desipere, delirare, dementes esse,Cic. N. D. 1, 34, 94: licet me desipere dicatis,id. Planc. 37; Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 46; id. Div. 2, 23, 51; Hor. S. 2, 3, 47; id. Ep. 1, 20, 9 al.: dulce est desipere in loco,to indulge in trifli...

desisto.definition: dē-sisto, stĭti, stĭtum, 3 ( Perf. destitĕrunt, Lucr. 4, 975), and n. (for syn. v. desino init.). Act., to set down: in scopulo puellam, Ap. M. 4, p. 157 (Anthol. Lat. 3, 174, 1). Neutr.

desitus.definition: dēsĭtus, a, um, Part., from desino.

desolatio.definition: desolo A desolating, desolation (eccl. Lat.). Abstr.: in sua desolatione,Vulg. Baruch, 4, 33; Salv. Gub. Dei, 6, p. 214: templi, Hilar. in Psa. 58, 7 al. Concr., a desert, Vulg. Jer. 7, 34; id. 44, 22.

desolator.definition: desolo A waster, one who makes lonely or desolate, Aug. Serm. 115, no. 5; Hieron. in Amos, III. ad 7, 4 sq.

desolatorius.definition: dēsōlātōrĭus, a, um, id. That makes lonely or desolate (eccl. Lat.), Vulg. Psa. 120, 4; Hier. Ep. 18, no. 14.

desolo.definition: dē-sōlo, āvi, ātum, 1 V. a., to leave alone, to forsake, abandon, desert (not anteAug., perh. first used by Verg.; most freq. in the part. perf.).

desorbeo.definition: dē-sorbĕo, ēre V. a., to swallow down: vortex,Tert. Idol. 24 al.; Mart. Cap. 8, § 804.

despectator.definition: id. One who looks down; trop., a despiser: divinarum sententiarum,Tert. ad Uxor. 8.

despecto.definition: dēspecto, āre V. intens. a. [id.], to look down upon any thing from a height (perh. not ante-Aug.). Prop.: ex alto terras,Ov. M. 4, 624; so, terras,Verg. A. 1, 396: humum,Ov. M. 2, 710: aquas,id. ib. 15, 699: flammas,Verg. A. 10, 409: procul palantes animos,Ov. M. 15, 151 al. Trop., to look down upon, to despise (used by Tac.): liberos infra,Tac. A. 2, 43: ne ut victi et ignavi despectarentur,id. H. 2, 30.

despector.definition: despicio, no. II. A despiser, Tert. adv. Marc. 2, 23.

despectrix.definition: despector She that despises, a despiser: mundi (virtus),Tert. Anim. 23.

despectus.definition: dēspectus, a, um, Part., from despicio.

desperabilis.definition: dēspērābĭlis, e, despero Incurable, desperate: plaga mea,Vulg. Jer. 15, 18.

desperate.definition: dēspērātē Adv., hopelessly, etc., v. despero, P. a., no. 2. fin.

desperatio.definition: despero Hopelessness, despair: desperatio est aegritudo sine ulla rerum exspectatione meliorum,Cic. Tusc. 4, 8, 18. Prop. (good prose and very freq.). Meton., desperate boldness, foolhardiness: desperatio truculentae feminae, Ap. M. 10, p. 251: periculosa,Vulg. 2 Reg. 2, 26; id. Sirach, 27, 24.

desperatus.definition: dēspērātus, a, um, Part. and , from despero.

desperno.definition: dē-sperno, ĕre V. a., to despise greatly, disdain: opes, Col. poët. 10, 298.

despero.definition: dē-spēro, āvi, ātum, 1, and A., to be hopeless; to have no hope of, to despair of, to give up (freq. and class.).—Constr. most freq. with de, the acc., or acc. and inf.; less freq. with the dat. or absol.

despicabilis.definition: dēspĭcābĭlis, e, despicor Contemptible, despicable (post-class.): homo,Amm. 26, 8, 5; Ambros. in Psa. 28, § 3 al.— Comp., Sid. Ep. 2, 10.

despicatus.definition: dēspĭcātus, a, um, Part. and , from despicor.

despicientia.definition: despicio A despising, contempt (very rare; perh. only in Cic.): in omnium rerum humanarum contemptione ac despicientia,Cic. Tusc. 1, 40: rerum externarum,id. Off. 1, 20: animi,id. ib. 2, 11: in contemnendis honoribus,id. Part. Or. 23, 81.

despicio.definition: dē-spĭcĭo, exi, ectum, 3 ( Inf. perf. despexe, Plaut. Mil. 2, 6, 72), v. n. and a. To look down upon any thing (for syn. cf.: contemno, sperno, aspernor). To look away, not to regard, not to attend: simul atque ille despexerit,Cic. Rosc. Am. 8, 22.— Hence, P. a., dēspectus, a, um, contemptible, despicable: natura ejus,Tac. A. 13, 47: Euphrates, ingens modo, inde tenuis rivus, despectus emoritur, Mela, 3, 8, 5.—Comp.: improbos despectiores facere,...

despicor.definition: dēspĭcor, ātus, 1 V. dep. a. [despicio, no. I. B.), to despise, disdain (very rare): aliquem, Q. Pompeius ap. Prisc. p. 793 P.; Aur. Vict. Vir. Ill. 23.—Hence, dēspĭcā-tus, a, um, in a pass. sense, despised: vir me habet despicatam,Plaut. Cas. 2, 2, 15 and 19; cf. Ter. Eun. 2, 3, 92.

desplendesco.definition: dē-splendesco, ĕre V. n. inch., to cease to shine, to lose its brightness, Paul. Nol. Ep. 39 fin.

despoliatio.definition: despolio A robbing, despoiling, Tert. Res. Carn. 7; of a fine, Cod. Theod. 9, 17, 6.

despolio.definition: dē-spŏlĭo, āvi, ātum, 1, (also Dep.: quos despoliatur, with depopulatur, Afran. ap. Non. 480, 13), to rob, plunder, despoil (rare, but good prose).—Constr., aliquem (aliquid) aliqua re: ne se armis despoliaret, * Caes. B. G. 2, 31, 4: me despoliat,Plaut. Men. 5, 2, 53; cf. id. Cas. 4, 4, 4; Ter. And. 4, 5, 21; Cic. Att. 7, 9: Dianae templum,Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 21 fin.: digitos suos,Plaut. Mil. 4, 2, 57: despoliari triumpho,Liv. 45, 36.

despondeo.definition: dē-spondĕo, spondi, sponsum, 2 ( Perf. despopondisse, Plaut. Trin. 3, 1, 2; plqpf. despoponderas, id. Truc. 4, 3, 51; with despondi,id. Aul. 2, 3, 4: despondisse,id. Trin. 5, 2, 9 et saep.), v. a., to promise to give, to promise, pledge. Lit. Trop.

desponsatio.definition: desponso A betrothing, betrothal, Tert. Verg. vel. 11; Vulg. Cant. 3, 11.

desponsio.definition: despondeo A despairing, desponding, Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 18, 176: animi,id. ib. 2, 32, 167.

desponso.definition: dē-sponso, no Perf., ātum, 1, v. a., to betroth (post-Aug.), Suet. Caes. 1; id. Claud. 27; Aur. Vict. Orig. 13: viro justo,Ambros. in Luc. 10, 21; Vulg. Matt. 1, 18.

despumatio.definition: despumo A skimming off, Tert. Carn. Chr. 19.

despumo.definition: dē-spūmo, āvi, ātum, 1, and n. (perh. not ante-Aug.). Act. Neutr., to cease foaming, to slacken, abate: ut nimius ille fervor despumet,Sen. Ira, 2, 20: cum aliquid lacrymarum affectus despumaverit,id. Ep. 99, 27: aetas,id. ib. 68fin.

despuo.definition: dē-spŭo, ĕre, and A., to spit out, to spit. Prop., Liv. 5, 40; Naev. ap. Gell. 2, 19, 6; esp. as a religious observance for averting a disease, etc.; so, act. morbos, Plin. 28, 4, 7, § 35: tenerum ignem, Claud. rapt. Pros. 2, 52; neutr., Varr. R. R. 1, 2, 27; Tib. 1, 2, 54; Plin. 10, 23, 33, § 69.— Hence Trop., to reject, abhor (syn.: deprecari, aspernari, spernere, etc.),Plaut. As. 1, 1, 26: preces alicujus, Catull. 50, 19: voluptates (with sper...

desputum.definition: id. Spittle (late Lat.), Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 20, 195.

desquamo.definition: no Perf., ātum, 1, v. a., to scale off, to scale. Prop.: pisces,Plaut. Aul. 2, 9, 1. Transf.

desterno.definition: dē-sterno, strāvi, 3 V. a., to free from its covering (stratum), to unsaddle, ungird: camelos,Vulg. Gen. 24, 32.

destico.definition: dēstĭco, āre V. n., to squeak, of the noise made by the shrew-mouse, Auct. Carm. Philom. 62.

destillatio.definition: destillo A dripping down, distilling; in medic. lang., a rheum, catarrh, running, Cels. 1, 2; 4, 2; Plin. 20, 17, 71, § 183; 22, 25, 68, § 139 et saep.: jecoris,an abscess,Amm. 14, 11, 24.

destillo.definition: dē-stillo (or di-stillo), āvi, ātum, 1, and n. To drip or trickle down, to distil (not in Cic.). Prop.: lentum destillat ab inguine virus, * Verg. G. 3, 281; cf.: ex athere,Sen. Q. N. 2, 12: de capite in nares humor (from a cold),Cels. 4, 2, 4: nubes distillaverunt aquis,Vulg. Judic. 5, 4 al. Transf.: tempora nardo,to drop, distil,Tib. 2, 2, 7; cf.: destillante arboribus odore mirae suavitatis,Plin. 6, 31, 36, § 198.

destinate.definition: dēstĭnātē Adv., resolutely, obstinately, etc.; v. destino fin.

destinatio.definition: destino A setting fast, establishing; a resolution, determination, purpose, design (perh. not ante-Aug.): depascitur segetes destinatione ante determinata in diem,Plin. 8, 25, 39, § 95: porticum ex destinatione M. Agrippae a sorore ejus inchoatam peregit,id. 3, 2, 3, § 17; cf. Tac. H. 1, 77: nulli' placere partium destinatio,Liv. 32, 35 fin.: consulum, i. e. the election (opp. renuntiatione), Plin. Pan. 77, 1; cf. Tac. H. 2, 79; Plin. Pan. 95, 2:...

destinatus.definition: dēstĭnātus, a, um, see the foll. art.

destino.definition: dē-stĭno, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.obs. stanare; a particip. stem from root STA, v. sto; and cf.: dono, digno, etc., Corss. 2, 416 To make fast, make firm, bind (class.; esp. freq. in the trop. sense—for syn. cf.: decerno, scisco, statuo, jubeo, constituo, sancio, definio). Lit.: antemnas ad malos,Caes. B. G. 3, 14, 6: rates ancoris,id. B. C. 1, 25, 7: falces (laqueis),id. B. G. 7, 22, 2: arcas,Vitr. 5, 12, 3; dub., v. destina. Trop., to establish, det...

destituo.definition: dē-stĭtŭo, ŭi, ūtum, 3, statuo. To set down; to set, place anywhere (ante-class. and freq. in Liv.; elsewh. rare): destituit omnes servos ad mensam ante se, Caecil. ap. Non. 280, 3: navem in alto ancoris, Naev. ib.: palum in foro, C. Gracchus ap. Gell. 10, 3, 3: aliquem in convivio (sc. ludendi causa),Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 26 fin.: armatos in medio,Liv. 7, 10: aliquem ante tribunal,id. 2, 12; cf. id. 23, 10: cohortes extra vallum,id. 10, 4: duo signa ...

destitutio.definition: destituo A forsaking, deserting; deceiving, a failure, disappointment (very rare), Cin. Clu. 26, 71; id. Quint. 5, 20; Suet. Dom. 14. A putting away, abandoning: peccati,Vulg. Heb. 9, 26.

destitutus.definition: dēstĭtūtus, a, um, Part., from destituo.

destrictivus.definition: dēstrictīvus, a, um, destringo Dissolving, loosening, opp. constrictivus, Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 29.

destrictiuus.definition: dēstrictīvus, a, um, destringo Dissolving, loosening, opp. constrictivus, Cael. Aur. Acut. 2, 29.

destrictus.definition: dēstrictus, a, um, Part., from destringo

destringo.definition: dē-stringo, inxi, ictum, 3 To strip off. To touch gently, to graze, skim, skirt (perh. only in the poets).

destructibilis.definition: dēstructĭbĭlis, e, destruo Destructible: omnia, Lact. de Ira D. fin. (al. destructilia).

destructilis.definition: dēstructĭlis, e, id. Destructible: aedes, Prud. στεφ. 10, 357; Lact. de Ira Dei, 23, § 28.

destructio.definition: id. A pulling down, destruction. Prop.: murorum,Suet. Galb. 12: munitionum,Vulg. 2 Cor. 10, 4. Trop.: sententiarum (opp. confirmatio),a refuting, refutation,Quint. 10, 5, 12: appetentiae,disturbance,Cael. Aur. Acut. 3, 21, 203.

destructivus.definition: dēstructīvus, a, um, id. Destructive: adjutorium,Cael. Aur. Tard. 1, 4, 84.

destructiuus.definition: dēstructīvus, a, um, id. Destructive: adjutorium,Cael. Aur. Tard. 1, 4, 84.

destructor.definition: id. One who pulls down, a destroyer: rerum, opp. aedificator,Tert. Apol. 46: Trojae, Cass. Var. 14, 15; Hier. Ep. 112, 10 fin.

destruo.definition: dē-strŭo, xi, ctum, 3 V. a., to pull or tear down any thing built (opp. construo— for syn. cf.: demolior, diruo). Prop. (rare but class.): navem, aedificium idem destruit facillime, qui construxit,Cic. de Sen. 20, 72; so, templum prope funditus,Suet. Vesp. 9: moenia,Verg. A. 4, 326: aras,Vulg. Exod. 34, 13 et saep. Trop., to destroy, ruin, weaken (perh. not ante-Aug.): destruere ac demoliri aliquid,Liv. 34, 3: tyrannidem,Quint. 1, 10, 48: oration...

desubito.definition: dē-sŭbĭtō (by many written separately, de subito) Adv., on a sudden, suddenly (except once in Cic., only ante-class.), Plaut. Bac. 1, 1, 46; id. Capt. prol. 62; id. Most. 2, 1, 63; id. Stich. 5, 4, 39; Lucil., Enn., Naev., al. ap. Non. 517, 13-518, 1; Lucr. 2, 265; 3, 643; Cic. Rep. 6, 2, 2 (ap. Non. p. 517).

desubulo.definition: dē-sūbŭlo, āre, subula To bore in deeply: perforare,Non. 99, 30; trop.: viam, Varr. ap. Non. 99, 32.

desudo.definition: dē-sūdo, āvi, ātum, 1, and A. (mostly post-Aug.). Neutr., to sweat greatly. Act., to sweat out, exude.

desuesco.definition: dē-sŭesco, sŭēvi, sŭētum, 3, and n. (mostly poet., or in post-Aug. prose; in Cic. and Caes. not at all; cf., however, desuefacio). Act., to disuse, to lay aside a custom or habit, to disaccustom, to put out of use: desuevi, ne quo ad cenam iret, Titin. ap. Non. 95, 1: arma diu desueta,Verg. A. 2, 509; cf.: rem desuetam usurpare,Liv. 3, 38: desueta sidera cerno (i. e. quae cernere desuevi),Ov. M. 5, 503; cf.: voces jam mihi desuetae,id. ib. 7, 646...

desuetudo.definition: desuesco Discontinuance of a practice or habit, disuse, desuetude: armorum,Liv. 1, 19: bellandi, Fronto, princ. hist. p. 3, 7: desuetudine tardi,Ov. M. 14, 436; so absol., id. Tr. 5, 7, 57; Dig. 1, 3, 32 al.

desuetus.definition: dēsŭētus, a, um, Part., from desuesco.

desugo.definition: dē-sūgo, no Perf., ctum, 3, v. a., tosuck from any thing, to suck in (late Lat.), Pall. 1, 9, 4; 1, 37, 2.

desulto.definition: dēsulto, āre V. intens. n. [desilio], to leap down: mari,into the sea,Tert. Anim. 32.

desultor.definition: id. A leaper, vaulter, the technical designation of a sort of riders, who, in the circus-games, leaped from one horse to another without stopping. Prop., Varr. R. R. 2, 7, 15; Liv. 23, 29; 44, 9; Manil. 5, 85. Trop., a fickle, inconstant person: amoris,an inconstant lover,Ov. Am. 1, 3, 15; cf. bellorum,Sen. Suas. 1, § 8.

desultorius.definition: dēsultōrĭus, a, um, desultor. Of or belonging to a vaulter (desultor): equi,Suet. Caes. 39: levitas,Mart. Cap. 1, § 88.—Subst.: desultorius, ii, m., Cic. Mur. 27, 57. Desultory, superficial, Ap. M. 1, p. 102, 14.

desultrix.definition: dēsultrix, īcis, f., id. Inconstant (late Lat.): virtus,Tert. adv. Val. 38.

desumo.definition: dē-sūmo, mpsi (msi), 3, Lit. To take for one's self from a multitude or mass; hence, to pick out, choose, select (syn. deligere); to take upon one's self, undertake (rare, and perh. not ante-Aug.— syn. suscipere): sibi consules asservandos desumunt,Liv. 4, 55, 3: sibi hostes,id. 38, 45; cf.: sibi pugnas,Tac. Or. 37; and: cursum certamenque,Plin. Ep. 8, 20, 7: sibi vacuas Athenas, *Hor. Ep. 2, 2, 81.

desuper.definition: dē-sŭper Adv., from above, from overhead (repeatedly in the historians and poets; not in Cic.): qui in phalangas insilirent et desuper vulnerarent,Caes. B. G. 1, 52, 5 (a false reading in Caes. B. C. 1, 79, 2; but v. Lachm. ad Lucr. 6, 511; cf. Tac. A. 2, 16): aprum jaculis desuper petit,Suet. Tib. 72; Sen. Ep. 74: desuper atrum nemus imminet,Verg. A. 1, 165; 2, 47; 4, 122 al.: nunc desuper Alpis colles abripimur,Luc. 1, 688 (the construction as ...

desuperne.definition: dē-supernē Adv., from above, Vitr. 10. 16, 10 (dub. v. Lachm. ad Lucr. 6, 511).

desurgo.definition: dē-surgo, ĕre V. n., to rise from any place; to rise (extremely rare). Prop.: certa desurgere parte, *Lucr. 5, 703: cenă, *Hor. S. 2, 2, 77. Transf., to go to stool, Scrib. Comp. 140 and 142; Plin. 28, 14, 59, § 211.

desursum.definition: dē-sursum, ( = desuper) From above, Tert. de Praescr. 46 al.: descendens,Vulg. Jacob, 3, 15 al.

detector.definition: id. An uncoverer; trop., revealer (eccl. Lat.): creatoris,Tert. adv. Marc. 4, 36 med.: conscientiae,id. adv. Val. 3.

detego.definition: dē-tĕgo, xi, ctum, 3 V. a., to uncover, expose, lay bare (freq. in the Aug. per.). Lit.: ventus detexit villam,unroofed,Plaut. Rud. 1, 1, 3: aedem Junonis ad partem dimidiam,Liv. 42, 3: regiam Caci,Verg. A. 8, 241: juga montium detexerat nebula,Liv. 33, 7 et saep.: capite detecto,Suet. Caes. 57; cf. poet. transf. and in Gr. construction: caput puer detectus,Verg. A. 10, 133: faciem,Suet. Ner. 48: corpora,Tac. A. 13, 38: ossa,Suet. Caes. 81; Ov. M...

detendo.definition: dē-tendo, no Perf., sum, 3, v. a., to unstretch, relax a thing strained (very rare): tabernacula, to strike the tents, * Caes. B. C. 3, 85, 3; Liv. 41, 3, 1.

detentator.definition: detento One who holds or keeps back something, a detainer, Cod. 7, 39, 7; 11, 59, 2.

detento.definition: dētento, no Perf., ātum, 1, v. intens. a. [id.], to hold or keep back, to detain (late Lat.), Ven. Carm. 11, 21: servos, Cod. Th. 7, 13, 16 al.

detentus.definition: dētentus, a, um, Part., from detineo.

detepesco.definition: dē-tĕpesco, ĕre V. inch. n., to cease to be lukewarm, to grow cool, Sid. Ep. 5, 17.

detergeo.definition: dē-tergĕo, si, sum, 2 (also post-class.: Detergis,Claud. Cons. Mall. Theod. 191: detergunt, id. ap. Eutr. 2, 375: detergantur,Dig. 33, 7, 12, § 21; Ap. Mag. 59, p. 312, 26; Sen. Ep. 47, 4, v. tergeo) To wipe off, wipe away (class.). To strip off, break off; to break to pieces: remos,Caes. B. C. 1, 58; Liv. 28, 30 fin.: pinnas asseribus falcatis,id. 38, 5: palmites,Col. 4, 27 fin.

deterioro.definition: dētĕrĭōro, āvi, ātum, 1, deterior To make worse, to deteriorate (late Lat.), Claud. Mam. de Statu an. 1, 3 al.

determinabilis.definition: dētermĭnābĭlis, e, determino That has an end, finite: materia,Tert. adv. Herm. 41.

determinatio.definition: id. A boundary, conclusion, end: extrema ora et d. mundi, Cic. N. D. 2, 40, 101: exitus et determinatio orationis,id. Inv. 1, 52, 98.

determinator.definition: id. One who prescribes or determines: disciplinae,Tert. Pudic. 11.

determino.definition: dē-termĭno, āvi, ātum, 1 V. a., to enclose within boundaries, to bound; to limit, prescribe, determine (rare but class.). Prop.: regiones, limites, confinia,Plaut. Poen. prol. 49: augur regiones ab oriente ad occasum determinavit,Liv. 1, 18 fin.; cf. Asiam ab oriente Armenia minore, ab occidente Phrygia, etc.,Plin. 5, 27, 28, § 102: imaginem templi scipione in solo,id. 28, 2, 4, § 15. Transf., to fix, settle, determine: teli ictus,Lucr. 6, 403: s...

detero.definition: dē-tĕro, trīvi, trītum, 3 V. a., to rub away, to wear away, to wear out (mostly poet. and in post-Aug. prose; not in Cic. or Caes.). Prop.: strataque jam volgi pedibus detrita viarum saxea,Lucr. 1, 315: a catena collum detritum cani,Phaedr. 3, 7, 16; so, vestem usu,Plin. 8, 48, 73, § 191; cf.: detrita tegmina,Tac. A. 1, 18: aurum usu,Plin. 33, 3, 19: pedes (viă longă),Tib. 1, 9, 16: frumenta,to thresh out,Col. 1, 6, 23; cf. milium,id. 6, 12, 4: s...

deterreo.definition: dē-terrĕo, ŭi, ĭtum, 2 To frighten from any thing; to deter, discourage from, prevent, hinder (class.).—Constr. In Augustan authors, sometimes with an inanimate object, like defendere, prohibere, etc., to avert, keep off: vim a censoribus,Liv. 4, 24 fin.: d. nefas et inhibere bipennem,Ov. M. 8, 767.

detersio.definition: detergeo A cleansing: mitissima,Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 14, 203.

detestabilis.definition: dētestābĭlis, e, detestor Execrable, abominable, detestable (good prose): omen,Cic. Phil. 11, 5, 11; cf.: exsecratus populo Romano, detestabilis, etc.,id. ib. 2, 26 fin.: nihil esse tam detestabile tamque pestiferum quam voluptatem,id. de Sen. 12, 41; cf. res (with tetra, misera),id. Tusc. 3, 11 fin.: scelus,id. Lael. 8, 27: exemplum,Liv. 26, 48: voce,Suet. Vit. 10 et saep.—Comp., Cic. Off. 1, 17, 57; Vulg. Sap. 19, 13.—Sup. appears not to occur....

detestatio.definition: id.. In relig. lang. In judicial lang., a formal renunciation under oath: detestatio est denuntiatio facta cum testatione,Dig. 50, 16, 40; cf. detestor, no. II.—So detestatio sacrorum, the solemn renunciation of the family sacred rites, and thereby of the gens itself, which in arrogatio was made by the son, Gell. 15, 27, 3; cf.: Liber (Servii Sulpicii) de sacris detestandis,id. 6, 12, 1.

detestator.definition: detestor, no. I. One who execrates, a curser (eccl. Lat.), Tert. adv. Marc. 4, 27 al.

detesto.definition: dētesto, āvi, 1, act. collat. form of detestor To execrate (very rare): detestabant,Amm. 26, 6, 17; v. also detestor fin.

detestor.definition: dē-testor, ātus, 1 V. dep. a. In relig. lang. Transf., to avert from one's self by entreaty, to ward off, avert, remove, sc. an evil from one's self or others, = deprecari, to deprecate: ut a me quandam prope justam patriae querimoniam detester ac deprecer,Cic. Cat. 1, 11: memoriam consulatus tui a republica,id. Pis. 40, 96: invidiam,id. N. D. 1, 44, 123: o di immortales, avertite ac detestamini hoc omen,id. Phil. 4, 4, 10.
