enarratio.definition: enarro A detailed exposition, interpretation: ineffabilis sanctusque sermo, cujus enarratio modum hominis excedat, Lact. 4, 9, 3; Quint. 1, 4, 2 sq.; 1, 8, 18 al. Esp., the reckoning in metre, scanning: syllabarum,Sen. Ep. 88, 3.

enarro.definition: ē-narro, āvi, ātum, 1 To explain in detail, to expound, interpret (rare but class.): omnem rem modo seni, Quo pacto haberet, enarramus ordine,Ter. Ad. 3, 3, 11; Plaut. Am. 1, 3, 27; id. Mil. 2, 1, 1; Ter. Heaut. 2, 3, 32; Cic. Inv. 1, 20; id. Div. 1, 26; Liv. 27, 50; Quint. 10, 1, 101 Spald.: poëmata,id. 1, 2, 14 Spald.; Plin. 36, 13, 19, § 87; Gell. 13, 10, 2; 18, 9, 4.—Hence, ēnarrātĭus, adv. comp., more explicitly: scribere,Gell. 10, 1, 7 (opp...

enascor.definition: ē-nascor, -nātus, 3 V. dep. n., to issue forth, to sprout or spring up, to arise, to be born (not freq. till after the Aug. per.; in Plaut., Ter., and Cic. not at all): quod enasci colicoli vix queunt,Varr. R. R. 1, 41, 4; so of plants,Col. 5, 4, 2; 11, 3, 48; Liv. 32, 1 fin.; 43, 13; Quint. 6, 3, 77; Suet. Aug. 94 al.; also: rami enati, shot out, * Caes. B. G. 2, 17, 4; v. G. Long ad h. l.: dentes ex mento,Varr. R. R. 2, 9, 3; cf.: cornua (cervo...

enato.definition: ē-năto, āvi, 1 To swim out or away, to escape by swimming (very rare). Lit., Vitr. 6 praef.; Hor. A. P. 20; Phaedr. 4, 21, 14; App. M. p. 121, 3 al. Trop., to extricate one's self, to get off: reliqui habere se angustius videntur; enatant tamen,Cic. Tusc. 5, 30, 87; Petr. 57, 10.

enavigo.definition: ē-nāvĭgo, āvi, ātum, 1, and A. Neutr., to sail out, sail away. Act., to traverse by sailing, to sail over: undam,Hor. C. 2, 14, 11: sinum,Plin. 9, 3, 2, § 6: (Indum),id. 6, 17, 21, § 60.

enauigo.definition: ē-nāvĭgo, āvi, ātum, 1, and A. Neutr., to sail out, sail away. Act., to traverse by sailing, to sail over: undam,Hor. C. 2, 14, 11: sinum,Plin. 9, 3, 2, § 6: (Indum),id. 6, 17, 21, § 60.

encaenio.definition: encaenĭo, āre To consecrate: novam tunicam,Aug. in Joann. 84.

encomboma.definition: A white garment worn by girls, Varr. ap. Non. 543, 1.

endromis.definition: A coarse woollen cloak in which the heated athletae wrapped themselves after their exercises, Mart. 4, 19; 14, 126; Juv. 3, 102. But afterwards a fine sort worn as an article of luxury: Tyriae,id. 6, 246 Rup.

eneco.definition: ē-nĕco or ēnĭco, cŭi (enicavit, Plaut. As. 5, 2, 71), ctum (less freq. enecatum; in the Part. enecatus, Plin. 18, 13, 34, § 127; 30, 12, 34, § 108; and, enectus,id. 7, 9, 7, § 47; 26, 15, 90, § 159), 1 (old form of the fut. perf. enicasso, Plaut. Most. 1, 3, 55 and 66), , to kill off, kill completely, to kill, stay (freq. and class., esp. in the transf. signif.; syn.: neco, interficio, interimo, conficio, caedo, occido, concido, trucido, jugulo, ...

enervis.definition: ē-nervis, e, nervus Nerveless, enervated, weak, effeminate (rare and postAug., for enervatus; cf. enervo): corpus, Petr. poët. 119, 25: homo,Sen. Thyest. 176: compositio (with effeminata),Quint. 9, 4, 142; cf. orator (with solutus),Tac. Or. 18 fin.: et fluxum spectaculum,Plin. Pan. 33, 1; Val. Max. 6, 4, 2; 8, 8 init. al.—Adv.: enervĭter, weakly: blandus, August. cont. Faust. 22, 50.

eneruis.definition: ē-nervis, e, nervus Nerveless, enervated, weak, effeminate (rare and postAug., for enervatus; cf. enervo): corpus, Petr. poët. 119, 25: homo,Sen. Thyest. 176: compositio (with effeminata),Quint. 9, 4, 142; cf. orator (with solutus),Tac. Or. 18 fin.: et fluxum spectaculum,Plin. Pan. 33, 1; Val. Max. 6, 4, 2; 8, 8 init. al.—Adv.: enervĭter, weakly: blandus, August. cont. Faust. 22, 50.

enervo.definition: ē-nervo, āvi, ātum, 1 (scanned ĕnervans and ĕnervātum in Prud. Cath. 8, 64; contra Symm. 2, 143), v. a. enervis To take out the nerves or sinews. Prop. (rare and post-class.): poplites securi,App. M. 8, p. 215: cerebella,Apic. 4, 2; 7, 7: enervatus Melampus,i. e. unmanned,Claud. in Eutr. 1, 315. Transf., in gen., to enervate, weaken, render effeminate (class.; esp. freq. in the part. perf.): non plane me enervavit senectus,Cic. de Sen. 10, 32: co...

eneruo.definition: ē-nervo, āvi, ātum, 1 (scanned ĕnervans and ĕnervātum in Prud. Cath. 8, 64; contra Symm. 2, 143), v. a. enervis To take out the nerves or sinews. Prop. (rare and post-class.): poplites securi,App. M. 8, p. 215: cerebella,Apic. 4, 2; 7, 7: enervatus Melampus,i. e. unmanned,Claud. in Eutr. 1, 315. Transf., in gen., to enervate, weaken, render effeminate (class.; esp. freq. in the part. perf.): non plane me enervavit senectus,Cic. de Sen. 10, 32: co...

enervus.definition: ēnervus, a, um, , = enervis Enervated, weak: enerva et exossa saltatio,App. M. 2, p. 104, 3.

eneruus.definition: ēnervus, a, um, , = enervis Enervated, weak: enerva et exossa saltatio,App. M. 2, p. 104, 3.

enim.definition: ĕnim Conj. [comp. of ĕ for pronom. stem i, and nam], a demonstrative corroborative particle. (Its position is regularly after the first word, or the first two or more closely connected words in the sentence; only in the comic writers sometimes at the beginning. Put after est in the fourth place: in eo est enim illud,Cic. Off. 1, 20, 67: ab omnibus est enim, etc.,id. Deiot. 13, 37; al., see below. Put after quoque: id quoque enim traditur,Liv. 2, ...

eniteo.definition: ē-nĭtĕo, tŭi, 2 To shine forth, shine out, gleam, brighten (class.). Lit.: fruges enitent, Att. ap. Cic. Tusc. 2, 5; cf.: myrtus floridis ramulis,Cat. 61, 21: campus,Verg. G. 2, 211: caelum,i. e. to become fine again, clear up,Gell. 19, 1, 7: tantum egregio decus enitet ore,Verg. A. 4, 150. Trop., to shine forth, to be eminent, distinguished (a favorite expression of Cicero): quod in eis orationibus, quae Philippicae nominantur, enituerat Demosth...

enitesco.definition: ē-nĭtesco, -nitŭi, 3 V. inch. n., to shine forth, shine out, become bright (freq. in the post-Aug. per.). Lit.: ut (oculi) in hilaritate enitescant,Quint. 11, 3, 75.—Poet.: enitescis pulchrior multo (Barine),Hor. C. 2, 8, 6. Trop., to shine forth, become distinguished: sibi novum bellum exoptabat, ubi virtus enitescere posset,Sall. C. 54, 4: gloria,Auct. Her. 4, 44, 57; cf. Gell. 17, 21, 33: facundia,Quint. 10, 5, 14; cf. Tac. Or. 20: utque studi...

enitor.definition: ē-nītor, -nīsus or -nixus (enixus, of bodily exertion, esp. of childbirth: enisus, of labor for an end, esp. of mental effort, etc. V.infra), 3, v. dep. n. and act. Neutr. Act. (perh. not ante-Aug.).

enixe.definition: ēnixē and ēnixim Advv., v. preced. fin.

eno.definition: ē-no, āvi, 1, and A. Neutr., to swim out, swim away, escape by swimming. Act., to traverse by swimming, i. e. to sail through a place (in post-Aug. poets): orbem fretis,Val. Fl. 5, 316: has valles,Sil. 3, 662.

enodatio.definition: enodo A denouement, development, explanation, Cic. Top. 7, 31; id. N. D. 3, 24, 62.

enodis.definition: ēnōdis, e, nodus Free from knots, without knots (poet. and in post-Aug. prose). Prop.: trunci,Verg. G. 2, 78; cf. cedri,Claud. Rapt. Pros. 3, 360: nitor arborum,Plin. 5, 1, 1, § 14: harundo,Mart. Cap. 9, § 906. Trop., of speech, clear, plain, intelligible: elegi,Plin. Ep. 5, 17, 2; Ambros. Ep. 1, 12; id. in Luc. 7, § 136 init.

enodo.definition: ē-nōdo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. To free from knots. Lit.: vitem,Cato, R. R. 33, 1; 44; Col. 5, 6, 14. Trop., of speech, to free from obscurity, i. e. to make plain, to explain, elucidate, unfold, declare (mostly ante-class.; syn.: expedio, extrico, enucleo, expono, interpretor, explano, explico): quod quaero abs te enoda, et qui sis explica, Att. ap. Non. 15, 7; cf. Enn. Pac., Turp., and Varr. ib. 11 sq.: nomina,Cic. N. D. 3, 24, 62: praecepta,id. In...

enormis.definition: ē-normis, e, adj.norma Out of rule (post-Aug.). Irregular, unusual: toga,Quint. 11, 3, 139: vici (with huc et illuc flexi),Tac. A. 15, 38.—Far more freq. Immoderate, immense, enormous (cf.: immensus, immodicus, summus, maximus, effusus): enormes sunt (umbrae) cerasis,Plin. 17, 12, 17, § 88: spatium (with immensum),Tac. Agr. 10; cf. hastae (with immensa scuta),id. A. 2, 14: gladii (opp. parva scuta),id. Agr. 36: Colossi,Stat. S. 1, 3, 51; cf. corp...

ens.definition: sum A thing; formed, like essentia, after the Gr. οὐσία, by Flavius (or Fabianus), acc. to Quint. 8, 3, 33 Spald. N. cr., but first used by Caesar, acc. to Prisc. 18, 8, 75: entia (= τὰὄντα), Quint. 2, 14, 2.

ensis.definition: Sanscr. root as-, asyati, hurl; asi, sword A sword, brand. Prop. (almost exclusively in the poets; synon. with gladius, acc. to Quint. 10, 1, 11; cf. also spatha, acinaces, sica, mucro, pugio),Lucr. 5, 1293; Cic. poët. ap. Gell. 15, 6, 3; and id. N. D. 2, 63 fin.; Tib. 1, 3, 47; 1, 10, 1: ensem haesurum jugulo puto,Ov. Tr. 1, 1, 484; Verg. A. 2, 393; 553 et saep.; Liv. 7, 10, 9. Meton.

entelechia.definition: in the lang. of the Aristotelian philosophy Actuality, Tert. Anim. 32; Macr. Somn. Scip. 1, 14; cf. Cic. Tusc. 1, 10, 22 (v. Lidd. and Scott, s. v. ἐντελέχεια).

entheca.definition: . A store, Cod. Th. 14, 3, 7; Dig. 32, 67, § 2 al. A magazine, Cod. Th. 15, 1, 12. A hoard, August. Serm. 355, 4.

enthymema.definition: rhetor. and dialect. t. t. A reflection, meditation, an argument (pure Lat. commentatio), Quint. 5, 10, 1; 5, 14, 1; 24; 8, 5, 4 et saep.; Cic. Top. 14; Juv. 6, 450. A conclusion drawn from the contrary, Cic. Top. 13, 55; Quint. 8, 5, 9.

enubilo.definition: ē-nūbĭlo, āvi, ātum, 1 To free from clouds, to make clear (eccl. Lat.). Lit., Tert. Apol. 35. Trop.: veritatem,Paul. Carm. 21, 667 al.

enubo.definition: ē-nūbo, psi, 3, (a Livian word). To marry out of one's rank: e patribus,Liv. 4, 4, 7; 10, 23, 4. In gen., to marry and leave the paternal house, Liv. 26, 34, 3, v. Weissenb. ad Liv. 39, 19, 5.

enucleatus.definition: ēnūclĕātus, a, um, Part. and , from enucleo.

enucleo.definition: ē-nūclĕo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. To take out the kernels, to clear from the husk. Lit.: bacas, Scribon. Comp. 233; Marc. Emp. 20; Apic. 4, 5: uva passa enucleata,id. 10, 1. Trop., to lay open, make clear, explain (cf.: enodo, extrico, expedio, etc.): haec nunc enucleare non ita necesse est,Cic. Tusc. 5, 8, 23; id. Part. 17; Gell. 19, 8, 14; Cod. Just. 1, 17 in lemm. —Hence, ēnūclĕātus, a, um, P. a.

enumeratio.definition: enumero A counting up, enumerating. In gen.: malorum,Cic. Leg. 3, 10: bonorum et malorum,id. Part. Or. 17, 58: singulorum argumentorum,id. Clu. 24: oratorum,id. Brut. 36 fin. In rhetor. lang., a recapitulation (Gr. ἀνακεφαλαίωσις), Cic. Inv. 1, 29, 45; 1, 52; Quint. 5, 14, 11; 6, 1, 1 al.

enumero.definition: ē-nŭmĕro, āvi, ātum, 1 To reckon up, count over, count out (class.). In gen.: jamne enumerasti id, quod ad te rediturum putes?Ter. Ad. 2, 2, 28: dies, * Caes. B. C. 3, 105, 2: peculium,i. e. to rate, estimate,Plaut. As. 2, 4, 91: pretium,to count out, to pay,Cic. Rosc. Am. 46, 133. In partic., to enumerate in speaking, to recount, relate (so most freq.): enumerare possum, quae sit in figuris animantium descriptio partium,Cic. N. D. 2, 47, 121; cf...

enuntiatio.definition: (), , enuntio, in rhetor. and dialect. lang. A declaration, enunciation, proposition, Cic. Fat. 1; 10; 12; Quint. 7, 3, 2; 9, 1, 23.

enuntio.definition: ē-nuntĭo (enuncio), āvi, ātum, 1 To say out (esp. something that should be kept secret), to divulge, disclose, to report, tell. Prop. (good prose): ut, quod meae concreditumst taciturnitati clam, ne enuntiarem, quoiquam,Plaut. Trin. 1, 2, 106: sociorum consilia adversariis,Cic. Rosc. Am. 40, 117; cf. Caes. B. G. 1, 17, 5: rem Helvetiis per indicium,id. ib. 1, 4, 1; cf.: dolum Ciceroni per Fulviam,Sall. C. 28, 2: mysteria,Cic. Mur. 11, 25; id. de ...

enutrio.definition: ē-nūtrĭo, īvi or ii, ītum, 4 To bring up, to nourish, feed, support (rare and not ante-Aug.). Lit.: puerum sub antris,Ov. M. 4, 289: purpurae lutense genus,Plin. 9, 37, 61, § 131: platanum, id. 12, 1, 4, § 8. Trop., to promote, nourish: unde origines aedificiorum sint institutae, et quibus rationibus enutritae et progressae sint gradatim ad hanc finitionem,Vitr. 2, 1 fin.: ingenia,Quint. 8 prooem. 2: verbis fidei,Vulg. 1 Tim. 4, 6.

eo.definition: ĕo, īvi or ii (īt, Verg. A. 9, 418 al.; cf. Lachm. ad Lucr. vol. 2, p. 206 sq.: isse, issem, etc., for ivisse, etc.,Ter. Hec. 2, 1, 25; Cic. Rosc. Am. 23, 64; id. Phil. 14, 1, 1; Ov. M. 7, 350 et saep.: isti, Turp. ap. Non. 4, 242: istis,Luc. 7, 834, etc., v. Neue Formenl. 2, 515), īre (inf. pass. irier, Plaut. Rud. 4, 7, 16), ĭtum, root i-, Sanscr. ēmi, go; Gr. εἶμι; causat. ἵημι = jacio, Georg Curtius Gr. Etym. p. 403, to go (of every kind ...

eodem.definition: ĕōdem, old dat. and abl. of idem, of place. Of the place in which, with gen. loci, in the same place (rare): res eodem est loci quo reliquisti,Cic. Att. 1, 13, 5: additi eodem (i. e. in Aventino) novi cives,Liv. 1, 33, 2: arduum est eodem loci potentiam et concordiam esse,Tac. A. 4, 4; Suet. Aug. 65; id. Calig. 53. Of the place to which.

epastus.definition: ē-pastus, a, um, Part. [pasco] Eaten up: escae,Ov. Hal. 119.

ephebia.definition: ἐφηβεία or ἐφηβία. Puberty, Don. ad Ter. And. 1, 1, 24. = ephebeum, Vulg. 2 Macc. 4, 9.

ephebus.definition: ( Gen. plur. contr. ephebūm, Stat. Th. 4, 232), m., = ἔφηβος, a male Greek youth from 18 to 20 years of age (cf.: puer, adolescens, juvenis, adultus, pubes),Ter. Eun. 5, 1, 8; Cic. Fl. 21, 51; id. N. D. 1, 28, 79; Suet. Aug. 98; id. Ner. 12; Hor. Ep. 2, 1, 171; Ov. A. A. 1, 147 al.: is postquam excessit ex ephebis (after the Gr. ἐξελθεῖν ἐξ ἐφήβων), i. e. after he had come to the age of manhood, Ter. And. 1, 1, 24 Ruhnk. (also cited in Cic...

ephemeris.definition: A day-book, diary, ephemeris (cf.: commentarius, tabulae, scriptio, acta, etc.),Cic. Quint. 18, 57; Nep. Att. 13, 6; Sen. Ep. 123; Plin. 29, 1, 5, § 9; Prop. 3 (4), 23, 20; Ov. Am. 1, 12, 25 al.: ephemeridas ejus vitae composuit, Treb. Poll. Gallien. 18, 6.

ephesius.definition: Ephĕsius, a, um, , see the foll. art.

ephesus.definition: Ephĕsus, i, f., = Ἔφεσος An old and celebrated commercial city of Ionia, with a temple to Diana, now ruins near the village of Ayasaluk, Mel. 1, 17, 2; Plin. 5, 29, 31, § 131 sqq.; Plaut. Bacch. 2, 1, 2; 2, 3, 75; 102; 4, 9, 124 et saep.—Derivv. Ephĕsĭus, a, um, , Ephesian: Diana,Plaut. Bacch. 2, 3, 73; id. Mil. 2, 5, 1; Cic. Div. 1, 23 fin.: mater,born at Ephesus,id. Phil. 3, 6, 15: pecunia,deposited in the temple there,Caes. B. C. 3, 33 fin.;...

ephi.definition: A Hebrew measure, used for grain, oil, etc.; an ephah, Vulg. Exod. 16, 36 et saep.

ephippiatus.definition: ĕphippĭātus, a, um Furnished with an ephippium: equites,Caes. B. G. 4, 2, 5.

ephippium.definition: A horse-cloth, caparison, housing (cf. clitellae): tegimen equi ad mollem vecturam paratum,Non. p. 108, 30 (pure Lat. stragulum); Varr. R. R. 2, 7, 15; id. ap. Non. l. l.; Caes. B. G. 4, 2, 4; Cic. Fin. 3, 4, 15; Gell. 5, 5, 3 al.—Prov.: optat ephippia bos piger, optat arare caballus,i. e. each envies the other's condition,Hor. Ep. 1, 14, 43.

ephod.definition: Part of the clothing of the Hebrew priest, Vulg. Exod. 25, 7 al.

ephorus.definition: ( Nom. plur. ephoroe = ἔφοροι, Val. Max. 1, 41, ext. 8), m., = ἔφορος, a member of a well-known body of Spartan magistrates, the Ephori, Cic. Leg. 3, 7, 16; id. Tusc. 1, 42, 100; id. Off. 2, 23; Nep. Them. 7, 2; id. Ages. 4.

epicopus.definition: ĕpĭcōpus, a, um Furnished with oars: phaselus,Cic. Att. 14, 16 init.

epicus.definition: ĕpĭcus, a, um Epic: poëta (Ennius),Cic. Opt. Gen. 1, 2: poëma,id. ib. 1, 1; cf. carmen,Quint. 10, 1, 62; Fulg. Myth. 1, 2.—Plur. as subst.: Epĭci, ōrum, m., the epic poets, Quint. 10, 1, 51.

epicyclus.definition: A small circle having its centre on the circumference of a greater circle, an epicycle, Mart. Cap. 8, § 879.

epidicticus.definition: ĕpĭdīctĭcus, a, um For display, declamatory: in illo epidictico genere, quod diximus proprium sophistarum,Cic. Or. 13, 42 (written as Greek, id. ib. 11, 37; 61, 207).

epigramma.definition: ( Dat. plur. epigrammatis, Cic. Att. 1, 16, 15.—Gen. plur.: epigrammatōn,Mart. 1 praef.; 1, 2; -matum,Suet. Aug. 85), = ἐπίγραμμα. An inscription; on the base of a statue, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 57; on an offering,Nep. Paus. 1, 3; on tombstones,Petr. 115 fin.; as a brand,id. ib. 103, 4. An epigram, Cic. Tusc. 1, 34, 84; id. Arch. 10, 25; Quint. 1, 5, 20; Suet. Caes. 73 et saep.; so the Epigrammata of the poet Martial.

epilepsia.definition: The falling sickness, epilepsy, Lat. morbus comitialis, Lampr. Heliog. 20: boum,Veg. Vet. 5, 32; Cael. Aur. Tard. 1, 4, 60 sq.

epilepticus.definition: ĕpĭlēptĭcus, i, m. Epileptic, Auct. Fragm. Jur. Antejust. p. 38 ed. Mai.: passio = morbus comitialis,epilepsy,Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 30, 162.

epilogus.definition: A winding up of a speech, peroration, epilogue (= peroratio or conclusio), Cic. Brut. 33 fin.; Quint. 6, 1, 55; 4, 1, 28; Cic. de Or. 2, 69; id. Tusc. 1, 47; id. Planc. 34; id. Att. 4, 15, 4; Quint. 6, 1, 37; 50 et saep.

epiphania.definition: or , , , = Ἐπιφάνεια A city of Cilicia, Plin. 5, 27, 22, § 93; Cic. Fam. 15, 4, 7 sq.

epiphora.definition: . An afflux; as a disease, a defluxion of humors, Col. 6, 17, 8; Plin. 20, 9, 40, § 103; 29, 6, 38, § 118 al. (in Cic. Fam. 16, 23, written as Greek). As a rhet. fig., a repetition, Rufin. de Fig. 1, 8, p. 30.

epiredium.definition: ἐπί-reda; perh. derived immediately from the Greeks, who adopted the Gallic reda into their language A thong by which a horse was attached to a cart, Juv. 8, 66; Quint. 1, 5, 68.

episcopalis.definition: ĕpīscŏpālis, e, episcopus Episcopal: solium, Prud. στεφ. 33.—Adv.: ĕpīscŏpālĭter, episcopally, Aug. Conf. 5, 13.

episcopatus.definition: id. The office and dignity of a bishop, episcopate, Tert. Bapt. 17; Amm. 27, 3, 12; Vulg. Psa. 108, 7 al.

episcopus.definition: An overseer, superintendent. In gen., Dig. 50, 4, 18, § 7; Inscr. Orell. 4024 (in Cic. Att. 7, 11 fin., written as Greek). In partic., a bishop (eccl. Lat.), Amm. 15, 7, 7; Vulg. Phil. 1, 1 al.

epistolium.definition: ἐπιστόλιον A short letter, note, Cat. 68, 2.

epistula.definition: (also in Cic. and ante- and post-class., , Corss. Ausspr. 2, 141; but cf. Brambach, Hülfsb. p. 35 sq. Ritschl, Opusc. 2, 493 note), , , = . In gen., a written communication, a letter, epistle (cf.: litterae, codicilli): venio nunc ad tuas litteras, quas pluribus epistolis accepi,Cic. Q. Fr. 3, 1, 3, § 8; Plaut. Bacch. 3, 6, 32; 4, 9, 83; id. Mil. 4, 6, 10 et saep.; Cic. Phil. 2, 31; Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 69 fin.; id. Fam. 2, 4 et saep.; Hor. Ep. 2, 2,...

epistularis.definition: ĕpistŭlāris (epistol-, v. epistula Init.), e, epistula, of or belonging to a letter, epistolary. Adj.: chartae,letter-paper,Mart. 14, 11in lemm.;Dig. 33, 9, 3, § 10: colloquium,epistolary,Aug. Ep. ad Marcell. 5. Subst.: epistŭlāris, is, f., a messenger of the Eagle of Jupiter: epistularis tua,Mart. Cap. 9, § 896.—Plur.: epistulāres, ium, m., state secretaries, Cod. Th. 6, 30, 7.

epistylium.definition: in arch. The cross-beam that rests on the columns, the architrave, Vitr. 3, 1 sq.; 4, 3; 5, 1; Varr. R. R. 3, 5, 11; Plin. 36, 14, 21, § 96; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 82, 11 Müll. Isid. Orig. 15, 8, 15; 19, 10, 24; Vulg. 3 Reg. 7, 6 al.

epitaphium.definition: n., = ἐπιτάφιον, or , m., = ἐπιτάφιος λόγος A funeral oration, eulogy. In gen., Inscr. Drell. 1022; 4518. Esp., of the famous oration of Pericles over the fallen Athenians, in Plato's Menexenus, Cic. Tusc. 5, 12, 36.

epithalamium.definition: A nuptial song, epithalamium, Treb. Poll. Gallien. 11. Quintilian calls the wellknown Carmen nuptiale of Catullus (62) Epithalamium, Quint. 9, 3, 16.

epitomo.definition: ĕpĭtŏmo, āvi, ātum, 1, epitome To abridge, epitomize (post-class.; cf.: excerpo, abbrevio): historiam, Treb. Poll. XXX. Tyr. 30 fin.: aliquid,Veg. M. 1, 8 fin.

epitonium.definition: ἐπιτόνιον (also written = ἐπιστόμιον) A bung, stopple, the cock in a water-pipe, Varr. R. R. 3, 5, 16; Vitr. 9, 8, 11 al.; Sen. Ep. 86, 6; Dig. 19, 1, 17, § 8.

epops.definition: The hoopoe, Ov. M. 6, 674; Verg. Cul. 251; cf. upupa.

eporedorix.definition: Ἐπορέδοριξ, Paraphr. A noble Aeduan, who served in Caesar's army, Caes. B. G. 7, 38 sq.; 7, 54 sq.; 7, 76. Another Aeduan of the same name, Caes. B. G. 7, 67 fin.

epos.definition: (occurring only in the nom. and acc.) A heroic poem, an epic; nom., Hor. S. 1, 10, 43; acc., Mart. 12, 95; Aus. Prof. 5, 10.

epoto.definition: ē-pōto (ex-poto, Plaut. Trin. 2, 4, 5 V.infra), āvi, pōtum (in late Lat. potatum, v. fin.), 1, , to drink out, off, or up, to drain, quaff, swallow (in the verb. finit. rare, and only post-Aug.; in the part. perf. class.): epotum venenum,Cic. Clu. 62, 173: medicamentum,Liv. 8, 18: potionem,Quint. 7, 2, 17; 25; Ov. M. 5, 453 al.: epoto poculo,Cic. Clu. 60, 168: poculum,Liv. 40, 24: amphoram,Suet. Tib. 42; Phaedr. 3, 1, 1; Vulg. Ezech. 23, 34: reme...

epotus.definition: ēpōtus, a, um, Part., v. epoto Init.

epulor.definition: ĕpŭlor, ātus, 1 V. dep. n. and a. [epulum], to hold an entertainment, to feast, banquet. Neutr. (class.): ut in voluptate sit, qui epuletur,Cic. Fin. 2, 5, 16; id. de Sen. 13, 45; id. Tusc. 1, 47, 113; id. Att. 5, 9; Liv. 42, 56; 44, 31; Tac. H. 3, 38.—With abl., to feast upon, Verg. A. 3, 224; id. G. 2, 537; Vulg. Deut. 12, 12 al. Act., to eat, feast upon (not ante-Aug.): aliquem epulandum ponere mensis,Verg. A. 4, 602; cf. Ov. M. 15, 111; Sen. ...

epulum.definition: n., and in the plur. heterocl. , (EPULAM antiqui etiam singulariter posuere, Paul. ex Fest. p. 82, 14 Müll.), f. etym. dub.; perh. contr. from edipulum, from edo Sumptuous food or dishes (cf.: daps, commissatio, convivium, cena, etc.). Prop. (only in the plur.): si illi congestae sint epulae,Plaut. Trin. 2, 4, 70: mensae conquisitissimis epulis exstruebantur,Cic. Tusc. 5, 21, 62: vino et epulis onerati,Sall. J. 76 fin.; so opp. vinum,Liv. 8, 16; ...

equa.definition: equus A mare, Varr. R. R. 2, 7, 4; Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 10; Verg. G. 1, 59; 3, 266; Hor. C. 2, 16, 35 et saep.—Dat. and abl. plur. equis, Varr. R. R. 2, 1, 19; Col. 6, 37, 8; Plin. 11, 41, 96, § 237; 8, 42, 64, § 156; Dig. 50, 13, 2; also, equabus,Pall. Mart. 13, 1 and 5; Serv. Verg. G. 3, 268; Cod. Just. 11, 75, 1.

eques.definition: id. A horseman, rider. In gen.: it eques et plausu cava concutit ungula terram, Enn. ap. Macr. S. 6, 1 (Ann. v. 419 ed. Vahlen); Liv. 26, 2; 28, 9; Dig. 9, 2, 57; Ov. F. 5, 700 (of Castor; cf. Hor. C. 1, 12, 26; id. S. 2, 1, 26); Hor. C. 4, 11, 27 (of Bellerophon; cf. id. ib. 3, 12, 8); id. Ep. 1, 2, 65; 1, 10, 38 al.—Poet. transf., of horse and rider: quadrupes, Enn. ap. Non. 106, 31; Gell. 18, 5; and Macr. S. 6, 9 (who, like the other ancient g...

equester.definition: ĕquester, tris, tre (m. equestris, Liv. 27, 1, 11; Verg. A. 5, 667 al.; v. Zumpt, Gram. § 100, A. 1.; like acris, celebris, celeris, etc.), adj. eques Belonging to a horseman, equestrian. In gen. (very rare): equestres statuae inauratae,Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 61; id. Phil. 6, 5; 9, 6; Suet. Tit. 2: equi,riding - horses,Vulg. 3 Reg. 4, 26.—Far more freq. In partic.

equidem.definition: ĕquĭdem, adv.comp. of the interj. ĕ and quidem enclit.; cf. edepol, a demonstrative corroborative particle Verily, truly, indeed, at all events, = certe, revera, etc. (freq. and class.). In gen. In partic.

equile.definition: id.; cf.: bubile, caprile, ovile, etc. A stable for horses, Cato, R. R. 14, 2; Varr. R. R. 2, 7, 15; Suet. Calig. 55.

equinus.definition: ĕquīnus, a, um, equus Of or belonging to horses: pecus,Varr. R. R. 2, 7, 7; cf. genus,Col. 6, 27, 1: lac,Varr. R. R. 2, 11, 1: stercus,id. ib. 1, 38, 3 al.: cervix,Hor. A. P. 1: cauda,id. Ep. 2, 1, 45: ubera,id. Epod. 8, 8: pedes,Plin. 4, 13, 27, § 95: seta, * Cic. Tusc. 5, 21, 62: emptio (i. e. equorum),Varr. R. R. 2, 7, 6: pullus,Vulg. Sir. 23, 30.

equiso.definition: equus A groom, stableboy (ante- and post-class.), Varr. ap. Non. 105, 14; 32 sq.; Val. Max. 7, 3 ext. 2; App. M. 7, p. 194: equisones nautici, who draw vessels along by ropes, Varr. ap. Non. 106, 1; id. 451, 4.

equitatus.definition: id.. * In abstr., = equitatio, a riding: atteri equitatu,Plin. 28, 15, 61, § 218. In concr.

equito.definition: ĕquĭto, āvi, ātum, 1, and A. [eques], to ride. Neutr. Act., to ride through (post-Aug.).—In pass.: flumen equitatur,Flor. 3, 4, 5: equitataque Culmina Taÿgeti,Claud. Bell. Get. 192: fluxis equitata Bactra Parthis,Sid. Carm. 23, 249.

equuleus.definition: or , , dim. equus A young horse, a colt, foal. Lit., Varr., Pompon., and Cic. ap. Non. 105, 11 sq.; Liv. 31, 12. Transf.

equus.definition: ( Gen. plur. equūm, Verg. G. 2, 542; Stat. Th. 4, 409 al.), m. Sanscr. acvas; Gr. ἵππος (ἴκκος); cf. Epŏna; root, ak-, to be sharp or swift; cf. Gr. ἄκρος, ὠκύς; Lat. acus, ocior, a horse, steed, charger. Prop. Meton.

era.definition: (less correctly, ; v. erus), ae (archaic Gen. sing. ĕrāï, Aus. Idyll. 7, 5), f. erus. Prop., the mistress of a house, with respect to the servants; the mistress, lady: nunquam era errans (i. e. Medea), etc., Enn. ap. Auct. Her. 2, 22, 34 (Trag. v. 287 Vahl.): servus Dat (puellam) erae suae,Plaut. Cas. prol. 44 sq.; so id. ib. 2, 5, 3; 2, 8, 70; id. Am. 1, 1, 105; Ter. And. 4, 2, 4; id. Eun. 4, 3, 12; 5, 3, 8. So, era major and era minor, the old ...

eradico.definition: ē-rādīco (exr-), āvi, ātum, 1 (archaic Inf. eradicarier, Plaut. Aul. 2, 4, 21), , to pluck up by the roots, to root out, eradicate (an ante-class. word). Lit.: ex terra enata,Varr. R. R. 1, 27, 2: plantationem,Vulg. Matt. 15, 13; 13, 29 al. Trop.: pugnis memorandis suis hominum aures, i. e. to wear out, pester with talking, Plaut. Ep. 3, 3, 53.

erado.definition: ē-rādo, si, sum, 3 To scratch out, scrape off (ante-class. and since the Aug. per.). Lit.: eradere atque eruere terram,Varr. L. L. 5, § 136 Müll.: muscum,Col. 4, 24, 6: medullam,id. Arb. 9 fin.; Plin. 17, 21, 35, § 162: aliquem (albo),to strike out, erase,Plin. Pan. 25, 3; Tac. A. 4, 42 fin.; cf.: inscriptos titulos monumento,Paul. Sent. 1, 21, 8; Amm. 15, 6, 2: corticem,Vulg. Sap. 13, 11.—Poet. transf.: genas, i. e. to shave off the beard (for w...

erectio.definition: erigo A setting up, erecting: tignorum,Vitr. 10, 5 fin.; 8 praef.; Vulg. Num. 10, 21. Trop., pride, insolence, Vulg. Job, 22, 20.

erectus.definition: ērectus, a, um, Part. and , from erigo.

eremita.definition: ae. An eremite, hermit, Sulpic. Sever. Dial. 17.

eremitis.definition: ĕrēmītis, ĭdis Adj. f., = ἐρημιτίς, solitary, recluse, Sid. Ep. 9, 3.

eremus.definition: ĕrēmus (ĕrĕmus, Prud. Cathem. 5, 89; id. Psych. 371), a, um Waste, desert (late Lat.). Adj.: loca,Cod. Just. 11, 57, 4. Subst.: ĕrēmus, i, m. (sc. locus), or f. (sc. regio), a wilderness, desert, Tert. Idol. 5; Sulpic. Sever. Dial. 1, 15; Vulg. Deut. 1, 19 al.

ereptio.definition: id. A forcible taking away, seizure of a possession, Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 5: animae,Tert. Spect. 2.

erga.definition: ergā Praep. [syncop. for e-regā, from ex and root rag-, to reach upward, be upright; cf. ergo, v. Corss. Ausspr. 1, 448 sqq.], over against, opposite to (cf.: adversus, versus, contra, e regione, e contrario). Lit., of locality (ante- and post-classical and rare): quae med erga aedes habet,i. e. opposite me,Plaut. Truc. 2, 4, 55 (al. modo erga): erga regiam,App. Dogm. Plat. p. 9, 21. Trop.: aliquem, more rarely aliquid, of feelings and conduct to...

ergastulum.definition: ἐργάζομαι A workhouse for offenders (slaves, debtors, etc.), a house of correction, penitentiary. Prop., Col. 1, 6, 3; 1, 8, 16; Cic. Clu. 7, 21; id. Rab. Perd. 7, 20; Liv. 2, 23; 7, 4; Suet. Aug. 32; id. Tib. 8 al.; Vulg. Exod. 6, 6 al. Transf., in plur., , , (like stabula, servitia, mancipia, etc.), the inmates of a workhouse, penitentiary convicts, * Caes. B. C. 3, 22, 2; Brutus ap. Cic. Fam. 11, 13, 2; Plin. 18, 6, 7, § 36; Flor. 4, 8, 1; J...

ergo.definition: ergō (rarely with short O in Ov. and the post-Aug. poets, Ov. H. 5, 59 Lennep.; id. Tr. 1, 1, 87; Luc. 9, 256; Val. Fl. 2, 407; Claud. Ep. 4, 17), for e-regō, from ex and root rag-, to extend upward; cf. Gr. ὀρέγω, L. rego, Germ. ragen; v. erga, and Corss. Ausspr. 1, 448 sqq., proceeding from or out of. With gen. (placed after it, like causa and gratia), in consequence of, on account of, because of (ante-class, but not in Plaut. or Ter.): quoju...

ericius.definition: er A hedgehog, urchin. Prop., Varr. ap. Non. 49, 10, and 106, 18; cf. Isid. Orig. 12, 3, 7; Vulg. Isa. 14, 23; 34, 11 (as translation of Heb. kipōd, which was probably a bird—perh. the bittern. But the LXX. and Gesenius, Thes. Heb. s. v., sustain the Vulgate). Transf., in milit. lang., a beam armed with sharp spikes to keep off assailants, Caes. B. C. 3, 67, 5 and 6; Sall. Fragm. ap. Non. 555, 2.

erigo.definition: ē-rĭgo, rexi, rectum, 3, v. a.rego To raise or set up, to erect (very freq. and class.). Lit. Trop.

erilis.definition: ĕrīlis (less correctly hĕrīlis, v. erus), e, erus Of the master or mistress of a family, the master's, the mistress's (poet.; esp. in Plaut.): erum fefelli, in nuptias conjeci erilem filium,Ter. And. 3, 4, 23; cf. id. Ad. 3, 2, 3; so, filius,Plaut. Bacch. 2, 3, 117; id. Most. 1, 1, 20; 79; Ter. Eun. 2, 2, 58; id. ib. 5, 5, 20; id. Phorm. 1, 1, 5: filia,Plaut. Aul. 1, 1, 35; id. ib. 2, 3, 8; id. Cist. 2, 3, 8: amica,id. Mil. 2, 1, 37; 44; id. ib. ...

erinaceus.definition: (), , er; cf. ericius A hedgehog, Plin. 8, 37, 56, § 133; 10, 63, 83, § 174 al. (Sillig; dub.—Jan. irenaceus).

eripio.definition: ē-rĭpĭo, ĭpŭi, eptum, 3, v. a.rapio To snatch, tear, or pull out; to snatch away, take away (freq. and class.; cf.: capio, prehendo, sumo, demo, adimo, rapio, furor). Lit. Trop., to take away, snatch away: responsiones omnes hoc verbo,Plaut. Most. 3, 1, 63; cf.: orationem alicui ex ore,id. Merc. 1, 2, 64: primam vocem ab ore loquentis,Verg. A. 7, 119: alicui jus suum,Plaut. Rud. 3, 4, 6: libertatem (hostis),id. Capt. 2, 2, 61; cf. Cic. Rep. 1, 17...

erogatio.definition: erogo. A giving out, paying out, a division, distribution: pecuniae, * Cic. Att. 15, 2 fin.; so Dig. 25, 1, 3; 50, 4, 14; Cod. Just. 12, 38, 16 al.: aquarum,Front. Aquaed. 77; so in the plur., id. ib. 3; cf. Plin. Ep. 10, 35; id. Pan. 41, 1; Tac. A. 13, 50 al.—* A repeal, abrogation: legis,Tert. Idol. 5.

erogo.definition: ē-rŏgo, āvi, ātum, 1 Orig., a pub. law t. t., to expend, pay out money from the public treasury, after asking the consent of the people: pecunias ex aerario,Cic. Vat. 12; cf. Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 71; 2, 5, 19; id. Q. Fr. 1, 2, 4, § 14; Liv. 22, 23; 33, 47 al.; cf.: pecuniam in classem,Cic. Fl. 13: in aes alienum,id. Att. 6, 1, 21: unde in eos sumptus, pecunia erogaretur,Liv. 1, 20; Vulg. Marc. 5, 26. To entreat, prevail on by entreaties: precibus ero...

errabundus.definition: errābundus, a, um, erro Wandering to and fro, wandering about (rare; not in Cic. or Caes.): odor,floating about,Lucr. 4, 692: nunc errabundi domos suos pervagarentur,Liv. 1, 29; cf. Suet. Caes. 31: naves (with dispersae), Auct. B. Afr. 2, 4: naves vagabantur,ib. 21, 3: trieris,ib. 44, 2: agmen,Curt. 8, 4, 6.—Poet. transf.: vestigia bovis,Verg. E. 6, 58.

erraticus.definition: errātĭcus, a, um, id. Wandering to and fro, wandering about, roving, erratic (mostly ante-class. and post-Aug.). In gen.: stellae, planets, Auct. ap. Gell. 3, 10, 2; 14, 1, 11; 18; Sen. Q. N. 7, 23: Delos,Ov. M. 6, 333: homo,Gell. 9, 2, 6: sanguis,i. e. herpetic,Plin. 26, 13, 84, § 136; cf. transf.: vitis serpens multiplici lapsu et erratico, * Cic. de Sen. 15, 52. Esp. in botany, of plants that spring up here and there wild, i. q. silvestris, wi...

erro.definition: erro, āvi, ātum, 1, and A. [root er-, to go; desiderative forms, ἔρχομαι (ἐρσκ-); and Lat. (ers-o) erro, to seek to reach; hence, to wander; cf. Germ. irren; Engl. err, etc., v. Georg Curtius Gr. Etym. p. 546 sq.]. Neutr. Act. in Aug. poets (only in part. perf.), to wander over or through: immensum est erratas dicere terras,Ov. F. 4, 573: ager,id. ib. 3, 655: orbis,Val. Fl. 4, 447: litora,Verg. A. 3, 690.

erroneus.definition: errōnĕus, a, um, id. Wandering about, straying: vagus atque erroneus,Sen. Ben. 6, 11, 2: canes,Col. 7, 12, 5: erroneus, ἀλήτης, πλάνος, Gloss. Labb.

error.definition: id. A wandering. In gen., a wandering, straying or strolling about (rare and mostly poet.). In partic., a wandering from the right way, a going astray.

erubesco.definition: ē-rŭbesco, bŭi, 3 V. inch. n. and a. Neutr., to grow red, to redden. Act., with acc.: jura fidemque Supplicis erubuit,he respected,Verg. A. 2, 542: fratres,to blush on account of,Prop. 3, 14, 20 (4, 13, 20 M.): soloecismum,Sen. Ep. 95, 9 (dub. al. soloecismo).—In the part. fut. pass. erubescendus, a, um, of which one should be ashamed: ignes (amoris),Hor. C. 1, 27, 15: id urbi Romanae fore erubescendum,Liv. 38, 59, 11; Vell. 2, 130, 4; Curt. 4, 2...

eruca.definition: A caterpillar, cankerworm, Col. 11, 3, 63, p. 464 Bip.; Pall. 1, 35 saep.; Col. 10, 333; Plin. 17, 24, 37, § 229, but here Sillig reads uruca, q. v. A sort of cole-wort, Brassica eruca, Linn.; Col. 11, 3, 29; 10, 109; 372; Plin. 19, 8, 44, § 154; Hor. S. 2, 8, 51; Mart. 3, 75; Vulg. Amos, 4, 9.

eructo.definition: ē-ructo, āre To belch or vomit forth, to throw up (rare but class.). Ingen., to cast forth, emit, exhale: Tartarus horriferos eructans faucibus aestus,Lucr. 3, 1012: aquam,Varr. R. R. 3, 14, 2: odorem,id. ib. 1, 4, 4: noxium virus,Col. 1, 5, 6: harenam,Verg. A. 6, 297: flammas, vaporem, fumum,Just. 4, 1, 4.

erudio.definition: ē-rŭdĭo, īvi or ii, ītum, 4, v. a., qs. to free from roughness, i. e. To polish, educate, instruct, teach (freq. and class.; cf.: doceo, edoceo, praecipio, instituo). Prop.: studiosos discendi erudiunt atque docent,Cic. Off. 1, 44, 156: aliquem,id. Div. 2, 2 (with docere); id. de Or. 3, 9, 35 (with instituere); id. ib. 2, 1, 12; Quint. prooem. § 1; 6 et saep.: filios ad majorum instituta (with instituere),Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 69; cf. id. Tusc. 1, 26:...

eruditio.definition: erudio An instructing, instruction (cf.: doctrina, disciplina, scientia, intellegentia, cognitio). Prop.: de ejus eruditione quod labores, nihil est, quoniam ingenium ejus nosti,Cic. Q. Fr. 3, 1, 4 fin.; cf. Quint. 2, 3, 10; Gell. 11, 7, 3.— Far more freq. Transf., learning, knowledge, erudition, obtained by instruction: qui praeclara eruditione atque doctrina aut utraque re ornati,Cic. Off. 1, 33; id. de Or. 2, 1; id. Fin. 1, 21, 71; id. Tusc. 1...

eruditus.definition: ērŭdītus, a, um, Part. and , from erudio.

erugo.definition: ē-rūgo, āre To clear from wrinkles, to smooth, Plin. 13, 12, 26, § 82; 21, 19, 74, § 127; 28, 12, 50, § 183.

erumpo.definition: ē-rumpo, rūpi, ruptum, 3, and n. Act., to cause to break or burst forth; to burst, sunder (rare; mostly ante-class.). Neutr., to break out, to burst or sally forth.

eruo.definition: ē-rŭo, ŭi, ŭtum, 3 To cast forth, throw out; to dig, tear, or pluck out (freq. and class.). Lit. Trop.

eruptio.definition: erumpo, II. A breaking out, bursting forth. Lit. Trop.: vitiorum,Sen. Clem. 1, 2, 2.

erus.definition: (less correctly V.infra), , m.Sanscr. root, har-; har-āmi, I seize; har-anam, hand; Gr. χείρ, χέρης; Lat. heres, hirudo; but the form erus is that of the best MSS.; cf. Ritschl, Opusc. 2, 409; Brix ad Plaut. Trin. 1, 2, 24. Lit., the master of a house or family, in respect to servants: erum atque servom saluere,Plaut. Trin. 2, 4, 34: iis, qui vi oppressos imperio coercent, sit sane adhibenda saevitia, ut eris in famulos, si aliter teneri non po...

erutor.definition: eruo A rescuer: erutor meus es tu, Domine, Vers. Lat. Psa. 69, 6, ap. August. in Psa. 69 (cf.: implicatus sum, erue, August. ib.).

ervilia.definition: ervum A kind of pulse, the bitter vetch, Varr. R. R. 1, 32, 2; Col. 2, 13, 1; Ser. Samon. 585; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 82, 21 Müll.

eruilia.definition: ervum A kind of pulse, the bitter vetch, Varr. R. R. 1, 32, 2; Col. 2, 13, 1; Ser. Samon. 585; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 82, 21 Müll.

ervum.definition: (), , Gr. ἐρέβινθος, ὄροβος; root, ar- for al-; cf. alo A kind of pulse, the bitter vetch, ervum ervilia, Linn.; Verg. E. 3, 100 Voss.; Col. 2, 10, 34; 11, 2, 10; Pall. Jan. 8; Ov. Med. fac. 55; Hor. S. 2, 6, 117.

eruum.definition: (), , Gr. ἐρέβινθος, ὄροβος; root, ar- for al-; cf. alo A kind of pulse, the bitter vetch, ervum ervilia, Linn.; Verg. E. 3, 100 Voss.; Col. 2, 10, 34; 11, 2, 10; Pall. Jan. 8; Ov. Med. fac. 55; Hor. S. 2, 6, 117.

erysisceptrum.definition: A low thorny shrub, also called adipsatheon, Plin. 24, 13, 69, § 112 al.; App. Herb. 109.

erythinus.definition: A red kind of sea-mullet, Plin. 9, 16, 23, § 166; Ov. Hal. 104.

esca.definition: ( Gen. sing. escas, Liv. Andron. ap. Prisc. p. 679 P.), f. for edca, v. esco, and edo; cf. Varr. L. L. 6, § 84 Müll., food, both of men and beasts (class.; cf.: victus, cibus, cibaria, alimenta, edulia, opsonium, pulmentum; epulae, daps, etc.). In gen. In partic., bait for catching animals.

escarius.definition: escārĭus, a, um, id.. Pertaining to food, eating: mensa,Varr. L. L. 5, § 120 Müll.; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 77, 11 Müll.: vasa,Plin. 36, 26, 67, § 198; cf. argentum,Dig. 34, 2, 19, § 12; 34, 2, 32, § 2; and absol.: escāria, ōrum, n., Juv. 12, 46: uvae,fit for eating,Plin. 14, 3, 4, § 42. —* Of or belonging to bait: vincla,Plaut. Men. 1, 1, 18.

escendo.definition: ē-scendo (exs-), di, sum, 3, and A. [scando]. Neutr., to climb up, mount up, ascend from a place (cf. ascendo init.; also: scando, peto, incedo, ingredior; rare but class.). Act., to mount, ascend a thing: pars equos escendere,Sall. J. 97, 5: vehiculum,Sen. Vit. Beat. 23: suggestum,Tac. A. 13, 5; cf. rostra,id. ib. 15, 59.

esculentus.definition: escŭlentus, a, um, id. Fit for eating, good to eat, eatable, edible, esculent; cf. poculentus: frusta,Cic. Phil. 2, 25 fin.; cf. id. N. D. 2, 49; 56 fin.; Scaev. ap. Gell. 4, 1, 17; Dig. 33, 9, 3. § 3: animalia (with innocua),Plin. 8, 55, 81, § 219: merces,Col. 11, 3, 50: ōs,i. e. filled with food.Plin. 8, 25, 37, § 90.—Comp.: a vino et esculentioribus cibis abstinere, i. e. more delicate, Hier. Ep. 22, 11.

essedarius.definition: essĕdārĭus, a, um, essedum Of or belonging to a war-chariot: mulier,Petr. 45, 7.—Hence, as subst.: essedari-us, i, m. A fighter in a (Gallic or British) war-chariot, Caes. B. G. 4, 24, 1; 5, 15, 1; 5, 19, 1; Cic. Fam. 7, 6 fin. In the Roman circus, a gladiator, Petr. 36, 6; Suet. Calig. 35; id. Claud. 21; Inscr. Orell. 2566; v. essedum.

essentia.definition: sum The being or essence of a thing; transl. of the Gr. οὐσία: haec interpretatio (rhetorices) non minus dura est, quam illa Flavii essentia atque entia,Quint. 2, 14, 2; 3, 6, 23; 8, 3, 33: cupio, propitiis auribus tuis, essentiam dicere. Ciceronem auctorem hujus verbi habeo,Sen. Ep. 58, 6.

essentialiter.definition: essentĭālĭter, essentia Essentially (late Lat.), Aug. de Trin. 7, 2.

esuries.definition: 1. esurio Hunger (postclass.). Lit., Hier. Ep. 125, 33; Alcim. 2, 18; Vulg. Deut. 28, 20. Trop.: avida ignorantiae,Sid. Ep. 6, 6.

esurio.definition: ēsŭrĭo (ess-), no Perf., ītum, īre (fut. esuribo, Pompon. and Nov. ap. Non. 479 sq.; Pompon. v. 64; Nov. v. 22 Rib.), v. desid. n. and a. [1. edo], to desire to eat, to suffer hunger, be hungry, to hunger. Lit. (class.), Plaut. Capt. 4, 2, 86; 4, 4, 4; id. Cas. 3, 6, 6 et saep.; Cic. Tusc. 5, 34; Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 34; Cael. ap. Cic. Fam. 8, 17 fin.; Hor. S. 1, 2, 115; 1, 3, 93 et saep.: esuriendi semper inexplebilis aviditas,canine hunger,Plin. 11...

esuritio.definition: id. A hungering, hunger (rare; not in Cic.),Cat. 23, 14; Gell. 16, 3, 3 sq.; Mart. 1, 100.—In plur, Cat. 21, 1.

esus.definition: ēsus, a, um, Part., v. 1. edo.

et.definition: ĕt Conj. [Sanscr. ati, beyond; Gr. ἔτι, besides, yet; Lat. et-iam, at-avus], serves to connect, in the most general manner, single words or entire sentences, and. In gen.: qui illius impudentiam norat et duritudinem, Cato ap. Gell. 17, 2, 20: te sale nata precor, Venus et genetrix patris nostri, Enn. ap. Non. 378, 16 (Ann. v. 53 ed. Vahlen): blande et docte percontat, Naev. ap. Non. 474, 7: ut, quoad possem et liceret, a senis latere numquam di...

etenim.definition: ĕt-ĕnim Conj., subjoins a corroborative clause, or one which contains the reason of a preceding statement, for, truly, and indeed, because that, since (not freq. till class. times, esp. in Cic.): verum profecto hoc petere me precario a vobis jussit ... Etenim ille, etc.,Plaut. Am. prol. 26; Ter. And. 2, 6, 9; id. Eun. 5, 9, 44: praeclare quidem dicis; etenim video jam, quo pergat oratio,Cic. Rep. 3, 32; id. de Sen. 5 fin. et saep.: quippe etenim,...

ethicus.definition: ēthĭcus, a, um, (scanned ĕthĭcīs, Prud. Hamart. 583), adj. Moral, ethic (post-class.): res,ethics,Gell. 1, 2, 4: dictio,which shows the character,Sid. Ep. 8, 11.— Hence adv.: ēthĭcos = ἠθικῶς, morally: dicere,Sen. Contr. 2, 12, 8.

ethnicus.definition: ethnĭcus, a, um Heathenish, pagan; and subst.: ethni-cus, i, m., a heathen, Tert. Pud. 9; Vulg. Matt. 5, 47; 18, 17.—Adv.: ethnĭce, heathenishly: vivere,Tert. Pud. 9.

ethologia.definition: The art of depicting or imitating character, Quint. 1, 9, 3; Sen. Ep. 95, 66; Suet. Gramm. 4.

ethologus.definition: One who jestingly imitates the manners, actions, gestures, etc., of others, a mimic: mimus,Cic. de Or. 2, 59, 242; 2, 60, 244.

etiam.definition: ĕtĭam Conj. [cf. Gr. ἔτι; with ending -am, as in quoniam, nunciam, etc.; cf. Brix ad Plaut. Trin. prol. 3], annexes a fact or thought to that which has already been said, and also, and furthermore, also, likewise, besides (syn. quoque). In gen.: hoc etiam ad malum accersebatur malum,Plaut. Bacch. 3, 3, 22; cf. Ter. And. 1, 3, 10; Cic. de Sen. 6, 16; id. N. D. 2, 52, 130: tute istic (dixisti) etiam astante hoc Sosia,Plaut. Am. 2, 2, 115: sed eti...

etiamnum.definition: ĕtĭam-numand (more freq., always in Cic. and Caes.) ĕtĭam-nunc (also written separately, etiam num ... nunc) Conj., yet, till now, still, even now, even to this time, even at this time. In gen. (in all periods): Ev. Etiamnunc mulier intu'st? Sy. Etiam, Plaut. Merc. 4, 5, 14; Varr. R. R. 3, 2, 3; Plaut. Stich. 5, 4, 16; Varr. ap. Non. 11, 15; Sen. Contr. 4, 26: de materia loquor orationis etiamnunc, non ipso de genere dicendi,Cic. Or. 34, 119: ut ...

etiamsi.definition: ĕtĭam-si (also written separately), a concessive conditional particle, = καὶ εἰ, more emphatic than etsi Even if, although, albeit.

etiamtum.definition: ĕtĭam-tumand (more rarely) ĕtĭam-tunc Conj., even then, till that time, till then, still. With imperf. tense (so usually): omnes etiamtum retinebant illum Pericli sucum; sed erant paulo uberiore filo,Cic. de Or. 2, 22 fin.: etiamtum vita hominum sine cupiditate agitabatur,Sall. C. 2, 1; id. J. 63, 6: manebant etiamtum vestigia monentis libertatis,Tac. A. 1, 74: nam etiamtum Agricola Britanniam obtinebat,id. Agr. 39; Suet. Tib. 42; so with cum, wh...

etsi.definition: et-si Conj. [et, II. H.], like etiamsi, a concessive conditional particle, though, although, albeit. Prop. Transf., sometimes like quamquam, to restrict or correct a preceding proposition, although, and yet, but, καίπερ, καίτοι: vale atque salve: etsi aliter ut dicam meres,Plaut. Capt. 3, 5, 86: utram (conditionem) malis vide: etsi hoc consilium rectum esse scio,Ter. Heaut. 2, 3, 85: habet enim res deliberationem: etsi ex parte magna tibi assen...

etymologia.definition: Etymology, Cic. Ac. 1, 8, 32; Quint. 1, 6, 1; 28; 7, 3, 25 et saep. (Cic. Top. 8, 35, written as Greek, and transl. by veriloquium).

eu.definition: eu Well! well done! bravo! an exclamation of joy or approbation, Plaut. Most. 1, 4, 26; Ter. Phorm. 3, 1, 14; Plaut. Mil. 4, 4, 10; Ter. Eun. 1, 2, 74; Hor. A. P. 328.—Esp.: Eu Hercle!Plaut. Men. 5, 1, 31; id. Rud. 3, 5, 41; id. Most. 3, 1, 58 al. Cf. Hand, Turs. II. p. 609 sq.; and see euge.

eucharis.definition: euchăris, is Agreeable, grateful, Vulg. Sir. 6, 5.

eucharistia.definition: . A thanksgiving, Tert. adv. Haer. 47. The Lord's supper in the Christian Church, the eucharist, Cypr. Ep. 10.

euge.definition: eugĕ (eugē or eugae, Ter. And. 2, 2, 8), , = , an exclamation of joy, applause, admiration, etc. Well done! good! bravo! (cf. eu; freq. in Plaut. and Ter., and in the Vulg.). In gen.: euge, euge, perbene, Ab saxo avortit fluctus ad litus scapham,Plaut. Rud. 1, 2, 75; id. Aul. 4, 6, 11; id. Ep. 3, 2, 21; id. Stich. 5, 6, 5; id. Mil. 4, 1, 20 et saep.; Ter. And. 2, 2, 8; id. Heaut. 4, 2, 10; Pers. 5, 167; 1, 75; as an indecl. subst., n.: euge tuum,...

eugeneus.definition: eugĕnēus or -īus, a, um Well-born, i. e. noble, generous; applied to wine of good quality: (vinum),Cato R. R. 6, 4; Varr. R. R. 1, 25: (uvae),Col. 3, 2, 16.

euhius.definition: Euhius (cf. Lach. ad Lucr. 5, 743; also, Euius; less correctly, as in some edd., Evius), ii, m. A surname of Bacchus, Lucr. 5, 742; Cic. Fl. 25, 60; Hor. C. 1, 18, 9; 2, 11, 17; Col. poët. 10, 424.—Acc. Euhion, Pers. 1, 102; Ov. A. A. 1, 563; voc. Euhie, Stat. Th. 2, 72; Col. poët. 10, 224.—Hence

euhoe.definition: euhoe (dissyl.; also, euoe; less correctly, ēvoe; cf. Lach. ad Lucr. 5, 743), , = εὐοῖ A shout of joy at the festivals of Bacchus: euhoe Bacche,Plaut. Men. 5, 2, 82; Ov. A. A. 1, 563; Cat. 64, 255; Verg. A. 7, 389; Hor. C. 2, 19, 5 and 7; cf.: euhan euhoe euhoe euhius,Enn. Tr. 150.

eunuchus.definition: A eunuch. Prop., Cic. Or. 70, 232; Mart. 3, 82; Juv. 6, 366; 378; 12, 35; Vulg. Gen. 37, 36 et saep. (Sc. fabula.) Fem., the name of one of Terence's comedies.

euphrates.definition: Euphrātes (in Inscr. also EVFRATES), is, m., = Εὐφράτης A wellknown river in Syria, which rises in Armenia, and, after its junction with the Tigris, empties into the Persian Gulf, now Frat, Mel. 1, 11, 2; 3, 8, 5; Plin. 5, 24, 20, § 83 sqq.; Prud. Ham. 562; Cic. N. D. 2, 52, 130; Plin. Pan. 14; abl. Euphratē, Luc. 8, 358. A philosopher in the time of the younger Pliny, Plin. Ep. 1, 10.—‡ A rare Roman surname: M. IVNIVS EVFRATES, Inscr. in Bull....

euripus.definition: (), , , = εὔριπος A narrow channel, strait. Prop. Transf., a canal, conduit, aqueduct.

euronotus.definition: The south-southeast wind, that which is between eurus and notus, Col. 11, 2, 42; Plin. 2, 47, 46, § 120; Vitr. 1, 6.

europa.definition: Eurōpa, ae, and Eurōpe, ēs, f., = Εὐρώπη. Daughter of the Phoenician king Agenor, sister of Cadmus, and mother of Sarpedon and Minos by Jupiter, who, under the form of a bull, carried her off to Crete, Ov. M. 2, 836 sq.; Hyg. Fab. 155; 178; nom. Europe, Hor. C. 3, 27, 25; 57; Prop. 2, 28, 52; gen. Europae, Mel. 2, 7, 12; acc. Europen, Ov. A. A. 1, 323; Juv. 8, 34: Europam,Varr. R. R. 2, 5, 5; Ov. H. 4, 55. The continent of Europe, named after h...

eurous.definition: eurōus, a, um, eurus; cf.: arctous, Lesbous Eastern, orient: fluctus,Verg. A. 3, 533.

eurus.definition: The southeast wind (pure Lat. Vulturnus), Col. 11, 2, 65; 5, 5, 15; Sen. Q. N. 5, 16; Plin. 2, 47, 46, § 119; Gell. 2, 22, 7 sq.; Vitr. 1, 6; Hor. C 1, 28, 25; 2, 16, 24 al.—In plur., Verg. G. 2, 339; 441; Ov. H. 11, 9 al. Transf.

eusebius.definition: A Latin rhetorician, Rufin. p. 191 Bait.

eutrapelus.definition: Εὐτράπελος (witty) A surname given to P. Volumnius, a friend of Marc Antony, Cic. Att. 15, 8, 1; Hor. Ep. 1, 18, 31 al.

eva.definition: (, Vulg. Gen. 4, 1; id. 2 Cor. 11, 3 al.) Eve, the first woman, Tert. Virg. vel. 5; Prud. Hamort. 741.

eua.definition: (, Vulg. Gen. 4, 1; id. 2 Cor. 11, 3 al.) Eve, the first woman, Tert. Virg. vel. 5; Prud. Hamort. 741.

evacuo.definition: ē-văcŭo, no Perf., ātum, 1, , to empty out, evacuate (post-Aug.). Lit.: alvum,Plin. 20, 6, 23, § 52; 32, 9, 33, § 104. Trop.

euacuo.definition: ē-văcŭo, no Perf., ātum, 1, , to empty out, evacuate (post-Aug.). Lit.: alvum,Plin. 20, 6, 23, § 52; 32, 9, 33, § 104. Trop.

evado.definition: ē-vādo, si, sum, 3 ( Perf. sync. evasti, Hor. S. 2, 7, 68; Sil. 15, 796; perf. evadi. Treb. Poll. Trig. Tyr. 5, 6), and a. Neutr., to go or come out, go forth (freq. and class.). Act. (mostly poet. and post-Aug.; not in Cic.), to pass over or pass a thing, to get over, pass beyond, leave behind.

euado.definition: ē-vādo, si, sum, 3 ( Perf. sync. evasti, Hor. S. 2, 7, 68; Sil. 15, 796; perf. evadi. Treb. Poll. Trig. Tyr. 5, 6), and a. Neutr., to go or come out, go forth (freq. and class.). Act. (mostly poet. and post-Aug.; not in Cic.), to pass over or pass a thing, to get over, pass beyond, leave behind.

evagino.definition: ē-vāgīno, no Perf., ātum, 1, vagina, to draw out of the scabbard, to unsheath (post-class.): gladio sua sponte evaginato,Just. 1, 9, 8; Hyg. Fab. 164; Vulg. Exod. 15, 10: pugionem, id. Judith, 13, 9.

euagino.definition: ē-vāgīno, no Perf., ātum, 1, vagina, to draw out of the scabbard, to unsheath (post-class.): gladio sua sponte evaginato,Just. 1, 9, 8; Hyg. Fab. 164; Vulg. Exod. 15, 10: pugionem, id. Judith, 13, 9.

evagor.definition: ē-văgor, ātus, 1 V. dep. n. and a. Neutr., to wander forth, to roam about; to scatter or spread about, to extend (class.). Act., to stray beyond,to overstep any thing: ordinem,Hor. C. 4, 15, 10.

euagor.definition: ē-văgor, ātus, 1 V. dep. n. and a. Neutr., to wander forth, to roam about; to scatter or spread about, to extend (class.). Act., to stray beyond,to overstep any thing: ordinem,Hor. C. 4, 15, 10.

evalesco.definition: ē-vălesco, lŭi, 3 V. inch. n., to become strong, increase in strength, to increase, grow (cf.: vix illa, quae παραγόμενα vocant, nobis permittimus, sed hoc feliciter, evaluit, Quint. 8, 6, 32; not ante-Aug.). Lit.: cum evaluissent flagella pedes binos,Plin. 17, 15, 25, § 116; cf. rami,id. 16, 30, 54, § 125. Trop.

eualesco.definition: ē-vălesco, lŭi, 3 V. inch. n., to become strong, increase in strength, to increase, grow (cf.: vix illa, quae παραγόμενα vocant, nobis permittimus, sed hoc feliciter, evaluit, Quint. 8, 6, 32; not ante-Aug.). Lit.: cum evaluissent flagella pedes binos,Plin. 17, 15, 25, § 116; cf. rami,id. 16, 30, 54, § 125. Trop.

evanesco.definition: ē-vānesco, nŭi, 3 ( Part. fut. evaniturus, Lact. 5, 4 fin.), v. inch. n., to vanish or pass away, to die away, to disappear (class.). Lit. Trop.: ne cum poëta scriptura evanesceret, to die away, sink into oblivion, Ter. Hec. prol. alt. 5; cf.: omnis eorum memoria sensim obscurata est et evanuit,Cic. de Or. 2, 23, 95: orationes,id. Brut. 27 fin.: Hortensius,id. ib. 94: sententiae Aristonis, Pyrrhonis (opp. stabilitatem habere),id. Tusc. 5, 30, 85 ...

euanesco.definition: ē-vānesco, nŭi, 3 ( Part. fut. evaniturus, Lact. 5, 4 fin.), v. inch. n., to vanish or pass away, to die away, to disappear (class.). Lit. Trop.: ne cum poëta scriptura evanesceret, to die away, sink into oblivion, Ter. Hec. prol. alt. 5; cf.: omnis eorum memoria sensim obscurata est et evanuit,Cic. de Or. 2, 23, 95: orationes,id. Brut. 27 fin.: Hortensius,id. ib. 94: sententiae Aristonis, Pyrrhonis (opp. stabilitatem habere),id. Tusc. 5, 30, 85 ...

evangelicus.definition: ēvangĕlĭcus (eua-), a, um Evangelical: scriptura,Tert. adv. Marc. 39: vox,Prud. Apoth. 495 et saep.

euangelicus.definition: ēvangĕlĭcus (eua-), a, um Evangelical: scriptura,Tert. adv. Marc. 39: vox,Prud. Apoth. 495 et saep.

evangelista.definition: () An evangelist, Prud. Cathem. 6, 77 et saep.; Vulg. Act. 21, 8.

euangelista.definition: () An evangelist, Prud. Cathem. 6, 77 et saep.; Vulg. Act. 21, 8.

evangelium.definition: (), , , = . Good news, Cic. Att. 2, 3, 1, written as Greek, εὐαγγέλια. The Gospel (eccl. Lat.), Vulg. Matt. 4, 23 et saep.

euangelium.definition: (), , , = . Good news, Cic. Att. 2, 3, 1, written as Greek, εὐαγγέλια. The Gospel (eccl. Lat.), Vulg. Matt. 4, 23 et saep.

evangelizator.definition: (), , evangelium A preacher of the Gospel, Tert. Cor. Mil. 9; id. Praescr. 4.

euangelizator.definition: (), , evangelium A preacher of the Gospel, Tert. Cor. Mil. 9; id. Praescr. 4.

evangelizo.definition: ēvangĕlīzo (eua-), āvi, ātum, 1, and n., = εὐαγγελίζω (eccl. Lat.). Act., to preach, declare, proclaim, always with the accessory notion of bringing good tidings, proclaiming the Gospel: vobis gaudium magnum,Vulg. Luc. 2, 10: Christum Iesum,id. Deiot. 14, 40; cf. indicium,Plin. 28, 4, 12, § 47: iram, Sen. de Ira, 3, 8: risum lugentibus,id. Ep. 29: ad aliquem honorem evocatus,Caes. B. G. 7, 57, 3: eas (ta...

evolo.definition: ē-vŏlo, āvi, ātum, 1 To fly out or forth, to fly away, to fly up (class.). Lit.: ex quercu (aquila),Cic. Leg. 1, 1, 2: extra septa,Varr. R. R. 3, 9, 15.—Absol.: evolandi potestas,Col. 8, 15, 1: longius,Dig. 41, 1, 5, § 6: aut saepe ex humili sede sublima evolat, Att. ap. Non. 489, 5 (Rib. Trag. Fragm. p. 211): evolare ubi nec Pelopidarum facta neque famam audiam, Poet. ap. Cic. Att. 15, 11, 3; id. Fam. 7, 30, 1; cf. id. ib. 7, 28; id. Att. 14, 12...

euolo.definition: ē-vŏlo, āvi, ātum, 1 To fly out or forth, to fly away, to fly up (class.). Lit.: ex quercu (aquila),Cic. Leg. 1, 1, 2: extra septa,Varr. R. R. 3, 9, 15.—Absol.: evolandi potestas,Col. 8, 15, 1: longius,Dig. 41, 1, 5, § 6: aut saepe ex humili sede sublima evolat, Att. ap. Non. 489, 5 (Rib. Trag. Fragm. p. 211): evolare ubi nec Pelopidarum facta neque famam audiam, Poet. ap. Cic. Att. 15, 11, 3; id. Fam. 7, 30, 1; cf. id. ib. 7, 28; id. Att. 14, 12...

evolutio.definition: evolvo, I. B. 1. An unrolling or opening of a book; hence, a reading: quid poëtarum evolutio voluptatis affert?Cic. Fin. 1, 7, 25.

euolutio.definition: evolvo, I. B. 1. An unrolling or opening of a book; hence, a reading: quid poëtarum evolutio voluptatis affert?Cic. Fin. 1, 7, 25.

evolvo.definition: ē-volvo, volvi, vŏlūtum, 3 ( Per diaeresin ēvŏlŭam, Cat. 66, 74: ēvŏlŭisse,Ov. H. 12, 4), , to roll out, roll forth; to unroll, unfold (class.). Lit.: (vis venti) Arbusta evolvens radicibus haurit ab imis,Lucr. 6, 141; cf. silvas,Ov. M. 12, 519: cadavera turribus,Luc. 6, 171: montes corpore,Ov. M. 5, 355: saxa nudis lacertis,Luc. 3, 481: intestina,Cels. 7, 16 et saep.: vestes,to open, unfold,Ov. M. 6, 581: volumen epistolarum,to open,Cic. Att. 9,...

euoluo.definition: ē-volvo, volvi, vŏlūtum, 3 ( Per diaeresin ēvŏlŭam, Cat. 66, 74: ēvŏlŭisse,Ov. H. 12, 4), , to roll out, roll forth; to unroll, unfold (class.). Lit.: (vis venti) Arbusta evolvens radicibus haurit ab imis,Lucr. 6, 141; cf. silvas,Ov. M. 12, 519: cadavera turribus,Luc. 6, 171: montes corpore,Ov. M. 5, 355: saxa nudis lacertis,Luc. 3, 481: intestina,Cels. 7, 16 et saep.: vestes,to open, unfold,Ov. M. 6, 581: volumen epistolarum,to open,Cic. Att. 9,...

evomo.definition: ē-vŏmo, ŭi, ĭtum, 3 To spew out, vomit forth (class.). Lit.: (haec avis scribitur) conchas cum concoxerit, evomere,Cic. N. D. 2, 49; Suet. Claud. 44; id. Ner. 2; Tac. A. 12, 67; Vulg. Jonah, 2, 11 al. Trop.: virus acerbitatis suae apud aliquem,Cic. Lael. 23, 87: in aliquem orationem ex ore impurissimo,id. Phil. 5, 7, 20: iram in aliquem,Ter. Ad. 3, 2, 14; cf. id. ib. 3, 4, 65; id. Hec. 3, 5, 65.

euomo.definition: ē-vŏmo, ŭi, ĭtum, 3 To spew out, vomit forth (class.). Lit.: (haec avis scribitur) conchas cum concoxerit, evomere,Cic. N. D. 2, 49; Suet. Claud. 44; id. Ner. 2; Tac. A. 12, 67; Vulg. Jonah, 2, 11 al. Trop.: virus acerbitatis suae apud aliquem,Cic. Lael. 23, 87: in aliquem orationem ex ore impurissimo,id. Phil. 5, 7, 20: iram in aliquem,Ter. Ad. 3, 2, 14; cf. id. ib. 3, 4, 65; id. Hec. 3, 5, 65.

evulgo.definition: ē-vulgo (evolgo), āvi, ātum, 1 To bring out among the people, to publish, divulge (not ante-Aug., and very rare): civile jus repositum in penetralibus pontificum evulgavit,Liv. 9, 46: arcanum,Tac. H. 1, 4: injurias,id. A. 13, 19: pudorem,id. ib. 14, 14.—With an object-sentence in direct discourse: sic evulgari jussit,Tac. A. 13, 9.

euulgo.definition: ē-vulgo (evolgo), āvi, ātum, 1 To bring out among the people, to publish, divulge (not ante-Aug., and very rare): civile jus repositum in penetralibus pontificum evulgavit,Liv. 9, 46: arcanum,Tac. H. 1, 4: injurias,id. A. 13, 19: pudorem,id. ib. 14, 14.—With an object-sentence in direct discourse: sic evulgari jussit,Tac. A. 13, 9.

evulsio.definition: evello A pulling out: dentis,Cic. N. D. 3, 22, 57. Eradication, utter destruction, Vulg. Jerem. 12, 17.

euulsio.definition: evello A pulling out: dentis,Cic. N. D. 3, 22, 57. Eradication, utter destruction, Vulg. Jerem. 12, 17.

ex.definition: ex or ē (ex always before vowels, and elsewh. more freq. than e; e. g. in Cic. Rep. E occurs 19 times, but ex 61 times, before consonants—but no rule can be given for the usage; cf., e. g., ex and e together: qui ex corporum vinculis tamquam e carcere evolaverunt,Cic. Rep. 6, 14. But certain expressions have almost constantly the same form, as ex parte, ex sententia, ex senatus consulto, ex lege, ex tempore, etc.; but e regione, e re nata, e vest...

exacerbatio.definition: exacerbo An exasperation, Rufin. de Schem. 11, p. 274: peccatorum, i. e. because of, Salv. Gub. Dei, 4, 7. Esp., of the stirring of divine anger by the Jews in the wilderness, the provocation, Vulg. Hebr. 3, 8; 15.

exacerbo.definition: ex-ăcerbo, āvi, ātum, 1, (not anteAug.). To exasperate, irritate, provoke, make angry; to grieve, afflict: ut recenti aliqua ira exacerbarentur animi,Liv. 2, 35 fin.; 46; 6, 18; 8, 33; Suet. Tib. 62; 75; Plin. Ep. 8, 5, 2; Vulg. Psa. 9, 24 al. In jurid. Lat., to aggravate, increase a punishment: supplicia,Dig. 48, 19, 16 fin.; cf.: crimen verbis impiis,Paul. Sent. 5, 29, 1; pass. impers.: crimine majestatis facto maxime exacerbatur in milites,ib....

exactio.definition: exigo. * A driving out, expelling: (regum),Cic. de Or. 1, 9, 37 (perh. only on account of the preceding exactis regibus). A demanding, exacting, requisition. A finishing, completion, Vitr. 3, 1; 6, 11; Aus. Idyll. 11, 5.

exactor.definition: id.; cf. also exactio. * A driver-out, expeller: regum (Junii Valeriique),Liv. 9, 17, 11. A demander, exactor (cf.: redemptor, manceps, magister; also: publicanus, portitor).

exactus.definition: exactus, a, um, Part. and , from exigo.

exacuo.definition: ex-ăcŭo, ŭi, ūtum, 3 To make very sharp, to sharpen, make pointed (class.). Lit.: ferramenta cote,Plin. 28, 4, 12, § 47; 34, 14, 41, § 146: ridicas,Col. 11, 2, 12: vallos furcasque bicornes,Verg. G. 1, 264: spicula,id. ib. 4, 74: dentes,id. ib. 3, 255: metas in angustissimas vertices,Col. 2, 18, 2: cornua in leve fastigium,Plin. 11, 37, 45, § 124 et saep. Trop.

exadversum.definition: ex-adversum (-vors-) and ex-adversus (-vors-), and Praep.Lit. from opposite; hence, over against, opposite, vis-a\-vis. Adv.: apud ipsum lacum est pistrilla, et exadversum fabrica,Ter. Ad. 4, 2, 44: video exadvorsum Pistoclerum,Plaut. Bacch. 4, 7, 37: ea sita erat exadvorsum,Ter. Phorm. 1, 2, 47: inque earum locum bina castra exadversum constituta erant,Suet. Caes. 40 Roth; App. Flor. p. 353; Amm. 23, 6, 72.—With dat.: exadvorsum ei loco Tonstrin...

exaduersum.definition: ex-adversum (-vors-) and ex-adversus (-vors-), and Praep.Lit. from opposite; hence, over against, opposite, vis-a\-vis. Adv.: apud ipsum lacum est pistrilla, et exadversum fabrica,Ter. Ad. 4, 2, 44: video exadvorsum Pistoclerum,Plaut. Bacch. 4, 7, 37: ea sita erat exadvorsum,Ter. Phorm. 1, 2, 47: inque earum locum bina castra exadversum constituta erant,Suet. Caes. 40 Roth; App. Flor. p. 353; Amm. 23, 6, 72.—With dat.: exadvorsum ei loco Tonstrin...

exaedifico.definition: ex-aedĭfĭco, āvi, ātum, 1 To finish building, to build up, erect, construct (rare but class.). To turn out of doors: me ex his aedibus,Plaut. Trin. 5, 2, 3.

exaequo.definition: ex-aequo, āvi, ātum, 1 To make even or level with any thing. To equal, be equal to any one; with acc. (cf. aequo): ut longitudo aut plenitudo harum (syllabarum) multitudinem alterius assequatur et exaequet,Auct. Her. 4, 20, 28: tetricas Sabinas,Ov. Am. 3, 8, 61.

exaestuo.definition: ex-aestŭo, āvi, ātum, 1, and A., to boil up, foam up, ferment (not freq. till after the Aug. period; in Cic. and Caes. not at all). Neut. Act., to boil up with, to give forth, exhale (very rarely): hos igitur tellus omnes exaestuat aestus,Lucr. 6, 816; so, aestus,id. 2, 1137.

exaggero.definition: ex-aggĕro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. To raise a mound, dam, or dike; to heap up (class.; cf.: acervo, coacervo, cumulo, aggero). Lit.: aggesta humo planitiem,Curt. 6, 5: terram,Plin. 19, 8, 41, § 139: clivum super capita columnarum,id. 36, 14, 21, § 96: locum operibus,to surround with ramparts,Vitr. 10, 22: pluribus stramentis exaggerandum est aviarium,to be abundantly filled, supplied,Col. 8, 11, 9. Trop.: hic alteri alteris mortem morti exaggerabant,...

exagito.definition: ex-ăgĭto, āvi, ātum, 1 To drive out of its position or place; to stir up, rouse up, disturb. Lit. (very seldom): ut quicquid faecis subsederit exagitet, et in summum reducat,Col. 12, 19, 4: vis (venti) exagitata foras erumpitur,Lucr. 6, 583. —Poet.: lustra ferarum Venatu,to disturb,Sil. 16, 553: lepus hic aliis exagitandus erit,to rouse, start,Ov. A. A. 3, 662; cf. Petr. 131, 7. Trop., to rouse up (qs. like a wild beast), to disquiet, harass, per...

exaltatio.definition: exalto. Exaltation, elevation (eccl. Lat.): ab exaltatione tua dispersae sunt gentes,Vulg. Isa. 33, 3. Trop., pride, haughtiness: non congruit professoribus humilitatis,Tert. Cult. Fem. 3; cf. oculorum,Vulg. Prov. 21, 4: stultorum,id. ib. 3, 35.

exalto.definition: ex-alto, āvi, ātum, 1, altus (postAug.; mostly eccl. Lat.). To raise, elevate, exalt: deus alia exaltat, alia submittit,Sen. Q. N. 3 prooem.: TERMINOS VETVSTATE COLLAPSOS,Inscr. Fabr. p. 748, no. 555: solium,Vulg. Isa. 14, 13. To deepen: fodiunt (sulcos) et exaltant in tres pedes,Col. 3, 13, 4: sulcum,id. 3, 13, 9: orbem ablaqueationis,id. 4, 4, 2.

examen.definition: for ex-agmen, from ex and ago; cf. contamino and contagies, flamen and flagrare. A multitude issuing forth or flying out, a swarm. Primarily and class. of a swarm of bees: res rusticae laetae sunt tum pecudum pastu, apium examinibus, florum omnium varietate,Cic. de Sen. 15 fin.; so, apium,id. Off. 1, 44, 157; id. Div. 1, 33 fin.; Liv. 4, 33 et saep.; cf. Varr. R. R. 3, 16, 29; Col. 9, 3 fin.; 9, 4 fin. et saep.; Plin. 11, 10, 10, § 23; Verg. G. 2...

examinator.definition: id.. * Lit., a weigher, Cassiod. Var. 6, 18 fin. Trop., an examiner (late Lat.), Tert. Apol. 9; Aug. contr. Cresc. 3, 73.

examinatus.definition: exāmĭnātus, a, um, Part. and , from examino.

examino.definition: exāmĭno, āvi, ātum, 1, v. n. and A. [examen]. * (acc. to examen, I.).— Neut., to form swarms, to swarm: examinant alvi,Col. 9, 14, 5. (acc. to examen, II.).

exanimalis.definition: ex-ănĭmālis, e Adj. pass. (perh. only in Plaut.), lifeless, dead: ni illum exanimalem faxo,Plaut. Bacch. 4, 8, 7.—Act., deadly: curae exanimales,id. Rud. 1, 4, 2.

exanimis.definition: ex-ănĭmis, e, and ex-ănĭmus, a, um (cf. Wagner ad Verg. A. 4, 8; the latter form common in the plur., of which the former has only exanimes, nom. and acc.), anima Lifeless, dead (mostly postAug.; not in Cic. and Caes.; cf.: inanimis, exanimatus, mortuus). Lit. Transf., half dead with fear, terrified, dismayed (very rare; only in form exanimis): audiit exanimis,Verg. A. 4, 672; cf. Hor. S. 1, 1, 76; 2, 6, 114; Liv. 1, 25, 6.

exanimo.definition: ex-ănĭmo, āvi, ātum, 1 To deprive of air or wind. To deprive of life, to kill (freq. and class.).

exaperio.definition: ex-ăpĕrĭo, īre To open wide, throw open (very rare): exapertae repente delubri fores, et audita major humana vox,Tac. H. 5, 13: implicatissimam nodositatem,to undo, unloose,Aug. Conf. 10.

exardesco.definition: ex-ardesco, arsi, arsum, 3 V. inch. n., qs. to blaze out, i. e. to kindle, take fire (class.; esp. freq. in the trop. sense and in Cic.; cf.: ardeo, ferveo, caleo, flagro, candeo, uro, etc., incendor, inflammor, etc.). Lit.: nulla materies tam facilis ad exardescendum est, quae, etc.,Cic. de Or. 2, 45 fin.: sulphur exardescens,Plin. 35, 15, 50, § 175. Trop., to be kindled, inflamed, to break out (in a good and bad sense).

exaresco.definition: ex-āresco, rŭi, 3 V. inch. n., to dry up, become completely dry (rare, but class.). Lit.: vestimenta uvida,Plaut. Rud. 2, 7, 20: frumentum,Varr. R. R. 1, 32: silva omnis radicitus,Suet. Galb. 1: amnes,Cic. Pis. 33, 82; id. Div. 1, 19 fin.; cf. fontes, * Caes. B. C. 3, 49, 5: lacus et stagna,Dig. 41, 1, 12: lacrimae,to dry up,Cic. Att. 10, 14. Trop.: neque dum exarui ex amoenis rebus et voluptariis,Plaut. Mil. 3, 1, 46: sic omnis fetus repressus, ...

exarmo.definition: ex-armo, āvi, ātum, 1 To deprive of arms, to disarm (post-Aug.). Lit.: cohortes,Tac. H. 2, 76 fin.: dextras,Luc. 5, 356: Medos,id. 8, 387; Col. 7, 3, 5; cf. Lampr. Hel. 21. Trop., to disarm: filium mater Veturia lacrimis suis exarmavit,Flor. 1, 22, 3 Duker.; cf.: nautas mirabili forma,Petr. 105, 7: accusationem,Plin. Ep. 3, 9, 29.

exaro.definition: ex-ăro, āvi, ātum, 1 To plough or dig up (class.). Lit.: radices, Cato. R. R. 61; id. ap. Plin. 17, 18, 30, § 127; Plin. 18, 6, 8, § 46: sepulcra,Cic. Leg. 2, 23, 58: terminos (with deicere),Dig. 10, 1, 4, § 4: deum, puerum,Cic. Div. 2, 23, 51; 2, 38, 80. Transf.

exasperatio.definition: exaspero A roughness, Scrib. Comp. 222; Veg. Vet. 5, 61, 1. Bitterness, exasperation, Tert. adv. Marc. 2, 16; Macr. S. 7, 12, 38.

exasperatrix.definition: id. She who irritates or exasperates, Vulg. Ezech. 2, 8.

exaspero.definition: ex-aspĕro, āvi, ātum, 1 To make rough, to roughen (not ante-Aug.). Lit.: fauces,Cels. 1, 3; cf.: summam cutem,id. 3, 27: arterias,Plin. 22, 23, 48, § 100: corpus,id. 31, 6, 34, § 67: tussim,id. 23, 4, 51, § 97: faucium vitio exasperatur vox,Quint. 11, 3, 20: undas,to roughen, stir up,Ov. Am. 2, 11, 27: mare fluctibus,Liv. 37, 12 fin. (cf. aspero).—Poet.: aegida innumeris signis,i. e. to adorn with raised sculptures,Claud. III. Cons. Honor. 193: e...

exauctoro.definition: ex-auctōro, āvi, ātum, 1, Milit. t. t. To discharge from service (after sixteen years of service, before the end of the usual term of twenty years, i. e. before the regular missio; see missio. This discharge was either an honorable one or a punishment. The honorably discharged soldiers remained four years in the army as a separate corps under a vexillum, with peculiar privileges; cf. mitto, dimitto). Prop. Trop.: verba exauctorata a sequenti aeta...

exaudibilis.definition: exaudībĭlis, e, exaudio That may be heard or listened to, Aug. Sol. 1, 1. Giving ear to requests, listening, Schol. Juv. 13, 248.

exaudio.definition: ex-audĭo, īvi or ii, ītum, 4 To hear or perceive clearly (class.): Nec satis exaudiebam, nec sermonis fallebar tamen, Quae loquerentur,Plaut. Epid. 2, 2, 55; cf. id. Merc. 4, 3, 8; id. Men. 3, 2, 13; id. Trin. 3, 3, 25: cum aliquantulum progressus esset, subito exaudivit hinnitum,Cic. Div. 1, 33 fin.; cf. id. Att. 13, 48; Caes. B. G. 6, 39, 1; 7, 61, 3; id. B. C. 1, 66, 1; 3, 105, 3; Liv. 1, 29; 2, 27; 5, 52; 8, 33 et saep.: maxima voce, ut omnes...

exauditio.definition: exaudio, II. B. A hearkening to, granting: oratio exauditione dei dignior,Aug. Civ. D. 21, 24; Vulg. 2 Chron. 33, 19.

exauditor.definition: id. One who hearkens to, grants, Vulg. Sirach, 35, 19.

exauguratio.definition: exauguro A desecrating, profaning: omnium sacellorum exaugurationes,Liv. 1, 55, 3.

excaeco.definition: ex-caeco, āvi, ātum, 1 To blind, make blind (rare). Lit.: num ergo is excaecat nos aut orbat sensibus? etc., * Cic. Ac. 2, 23, 74; Plin. 20, 18, 76, § 200; Flor. 2, 20, 5. Trop.: oculos animosque (fama),Petr. 141, 5: formam,i. e. to render uncomely, to disfigure,id. 128, 3: nec accipies munera quae excaecant prudentes,Vulg. Exod. 23, 8.

excalceo.definition: ex-calcĕo (-calcĭo), āvi, ātum, 1, (the deponent form, v. below) To take off the shoes. In gen.: petiit, ut sibi pedes praeberet excalciandos,Suet. Vit. 2.—More freq. with a personal object and in the part. perf.: excalciatus cursitare,unshod, barefoot,Suet. Vesp. 8; Mart. 12, 88; cf. mid. in the verb. finit.: neque umquam aut nocte aut die excalcearetur aut discingeretur,Vell. 2, 41 fin.; and as a verb. dep.: ut nemo se excalceatur, Varr. ap. No...

excalfactorius.definition: excalfactōrĭus, a, um, id. Warming, heating (a Plinian word), Plin. 21, 18, 72, § 120; 24, 11, 64, § 105; 25, 13, 95, § 152.

excandescentia.definition: excandesco Nascent anger, passionateness, irascibility, Cic. Tusc. 4, 9, 21; cf. App. Dogm. Plat. 1 fin.

excandesco.definition: excandesco, dŭi, 3 V. inch. n., to grow hot, to take fire, kindle, to glow (class.). Lit.: cum bitumen et sulphur additum est, excandescet,Cato R. R. 95; Col. 7, 5, 16. Trop., to glow, to burn, esp. with anger: haec nullam habent vim, nisi irā excanduit fortitudo, * Cic. Tusc. 4, 19, 43: id postquam resciit, excanduit, Cael. ap. Cic. Fam. 8, 12, 2; cf. Petr. 53, 8; 57, 1; Suet. Claud. 40; id. Ner. 40: in aliquem,id. Vesp. 14; cf.: in exteros,Col....

excarnifico.definition: ex-carnĭfĭco, no Perf., ātum, 1, , to cut or tear any one to pieces (a rare word). Lit.: aliquem,Cic. N. D. 3, 33 fin.; Suet. Vit. 17; Sen. Ep. 24. Trop., to torment, torture: aliquem,Ter. Heaut. 4, 6, 9: excarnificatus animus, Sen. de Ira, 3, 4: comitem,Amm. 14, 5, 1; 14, 9, 6.

excavo.definition: ex-căvo, no Perf., ātum, 1, , to hollow out. Lit.: trullam,Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 27 fin.: cavernam sibi rostro,Plin. 9, 27, 43, § 82: ripas,id. 10, 33, 49, § 95: terram,id. 33 prooem.: lapides excavant aquae,Vulg. Job, 14, 19. Transf., in mal. part., Auct. Priap. 51, 4.

excauo.definition: ex-căvo, no Perf., ātum, 1, , to hollow out. Lit.: trullam,Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 27 fin.: cavernam sibi rostro,Plin. 9, 27, 43, § 82: ripas,id. 10, 33, 49, § 95: terram,id. 33 prooem.: lapides excavant aquae,Vulg. Job, 14, 19. Transf., in mal. part., Auct. Priap. 51, 4.

excedo.definition: ex-cēdo, cessi, cessum, 3 ( Subj. perf. sync. excessis, Ter. And. 4, 4, 21), and a. Neut., to go out, go forth or away, to depart, retire, withdraw (freq. and class.; cf.: discedo, deficio, destituo, desero, linquo, relinquo). Act. (post-Aug.).

excellenter.definition: excellenter, adv. Excellently; v. excello, P. a. 1. fin.

excellentia.definition: excellentia, ae, f.excello, 1. Superiority, excellence, perfection (abstr. and rel.): magna cum excellentia praestantiaque animantium reliquarum,Cic. Off. 1, 28; cf. id. ib. 1, 27 fin.: animi excellentia magnitudoque,id. ib. 1, 5, 17; so, picturae,Plin. 35, 14, 49, § 173: crurum,id. 34, 8, 19, § 82; Prud. στεφ. 10, 52: propter excellentiam, pre-eminence, Gr. κατ̓ ἐξοχήν, ut Homerus propter excellentiam commune poëtarum nomen efficit apud Graeco...

excello.definition: ex-cello, cellŭi, celsum, 3 (also acc. to the 2d conj. Praes. indic. excellet, Aem. Mac. ap. Diom. p. 371 P., and subj. excelleat, Cic. Fragm. ap. Prisc. p. 838 and 896 P.), v. a. and n. cello. Act., to raise up, elevate; only: recellere reclinare, et excellere in altum extollere,Fest. p. 274, 31; and Paul. ib. 275, 11 Müll.; cf. the P. a. excelsus, below. Neut., to rise, elevate itself (cf.: antecello, praesto, antecedo, emineo, floreo, vigeo).

excelse.definition: excelsē, adv., v. excello, P. a. 2. Fin.

excelsitas.definition: excelsus Loftiness, height. Lit.: montium,Plin. 2, 64, 64, § 160: harundinis,id. 16, 36, 66, § 167: lilii,id. 21, 5, 11, § 23. Trop.: excelsitas animi et magnitudo,Cic. Off. 3, 5, 24.

excelsus.definition: excelsus, a, um, , v. excello Fin. 2.

exceptio.definition: id. An exception, restriction, limitation [good prose and very freq., esp. in Cic.). In gen.: consiliorum, voluntatum sine ulla exceptione communitas,Cic. Lael. 17; so, sine (ulla) or cum exceptione,id. Fam. 6, 5, 1; id. Caecin. 8 fin.; Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 31; id. Att. 8, 4, 2; id. Q. Fr. 1, 1, 13; id. Inv. 2, 57, 172; Quint. 7, 1, 50; Plin. Ep. 1, 2, 5 et saep.; cf. in plur.: unus imperitat nullis jam exceptionibus,Tac. G. 44: quod si exceptio faci...

excepto.definition: excepto, āvi, ātum, 1, excipio To take out, to take up, catch (very rare): barbatulos nullos exceptans de piscina, * Cic. Par. 5, 2, 38; so, aliquem, * Caes. B. G. 7, 47 fin.: (equae) exceptant leves auras, catch up., i. e. snuff up, * Verg. G. 3, 274; cf. poet.: per pectora saevas Exceptat mortes, * Sil. 9, 369.

exceptus.definition: exceptus, a, um, Part., from excipio.

excerebro.definition: ex-cĕrēbro, ārecerebrum To deprive of brains, i. q. to make senseless: canem,Vulg. Isa. 66, 3.—Part.: ex-cerēbrā-tus, a, um, deprived of brains, i. q. rendered senseless, stupefied: excerebratus es novo vino,Tert. adv. Marc. 4, 11.

excerpo.definition: ex-cerpo, psi, ptum, 3, carpo To pick or take out. * Lit.: semina pomis,Hor. S. 2, 3, 272. Trop. (class.).

excessus.definition: excedo, I. A. 2. and B. 2.. A departure. A standing out, projecting beyond a certain limit. *

excetra.definition: perh. corrupted from ἔχιδνα A snake, serpent (very rare). Prop., Plaut. Pers. 1, 1, 3 sq.; * Cic. poet. Tusc. 2, 9, 22. Transf., a reproachful epithet for a bad, intriguing woman, Plaut. Cas. 3, 5, 19; id. Ps. 1, 2, 82; Liv. 39, 11.

excidium.definition: (sometimes written , as if from exscindo), , usually referred to ex-cīdo Overthrow, demolition, subversion, ruin (especially of cities, buildings, etc.), destruction (not freq. till the Aug. per.; not in Caes. and Cic.): urbis,Liv. 27, 39 fin.; Tac. H. 1, 80; 3, 76; Verg. A. 5, 626.—In plur.: petit urbem excidiis,Verg. G. 2, 505; id. A. 2, 643; 10, 46; Liv. 9, 45; 29, 1 al.: castellorum,Tac. H. 4, 15: arcium,Verg. A. 12, 655: Libyae,id. ib. 1, 22...

excido.definition: ex-cĭdo, cĭdi, 3, cado To fall out or down, to fall from (class.; esp. freq. in the trop. sense). Lit. Trop.

excio.definition: ex-cĭo, īvi or ii, itum (long and short equally freq.; cf. excĭtus, Enn. ap. Cic. Div. 1, 20, 40; Lucr. 4, 1207; Cat. 61, 11; 63, 42; 64, 56; Verg. A. 4, 301; 7, 376; 12, 445; Ov. M. 2, 779 al.: Excītus,Lucr. 4, 1215; Verg. A. 3, 675; 7, 642; 10, 38; Ov. M. 8, 338; 11, 384; Sil. 7, 635; Luc. 1, 239 al.; also acc. to cieo, ēre: excies,Att. Trag. 300 (Rib. Trag. Fragm. p. 175): exciet,Plaut. Ps. 5, 2, 1; inf. exciere, Liv. 7, 11, 11; imperf. exciba...

excipio.definition: ex-cĭpĭo, cēpi, ceptum, 3, capio. (With the notion of the ex predominating.) To take or draw out. (With the notion of the verb predominating.) To take a thing to one's self (in a good or bad sense), to catch, capture, take, receive.

excisus.definition: excīsus, a, um, Part., from excīdo.

excito.definition: excĭto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. freq. a.excio To call out or forth, to bring or send out, to wake or rouse up (freq. and class.; cf.: provoco, evoco; irrito, lacesso, invito). Lit.: unde (Acherunte) animae excitantur obscura umbra, Poëta ap. Cic. Tusc. 1, 16, 37: aliquem a portu,Plaut. Am. 1, 1, 10: aliquem huc foras,id. Rud. 1, 5, 2: si excitatus fuerit de spectaculis,turned out, expelled,Quint. 3, 6, 19: dormientes spectatores e somno,to wake up,Plaut...

exclamatio.definition: exclamo A loud calling or crying out (very rare). In gen.: acuta atque attenuata nimis,Auct. Her. 3, 12, 21: acutas vocis exclamationes vitare debemus,id. ib.; Quint. 11, 3, 179; Vulg. Sirach, 35, 13. In partic., as a figure of rhetoric, an exclamation, Auct. Her. 4, 15, 22; Cic. de Or. 3, 54, 207; id. Or. 39, 135; Quint. 9, 1, 34; 9, 2, 27; 9, 3, 97; Tac. Dial. 26; 31.

exclamo.definition: ex-clāmo, āvi, ātum, 1, and A. Neut., to call or cry aloud, to call or cry out, to exclaim: cum exclamasset Laelius,Cic. Rep. 6, 12 fin.: in stadio cursores exclamant quam maxime possunt,id. Tusc. 2, 23, 56; cf. Plaut. Most. 2, 2, 57: majus,Cic. Tusc. 2, 24, 56: contiones saepe exclamare vidi, cum apte verba cecidissent,i. e. to applaud loudly,id. Or. 50, 168; cf. Quint. 1, 6, 45.—Pass. impers.: quoties exclamandum erit, lateris conatus sit ille,...

excludo.definition: ex-clūdo, si, sum, 3 ( Perf. sync. exclusti for exclusisti, Ter. Eun. 1, 2, 18) [cludo, claudo], to shut out, exclude; to cut off, remove, separate from any thing (class.). Lit. Trop., to exclude, except, remove, hinder, prevent: Crassus tres legatos decernit, nec excludit Pompeium,Cic. Fam. 1, 1, 3: excludi ab omni doctrina,id. de Or. 1, 11, 46; cf.: exclusit illum a re publica,id. Phil. 5, 11, 29: ab hereditate fraterna excludi,id. Clu. 11, 31;...

exclusio.definition: excludo A shutting out, exclusion (very rare; not in Cic.): de exclusione verbum nullum,Ter. Eun. 1, 2, 8: ventorum,Vitr. 1, 6: exceptio est quasi quaedam exclusio, etc.,Dig. 44, 1, 2.

excogitatio.definition: excogito A thinking out, a contriving, devising, inventing (syn. inventio): quid? illa vis quae tandem est, quae investigat occulta, quae inventio atque excogitatio dicitur?Cic. Tusc. 1, 25, 61: excogitationem non habent difficilem, may be thought out without difficulty, id. de Or. 2, 27, 120: hominum malae artis,Vulg. Sap. 15, 4.

excogito.definition: ex-cōgĭto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. To find out by thinking, to contrive, devise, invent (freq. and class.; cf.: comminiscor, simulo, confingo, fingo, etc.): quid enim mali aut sceleris fingi aut excogitari potest, quod non ille conceperit?Cic. Cat. 2, 4, 7: ad haec igitur cogita, mi Attice, vel potius excogita,id. Att. 9, 6, 7: quid igitur causae excogitari potest, cur? etc.,id. Deiot. 7, 20: novam interregni ineundi rationem,id. Rep. 2, 12: aliquid ...

excolo.definition: ex-cŏlo, cŏlŭi, cultum, 3 To work carefully, to tend, cultivate. Lit. (very rare, and mostly post-Aug.): vineas,Plin. 14, 4, 5, § 48; cf. rura, Claud. ap. Eutr. 2, 196: victum hominum (boves),Plin. 8, 47, 72, § 187: lanas rudes,i. e. to spin fine,Ov. A. A. 2, 220. Trop.

excommunicatio.definition: excommunico Ban of the Church, excommunication, Aug. de Fide, 3 et saep.

excommunico.definition: ex-commūnĭco, āvi, ātum, 1, (lit., to put out of the community; hence, in eccl. Lat.) To lay under the ban of the Church, to excommunicate, Hier. adv. Ruf. 2, 18: aliquem excommunicatum habere, Hilar. Op. Hist. Fragm. 11, 4.

excoquo.definition: ex-cŏquo, xi, ctum, 3 To boil out, melt out, dry up. Lit.: usque coquito, dum dimidium excoquas,i. e. you boil away,Cato, R. R. 107, 2: mustum ad dimidium,Col. 12, 19, 1: testudinem vino,to boil thoroughly,Plin. 32, 4, 14, § 38: glebas melle,id. 37, 12, 74, § 194: ferrum (ignis),i. e. to harden,Ov. M. 14, 712: harenas admixto nitro in vitrum,Tac. H. 5, 7: lapide cremato in caminis donec excoquatur in rubricam,Plin. 34, 13, 37, § 135: ignis vitium...

excorio.definition: ex-cŏrĭo, āre, corium To strip of its skin or covering, to skin, strip, Cassiod. Hist. Eccl. 10, 30; Vulg. Micah, 3, 3. In mal. part., App. M. 10, p. 717 Oud. dub.; cf. Hildebr. ed. min. p. 137, note 3.

excors.definition: ex-cors, cordis, cor, the heart, as the seat of intelligence; v. cor Without intelligence, without understanding, senseless, silly, stupid (class.; cf.: amens, demens, vecors, insanus, vesanus, delirus): aliis cor ipsum animus videtur: ex quo excordes, vecordes, concordesque dicuntur,Cic. Tusc. 1, 9, 18; cf.: an quod aspexit (taurus) vestitu purpureo excordem Caesarem, ipse corde privatus est?id. Div. 2, 16, 36: excors, caecus, incogitabilis,Plau...

excrementum.definition: excerno. What is sifted out, the refuse, Col. 8, 5, 25; Pall. Febr. 26, 3; id. Nov. 20, 4.—More freq. What passes from the body, excrement, ordure, Plin. 11, 26, 32, § 94; 9, 45, 68, § 147: oris,spittle,Tac. H. 4, 81: narium,mucus of the nose,id. A. 16, 4.

excresco.definition: ex-cresco, crēvi, crētum, 3 V. inch. n., to grow out or forth, to grow up, rise up (not ante-Aug.). Lit. Trop., to grow immoderately, to increase, enlarge: nec minus evitanda est immodica ejus prooemii longitudo, ne in caput excrevisse videatur,Quint. 4, 1, 62: fructus in tantum excrevit, ut, etc.,Dig. 36, 1, 27, § 16 fin.: litium series,Suet. Vesp. 10.—Hence, ex-crētus, a, um, , grown up, fullgrown: animalia,Lact. 2, 11 med. al. (so, haedi, Verg...

excrucio.definition: ex-crŭcĭo, āvi, ātum, 1 (archaic Inf. praes. excruciarier, Ter. Heaut. 3, 1, 4), , to torment greatly, to torture, rack, plague (class.). Physically: perii! excruciabit me herus,Plaut. Mil. 3, 2, 45: servos fame vinculisque,Caes. B.
