Priap. 14, 1; 34, 1; and sarcastically: salacissimus Juppiter, Sen. ap. Lact. 1, 16, 10. Poet. transf., that provokes lust, provocative: erucae...

salebra.definition: sălĕ_bra, ae (orig. , sc. via), f. salio A jolting-place, roughness in a road. Lit. (poet. and in post-Aug. prose): demonstrant astra salebras,Prop. 3, 16 (4, 15), 15; Hor. Ep. 1, 17, 53; Mart. 9, 58, 5: salebris sollicitari,Col. 9, 8, 3. Transf.: senile guttur salebris spiritŭs praegravavit,irregular breathing, panting,Val. Max. 9, 12, ext. 6. Trop.

salebrosus.definition: sălĕ_brōsus, a, um, id. Full of joltings, rough, rugged, uneven (not anteAug.; cf.: confragosus, horridus, asper). Lit.: semita,App. M. 8, p. 208, 37: furfures multo lapide,id. ib. 7, p. 194, 38. Trop., of speech: resistens ac salebrosa oratio,Quint. 11, 2, 46: compositio Pollionis Asinii,Sen. Ep. 100, 7.—Of the writer himself: Sanctra,Mart. 11, 2, 7.

salgamum.definition: salgama Nourish-ment, food, sustenance, Cod. Just. 12, 42; Cod. Th. 7, 9, § 1 sq.

salictum.definition: contr. from salicetum, from salix A plantation or thicket of willows, Cato, R. R. 1, 7; 1, 9; 33, 5; Enn. ap. Cic. Div. 1, 20, 40 (Ann. v. 40 Vahl.); Plaut. Aul. 4, 6, 9; Cic. Agr. 2, 14, 36; Verg. E. 1, 55; id. G. 2, 13; 2, 415; Hor. C. 2, 5, 8; Liv. 29, 17; Ov. M. 11, 363; Juv. 11, 67; Col. 4, 30, 3.

saligneus.definition: sălignĕus, a, um, v. salignus Init.

salignus.definition: sălignus (collat. form sălignĕus, Col. 6, 2, 4; 9, 15, 12; 11, 3, 33; Dig. 47, 7, 3), a, um, salix Of willow or willowwood, willow-: cunei,Cato, R. R. 20, 1: fustis,Hor. S. 1, 5, 22: verua,Ov. F. 2, 363: lectus,id. M. 8, 659; cf. pes,id. ib. 8, 657: frons,id. ib. 9, 99: umbonum crates,Verg. A. 7, 632: crates,Petr. 135.

salillum.definition: dim.for salinulum, from salinum A little salt-cellar, Cat. 23, 19.—In comic lang.: salillum animae, perh. little measure, brief span of life, Plaut. Trin. 2, 4, 91.

salinum.definition: sal (sc. vas; Masc. collat. form, plur., , Varr. ap. Non. 546, 14), a salt-cellar, Plaut. Pers. 2, 3, 15; Hor. C. 2, 16, 14; Pers. 3, 25; 5, 138; also used at sacrifices,Liv. 26, 36; Val. Max. 4, 4, 3; Arn. 2, 91.—Prov.: salinum cum sale obsignare,Plaut. Pers. 2, 3, 15.

salio.definition: sălĭo (sall-), no Perf., ītum, 4 (collat. form sălo or sallo, no perf., salsum, 3: salunt, Varr. ap. Diom. p. 372 P.: salerent, Sall. Fragm. ap. Prisc. p. 909: salere, Lucil. ib.: salsurus, Mummius ap. Prisc. p. 910 P.; part. salsus, v.infra P. a.), v. a. id.. To salt down, to salt: pernas, Cato ap. Varr. R. R. 1, 2 fin.: oleas caducas,Cato, R. R. 23, 1: pisces, Sisenn. ap. Prisc. p. 909 P.; Cels. 2, 18: saliturus istaec mittam salem, Naev. ap. P...

saliunca.definition: An odoriferous plant, the wild or Celtic nard: Valeriana Celtica, Linn.; Plin. 21, 7, 20, § 43; Verg. E. 5, 17; Scrib. Comp. 195; 258; Vulg. Isa. 55, 13.

saliva.definition: kindr. with σίαλον Spittle, saliva (in gen., while sputum is that already spit out; equally used in sing. and plur.). Lit., sing., Cat. 23, 16; 78, 8; 99, 10; Juv. 6, 623; Sen. Ira, 3, 38, 2; Plin. 27, 6, 24, § 41; 28, 12, 53, § 193: in manum ingerere,id. 28, 4, 7, § 37 al.—Plur., Lucr. 4, 638; 4, 1108; Col. 6, 9, 3: unā salivā,without interruption,Hier. ad Pam. 61, 4. Trop., taste, flavor; longing, appetite (poet., and in post-Aug. prose): Meth...

saliua.definition: kindr. with σίαλον Spittle, saliva (in gen., while sputum is that already spit out; equally used in sing. and plur.). Lit., sing., Cat. 23, 16; 78, 8; 99, 10; Juv. 6, 623; Sen. Ira, 3, 38, 2; Plin. 27, 6, 24, § 41; 28, 12, 53, § 193: in manum ingerere,id. 28, 4, 7, § 37 al.—Plur., Lucr. 4, 638; 4, 1108; Col. 6, 9, 3: unā salivā,without interruption,Hier. ad Pam. 61, 4. Trop., taste, flavor; longing, appetite (poet., and in post-Aug. prose): Meth...

salix.definition: Lit., a willow-tree, willow, sallow, Cato, R. R. 6, 4; Varr. R. R. 1, 24, 4; Col. 4, 30, 4; Plin. 16, 37, 68, § 174; 24, 9, 37, § 56; Lucr. 2, 361; Verg. E. 3, 65; 83; 5, 16 et saep.—* Meton., a willowbranch, withy, osier, Prud. στεΦ. 10, 703.

sallo.definition: sallo and sălo, ĕre, v. 1. salio.

salmoneus.definition: (), , , = Σαλμωνεύς A son of Aeolus, brother of Sisyphus, who imitated lightning with burning torches, and was on that account hurled into Tartarus by a thunderbolt from Jupiter, Hyg. Fab. 60; 61; 250; Verg. A. 6, 585 Serv.; Claud. in Rufin. 2, 514; Epigr. ap. Sphaer. Archim. 18.—Hence, , , , = Σαλμωνίς, Tyro, a daughter of Salmoneus, mother of Neleus and Pelias by Neptune, who assumed the form of Enipeus, Prop. 3, 19 (4, 18), 13; 1, 13, 21; Ov...

salomon.definition: Sălŏmon (Sŏlŏmon), ōnis, m., = Σαλωμών, Σαλομών, Σολομών [] Solomon, son of David, Prud. Hamart. 581; Juvenc. 2, 717; Alcim. 6, 387; Lact. 4, 16. —Hence

salpa.definition: A kind of stock-fish, Plin. 9, 18, 32, § 68; Ov. Hal. 121.

salsamentum.definition: salsus. * Fish-pickle, brine, * Cic. Div. 2, 57, 117. Salted or pickled fish (usu. in plur.): salsamenta Fac macerentur,Ter. Ad. 3, 3, 26; Varr. R. R. 3, 17, 7; Col. 8, 17, 12; Plin. 32, 2, 9, § 18; 32, 7, 26, § 79; 32, 9, 34, § 106 al.—Sing., Col. 12, 55, 4; Gell. 2, 24, 7.

salsugo.definition: (collat. form , Plin. 31, 7, 42, § 92; 18, 12, 32, § 124), , salsus Saltness, brackishness, Vitr. 1, 4; Plin. 36, 23, 55, § 176; 19, 5, 26, § 84 al.: terra salsuginis,i. e. a desert,Vulg. Job, 39, 6; id. Jer. 17, 6. Transf., salt-water, brine, Plin. 19, 5, 26, § 85; 31, 7, 42, § 92.

saltatio.definition: id. A dancing; concr., a dance, Quint. 1, 11, 18 sq.; 2, 18, 1; Scipio Afric. ap. Macr. S. 2, 10: multarum deliciarum comes est extrema saltatio,Cic. Mur. 6, 13; id. Brut. 62, 225; id. Fin. 3, 7, 24; Quint. 11, 3, 128; Suet. Tit. 7 al.—Plur., Plaut. Stich. 5, 2, 11.

saltatiuncula.definition: dim.saltatio A little dance (late Lat.), Vop. Aur. 6.

saltator.definition: salto A dancer (generally among the Romans with an accessory contemptuous signif.), Cic. Off. 1, 42, 150; id. Mur. 6, 13; id. Deiot. 10, 28; id. Fin. 3, 7, 24; Quint. 1, 12, 14; 11, 3, 89; Suet. Calig. 54; id. Ner. 6; Macr. S. 2, 10 al.

saltatorius.definition: saltātōrĭus, a, um, salto Of or belonging to dancing, dancing-, saltatory (class.): ludus, a dancing-school, Scipio Afric. ap. Macr. S. 2, 10, § 7; cf. Macr. S. 2, 10, 4: orbis,a dancing in a ring,Cic. Pis. 10, 30; Arn. 2, 73.—* Adv.: saltātōrĭē, like a dancer, in a dancing attitude: procurrens,App. M. 10, p. 253, 36.

saltatricula.definition: dim.saltatrix A little dancing-girl (post-class.), Gell. 1, 5 fin.

saltatrix.definition: saltator A female dancer, dancing-girl, Cic. Pis. 8, 18; Plin. 10, 23, 33, § 68; Macr. S. 2, 10, 1; Vulg. Ecclus. 9, 4.

saltatus.definition: salto A (religious) dance (not ante-Aug., and very rare): (Numa Salios) per urbem ire canentes carmina cum tripudiis sollennique saltatu jussit,Liv. 1, 20; so Sen. Troad. 786; Lact. 1, 21 fin.—Plur.: saltatibus apta juventus,Ov. M. 14, 637.

saltem.definition: saltem (sometimes in MSS. saltim; cf. Aus. Ep. 7, 23; and Prisc. p. 1013 P.), old acc. form, from salvus, salus. prop. Saved, reserved (salvā re; compare Engl. save, except). It serves to point out that which still remains or holds good, in spite of or by way of exception to something opposed to it; and accordingly is used (like certe, II.) as a restrictive particle, at least, at the least, at all events, anyhow. Affirmatively (class.). With the ...

saltito.definition: saltĭto, āre V. freq. n. [salto], to dance much or vigorously (post-Aug. and very rare), Quint. 9, 4, 142; Macr. S. 2, 4, 14; 2, 10 fin.; Arn. 2, 73.

salto.definition: salto (once salĭto, Varr. L. L. 5, § 85 Müll., Salii a salitando), āvi, ātum, 1 V. freq. n. and a. [2. salio], to dance (in the widest signif. of the word, including pantomime and gesticulation; mostly with a contemptuous accessory signif.). Neutr.: vidi in his unum puerum bullatum, non minorem annis duodecim, cum crotalis saltare, quam saltationem impudicus servulus honeste saltare non posset, Scipio Afric. ap. Macr. S. 2, 10 (v. the whole chapt...

saltuosus.definition: saltŭōsus, a, um, id. Full of woods or forests, well-wooded, woody: loca,Sall. J. 38, 1; Liv. 27, 12; Tac. A. 4, 45; 6, 34: convalles,Plin. 6, 7, 7, § 19: per saltuosos tramites,Amm. 19, 9, 5.

saltus.definition: 2. salio A leaping, leap, spring, bound (class.), Sen. Ep. 15, 4: saltu uti, * Cic. Sen. 6, 19: cum alacribus saltu, cum velocibus cursu certabat, Sall. Fragm. ap. Veg. Mil. 1, 9 fin.: saltu pernici tollere corpus,Lucr. 5, 559; cf.: (monocoli) mirae pernicitatis ad saltum,Plin. 7, 2, 2, § 23: corpora saltu Subiciunt in equos,Verg. A. 12, 287: saltu Emicat in currum,id. ib. 12, 326; 9, 553: saltu superare viam,id. G. 3, 141: saltum dare,to make a ...

salubris.definition: sălūbris, e ( Masc. collat. form sălū-ber, Varr. R. R. 1, 2, 8; Ov. R. Am. 704; but salubris, m., Cic. Div. 1, 57, 130; Cels. 1, 3; 2, 1; 3, 6; abl. salubri, v. Neue, Formenl. 2, p. 30), adj. salus, health-giving, promoting health, healthful, wholesome, salubrious; salutary, serviceable, advantageous, beneficial (v. salutaris init.). Lit. (freq. and class.) Transf., in a neutr. sense, of the human body, healthy, sound, well, vigorous (very rare, ...

salubritas.definition: salubris. Healthfulness, wholesomeness, salubrity (class.): hostiarum exta, quorum ex habitu atque ex colore tum salubritatis, tum pestilentiae signa percipi,Cic. Div. 1, 57, 131: amoenitatem hanc (sc. hujus loci) et salubritatem sequor,id. Leg. 2, 1, 3; so of places,id. Agr. 2, 35, 95; Varr. R. R. 1, 4, 3 sq.; Suet. Tib. 11; Auct. B. G. 8, 52; cf.: aquarum,Liv. 42, 54 fin.; Tac. A. 12, 66; Plin. 5, 16, 15, § 72: nemorum,id. 37, 10, 77, § 201: ca...

salum.definition: ( Masc. collat. form, corresp. to the Gr. acc., undantem salum, Enn. ap. Non. 223, 24, or Trag. v. 226 Vahl.), = σάλος, the open sea, the high sea, the main, the deep; opp. to the sea near the coast or in a port (occurring only in sing., and mostly in the acc. and abl.). Lit. (rare but class.), Cic. Caecin. 30, 88: in salum nave evectus,Liv. 29, 14: paucas (naves) ante portum in salo habiturum,id. 37, 10: pars (classis) in salo ad ostium portūs ...

salus.definition: (archaic Gen. SALVTES, on a clay vessel, v. Ritschl de Fictilibus Litteratis, Berol, 1853, p. 18, n. 5; cf. APOLONES, from Apollo; dat. SALVTEI, Corp. Inscr. Lat. 587), f. root sar, to guard, whence servus, servare, salvus, sollus; cf. Gr. ὅλος, entire, a being safe and sound; a sound or whole condition, health, welfare, prosperity, preservation, safety, deliverance, etc. (very freq. and class.: cf.: valetudo, sanitas). Lit. Salus, personified,...

salutaris.definition: sălūtāris, e, adj.salus Of or belonging to well-being, healthful, wholesome, salutary, serviceable, beneficial, advantageous (in the most general sense, while the predominant meaning of salubris, in class. lang., is healthy in a medical sense; very freq. and class.). In gen. In partic.

salutatio.definition: saluto A greeting. saluting, salutation (rare but good prose). In gen.: quis te aditu, quis ullo honore, quis denique communi salutatione dignum putet?Cic. Pis. 40, 96: salutationem facere,Liv. 1, 1 fin.: salutationem reddere,Tac. A. 4, 61: salutatione acceptā ac redditā,Macr. S. 1, 6: mutuā salutatione factā,Curt. 10, 8, 23.—Of performing devotions: uti praetereuntes possint respicere (aedificia deorum) et in conspectu salutationes facere,Vitr. ...

salutator.definition: id. One who greets; a greeter, saluter. In gen.: salutator regum,Stat. S. 2, 4, 29. In partic. (cf. salutatio, II.), one who makes complimentary visits, who pays his respects to another, a visitor; also (in the time of the emperors), one who appears at court, a courtier, Q. Cic. Petit. Cons. 9, 34; Col. praef. § 9; Mart. 1, 71, 18; 10, 74, 2; Suet. Claud. 35; Juv. 5, 15.

salutatrix.definition: salutator (postAug.) She that salutes; occurring only in apposition. In gen.: pica,Mart. 7, 87, 6: charta,i. e. a letter of greeting,id. 9, 99, 2. In partic., she that makes complimentary visits, that pays court: turba,i. e. the crowd of clients who come to salute their patron in the morning,Juv. 5, 21.

salutificator.definition: salus-facio A bringer of safety, a savior (eccl. Lat.), Tert. Res. Carn. 47; id. Carn. Chr. 14 (al. salvificator).

saluto.definition: sălūto, āvi, ātum ( Gen. plur. salutantum, Lucr. 1, 318; Verg. G. 2, 462; Ov. M. 5, 295), 1, salus. * (Acc. to salus, I. A.) To keep safe, to preserve: sequenti anno palmites salutentur pro viribus matris singuli aut gemini,Plin. 17, 22, 35, § 177. (Acc. to salus, I. B.) To greet, wish health to, pay one's respects to, salute any one (freq. in all periods and kinds of composition; cf.: salvere jubeo).

salvatio.definition: id. Deliverance, salvation (late Lat.), Boëth. Duab. Nat. p. 953; Vulg. Joel, 2, 32.—Plur., Vulg. Psa. 27, 8.

saluatio.definition: id. Deliverance, salvation (late Lat.), Boëth. Duab. Nat. p. 953; Vulg. Joel, 2, 32.—Plur., Vulg. Psa. 27, 8.

salvator.definition: id.. In gen., a saviour, preserver (late Lat.; class. servator): Cicero Soterem salvatorem noluit nominare,Mart. Cap. 5, § 510; Vulg. Isa. 17, 10: IOVI SALVATORI,Inscr. Grut. 19. In partic., in the Vulg. and Christian fathers, as a transl. of σωτήρ and Jesus (Heb. ), the Saviour, Redeemer: Christus Jesus, id est Christus Salvator: hoc est enim Latine Jesus ... Salus Latinum nomen est: salvare et salvator non fuerunt haec Latina, antequam veniret...

saluator.definition: id.. In gen., a saviour, preserver (late Lat.; class. servator): Cicero Soterem salvatorem noluit nominare,Mart. Cap. 5, § 510; Vulg. Isa. 17, 10: IOVI SALVATORI,Inscr. Grut. 19. In partic., in the Vulg. and Christian fathers, as a transl. of σωτήρ and Jesus (Heb. ), the Saviour, Redeemer: Christus Jesus, id est Christus Salvator: hoc est enim Latine Jesus ... Salus Latinum nomen est: salvare et salvator non fuerunt haec Latina, antequam veniret...

salveo.definition: salvĕo, ēre, salvus. To be well, or in good health; so in the verb. finit. only once in a lusus verbb. with the foll.; v. II. 1. fin. In partic., as a term of salutation.

salueo.definition: salvĕo, ēre, salvus. To be well, or in good health; so in the verb. finit. only once in a lusus verbb. with the foll.; v. II. 1. fin. In partic., as a term of salutation.

salvifico.definition: salvĭfĭco, āre, salvus-facio To save, deliver (late Lat.): pater istā memet ab horā Salvifica,Sedul. 5, 7: me,Vulg. Johan. 12, 27: mundum,id. ib. 12, 47.

saluifico.definition: salvĭfĭco, āre, salvus-facio To save, deliver (late Lat.): pater istā memet ab horā Salvifica,Sedul. 5, 7: me,Vulg. Johan. 12, 27: mundum,id. ib. 12, 47.

salvificus.definition: salvĭfĭcus, a, um, id. Saving: corpus Christi,Alcim. Avit. ad Sor. 180.

saluificus.definition: salvĭfĭcus, a, um, id. Saving: corpus Christi,Alcim. Avit. ad Sor. 180.

salvo.definition: salvo, āvi, ātum, 1, salvus To save (late Lat.; opp. perdere; syn.: servo, conservo),Veg. Vet. 3, 23, 3; Lact. de Ira Dei, 5, 7; Hier. Ep. 20, 4; Vulg. Isa. 4, 2; id. Amos, 2, 14; Sedul. 1, 109.

saluo.definition: salvo, āvi, ātum, 1, salvus To save (late Lat.; opp. perdere; syn.: servo, conservo),Veg. Vet. 3, 23, 3; Lact. de Ira Dei, 5, 7; Hier. Ep. 20, 4; Vulg. Isa. 4, 2; id. Amos, 2, 14; Sedul. 1, 109.

salvus.definition: salvus (ante-class. -vos), a, um, adj. root sar, sal; v. salus Saved, preserved, unharmed, safe, unhurt, uninjured, well, sound, etc. In gen. (very freq. and class.; syn.: sospes, sanus, incolumis): Mars pater, te precor, pastores pecuaque salva servassis duisque bonam salutem valetudinemque mihi, etc., an ancient form of praver in Cato, R. R. 141, 3; cf.: si respublica populi Romani Quiritium ad quinquennium proximum salva servata erit hisce due...

saluus.definition: salvus (ante-class. -vos), a, um, adj. root sar, sal; v. salus Saved, preserved, unharmed, safe, unhurt, uninjured, well, sound, etc. In gen. (very freq. and class.; syn.: sospes, sanus, incolumis): Mars pater, te precor, pastores pecuaque salva servassis duisque bonam salutem valetudinemque mihi, etc., an ancient form of praver in Cato, R. R. 141, 3; cf.: si respublica populi Romani Quiritium ad quinquennium proximum salva servata erit hisce due...

sambuca.definition: A triangular stringed-instrument of a very sharp, shrill tone (and hence of slight esteem), Plaut. Stich. 2, 2, 57; Scipio Afric. ap. Mácr. S. 2, 10; Pers. 5, 95; Spart. Hadr. 26; cf. Fest. pp. 324 and 325 Müll.; Isid. 3, 20, 7; Vulg. Dan. 3, 5. Transf., a machine of like form used by besiegers; a sort of bridge for storming walls, Veg. Mil. 4, 21; Vitr. 10, 22; cf. Fest. 1. c.

sambucistria.definition: () A woman that plays on the sambuca (with psaltria), Liv. 39, 6; Arn. 2, n. 42; cf. Fest. pp. 324 and 325 Müll., and v. sambucina.

sambucus.definition: sambuca He who plays on the sambuca, Mart. Cap. 9, § 924.

samius.definition: Sămĭus, a, um, v. Samus, I.

sanabilis.definition: sānābĭlis, e, adj.sano That can be healed, curable, remediable (rare but class.); of the body: vulnus,Ov. P. 2, 2, 59; id. R. Am. 101: dolor sanabilior,Cels. 2, 8; of the mind, * Cic. Tusc. 4, 37, 80; Sen. Ep. 108, 3. —Sup. and adv. do not occur.

sancio.definition: sancĭo, xi, ctum, 4 ( Pluperf. sancierat, Pompon. ap. Diom. p. 368 P.; id. ap. Prisc. p. 904 ib.: sancivi,Prisc. 904; Diom. 368; part. perf. sancitum, Lucr. 1, 587; Cass. Sev. ap. Diom. l. l.), v. a. Sanscr. root sac, sak, to accompany, honor (cf. sequor); whence also sacer; cf. Gr. ἉΓ, ἅγιος, ἁγνός, to render sacred or inviolable by a religious act; to appoint as sacred or inviolable. Lit., mostly of legal ordinances or other public proceed...

sanctificatio.definition: sanctifico Sanctification (eccl. Lat.), Tert. Exhort. ad Cast. 1; Sid. Ep. 8, 14; Vulg. 1 Cor. 1, 30 et saep.

sanctifico.definition: sanctĭfĭco, āvi, ātum, 1, sanctusfacio To make holy or treat as holy, to sanctify, consecrate, dedicate (eccl. Lat.), Tert. Or. 3; id. Exhort. ad Cast. 7; Prud. Cath. 3, 15; Vulg. Gen. 2, 3 et saep.

sanctimonia.definition: sanctus; cf.: acrimonia, parsimonia, etc. Sacredness, sanctity, moral purity, virtuousness, chastity, etc. (rare but class.): ad deorum religionem et sanctimoniam demigrasse,Cic. Rab. Perd. 10, 30: habere domum clausam pudori et sanctimoniae, patentem cupiditati et voluptatibus,id. Quint. 30, 93: summa sanctimonia,id. ib. 17, 55: priscae sanctimoniae virgo,Tac. A. 3, 69 fin.; cf. id. ib. 2, 86: femina sanctimoniā insignis,id. ib. 12, 6: nuptiarum...

sanctimonialis.definition: sanctĭmōnĭālis, e, sanctimonia Holy; of Christians, pious, religious (late Lat.): vita,i. e. a monastic life,Cod. Just. 1, 3, 56: mulier,i. e. a nun,ib. 1, 2, 13. —As subst.: sanctĭmōnĭālis, is, f., a nun, Aug. Ep. 169; id. Retract. 2, 22.—Adv.: sanctĭmōnĭālĭter, holily, piously: degere,i. e. in a cloister,Cod. Just. 1, 3, 56.

sanctio.definition: sancio An establishing, ordaining, or decreeing as inviolable under penalty of a curse; a decree, ordinance, sanction: sanctiones sacrandae sunt ...poenā, cum caput ejus qui contra fecerit consecratur,Cic. Balb. 14, 33; 16, 36; cf.: legis sanctio poenaque,Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 66, § 149: sanctio legum, quae novissime certam poenam irrogat iis, qui praeceptis legis non obtemperaverint,Dig. 48, 19, 41; cf.: interdum in sanctionibus adicitur, ut qui ibi ...

sanctitas.definition: sanctus. Inviolability, sacredness, sanctity: tribunatūs,Cic. Sest. 37, 79: regum, Caes. ap. Suet. Caes. 6; cf.: regii nominis, Sall. Fragm. ap. Serv. Verg. G. 4, 211: sanctitas templi insulaeque,Liv. 44, 29: templo sanctitatem tribuere,Tac. A. 3, 62 fin.; cf.: augusti atque inviolati soli,Liv. 45, 5: fori,Quint. 11, 3, 58: mecum deorum et hominum sanctitates omnes et religiones afuerunt,Cic. Red. in Sen. 14, 34: propter sanctitatem aliquam, Mass...

sanctitudo.definition: sanctus. Mostly ante-class. for sanctitas, sacredness, sanctity: Jovis, Att. ap. Non. 173, 33: Apollinis,Turp. ib. 174, 5: nominis matronae sanctitudinem,Afran. ib. 174, 9: fani, Quadrig. ap. Gell. 17, 2, 19 sq.: sepulturae, Cic. Rep. Fragm. ap. Non. 174, 7 (4, 8 Mos.).—In plur., Att. ap. Non. 174, 2. In the postclass. per., transf., uprightness, purity, Capitol. Ver. 8: domum tuam decet sanctitudo, Domine,Vulg. Psa. 92, 5.

sanctor.definition: sancio An establisher, ordainer: legum,Tac. A. 3, 26 fin.

sanctuarium.definition: sanctus (postAug. for sacrarium). A place for keeping sacred things, a shrine, sanctuary, Aggen. Limit. p. 61 Goes.; Vulg. Dan. 8, 13 et saep. The private cabinet of a prince: Mithridatis,Plin. 23, 8, 77, § 149; Sicul. Fl. p. 16 Goes.; Inscr. Orell. 2388.

sanctus.definition: sanctus, a, um, Part. and of sancio.

sandaliarius.definition: sandălĭārĭus, a, um, sandalium Of or belonging to sandals: Apollo Sandaliarius, who had a statue in the Sandal-street (in the fourth region of Rome), Suet. Aug. 57.—Subst.: Sandălĭārĭus, ii, m. (sc. vicus), Sandal-street, Shoemakers'-street: in Sandaliario forte apud librarios fuimus,Gell. 18, 4, 1; cf. VICVS,Inscr. Grut. p. 79, 5.—Sandaliarius signifies also a sandal-maker in Inscr. Spon. Miscell. Ant. p. 114 (perh. in Plaut. Aul. 3, 5, 39, sand...

sandalium.definition: (plur. scanned sandālĭa, Albin. 2, 65) A slipper, sandal, Turp. ap. Non. 427, 28; Ter. Eun. 5, 7, 4; Vulg. Judith, 10, 3

sandapila.definition: A common kind of bier for people of the lower classes (persons of rank were borne on a lectica), Suet. Dom. 17 fin.; Mart. 8, 75, 14; 2, 81, 2; 9, 3, 12; Juv. 8, 175; Suet. Dom. 17; cf. Fulg. Expos. Serm. Ant. p. 558.

sanesco.definition: sānesco, ĕre V. inch. n. [sanus], to become sound, get well, heal (post-Aug.): insanientes sub somno sanescunt,Cels. 3, 18: corpus,id. 2, 8: ulcera,id. 3, 22; Plin. 17, 23, 35, § 214: vulnera,Col. 6, 7, 4: cutis,Cels. 8, 4 et saep.

sanguinarius.definition: sanguĭnārĭus, a, um (also late Lat. sanguĭnāris, e, Vulg. Ecclus. 42, 5), sanguis Of or belonging to blood, blood- Lit.: herba, an herb that stanches blood, the Gr. πολύγονον,Col. 7, 5, 19; also called sanguinaria alone,Plin. 27, 12, 91, § 113, and sanguinalis herba, Col. 6, 12 fin.; Cels. 2, 33; 3, 22fin.: latus sanguinare, coveredwith blood, Vulg. Ecclus. 42, 5. Trop., blood-thirsty, bloody, sanguinary (rare but class.): juventus,Cic. Att. 2, ...

sanguineus.definition: sanguĭnĕus, a, um, sanguis. Lit., of blood, consisting of blood, bloody, blood- (class.; a favorite word of the Aug. poets): imber, * Cic. Div. 2, 28, 60: guttae,Ov. M. 2, 360; 14, 408: dapes,Tib. 1, 5, 49: manus,Ov. M. 1, 143: lingua,id. ib. 3, 57: humus,id. H. 16, 334; cf. mater,id. M. 3, 125: hasta,Stat. Th. 8, 436: pulmo,Sen. Agam. 760; Plin. 11, 37, 72, § 188: caedes,Ov. M. 13, 85: rixae,Hor. C. 1, 27, 4: bellum,Val. Fl. 5, 308; 6, 134: crin...

sanguinolentus.definition: sanguĭnŏlentus (collat. form san-guĭlentus, Scrib. Comp. 182), a, um, sanguis Lit., full of blood, bloody (class., but, like sanguineus, mostly poet.; not in Cic.): torques, Quadrig. ap. Gell. 9, 13, 18; so, soror,Tib. 2, 6, 40: pectora,Ov. H. 3, 50: ille,id. F. 4, 844: Erinys,id. H. 6, 46: (Curetes) inter se armis Ludunt in numerumque exsultant sanguinolenti,Lucr. 2, 631; v. Lachm. ad h. l.: Allia...vulneribus Latiis,Ov. A. A. 1, 414: seditiones...

sanguis.definition: (acc. SANGVEM, Inscr. Fratr. Arval. tab. 41, 22; Inscr. Orell. 2270 and 5054; cf. ex-sanguis, acc. -em. Neutr. collat. form sanguen, ante-class., Enn. ap. Non. 224; id.ap.Cic.Rep. 1, 41, 64; id.ap.Cic. Fin. 5, 11, 31; Cic. de Or. 3, 58, 218; id. ap. Prisc. p. 708 P.; Cato ap. Gell. 3, 7, 19; Att. and Varr. ap. Non. l. l.; Lucr. 1, 837; 1, 860; Petr. 59, 1; Arn. 1, 36), m. etym. dub.; prob. root sak-, sag-, to drop, flow; cf. Angl.-Sax. sūc-an; Ge...

sanguisuga.definition: sanguis-sugo A blood-sucker, leech (called also hirudo), Cels. 5, 27, 16; Plin. 8, 10, 10, § 29; 32, 10, 42, § 123; Vulg. Prov. 30, 15.

sanies.definition: a weakened form of sanguis. Diseased or corrupted blood, bloody matter, sanies (cf.: pus, tabes): ex his (vulneribus ulceribusque) exit sanguis, sanies, pus. Sanguis omnibus notus est: sanies est tenuior hoc, varie crassa et glutinosa et colorata: pus crassissimum albidissimumque, glutinosius et sanguine et sanie, etc.,Cels. 5, 26, 20: saxa spargens tabo, sanie et sanguine atro, Enn. ap. Cic. Tusc. 1, 44, 107, and id. ap. Cic. Pis. 19 (Trag. v. 4...

sanitas.definition: sanus Soundness of body, health (class., = valetudo bona; opp. valetudo mala, imbecillitas; cf. also salus): est enim corporis temperatio, cum ea congruunt inter se, e quibus constamus, sanitas: sic animi dicitur, cum ejus judicia opinionesque concordant,Cic. Tusc. 4, 13, 30; cf. id. ib. 3, 5, 10. Lit.: Apollo, quaeso te, ut des Salutem et sanitatem nostrae familiae,Plaut. Merc. 4, 1, 13 (for which, in the old formula of prayer in Cato, R. R. 141...

sanna.definition: δάννας A mimicking grimace, esp. in mockery, derision, Pers. 1, 62; 5, 91; Juv. 6, 306.

sannio.definition: sanna One who makes mimicking grimaces, a buffoon (cf. scurra), Cic. de Or. 2, 61, 251; id. Fam. 9, 16, 10; Amm. 14, 6, 16.

sano.definition: sāno, āvi, ātum, 1, sanus To make sound, to heal, cure, restore to health (freq. and class.; syn.: curo, medeor, medico). Lit.: quam (vomicam) sanare medici non potuerant,Cic. N. D. 3, 28, 70: Ptolemaeum,id. Div. 2, 66, 135; so, aliquem,id. Phil. 2, 39, 101 Orell. N. cr.: oculorum tumor sanatur,id. Tusc. 4, 37, 81: tumores,Plin. 20, 6, 23, § 55: volnera,Cic. Rep. 1, 3, 5; Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 46, § 121; id. Fin. 4, 24, 66; id. Att. 5, 17, 6; Ov. M. 1...

sanqualis.definition: Sanquālis (Sanguālis), e, Sancus; cf. arquatus, from arcus Of or belonging to Sancus: avis, a bird sacred to Sancus, the ospray (ossifragus), Plin. 10, 7, 8, § 20; Liv. 41, 13; cf. Fest. p. 317 Müll.: sanqualis porta appellatur proxima aedi Sanci,Fest. p. 343, 34, and Paul. ex Fest. p. 345, 2 Müll.

sanus.definition: sānus, a, um (sanun', for sanusne, Plaut. Bacch. 3, 6, 37; id. Men. 5, 2, 66; id. Mere. 2, 2, 21; 2, 4, 21; id. Rud. 3, 2, 19; id. Truc. 2, 4, 13; cf. Sanan',id. Am. 3, 2, 48; id. Cure. 5, 2, 54; id. Cist. 4, 1, 14; id. Ep. 5, 1, 42; id. Men. 2, 3, 43; and sanin',id. Ps. 4, 7, 83), kindr. with ΣΑ, σῶς, sound, whole, healthy, physically or mentally (cf.: integer, incolumis, sospes, salvus). Lit., sound in body, whole, healthy, well: pars corporis...

sapa.definition: cf. Germ. Saft; Engl sap Must or new wine boiled thick, Varr. ap. Non. 551, 23; 551, 18; Col. 12, 19, 1; Plin. 14, 9, 11, § 80; 14, 19, 24, § 121; Ov. F. 4, 780; Mart. 7, 53, 6; Fest. s. v. burranica, p. 30.

sapidus.definition: săpĭdus, a, um, sapio (post-class.). Lit., well-tasted, relishing, savory: tucetum perquam sapidissimum,App. M. 2, p. 117, 32; 10, p. 344, 32: avis sapidior,Apic. 6, 6.—* Trop., wise, prudent: puellae,Alcim. 6 prooem.—* Adv.: să-pĭdē, savorily: femur sapidissime percoctum,App. M. 8 fin.

sapiens.definition: săpĭens, entis, Part. and , from sapio.

sapienter.definition: săpĭenter, , v. sapio P. a. fin.

sapientia.definition: sapiens. (Acc. to sapiens, A.) Prop., good taste, i. e. good sense, discernment, discretion, prudence, intelligence (class.; syn. prudentia): pellitur e medio sapientia, vi geritur res, Enn. ap. Gell. 20, 10, 4 (Ann. v. 272 Vahl.): non aetate verum ingenio adipiscitur sapientia,Plaut. Trin. 2, 2, 88; id. Mil. 4, 6, 36: fac participes nos tuae sapientiae,id. Ep. 2, 2, 73; cf.: neque habet (erus meus) plus sapientiae quam lapis,id. Mil. 2, 2, 81; i...

sapio.definition: săpĭo, īvi or ĭi (sapui, Aug. Civ. Dei, 1, 10; id. Ep. 102, 10; but sapivi, Nov. ap. Prisc. p. 879 P.; id. ap. Non. 508, 21: SaPisti,Mart. 9, 6, 7: sapisset,Plaut. Rud. 4, 1, 8), 3, v. n. and a. [kindr. with ὀπός, σαφής, and σοφός], to taste, savor; to taste, smack, or savor of, to have a taste or flavor of a thing (cf. gusto). Lit. (so only in a few examples). Trop.

sapo.definition: Germ. Soap, Plin. 28, 12, 51, § 191; Mart. 14, 26in lemm.;Ser. Samm. 11, 157.

sapor.definition: sapio, I.. Lit., a taste, relish, flavor, savor (objectively of the taste inherent in a thing; whereas gustatus is used subjectively, of the taste experienced by him who eats or drinks; class.),Lucr. 2, 679; cf.: si quem forte inveneritis, qui aspernetur oculis pulchritudinem rerum, non odore ullo, non tactu, non sapore capiatur, excludat auribus omnem suavitatem, Cic. Cael. 17, 42: ut mel, suo proprio genere saporis, dulce esse sentitur,id. Fin....

sapphirus.definition: (i short, Ven. Carm. 6, 2) A sapphire, Plin. 37, 9, 39, § 120; Vulg. Apoc. 21, 19; id. Isa. 54, 11.—Form sappir, Plin. 37, 9, 38, § 119.—Form sapphir, Tert. adv. Marc. 2, 10; Vulg. Exod. 28, 18; Hier. in Isa. 15, 54, v. 11 (as , Isid. 16, 9, 2).

sarcina.definition: id.. Lit., a package, bundle, burden, load, pack; more freq. in the plur., luggage (class. only in the plur.; not in Cic.); sing.: quid ego nunc agam? nisi uti sarcinam constringam et clipeum ad dorsum accommodem,Plaut. Trin. 3, 2, 93; 2, 4, 195: sarcinam inponam seni,id. Most. 2, 1, 83: essem militiae sarcina fida tuae,Prop. 4 (5), 3, 46. gravis,Hor. Ep. 1, 13, 6; Petr. 117, 11.—In plur.: sarcinas colligere,Sall. J. 97, 4; Varr. R. R. 1, 1, 1; C...

sarcinator.definition: sarcio A patcher, botcher, mender of old garments (anteand post-class.), Lucil. ap. Non. 175, 33; Plaut. Aul. 3, 5, 41; Dig. 4, 4, 5; 47, 2, 82; 14, 4, 1; cf. Serv. ad Verg. A. 12, 13.

sarcinula.definition: dim.id. A little pack, bundle, or fardel (mostly post-Aug. and in plur.); sing., Gell. 19, 1, 14.—Plur.: sarcinulas expedire,Cat. 28, 2; Petr. 10, 4: colligere,id. 81, 1: alligare,Plin. Ep. 4, 1, 2; Juv. 6, 146; Vulg. Judic. 19, 17 al.—Poet.: puellae,i. e. the wealth she brings her husband, her marriage-portion, dowry,Juv. 3, 160.

sarcio.definition: sarcĭo, sarsi, sartum, 4, v. a.etym. dub.; cf. Gr. ῥάπτω To patch, botch, mend, repair, restore, etc.: sarcire est integrum facere, Paul. ex Fest. s. v. sarte, p. 323 Müll. (class.; cf.: renovo, instauro, redintegro). Lit.: funes veteres, centones, cuculiones,Cato, R. R. 2, 3; cf.: in vestimento sartum quod comprehensum,Varr. L. L. 6, § 64 Müll.: corbulas,Cato, R. R. 23, 1; 31, 1: dolia,id. ib. 39, 1 sq.; Plin. 18, 26, 64, § 236: aedes,Plaut. M...

sarcophagus.definition: sarcŏphăgus, a, um, , = (flesh-devouring, carnivorous): sarcophagus lapis A kind of limestone used for coffins (so called because the corpses were quickly consumed by it), Plin. 2, 96, 98, § 211; 36, 17, 27, § 161.—In medicine, Plin. 28, 9, 37, § 140. Transf., subst.: sarcŏphăgus, i, m. (‡ sarcŏphă-gum, i, n., Inscr. Don. 7, 8), a grave, sepulchre (post-Aug.), Juv. 10, 172; Dig. 11, 7, 37; 34, 1, 18 fin.; Prud. Cath. 3, 203; Inscr. Orell. 194; 44...

sarculum.definition: ( Masc. collat. form, acc. plur., sarculos, Pall. 1, 43, 3) [sario = sarrio], an implement for loosening the soil, weeding, etc., a light hoe (cf.: ligo, pastinum),Cato, R. R. 10, 3; 155, 1; Varr. L. L. 5, § 134 Muüll.; Col. 2, 11, 10; Plin. 18, 7, 18, § 79 (Jahn, sacculo); 19, 6, 33, § 109; Ov. M. 11, 36; id. F. 1, 699; Hor. C. 1, 1, 11; Vulg. Isa. 7, 25.

sardinus.definition: sardīnus, a, um, v. sardius Fin.

sardius.definition: sardĭus, a, um, cf. 1. sarda, II. Sardian, carnelian (late Lat.): lapis,Vulg. Exod. 28, 17.—Hence, subst.: sardĭus, ii, m., the carnelian, a precious stone, Vulg. Exod. 39, 10; id. Apoc. 21, 20; Tert. adv. Marc. 2, 10; called lapis sardinus,Vulg. Apoc. 4, 3; cf. Hier. in Isa. 15, 54, v. 11 sq.

sardonyx.definition: sardŏnyx, ychis, m. and f. A precious stone, sardonyx; fem., Plin. 37, 6, 23, § 85; Pers. 1, 16; Juv. 7, 144. —Masc., Juv. 6, 382; Mart. 4, 28, 4; 4, 61, 6. —Gen. plur. sardonychum, Juv. 13, 139.— Hence, : sardŏnĭchus, a, um, of sardonyx: lapis,Vulg. Job, 28, 16.

sardus.definition: Sardus, a, um, v. Sardi, A.

sargus.definition: A kind of sea-fish esteemed by the Romans, Plin. 9, 17, 30, § 65; 9, 51, 74, § 162; Lucil. ap. Fest. p. 322 Müll.; Enn. ap. App. Mag. p. 299; Ov. Hal. 105.

sarisa.definition: (), , , = . A long Macedonian lance, Liv. 9, 19; 37, 42; 38, 7fin.; Curt. 7, 4, 36; 9, 7, 19; Ov. M. 12, 466; 12, 479 al.; cf. Fest. pp. 145 and 251. Poet., in gen., for Macedonians, Luc. 8, 298; 10, 47; cf.: denominatio est ...si quis Macedonas appellarit hoc modo: Non tam cito sarissae Graecia potiti sunt,Auct. Her. 4, 32, 43.

sarmata.definition: Sarmăta, ae, m., = Σαρμάτης A Sarmatian, Luc. 1, 430; Mart. Spect. 3, 4; Juv. 3, 79; Claud. Laud. Stil. 1, 111.—Plur.: Sarmătae (Gr. collat. form Saurŏ-mătae, Ov. Tr. 2, 198; 3, 3, 6; 3, 10, 5; 4, 1, 94; 5, 1, 74; Val. Fl. 7, 235; Mel. 1, 2, 6; 2, 1, 2; Plin. 6, 13, 15, § 38; cf. id. 4, 12, 25, § 80; v. also in the foll.), ārum, m., = Σαυρομάται, the Sarmatians, a great Slavic people, dwelling from the Vistula to the Don, in the mod. Poland and...

sarmentum.definition: sarpo Twigs, light branches, brushwood; a fagot, fascine (class.; usu. in plur.; only so in Cic. and Caes.; cf.: lignum, materia); sing., Varr. R. R. 1, 31, 2; Col. 3, 10, 1; Sil. 7, 314.— Plur., Col. 4, 24, 7; 5, 5, 16; Cic. Sen. 15, 52 and 53; id. de Or. 2, 21, 88; Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 27, § 69; * Caes. B. G. 3, 18 fin.; Liv. 22, 16 fin.; Quint. 2, 17, 19; Plin. 12, 25, 54, § 118; 22, 25, 72, § 150 al.

sarracum.definition: () A kind of wagon or cart (acc. to Quint. 8, 3, 21, belonging to vulgar lang.), Sisenn. ap. Non. 195, 29; Cic. Pis. Fragm. ap. Quint. l. l.; Vitr. 10, 1 fin.; Juv. 3, 255; Capitol. M. Aurel. 13; Amm. 31, 2, 18. Transf., the Wain, a constellation: frigida Bootae,Juv. 5, 23.

sarrio.definition: sarrio (sario), ŭi and īvi (the former in Cato, R. R. 161, 2; the latter in Col. 11, 2, 10), ītum, 4, ; in agricult. lang. To hoe the soil, plants, etc., for the purpose of destroying weeds; to weed, Cato, R. R. 161, 1 and 2; Varr. R. R. 1, 18, 8; 1, 29, 1; Col. 2, 11, 4; 11, 2, 9 sq.; Plaut. Capt. 3, 5, 5; Plin. 18, 21, 50, § 184; 18, 17, 45, § 158; Mart. 3, 93, 20; Vulg. Isa. 7, 25.

sarritor.definition: (collat. form ), , id.. A hoer, weeder, Varr. R. R. 1, 29, 2; Col. 2, 13, 1.—* Trop.: sator sartorque scelerum et messor maxime,i. e. cultivator,Plaut. Capt. 3, 5, 3.

sartago.definition: A frying-pan, baking-pan (post-Aug.), Plin. 16, 11, 22, § 55; Juv. 10, 63; Ambros. Ep. 100, § 9; Vulg. Lev. 7, 9.—* Trop.: sartago loquendi,a hotchpotch, mixture, medley,Pers. 1, 80.

sartor.definition: sarcio A patcher, botcher, mender, Non. 7, 28: sartoris arte se pascere, Aug. Civ. Dei, 22, 8, n. 10.

satago.definition: sătăgo, ĕre, v. satis, II. B.

satelles.definition: An attendant upon a distinguished person, esp. a prince, a lifeguard; in plur., attendants, escort, train, retinue (class.; syn.: stipator, apparitor, accensus). Lit.: regii satellites,Liv. 2, 12; 34, 36fin.; cf. Quint. 7, 2, 54: administri et satellites Sex. Naevii,Cic. Quint. 25, 80 (cf. infra, II.): habet sectatores vel potius satellites, qui, etc.,Tac. A. 16, 22: contumeliosum foret, si equites Romani satellites Numidae traderentur,Sall. J. 6...

satias.definition: (collat. form , Juvenc. 1, 637: Ad satiem,id. 3, 216; abl. satie, Plin. 8, 51, 77, § 209), f. satis, a sufficiency, abundance, plentifulness. In gen. (mostly ante- and post-class.; not found in Cic. or Caes.; commonly used only in nom. sing., the other cases being taken from satietas): quorum crudelitatem numquam ulla explet satias sanguinis, Att. ap. Non. 172, 7 (Trag. Rel. p. 133 Rib.); cf. id. ap. Cic. N. D. 3, 38, 90 (v. Charis. p. 70 P., and...

satietas.definition: satis A sufficiency, abundance (syn. saturitas). In gen. (very rare): neque ulla ornandi satis satietas est,Plaut. Poen. 1, 2, 6.—Plur.: quercus terrenis principiorum satietatibus abundans, parumque habens umoris et aëris,Vitr. 2, 9, 8; 2, 9, 9. In partic., subject., the state of being glutted or sated; a loathing, disgust, satiety (class. and very freq., esp. in the trop. sense and with Cicero; syn. fastidium).

satio.definition: sătĭo, āvi, ātum, 1, satis To fill, satisfy; to sate, satiate with food (class.; esp. freq. in the trop. sense; syn. saturo). Lit.: satiat semimodius cibi in diebus singulis vicenos et centenos turtures,Col. 8, 9, 3: se (orca),Plin. 9, 6, 5, § 14: desideria naturae,to satisfy, appease,Cic. Fin. 2, 8, 25: sitim,Mart. 6, 35, 5: famem,Ov. M. 11, 371.—In part. perf.: satiati agm ludunt,Lucr. 2, 320: canes sanguine erili,Ov. M. 3, 140: vultur humano c...

satis.definition: sătis, and abbreviated, săt (cf. the letter S.: satin', contr. for satisne; v.the foll.), root in Gr. ἄδην, ἅδην, orig. a comp. form, weakened from satius; cf.: magis, nimis, etc. Enough, sufficiently (objectively, so that one needs nothing more; whereas affatim subjectively, so that one wishes nothing more). Posit. Particular phrases.

satisdatio.definition: (or separately, ), , satis-do; v. satis, II. C.. The satisfaction of a creditor, Dig. 46, 3, 49. A giving of bail or security, Dig. 2, 8, 1; 4, 6, 28; 46, 5, 1; 50, 16, 61; Cic. Att. 5, 1, 2; Gai. Inst. 1, 200.—Transf.: capitalis, i. e. a pledging of or answering with one's life, Plin. 36, 5, 4, § 29.

satisfactio.definition: satisfacio; v. satis, II. D.. * A satisfying of a creditor by security; a giving security or bail: satisfactio pro solutione est,Dig. 46, 3, 52. An excuse, apology, plea, explanation (class.): (Caesar) Ubiorum satisfactionem accepit,Caes. B. G. 6, 9 fin.; cf. id. ib. 1, 41: hic tu me etiam insimulas, nec satisfactionem meam accipis,Cic. Fam. 7, 13, 1: ne aliquid satisfactio levitatis habere videatur,id. Att. 4, 6, 3: satisfactionem ex nullā consc...

sativus.definition: sătīvus, a, um, 1. sero That is sown or planted (opp. agrestis, silvestris, etc., that grows wild; very rare), Varr. ap. Gell. 17, 3, 4: morus,Plin. 24, 13, 73, § 120: corna,id. 32, 2, 11, § 22.—Neutr. plur.: sativa (opp. silvestria),Plin. 19, 12, 60, § 185.

satiuus.definition: sătīvus, a, um, 1. sero That is sown or planted (opp. agrestis, silvestris, etc., that grows wild; very rare), Varr. ap. Gell. 17, 3, 4: morus,Plin. 24, 13, 73, § 120: corna,id. 32, 2, 11, § 22.—Neutr. plur.: sativa (opp. silvestria),Plin. 19, 12, 60, § 185.

sator.definition: id.. Lit., a sower, planter, Varr. R. R. 1, 45, 3; Lucr. 2, 1168; Cic. N. D. 2, 34; Col. 3, 15, 3; Plin. 15, 1, 1, § 3; Vulg. Jer. 50, 16. Trop., a sower, promoter, author (very rare; not in Cic.): sator sartorque scelerum,Plaut. Capt. 3, 5, 3: litis,Liv. 21, 6, 2: turbarum. Sil. 8, 260.

satrapes.definition: and , (plur. satrapae), , = σατράπης [Persian; cf. Gesenius, under ] A governor of a province, a viceroy among the Persians, a satrap; nom. satrapes, Nep. Paus. 1, 2; id. Alcib. 10, 3; Curt. 8, 4, 21: satrapa,Ter. Heaut. 3, 1, 43; Curt. 3, 13, 1; Amm. 18, 6, 20: satraps,Sid. Carm. 2, 78; Alcim. 6, 392.—Gen. satrapis, Nep. Lys. 4, 1.—Acc. satrapen, Nep. Con. 2, 1: satrapam,Curt. 3, 13, 1.—Plur. nom. satrapae, Nep. Dat. 3, 1; id. Ages. 2, 2; Vulg....

satureia.definition: ( Neutr. collat. form in plur. (), , Ov. A. A. 2, 415; Mart. 3, 75, 4; though this is perh. another plant), the common name for the pot-herb cunila, savory, Col. 9, 4, 2; 9, 4, 6; 9, 10 (poet.), 233; 11, 3, 57; Plin. 19, 8, 50, § 165; Pall. Febr. 24, 2.

saturitas.definition: id. Fulness, repletion, satiety (mostly ante-class. and postAug. for the class. satietas; perh. only once in Cic.). Lit.: aperitur ostium, unde saturitate saepe ego exii ebrius,Plaut. Capt. 1, 1, 35; 4, 1, 4; 4, 2, 85; Aur. Vict. Epit. 45 fin.: quid causae est quin virgis te usque ad saturitatem sauciem?till you have enough,Plaut. Rud. 3, 4, 53 (for which usu. ad satietatem; v. satietas); Vulg. Exod. 16, 3.— Humorously personified as the goddess ...

saturninus.definition: A Roman surname. So esp. L. Appuleius Saturninus, a tribune of the people A.U.C. 654; who, with C. Servilius Glaucia, was pronounced guilty of treason and put to death, Cic. Rab. Perd. 6, 18; id. Brut. 62, 224; id. Cat. 1, 2, 4; id. Mil. 5, 14; Suet. Aug. 27; id. Calig. 38; Mart. 4, 11, 2.

saturo.definition: sătŭro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.satur To fill, glut, cloy, satiate (rare but class.; syn. satio). Lit.: animalia duce naturā mammas appetunt earumque ubertate saturantur,Cic. N. D. 2, 51, 128: armenta,Verg. A. 8, 213: nec cytiso saturantur apes,id. E. 10, 30: caede leones,Ov. M. 10, 541; id. Am. 2, 16, 25: testudines,Plin. 9, 10, 12, § 36: saturabat glebula talis Patrem ipsum,Juv. 14, 166: famem,i. e. to satisfy, appease,Claud. Phoen. 13; Vulg. Deut. ...

satus.definition: sătus, a, um, Part. of 1. sero.

satyriscus.definition: dim. A little Satyr, Cic. Div. 1, 20, 39.

satyrus.definition: A kind of ape, Plin. 7, 2, 2, § 24; 5, 8, 8, § 44; 10, 72, 93, § 199; Sol. 27 fin. A Satyr, one of the satyri, a kind of wood-deities resembling apes, with two goat's feet, and very lascivious; sing., Ov. M. 6, 110; 6, 383; Hor. Ep. 2, 2, 125; Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 60, § 135; Sil. 3 103.—Commonly plur.: capripedes Satyros,Lucr. 4, 580; Hor. C. 2, 19, 4; 1, 1, 31; id. Ep. 1, 19, 4; id. A. P. 221 sq.; Ov. F. 1, 397; id. M. 1, 193; 1, 692; 4, 25; Cic. N....

saucio.definition: saucĭo, āvi, ātum, 1, id. To wound, hurt. Lit. (class. but rare; not in Caes.; syn.: vulnero, laedo): Rubrius in turbā sauciatur,Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 26, § 67; id. Vatin. 5, 13: ut ictu tragulae sauciaretur, Sall. Fragm. ap. Non. 398, 8 (Hist. 2, 19 Dietsch): aliquem virgis,Plaut. Rud. 3, 4, 53: ungue genas,Ov. A. A. 3, 708: radices, Cato ap. Plin. 17, 22, 35, § 198: sive quis sauciatus in opere noxam ceperit,Col. 11, 1, 18.—* Trop. (anteand post-cla...

saucius.definition: saucĭus, a, um Wounded, hurt. Lit.: omnes saucios Convisit, Att. ap. Non. 398, 4: multis civibus sauciis,Varr. ib. 398, 13: videmus ex acie efferri saepe saucios,Cic. Tusc. 2, 16, 38; so, too, in milit. lang.,Caes. B. G. 3, 4 fin.; 5, 36; id. B. C. 3, 75; 3, 78 al.; cf. humorously: saucius factus sum in Veneris proelio: Sagittā Cupido cor meum transfixit, * Plaut. Pers. 1, 1, 24: taurus,Verg. A. 2, 223: funesto saucia morsu,Ov. M. 11, 373: bracch...

saul.definition: or The first king of the Jews, Alcim. ad Sor. 435; Paul. Nol. Carm. 13, 601; Vulg. 1 Reg. 9, 2; id. Act. 13, 21; gen. Saulis, id. Isa. 10, 29; dat. Sauli, id. Psa. 51, 1; acc. Saulem, id. 1 Reg. 15, 35.

saulus.definition: Saul, the name of St. Paul before his conversion, Prud. Ench. 186; Arat. A. Ap. 1, 709; Vulg. Act. 9, 1 et saep.

saxetum.definition: saxum A rocky place (very rare): asperum saxetum, * Cic. Agr. 2, 25, 67.—In plur., Col. 5, 10, 9 Schneid. N. cr. (al. saxosa).

saxeus.definition: saxĕus, a, um, id.. Lit., of rock, of stone, rocky, stony: saxea est verruca in summo montis vertice, Auct. ap. Quint. 8, 3, 48: moles, Att. ap. Cic. N. D. 2, 35, 89; Ov. M. 12, 283: scopulus,id. ib. 14, 73: saepta,Lucr. 4, 699: strata viarum,id. 1, 315: tecta,id. 5, 984; Ov. H. 10, 128: crepido,Plin. 12, 1, 5, § 9: effigies bacchantis,Cat. 64, 61: umbra,of the rocks,Verg. G. 3, 145 et saep.: mater ad auditas stupuit ceu saxea voces,Ov. M. 5, 509...

saxificus.definition: saxĭfĭcus, a, um, saxum-facio That turns into stone, petrifying (poet.): Medusa,Ov. Ib. 555; Sil. 10, 178; Luc. 9, 670; cf.: vultus Medusae,Ov. M. 5, 217: os (Medusae),Sen. Herc. Fur. 901.

saxosus.definition: saxōsus (collat. form saxŭōsus, Sicul. Fl. p. 11 Goes.), a, um, saxum Full of rocks or stones, rocky, stony: montes,Verg. G. 2, 111: valles,id. E. 5, 84: loca,Col. Arb. 21, 1: mare,id. ib. 8, 16, 8: Hypanis,Verg. G. 4, 370: Euphrates,Plin. 5, 24, 20, § 84: frutex,growing among stones,id. 15, 7, 7: Phlegethon saxosa incendia torquet,Sil. 13, 565.—As subst.: saxōsa, ōrum, n., rocky or stony places: piscium genera alia planis gaudent, alia saxosis,Q...

saxulum.definition: dim.id. A little rock: in asperrimis saxulis,Cic. de Or. 1, 44, 196.

saxum.definition: (in inscrr. also SAKSVM; from collat. form saxus; A vocative SAXE,Inscr. Orell. 2982), , n.root sak-; Sanscr. ska; cf. secare, any large, rough stone; a detached fragment of rock; a rock (in gen.; whereas rupes is a steep rock, crag, cliff). In gen., Lucr. 4, 266 sq.; cf. id. 1, 882: non est e saxo sculptus,Cic. Ac. 2, 31, 100: pars ludicre saxa Jactant, inter se licitantur, Enn. ap. Non. 134, 13 (Ann. v. 76 Vahl.): (Sisyphum) adverso nixantem tr...

scabellum.definition: (), , dim. scamnum; cf. Quint. 1, 4, 12. A low stool, footstool, cricket, Varr. L. L. 5, 35, 46 fin.; Cato, R. R. 10, 4; Vulg. Psa. 98, 5; id. Isa. 66, 1. Transf., an instrument of the nature of the castanet, played on by the foot, esp. used in dramatic representations, Cic. Cael. 27, 65; Suet. Calig. 54; Arn. 2, 73; Aug. Mus. 3 init.

scabies.definition: scabo A roughness, scurf. Lit. Trop. (acc. to I. B.), an itching, longing, pruriency (very rare): cujus (voluptatis) blanditiis corrupti, quae naturā bona sunt, quia dulcedine hac et scabie carent, non cernunt satis, * Cic. Leg. 1, 17, 47; so, scabies et contagia lucri,Hor. Ep. 1, 12, 14: nos hac a scabie (sc. rodendi, detrectandi) tenemus ungues,Mart. 5, 60, 11; so of lust, id. 6, 37, 4; 11, 7, 6.

scabiosus.definition: scăbĭōsus, a, um, id. (post-Aug.). Rough, scurfy: coralium,Plin. 32, 2, 11, § 22: far,old, spoiled,Pers. 5, 74. Scabby, mangy: boves, Col.11,2,83: (homo),Pers. 2, 13: anguli (oculorum),Plin. 29, 2, 10, § 36: macies mulorum,App. M. 9, p. 223.

scabo.definition: scăbo, scābi (no Sup.), 3, root skap-, skamp; Gr. σκάπτω, to dig; κάπετος, ditch; Lat. scaber, scabies, to scratch, to scrape (syn. rado): caput, Lucil. ap. Non. 472, 6; Hor. S. 1, 10, 71: scaberat ut porcus contritis arbore costis, Lucil. ap. Prisc. p. 884 P.: aures pedibus posterioribus,Plin. 11, 48, 108, § 260: se,id. 8, 27, 41, § 99; 10, 74, 95, § 204: tellurem,id. 10, 71, 91, § 196: laminas (doliorum),id. 18, 26, 64, § 236.—Prov.: mutuum s...

scabritia.definition: and , (in both forms post-Aug.; esp. freq. in Plin.), id.. In gen., roughness, ruggedness: digitorum,Plin. 34, 13, 34, § 131: unguium,id. 28, 9, 37, § 139: linguae,id. 31, 9, 45, § 100: chartae levigatur dente,id. 13, 12, 25, § 81: corticis,id. 21, 4, 10, § 17: ferramentorum,id. 28, 9, 41, § 148: arteriae,id. 27, 12, 105, § 130 et saep.—* The scab, the itch, Col. 7, 5, 8.

scabrosus.definition: scă_brōsus, a, um, id. Rough, scabrous: sorde,Prud. Psych. 106.

scaena.definition: (falsely , v. Prol. in Verg. p. 387 Rib.), , = σκηνή. Lit., the stage, boards, scene of a theatre: dum histrio in scaenă siet,Plaut. Poen. prol. 20: in scaenă esse Roscium intellegat,Cic. Brut. 84, 290: foris hic extra scaenam fient proelia,Plaut. Capt. prol. 60: cum scaena croco Cilici perfusa recens est,Lucr. 2, 416: scaenaique simul varios splendere decores,id. 4, 983: scaenae magnificentia,Cic. Mur. 19, 38: nec vero scaena solum referta est ...

scaenicus.definition: scaenĭcus (scen-), a, um Of or belonging to the stage, scenic, dramatic, theatrical (class.). Lit.: poëtae,dramatic poets,Varr. L. L. 9, § 17 Müll.: artifices,players, actors,Cic. Arch. 5, 10; Suet. Caes. 84: actores,Quint. 6, 1, 26; 11, 3, 4: ludi, stage-plays, theatrical representations, in a gen. sense (opp. to games of wrestling, racing, etc.), Liv. 7, 2; 31, 4; 34, 54; Ter. Hec. prol. alt. 37; Suet. Calig. 26; id. Ner. 11; cf. operae (with g...

scaevus.definition: scaevus, a, um, kindred with Sanscr. savya, laevus, sinister, as the Gr. σκαιός and the Germ. schief, oblique Left, that is on the left, towards the left side (rare; most freq. in Appul.; syn. laevus, sinister). Lit.: itinera portarum,i. e. running from right to left,Vitr. 1, 5, 2: iter,Serv. Verg. A. 3, 351. Trop.

scaeuus.definition: scaevus, a, um, kindred with Sanscr. savya, laevus, sinister, as the Gr. σκαιός and the Germ. schief, oblique Left, that is on the left, towards the left side (rare; most freq. in Appul.; syn. laevus, sinister). Lit.: itinera portarum,i. e. running from right to left,Vitr. 1, 5, 2: iter,Serv. Verg. A. 3, 351. Trop.

scala.definition: (acc. to the ancient grammarians, not used in sing.; cf. Varr. L. L. 9, §§ 63 and 68; 10, § 54 Müll.; Quint. 1, 5, 16 Spald.; Charis. p. 20 P. p. 72 ib.; Diom. p. 315 ib. al.; but V.infra), f.for scandla, from scando; cf. mala, from mando, mostly plur.: , , a flight of steps or stairs, a staircase; a ladder, scaling-ladder. Plur. Sing. (post-class.).

scalmus.definition: A peg to which an oar was strapped; a thole, tholepin, Vitr. 10, 8 med.; Cic. Brut. 53, 197; id. de Or. 1, 38, 174; Vell. 2, 43, 1: venit (Canius) mature: scalmum nullum videt, not even a thole-pin, i. e. no trace of a boat, Cic. Off. 3, 14, 59.

scalpellum.definition: n. (collat. form , , m., Cels. 2, 10 twice), dim. scalprum A small surgical knife, a scalpel, a lancet: scalpellum adhibere,Cic. Sest. 65, 135; id. Div. 2, 46, 96; Col. 6, 32, 3; Plin. 28, 8, 28, § 110; Veg. Vet. 1, 26, 2; Sen. Ira, 2, 27, 4: scribae,a penknife,Vulg. Jer. 36, 23.

scalpo.definition: scalpo, psi, ptum, 3, root skalp-; Gr. σκάλοψ, mole; Lat. talpa; cf. scalprum; also Gr. γλύφω. To cut, carve, scrape, scratch, engrave (class.; syn. caelo), said of surface work, = ξέειν; sculpo, of deeper work, high relief, or statuary, = γλύφω: ad pingendum, ad fingendum, ad scalpendum apta manus est,Cic. N. D. 2, 60, 150: Phidiam tradunt scalpsisse marmora,Plin. 36, 5, 4, § 15: marmora ac scyphos,id. 35, 11, 40, § 128 (Sillig, sculpsit): g...

scalpratus.definition: scalprātus, a, um, scalprum Having a sharp or cutting edge: ferramentum,Col. 9, 15, 9.

scalprum.definition: n. (collat. form , , m., Cels. 8, 3) [scalpo] A sharp cutting instrument; a chisel, knife, etc., of sculptors, husbandmen, shoemakers, surgeons, etc., Liv. 27, 49; Col. 4, 25, 1; Hor. S. 2, 3, 106; Cels. 8, 3 sq.; Sen. Ep. 65, 13.—A penknife, Tac. A. 5, 8; Suet. Vit. 2.—Of a pruning-knife, Plin. 17, 16, 26, § 119.

scamnum.definition: for scap-num; root skap-; Gr. σκήπτω, to support; cf.: scabellum, scapus, scipio A bench, stool, step, etc. In gen.: quă simplici scansione scandebant in lectum non altum, scabellum; in altiorem, scamnum,Varr. L. L. 5, § 168 Müll.; Ov. A. A. 2, 211; 1, 162: longis considere scamnis,id. F. 6, 305; Cels. 2, 15: sedere in scamnis equitum,Mart. 5, 41, 7.— Of horizontal branches of trees serving as seats, Plin. 12, 1, 5, § 10: ramorum,id. 17, 23, 35,...

scandalizo.definition: scandălizo, āvi, ātum, 1 To cause to stumble, tempt to evil (eccl. Lat.), Tert. Virg. Vel. 3; id. Cor. Mil. 14; id. adv. Marc. 15, 18 fin.; Vulg. Mal. 2, 8; id. Matt. 5, 30.

scandalum.definition: That which causes one to stumble, a stumblingblock (eccl. Lat.). * Lit., Prud. Apoth. 47 praef. Trop., an inducement to sin, a temptation, cause of offence, Tert. Virg. Vel. 3; id. adv. Jud. 14; id. adv. Marc. 3, 1; Vulg. Psa. 118, 165; id. 1 Johan. 2, 10.

scandix.definition: The herb chervil: Scandix caerefolium, Linn.; Plin. 21, 15, 52, § 89; 22, 22, 38, § 81.

scando.definition: scando (no Perf. or sup.; cf.: ascendo, descendo, etc.), 3, and n. Sanscr. root skand-, to climb; cf. Gr. σκάνδαλον, σκανδάληθρον. Act., to climb, mount, clamber or get up; to ascend. Neutr., to mount, rise, arise, ascend (not freq. till after the Aug. period).

scapha.definition: σκάφη; cf. scabo A light boat, a skiff (cf.: lembus, cymba): de navi timidae desiluerunt in scapham,Plaut. Rud. prol. 75; 1, 2, 74; 1, 2, 76; 1, 2, 84; 2, 3, 36; 2, 3, 38; Cic. Inv. 2, 51, 154; Auct. Her. 1, 11, 19; Sall. Fragm. ap. Non. 535, 11; Liv. 44, 42: biremis, * Hor. C. 3, 29, 62: piscatoria,Just. 2, 13, 9 et saep.; Vulg. Act. 27, 16.

scaphium.definition: () In gen., a concave vessel or basin in the form of a boat (cf. cymbium), Lucr. 6, 1046; Vitr. 8, 1 med. In partic.

scapula.definition: Scăpŭla, ae, m. A Roman surname. A partisan of Pompey, the main instigator of the Spanish war, Auct. B. Hisp. 33; Cic. Fam. 9, 13, 1. A usurer in the time of Cicero, Cic. Quint. 4, 17.—Hence, Scă-pŭlānus, a, um, , named after one Scapula: horti,Cic. Att. 12, 40, 4.

scapus.definition: root skap-; Gr. σκήπτω, to prop, σκῆπτρον; Doric, σκᾶπος; cf.: scipio, scamnum, scopus; Engl. shaft A shaft, stem, stalk, trunk, etc. In gen., Varr. R. R. 1, 31, 5; Col. 9, 4, 4; Plin. 18, 10, 21, § 95; Sen. Ep. 86, 17. In partic.

scatebra.definition: scateo A bubbling or gushing up of water (not ante-Aug., and very rare): fontium,Plin. 5, 1, 1, § 6: fonticuli,id. 31, 10, 46, § 108.

scateo.definition: scăteo, ēre (ante-class. also scatit, Lucr. 5, 40; 6, 891; and scatĕre, Enn. ap. Cic. Tusc. 1, 28, 69, or Trag. v. 196 Vahl.; Lucr. 5, 598; 5, 952; 6, 896; Perf. and sup. wanting), etym. dub.; cf. Lith. skas-, leap, to bubble, gush, well, spring, or flow forth (poet.; not before the Aug. period in prose). Lit.: fontes scatere, Enn. l. l.; cf.: fons dulcis aquaï qui scatit et salsas circum se dimovet undas,Lucr. 6, 891 sq.; and (with erumpere) id....

scaurus.definition: Scaurus, i, m.1. scaurus A frequent surname in the gens Aemilia and Aurelia. So, M. Aemilius Scaurus, whom Cicero defended in an oration, part of which is still extant.—Hence, Scaurĭānus, a, um, , relating to Scaurus: oratio,Mart. Cap. 5, § 441.

scazon.definition: (limping) An iambic trimeter, with a spondee or trochee in the last foot, Plin. Ep. 5, 11, 2; cf. Mart. 1, 97, 1; 7, 25, 1.

sceleratus.definition: scĕlĕrātus, a, um, Part. and of scelero.

scelero.definition: scĕlĕro, no Perf., ātum, 1, v. a.id., to pollute, defile, contaminate, desecrate (in the verb. finit. rare, and only poet.; syn.: temero, polluo): impia non verita est divos scelerare parentes,Cat. 64, 405; cf. Stat. Th. 2, 663: sanguine fauces,id. ib. 8, 761: parce pias scelerare manus,Verg. A. 3, 42: Cererem,Juv. 9, 25: animum,Sil. 16, 122; cf.: dextram sanguine,Stat. Th. 9, 666. —Hence, scĕlĕrātus, a, um, P. a., polluted, profaned by crime.

scelerosus.definition: scĕlĕrōsus, a, um, scelus Full of wickedness, vicious, abominable, accursed (ante- and post-class.): ubi ego illum scelerosum et impium inveniam?Ter. Eun. 4, 3, 1: scelerosa et polluta mulier,App. M. 10, p. 253, 2: scelerosa atque impia facta,Lucr. 1, 82: o diem scelerosum et indignum, Afr. ap. Non. 174, 29.—As subst.: scĕlĕrōsus, i, m., a wicked or vicious person, a wretch, Lucil. ap. Non. 174, 27.

scelestus.definition: scĕlestus, a, um, scelus; like funestus, from funus Wicked, villanous, infamous, accursed, abominable; knavish, roguish; and subst., a wicked person, a knave, rogue, scoundrel, miscreant (freq. ante-class. in Plaut. and Ter.; after the class. per. sceleratus is more freq.; by Cic. not used of persons). Lit., of persons: ego sum malus, Ego sum sacer, scelestus,Plaut. Bacch. 4, 6, 14: eheu, scelestus galeam in navi perdidi,id. Rud. 3, 5, 22: perjur...

scelus.definition: Sanscr. root skhal, to fall, akin to khal-, to deceive; cf. Goth. skal, to owe An evil deed; a wicked, heinous, or impious action; a crime, sin, enormity, wickedness (the strongest general term for a morally bad act or quality; very freq. both in sing. and plur.; cf. nefas). Lit. Transf.

scenofactorius.definition: scēnŏfactōrĭus, a, um, σκῆνος -facio Of or belonging to the making of tents: ars,the business of tent-making,Vulg. Act. 18, 3.

scenopegia.definition: σκηνοπηγία The Jewish Feast of Tabernacles (eccl. Lat.), Vulg. 1 Macc. 10, 21; id. 2 Macc. 1, 18; id. Johan. 7, 2.

sceptrum.definition: (less correctly ) A royal staff, a sceptre. Lit.: (rex Ptolemaeus) sedens cum purpurā et sceptro et illis insignibus regiis,Cic. Sest. 26, 57; Quint. 9, 3, 57; 11, 3, 158; Suet. Aug. 94: Augusti,id. Galb. 1; Verg. A. 7, 247: dextrā sceptrum gerebat,id. ib. 12, 206; Ov. M. 7, 103; 1, 178; 2, 847; 5, 422. Also borne by a king's daughter,Verg. A. 1, 653 Heyne: exitiale,Stat. Th. 1, 34; of a triumphant general,Liv. 5, 41; Juv. 10, 43.—Poet., in the p...

sceptuchus.definition: A sceptre-bearer, a high officer of state in the East, Tac. A. 6, 33.

schedula.definition: (), , dim. scheda or scida A small leaf of paper, Hier. in Ruf. 3, 2.

schema.definition: (cf.: Diadema, dogma, etc.,Prisc. p. 679 P.), and (mostly post-Aug.) , (dat. and abl. plur. schemasin, Varr. ap. Charis. p. 38; but schematibus,Lampr. Heliog. 19), = σχῆμα. In gen., a shape, figure, form, fashion, manner, posture, attitude, etc. (so mostly ante-class.; not in Cic.). In partic., as in rhet., a figure of speech, rhetorical figure (pure Lat. figura; freq. in Quint.; in Cic. written as Greek),Sen. Contr. 1, praef. § 23 sq.; 1, 1, 25...

schisma.definition: A split, separation, disunion, schism (eccl. Lat.), Tert. Praescr. 5; Prud. στεφ. 11, 19; 11, 30; Vulg. Johan. 9, 16.

schismaticus.definition: A separatist, seceder, schismatic (eccl. Lat.): schismaticos non fides diversa facit, sed communionis disrupta societas,Aug. Quaest. in Matt. 11.

schoenus.definition: ( Neutr. collat. form , Col. 12, 20, 2 and 5, somewhat dub.), = σχοῖνος, ὁ. A rush, of an aromatic kind (pure Lat. juncus), used by the Romans to season wine, Cato, R. R. 105, 2; 113, 1; Col. 12, 20, 2; 12, 20, 5; 12, 53, 2; low women anointed themselves with a perfume made from it: schoeno delibutae,Plaut. Poen. 1, 2, 55 (where others read caeno delibutae); cf. also schoeniculae. A measure of distance among the Persians (= 40 stadia), Plin. 6,...

schola.definition: (), , , = (spare time, leisure; hence, in partic.) Leisure given to learning, a learned conversation or debate, a disputation, lecture, dissertation, etc.: in quam exercitationem (disputandi) ita nos studiose operam dedimus, ut jam etiam scholas Graecorum more habere auderemus ... Itaque dierum quinque scholas, ut Graeci appellant, in totidem libros contuli,Cic. Tusc. 1, 4, 7; 8: separatim certae scholae sunt de exsilio, de interitu patriae, etc....

scholaris.definition: schŏlāris, e, schola. Of or belonging to a school (late Lat.): incohamenta,Mart. Cap. 3, § 326: murmur, Prud. στεφ. 9, 16: declamatio,Hier. Ep. 36, 14. (Acc. to schola, I. B. 2. b.) Subst.: schŏlāres, ĭum, m., the imperial guard, Cod. Th. 11, 18, 1; 7, 4, 34; Cod. Just. 12, 38, 14.

scholasticus.definition: schŏlastĭcus, a, um. Adj. = σχολαστικός, of or belonging to a school, scholastic (post-Aug., and in gen. referring to the schools of rhetoric): controversiae,Quint. 4, 2, 92; 4, 2, 97; Tac. Or. 14 fin.: materia,Quint. 11, 1, 82: declamationes,Gell. 15, 1, 1: scholasticae atque umbraticae litterae,Plin. Ep. 9, 2, 3: lex,id. ib. 2, 20, 9.— As subst.: schŏlastĭca, ōrum, n. plur., school-exercises: in scholasticis nonnumquam evenit, ut pro narration...

scibilis.definition: scībĭlis, e, scio That can be known, knowable, discernible (post-class.): Deus non omnibus scibilis,Tert. adv. Marc. 5, 16: scientia rei,Mart. Cap. 4, § 375.

scida.definition: or , , , = σχίδν, σχέδη A strip of papyrus bark, Plin. 13, 12, 23, § 77.—Form scheda, a leaf or sheet of paper, Cic. Att. 1, 20, 7; id. Fam. 15, 16, 1; Quint. 1, 8, 19; Mart. 4, 89, 4 (form scheda; al. scida).

sciens.definition: scĭens, entis, Part. and , from scio.

scienter.definition: scĭenter, , v. scio P. a. fin.

scientia.definition: (plur. only Vitr. 1, 1, 18; 3, praef. 1) [sciens] A knowing or being skilled in any thing, knowledge, science, skill, expertness, = cognitio, eruditio (freq. and class.).

scilicet.definition: scīlĭcet, contr. from sci- (root of scire) licet; cf. vide-licet, i-licet, or scīre lĭcet, as it is freq. written in Lucr. and in archaic lang. in Liv., and sometimes in Cels.; prop., you may understand or know, = Gr. δηλονότι, and serving to imply that a statement is in itself obviously true, and is not overlooked by the speaker (cf. Madv. ad Cic. Fin. 5, 1, 3). Lit., it is evident, clear, plain, or manifest; of course, naturally, evidently, ce...

scilla.definition: () A sea-onion, sea-leek, squill: Scilla maritima, Linn.; Plin. 19, 5, 30, § 93; 20, 9, 39, § 97; 21, 17, 66, § 106; Varr. R. R. 2, 7, 8; Col. 12, 33; 12, 34; Pall. Febr. 29, 2; id. Mart. 10, 4; id. Jul. 8, 1 al. A small fish of the lobster kind, which defends the pinna, a prawn, shrimp: Cancer squilla, Linn.; in this sense more usually written squilla,Cic. N. D. 2, 48, 123; Plin. 9, 42, 66, § 142; Lucil. ap. Cic. Fin. 2, 8, 24; Hor. S. 2, 4, 58;...

scindo.definition: scindo, scĭdi, scissum, 3 (old Perf. redupl. scicidi, Enn., Naev., Att, and Afran. ap. Prisc. p. 890 P.; or Enn. p. 133 Vanl.; Com. Rel. pp. 19 and 164 Rib.; cf. also, sciciderat. Gell 6, 9, 16), v. a. akin to Gr. σχίζω, to split; cf. Germ. scheiden, and Lat. scio, to cut, tear, rend, or break asunder; to split, cleave, divide, or separate by force, etc. (freq. and class.; but in tempp.perf.ante-class.and postAug.; syn.: findo, rumpo). Lit.: quo...

scintilla.definition: dim.kindr. with σπινθήρ A spark (class.). Lit.; sing.: videmus Accedere ex unā scintillā incendia passim,Lucr. 5, 609; 4, 606; Verg. A. 1, 174; Ov. M. 7, 80; Liv. 38, 7 al.: parva saepe scintilla contempta excitavit incendium,Curt. 6, 3, 11.—Plur., Lucr. 2, 675; 6, 163; Verg. A. 12, 102; Quint. 8, 5, 29 al. Trop., a spark, glimmer, faint trace: scintilla ingenii,Cic. Rep. 2, 21, 31: belli,id. Fam. 10, 14, 2: isti tantis offusis tenebris ne scint...

scintillo.definition: scintillo, āvi, 1, scintilla To sparkle, glitter, glow, gleam, flash (poet. and in post-Aug. prose; cf. fulguro). Lit.: templa caeli,Lucr. 6, 644: fulgetra,Plin. 2, 43, 43, § 113: clipeus ardens,id. 2, 34, 34, § 100: testā ardente oleum,Verg. G. 1, 392: oculi,Plaut. Men. 5, 2, 77: carbunculi contra radios solis,Plin. 37, 7, 25, § 95: cristae,Sil. 7, 593. Trop.: scintillavit cruentis Ira genis,Sil. 9, 562: tunc Venus et calidi scintillat fervor am...

scintillula.definition: dim.id. A little spark, sparklet (rare): eas in pueris virtutum quasi scintillulas videmus, e quibus accendi philosophi ratio debet,Cic. Fin. 5, 15, 43: vitae,Tert. Anim. 23: animae,Plaut. Trin. 2, 4, 91 Fleck.

scio.definition: scĭo, īvi, ītum, 4 (old Imperf. scibam, Plaut. As. 2, 2, 34; 2, 4, 89; id. Ps. 1, 5, 84; 1, 5, 86; Ter. Heaut. 2, 3, 68; id. Phorm. 4, 1, 16: scibas,Plaut. Aul. 4, 10, 24; id. Ps. 1, 5, 85: scibat,id. Am. prol. 22; Lucr. 5, 934: scibatis,Plaut. Rud. 2, 3, 47: scibant,Lucr. 5, 949; 5, 953; Cat. 68, 85.—Fut. scibo, Plaut. As. 1, 1, 13; id. Most. 4, 3, 5; id. Men. 2, 3, 35; 5, 2, 57; id. Ps. 1, 2, 41; 1, 5, 65; id. Truc. 2, 6, 69; Ter. Eun. 4, 4, 58...

sciolus.definition: scius A smatterer, sciolist, Arn. 2, 86 dub.; Hier. Ep. 48, 18; 58, 5; 125, 16.

scipio.definition: root skap-; Gr. σκήπτω, to support, σκίπων, = σκῆπτρον, a staff; cf.: scāpus, scopio, scamnum A staff (carried by persons of wealth, rank, high official station, etc.): unde ornatu hoc advenis? quid fecisti scipione?Plaut. Cas. 5, 4, 6; id. Am. 1, 3, 22; id. As. 1, 1, 111; id. Men. 5, 2, 103; Cat. 37, 10; Plin. 28, 2, 4, § 15: eburneus, carried by the viri triumphales,Liv. 5, 41 fin.; cf. Val. Max. 4, 4, 5; in the time of the emperors, also by...

scirpiculus.definition: scirpĭcŭlus (sirp- and surp-), a, um id.. Of or made of rushes. So with falces (their use is unknown), Cato, R. R. 11, 4; Varr. R. R. 1, 22, 5; id. L. L. 5, § 137 Müll.: fiscella,Vulg. Exod. 2, 3.—More freq. Subst.: scirpĭcŭlus (sirp-, surp-), i, m., a basket made of rushes, a rush-basket: surpiculi olerorum, Lucil. ap. Non. 490, 24; Varr. R. R. 2, 2, 10; Col. poët. 10, 305; Prop. 4 (5), 2, 40. piscarii,wears, weels,Plaut. Capt. 4, 2, 36.

scirpo.definition: scirpo (sirpo), no Perf., ātum, 1, id., to plait of rushes, Varr. L. L. 5, § 137 sq.; id. ap. Non. 83, 24.

scirpus.definition: (sometimes ) A rush, bulrush, Plin. 16, 37, 70, § 178; 7, 56, 57, § 206; Fest. p. 330 Müll.; Plaut. Rud. 2, 6, 39; Vulg. Job, 8, 11. Transf., deriving the idea of intricacy from plaited work of rushes, a riddle, enigma: quae Graeci dicunt aenigmata, hoc genus quidam e nostris veteribus scirpos appellaverunt,Gell. 12, 6, 1.

sciscitor.definition: sciscĭtor, ātus, 1 V. dep. a. [scisco], to inform one's self; to ask, inquire, question, examine, interrogate, etc. (class.; syn.: percontor, interrogo); constr. regularly, ex (ab) aliquo aliquid, de aliquā re, with a rel.clause or absol.; also (post-Aug.) with aliquem quid.

scisco.definition: scisco, scīvi, scītum, 3 ( Dep. collat. form sciscor, acc. to Prisc. p. 799 P.), v. inch. a. [scio], to seek to know; to search, inquire. Lit. (ante-class. and very rare; cf., on the other hand, the deriv. sciscitor): praefestinamus, quae sit causa, sciscere, Afran. ap. Charis. p. 186 P.: ibo ad eam, ut sciscam, quid velint, Att. ap. Non. 505, 12; cf. Plaut. Am. 5, 1, 17. Transf.

scissilis.definition: scissĭlis, e, scindo. That may easily be split, cleft, or rent: alumen,Cels. 5, 2; 6, 11: lapis,id. 6, 6, 30. (Postclass.) scissus, a, um, rent, torn: palliastrum,App. M. 1, p. 104, 27; cf. centunculus,id. 9, p. 222, 27: fasciae,Veg. 3, 47, 3.

scissor.definition: scinde. One who cleaves or divides, a carver, Petr. 36, 6. A kind of gladiator, Inscr. Orell. 2569.

scissura.definition: id. A tearing, rending, dividing; a rent, cleft, scissure (postAug.). Lit., Sen. Q. N. 6, 2: ad scissuram Nili,Plin. 5, 9, 9, § 50; 11, 28, 34, § 100: sal rectis scissuris,id. 31, 7, 39, § 79; Pall. Mai, 12; Vulg. Matt. 9, 16. Trop.: domestica turbat rem populi,Prud. Psych. 756: audio scissuras esse inter vos,Vulg. 1 Cor. 11, 18.

scitor.definition: scītor, ātus, 1 (old Inf. scitarier, Ov. M. 2, 741), v. freq. dep. a. [scio], to seek to know; to ask, inquire (poet. and late Lat.; in Cic. Or. 16, 52, read sciscitari; cf.: interrogo, percunctor): scitari et quaerere causas,Verg. A. 2, 105: causam viae,Ov. M. 2, 511: causam adventūs,id. ib. 2, 741: omnia,id. ib. 2, 548: digna relatu,id. ib. 4, 793: scitanti deus huic de conjuge dixit,id. ib. 10, 564: quid veniat, scitatur,id. ib. 11, 622: Euryp...

scitulus.definition: scītŭlus, a, um Adj. dim. [1. scitus, A. 2.], handsome, pretty, neat, trim, elegant (ante- and post-class.): facies,Plaut. Rud. 2, 7, 7: forma atque aetatula,id. ib. 4, 1, 3; App. M. 2, 113, 19: juvenem formulae scitulae,id. ib. 3, 136, 13: caupona,id. ib. 1, p. 105, 23: pusiones,Arn. 5, 179.—Adv.: scītŭlē, elegantly, gracefully, App. M. 2, p. 123, 8; 7, p. 192, 35; 10, p. 253, 38.

scitum.definition: scītum, i, n., v. scisco, , A. 1. and B.

scitus.definition: scītus, a, um, Part. and of scisco.

scius.definition: scĭus, a, um, scio Knowing, having knowledge of a thing (mostly ante- and post-class., and rare for sciens, gnarus, peritus).

scobis.definition: (collat. form , only acc. to Prisc. p. 751 P.; but scobis is found in Cels. 5, 5; 8, 2; Col. 4, 29, 15; 7, 10, 4; cf. scrobis Init.), , f. (m., Vitr. 8, 3; Pall. Febr. 17, 6) [scabo], powder or dust produced by sawing, rasping, etc.; sawdust, scrapings, filings, etc., Cels. 1. 1.; Col. 1. 1.; Hor. S. 2, 4, 81; Plin. 34, 11, 26, § 111; Juv. 14, 67 al.: citreus,i. e. grated lemon-peel,Vitr. 8, 3, 8: cutis, scurf, etc., Plin. 30, 4, 10, § 28.

scomber.definition: A kind of tunny, a mackerel: Scomber scomber, Linn.; Plin. 9, 15, 19, § 49; 31, 8, 43, § 94; 32, 11, 53, § 151; Col. 8, 17, 12; Plaut. Capt. 4, 2, 71; Cat. 95, 8; Pers. 1, 43; Mart. 3, 50, 9; 4, 87, 8; 13, 102, 2.

scopa.definition: and plur.: , (cf. on plur., Varr. L. L. 8, § 7 Müll.; 10, § 24 ib.; Quint. 1, 5, 16; Charis. p. 20 P.; 72 ib.; Diom. p. 315 ib.; sing. V.infra, B.), f.root skap-, to support; cf.: scipio, scamnum. Lit., thin branches, twigs, shoots (rare), Cato, R. R. 152; Pall. 3, 24, 8; 4, 9, 12; Auct. B. Afr. 47, 5; Plin. 20, 22, 89, § 241; 22, 18, 21, § 46 al. Meton., a broom, besom made of twigs (class. in plur.): munditias volo fieri: efferte huc scopas, et...

scopo.definition: scŏpo, ĕreσκοπέω To investigate, test, search: spiritum suum,Vulg. Psa. 76, 7.

scopulus.definition: σκόπελος A projecting point of rock; a rock, cliff, crag, esp. a rock, shelf, ledge in the sea. Lit. (mostly poet.; not in Cic., but v.infra, II.; cf.: rupes, cautes), in the sea: ut pars (remigum) ad scopulos allisa interficeretur,Caes. B. C. 3, 27 fin.; id. B. G. 3, 13; Poët. ap. Cic. de Or. 3, 41, 166; Verg. G. 3, 261; id. A. 1, 145; 5, 270; Ov. M. 4, 524; 9, 592: frequentes,Juv. 13, 246: vomentes aequor,Luc. 6, 24: immanes,Ov. M. 14, 182; cf...

scorpio.definition: (poet. collat. forms and , , corresp. to the Greek) A scorpion. Lit., Plin. 11, 37, 62, § 86; 28, 2, 5, § 24; 29, 4, 29, § 91; Vulg. Deut. 8, 15. —In the form scorpius, Ov. M. 15, 371 scorpios, id. F. 4, 164; acc. scorpion, id. ib. 5, 541. Transf.

scortator.definition: scortor A whoremonger, fornicator, Plaut. Am. 1, 1, 131; Hor. S. 2, 5, 75; Hier. ad Ephes. 1, 13.

scorteus.definition: scortĕus, a, um, scortum, I. Made of hides or leather, leathern: etiam nunc dicimus scortea ea, quae ex corio ac pellibus sunt facta,Varr. L. L. 7, § 84 Müll.; cf. Ov. F. 1, 629; and Fest. s. v. scorta, p. 330 Müll.: fascinum,Petr. 138, 1: pulvinus,Cels. 8, 12: asses, Hier. Chron. ad annum MCCC.—In a lusus verbb.: scorteum scortum,i. e. wrinkled, old,App. M. 1, p. 105, 36. —Subst.: scortĕa, ae, f. (sc. vestis), a garment of skins or leather, Sen....

scortillum.definition: dim.scortum, II. A little or young harlot, Cat. 10, 3; cf. ‡ scortulum.

scortor.definition: scortor, āri (old Inf. scortarier, Plaut. Merc. 5, 4, 58), v. dep. n. [id.], to employ or associate with harlots (ante- and post-class.): scortari est saepius meretriculam ducere,Varr. L. L. 7, § 84 Müll.; Plaut. As. 2, 2, 4; id. Merc. 5, 4, 25; 5, 4, 58; id. Ps. 4, 7, 35; Ter. Heaut. 1, 2, 32; id. Ad. 1, 2, 22; Vulg. 2 Macc. 6, 4.

scortum.definition: cf. Gr. χόριον, corium; Lith. skurà, skin. Lit., a skin, hide (post-class. and rare): pellem antiqui dicebant scortum,Varr. L. L. 7, § 84 Müll.: jam Omphale in Herculis scorto designata descripsit,Tert. Pall. 4 med. Transf., a harlot, strumpet, prostitute (freq. and class.): scorta appellantur meretrices, quia ut pelliculae subiguntur. Omnia namque ex pellibus facta scortea appellantur, Fest. pp. 330 and 331 Müll.—Sing., Plaut. Am. 1, 1, 132; id...

scotia.definition: in architect. A hollow moulding in the base of a column, a scotia, Vitr. 3, 5, 2. A gutter at the end of a cornice, Vitr. 4, 3, 6.

screatus.definition: id. A hawking, hemming, Ter. Heaut. 2, 3, 132.

screo.definition: scrĕo, āre To hawk, hem, Plaut. Curc. 1, 2, 22.

scriba.definition: scribo A public or official writer, a clerk, secretary, scribe (whereas librarius or scriba librarius denotes a private secretary or amanuensis; notarius, a short-hand writer): scribas proprio nomine antiqui et librarios et poëtas vocabant. At nunc dicuntur scribae quidem librarii, qui rationes publicas scribunt in tabulis, etc.,Fest. p. 333 Müll.: (scribarum) ordo est honestus, quod eorum hominum fidei tabellae publicae periculaque magistratuum ...

scriblita.definition: () A kind of tart, Cato, R. R. 78; Plaut. Poen. prol. 43; Petr. 35, 4; 66, 3; Mart. 3, 17, 1.

scribo.definition: scrībo, psi, ptum, 3 ( Perf. sync. scripsti, Plaut. As. 4, 1, 57: scripstis, Enn. ap. Non. 153, 28, or Trag. v. 239 Vahl.; inf. scripse, Aus. Sept. Sap. Lud. 1; cf. 2. dico init.), root skrabh-, to dig; whence, Gr. γράφω; Lat. scrobis, scrofa; cf. Germ. schreiben, prop., to scratch, grave, engrave with a sharp point; hence In gen. In partic., with the accessory idea of intellectual action, of written composition of every kind, to write, write do...

scrinium.definition: scribo. Lit., a case, chest, or box for keeping books, papers, letters, etc.; a book-box, letter-case, escritoir (not in Cic.; syn.: capsa, cista): Flaccum praetorem scrinium cum litteris, quas a legatis acceperat, codem afferre jubet,Sall. C. 46, 6: epistularum,Sen. Ira, 2, 23, 4; Plin. 7, 25, 26, § 94: vigil calamum et chartas et scrinia posco,book-boxes,Hor. Ep. 2, 1, 113; id. S. 1, 1, 120; Ov. P. 1, 1, 24; id. Tr. 1, 1, 106; Cat. 14, 17; Juv....

scriptor.definition: scribo One who writes. In gen. (acc. to scribo, I.), a writer, scribe, secretary (syn. librarius; very rare): addebat etiam, scriptores illos male multatos exisse cum Galbā,Cic. Brut. 22, 88; cf.: scriptor librarius,Hor. A. P. 354: ex ejus (Crassi) scriptore et lectore Diphilo suspicari liceret,Cic. de Or. 1, 30, 136: (Seneca) advocatis scriptoribus pleraque tradidit, quae, etc.,Tac. A. 15, 63 fin.; Vulg. Ezech. 9, 2. In partic. (acc. to scribo, ...

scriptorius.definition: scriptōrĭus, a, um, id. Of or belonging to writing, writing-: atramentum,Cels. 6, 4 fin.; 8, 4: calamus,id. 5, 28, 12.— Subst.: scriptōrĭum, ii, n., = γραφίον, a metallic style for writing on wax tablets, Isid. 6, 9, 2.

scriptulum.definition: scriptŭlum, i, v. scrupulus, I. B.

scriptura.definition: scribo A writing, written characters. In gen. (acc. to scribo, I.; Cic. uses scriptio instead): minium in voluminibus quoque scriptura usurpatur clarioresque litteras vel in auro vel in marmore etiam in sepulchris facit,Plin. 33, 7, 40, § 122: (meorum librorum) scriptura quanti constet,Mart. 1, 67, 3; Suet. Aug. 80: mendum scripturae, an error in writing, Caecin. ap. Cic Fam. 6, 7, 1.—* In partic. (freq. and class.).

scriptus.definition: scriptus, a, um, Part., from scribo.

scripulum.definition: (, ), , , corrupt collat. form of scrupulus, which became the prevailing one in the sense of A scruple, a small weight; v. scrupulus, I. B.

scrobis.definition: (collat. form , only acc. to Prisc. p. 751 P., and by a false read. in some edd. in Col. 4, 4, 1; 5, 5, 1 sq.; 5, 6, 18; 5, 10, 4), , m., less freq. f. root skrabh-, v. scribo. Lit., a ditch, dike, trench (syn. fossa; class.); masc., Plaut. Fragm. ap. Non. 225; 7; 8; Varr. Fragm. ib. 11; Cic. Fragm. ap. Serv. Verg. G. 2, 288; Col. 4, 1, 5; 5, 5, 2; 5, 5, 4; 5, 6, 18 et saep.— Fem., Gracchus ap. Serv. Verg. G. 2, 288; Ov. M. 7, 243; Luc. 8, 756; C...

scrofa.definition: root skrabh-, v. scribo A breeding-sow, Varr. R. R. 2, 4, 4; Col. 7, 9, 2; 7, 11, 3; Pall. Febr. 26, 1; Juv. 6, 177; 12, 73.

scrotum.definition: perh. for scortum, I. The scrotum, Cels. 7, 19; 7, 20.

scrupeus.definition: scrūpĕus, a, um, scrupus. Lit., consisting of pointed or sharp stones; sharp, rough, steep, rugged (poet. and rare): saxum, Enn. ap. Fest. s. v. scrupi, p. 333 Müll. (Trag. v. 139 Vahl.): spelunca,Verg. A. 6, 238: vada (undae),Sen. Agam. 556; cf. ora (Ismeni),Stat. Th. 9, 411: rupes,Ambros. Ep. 6, 13. Trop., hard, severe: ille (Achilles) scrupeā scholā eruditus,Tert. Pall. 4: difficultas,Aus. Idyll. 12 praef.—Subst.: scrūpĕa, ae, f., difficulty: ...

scruposus.definition: scrūpōsus, a, um, scrupus. Lit., full of sharp or rough stones, jagged, rough, rugged (poet. and in post-class. prose): specus, Att. ap. Non. 223, 2; cf. saxa,Luc. 5, 675; App. M. 6, p. 187, 6: Pyrene,Grat. Cyn. 514: via,Plaut. Capt. 1, 2, 82: ager,App. Flor. 2, p. 348, 20: per asperitates scruposas,Amm. 31, 8, 4.—* Trop., rough, hard, arduous: ratio,Lucr. 4, 523.

scrupulositas.definition: scrupulosus (very rare) Over-nicety, scrupulosity: in hac ruris disciplinā non desideratur ejusmodi scrupulositas: sed quod dicitur pingui Minervā, etc.,Col. 11, 1, 32; Tert. Virg. Vel. 11 med.; Hier. Ep. Gal. prol.

scrupulosus.definition: scrūpŭlōsus, a, um, adj.scrupulus. Lit., full of small sharp or pointed stones, rough, rugged, jagged (rare but class.): specus, Pac. ap. Prisc. p. 713 P.: tamquam e scrupulosis cotibus enavigavit oratio, * Cic. Tusc. 4, 14, 33: ruminatio corticis,Plin. 15, 23, 25, § 94: saltibus degressi scrupulosis et inviis,Amm. 19, 13, 1: vulnera aurium,for wearing jewelled drops,Tert. Cult. Fem. 10, 2. Trop. (only post-Aug.), very nice, exact, precise, anxio...

scrupulum.definition: scrūpŭlum, i, v. scrupulus, I. B.

scrupulus.definition: (, etc. V.infra, B.), , m.dim.scrupus. * Lit., a small sharp or pointed stone: ater scrupulus,Sol. 7. Trop., a pricking, stinging, uneasy sensation; hence

scrupus.definition: Lit., a rough or sharp stone: * scrupi dicuntur aspera saxa et difficilia attrectatu, Fest. pp. 332 and 333 Müll. (very rare): cum horā paene totā per omnes scrupos traxissemus cruentos pedes,Petr. 79, 3: scrupus proprie est lapillus brevis,Serv. Verg. A. 6, 238; Avien. Descr. Orb. 503. Trop., anxiety, solicitude, uneasiness (for the usual scrupulus, q. v. II.): quod vacua metu, curā, sollicitudine, periculo vita bonorum virorum sit: contra autem...

scruta.definition: sibilated from γρύτη Old or broken stuff, trash, frippery, trumpery, Lucil. ap. Gell. 3, 14, 10; Hor. Ep. 1, 7, 65; Petr. 62, 1; Vulg. 3 Reg. 10, 15; id. 2 Esdr. 3, 30.

scrutarius.definition: scrūtārĭus, a, umscruta. Adj., of or belonging to trash, frippery, or trumpery: SERVVS, perh. a dealer in such things, Inscr. Orell. 2954. Subst. *

scrutatio.definition: scrutor A searching, examining, investigating (post-Aug. and very rare). Lit.: domus,a searching, search,Sen. Vit. Beat. 23. Trop.: insulsa nimis et odiosa,Gell. 9, 10, 5; Oros. praef. p. 5.

scrutinium.definition: scrutor A search, inquiry, investigation, scruting (post-class.), App. M. 9, p. 237, 5; Vulg. Psa. 63 (64), 7.

scrutor.definition: scrūtor, āri, ātus V. dep. a. [scruta; cf.: γρυτεύει, scrutatur, Gloss. Philox.], qs. to search even to the rags, i. e. to search carefully, examine thoroughly, explore a thing; to search, examine a person (syn.: indago, rimo). Lit., of things: domos, naves,Cic. Vatin. 5, 12: loca abdita,Sall. J. 12, 5: omnia foramina parietum scrutatur,Petr. 98, 1: paleam,id. 33, 4: terraï abdita ferro,Lucr. 6, 809: ignem gladio,Hor. S. 2, 3, 276: lumina manibu...

sculpo.definition: sculpo, psi, ptum, 3, cf. γλύφω, to hollow out, grave; also scalpo, γλάφω To carve, cut, grave, chisel in stone, brass, wood, etc.; to form, fashion, or produce by carving, graving, etc. (very rare but class.; in the MSS. very freq. interchanged with scalpere). Lit.: non est e saxo sculptus aut e robore dolatus, * Cic. Ac. 2, 31, 100: niveum mirā arte Sculpsit ebur,Ov. M. 10, 248: quid sculptum infabre, quid fusum durius esset,Hor. S. 2, 3, 22:...

sculptilis.definition: sculptĭlis, e, sculpo Formed or produced by carving, graving, etc., sculptile (poet.): opus dentis Numidae,Ov. P. 4, 9, 28: forma in aere, Prud. στεφ. 10, 266. —Subst.: sculptĭle, is, n., a carved image, statue, Vulg. Judic. 17, 3: sculptilia deorum,id. 1 Macc. 5, 68: deos et sculptilia,id. Dan. 11, 8.

sculptor.definition: id. One who cuts, carves, or engraves in stone, wood, etc. (cf.: fictor, plastes),a stone-cutter, graver, sculptor,Plin. 29, 6, 38, § 132; 36, 5, 4, § 11 (Jahn reads throughout scalptor); Plin. Ep. 1, 10, 4: opere sculptoris,Vulg. Exod. 23, 11; Cassiod. Var. 7, 5 (sometimes confounded with scalptor).

scurra.definition: Orig., an elegant, town-bred man; a fine gentleman, gallant, dandy: tu urbanus vero scurra, deliciae popli, Rus mihi tu objectas?Plaut. Most. 1, 1, 14; cf. (opp. militaris) id. Ep. 1, 1, 13; id. Curc. 2, 3, 17.—Also of an elegant debauchee, Cic. Sest. 17, 39; Auct. Har. Resp. 20, 42. Transf.

scurrilitas.definition: scurrilis Buffoonery, scurrility (post-Aug.), Quint. 11, 1, 30: insulsa,Tac. Or. 22; Vulg. Eph. 5, 4.

scutarius.definition: scūtārĭus, a, um, id.. Of or belonging to a shield: fabricae,shield-factories,Veg. Mil. 2, 11. Subst.: scū-tārĭus, ii, m.

scutatus.definition: scūtātus, a, um, adj.id.. Armed with a scutum (long shield): cohortes, * Caes. B. C. 1, 39: milites,Liv. 8, 8; 33, 14: equites,Verg. A. 9, 370: manus,Sil. 6, 211. Subst.

scutella.definition: (scutella, Ven. Carm. 11, 10, 7), , dim. scutra; cf. 1. scutula A salver or waiter, of a nearly square form: dulciculae potionis,Cic. Tusc. 3, 19, 46.— Also as a stand for vases,Dig. 34, 2, 19, § 10; Ven. Fort. 3, 13, 4; 11, 10, 7.

scutica.definition: A lash, whip (milder than flagellum): ne scuticā sectere,Hor. S. 1, 3, 119; Juv. 6, 480; Ov. H. 9, 81; Mart. 10, 62, 8 (dub.): si quis Orbilius ferulā scuticāque cecidit, Domit. ap. Suet. Gram. 9.

scutra.definition: A flat tray, dish, or platter of a nearly square form, Cato, R. R. 157, 11; Plaut. Pers. 1, 3, 8; Vulg. 3 Reg. 7, 40; 7, 45.—Collat. form , , Lucil. ap. Prisc. p. 618 P

scutula.definition: dim.scutra; cf. scutella. Lit., a little dish or platter of a nearly square form (cf. lanx), Cato, R. R. 68, 1; Mart. 11, 31, 19; 8, 71, 7.
