Resp. 21, 44; cf.: strophium est fascia brevis, quae virginalem tumorem cohibet papillarum, Non. l. l. A head-band, chaplet, Verg. Copa, 32; Prud. Cath. 3, 26; esp. of priests; cf. Fest. s. v. stroppus, p...

structilis.definition: structĭlis, e, struo Of or belonging to building; that is built or constructed; that is designed or used for building (postAug.): canales,walled,Vitr. 8, 7; so, cloacae,id. 5, 9 med.: columnae,Dig. 8, 5, 8: bases,ib. 50, 16, 245: opus,ib. 50, 16, 241: gemellar, Col. 12, 52, 10: caementum, building - cement, i. e. that is used in building, Mart. 9, 76, 1.

structor.definition: id.. One who erects a building, a builder, mason, carpenter: res agebatur multis structoribus,Cic. Q. Fr. 2, 6, 2; id. Att. 14, 3, 1; Cod. Just. 10, 64, 1; Dig. 50, 6, 6; Capitol. Ver. 5; Lampr. Heliog. 27 al. One who spreads the table or serves up food and carves; a server, carver (post-Aug.): ferculorum compositor, Serv. ap. Verg. A. 1, 703; Petr. 35, 2; Mart. 10, 48, 15; Juv. 5, 120; 11, 136.

structura.definition: struo A fitting together, adaptation, adjustment. Lit. Trop., of language, an arrangement, order, structure (in Cic. only as a figure of speech, with quasi or quaedam; later in gen.): verborum quasi structura,Cic. Brut. 8, 33: quasi structura quaedam,id. Or. 44, 149: et verborum est structura quaedam,id. Opt. Gen. 2, 5: proprietates verborum exigit, et structuram et argumentationes,Sen. Ep. 89, 9: mei carminis,Ov. P. 4, 13, 4; Quint. 1, 10, 23; 8...

strues.definition: id. A heap, pile of things put together. In gen. (class.; syn.: acervus, cumulus, congeries): laterum,Cic. Att. 5, 12, 3: corporum,Liv. 23, 5; Tac. H. 2, 70; 3, 83: lignorum,Liv. 21, 37; Plin. 16, 11, 22, § 53: arma cum telis in strue mixta,Ov. P. 2, 1, 40: rogi,a funeral pile, pyre,Tac. G. 27; Luc. 8, 757; Sen. Phoen. 112; id. Oedip. 33: uvarum,Plin. 14, 4, 5, § 51 et saep.: (milites Macedones) confusa strue implicantur,a heap, mass, phalanx,Liv...

struix.definition: struo A heap, pile of things put together (ante- and post-class. for the class. strues). Lit.: struices antiqui dicebant exstructiones omnium rerum,Fest. p. 310 Müll.: tantas struices concinnat patinarias,Plaut. Men. 1, 1, 26: et Livius: per struices saxeas lapsu accidit, Livius ap. Fest. l. l.: lignorum struicibus incensis,Arn. 7, 222: caementiciae,Sol. 28. —* Trop.: struix malorum, Naev. ap. Serv. Verg. A. 4, 267 (Trag. Rel. v. 64 Rib.).

struma.definition: struo A scrofulous tumor, struma, Cels. 5, 28, 7; 1, 9fin.; Plin. 8, 51, 77, § 206; 22, 14, 16, § 38; 26, 5, 14, § 26 al.: qui exsecant pestem aliquam, tamquam strumam civitatis,Cic. Sest. 65, 135; cf. sarcastically: Vatinii strumam sacerdotii διβάφῳ vestiant, id. Att. 2, 9, 2.

strumosus.definition: strūmōsus, a, um, 1. struma Having a struma, scrofulous, strumous, Col. 7, 10, 3: homo,Juv. 10, 309: facies, Schol. Bob. ad Cic. Sest. 65.

struo.definition: strŭo, xi, ctum, 3, v. a.root στορ; Gr. στρώννυμι, to spread; cf. Sanscr. upa-star, to make ready; and v. sterno To place by or upon each other; to pile up, arrange, etc. Lit. Trop.

struthiocamelus.definition: m. (f., Plin. 11, 37, 56, § 155) An ostrich, Plin. 10, 1, 1, § 1; 10, 22, 29, § 56; 11, 37, 47, § 130 (Jahn, struthocamelus); Petr. 137, 5 al.—By later writers also called simply , , m., = στρουθίων, Capitol. Gord. 3 fin.; Lampr. Heliog. 30; Vopisc. Firm. 6; Vulg. Lev. 11, 16 et saep.

studeo.definition: stŭdĕo, ŭi, 2 ( Perf. studīvi, M. Aur. ap. Front. Ep. ad M. Caes. 5), and n. perh. kindr. with σπεύδω, σπουδή, to speed, haste, to be eager or zealous, to take pains about, be diligent in, anxious about, busy one's self with, strive after, to apply one's self to or pursue some course of action, etc.; to desire, wish, etc. (very freq. and class.; cf.: operam do). In gen. In partic.

studiosus.definition: stŭdĭōsus, a, um, adj.studium Eager, zealous, assiduous, anxious after any thing, fond or studious of any thing. In gen. In partic.

studium.definition: studeo A busying one's self about or application to a thing; assiduity, zeal, eagerness, fondness, inclination, desire, exertion, endeavor, study: stu dium est animi assidua et vehemens ad aliquam rem applicata magnā cum voluntate occupatio, ut philosophiae, poëticae, geometriae, litterarum, Cic. Inv. 1, 25, 36. In gen. In partic.

stultiloquium.definition: id. Silly talk, babbling, stultiloquy, Plaut. Mil. 2, 3, 25; Hier. Eph. 5, 3; Vulg. Eph. 5, 4.

stultitia.definition: stultus Folly, foolishness, simplicity, silliness, fatuity, etc.: delirationem incredibilem! Non enim omnis error stultitia dicenda est,Cic. Div. 2, 43, 90: stultitia atque insipientia,Plaut. Mil. 3, 3, 5: inscitiae meae et stultitiae ignoscas,id. ib. 2, 6, 62: utrum stultitiā facere ego hunc an malitiā Dicam,Ter. Phorm. 4, 3, 54: stultitiā ac temeritate vestrā Galliam prosternere,Caes. B. C. 7, 77: stultitia loquax,Cic. de Or. 3, 35, 142: num ti...

stultividus.definition: stultĭvĭdus, a, um, stultusvideo Simple-sighted, that sees things in a foolish light, Plaut. Mil. 2, 3, 64.

stultiuidus.definition: stultĭvĭdus, a, um, stultusvideo Simple-sighted, that sees things in a foolish light, Plaut. Mil. 2, 3, 64.

stultus.definition: stultus, a, um, adj.root star-; v. stolidus Foolish, simple, silly, fatuous, etc. (cf.: insulsus, ineptus, insipiens, brutus). Lit.: stulti, stolidi, fatui, fungi, bardi, blenni, buccones,Plaut. Bacch. 5, 1, 2; cf. Ter. Heaut. 5, 1, 4: inepte stultus es,Plaut. Most. 2, 2, 64: mulier stulta atque inscita,id. Men. 2, 3, 85: ex stultis insanos facere,Ter. Eun. 2, 2, 23: deum qui non summum putet, stultum (existumat), Caecil. ap. Cic. Tusc. 4, 32, 68...

stupefacio.definition: stŭpĕ-făcĭo, fēci, factum, 3, stupeo To make stupid or senseless, to benumb, deaden, stun, stupefy (rare; usu. in the part. perf.).

stupeo.definition: stŭpeo, ui, ēre, and A. [Sanscr. stūpas, cumulus; Gr. στύπος; Lat. stipes, a block, stump; cf. στείβω]. Neutr., to be struck senseless, to be stunned, benumbed; to be struck aghast, to be astonished, astounded, amazed, confounded, stupefied, etc. (freq. and class.; syn. torpeo): animus lassus curā confectus stupet,Ter. And. 2, 1, 4: cum hic etiam tum semisomnus, stupri plenus stuperet,Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 36, § 95: torpescunt scorpiones aconiti tac...

stupesco.definition: stŭpesco, ĕre V. inch. n. [stupeo], to grow astonished, become amazed, Cic. de Or. 3, 26, 102; Vulg. Ezech. 32, 10.

stupiditas.definition: stupidus Senselessness, dullness, stupidity (very rare), Att. ap. Non. 226, 22 (Trag. Rel. v. 287 Rib.): incredibilis, * Cic. Phil. 2, 32, 80.

stupidus.definition: stŭpĭdus, a, um, stupeo Strucksenseless, confounded, amazed. Lit. (rare but class.): stupida sine animo asto,Plaut. Poen. 5, 4, 79: quid stas stupida? quid taces?id. Ep. 4, 2, 13: stupidi timore obmutuerunt,Auct. Her. 4, 52, 65: Echionis tabula te stupidum detinet,Cic. Par. 5, 2, 37; cf.: populus studio stupidus,Ter. Hec. prol. 4. Transf.

stupor.definition: stupeo Numbness; dulness, insensibility, stupidity, stupor, stupefaction; astonishment, wonder, amazement (class.; syn. torpor): stupor in corpore,Cic. Tusc. 3, 6, 12: sensūs stupor,id. Phil. 2, 45, 115: stupor obstitit lacrimis,Ov. P. 1, 2, 29; cf.: stupor omnium animos tenet. Liv. 9, 2: oculos stupor urget inertes,Verg. G. 3, 523: stupor cordis,Cic. Phil. 3, 6, 16: stupor debilitasque linguae,id. Pis. 1, 1: tantus te stupor oppressit, ut, etc.,...

stuppa.definition: (less correctly ), , , = στύππη (στύπη) The coarse part of flax, tow, hards, oakum, Plin. 19, 1, 3, § 17; Varr. ap. Gell. 17, 3, 4; Lucr. 6, 880; Caes. B. C. 3, 101; Liv. 21, 8, 10; Verg. A. 5, 682; Pers. 5, 135; cf. Fest. p. 317 Müll.

stuppeus.definition: stuppĕus (stūpĕus), a, um, id. Made or consisting of tow: vincula,Verg. A. 2, 236: retinacula,Ov. M. 14, 547: verbera fundae,Verg. G. 1, 309: flamma,burning tow,id. A. 8, 694: messis,i. e. flax,Grat. Cyn. 36.

stupro.definition: stūpro, āvi, ātum, 1, id. To defile. In gen. (very rare): pulvinar,Cic. Har. Resp. 15, 33: stuprandis moribus,Tert. Apol. 6. In partic., to dishonor by unchastity, to debauch, deflour, ravish, stuprate (class.): qui illam stupravit noctu,Plaut. Aul. prol. 36: ne stupraretur (filia),Cic. Fin. 5, 22, 64; Plaut. Truc. 4, 3, 47: Lucretia vi stuprata,Cic. Fin. 2, 20, 66; Liv. 8, 22, 3: simillimi feminis mares stuprati et constupratores,Liv. 39, 15, 9;...

stuprum.definition: Defilement, dishonor, disgrace. In gen. (so only ante-class.): stuprum pro turpitudine antiquos dixisse apparet in Appii sententiis: qui animi compotem esse, ne quid fraudis stuprique ferocia pariat. Naevius: seseque ii perire mavolunt ibidem, quam cum stupro redire ad suos populares,Fest. p. 317 Müll. In partic., dishonor, disgrace by unchastity of any sort, debauchery, lewdness, violation, always implying the infliction of dishonor on the subje...

sturnus.definition: Gr. ψάρ; mod. Gr. ψαρόνι; Germ. star; Engl. star-ling A starling or stare: Sturnus vulgaris, Linn.; Plin. 10, 24, 35, § 72; 18, 17, 45, § 160; 10, 42, 59, § 120; Mart. 9, 55, 7; Stat. S. 2, 4, 18; Dig. 19, 2, 15.

stygius.definition: Stygĭus, a, um, v. Styx, II. 1.

styrax.definition: (, Sol. 33 med.; Isid. Orig. 17, 8, 5) A tree; and also the resinous gum of that tree, storax, Plin. 12, 25, 55, § 125; 24, 6, 15, § 24; Verg. Cir. 167.—Hence, , , of or made from storax: oleum,Cael. Aur. Tard. 2, 7.

styx.definition: Styx, ygis and ygos, f., = Στύξ. A fountain in Arcadia, the icy-cold water of which caused death, Plin. 2, 103, 106, § 231; Sen. Q. N. 3, 25, 1; Vitr. 8, 3, 16; Just. 12, 14, 7; Curt. 10, 10, 17. In mythology, a river in the infernal regions, by which the gods swore, Cic. N. D. 3, 17, 43; Verg. G. 4, 480; Ov. M. 12, 322; id. A. A. 1, 635; Sil. 13, 570; Stat. Th. 8, 30; id. Achill. 1, 269 al.— Hence, poet., the infernal regions, the lower world, ...

suadela.definition: (less correctly ), , suadeo. Exhortation, suasion, persuasion (ante- and post-class.): jam perducebam illam ad me suadela mea,Plaut. Cist. 2, 3, 24: suadela depravata,App. Dogm. Plat. 2, p. 28, 15.—Plur.: his et hujusmodi suadelis, etc.,App. M. 9, p. 225, 20. Suadela, personified, the goddess of Persuasion, the Gr. Πειθώ, Hor. Ep. 1, 6, 38.

suadeo.definition: suādĕo, si, sum, 2 (scanned as a trisyl., sŭādent, Lucr. 4, 1157: suavis, Key, § 972), v. n. and A. [Sanscr. svad-, to taste, please; Gr. ἁδ-, ἁνδάνω, to please; Lat. suavis, suadela, etc.; Germ. süsz; Engl. sweet], to advise, recommend, exhort, urge, persuade (freq. and class.; cf.: hortor, moneo). In gen., constr. absol., with dat. of pers., and with acc. rei, an obj.-clause, ut or ne, or the simple subj.; rarely with acc. pers. In partic., ...

suadus.definition: suādus, a, um, id. Persuading, persuasive (poet.): delenifica et suada facundia,Symm. Ep. 3, 6: cruor,Stat. Th. 4, 453: majestas,App. M. 11, 272, 26: conjux,Mart. Cap. 1, § 3.—Hence, Suāda, ae, f., personified, the goddess of Persuasion, the Greek Πειθώ: Suadae medulla (Cethegus), Enn. ap. Cic. Brut. 15, 59; id. Sen. 14, 50; Gell. 12, 2, 3; cf. Quint. 2, 15, 4 (Ann. v. 309 Vahl.).

suasor.definition: id.. In gen., one who exhorts, advises, or persuades, an adviser, counsellor, persuader (class.): esse suasorem summum et studiosum robore belli, Enn. ap. Gell. 7, 2 (Ann. v. 375 Vahl.): me suasore et impulsore id factum,Plaut. Most. 3, 3, 13: suasor et impulsor profectionis,Cic. Att. 16, 7, 2: quid interest inter suasorem facti et probatorem?id. Phil. 2, 12, 29: suasoris finis est utilitas,Quint. 3, 8, 42: pacis,Ov. F. 4, 75. In partic., in publ...

suasorius.definition: suāsōrĭus, a, um, adj.id. Of or belonging to counselling or persuading, suasory, persuasive (post-Aug.). * In gen.: oscula,App. M. 5, p. 161, 29. In partic., in rhet., of or belonging to the suasory species of discourse, hortatory, suasory.

suasus.definition: suāsus, a, um, Part. of suadeo.

suaveolens.definition: suāvĕ-ŏlens (also written separately), entis, suavis-oleo Sweet-smelling, fragrant: amaracus,Cat. 61, 7: mala,id. 19, 13.

suaueolens.definition: suāvĕ-ŏlens (also written separately), entis, suavis-oleo Sweet-smelling, fragrant: amaracus,Cat. 61, 7: mala,id. 19, 13.

suaviatio.definition: (), , suavior A kissing (ante- and post-class.): suavis,Plaut. Bacch. 1, 2, 8; 1, 2, 12; id. Ps. 1, 1, 63.— Plur., Gell. 18, 2, 8.

suauiatio.definition: (), , suavior A kissing (ante- and post-class.): suavis,Plaut. Bacch. 1, 2, 8; 1, 2, 12; id. Ps. 1, 1, 63.— Plur., Gell. 18, 2, 8.

suavidicus.definition: suāvĭdĭcus, a, um, suavis-dico Sweet-spoken, pleasant: versus,Lucr. 4, 180.

suauidicus.definition: suāvĭdĭcus, a, um, suavis-dico Sweet-spoken, pleasant: versus,Lucr. 4, 180.

suaviloquens.definition: suāvĭlŏquens, entis, suavisloquor Sweet-spoken, pleasant-speaking (poet.): suaviloquenti ore Cetegus, Enn. ap. Cic. Brut. 15, 58 (Ann. v. 304 Vahl.); cf. Quint. 11, 3, 31; and v. suaviloquentia; so perh. in imitation of Ennius: jucunditas, Cic. Fragm. ap. Gell. 12, 2, 7 (hence, expressly censured by Seneca as Ennian): carmen,Lucr. 1, 945.

suauiloquens.definition: suāvĭlŏquens, entis, suavisloquor Sweet-spoken, pleasant-speaking (poet.): suaviloquenti ore Cetegus, Enn. ap. Cic. Brut. 15, 58 (Ann. v. 304 Vahl.); cf. Quint. 11, 3, 31; and v. suaviloquentia; so perh. in imitation of Ennius: jucunditas, Cic. Fragm. ap. Gell. 12, 2, 7 (hence, expressly censured by Seneca as Ennian): carmen,Lucr. 1, 945.

suaviloquentia.definition: suaviloquens Sweetness of speech, suaviloquence: et oratorem appellat (Ennius Cethegum) et suaviloquentiam tribuit,Cic. Brut. 15, 58; cf. suaviloquens.

suauiloquentia.definition: suaviloquens Sweetness of speech, suaviloquence: et oratorem appellat (Ennius Cethegum) et suaviloquentiam tribuit,Cic. Brut. 15, 58; cf. suaviloquens.

suaviolum.definition: (), , dim. suavium A little kiss, perh. only in Cat. 99, 2 and 14.

suauiolum.definition: (), , dim. suavium A little kiss, perh. only in Cat. 99, 2 and 14.

suavis.definition: suāvis, e (sŭāves, trisyl., Sedul. 1, 274), adj. Gr. root ἁδ-, ἁνδάνω, to please; ἡδύς, sweet; Sanscr. svad-, taste; cf. suadeo Sweet, pleasant, agreeable, grateful, delightful (freq. and class.; cf.: dulcis, jucundus). As affecting the senses: quod suave est aliis, aliis fit amarum,Lucr. 4, 658: odor suavis et jucundus,Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 9, § 23: elixus esse quam assus soleo suavior,Plaut. Most. 5, 1, 66: vidimus et merulas poni et sine clune...

suauis.definition: suāvis, e (sŭāves, trisyl., Sedul. 1, 274), adj. Gr. root ἁδ-, ἁνδάνω, to please; ἡδύς, sweet; Sanscr. svad-, taste; cf. suadeo Sweet, pleasant, agreeable, grateful, delightful (freq. and class.; cf.: dulcis, jucundus). As affecting the senses: quod suave est aliis, aliis fit amarum,Lucr. 4, 658: odor suavis et jucundus,Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 9, § 23: elixus esse quam assus soleo suavior,Plaut. Most. 5, 1, 66: vidimus et merulas poni et sine clune...

suavitas.definition: suavis Sweetness, pleasantness, agreeableness (class. and freq.). To the senses: is (piscis) habet suavitatem,Plaut. As. 1, 3, 27: quid suavitatem piscium dicam?Cic. N. D. 2, 64, 160: (muriatica) Sine omni lepore et sine suavitate,Plaut. Poen. 1, 2, 33: cibi,Cic. Phil. 2, 45, 115: odorum,id. Sen. 17, 59: coloris,id. Opt. Gen. 3, 8: me tuus sonus et suavitas ista delectat: omitto verborum ... sed hanc dico suavitatem, quae erit ex ore,id. de Or. 3...

suauitas.definition: suavis Sweetness, pleasantness, agreeableness (class. and freq.). To the senses: is (piscis) habet suavitatem,Plaut. As. 1, 3, 27: quid suavitatem piscium dicam?Cic. N. D. 2, 64, 160: (muriatica) Sine omni lepore et sine suavitate,Plaut. Poen. 1, 2, 33: cibi,Cic. Phil. 2, 45, 115: odorum,id. Sen. 17, 59: coloris,id. Opt. Gen. 3, 8: me tuus sonus et suavitas ista delectat: omitto verborum ... sed hanc dico suavitatem, quae erit ex ore,id. de Or. 3...

suavium.definition: (), , id.. A mouth puckered up to be kissed (anteclass. and very rare; syn. osculum): dum semihiulco savio meo puellum savior, Poët. ap. Gell. 19, 11, 4; Plaut. Mil. 2, 1, 16; cf. id. As. 4, 1, 53; App M. 3, p. 135, 35. Transf., a kiss, a love-kiss, φίλημα (mostly ante-class.; esp. freq. in Plaut.; syn.: osculum, basium; cf.: sciendum osculum religionis esse, savium voluptatis; quamvis quidam osculum filiis dari, uxori basium, scorto savium dica...

suauium.definition: (), , id.. A mouth puckered up to be kissed (anteclass. and very rare; syn. osculum): dum semihiulco savio meo puellum savior, Poët. ap. Gell. 19, 11, 4; Plaut. Mil. 2, 1, 16; cf. id. As. 4, 1, 53; App M. 3, p. 135, 35. Transf., a kiss, a love-kiss, φίλημα (mostly ante-class.; esp. freq. in Plaut.; syn.: osculum, basium; cf.: sciendum osculum religionis esse, savium voluptatis; quamvis quidam osculum filiis dari, uxori basium, scorto savium dica...

sub.definition: sŭb (on the form sus from subs V.infra, III.), with acc. and abl. [perh. for es-ub, ens-ub, = ἐνς (εις) and ὑπό; Sanscr. upa; cf. Georg Curtius Gr. Etym. p. 290], under. With abl., to point out the object under which a thing is situated or takes place (Gr. ὑπό, with dat. or gen.), under, below, beneath, underneath. With acc., to point out the object under which a thing comes, goes, extends, etc. (Gr. ὑπό, with acc.), under, below, beneath.

subabsurdus.definition: sŭb-absurdus, a, um Somewhat or rather absurd (Ciceronian): sunt illa subabsurda,Cic. de Or. 2, 67, 274: subabsurda dicere,id. ib. 2, 71, 289: tempus discessūs,id. Att. 16, 3, 4: incompositus, reconditus et, quo Cicero utitur, subabsurdus,Quint. 1, 5, 65; cf. id. 6, 3, 23; 6, 3, 99.—Adv.: sŭbabsurdē, somewhat absurdly: aliquid subabsurde dicere,Cic. de Or. 2, 68, 275.

subaccuso.definition: sŭb-accūso, āre To blame or accuse somewhat (Ciceronian): alicujus discessum,Cic. Planc. 35, 86; id. Att. 16, 7, 1: subaccusa quaeso Vestorium,id. ib. 13, 46, 2.

subacidus.definition: sŭb-ăcĭdus, a, um Somewhat sour, sourish: vinum,Cato, R. R. 108, 2: sucus,Plin. 12, 25, 54, § 120.

subactio.definition: subigo. Lit., a working through, working up, preparing (rare): harena fluviatica bacillorum subactionibus in tectorio recipit soliditatem,Vitr. 2, 4 fin.: subactiones ciborum,Arn. 3, 107.—* Trop., preparation, discipline: subacto mihi ingenio opus est ... subactio autem est usus, auditio, lectio, litterae,Cic. de Or. 2, 30, 131.

subadiuva.definition: adjuvo An assistant (post-class.), Cod. Th. 6, 27, 3 fin.; Cod. Just. 12, 20, 4.

subadiuua.definition: adjuvo An assistant (post-class.), Cod. Th. 6, 27, 3 fin.; Cod. Just. 12, 20, 4.

subagitatio.definition: sŭbăgĭtātĭo, sŭbăgĭtātrix, sŭb-ăgĭto, v. subigitatio, etc.

subagrestis.definition: sŭb-ăgrestis, e Somewhat rustic, rather boorish (Ciceronian): subagreste quiddam planeque subrusticum,Cic. Brut. 74, 259: consilium,id. Rep. 2, 7, 12: ingenium,Amm. 14, 11, 11.

subalaris.definition: sŭb-ālāris, e That is under the arms, placed or carried under the arms: telum,Nep. Alcib. 10, 5: culcitae,Lampr. Heliog. 19 fin.—As substt.

subalbidus.definition: sŭb-albĭdus, a, um Rather whitish: pars corrupta,Cels. 5, 28, 8: folia,Plin. 21, 25, 96, § 168; Isid. 12, 1, 50.

subamarus.definition: sŭb-ămārus, a, um Somewhat bitter, bitterish (Ciceronian), Cic. Fat. 4, 8. —Adverb.: subamarum arridens,somewhat bitterly,Amm. 27, 11, 5.

subaquilus.definition: sŭb-ăquĭlus, a, um Somewhat dusky, brownish, tawny (ante- and postclass.): corpus. Plaut. Rud. 2, 4, 9: vultus, Trebell. XXX. Tyr. 30.

subarmalis.definition: sŭb-armālis, e, armus Passing under the arms (post-class.): vestis (perh. thrown back under the arm),Mart. Cap. 5, § 426.—As subst.: sŭbarmāle, is n., = subarmalis vestis, Valer. ap. Treb. Claud. 14; Spart. Sever. 6 fin.; Vop. Aur. 13; cf. subalaris.

subasso.definition: sŭb-asso, no Perf., ātum, 1, , to roast a little, Apic. 4, 2; 7, 2; 7, 5; 8, 8: squilla,Cael. Aur. Tard. 4, 3, 6.

subaudio.definition: sŭb-audĭo, ii, ītum, 4, (postclass.). To understand, supply a word omitted: subaudito jubeo,Dig. 28, 5, 1; Aug. Civ. Dei, 15, 7; 17, 11; Greg. M. in Job, 33, 17. To hear a little: nocturnis subaudiens vocibus,App. M. 5, p. 167, 4.

subausculto.definition: sŭb-ausculto, āvi, ātum, 1 To listen secretly, to eavesdrop (rare but class.): subauscultando excipere voces,Cic. de Or. 2, 36, 153: opprime os: is est, etiam subauscultemus,Plaut. As. 3, 2, 40: tace, subauscultemus, ecquid de me fiat mentio,id. Mil. 4, 2, 3: videntur subauscultare quae loquor,Cic. Att. 10, 18, 1: viris subauscultantibus pariete interposito,id. Top. 20, 75.

subausterus.definition: sŭb-austērus, a, um Rather harsh: vinum austerum vel certe subausterum,Cels. 3, 6, § 61; 6, 6. 8, § 68.

subbasilicanus.definition: basilica One who lounges around the basilicas, a lounger: quorum odos subbasilicanos omnes abigit,Plaut. Capt. 4, 2, 35 Brix ad loc.

subdiaconus.definition: A sub - deacon, Cod. Just. 1, 3, 6; Aug. Ep. 53; 63; Isid. 7, 12, 23.

subdifficilis.definition: sub-diffĭcĭlis, e Somewhat difficult: quaestio,Cic. Lael. 19, 67.

subdiffido.definition: sub-diffīdo, ĕre To be somewhat distrustful, Cic. Att. 15, 20, 2.

subdisiunctivus.definition: sub-disjunctīvus, a, um Subdisjunctive; said of two statements opposed to each other in such a way that neither of them may hold good (postclass.): haec verba: ille aut ille, non solum disjunctiva sed etiam subdisjunctivae orationis sunt, etc.,Dig. 50, 16, 124: conjunctiones,Prisc. p. 1029 P.

subdisiunctiuus.definition: sub-disjunctīvus, a, um Subdisjunctive; said of two statements opposed to each other in such a way that neither of them may hold good (postclass.): haec verba: ille aut ille, non solum disjunctiva sed etiam subdisjunctivae orationis sunt, etc.,Dig. 50, 16, 124: conjunctiones,Prisc. p. 1029 P.

subdistinguo.definition: sub -distinguo, xi, ctum, 3 To make a smaller interpunction (perh. a colon), Ascon. ad Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 13 fin.

subditicius.definition: subdĭtīcĭus (later -tĭus), a, um, subdo Substituted, supposititious, spurious, counterfeit (perh. only ante- and postclass., since the correct read. in Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 27, § 69, is subditivum; and in Quint. 1, 4, 3, subditos): servus,Plaut. Ps. 2, 4, 62: Antonius,Lampr. Heliog. 17; Amm. 14, 6, 15.

subditivus.definition: subdĭtīvus, a, um, id. Substituted, supposititious, spurious, counterfeit (rare but class.): de illo subditivo Sosia mirum nimis est,Plaut. Am. 2, 2, 198; 1, 2, 35: archipirata,Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 27, § 69: fratrem ut subditivum arguere,Suet. Ner. 7. —Subst.: Subdĭtīvus, i, m., the title of a comedy of Coecilius, Gell. 15, 9, 1 (Com. Rel. p. 39 sq. Rib.).

subditiuus.definition: subdĭtīvus, a, um, id. Substituted, supposititious, spurious, counterfeit (rare but class.): de illo subditivo Sosia mirum nimis est,Plaut. Am. 2, 2, 198; 1, 2, 35: archipirata,Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 27, § 69: fratrem ut subditivum arguere,Suet. Ner. 7. —Subst.: Subdĭtīvus, i, m., the title of a comedy of Coecilius, Gell. 15, 9, 1 (Com. Rel. p. 39 sq. Rib.).

subditus.definition: subdĭtus, a, um, Part., from subdo.

subdo.definition: sub-do, dĭdi, dĭtum, 3 To put, place, set, or lay under (syn.: suppono, sterno). To put in the place of another person or thing, to substitute (rare but class.).

subdolus.definition: sub -dŏlus, a, um Somewhat crafty, cunning, sly, subtle, deceptive, or deceitful (mostly ante - class. and post - Aug.; syn.: fallax, astutus): homo et sycophanta et subdolus,Plaut. Poen. 5, 2, 72; id. Mil. 2, 4, 2; id. Men. 3, 2, 24; id. Aul. 2, 5, 8; id. Poen. 5, 2, 129: ut viro subdola sies, memento,id. Cas. 4, 4, 5: subdola adversus senem,id. Ep. 2, 3, 13: jugurtha, cognitā vanitate legati, subdolus ejus augere amentiam,Sall. J. 38, 1: occult...

subduco.definition: sub-dūco, xi, ctum, 3 ( Perf. sync. subduxti, Ter. Eun. 4, 7, 25; inf. subduxe, Poët. ap. Varr. R. R. 2, 1, 6), v. a., to draw from under or from below. Without the idea of removal. With the idea of removal implied, to draw away from among; to take away, lead away, carry off; to withdraw, remove, etc. (class.; syn. subtraho).

subductio.definition: id.. (Acc. to subduco, I. B. 1.) Naut. t. t., a hauling ashore of a ship: ad celeritatem onerandi subductionesque paulo facit humiliores (naves), * Caes. B. G. 5, 1: navium,Vitr. 10, 2, 10.—* (Acc. to subduco, II. B.) A reckoning, Cic. Or. 2, 30, 132.

subedo.definition: sŭb-ĕdo, ēdi, 3 To eat, waste, or wear away below: e scopulo, quem rauca subederat unda,Ov. M. 11, 783; Hier. in Jer. 1, 2, 37.

suber.definition: The cork-oak, cork-tree: Quercus suber, Linn.; Plin. 16, 8, 13, § 34; 16, 25, 41, § 98; Col. 4, 26, 1; 9, 6, 1; Verg. A. 7, 742. Transf., cork: silvestre,Verg. A. 11, 554; cf.: ut ramale vetus vegrandi subere coctum, i. e. a thick bark, like that of the cork-tree, Pers. 1, 97.—The tree is called , , , Lucil. ap. Fest. p. 294 Müll.; cf. Isid. Orig. 17, 7, 27.

subhorridus.definition: sŭb-horrĭdus, a, um Somewhat rough, roughish: subhorridus atque incultus,Cic. Sest. 9, 21.

subicio.definition: sūb-ĭcĭo (less correctly subjĭcĭo; post-Aug. sometimes sŭb-), jēci, jectum, 3, v. a. sub-jacio. Lit., to throw, lay, place, or bring under or near (cf. subdo); in all senses construed with acc. and dat., or with acc. and sub and acc.; not with sub and abl. (v. Madvig. ad Cic. Fin. 2, 15, 48; cf. II. B. 2. infra). Trop.

subigitatio.definition: (), , subigito Illicit intercourse, Plaut. Capt. cat. 2.

subigito.definition: sŭbĭgĭto (sŭbăgĭto), āre, sub-agito. Lit., to lie with illicitly (ante-class.): scortum,Plaut. Mil. 3, 1, 53 (649 Ritschl): aliquam,id. ib. 5, 9; id. Cas. 5, 4, 2 (al. subicitare); id. Merc. 1, 2, 91; Ter. Heaut. 3, 3, 6. Trop., to work upon, incite to any thing (post-class.): aliquem, M. Aurel. ap. Front. Ep. ad M. Caes. 4, 5: mulierem blanditiis,App. Mag. p. 329, 3.

subigo.definition: sŭbĭgo, ēgi, actum, 3 (sūbĭgĭt, scanned with u long, Cic. poët. Div. 1, 47, 106), sub-ago To bring under, get under; bring or get up, or up to any place. Lit. (mostly poet.): sues antequam aestus incipiat, subigunt in umbrosum locum,Varr. R. R. 2, 4, 6: qui adverso flumine lembum Remigiis subigit,i. e. rows up stream,Verg. G. 1, 202: naves ad castellum,Liv. 26, 7: classem ad moenia,Sil. 15, 218: saxum contra ardua montis,id. 13, 610: frondosum ap...

subimpudens.definition: sŭb-impŭdens, entis Somewhat shameless or impudent: saepe,Cic. Fam. 7, 17, 1.

subinanis.definition: sŭb-ĭnānis, e Somewhat empty or vain: quod est subinane in nobis,Cic. Att. 2, 17, 2.

subinde.definition: sŭb-inde, , a particle of time. In gen., immediately after, just after, presently, forthwith, thereupon (not ante-Aug.): primum gaudere, subinde Praeceptum auriculis hoc instillare memento,Hor. Ep. 1, 8, 15: ager primum aretur ultimā parte mensis Augusti, subinde Septembri sit iteratus,Col. 2, 4, 11: primo auctumno arandi et subinde conserendi,id. 11, 2, 8; Tac. Agr. 14: sparge subinde,Hor. S. 2, 5, 103: aliud subinde bellum cum alterius orae Gra...

subinsulsus.definition: sŭb-insulsus, a, um Somewhat tasteless or insipid: si quid absurdum ... aut subinsulsum est,Cic. Opt. Gen. 3, 7.

subintellego.definition: sŭb-intellĕgo, ĕre To understand or perceive a little (late Lat.), Tert. adv. Marc. 5, 3; Hier. Ep. 145 med. To supply in thought, understand in addition, Aug. Trin. 6, 4; id. Serm. 104, 3 fin.; Greg. M. in Job, 33, 7 al.

subintro.definition: sŭb-intro, āvi, ātum, 1 To go into secretly, to enter by stealth, steal into (late Lat.); trop.: populo bellicoso ludorum scenicorum subintravit insania, Aug. Civ. Dei, 1, 32; so Tert. adv. Marc. 5, 3 al.

subinvideo.definition: sŭb-invĭdĕo, no Perf., sum, 2 To envy a little or slightly, to be somewhat envious of (Ciceronian): subinvideo tibi, ultro te etiam arcessitum ab eo,Cic. Fam. 7, 10, 1.—* Part. perf., a little disliked, somewhat odious: subinvisum apud malevolos Postumi nomen,Cic. Rab. Post. 14, 40.

subinuideo.definition: sŭb-invĭdĕo, no Perf., sum, 2 To envy a little or slightly, to be somewhat envious of (Ciceronian): subinvideo tibi, ultro te etiam arcessitum ab eo,Cic. Fam. 7, 10, 1.—* Part. perf., a little disliked, somewhat odious: subinvisum apud malevolos Postumi nomen,Cic. Rab. Post. 14, 40.

subinvito.definition: sŭb-invīto, āvi, 1 To invite slightly: aliquem, ut ad se scriberet,Cic. Fam. 7, 1, 6.

subinuito.definition: sŭb-invīto, āvi, 1 To invite slightly: aliquem, ut ad se scriberet,Cic. Fam. 7, 1, 6.

subirascor.definition: sŭb-īrascor, ātus, 3 V. dep. n., to be somewhat angry (Ciceronian): interdum soleo subirasci,Cic. Fin. 2, 4, 12: brevitati litterarum,id. Fam. 11, 24, 1: in Epirum quod me non invitas, subirascor,id. Att. 9, 7, 7.—Hence, sŭbīrātus, a, um, , somewhat angry: tibi,Cic. de Or. 1, 16, 72; id. Fam. 3, 9, 1: anus subiratior,App. M. 4, p. 154 (dub. al. iratior).

subitaneus.definition: sŭbĭtānĕus, a, um, subitus Sudden: imber,Col. 1, 6, 24; 2, 4, 4; Sen. Q. N. 7, 22, 1; Vulg. Sap. 17, 6; 17, 14; 19, 16.

subitarius.definition: sŭbĭtārĭus, a, um, id. Done suddenly or in haste, sudden, hasty: ad eum exercitum explendum Latini Hernicique dare Quintio subitarios milites (ita tum repentina auxilia appellabant) jussi,Liv. 3, 4, 11; so, milites (corresp. to tumultuarii),id. 40, 26, 6: exercitus,id. 3, 30, 3; 31, 2, 6; 41, 17, 9: res,Plaut. Mil. 2, 2, 70: aedificia,Tac. A. 15, 39: gradus theatri (with scena in tempus structa),id. ib. 14, 20: dictio,a speaking extempore,Gell. 9...

subito.definition: sŭbĭtō, , v. subeo P. a. fin.

subiaceo.definition: sub-jăcĕo, cŭi, 2 To lie under or near any thing (post-Aug.). Lit.: feles coeunt mare stante, feminā subjacente,Plin. 10, 63, 83, § 174: frumentum si tegulis subjaceat,id. 18, 30, 73, § 301: fenestris subjacet vestibulum villae,Plin. Ep. 2, 17, 15; cf.: subjacentes petrae,Curt. 5, 3, 18: campus aedificio subjacet,adjoins, lies close to the building,Col. 1, 2, 3; so, monti,Plin. Ep. 5, 6, 2: fenestra subjacens,id. ib. 2, 17, 6. Trop., to be under,...

subiectio.definition: id. A laying, putting, or placing under. Lit. A subjugation, reduction to obedience: provinciarum,Oros. 3, 14 fin.: mentium,Ambros. in Psa. 118, Serm. 12, § 27: in omni subjectione,in all submissiveness,Vulg. 1 Tim. 2, 11; the state of slavery, Jornand. Get. 32.

subiectivus.definition: subjectīvus, a, um, subjectus Of or belonging to the subject of a proposition, subjective: pars,i. e. the subject,App. Dogm. Plat. 3, p. 30, 30; Mart. Cap. 4, § 393; Tert. Virg. Vel. 4 fin.—Adv.: subjectīvē, subjectively, Mart. Cap. 4, § 393.

subiectiuus.definition: subjectīvus, a, um, subjectus Of or belonging to the subject of a proposition, subjective: pars,i. e. the subject,App. Dogm. Plat. 3, p. 30, 30; Mart. Cap. 4, § 393; Tert. Virg. Vel. 4 fin.—Adv.: subjectīvē, subjectively, Mart. Cap. 4, § 393.

subiecto.definition: subjecto (also written subjacto, Varr. R. R. 1, 52, 2), āre, subicio To lay, place, or put under; to throw out from below (mostly poet.; not in Cic.): manus,Ov. M. 4, 359: acres Subjectat lasso stimulos,Hor. S. 2, 7, 94: saxa,Lucr. 6, 700: nigram alte harenam,to cast up from its depths,Verg. G. 3, 241; so, grana e terrā,Varr. R. R. 1, 52, 2.

subiector.definition: id. One who substitutes, a substitutor, forger: testamentorum,Cic. Cat. 2, 4, 7.

subiectum.definition: subjectum, i, v. subicio, II. C.

subiectus.definition: subjectus, a, um, Part. and , from subicio.

subiugalis.definition: sub-jŭgālis, e, adj. Accustomed to the yoke: subjugales beluae, Prud. στεφ. 10, 333.—Subst., a beast of burden, Vulg. Matt. 21, 5.

subiugo.definition: subjŭgo, āvi, ātum, 1, id. (postclass.) To bring under the yoke: decus publicum,Arn. 4, p. 129: exercitum,Eutr. 4, 17. In gen., to subject, subjugate: ORBEM TERRAE ROMANO NOMINI,Inscr. Grut. 281, 2: hostes,Claud. VI. Cons. Hon. 249: provinciam, Ps.-Ascon. ad Cic. Verr. 1, 21: multi periculo subjugati sunt,Lact. Mort. Pers. 34.—With dat.: aliquem poenae, Dig 4, 8, 43: aliquem personali muneri,ib. 50 4, 18, § 9: ingratum populum legi,Lact. 4, 10, 1...

subiungo.definition: sub-jungo, xi, ctum, 3 ( Inf. pass. subjungier, Prud. ap. Symm. 2, 586), , to yoke, harness (rare): curru subjungere tigres,Verg. E. 5, 29: (juvencos) plostro,Col. 6, 2, 8: carpento suo equas,Plin. 11, 49, 109, § 262. Transf., in gen.

sublabor.definition: sub-lābor, lapsus, 3 V. dep. n., to fall, glide, or sink under or down, to sink (poet. and in post-Aug. prose). Lit.: imperfecta necesse est labent et modo prodeant, modo sublabantur aut succidant,Sen. Ep. 71, § 34: aedificia vetustate sublapsa,Plin. Ep. 10, 75, 1; cf. poet. transf.: annis sublapsa vetustas,Verg. A. 12, 686.—* Trop.: retro sublapsa Spes,Verg. A. 2, 169: memoria senum,Sen. Oedip. 817.

sublatus.definition: sublātus, a, um, Part. of tollo; as , v. tollo Fin.

sublecto.definition: sublecto, āre, sub-lacio To wheedle, cajole: os,Plaut. Mil. 4, 2, 74.

sublego.definition: sub-lĕgo, lēgi, lectum, 3 To gather from below, to gather or search for underneath, to gather up: (puer) sublegit quodcumque jaceret inutile quodque Posset cenantes offendere,Hor. S. 2, 8, 12: baca tempestatibus in terram decidit et necesse est eam sublegere,Col. 12, 52, 1: ficum viridem,id. 12, 17, 1. To choose or elect in the place of another, to substitute: collegae, qui una lecti: et qui in eorum locum suppositi, sublecti: additi, allecti,Var...

sublestus.definition: sublestus, a, um, acc. to Döderl. Synon. 2, p. 101 sq., perh. from sublevo; and hence, light Slight, trifling, trivial (ante-class.): sublesta antiqui dicebant infirma et tenuia,Plaut. Pers. 3, 1, 20: fides sublestior, id est, infirmior. Idem in Nervolaria vinum ait sublestissimum, quia infirmos faciat vel corpore vel animo, Fest. pp. 294 and 295 Müll.; cf.: sublestum est leve, frivolum,Non. 177, 11: sublestus infirmus, tristis, Gloss. Isid.: fid...

sublevatio.definition: sublevo, II. B. A lightening, alleviation; trop.: sublevatio et medicina,Cic. Rep. 2, 34, 59.

subleuatio.definition: sublevo, II. B. A lightening, alleviation; trop.: sublevatio et medicina,Cic. Rep. 2, 34, 59.

sublevo.definition: sub-lĕvo, āvi, ātum, 1 To lift up from beneath, to raise up, hold up, support (class.: esp. freq. in the trop. sense; syn.: extollo, erigo). Lit.: qui nos sibi quondam ad pedes stratos ne sublevabat quidem,Cic. Att. 10, 4, 3: in ascensu sublevati,Caes. B. C. 2, 34; id. B. G. 7, 47: alterni innixi sublevantesque invicem et trahentes alii alios,Liv. 5, 47, 2; 28, 20, 5; cf.: jubis equorum sublevati,Caes. B. G. 1, 48: erigere se aut sublevare,id. ib...

subleuo.definition: sub-lĕvo, āvi, ātum, 1 To lift up from beneath, to raise up, hold up, support (class.: esp. freq. in the trop. sense; syn.: extollo, erigo). Lit.: qui nos sibi quondam ad pedes stratos ne sublevabat quidem,Cic. Att. 10, 4, 3: in ascensu sublevati,Caes. B. C. 2, 34; id. B. G. 7, 47: alterni innixi sublevantesque invicem et trahentes alii alios,Liv. 5, 47, 2; 28, 20, 5; cf.: jubis equorum sublevati,Caes. B. G. 1, 48: erigere se aut sublevare,id. ib...

sublica.definition: A stake or pile driven into the ground, a palisade (cf.: palus, sudes, stipes),Caes. B. C. 3, 49; Liv. 23, 37; Vitr. 3, 3.—Esp., of the piles for a bridge, Caes. B. G. 4, 17; 7, 35; Liv. 1, 37.—In the form sublices, Sall. H. Fragm. 4, 77; cf. Gloss. Labb.

sublicius.definition: sublĭcĭus, a, um, sublica Consisting of or resting upon piles: Pons Sublicius, the pile-bridge, a wooden bridge across the Tiber, built by Ancus Marcius, Liv. 1, 33; 2, 10; Sen. Vit. Beat. 25, 1; Plin. 36, 15, 23, § 100; Tac. H. 1, 86; Varr. L. L. 5, § 83, and 6, § 44 Müll.; Fest. p. 293 ib.; cf. Becker, Antiq. 1, p. 693 sq.—As the place where beggars sat,Sen. Vit. Beat. 25.

subligaculum.definition: subligo A waistband, breech - cloth, Cic. Off. 1, 35, 129; cf. Non. 19, 21.—Called subsequently , , , Mart. 3, 87, 4; Juv. 6, 70; Plin. 12, 14, 32, § 59; and , , , Theod. Prisc. 1, 26.

subligo.definition: sub-lĭgo, āvi, ātum, 1 To bind or tie below, to bind on (mostly poet.; not in Cic.; syn. subnecto): vites,Cato, R. R. 33, 4; Plin. 17, 22, 35, § 197: lateri atque umeris ensem,Verg. A. 8, 459: clipeum sinistrae,id. ib. 11, 11: arma,Val. Fl. 5, 445; cf. poet., transf.: quem (virum) balteus asper Subligat,girds,id. 5, 579: tiaram extremā cervice,id. 6, 700 et saep.: subligata ludit,trussed up, tucked up,Mart. 7, 67, 4.

sublimatio.definition: sublimo A lifting up, deliverance, Alcim. Ep. 2.

sublimis.definition: sublīmis, e (collat. form sublīmus, a, um: ex sublimo vertice, Cic. poët. Tusc. 2, 7, 19; Enn. ap. Non. 169; Att. and Sall. ib. 489, 8 sq.; Lucr. 1, 340), etym. dub.; perh. sub-limen, up to the lintel; cf. sublimen (sublimem est in altitudinem elatum, Fest. p. 306 Müll.) Uplifted, high, lofty, exalted, elevated (mostly poet. and in postAug. prose; not in Cic. or Caes.; syn.: editus, arduus, celsus, altus). Lit. Trop., lofty, exalted, eminent, dis...

sublimitas.definition: sublimis Height, loftiness (post-Aug.; cf. altitudo). Lit.: corporis,Quint. 12, 5, 5: cellarum,Col. 8, 3, 3: cucurbitarum,Plin. 19, 5, 24, § 69.—In plur.: lunae,Plin. 2, 16, 13, § 68. Trop.

sublimo.definition: sublīmo, āvi, ātum, 1, id. To lift up on high, to raise, elevate (ante- and postclass.). Lit.: facem (sol), Enn. ap. Non. 170, 11 (Trag. v. 319 Vahl.): se nubium tenus,App. Flor. p. 340, 38; cf. mid.: sublimata in altum,id. M. 3, p. 138, 34; Vitr. 6, 6, 4; Vulg. 1 Reg. 2, 10. Trop.: sublimavit dixit (Cato), id est in altum extulit, Originum, l. II.: in maximum decus atque in excelsissimam claritudinem sublimavit,Fest. p. 306 Müll.: aliquem,Macr. ...

sublimus.definition: sublīmus, a, um, v. sublimis Init.

sublingio.definition: sub-lingo A lick-dish, under-scullion: coqui,Plaut. Ps. 3, 2, 103.

sublino.definition: sub-lĭno, lēvi, lĭtum, 3 To besmear or anoint beneath, to lay on as a groundcolor, to prime with any thing (ante-class. and post-Aug.). Lit.: chrysocollam atramento,Plin. 33, 5, 27, § 90: caeruleum,id. 35, 6, 26, § 45: argentum vivum,id. 33, 6, 32, § 100: sanguinem lacertae,id. 30, 9, 23, § 80. Transf.

subluceo.definition: sub-lūcĕo, ēre To shine a little, to gleam faintly, to glimmer (poet. and in post - Aug. prose): aries sublucet corpore totus,Cic. Arat. 289: crepuscula sublucent,Ov. Am. 1, 5, 5: si fragmenta (picis), subluceant,Plin. 14, 20, 25, § 127: (liquor) nigrantis rosae colore sublucens,id. 9, 36, 60, § 126: violae sublucet purpura nigrae,Verg. G. 4, 275; cf.: candida nec mixto sublucent ora rubore,Ov. H. 21, 217.

sublucidus.definition: sub-lūcĭdus, a, um Somewhat light, lightish: lucus,App. M. 6, p. 174, 24.

subluo.definition: sub-lŭo, no Perf., lūtum, ĕre, , to wash or bathe underneath (very rare; not in Cic.). Lit.: aliquid aquā calidā,Cels. 4, 15; Col. 6, 32, 1: inguina,Mart. 6, 81, 2: subluto podice,id. 2, 42, 1. Transf., of rivers, to flow along the base of, to wash the foot of: hunc montem flumen subluebat,Caes. B. C. 3, 97: radices collis (flumina),id. B. G. 7, 69.—Pass.: Asia, quā Hellesponto, quā rubro mari subluitur,Curt. 9, 6, 20.

sublustris.definition: sublustris, e, sub-lux Giving some light, having a faint light, glimmering (not ante-Aug., and very rare). Lit.: nox,Hor. C. 3, 27, 31; Liv. 5, 47: umbra (noctis),Verg. A. 9, 373; Val. Fl. 3, 141.— * Trop.: eloquentiae Latinae lumina,Gell. 13, 24, 12.

subluvies.definition: subluo, that which is washed off Filth, dirt (post-Aug.). In gen.: via subluvie caenosā lubrica,App. M. 9, p. 221, 2: limosa,Amm. 15, 4. In partic., a disease in the feet of sheep, the foul, Col. 7, 5, 11; so in the feet of men,Plin. 30, 9, 23, § 80.—Called also , , , Marc. Emp. 18 fin.

subluuies.definition: subluo, that which is washed off Filth, dirt (post-Aug.). In gen.: via subluvie caenosā lubrica,App. M. 9, p. 221, 2: limosa,Amm. 15, 4. In partic., a disease in the feet of sheep, the foul, Col. 7, 5, 11; so in the feet of men,Plin. 30, 9, 23, § 80.—Called also , , , Marc. Emp. 18 fin.

subnascor.definition: sub-nascor, nātus, 3 V. dep. n., to grow up under, out of, or after; to follow after, succeed (not ante-Aug.): num vada subnatis imo viridentur ab herbis,Ov. Hal. 90: qui (cortex) subnascente alio expellitur,Plin. 17, 24, 37, § 234; so, folia,id. 16, 22, 34, § 84: poma,id. 12, 3, 7, § 15: castaneae,id. 17, 20, 34, § 148: pilus,id. 11, 39, 94, § 230: plumae,id. 11, 23, 27, § 78: ulcera,Sen. Brev. Vit. 5, 5: aqua, id. Ira, 2, 10, 5: ignis,Sil. 14, ...

subnecto.definition: sub-necto, nexui, xum, ĕre To bind or tie under, bind on beneath (poet. and in post-Aug. prose; syn. subligo). Lit.: antennis velum,Ov. M. 11, 483: cingula mammae,Verg. A. 1, 492: tenui de vimine circlos Cervici,id. G. 3, 167: subnectit fibula vestem,id. A. 4, 139: fragmentum clavi collo,Plin. 28, 4, 11, § 46: specieque comam subnexus utrāque,wreathed, garlanded,Stat. S. 5, 3, 113 et saep. Trop., to add, subjoin in speaking: ut inventioni judiciu...

subnego.definition: sub-nĕgo, āvi, 1 To half deny or refuse: quod praesenti tibi prope subnegāram,Cic. Fam. 7, 19 init.

subnervo.definition: subnervo, āvi, 1, sub-nervus, to cut the sinew beneath To hamstring, hough (post-class.). Taurum, Tert. adv. Jud. 10 med.: equos,Vulg. Jos. 11, 6: jugales,id. 2 Reg. 8, 4.—* Trop., to invalidate, refute: calumnias,App. Mag. p. 327.

subneruo.definition: subnervo, āvi, 1, sub-nervus, to cut the sinew beneath To hamstring, hough (post-class.). Taurum, Tert. adv. Jud. 10 med.: equos,Vulg. Jos. 11, 6: jugales,id. 2 Reg. 8, 4.—* Trop., to invalidate, refute: calumnias,App. Mag. p. 327.

subnixus.definition: sub-nixus (-nīsus), a, um, Part. [nitor] Supported from beneath, under-propped, propped up, supported by, resting or leaning upon any thing, etc. (class., esp. in the trop. sense; cf. suffultus). Lit.: (duos circulos) caeli verticibus ipsis ex utrāque parte subnixos vides,Cic. Rep. 6, 20, 21: solioque alte subnixa resedit,Verg. A. 1, 506: parva Philoctetae subnixa Petelia muro, supported, i. e. defended by, id. ib. 3, 402: subnixae nubibus altis,...

subnotatio.definition: subnoto A signing underneath, subscription (post-class.), Cod. Just. 1, 23, 6; Cod. Th. 8, 5, 22; Hier. Ep. 123.

subnoto.definition: sub-nŏto, āvi, ātum, 1, (post-Aug.). To mark, note, or write underneath (cf. subscribo): in inferiori lineā particulares propositiones subnotentur,App. Dogm. Plat. 3, p. 31, 27: nomina palam,to write down,Suet. Calig. 41.—Transf.: libellos,to subscribe,Plin. Ep. 1, 10, 9. To note secretly, to mark, watch, observe: et non sobria verba subnotasti,Mart. 1, 28, 5: aliquem vultu digitoque,id. 6, 82, 3.

subnuba.definition: sub-nubo A rival: lecti subnuba nostri,Ov. H. 6, 153.

subnubilus.definition: sub-nūbĭlus, a, um Somewhatcloudy or overcast, rather gloomy: nox, * Caes. B. C. 3, 54: limes,Ov. R. Am. 599.

subo.definition: sŭbo, āre To be in heat. Prop. of sows, Plin. 10, 63, 83, § 181. Transf.

subobscenus.definition: sŭb-obscēnus (-caenus), a, um Somewhat smutty or obscene: ridiculum,Cic. Or. 26, 88.

subobscurus.definition: sŭb-obscūrus, a, um Somewhat obscure; trop., of language: breves et ob eam ipsam causam interdum subobscuri,Cic. Brut. 7, 29: ingressio,id. Or. 3, 11: cicatrix,Vulg. Lev. 13, 21.—Adv.: sŭbob-scūrē, somewhat obscurely: dixit,Gell. 10, 1, 7: explicat,id. 3, 14, 6.

subodiosus.definition: sŭb-ŏdĭōsus, a, um Somewhat vexatious or odious, Cic. Att. 1, 5, 4.

suboffendo.definition: sub-offendo, ĕre To give some offence: apud faecem populi,Cic. Q. Fr. 2, 6, 5.

suboleo.definition: sŭb-ŏlĕo (-ŏlo Pres. subj. subolat, Ter. Heaut. 5, 1, 26; cf. oleo init.), ēre, (prop. to emit a smell; only trop. and in third pers. sing.): hoc subolet alicui, or impers. subolet (alicui), to smell, scent, perceive any thing; I (thou, etc.), perceive, detect, etc. (ante-class.): id jam pridem sensi et subolet mihi,Plaut. Ps. 1, 5, 7; id. Cas. 2, 3, 59; 3, 2, 24; Ter. Phorm. 3, 1, 10: propemodum quod illic festinet, sentio et subolet mihi,Plaut....

suboles.definition: (less correctly ), , sub- 2. oleo, olesco A sprout, shoot, offshoot, twig, spray: suboles ab olescendo, id est crescendo, ut adulescentes quoque et adultae et indoles dicitur,Fest. p. 309 Müll. Lit. (very rare; syn. surculus), of plants: ulmum serere ex subolibus,Col. 5, 6, 2: caepa, quae non habuit suboles adhaerentes,id. 12, 10; Plin. 17, 10, 12, § 65 et saep. —Of the hair: ex subolibus parvuli (capilli) demittebantur, Varr. ap. Non. 456, 7: cu...

subolesco.definition: sŭb-ŏlesco, ĕre V. inch. n., to grow up (very rare): juventus subolescens,Liv. 29, 3: subolescere imperio adultos ejus filios,Amm. 14, 11, 3.

suborior.definition: sŭb-ŏrĭor, īri V. dep. n., to spring up, arise, proceed (very rare), Lucr. 1, 1036; 1, 1049; 2, 1138: metallorum opulentia tot saeculis suboriens,Plin. 2, 93, 95, § 207; Arn. 3, 9.

suborno.definition: sŭb-orno, āvi, ātum, 1 With the idea of the verb predominating, to fit out, furnish, provide, equip, adorn (class.; syn. instruo): aliquem pecuniā, Anton. ap. Cic. Phil. 13, 16, 32: vigilanter nervoseque nos, qui stamus in acie, subornes, Planc. ap. Cic. Fam. 10, 23, 6: paenulati isti in militum cultum subornati,Sen. Ben. 3, 28, 4: praeturae insignia invasit, praecedentibus in modum lictorum subornatis,Val. Max. 7, 3, 10: qui se ipse norit, intel...

subortus.definition: suborior A rising or springing up, Lucr. 5, 303.

subsannatio.definition: subsanno Mockery by gestures, derision in pantomime, Vulg. Psa. 34, 16; 43, 14.

subsannator.definition: id. One who insults or mocks by gestures, Vulg. Ecclus. 33, 6.

subsanno.definition: sub-sanno, āre, sanna To insult by derisive gestures, to deride, mock (late Lat.): ecce ipsi quasi subsannantes,Tert. adv. Jud. 11 med.; Hier. Ep. 40, 2; Vulg. Psa. 34, 16; id. Isa. 37, 22.

subscribendarius.definition: scribo An under-secretary (late Lat.), Cod. Th. 7, 4, 1; 7, 84, 8 al.

subscribo.definition: sub-scrībo, psi, ptum, 3 To write underneath or below (class.; cf. subnoto). (With the idea of the verb predom.) To write or note down (=notare; very rare): numerum aratorum,Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 51, § 120: audita,Quint. 12, 8, 8: quaedam,Suet. Aug. 27; cf.: suspiria nostra (a delatoribus),Tac. Agr. 45 (acc. to others this passage belongs to B. 1.).

subseco.definition: sub-sĕco, cui, ctum, 1 To cut under, cut away below; to clip, pare (rare; not in Cic.): stramentum et manipulum falce,Varr. R. R. 1, 50, 1: herbam. id. ib. 1, 49, 1: legumina,id. ib. 1, 23, 3: radices,Col. 2, 9, 10: partes, unde creatus erat (Saturnus),Ov. Ib. 276: ungues ferro,id. F. 6, 230: papavereas ungue comas,id. ib. 4, 438; Cels. 7, 33.

subsellium.definition: sub-sella A low bench (quod non plane erat sella, subsellium, Varr. L. L. 5, § 128 Müll.); hence, transf., a bench for sitting upon, a seat of any kind (in a house, the theatre, the curia, a court, etc.; syn.: scamnum, sedile). In gen., Plaut. Stich. 5, 4, 21; 1, 2, 36; id. Capt. 3, 1, 11; Suet. Ter. 2; cf. Cels. 7, 26, 1.—Of places in the theatre: ut conquisitores singuli in subsellia Eant per totam caveam, etc.,Plaut. Am. prol. 65; id. Poen. pr...

subsentio.definition: sub-sentĭo, si, 4 To notice or perceive secretly, to smell out: etsi subsensi id quoque, Illos ibi esse,Ter. Heaut. 3, 1, 62.

subsequor.definition: sub-sĕquor, cūtus, 3, v. n. and A., to follow close after or immediately; to follow, succeed, ensue (class.). Lit. Trop., to follow after, mentally or in opinion, to follow, adhere to, comply with, conform to, imitate a person or thing; with acc.: Speusippus Platonem avunculum subsequens,Cic. N. D. 1, 13, 32; cf. id. Div. 1, 3, 6: ut locupletes omnes summum ordinem subsequantur,id. Phil. 13, 10, 23: te imitari. te subsequi student,Plin. Pan. 84, ...

subsericus.definition: sub-sērĭcus, a, um Half-silken: vestis,Lampr. Heliog. 26; Gall. ap. Treb. Claud. 17; Vop. Aur. 15, 4.

subsero.definition: sub-sĕro, ĕre To sow or plant after, Col. 4, 15, 1; Dig. 7, 1, 13. Trop., to plant or distribute secretly: nutrimenta fictis criminibus,Amm. 14, 11, 3.

subsicivus.definition: subsĭcīvus, less correctly subsĕcī-vus (also transp. subcĭsīvus or suc-cĭsīvus), a, um, [sub-seco). Lit., as t. t. of the agrimensores, that is cut off and left remaining, in surveying lands.— Subst.: subsĭcīvum, i, n., a remainder or small patch of land, etc.: subsiciva, quae divisis per veteranos agris carptim superfuerunt, etc.,Suet. Dom. 9 fin.; Auct. Rei Agr. ap. Goes. p. 17; 23; 39: mensores nonnumquam dicunt in subsicivum esse unciam agri,...

subsiciuus.definition: subsĭcīvus, less correctly subsĕcī-vus (also transp. subcĭsīvus or suc-cĭsīvus), a, um, [sub-seco). Lit., as t. t. of the agrimensores, that is cut off and left remaining, in surveying lands.— Subst.: subsĭcīvum, i, n., a remainder or small patch of land, etc.: subsiciva, quae divisis per veteranos agris carptim superfuerunt, etc.,Suet. Dom. 9 fin.; Auct. Rei Agr. ap. Goes. p. 17; 23; 39: mensores nonnumquam dicunt in subsicivum esse unciam agri,...

subsidialis.definition: subsĭdĭālis, e, subsidium Of or belonging to a reserve, subsidiary (late Lat. for the class. subsidiarius): acies,Amm. 14, 6, 17: manus,id. 27, 10, 15.

subsidiarius.definition: subsĭdĭārĭus, a, um, adj.id.; in milit. lang. Of or belonging to a reserve, reserve-, subsidiary. Lit. Transf., in gen., out of the military sphere, serving for support, subsidiary: palmes, = resex,Col. 4, 24, 13 and 16.

subsidium.definition: subsideo. Milit. t. t. Transf., in gen., support, assistance, aid, help, protection, etc. (syn. adjumentum).

subsido.definition: sub-sīdo, sēdi, sessum, 3 (collat. form acc. to 2d conj., subsīdent, Luc. 1, 646; Amm. 28, 4, 22), and A. Neutr., to sit down, crouch down, squat; to set one's self down, settle down, sink down (class.). Act. (acc. to I. A. 2. b.), to lie in wait for, to waylay any one (poet. and in post-class. prose): devictam Asiam (i. e. Agamemnonem) subsedit adulter,Verg. A. 11, 268: leonem,Sil. 13, 221: copiosos homines,Amm. 28, 4, 22: insontem,id. 16, 8, 3:...

subsignanus.definition: subsignānus, a, um, sub-signum That is or serves under the standard: miles,a kind of legionary soldiers kept in reserve to strengthen the centre,Tac. H. 1, 70 fin.; 4, 33; Amm. 29, 5, 23.

subsilio.definition: sub-sĭlĭo, lŭi, 4, salio To spring upwards, leap up (mostly poet.; not in Cic.). Lit.: decido de lecto praeceps, subsilit,Plaut. Cas. 5, 2, 50; cf. id. Curc. 1, 2, 64: non subsilis ac plaudis? Varr. ap. Non. 135, 28: semper damnosi subsiluere canes,Prop. 4 (5), 8, 46.Pegasus adusque caelum subsilit ac resultat,App. M. 8, p. 208, 33: subsiliunt ignes ad tecta domorum,Lucr. 2, 191.—* To leap into: jamdudum flammis dexteram objecimus aut voluntariam...

subsistentia.definition: subsisto, = ὑπὀστασις The substance, reality, Cassiod. Hist. Eccl. 5, 38; 9, 3; 12, 4fin.; Boëth. Duab. Nat. p. 950.

subsisto.definition: sub-sisto, stĭti, 3, and A. Neutr., to take a stand or position, to stand still, remain standing; to stop, halt. Act. (acc. to I. A. 2. c.), to make a stand against, withstand, encounter any one (very rare): praepotentem armis Romanum subsistere,Liv. 9, 31: feras,id. 1, 4.

subsortior.definition: sub-sortĭor, tītus, 4, , jurid. t. t. To choose by lot as a substitute, sc. a judge in place of one rejected by the parties: judicem,Cic. Clu. 35, 96.—Absol.: subsortiemur etiam in M. Metelli locum,Cic. Verr. 1, 10, 30.—Part. in pass. sense: si ex lege subsortitus non erat Junius,Cic. Clu. 34, 92.

subsortitio.definition: subsortior A choosing of substitutes by lot, sc. of other judges in place of those rejected by the parties, Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 61, § 157; id. Clu. 33, 91; a selection of citizens to receive corn in place of those who had died: subsortitio a praetore fieret,Suet. Caes. 41 fin.

substantia.definition: substo That of which a thing consists, the being, essence, contents, material, substance (post - Aug.): hominis,Quint. 7, 2, 5: rerum,id. 2, 21, 1: placidae et altae mentis,id. 6, prooem. § 7: rhetorices,id. 2, 15, 34: de substantiā aut de qualitate,id. 3, 6, 38: singula animalia singulas habere debent substantias,Sen. Ep. 113, 4: esse diversae substantiae,Front. Strat. 4 praef.: earum rerum pretium non in substantiā, sed in arte positum est,in t...

substantialis.definition: substantĭālis, e, substantia. Lit., of or belonging to the essence or substance, essential, substantial (post - class.): differentia,Tert. Res. Carn. 45 fin. Transf., substantial, substantive: potestates,i. e. spirits,Amm. 21, 1, 8.—Adv.: sub-stantĭālĭter, essentially, substantially, Tert. adv. Valent. 7, 4; id. adv. Marc. 35 fin.

substantialitas.definition: substantialis The quality of being substantial or essential, Hier. in Didym. Spir. Sanc. 15; Cassiod. Hist. Eccl. 7, 14.

substantivus.definition: substantīvus, a, um, substantia Self-existent, substantive (post - class.). In gen.: res,Tert. adv. Prax. 26; id. adv. Hermog. 26. In gram.: substantivum verbum, the substantive verb, i.e. sum (a transl. of the Gr. ὑπαρκτικόν), Prisc. p. 812 fin. P.

substantiuus.definition: substantīvus, a, um, substantia Self-existent, substantive (post - class.). In gen.: res,Tert. adv. Prax. 26; id. adv. Hermog. 26. In gram.: substantivum verbum, the substantive verb, i.e. sum (a transl. of the Gr. ὑπαρκτικόν), Prisc. p. 812 fin. P.

substerno.definition: sub-sterno, strāvi, strātum, 3 To strew, scatter, spread, or lay under or beneath (class.; cf. subicio). Lit.: segetem ovibus,Cato, R. R. 37, 2: verbenas,Ter. And. 4, 3, 12: casias et nardi lenis aristas,Ov. M. 15, 398; Plin. 20, 14, 56, § 158: folia,id. 20, 21, 84, § 226: semina hordei,Col. 5, 9, 9: fucum marinum,to spread underneath, lay as a ground - color,Plin. 26, 10, 66, § 103 (syn. sublino): se (mulier), to submit, in mal. part., Cat. 64, ...

substituo.definition: sub-stĭtŭo, ŭi, ūtum, 3, statuo. To set, put, place, or lay under, to set or place next to any thing (so rare and mostly post - Aug.). To put instead or in the place of another, to substitute (class.; syn.: suppono, subrogo).

substitutio.definition: substituo, II.. In gen., a putting in the place of another, substitution, Arn. 3, p. 104. In partic., in jurid. lang., the appointment of a second or alternate heir, Gai. Inst. 2, § 174 sq.; Dig. 28, tit. 6.

substitutus.definition: substĭtūtus, a, um, Part. of substituo.

substramen.definition: substerno What is strewn under, litter: molle,Varr. R. R. 3, 10, 4; 3, 6, 5; 3, 9, 8. Transf., supports: lubrica roboreis aderant substramina plaustris,i. e. rollers,Sil. 12, 444.

substrictus.definition: sub-strictus, a, um, Part. and of substringo.

substringo.definition: sub -stringo, nxi, ctum, 3, v. a. To bind beneath; to bind, tie, or draw up (poet. and in post-Aug. prose; syn. subligo). Lit.: crinem nodo,Tac. G. 38: ligatas auro comas,Luc. 3, 281: sinus,Sen. Troad. 88: lintea malo,Sil. 1, 689: caput equi loro,Nep. Eum. 5, 5: carnem fasciā,Suet. Galb. 21. Transf., to bind or draw together; to draw up, contract, check: aurem, i. e. to point or prick the ear, Hor. S. 2, 5, 95: lacrimas,Marc. Emp. 8: bilem,Juv. 6...

substructio.definition: substruo An under - building, foundation, substructure, Vitr. 1, 5: maxima debet esse cura substructionum,id. 6, 11: maximae,Caes. B. C. 2, 25: insanae,Cic. Mil. 20, 53; 31, 85; Liv. 38, 28; Front. Aquaed. 3, 5 sq.; Col. 1, 5, 9; v. substruo fin.

substruo.definition: sub-strŭo, xi, ctum, 3, v. a. To build beneath, to underbuild, lay; lit.: fundamentum,Plaut. Most. 1, 2, 40: intervalla montium,Vitr. 8, 7 med.; cf.: intervalla substructis canalibus junguntur,Plin. 33, 4, 21, § 74: locus substructus,Varr. L. L. 5, § 155 Müll.: Capitolium saxo quadrato,Liv. 6, 4: substruendo iter facere,Dig. 8, 1, 10: vias glareā,i. e. to lay, to pave,Liv. 41, 27.—Absol.: non alte substruitur, the foundation is not laid deeply, V...

subsulto.definition: subsulto, āre V. freq. n. [id.], to spring up, to leap, jump, hop (rare; not in Cic.). Lit., Plaut. Cas. 2, 7, 10: tu subsultas, ego miser vix asto,id. Capt. 3, 4, 104. Trop.: ne sermo subsultet imparibus spatiis,Quint. 11, 3, 43: compositio multis clausulis concisa,id. 9, 4, 42.

subsutus.definition: sub-sūtus, a, um, Part. [suo] Sewn beneath or at the lower part: vestis, trimmed, edged, or fringed at the bottom, Hor. S. 1, 2, 29.

subtalaris.definition: sub-tālāris, e, sub-talus Lying under the heel: calcei,Isid. Orig. 19, 34, 7.

subtemen.definition: (), , contr. from subteximen, subtecmen, from sub-texo That which is wrought or woven in, the woof, weft of a web: inseritur medium radiis subtemen acutis, etc.,Ov. M. 6, 56; Varr. L. L. 5, § 113 Müll.; Verg. A. 3, 483; Vitr. 10, 1 med.; Plin. 11, 24, 28, § 81; 13, 12, 24, § 79. Meton. (pars pro toto), any thing spun, thread, yarn (rare, and mostly poet.): subtemen tenue nere,Plaut. Merc. 3, 1, 20: nere,Ter. Heaut. 2, 3, 52; Front. Nep. Am. 2 med...

subtendo.definition: sub-tendo, no Perf., tum, 3, and n. Act., to stretch underneath: lectos loris,Cato, R. R. 10, 5; 10, 25.—* Neutr., to extend underneath: linea,Front. Expos. Form. p. 32 Goes.

subter.definition: subter (also supter), adv. and prep. sub. Adv., below, beneath, underneath: navem in fugam transdunt subter saxa, Att. ap. Non. 155, 8 (Trag. Rel. v. 630 Rib.): terram fac ut esse rearis Subter item, ut supera,Lucr. 6, 537: partim quod supter per terras diditur omnis,id. 5, 268: aliam naturam supter habere,id. 5, 536: omnia haec, quae supra et subter, unum esse,Cic. de Or. 3, 5, 20; id. poët. N. D. 2, 42, 106: anulus subter adhaerens,Lucr. 6, 914...

subterduco.definition: subter-dūco, xi, 3 To carry off secretly, to steal away any thing (Plautin.): ne tibi clam se subterducat istinc,Plaut. Mil. 2, 3, 72: si huic occasioni tempus sese subterduxerit,id. As. 2, 2, 12.

subterfugio.definition: subter-fŭgĭo, fūgi, 3, and A. Neutr., to flee secretly or by stealth, to get off (so very rare): subterfugisse sic mihi hodie Chrysalum,Plaut. Bacch. 4, 6, 2; Dig. 42, 6, 20. Act., to escape, evade, avoid, shun (class.; a favorite word of Cic.): mare,Plaut. Merc. 1, 2, 83: vim criminum,Cic. Verr. 1, 3, 8: imprudentiam,id. ib. 1, 4, 13: militiam,id. Off. 3, 26, 97: poenam aut calamitatem, id. Caecin. 34, 100: periculum,id. Fam. 15, 1, 4: omnia qua...

subterlabor.definition: subter-lābor, lābi V. dep. n. Lit., to glide or flow under (mostly poet.): fluctus Sicanos,Verg. E. 10, 4: flumina subterlabentia muros,flowing close by,id. G. 2, 157: subterlabens Mosella,Aus. Idyll. 10, 21. Transf., to slip away, escape: celeritate subterlabentem,Liv. 30, 25 (dub.).

subtero.definition: sub-tĕro, trīvi, trītum, 3 To rub off or wear away underneath; to rub, bruise, or grind to pieces (rare; not in Cic.): boves ne pedes subterant,Cato, R. R. 72; so, pedes,Col. 6, 15, 2; Plin. 28, 16, 62, § 221: ungulas,Plaut. As. 2, 2, 73: jumenta cito subteruntur,Sen. Ep. 51, 9: salis sextarium subterito, et subtritum, etc.,pound, triturate,Col. 12, 5, 1: caepam aridam,id. 12, 5, 56; 2, 10, 25; Plin. 20, 20, 82, § 218; 30, 9, 23, § 80.

subterraneus.definition: sub-terrānĕus, a, um, terra Underground, subterranean (class.): specus,Cic. Att. 15, 26, 4; cf.: supterraneos specus aperire,Tac. G. 16: ergastulum,Col. 1, 6, 3: structura,Plin. 36, 22, 50, § 170: regna,Juv. 2, 149: animalia,Pall. Sept. 3, 2: mures,Sen. Q. N. 3, 16, 3: subterraneis venis in mare defluunt,Plin. 9, 15, 20, § 53: domus,id. 36, 13, 19, § 88: cubiculum,Plin. Ep. 4, 11, 9: subterraneis dolis peractum urbis excidium,Flor. 1, 12 fin.—Sub...

subtexo.definition: sub-texo, xŭi, xtum, 3 To weave under or below any thing; hence, to join on, fasten, affix (mostly poet. and in post-Aug. prose; not in Cic.). Lit. (very rare): lunam alutae,Juv. 7, 192.—Poet.: patrio capiti nubes, i. e. soli,to draw before, veil,Ov. M. 14, 368; cf.: nox subtexta polo,Luc. 4, 104: sol diem subtexit Olympo,spreads around Olympus,Val. Fl. 5, 414.—To cover, hide, darken, obscure, conceal, with acc. of thing concealed: subtexunt nubi...

subtilis.definition: subtīlis, e, adj.sub-tela; and therefore, prop., woven fine; hence Fine, not thick or coarse, thin, slender, minute (syn. tenuis). Lit. (mostly poet. and in postAug. prose; not in Cic.): quae vulgo volitant subtili praedita filo,Lucr. 4, 88: ventus subtili corpore tenuis,id. 4, 901; cf. id. 3, 195; Cat. 54, 3: acies gladii,Sen. Ep. 76, 14: farina,Plin. 18, 7, 14, § 74: mitra,Cat. 64, 63: ignis,Lucr. 6, 225: subtilia et minuta primordia rerum,id. ...

subtilitas.definition: (), , subtilis Fineness, thinness, slenderness, minuteness (syn. tenuitas). Lit. (mostly post-Aug.; not in Cic.): linearum,Plin. 35, 10, 36, § 82: ferramentorum,the keen edge, sharpness,id. 28, 9, 41, § 148: inenarrabilis florum,id. 21, 1, 1, § 1: muliebris,Vitr. 4, 1 med.: immensa animalium,Plin. 11, prooem. 1. § 1: caelandi fingendique ac tingendi,id. 35, prooem. § 1: umoris,id. 2, 65, 65, § 163. Trop.

subtractio.definition: subtraho A drawing back, Vulg. Ep. ad Hebr. 10, 39 (transl. of the Gr. ὑποστολή).

subtraho.definition: sub-trăho, xi, ctum, 3 To draw away from underneath or by stealth; also, in gen., to draw off, carry off, withdraw, take away, remove, etc. (class.; syn. subduco). Lit.: subtractus Numida mortuo superincubanti Romano vivus,Liv. 22, 51, 9 (Weissenb. substratus): pedibus raptim tellus subtracta,Lucr. 6, 605: effracto colla jugo,Ov. Tr. 5, 2, 40: viro (peculium),Plaut. Cas. 2, 2, 28: (impedimenta) clandestinā fugā,Hirt. B. G. 8, 33: aggerem cuniculi...

subtriplus.definition: sub-triplus, a, um Contained three times in a larger number, Boëth. Inst. Arith. 1, 23.

subtristis.definition: sub-tristis, e Somewhat sad or sorrowful (ante- and post-class.): subtristis visus est mihi,Ter. And. 2, 6, 16; Hier. Ep. 107, 9.—Comp.: cera subtristior,Hier. Ep. 60, 1.

subturpiculus.definition: sub-turpĭcŭlus, a, um Somewhat mean or disgraceful, Cic. Att. 4, 5, 1.

subturpis.definition: sub-turpis, e Somewhat mean or disgraceful: quae sint, quod ridiculi proprium est, subturpia,Cic. de Or. 2, 66, 264.

subtus.definition: subtus, from sub; like intus, from in Below, beneath, underneath (mostly ante-class.; not in Cic. or Caes.): subtus ambulare,Cato, R. R. 48, 2: labra subtus pendula,Varr. R. R. 2, 9, 3: Romani aggere et vineis et omnibus supra terram operibus, subtus Macedones cuniculis oppugnabant,Liv. 36, 25; cf. Plaut. Cas. 5, 2, 26; Varr. L. L. 5, § 131 Müll.

subtusus.definition: sub-tūsus, a, um, Part. [tundo] Somewhat bruised: flet teneras subtusa genas,Tib. 1, 10, 55: angulus, an obtuse angle, Boëth. Geom. 1, p. 1180.

subucula.definition: sub - UO; whence exuo. A man's under-garment, a shirt: postea quam binas tunicas habere coeperunt, instituerunt vocare subuculam et indusium, Varr. ap. Non. 542, 24; id. L. L. 5, § 131 Müll.; Hor. Ep. 1, 1, 95; Suet. Aug. 82. — Of the priest's dress,Vulg. Lev. 8, 7. Subuculam Aelius Stilo et Cloatius iisdem fere verbis demonstrant vocari, quod dis detur ex alicā et oleo et melle. Nam de tunicae genere notum est omnibus, Fest. pp. 308 and 309 Müll...

subula.definition: Lit., an awl, Mart. 3, 16, 2: aënea,Col. 6, 5, 4; Pall. Jun. 14, 3: perforabit aurem ejus subulā,Vulg. Exod. 21, 6; id. Deut. 15, 17. Transf., a very small weapon: subulā armatus,Sen. Ep. 85, 1; cf. prov.: subulā leonem excipis,id. ib. 82, 25.

subulcus.definition: from sus; formed in analogy with bubulcus A swine-herd, Varr. R. R. 2, 4, 14 and 20; Mart. 10, 98, 10; Verg. E. 10, 19 Wagn. (al. bubulci).

subura.definition: Sŭbūra, ae (abbrev. SVG.; V.infra), f., a quarter in Rome, in the second region, between the Esquiline, Viminal, and Quirinal, where provisions were sold, and where many prostitutes dwelt: Subura Junius scribit ab eo, quod fuerit sub antiquā Urbe: quoi testimonium potest esse, quod subest ei loco, qui Terreus murus vocatur. Sed ego a pago potius Succusano dictam puto Succusam, quod in notā etiam nunc scribitur tertia littera C, non B,Varr. L. L. ...

suburbanitas.definition: suburbanus Nearness to the city of Rome: suburbanitas hujusce provinciae (Siciliae), * Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 3, § 7; Symm. Ep. 2, 22; Sid. Ep. 7, 2 med.

suburbanus.definition: sŭb-urbānus, a, um Situated near the city of Rome, suburban. Adj.: rus suburbanum,Cic. Rosc. Am. 46, 133: fundus,id. Q. Fr. 3, 1, 3, § 9: ager,id. Div. 2, 32, 69: gymnasium,id. de Or. 1, 21, 98: regio Italiae,Col. 11, 2, 61; cf. Italia,Plin. 26, 4, 9, § 19: caulis,Hor. S. 2, 4, 15: peregrinatio,Tac. A. 3, 47: crimina,id. ib. 13, 43 et saep. Substt.

suburbium.definition: urbs A suburb: in suburbium ire,Cic. Phil. 12, 10, 24.

suburgeo.definition: sŭb-urgĕo (also written sŭbur-guĕo), ēre To drive or urge close to: proram ad saxa,Verg. A. 5, 202.

subvectio.definition: subveho A carrying, transporting, conveying, conveyance: frumenti,Liv. 44, 8; Tac. A. 13, 51 fin.— Plur.: durae subvectiones,Caes. B. G. 7, 10: marinae,Vitr. 1, 5, 1.

subuectio.definition: subveho A carrying, transporting, conveying, conveyance: frumenti,Liv. 44, 8; Tac. A. 13, 51 fin.— Plur.: durae subvectiones,Caes. B. G. 7, 10: marinae,Vitr. 1, 5, 1.

subvecto.definition: subvecto, āvi, ātum, 1, id. To bring up from below (on the shoulder, by ship, etc.), to bring, carry, convey, transport to a place (poet. and in post-Aug. prose): asini, qui tibi subvectabant rure huc virgas ulmeas,Plaut. As. 2, 2, 74: saxa umeris,Verg. A. 11, 131: saxa,Sil. 4, 21: onera,Col. 6, praef. 3: panaria candidasque mappas,Stat. S. 1, 6, 32: corpora cymbā,Verg. A. 6, 303: naves, quae frumentum Tiberi subvectassent,Tac. A. 15, 43.

subuecto.definition: subvecto, āvi, ātum, 1, id. To bring up from below (on the shoulder, by ship, etc.), to bring, carry, convey, transport to a place (poet. and in post-Aug. prose): asini, qui tibi subvectabant rure huc virgas ulmeas,Plaut. As. 2, 2, 74: saxa umeris,Verg. A. 11, 131: saxa,Sil. 4, 21: onera,Col. 6, praef. 3: panaria candidasque mappas,Stat. S. 1, 6, 32: corpora cymbā,Verg. A. 6, 303: naves, quae frumentum Tiberi subvectassent,Tac. A. 15, 43.

subvectus.definition: subvectus, a, um, Part. of subveho.

subuectus.definition: subvectus, a, um, Part. of subveho.

subveho.definition: sub-vĕho, vexi, vectum, 3 To bring up from below (on the shoulder, by ship, etc.), to bring, carry, convey, conduct to a place, to bring or carry up stream, etc. (not freq. till after the Aug. per.; not in Cic.): ast alium (aërem fluere) subter, contra qui subvehat orbem,Lucr. 5, 515: frumentum flumine Arari navibus, * Caes. B. G. 1, 16: adversum remis superes subvectus ut amnem,Verg. A. 8, 58: subvecta ponto Barbara agmina,Ov. M. 6, 423: matris ...

subueho.definition: sub-vĕho, vexi, vectum, 3 To bring up from below (on the shoulder, by ship, etc.), to bring, carry, convey, conduct to a place, to bring or carry up stream, etc. (not freq. till after the Aug. per.; not in Cic.): ast alium (aërem fluere) subter, contra qui subvehat orbem,Lucr. 5, 515: frumentum flumine Arari navibus, * Caes. B. G. 1, 16: adversum remis superes subvectus ut amnem,Verg. A. 8, 58: subvecta ponto Barbara agmina,Ov. M. 6, 423: matris ...

subvenio.definition: sub-vĕnĭo, vēni, ventum, 4 (old Fut. subvenibo, Plaut. Men. 5, 7, 20), , to come up or advance to one's assistance (the figure taken from the advance of a military reserve; v. subsidium), to come to one's assistance, to aid, assist, relieve, succor; to obviate, remedy, heal, cure a disease, an evil, etc. (freq. and class.; syn.: adjuvo, succurro, sublevo). In gen., to come up, come (very rare).

subuenio.definition: sub-vĕnĭo, vēni, ventum, 4 (old Fut. subvenibo, Plaut. Men. 5, 7, 20), , to come up or advance to one's assistance (the figure taken from the advance of a military reserve; v. subsidium), to come to one's assistance, to aid, assist, relieve, succor; to obviate, remedy, heal, cure a disease, an evil, etc. (freq. and class.; syn.: adjuvo, succurro, sublevo). In gen., to come up, come (very rare).

subvento.definition: subvento, āre V. freq. n. [id.], to come with assistance to one: spes bona, opsecro, subventa mihi,Plaut. Rud. 1, 4, 11.

subuento.definition: subvento, āre V. freq. n. [id.], to come with assistance to one: spes bona, opsecro, subventa mihi,Plaut. Rud. 1, 4, 11.

subversio.definition: subverto An overturn, overthrow, ruin, destruction (late Lat.): humani generis,Arn. 1, 7: urbium,Vulg. Gen. 19, 29.—Plur.: animorum,Arn. 5, 165.

subuersio.definition: subverto An overturn, overthrow, ruin, destruction (late Lat.): humani generis,Arn. 1, 7: urbium,Vulg. Gen. 19, 29.—Plur.: animorum,Arn. 5, 165.

subverto.definition: sub-verto (-vorto), ti, sum, 3 To turn upside down; to upset, overturn, overthrow (not in Cic. or Caes.). Lit.: lupinum aratro,Col. 11, 2, 44: mensam,Suet. Ner. 47: statuas,id. Calig. 34: tantas operum moles,Ov. F. 6, 645: silvam,Luc. 3, 436: subversi montes,Sall. C. 13, 1: Arisbe terrarum motu subversa,Plin. 5, 31, 39, § 139: Silvani simulacrum,id. 15, 18, 20, § 77: obices portarum,Tac. A. 13, 39. — Absol., Quadrig. ap. Gell. 9, 13, 17: calceus ...

subuerto.definition: sub-verto (-vorto), ti, sum, 3 To turn upside down; to upset, overturn, overthrow (not in Cic. or Caes.). Lit.: lupinum aratro,Col. 11, 2, 44: mensam,Suet. Ner. 47: statuas,id. Calig. 34: tantas operum moles,Ov. F. 6, 645: silvam,Luc. 3, 436: subversi montes,Sall. C. 13, 1: Arisbe terrarum motu subversa,Plin. 5, 31, 39, § 139: Silvani simulacrum,id. 15, 18, 20, § 77: obices portarum,Tac. A. 13, 39. — Absol., Quadrig. ap. Gell. 9, 13, 17: calceus ...

subvexus.definition: subvexus, a, um, subveho Sloping upwards (opp. devexus): omnia fastigio leni subvexa,Liv. 25, 36.

subuexus.definition: subvexus, a, um, subveho Sloping upwards (opp. devexus): omnia fastigio leni subvexa,Liv. 25, 36.

subviridis.definition: sub-vĭrĭdis, e Somewhat green, greenish: folia,Plin. 25, 9, 65, § 113: balanitae,id. 37, 10, 55, § 149: emplastrum,Scrib. Comp. 201 and 202.

subuiridis.definition: sub-vĭrĭdis, e Somewhat green, greenish: folia,Plin. 25, 9, 65, § 113: balanitae,id. 37, 10, 55, § 149: emplastrum,Scrib. Comp. 201 and 202.

subvolo.definition: sub-vŏlo, āre To fly up or upwards (rare but class.): hae (partes corporum) sursum in caelestem locum subvo lent, Cic. Tusc. 1, 17, 40: avis,Ov. M. 11, 790: ex agmine,id. ib. 14, 507: praepes,id. ib. 14, 577: ad capita, Aug. Civ. Dei, 18, 16 fin.: alte,Aur. Vict. Vir. Ill. 6, 3.

subuolo.definition: sub-vŏlo, āre To fly up or upwards (rare but class.): hae (partes corporum) sursum in caelestem locum subvo lent, Cic. Tusc. 1, 17, 40: avis,Ov. M. 11, 790: ex agmine,id. ib. 14, 507: praepes,id. ib. 14, 577: ad capita, Aug. Civ. Dei, 18, 16 fin.: alte,Aur. Vict. Vir. Ill. 6, 3.

subvolvo.definition: sub-volvo, ĕre To roll up or along: manibus saxa,Verg. A. 1, 424.

subuoluo.definition: sub-volvo, ĕre To roll up or along: manibus saxa,Verg. A. 1, 424.

succavus.definition: suc-căvus (subc-), a, um Hollow below or underneath (ante- and postclass.): areae,Cato, R. R. 151, 3: loca,Lucr. 6, 557; Auct. Limit. pp. 252, 260, 303 Goes.: natura Aetnae,Lucr. 6, 682.

succauus.definition: suc-căvus (subc-), a, um Hollow below or underneath (ante- and postclass.): areae,Cato, R. R. 151, 3: loca,Lucr. 6, 557; Auct. Limit. pp. 252, 260, 303 Goes.: natura Aetnae,Lucr. 6, 682.

succedo.definition: suc-cēdo, cessi, cessum, 3, and A. [sub]. To go below or under (so mostly poet.; syn. subeo). To approach, draw near (class. and freq.).

succendo.definition: suc-cendo, di, sum, 3, sub-candeo; v. accendo To kindle or set on fire from below (syn. inflammo). Lit. (class.): (sapiens) etiamsi in Phalaridis tauro inclusus succensis ignibus torreatur,Cic. Pis. 18, 42: aggerem cuniculo hostes succenderant,Caes. B. G. 7, 24: arma cumulata in ingentem acervum ipse imperator face subditā succendit,Liv. 45, 33; cf. Quadrig. ap. Gell. 15, 1, 7; Caes. B. G. 5, 43: rogum,Liv. 28, 23: pontem,id. 1, 37: pinus duabus ...

succenturio.definition: suc-centŭrĭo (subc-), no Perf., ātum, 1, , to receive as a recruit into a centuria; hence, transf., to put in the place of another, receive as a substitute (very rare): succenturiare est explendae centuriae gratiā supplere, subicere, Plaut. ap. Saturione: succenturia, centum require, qui te delectent domi,Fest. p. 306 Müll.: nunc prior adito tu, ego in insidiis hic ere Succenturiatus, si quid deficies, as a reserve, Ter. Phorm. 1, 4, 55; cf.: tot...

successio.definition: succedo, II.. A coming into the place of another, a following after, succeeding, succession in office, possession, etc. (mostly post-Aug.): si merces Antonii oppressi poscitur in Antonii locum successio, Brut. ap. Cic. Ep. ad Brut. 1, 17, 2: Neronis principis successio,Plin. 7, 13, 11, § 58: quorum non dubia,Tac. A. 4, 12; Suet. Tib. 15; 25; 55: ad spem successionis admoveri,id. Calig. 12; id. Oth. 4 fin.: regni,Just. 9, 2; App. M. 8, p. 210, 33;...

successivus.definition: successīvus, a false read. for succissiva, Lact. Opif. Dei, 12, 15 Bünem. ad loc.

successiuus.definition: successīvus, a false read. for succissiva, Lact. Opif. Dei, 12, 15 Bünem. ad loc.

successor.definition: succedo, II. A follower, successor in office, possession, time, etc. (class.; cf. vicarius): conjunctissimus,Cic. Fam. 3, 3, 1; cf.: successori decessor invidit,id. Scaur. Fragm. 33; id. Prov. Cons. 15, 37; id. Fl. 14, 33; id. Fam. 3, 6, 2: successorem alicui mittere,to remove from office,Liv. 23, 27, 12; cf. id. 32, 28, 1: legato eum consulari successorem dedisse,Suet. Aug. 88; id. Dom. 1: successorem accipere,to be removed,Plin. Ep. 8, 13, 23: ...

successus.definition: successus, a, um, Part. of succedo.

succidia.definition: 2. succido. A leg or side of meat cut off, esp. of pork; a leg of pork, flitch of bacon, Varr. L.L. 5, § 110 Müll.; id. R. R. 2, 4, 3: jam hortum ipsi agricolae succidiam alteram appellant,their second flitch,Cic. Sen. 16, 56. — * Transf., a slaughtering: succidias humanas facere, Cato ap. Gell. 13, 24, 12.

succido.definition: suc-cĭdo, ĭdi, 3, sub-cado To fall under any thing. * In gen.: lorica quod e loris de corio crudo pectoralia faciebant: postea succidit Gallica e ferro sub id vocabulum,i. e. were comprehended under the word,Varr. L. L. 5, § 116 Müll. Pregn., to sink under one's self, sink down, sink (poet. and in post-Aug. prose).

succiduus.definition: succĭdŭus, a, um, 1. succido Sinking down, sinking, failing (poet.). Lit.: genu,Ov. H. 13, 24: poples,id. M. 10, 458: gradus,Stat. Th. 4, 661: flammae,id. ib. 10, 116 et saep. Trop.: benedictio,faltering, trembling,Sid. Ep. 7, 6 fin. = succidaneus (late Lat.), Ven. Misc. 4, 25, 10.

succinericius.definition: suc-cinĕrīcius (subc-), a, um, id. Prepared under the ashes (late Lat.): panis,baked under the ashes,Vulg. Gen. 18, 6; id. Exod. 12, 39; id. Osee, 7, 8 al.; cf. Isid. Orig. 20, 21.

succingo.definition: suc-cingo (subc-), nxi, nctum, 3, v. a. To gird below or from below, to tuck up, gird, gird about, girdle (mostly poet. and in postAug. prose; cf. subligo). Lit.: crure tenus medio tunicas,Juv. 6, 455: astricti succingant ilia ventres,Grat. Cyn. 271; cf.: Virginem et Leonem Anguis intortus succingit,Vitr. 9, 5 (7), 1: illa (Scylla) feris atram canibus succingitur alvum,Ov. M. 13, 732; cf. Lucr. 5, 892; Tib. 3, 4, 89: eāpse sic succincta,tucked up...

succingulum.definition: (), , succingo An under-girdle, lower girdle, Plaut. Men. 1, 3, 17; cf. Fest. p. 302 Müll.

succino.definition: suc-cĭno (subc-; also succăno, Varr. L. L. 6, § 75 Müll.), ĕre, and n. cano To sing to, accompany (rare). Lit.: tubicines imitatus est succinente Habinnā,Petr. 69, 4: cantibus iste tuis alterno succinet ore,Calp. Ecl. 4, 79. Transf., to accord, agree: (agricultura) succinit pastorali,Varr. R. R. 1, 2, 16: clamat: Victum date. Succinit alter: Et mihi, etc.,another chimes in,Hor. Ep. 1, 17, 48.

succlamatio.definition: succlamo A calling or crying out, a shouting, acclamation after any thing (rare; perh. not anteAug.); only plur.: ultro territuri succlamationibus,Liv. 28, 26, 12; 40, 36, 4; 42, 28, 2; Suet. Ner. 24.

succlamo.definition: suc-clāmo (subc-), āvi, ātum, 1 To call or cry out, to shout, exclaim after or in reply to any thing (not in Cic. or Caes.); with obj.-clause: haec Virginio vociferanti succlamabat multitudo, nec illius dolori nec suae libertati se defuturos,Liv. 3, 50, 10: quidam ausi sunt mediā ex contione succlamare: Abite hinc, ne, etc.,id. 44, 45; cf.: si esset libera haec civitas, non tibi succlamassent,id. 6, 40: cum centuria fre quens succlamasset, nihil ...

succollo.definition: suc-collo (subc-), āvi, ātum, 1, collum To take upon the neck or shoulder, to shoulder (very rare): apes fessum (regem) sublevant, et si nequit volare, succollant,Varr. R. R. 3, 16, 8 (for which: attollunt umeris,Verg. G. 4, 217): vicissim succollantibus (lecticam),Suet. Claud. 10 med.: succollatus et a praesente comitatu imperator consalutatus,id. Oth. 6 med.; Plin. 35, 10, 37, § 117.

succontumeliose.definition: suc-contŭmēlĭōsē (subc-) Somewhat insolently or contumeliously: tractari,Cic. Att. 2, 7, 3.

succresco.definition: suc-cresco (subc-), ĕre V. inch. n., to grow under or from under any thing; to grow up (very rare). Lit.: sub ordine naturali pilorum (in palpebris) alius ordo succrescit,Cels. 7, 7, 8: succrescit ab imo,Ov. M. 9, 352: ne patiantur herbam succrescere,Col. 4, 14, 2; cf.: mores mali, Quasi herba irrigua, succrevere uberrime,Plaut. Trin. 1, 1, 9. Trop.: non enim ille mediocris orator vestrae quasi succrescit aetati, grows up after, succeeds, * Cic. ...

succrispus.definition: suc-crispus (subc-), a, um Somewhat curled, frizzled, or crisped: capillus,Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 44, § 108: juba equi,Varr. R. R. 2, 7, 5: pars inferior caudae,id. ib. 2, 5, 8.

succumbo.definition: suc-cumbo (subc-), cŭbŭi, cŭbĭtum, 3 To lay or put one's self under any thing; to fall down, lie, or sink down. Lit. (rare; not in Cic.; cf. subsido). Trop., to yield, be overcome; to submit, surrender, succumb (the predom. and class. signif.; cf.: cedo, me summitto).

succurro.definition: suc-curro (subc-), curri, cursum, 3 To run under. Lit. Trop. *

succussus.definition: succussus, a, um, Part. of succutio.

succutio.definition: suc-cŭtĭo (subc-), ussi, ussum, 3, sub-quatio To fling up from below, fling aloft, toss up (poet. and in post-Aug. prose). Lit.: orbes rotarum,Lucr. 6, 551: currus alte,Ov. M. 2, 166: mare,Sen. Q. N. 5, 1, 1: vasculum,App. M. 2, p. 166: caput,id. Mag. p. 333 et saep.—* Trop.: vultūs succussus,Val. Max. 6, 9 ext. 5.

sucidus.definition: sūcĭdus (succ-), a, um, id. Juicy, sappy; fresh (very rare; not in Cic.): solum,App. Mag. p. 289: tonsurae tempus inter aequinoctium vernum et solstitium, cum sudare inceperunt oves; a quo sudore recens lana tonsa sucida appellata est,Varr. R. R. 2, 11, 6: lana,Mart. 11, 27, 8; Juv. 5, 24; Fest. p. 118 Müll.; such wool was much used in medicine,Cels. 8, 3 fin.; Plin. 29, 2, 9, § 30; and was called sucidae sordes,id. 29, 2, 10, § 35: (puella) fres...

sucinum.definition: (), , sucus Amber, usu. called electrum, Plin. 37, 2, 11, § 30; Mart. 3, 65, 5; 5, 37, 11; Juv. 6, 573 al.

sucinus.definition: sūcĭnus (succ-), a, um, sucinum Of amber: gutta,Mart. 6, 15, 2: gemma,id. 4, 59, 2: novacula,Plin. 22, 23, 47, § 99.

sucus.definition: (), (collat. form Gen. sing. sucūs, Isid. 17, 9, 28; gen. plur. sucuum, App. M. 10, p. 244, 32), m. sugo, juice, moisture, sap (class.; cf.: liquor, latex). Lit. Trop., strength, rigor, energy, spirit: sucus ac sanguis (civitatis),Cic. Att. 4, 16, 10: ingenii, Quint. prooem. § 24.

sudarium.definition: sudor A cloth for wiping off perspiration, a handkerchief, Cat. 12, 14; 25, 7; Mart. 11, 39, 3; Petr. 67: sudario candido tergere frontem,Quint. 6, 3, 60; 11, 3, 148; Suet. Ner. 25; 48; 51; Val. Max. 9, 12, 7; App. Mag. p. 309, 28.

sudatorius.definition: sūdātōrĭus, a, um, sudo Belonging to or serving for sweating, sudatory. Adj.: unctiones,Plaut. Stich. 1, 3, 73: qualitas,Cassiod. Var. 2, 39 med. Subst.: sūdātōrĭum, ii, n., a sweatingbath, sweating-room, a sudatory: circa balinea ac sudatoria,Sen. Vit. Beat. 7, 2; id. Ep. 51, 6.
