Ep. 9, 4, 2: ignes transsiliunt protinus in naphtham undecumque visam,Plin. 2, 105, 109, § 23...

undique.definition: undĭquĕ Adv. indef. [unde-que, prop. whencesoever; hence], from all parts, sides, or places, from every quarter, on all sides, on every part, everywhere: ut undique uno tempore in hostes impetus fieret,Caes. B. G. 1, 22: vicus altissimis montibus undique continetur,id. ib. 3, 1: cinctus periculis,Cic. Imp. Pomp. 11, 30: rebus undique collectis, arcessitis, comportatis,id. de Or. 3, 24, 92; cf.: carpere et colligere,id. ib. 1, 42, 191: carpere atq...

undisonus.definition: undĭsŏnus, a, um, unda-sono Wave-sounding, sounding or roaring with the waves (poet.): rupes,Stat. Achill. 1, 198: saxum,Val. Fl. 4, 44: Psamathe,id. 1, 364: dei,i. e. sea-gods,Prop. 3 (4), 21, 18.

undo.definition: undo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. n. and A. [unda]. Neutr., to rise in waves or surges, to throw up waves, to surge, swell (poet. and in postAug. prose). Act. (very rare), to overflow, inundate, deluge: sanguine campos,Stat. Achill. 1, 87: sinus cruore,Claud. in Ruf. 2, 67.—P. a.: undātus, a, um, in a wavy or wave-like form: concharum genera imbricatim undata, cancellatim reticulata,Plin. 9, 33, 52, § 103.—Hence, undan-ter, adv., in a waving manner, like wa...

undosus.definition: undōsus, a, um, unda Full of waves or surges, surgy, billowy: aequor,Verg. A. 4, 313: Plemyrium,id. ib. 3, 693: regna,Sil. 5, 21.—Comp.: fluctus,Sol. 12 fin.—Sup.: torrentes, Aug. Civ. Dei, 27, 11. —Adv.: undōsē, in waves; comp.: undosius labens,Amm. 27, 4, 7.

unetvicesimus.definition: ūnetvīcēsĭmus (ūnăet-), a, um, unus-et-vicesimus The twentyfirst: legio,Tac. A. 1, 45 (al. undevicesimus).

unetuicesimus.definition: ūnetvīcēsĭmus (ūnăet-), a, um, unus-et-vicesimus The twentyfirst: legio,Tac. A. 1, 45 (al. undevicesimus).

ungo.definition: ungo or unguo, nxi, nctum, 3, root in Sanscr. ang, to besmear; cf. Gr. ἄγος To smear, besmear, anoint with any fat substance, an unguent, oil, etc. (class.; syn.: lino, linio): unguentis,Cic. Verr. 2, 4, 35, § 77: aliquam unguentis,Plaut. Most. 1, 3, 115; id. Truc. 2, 2, 34: unctus est, accubuit,Cic. Att. 13, 52, 1: gloria quem supra vires unguit,Hor. Ep. 1, 18, 22; Aug. ap. Suet. Aug. 76.—Of the anointing of corpses, Enn. ap. Serv. Verg. A. 6,...

unguen.definition: id. A fatty substance, fat; an ointment, unguent: in aënum caldum unguen indito,Cato, R. R. 79; 80: pingues unguine ceras, Verg. G. 3, 450: cras. sum,Pers. 6, 40: pingue,Val. Fl. 6, 360; 8, 302 al.

unguentarius.definition: unguentārĭus, a, um, unguentum Of or belonging to ointments or unguents, ointment-. Adj.: taberna, Varr L. L. 8, 30, 117; Sen. Ep. 108, 4; Suet. Aug. 4: cella,Sid. Ep. 2, 2: vasa,Plin. 36, 8, 12, § 60. Substt.

unguentum.definition: ( Gen. plur. unguentūm, Plaut. Curc. 1, 2, 5; id. Poen. 3, 3, 88), n. unguo, an ointment, unguent, perfume: non omnes possunt olere unguenta exotica,Plaut. Most. 1, 1, 41; 1, 3, 115 sq.; Cic. Verr. 2, 3, 25, § 62; id. Cat. 2, 3, 5; id. Sest. 8, 18; id. Cael. 11, 27; id. Tusc. 5, 21, 62; Hor. C. 2, 3, 13; 2, 7, 23; id. A. P. 375; Prop. 3, 16 (4, 15), 23; Ov. F. 3, 561; Mart. 11, 54, 1; Plin. 1, 1, 1, § 3.

unguiculus.definition: dim.unguis A finger-nail: integritas unguiculorum omnium,Cic. Fin. 5, 27, 80; Plaut. Ep. 5, 1, 17; Sen. Q. N. 6, 2, 5.—Prov.: a teneris unguiculis, a transl. of the Gr. ἐξ ἁπαλῶν ὀνύχων, from early infancy, from childhood, Cic. Fam. 1, 6, 2 (for which: de tenero ungui,Hor. C. 3, 6, 24): ex unguiculis (= ἐξ ὀνύχων), from the very finger-tips, i. e. through and through, Plaut. Stich. 5, 5, 20; App. M. 10, p. 249, 11.

unguis.definition: (abl. ungui, Cat. 62, 43; Hor. Ep. 1, 19, 46; id. C. 2, 8, 4; Prop. 1, 20, 39; cf. Charis. p. 120), cf. Gr. ΟΝΥΧ-, ὄνυξ; Sanscr. nakha A nail of a person's finger or toe. Lit., Plin. 11, 45, 101, § 247; 10, 35, 52, § 106; 28, 2, 5, § 28; Hor. Ep. 1, 7, 51; 1, 19, 46; id. S. 1, 3, 101; Prop. 1, 20, 39; Ov. Am. 1, 7, 64; 2, 6, 4; id. A. A. 3, 708. Transf.

ungula.definition: unguis. Lit., a hoof, claw, talon; of a horse: totam quatit ungula terram, Enn. ap. Macr. S. 6, 1 (Ann. v. 231 Vahl.); Verg. A. 8, 596; cf. Cic. N. D. 3, 5, 11.—Of a swine, Cato, R. R. 158, 1; Cels. 2, 17; 4, 14.—Of oxen: bisulca,Plin. 8, 21, 30, § 72.—Of the claws of hens, Plaut. Aul. 3. 4, 8.—Of vultures' and eagles' talons, Plaut. Ps. 3, 2, 63.—Prov.: toto corpore atque omnibus ungulis, i. e., as we say,with tooth and nail, with might and main...

unicaulis.definition: ūnĭ-caulis, e, id. Having a single stalk: genus carduorum silvestrium,Plin. 20, 23, 99, § 262: faba leguminum,id. 18, 7, 10, § 57: cuminum,id. 19, 10, 57, § 176.

unicolor.definition: ūnĭ-cŏlor, ōris (collat. form Acc. plur. unicoloras animas, Prud. Ham. 821), unus, of one color, all of one or the same color (opp. varius, differens): sues,Varr. R. R. 2, 4, 3: oculus,Plin. 11, 37, 54, § 145: torus,Ov. M. 11, 611.

unicornis.definition: ūnĭcornis, e, adj.unus-cornu Onehorned, having a single horn. Adj.: Indici boves,Plin. 8, 21, 30, § 72: animal,id. 11, 46, 106, § 255: rhinoceros,Tert. adv. Marc. 3, 18; id. adv. Jud. 10. Subst., Vulg. Psa. 91, 11.

unicornuus.definition: unicornis, pure Lat. for monoceros The unicorn, Tert. adv. Marc. 3, 18; id. adv. Jud. 10; Ambros. Off. Min. 2, 16, 85.

unicus.definition: ūnĭcus, a, um, adj.id. One and no more, only, sole, single (class.). Lit., of number: tuus unicus gnatus,Plaut. As. 1, 1, 1: gnatus,id. Poen. prol. 68; Ter. Heaut. 1, 1, 79; 3, 2, 29: gnata,id. And. 3, 3. 8; 1, 1, 73: filius,Plaut. Poen. prol. 65; id. Cas. 2, 3, 45; Ter. Heaut. 1, 1, 41; Cic. Rosc. Am. 14, 41: quid me patrem par facere'st, quoi ille'st unicus?Plaut. Capt. 1, 2, 38 (44): filia,Ter. Phorm. 4, 3, 41; Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 41, § 104; Verg...

uniformis.definition: ūnĭ-formis, e, unus-forma Having only one shape or form, uniform (postAug.): simplex quiddam et uniforme doceri,Tac. Or. 32: facies deorum dearumque,App. M. 11, p. 259, 3: humanum genus,id. Asclep. p. 98, 18: alimonia,Macr. S. 7, 5: institutum,Aur. Vict. Epit. 9 med.—Adv.: ūnĭformĭter, in one and the same manner, uniformly, App. Asclep. p. 77, 18; Arn. 2, 88.

uniformitas.definition: uniformis Uniformity (opp. varietas; post-class.),Macr. S. 7, 5 med.; Arn. 7, 212; Tert. Anim. 17 med.

unigena.definition: ūnĭgĕna, ae (collat. form oenĭgĕ-nŏs unigenitus, Paul. ex Fest. p. 195 Müll.), unus-gigno. Only-begotten, only: idcirco singularem deus hunc mundum atque unigenam procreavit,Cic. Univ. 4, 10.—In Christian authors, of Christ: dominus deusque,Paul. Nol. Carm. 5, 46; cf. unigenitus. Born of one parent, of one or the same family (poet.): te, Phoebe, relinquens Unigenamque simul cultricem montibus Idri, i. e. Diana, sister of Phoebus. Cat. 64, 301; of...

unigenitus.definition: ūnĭ-gĕnĭtus, a, um, id. Onlybegotten, only (eccl. Lat.; cf. unicus): unigenitus ille vocatur, qui parentibus solus sit, Hier. adv. Helv. 9: filius, Tert. adv Gnost. 7; Aug. Civ. Dei, 11, 24; Vulg. Johan 1, 14.

unimanus.definition: ūnĭmănus, a, um, unus-manus Having only one hand, one-handed. In gen.: puer natus,Liv. 35, 21, 3; 41, 21, 12 Unimanus, the surname of a certain Claudius. Flor. 2, 17, 16.

unio.definition: ūnĭo, ĭi, ītum, 4, unus To join together, unite (post-Aug. and very rare; cf. conjungo): caelum mari,Tert. Anim. 17, Sulp. Sev. Chron. 2, 43, 1: corpora,Sen. Q. N. 2, 2, 4; Dig. 39, 2, 15, § 13; App. Mag. p. 283, 30.

unitas.definition: unus The state of being one, oneness, unity. Lit.: singularis numeri unitas. Gell. 19, 8, 11: linum duplex triplexve sic tortum. ut unitas in eo facta sit,Cels. 7, 4, 4: Monotes et Henotes, id est solitas et unitas,Tert. adv. Valent. 37: alv ei,Plin. 5, 9, 9, § 48: mundi,Just. 2, 1, 14: in unitatem coire,Cels. 4, 19: inter se implicantur et quasi unitatem faciunt,Col. 11. 3, 43. Trop.

uniter.definition: ūnĭter, id. Into one, together in one, conjointly, = in unum (Lucretian): cum corporis atque animaï Discidium fuerit, quibus e sumus uniter apti,Lucr. 3, 839; 3, 846; 5, 555; 5, 558: cedere, Schol. Juv. 3, 298.

universalis.definition: ūnĭversālis, e, universus Of or belonging to all or the whole, universal (post-Aug.): praecepta universalia vel perpetualia,Quint. 2, 13, 14; so, quaestiones,id. 3, 5, 5; 3, 5, 12: vox,id. 8, 5, 3: nihil inveniebam aut proprium aut universale,Plin. Ep. 10, 71, 2.

uniuersalis.definition: ūnĭversālis, e, universus Of or belonging to all or the whole, universal (post-Aug.): praecepta universalia vel perpetualia,Quint. 2, 13, 14; so, quaestiones,id. 3, 5, 5; 3, 5, 12: vox,id. 8, 5, 3: nihil inveniebam aut proprium aut universale,Plin. Ep. 10, 71, 2.

universaliter.definition: ūnĭversālĭter, universalis All together: si grex venierit universaliter uno pretio,Dig. 18, 1, 35 fin.

uniuersaliter.definition: ūnĭversālĭter, universalis All together: si grex venierit universaliter uno pretio,Dig. 18, 1, 35 fin.

universitas.definition: id. The whole. Lit.: universitas generis humani,Cic. N. D. 2, 65, 164: in universitate rerum,i. e. in the universe,id. ib. 1, 43, 120: communem rerum naturam universitatemque omnia continentem,id. ib. 1, 15, 39 B. and K.: hoc interdictum ad universitatem bonorum, non ad singulas res pertinet,Dig. 43, 2, 1: aedificii,ib. 41, 1, 7: aedium,ib. 41, 3, 23: non tantum universitati ejus attendas, verum etiam particulas persequaris,Plin. Ep. 1, 8, 3: ora...

uniuersitas.definition: id. The whole. Lit.: universitas generis humani,Cic. N. D. 2, 65, 164: in universitate rerum,i. e. in the universe,id. ib. 1, 43, 120: communem rerum naturam universitatemque omnia continentem,id. ib. 1, 15, 39 B. and K.: hoc interdictum ad universitatem bonorum, non ad singulas res pertinet,Dig. 43, 2, 1: aedificii,ib. 41, 1, 7: aedium,ib. 41, 3, 23: non tantum universitati ejus attendas, verum etiam particulas persequaris,Plin. Ep. 1, 8, 3: ora...

universus.definition: ūnĭversus, a, um (poet. contr., unvorsum, Lucr. 4, 262; plur. OINVORSEI, S. C. Bacch.), adj. unus-verto, turned into one, combined into one whole All together, all taken collectively, whole, entire, collective, general, universal (opp. singuli). Substt.

uniuersus.definition: ūnĭversus, a, um (poet. contr., unvorsum, Lucr. 4, 262; plur. OINVORSEI, S. C. Bacch.), adj. unus-verto, turned into one, combined into one whole All together, all taken collectively, whole, entire, collective, general, universal (opp. singuli). Substt.

univira.definition: (, Treb. XXX. Tyrann. 32; Inscr. Grut. 307, 3), , unusvir A woman that has had only one husband (post-class.), Tert. Exhort. ad Castit. 13; Hier. adv. Jovin. 1, 11.—Adj.: univira viduitas,Tert. adv. Psych. 8.

uniuira.definition: (, Treb. XXX. Tyrann. 32; Inscr. Grut. 307, 3), , unusvir A woman that has had only one husband (post-class.), Tert. Exhort. ad Castit. 13; Hier. adv. Jovin. 1, 11.—Adj.: univira viduitas,Tert. adv. Psych. 8.

univiratus.definition: univira The state or condition of a woman who has married but once, Tert. Exhort. ad Castit. 13; id. ad Uxor. 1, 9; 2, 1.

uniuiratus.definition: univira The state or condition of a woman who has married but once, Tert. Exhort. ad Castit. 13; id. ad Uxor. 1, 9; 2, 1.

univocus.definition: ūnĭvŏcus, a, um, unus-vox That has but one meaning, univocal (logical t. t.): univocis aequivoca conectere,Mart. Cap. 4, § 339; 4, § 356.

uniuocus.definition: ūnĭvŏcus, a, um, unus-vox That has but one meaning, univocal (logical t. t.): univocis aequivoca conectere,Mart. Cap. 4, § 339; 4, § 356.

unoculus.definition: ūnŏcŭlus, a, um, unus-oculus One-eyed: Cyclops, Att. ap. Gell. 3, 11, 5: gens (Arimaspi),Sol. 15med.—Subst.: ūnŏcŭlus, i, m., a one-eyed person, Plaut. Curc. 3, 22 sqq.

unus.definition: ūnus (old forms OINOS and OENOS; cf. Cic. Leg. 3, 3, 9; C. I. L. 1, 32, 35), a, um (scanned Gen. sing. unĭus, Lucr. 2, 379; Verg. A. 1, 41; Hor. S. 1, 6, 13 al.: unīus,Verg. A. 1, 251; Ov. M. 13, 181 al.; ante-class. collat. form of the gen. sing. uni, Titin. ap. Prisc. pp. 694 and 717 P.; dat. m. uno, Varr. R. R. 1, 18, 6; dat. f. unae, Cato, R. R. 19, 1; acc. OINO, C. I. L. l. l.; voc. une, Plaut. ap. Prisc. p. 673 P.; Cat. 37, 17; cf. Varr. L....

upilio.definition: (eollat. form of ōpĭlĭo, q. v.), , ovis A shepherd, Verg. E. 10, 19; App. Mag. p. 279, 35.

upupa.definition: ἔποψ. Lit., a hoopoe, Plin. 10, 29, 44, § 86; 10, 25, 36, § 73; Varr. L. L. 5, § 75 Müll.; cf. epops. Transf., a kind of hoe or mattock, Plaut. Capt. 5, 4, 7.

urbanitas.definition: id. A living in a city, city life. Lit.: desideria urbis et urbanitatis,Cic. Fam. 7, 6, 1: in urbis urbanitatisque desiderio,id. ib. 7, 17, 1. Transf., city fashion, city manners, both in a good and in a bad sense.

urbanus.definition: urbānus, a, um, urbs Of or belonging to the city or town, city-, town- (opp. rusticus; cf.: urbicus, oppidanus). Lit. Transf., in the city fashion, in the city style, citizenlike, both in a good and a bad sense.

urbicapus.definition: urbs-capio A city taker, taker of cities: urbicape, occisor regum,Plaut. Mil. 4, 2, 64.

urbicarius.definition: urbĭcārĭus, a, um, urbicus Of or belonging to the city (post-class.): regiones, Cod. Th. 11, 28, 14: praefectura,Cod. Just. 3, 24, 1.

urbs.definition: (dat. VRBEI, Corp. Inscr. Lat. 206), Sanscr. vardh-, to make strong; cf. Pers. vard-ana, city A walled town, a city. Lit. Trop.: urbem philosophiae, mihi crede, proditis, dum castella defenditis,i. e. the main point,Cic. Div. 2, 16, 37.

urceolus.definition: dim.urceus A little pitcher or water-pot, Col. 12, 16, 4; Juv. 3, 203; 10, 64; Mart. 14, 105 in lemm.

urceus.definition: ( Neutr. collat. form , Cato, R. R. 13, 1) [Gr. ὔρχα, a jar; cf. orca],a pitcher, water-pot, ewer,Dig. 33, 7, 18, § 3; Hor. A. P. 22; Plaut. Mil. 3, 2, 18; Cn. Matius ap. Gell. 10, 24, 10; Plin. 19, 5, 24, § 71; Col. 12, 52, 8; Mart. 11, 56, 3; 12, 32, 16 al.

uredo.definition: uro. A blast, blight of plants, Cic. N. D. 3, 35, 86; Plin. 18, 28, 69, § 279; Col. 3, 20, 1. A burning itch, Plin. 9, 45, 68, § 147; cf. App. M. 8, p. 215, 18.

urgeo.definition: urgeo (less correctly urgueo), ursi ( Perf. rare; past part. not found), 2, v. a. Gr. ϝεργ-, εἵργνυμι, to shut in; Sanscr. varg-, vargami, prevent; Germ. Merk; Engl. work, to press, push, force, drive, impel, urge. Lit. (mostly poet.; syn.: pello, trudo): unda impellitur undā Urgeturque eadem veniens urgetque priorem,Ov. M. 15, 182: urgeris turbā circum te stante,Hor. S. 1, 3, 135: angustoque vagos pisces urgere catino,id. ib. 2, 4, 77: trepidi...

urina.definition: kindr. with Sanscr. vāri, water; Gr. οὖρον; cf. urna and urceus Urine. Lit., Cic. Fat. 3, 5; Cels. 2, 7; 2, 19; Plin. 24, 11, 56, § 94; 24, 6, 17, § 27; Juv. 6, 313.—Plur., Plin. 24, 13, 71, § 115; Suet. Aug. 80 fin.; id. Ner. 56; id. Vesp. 23; Gell. 19, 4, 3 et saep. Transf.: genitalis,seed, semen,Plin. 8, 43, 68, § 168; cf.: urina concepta,Juv. 11, 170.—Plur., Veg. Vet. 3, 15, 19.

urinator.definition: urinor A diver, Varr. L. L. 5, § 126 Müll.; Liv. 44, 10; Dig. 14, 2, 4; Inscr. Orell. 4115.

urinor.definition: ūrīnor, āri, (ante-class. collat. form ūrīno, āre) [urina; Gr. οὐρέω] To plunge under water, to dive: urinare est mergi in aquam,Varr. L. L. 5, § 126 Müll.; Cic. Fragm. ap. Non. 474, 27; Plin. 11, 37, 72, § 188.—Part.: urinantes,Plin. 9 30, 48, § 91.

urna.definition: prop. a vessel of burnt clay; root uro A vessel for drawing water, a water-pot, water-jar, urn. Lit.: urnae dictae, quod urinant in aquā hauriendā ut urinator,Varr. L. L. 5, § 126 Müll.; Plaut. Ps. 1, 2, 24; Prop. 4 (5), 4, 16; 4 (5), 11, 28; Ov. F. 3, 14; id. M. 3, 37; 3, 172; Hor. C. 3, 11, 22; id. S. 1, 5, 91; 1, 1, 54.—As an attribute of personified rivers, Verg. A. 7, 792; Sil. 1, 407.—Of the constellation Aquarius, Ov. F. 2, 457; Sen. Thyes...

uro.definition: ūro, ussi, ustum, 3, for uso from root us; cf. Gr. εὔω, to singe; αὔω, to kindle To burn (class.). Lit. Trop., to burn, inflame, consume with passion; in pass., to burn, glow, be heated, be inflamed, be enamored; of love or lust: me tamen urit amor,Verg. E. 2, 68: Daphnis me malus urit,id. ib. 8, 83: vires urit videndo Femina,id. G. 3, 215: urit me Glycerae nitor, Urit grata protervitas,Hor. C. 1, 19, 5 sq.— Pass.: uritur infelix Dido,Verg. A...

ursa.definition: ursus A she-bear. Lit., Ov. M. 2, 485; 13, 803; 13, 836; 15, 379; id. F. 2, 181; Mart. 6, 25, 2. Transf.: Ursa, as a constellation, either Ursa Major, the Greater Bear, or Ursa Minor, the Lesser Bear, Ov. H. 18 (17), 152; id. Tr. 1, 4, 1; 3, 11, 8; 5, 3, 7; Val. Fl. 4, 724; Suet. Aug. 80.

ursinus.definition: ursīnus, a, um, id. Of or belonging to a bear, bear's-. Adj.: sanguis,Col. Arb. 15: fel,Plin. 28, 16, 62, § 219: adeps,id. 28, 17, 71, § 235: rabies,id. 8, 36, 54, § 130: allium, a kind of wild garlic, id. 19, 6, 34, § 116. Subst.: ursīna, ae, f., bear's meat, Petr. 66.

ursus.definition: for urcsus; Sanscr. arća; Gr. ἄρκτος A bear, Plin. 8, 36, 54, § 131; Ov. M. 2, 494; 10, 540; Hor. Epod. 16, 51; id. C. 3, 4, 18; id. A. P. 472; Juv. 4, 106; Sen. Ira, 2, 31, 6; 3, 43, 2; cf. Varr. L. L. 5, § 100 Müll.—Prov.: fumantem nasum vivi tentaveris ursi,i. e. to provoke a dangerous person.Mart. 6, 64, 28: ursum poscunt,a bear-baiting in the circus,Hor. Ep. 2, 1, 186.

urtica.definition: uro. Lit. Trop., lustful desire, pruriency, Juv. 2, 128; 11, 166 (168).

urus.definition: Celtic A kind of wild ox, a ure-ox, urus, Caes. B. G. 6, 28; Plin. 8, 15, 15, § 38; Verg. G. 2, 374; 3, 532; cf. Macr. S. 6, 4 fin.

usitatus.definition: ūsĭtātus, a, um, Part. and of usitor.

uspiam.definition: uspĭam, us-piam, v. usque At or in any place, anywhere, somewhere (rare but class; mostly in affirmative clauses; cf. usquam): sive est illa (lex) scripta uspiam, sive nusquam,Cic. Leg. 1, 15, 42: si avenam uspiam videris,id. Fin. 5, 30, 91: non dubitabam, quin te ille aut Dyrrhachii aut in istis locis uspiam visurus esset, id. Att. 1, 17, 2: utrum consistere uspiam velit, an mare transire, nescitur,id. ib. 7, 12, 2: malo esse in Tusculano aut us...

usquam.definition: usquam, us for ubs, from ubi; indef. suffix quam, as in quisquam, etc.; cf. usque At or in any place, anywhere (usu. in neg. clauses, while uspiam, corresp. to quispiam, is used also affirmatively). Lit.: iste, cui nullus esset usquam consistendi locus, etc.,Cic. Fl. 21, 50: numquam etiam fui usquam, quin, etc.,Ter. Eun. 5, 9 (8), 62: neque quiescam usquam noctu neque interdiu,Plaut. Merc. 5, 2, 21: nec usquam insistentes,Quint. 10, 7, 6: neque o...

usque.definition: usquĕ, us- for ubs-, from ubi with locative s; and que for qued, old abl. of quis; v. Corss. Ausspr. 2, 471; 838; cf.: quisque, usquam. Lit., all the way to or from any limit of space, time, etc. (cf.: fine, tenus); of place, all the way, right on, without interruption, continuously, constantly. Meton.

usquequaque.definition: usquĕquāque, v. usque, I. B. 2.; II. A. 3. e.; II. B. 3.

ustio.definition: uro A burning, searing, or cauterizing (post-Aug. and very rare): si costa cariosa est, inutilis ustio,Cels. 8, 2 fin.: quaedam ustione sanantur,Plin. 34, 15, 44, § 151: vehementior sinapis,id. 20, 22, 87, § 239.

ustor.definition: id. A burner of dead bodies, a corpse-burner, Cic. Mil. 33, 90; Cat. 59, 5; Mart. 3, 93, 26; Luc. 8, 738.

ustulo.definition: ustŭlo, āvi, ātum, 1, id.. Lit. Transf., to pinch, nip, or blast with cold: gemmas (arboris) frigoris aurā,Auct. Priap. 62.

usualis.definition: ūsŭālis, e, adj.2. usus. That is for use, fit for use (post-class.): mancipia,Dig. 39, 4, 16, § 3.—* Usual, common, ordinary: sermo,Sid. Ep. 4, 10; Ambros. in Luc. 7, n. 150.—Hence, adv.: ūsŭālĭter, in the usual manner (late Lat.), Cassiod. Var. 2, 39.

usuarius.definition: ūsŭārĭus, a, um, id. Of or belonging to use, usuary, viz. Pass., that is used, made use of: servus,i. e. whom one has the use of, but does not own,Dig. 7, 8, 14; Gell. 4, 1, 23. Act., as subst.: ūsŭā-rĭus, ii, m., one who uses or has the use of a thing, but no right of property in it: usus aquae personalis est: et ideo ad heredem usuarii transmitti non potest,Dig. 7, 8, 21: eadem et in usuario dicenda sunt,ib. 7, 1, 13, § 2.

usucapio.definition: ūsū-căpĭo (in recent edd. usually separate, ūsū căpĭo), cēpi, captum, 3, id.; jurid. t. t. To acquire ownership of a thing by long use, to acquire by prescription or usucaption: quoniam hereditas usu capta esset,Cic. Att. 1, 5, 6: scio jam biennium transisse, omniaque me usucepisse,Plin. Ep. 5, 1, 10: nullam penes se culpam esse, quod Hannibal jam velut usu cepisset Italiam,Liv. 22, 44, 6: subsiciva, ut usu capta, concessit,Suet. Dom. 9 fin.: fil...

usura.definition: utor A using, use, or enjoyment of a thing (class.). In gen.: solis usura, Att. ap. Non. 231, 4: hujus lucis,Cic. Rab. Post. 17, 48: unius horae,id. Cat. 1, 12, 29: parva exigui temporis,id. Agr. 3, 1, 2: longi temporis,id. Fam. 3, 1, 1: vitae,id. Tusc. 1, 39, 93: corporis, Plaut Am. prol. 108; cf. id. Trin. 1, 2, 144 gloriae, Vell. 2, 34, 2. In partic., in mercantile lang., a use of money lent: ab aliquo pecuniam pro usurā auferre,Cic. Verr. 2, ...

usurarius.definition: ūsūrārĭus, a, um, usura. That serves or is fit for use, of which one has the use or enjoyment, = usuarius: puer,Plaut. Curc. 3, 12: uxor,id. Am. 1, 2, 36. Of or belonging to interest or usury, that pays interest: aera,Plaut. Truc. 1, 1, 53: pecunia,at interest,Dig. 16, 2, 11: debitum,ib. 3, 5, 5 fin.; 3, 5, 37 fin.: debitor,ib. 21, 1, 7.

usurpatio.definition: id. A taking into use, a making use, using, use of a thing (cf. usus). In gen.: usurpatio et renovatio doctrinae,Cic. Brut. 71, 250: civitatis,Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 64, § 166: vocis,Liv. 27, 19, 5: superba nominis,Plin. 33, 2, 7, § 31: vetustatis,Cic. Agr. 2, 12, 31: itineris insoliti,the undertaking of a journey so uncommon,Liv. 41, 23, 14: bonae mentis,enjoyment, possession,Val. Max. 4, 4, 1. In partic., in jurid. lang.

usurpo.definition: usurpo, āvi, ātum, 1, perh. contr. from usu rapio, to seize to one's own use To take into use; to make use of; to use, employ, apply, practise, exercise, enjoy (class.; cf. utor). In gen.: inter novam rem verbum usurpabo vetus,Plaut. Cist. 2, 1, 29: nomen tantum virtutis usurpas: quid ipsa valeat, ignoras,Cic. Par. 2, 17: at quam crebro usurpat Et consul, et Antonius!id. Phil. 2, 28, 70; cf.: praeclare est hoc usurpatum a doctissimis,id. Par. 5, ...

usus.definition: ūsus, a, um, Part. of utor.

ut.definition: ut or ŭtī (old form ŭtei, C. I. L. 1, 196, 4 sq.; 1, 198, 8 et saep.), and Conj. [for quoti or cuti, from pronom. stem ka-, Lat. quo-, whence qui, etc., and locat. ending -ti of stem to-, whence tum, etc.]. As adv. of manner. Conj.

utcumque.definition: ut-cumque (-cunq-; ante-class. ut quomque), adv. In what way soever, howsoever, however (class.). (Acc. to ut, I. B. 5.) At whatever time, whenever, = quandocumque (rare): utcumque exaestuat aut deficit mare,Liv. 26, 42, 8: utcumque defecere mores, Indecorant bene nata culpae,Hor. C. 4, 4, 35: ibimus, ibimus, Utcumque praecedes,id. ib. 2, 17, 11; cf.: utcumque mecum vos eritis, libens Insanientem navita Bosporum Temptabo,id. ib. 3, 4, 29.

utensilis.definition: ūtensĭlis, e, utor, in econom. lang. That may be used, fit for use, of use, useful. Adj.: quid in Italiā utensile non modo non nascitur, sed etiam non egregium fit?Varr. R. R. 1, 2, 6: quid utensile, Aug. Civ. Dei, 4, 22. Subst.: ūtensilĭa, ĭum, n., things for use, i. e. utensils, materials, necessaries, etc. (syn.: supellex, vasa): utensilia, quibus aut alitur hominum genus aut etiam excolitur,Col. 12, praef. § 3: exutus omnibus utensilibus mile...

uter.definition: ( Neutr. collat. form of plur. utria, Liv. And. ap. Non. p. 231, 31; gen. plur. utrium, Sall. J. 91, 1) [kindr. with uterus; v. Isid. Orig. 20, 6, 7], a bag or bottle made of an animal's hide, a skin for wine, oil, water, etc., Plaut. Truc. 5, 11: unctos salire per utres,Verg. G. 2, 384; Curt. 7, 5, 10; Ov. Am. 3, 12, 29; Juv. 15, 20; Plin. 12, 7, 15, § 31; 28, 18, 73, § 240; Scrib. Comp. 84; Just. 1, 8, 13; Dig. 33, 6, 3. —Often inflated and use...

uterus.definition: (collat. form , Caecil. ap. Non. 188, 15; Neutr. collat. form , , Plaut. Aul. 4, 7, 10, acc. to Non. 229, 33; Turp. and Afran. ib.) [Sanscr. uttara, later; Gr. ὕστερος; cf. Gr. ὑστέρα, womb; Sanscr. udaram, belly; Engl. udder], the womb, matrix (syn. volva). Lit.: utero exorti dolores,Plaut. Am. 5, 1, 40: perii, mea nutrix, uterum dolet!id. Aul. 4, 7, 10; id. Truc. 1, 2, 96: quae te beluam ex utero, non hominem fudit, Cic. Fragm. ap. Serv. Ve...

utibilis.definition: ūtĭbĭlis, e, utor That can be used, fit, appropriate, useful, serviceable (colloq. and ante-class.): non utibilis hic locus factis tuis,Plaut. Merc. 5, 4, 45: servi eris,id. Most. 4, 1, 2; id. Men. 5, 6, 23: ad rem utibile,id. Mil. 3, 1, 19; cf. id. Trin. 3, 3, 19: quid minus utibile fuit quam hoc ulcus tangere?Ter. Phorm. 4, 4, 10: neque aqua utibilis reperta, Auct. Itin. Alex. 37.

utica.definition: Ŭtĭca, ae, f. A very old town in Africa Propria, north of Carthage, where the younger Cato killed himself, now Boushater, Mel. 1, 7, 2; Plin. 5, 4, 3, § 24; Liv. 25, 31; 28, 4; id. Epit. 114; Caes. B. C. 1, 31; 2, 36; Cic. Scaur. 2, 45; id. Att. 12, 2, 1; Vell. 1, 2, 6; Hor. Ep. 1, 20, 13.—Hence, Ŭtĭcensis, e, , of or belonging to Utica: ager,Liv. 27, 5: conventus, Auct. B. Afr. 68, 4: ptisana,Plin. 18, 7, 15, § 75; Cato ap. Plin. 7, 30, 31, § 11...

utilis.definition: ūtĭlis, e, adj.utor. In gen. In partic.

utilitas.definition: ( Gen. plur. utilitatum and utilitatium), f. utilis, use, usefulness, utility, serviceableness, service, expediency, benefit, profit, advantage (used equally in sing. and plur.): commodis utilitatique servire,Cic. Q. Fr. 1, 1, 8, § 24: enitendum est, ut ostendas, in eā re, quam defendas, aut dignitatem inesse aut utilitatem ... nihil ad utilitatem suam referre,id. de Or. 2, 51, 207: etiamsi nulla sit utilitas ex amicitiā,id. Fin. 1, 20, 69: si ea...

utinam.definition: ŭtĭ-nam, ut, II. A., a particle or wishing Oh that! I wish that! if only! would to heaven! would that! etc. Affirm atively. Negatively: utinam ne and utinam non (equally in use), oh that ... not; would that ... not: utinam ne in nemore Pelio securibus Caesa accidisset abiegna ad terram trabes, Enn. ap. Cic. Top. 16, 61: quod utinam ne Phormioni id suadere in mentem incidisset!Ter. Phorm. 1, 3, 5: illud utinam ne vere scriberem!Cic. Fam. 5, 17, 3:...

utique.definition: ŭtĭ-quĕ And that, v. ut (uti) and que.

utor.definition: ūtor (old form oetor, oesus, etc., from oitor, oisus, Lex. Thor. lin. 11; Inf. parag. oetier, Rogat. Tribun. ap. Fest. p. 246 Müll.; Cic. Leg. 3, 4), ūsus (inf. utier, Plaut. Cas. 2, 3, 4; Ter. Phorm. 4, 2, 13), 3, etym. dub.. Prop., to use. Transf. (through the intermediate idea of having and using).

utpote.definition: ut-pŏtĕ As namely, namely, as being, as, seeing that, inasmuch as, since (rare but class.; cf. quippe); introducing an explanation.

utrarius.definition: 1. uter, in milit. lang. One who brings water in skins, a water-carrier: sequi se utrarios ad mare jussit,Liv. 44, 33, 1.

utricularius.definition: 1. utriculus. A bagpiper, Suet. Ner. 54; Inscr. Orell. 4119 sq. The master of a raft floated on bladders, used for ferriage, Inscr. Grut. 431, 4; 428, 10; 547, 8; Inscr. Donat. p. 470, 9.

utriculus.definition: dim.1. uter A small skin or leathern bottle, Cels. 2, 17; App. M. 1, p. 108, 16.

utrimque.definition: ūtrimquĕ (ūtrinquĕ), uterque From or on both sides or parts, on the one side and on the other. Lit.: horrescit telis exercitus asper utrimque, Enn. ap. Macr. S. 6, 4 (Ann. v. 385 Vahl.): tollitur in caelum clamor exortus utrimque,id. ib. p. 500 (Ann. v. 422 ib.): clamor utrinque, undique concursus,Hor. S. 1, 9, 77: postquam utrimque exitum est maxumā copiā, Dispertiti viri ... tubae utrimque canunt: contra Consonat terra: clamorem utrimque efferu...

utrobique.definition: ūtrŏbīquĕ (ūtrŭbīquĕ), utrubi-que On both parts or sides, on the one side and the other (rare but class.): quia utrobique magnos inimicos habebam, Asin. ap. Cic. Fam. 10, 31, 2: utrobique autem conventicium accipiebant,Cic. Rep. 3, 35, 48: depopulatus Hypatensem primo, deinde Heracleensem agrum, inutili utrobique auxilio Aetolorum,Liv. 36, 16, 5: ut eodem tempore utrobique respublica prospere gereretur,id. 27, 40, 2: utrobique Eumenes plus valeba...

utrum.definition: ūtrum, uter. Introducing an alternative question (direct or indirect), with an beginning the second clause (v. an); in Engl. represented in direct questions simply by the tone of voice, and in indirect questions by whether. Introducing a disjunctive question with more than two members, with an beginning each clause after the first.

uva.definition: etym. dub.; perh. for ug-va, root ug-, to be moist; Gr. ὑγρός; Lat. uvere; cf.: umor, uvidus, etc.; so Corss.; Curt. refers it to root ug-; Sanscr. ugras, strong; Gr. ὑγιής, healthful. Lit. Transf.

uua.definition: etym. dub.; perh. for ug-va, root ug-, to be moist; Gr. ὑγρός; Lat. uvere; cf.: umor, uvidus, etc.; so Corss.; Curt. refers it to root ug-; Sanscr. ugras, strong; Gr. ὑγιής, healthful. Lit. Transf.

uvesco.definition: ūvesco, ĕre V. inch. n. [uveo, uvens], to grow or become moist, wet, damp, dank, or humid (poet.). Lit.: suspensae in litore vestes Uvescunt,Lucr. 1, 306; Avien. Arat. 254. Transf., poet., to moisten or refresh one's self, i. e. to drink freely, to tipple: seu quis capit acria fortis Pocula, seu modicis uvescit laetius, * Hor. S. 2, 6, 70.

uuesco.definition: ūvesco, ĕre V. inch. n. [uveo, uvens], to grow or become moist, wet, damp, dank, or humid (poet.). Lit.: suspensae in litore vestes Uvescunt,Lucr. 1, 306; Avien. Arat. 254. Transf., poet., to moisten or refresh one's self, i. e. to drink freely, to tipple: seu quis capit acria fortis Pocula, seu modicis uvescit laetius, * Hor. S. 2, 6, 70.

uvidulus.definition: ūvĭdŭlus, a, um Adj. dim. [uvidus], moist, wet: uvidulam a fletu,Cat. 66, 63.

uuidulus.definition: ūvĭdŭlus, a, um Adj. dim. [uvidus], moist, wet: uvidulam a fletu,Cat. 66, 63.

uvidus.definition: ūvĭdus, a, um, uveo, uvens; v. uva init. Moist, wet, damp, dank, humid. Lit. (mostly poet. and in post-Aug. prose; syn.: umidus, madidus): rete,Plaut. Rud. 4, 3, 5: vestimenta,id. ib. 2, 7, 15: (mulieres) id. ib. 2, 3, 78; Hor. C. 1, 5, 14: gemma,Ov. F. 3, 238: uvidus ventosusque status caeli,Col. 7, 3, 3; cf. Juppiter,Verg. G. 1, 418: Menalcas,wet with the dew,id. E. 10, 20: Tiburis ripae,i. e. well-watered,Hor. C. 4, 2, 30; cf.: rura assiduis a...

uuidus.definition: ūvĭdus, a, um, uveo, uvens; v. uva init. Moist, wet, damp, dank, humid. Lit. (mostly poet. and in post-Aug. prose; syn.: umidus, madidus): rete,Plaut. Rud. 4, 3, 5: vestimenta,id. ib. 2, 7, 15: (mulieres) id. ib. 2, 3, 78; Hor. C. 1, 5, 14: gemma,Ov. F. 3, 238: uvidus ventosusque status caeli,Col. 7, 3, 3; cf. Juppiter,Verg. G. 1, 418: Menalcas,wet with the dew,id. E. 10, 20: Tiburis ripae,i. e. well-watered,Hor. C. 4, 2, 30; cf.: rura assiduis a...

uxor.definition: (for the form VXSOR in inscrr. V. the letter X), f.etym. dub.; cf. Sanscr. vaca, wife, a wife, spouse, consort (syn. conjux). Lit.: licuit uxorem dotatam ducere,Plaut. Mil. 3, 1, 86: duxit me uxorem liberorum sibi quaesendūm gratia, Enn. ap. Fest. s. v. quaeso, p. 258 (Trag. v. 161 Vahl.); so very freq. ducere uxorem, v. duco: uxorem adjungere,Cic. Fin. 3, 20, 68: ridicule illud L. Nasica censori Catoni, cum ille Ex tui animi sententiā tu uxorem ...

uxorius.definition: uxōrĭus, a, um, id. Of or belonging to a wife or married woman. In gen. In partic., excessively fond of one's wife, uxorious: pulcramque uxorius urbem Exstruis,Verg. A. 4, 266: amnis (Tiberis), as the husband of Ilia,Hor. C. 1, 2, 19: Vulcanus, Claud. Nupt. Hon. et Mar. 59: juvenis, Auct. Paneg. ad Maxim. et Constantin. 4.

vacatio.definition: vaco A being free from a duty, service, etc.; freedom, exemption, immunity; a freeing, exempting, dispensation (class.; syn. immunitas). Lit. Transf., a sum paid for exemption from military service: vacationes annuas exsolvere,Tac. H. 1, 46: vacationes centurionibus ex fisco numerat,id. ib. 1, 58.

uacatio.definition: vaco A being free from a duty, service, etc.; freedom, exemption, immunity; a freeing, exempting, dispensation (class.; syn. immunitas). Lit. Transf., a sum paid for exemption from military service: vacationes annuas exsolvere,Tac. H. 1, 46: vacationes centurionibus ex fisco numerat,id. ib. 1, 58.

vacca.definition: Sanscr. vacā, cow; root vaç, to bellow; cf. vagire A cow, Varr. R. R. 2, 5, 6; Col. 6, 21, 1; Cic. N. D. 1, 27 77; Verg. E. 9, 31; id. G. 2, 524; 3, 177; id. A. 4, 61; Ov. M. 2, 694; Hor. C. 4, 2, 53: boves operariae, used in ploughing,Col. 6, 24. 4; Varr. R. R. 1, 20, 4.

uacca.definition: Sanscr. vacā, cow; root vaç, to bellow; cf. vagire A cow, Varr. R. R. 2, 5, 6; Col. 6, 21, 1; Cic. N. D. 1, 27 77; Verg. E. 9, 31; id. G. 2, 524; 3, 177; id. A. 4, 61; Ov. M. 2, 694; Hor. C. 4, 2, 53: boves operariae, used in ploughing,Col. 6, 24. 4; Varr. R. R. 1, 20, 4.

vaccinium.definition: The blueberry, whortleberry: Vaccinium myrtillus, Linn.; Plin. 16, 18, 31, § 77; Verg. E. 2, 18; 2, 50; 10, 39; Ov. Tr. 1, 1, 5; Vitr. 7, 14, 2.

uaccinium.definition: The blueberry, whortleberry: Vaccinium myrtillus, Linn.; Plin. 16, 18, 31, § 77; Verg. E. 2, 18; 2, 50; 10, 39; Ov. Tr. 1, 1, 5; Vitr. 7, 14, 2.

vaccinus.definition: vaccīnus, a, um, vacca Of or from cows: caro,Plin. 28, 12, 50, § 185: lac,id. 25, 8, 53, § 94: caseus,id. 28, 14, 58, § 204.

uaccinus.definition: vaccīnus, a, um, vacca Of or from cows: caro,Plin. 28, 12, 50, § 185: lac,id. 25, 8, 53, § 94: caseus,id. 28, 14, 58, § 204.

vaccula.definition: dim.id. A little cow or heifer, Cat. 20, 14; Val. Cat. Dir. 132.

uaccula.definition: dim.id. A little cow or heifer, Cat. 20, 14; Val. Cat. Dir. 132.

vacerra.definition: A log, stock, post. Lit., Col. 9, 1, 3; 9, 1, 9; 6, 19, 2. Transf., like stipes, and our stock, block, as a term of abuse applied to a stupid person: vecorde et malefica vacerra, Liy. Andron. ap. Fest. p. 375 Müll. (Com. Fragm. v. 7 Rib.).

uacerra.definition: A log, stock, post. Lit., Col. 9, 1, 3; 9, 1, 9; 6, 19, 2. Transf., like stipes, and our stock, block, as a term of abuse applied to a stupid person: vecorde et malefica vacerra, Liy. Andron. ap. Fest. p. 375 Müll. (Com. Fragm. v. 7 Rib.).

vacerrosus.definition: văcerrōsus, a, um, vacerra, II., freq. used by the emperor Augustus for cerritus Mad, crazed, crack-brained, acc. to Suet. Aug. 87.

uexillatio.definition: id.. A body of the vexillarii; acc. to others, a body of soldiers united under one flag (vexillum), a corps, battalion, Suet. Galb. 20; Inscr. Orell. 845; 2009 sq. al. A division of cavalry, a troop, squadron, Veg. Mil. 2, 1; Amm. 25, 1, 9; App. M. 7, p. 191, 3.

vexillum.definition: dim. of vēlum A military ensign, standard, banner, flag. In gen., Caes. B. G. 6, 36; Cic. Phil. 2, 40, 102; 5, 11, 29; id. Att. 10, 15, 2; id. Agr. 2, 32, 86; Tac. A. 1, 20 al. In partic., a red flag placed on the general's tent, as a signal for marching or for battle: vexillum proponere, to raise or display, Caes. B. G. 2, 20: vexillo signum dare,id. B. C. 3, 89 fin.

uexillum.definition: dim. of vēlum A military ensign, standard, banner, flag. In gen., Caes. B. G. 6, 36; Cic. Phil. 2, 40, 102; 5, 11, 29; id. Att. 10, 15, 2; id. Agr. 2, 32, 86; Tac. A. 1, 20 al. vexo.definition: vexo ( Inf. vexarier, Verg. Cir. 480), āvi, ātum, 1, veho, orig., to shake, jolt, toss in carrying; hence, in gen., to move violently, to shake, agitate. Lit. (rare; syn. quatio): vexasse grave verbum est, factumque ab eo videtur, quod est vehere; in quo inest jam vis quaedam alieni arbitrii. Non enim sui potens est, qui vehitur. Vexare autem, quod ex eo inclinatum est, vi atque motu procul dubio vastiore est. Nam qui fertur et raptatur atque huc...

viaticus.definition: vĭātĭcus, a, um, adj.via Of or belonging to a road or journey, viatic. Adj. (very rare): cena,a parting meal, farewell repast,Plaut. Bacch. 1, 1, 61; so perh. factum,id. Trin. 4, 2, 45; v. Ritschl ad h. l. Subst.: vĭātĭcum, i, n., travellingmoney, provision for a journey, viaticum (freq. and class.).

uiaticus.definition: vĭātĭcus, a, um, adj.via Of or belonging to a road or journey, viatic. Adj. (very rare): cena,a parting meal, farewell repast,Plaut. Bacch. 1, 1, 61; so perh. factum,id. viator.definition: vio. In gen., a wayfarer, traveller, Cic. Fat. 15, 34; id. Mil. 21, 55; Caes. B. G. 4, 5; Verg. G. 4, 97; id. Fragm. ap. Don. Vit. Verg.; Hor. C. 3, 4, 30; id. S. 1, 5, 17; Ov. Tr. 2, 271; id. P. 4, 10, 34; Phaedr. 2, 1, 5; Juv. 10, 22; Mart. 2, 6, 14; 11, 13, 1. In partic., a summoner, apparitor, an officer whose duty was to summon persons before the magistrate, Varr. ap. Gell. 13, 12, 6; Cic. Sen. 16, 56; id. Vatin. 9, 22; Liv. 2, 56, 13; 3, 56...

vibro.definition: vībro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. and n. cf. Sanscr. vip, to tremble. Act., to set in tremulous motion, to move rapidly to and fro, to brandish, shake, agitate (class.; syn.: quatio, ventilo). Neutr., to be in tremulous motion, etc.

viburnum.definition: The wayfaring-tree: Viburnum lantana, Linn.; Verg. E. 1, 26.

uiburnum.definition: The wayfaring-tree: Viburnum lantana, Linn.; Verg. E. 1, 26.

vicanus.definition: vīcānus (post-class. collat. form vī-cānĕus, Cod. Just. 11, 56), a, um, vicus Of or dwelling in a village. Adj.: Tmolites ille vicanus,villager,Cic. Fl. 3, 8: haruspices, who go about from village to village, Enn. ap. Cic. Div. 1, 58, 132. Subst.: vīcāni, ōrum, m., villagers, peasants, rustics, Liv. 38, 30, 8; Cod. Just. 11, 56.

uicanus.definition: vīcānus (post-class. collat. form vī-cānĕus, Cod. Just. 11, 56), a, um, vicus Of or dwelling in a village. Adj.: Tmolites ille vicanus,villager,Cic. vicaria.definition: vĭcārĭa, ae, v. vicarius, II. B.

uicaria.definition: vĭcārĭa, ae, v. vicarius, II. B.

vicarius.definition: vĭcārĭus, a, um, vicis That supplies the place of a person or thing, substituted, delegated, vicarious. Adj.: vicaria fides amicorum supponitur,Cic. Rosc. Am. 38, 111: manus,Quint. Decl. 6, 21: corpus,id. ib. 16, 7: mors,Hyg. Fab. 243; Quint. Decl. 9 fin. Substt.

vicatim.definition: vīcātim, vicus. From street to street, through the streets, Sisenn. ap. Non. p. 188, 26; Suet. Caes. 41 med.; Tac. H. 2, 95; Hor. Epod. 5, 97. From village to village, through the villages, in hamlets: habitare,Liv. 9, 13, 7: dispersa,Plin. 6, 26, 30, § 117.

uicatim.definition: vīcātim, vicus. From street to street, through the streets, Sisenn. ap. Non. p. 188, 26; Suet. Caes. 41 med.; Tac. H. 2, 95; Hor. Epod. 5, 97. From village to village, through the villages, in hamlets: habitare,Liv. 9, 13, 7: dispersa,Plin. 6, 26, 30, § 117.

vicennalis.definition: vīcennālis, e, vicennium Of twenty years, every twenty years (postclass.). Adj.: votis vicennalibus, Num. Alex. Sev. ap. Eckhel. D. N. V. 7, p. 275. Subst.: vīcennālĭa, ĭum, n., a festival on the twentieth anniversary of an emperor's reign, Lact. Mort. Pers. 17.

uicennalis.definition: vīcennālis, e, vicennium Of twenty years, every twenty years (postclass.). Adj.: votis vicennalibus, Num. Alex. Sev. ap. Eckhel. D. N. V. 7, p. 275. Subst.: vīcennālĭa, ĭum, n., a festival on the twentieth anniversary of an emperor's reign, Lact. Mort. Pers. 17.

vicesimarius.definition: vīcēsĭmārĭus, a, um, id. Of or belonging to the twentieth part. Adj.: aurum, of the tax called vicesima (v. h. v.), Liv. 27, 10, 11. Subst.: vīcēsĭmā-rĭus, ii, m., a receiver of the vicesima, Petr. 65.

uicesimarius.definition: vīcēsĭmārĭus, a, um, id. Of or belonging to the twentieth part. Adj.: aurum, of the tax called vicesima (v. h. v.), Liv. 27, 10, 11. Subst.: vīcēsĭmā-rĭus, ii, m., a receiver of the vicesima, Petr. 65.

vicinalis.definition: vīcīnālis, e, vicinus Neighboring, near: usus,Liv. 21, 26, 8: bella,Just. 41, 1, 3: via,a road over the fields used in common, a village-path,Dig. 43, 8, 2; 43, 7, 3; Front. Aquaed. 126; Sen. Ben. 5, 24, 9.

Ps. 1, 3, 93; Hor. C. 3, 23, 12; Verg. G. 2, 147; Cic. Att. 1, 13, 1; Caes. B. G. 6, 16; Liv. 45, 7, 1; Ov. M. 7, 162; id. F. 1, 335; Juv. 12, 113; Luc. 1, 611; Sen. Herc. Fur. 923 al. A village, hamlet, a country-seat: si quis Cobiamacho, qui vicus inter Tolosam et Narbonem est, deverterentur,Cic. Font. 5, 9; Caes. B. G. 1, 5; ...

Lat. vegeo, vigil, augeo To be lively or vigorous; to thrive, flourish, bloom; to be in honor, esteem, repute, etc. (class.; mostly of things, concrete and abstract; cf. valeo). vigilo.definition: vĭgĭlo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. n. and A. [vigil]. Neutr., to watch, i. e. to be or keep awake at night, not to sleep, be wakeful (class.; syn. excubo). S. 5, 5, 2: de Pieriis vocalis fontibus unda,id. ib. 1, 2, 6.—Adv.: vōcālĭter, with a loud cry, loudly (post-class.), App. M. 1, p. 112; Tert. adv. Prax. 3.

vocatio.definition: voco, a calling; hence, in partic. A citing before a court; a summons, Varr. and Atei. Capito ap. Gell. 13, 12, 6; Varr. ib. 13, 13, 3. A bidding, invitation to dinner, etc., Cat. 47, 5. In eccl. Lat., calling, Vulg. 1 Cor. 1, 26; id. Heb. 3, 1: in caelo, Hilar. in Matt. 4, 15.

vocatus.definition: voco A calling, calling upon, summoning, invocation (only abl. in prose). In partic., an invitation to dinner, etc.: misit qui diceret, cenaturum apud Caesarem vocatu ipsius, Suet Calig. 39.

volcanus.definition: Volcānus (less correctly Vulc-), i, m. Lit., Vulcan, the fire-god, son of Jupiter and Juno, Cic. N. D. 3, 22, 55 sq.; 1, 30, 83; Caes. B. G. 6, 21; Hor. C. 1, 4, 8; 3, 4, 59; id. volubilis.definition: vŏlūbĭlis, e, volvo That is turned round or (more freq.) that turns itself round, turning, spinning, whirling, circling, rolling, revolving. Lit.: buxum,i. e. a top,Verg. xeniolum.definition: dim.xenium A small gift or present, App. M. 2, p. 119, 24; Dig. 1, 16, 6.

xenium.definition: A gift or present made to a guest (pure Lat. lautia). Lit., Plin. Ep. 6, 31, 14; Vitr. 6, 10.—Hence, Xenia, the title of the thirteenth book of Martial's epigrams, because treating of such things as were usually presented to guests, Mart. 13, 3, 1. Transf., in gen., a gift. present, Plin. Ep. 5, 14, 8; Dig. 1, 16, 6; Vulg. Ecclus. 20, 31.

xenodochium.definition: or A public building for the reception of strangers, a caravansary, a stranger's hospital (syn. deversorium), Hier. Ep. 66, 11; Cod. Just. 1, 2, 17; 1, 3, 33; 1, 3, 35. —Called also , , Cod. Just. 1, 2, 19 al.

xenodochus.definition: One who receives strangers, a superintendent of the stranger's hospital, Cod. Just. 1, 8, 33 fin.

xenoparochus.definition: One who attends to or provides for strangers, Dig. 5, 4, 18.

xerxes.definition: (, Cic. Leg. 2, 10, 26), is (i, Nep. Reg. 1), , = Ξέρξης The celebrated king of Persia, son of Darius Hystaspis, vanquished by the Greeks at Salamis, Cic. Tusc. 5, 7, 20; id. N. D. 1, 41, 115.

xysticus.definition: xystĭcus, a, um Of or belonging to a xystus. Adj.: vanitas,i. e. of the athletes,Tert. Pud. 7 med. Subst.: xystĭci, ōrum, m., athletes, Suet. Aug. 45; Dig. 3, 2, 4; Inscr. Grut. 332, 6.

xystus.definition: m., or , , n., = ξυστός or ξυστόν. Among the Greeks, a covered portico or gallery, where the athletes exercised in winter, Vitr. 5, 11, 4; 6, 10, 5; Tert. Apol. 38.
